actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robust Policy Optimization with Clustered Correlation Bounds
PROPOSAL: Develop a policy optimization algorithm that generalizes ORPO by partitioning the state-action space into clusters based on the reference policy's occupancy measure, and applying ORPO separately to each cluster with a strengthened regularization term that accounts for the correlation constraint within each cluster.
CONTROLS: Compare against ORPO, a random policy, and a model-free REINFORCE baseline.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our proposed algorithm will outperform ORPO in scenarios where the proxy reward correlation is weak and the reference policy rarely visits parts of the state-action space. However, its increased computational cost may lead to slower convergence, especially in complex environments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Informative Proxy Reward Refinement via Prior Knowledge Integration
PROPOSAL: Propose an algorithm that incorporates prior knowledge about the true reward into proxy reward refinement by using a knowledge graph and a symmetrized KL divergence constraint, which encourages the proxy reward to match the true reward in regions supported by prior knowledge while respecting the assumed correlation constraint.
CONTROLS: Evaluate against a baseline that uses a standard KL divergence constraint, and a setting where prior knowledge is unavailable.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By leveraging prior knowledge, our algorithm will provide more interpretable and robust policies, especially in settings where the proxy reward is strongly informative about the true reward. However, integration of high-quality prior knowledge may still be challenging in practice.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Informative Proxy Reward Refinement via Prior Knowledge Integration
PROPOSAL: Modify the symmetrized KL divergence constraint in the prior knowledge integration algorithm to also account for the correlation constraint, ensuring that proxy reward refinement is consistent with the assumed correlation level, even when prior knowledge suggests a different correlation.
CONTROLS: Compare against the baseline that uses a standard KL divergence constraint and the original prior knowledge integration algorithm, as well as a new setting where prior knowledge conflicts with the assumed correlation.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This modification will enhance the robustness of our algorithm, particularly when prior knowledge is incomplete or noisy, but may lead to slightly less optimal proxy reward refinement in scenarios where prior knowledge accurately captures the true reward correlation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cluster-wise Correlation-aware Exploration
PROPOSAL: Develop an exploration strategy that adapts the level of exploration within each cluster to the strength of the correlation constraint within that cluster, allowing the agent to focus exploration in regions where the proxy reward is more informative about the true reward.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that uses uniform exploration, and ablate the contribution of the correlation-aware exploration strategy by comparing against an oracle that perfectly knows the correlation level in each cluster.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our explored policy will generalize better to novel scenarios where the proxy reward correlation is diverse and the reference policy does not thoroughly visit all regions. However, its performance may be less competitive in settings with more complex exploration landscapes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: TRACER: Trajectory-based Robustness Analysis for Correlation Exploration and Refinement
PROPOSAL: Introduce a new algorithm that analyzes the agent's learned trajectories to identify potential reward hacking vulnerabilities and identify regions where the proxy reward correlation might be weak, allowing for targeted refinement and exploration of these areas.
CONTROLS: Evaluate against a baseline that relies on state-action sampling, and compare against a knowledge-engineered setting where a human expert provides the same insights as TRACER.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: TRACER will be particularly effective in scenarios with complex policies or large state-action spaces, but may require additional computational resources and expertise to interpret its findings.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: TRACER: Trajectory-based Robustness Analysis for Correlation Exploration and Refinement
PROPOSAL: Modify TRACER to not only identify potential reward hacking vulnerabilities but also to provide actionable recommendations for refining the proxy reward or adjusting the correlation constraint, enabling more effective countermeasures against reward hacking.
CONTROLS: Compare against the previous TRACER implementation, as well as a baseline that does not receive recommendations from TRACER, and evaluate the effectiveness of these countermeasures in improving policy robustness and performance.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This modification will enhance the practical value of TRACER, but may also introduce additional complexity and potential for over-refining the proxy reward in some scenarios, potentially leading to overfitting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scenario-specific Correlation Metrics for Reward Hacking Detection and Mitigation
PROPOSAL: Introduce a framework for computing scenario-specific correlation metrics that capture the magnitude and direction of correlation between proxy and true rewards in different regions of the state-action space, allowing for more nuanced reward hacking detection and mitigation.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that uses a unified correlation metric across the entire state-action space, and evaluate the effectiveness of these scenario-specific metrics in improving policy robustness and performance in different scenarios.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach will lead to more accurate reward hacking detection and mitigation in complex scenarios, but may require additional computational resources and storage to store scenario-specific metrics.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Sampling for Early Detection of Reward Hacking Vulnerabilities
PROPOSAL: Develop an adaptive sampling method that prioritizes exploration of areas of the state-action space that are most likely to exhibit reward hacking vulnerabilities, as identified by TRACER and scenario-specific correlation metrics, allowing for early detection and mitigation of these vulnerabilities.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that uses uniform exploration and a random sampling strategy, and evaluate the effectiveness of adaptive sampling in improving policy robustness and performance in different scenarios.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach will enable earlier detection and mitigation of reward hacking vulnerabilities, but may require careful tuning of exploration strategies and prioritization heuristics to ensure effective sampling.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Interpretable Lottery Tickets for Reward Hacking Mitigation
PROPOSAL: Identify and extract interpretable "lottery tickets" from the policies learned using the proposed algorithms, which can be used to diagnose and mitigate reward hacking vulnerabilities by isolating critical components of the policy that contribute to these vulnerabilities.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that does not extract lottery tickets, and evaluate the effectiveness of this approach in improving policy interpretability and robustness to reward hacking in different scenarios.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach will provide valuable insights into the internal decision-making processes of policies and enable more targeted interventions to mitigate reward hacking vulnerabilities, but may require careful interpretation and analysis of the extracted lottery tickets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Framework for Reward Hacking Mitigation and Policy Interpretability
PROPOSAL: Unify the existing methods and algorithms into a comprehensive framework that provides a systematic approach to reward hacking mitigation and policy interpretability, while also enabling seamless transfer of techniques and interventions across different scenarios and domains.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that uses a traditional RL approach without reward hacking mitigation and policy interpretability techniques, and evaluate the effectiveness of the unified framework in improving policy robustness and interpretability in autonomous vehicle traffic control, pandemic response, blood glucose control, and LLM alignment via RLHF.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The unified framework will provide a powerful tool for addressing reward hacking and ensuring policy interpretability in real-world applications, but may require careful validation and adaptation to the specific needs and constraints of each scenario and domain.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dependence-regularized Policy Optimization
PROPOSAL: Design and evaluate an algorithm, called Dependence-regularized Policy Optimization (DPO), that learns a policy robust to variations in the proxy reward by regularizing the policy against a specific set of dependence constraints. The dependence constraints encode information about the relationships between the proxy reward and the true reward, within the regions of the state-action space reachable by the reference policy. DPO will incorporate techniques from variable dependence minimization and hierarchical structuring of policy decisions to learn an interpretable policy that provably resists reward hacking.
CONTROLS: ORPO baseline, as well as ablations with dependence penalties and hierarchical structuring components removed
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: DPO will exhibit higher robustness to proxy variations than ORPO and baseline algorithms, but with possible extra conservatism in regions of high uncertainty due to misspecified dependence constraints; expected failure modes include agents exploiting gaps in knowledge about the proxy-true relationship and overemphasizing easily manipulated features.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Conditional Correlation-based Exploration
PROPOSAL: Develop a modular architecture for Dependence-regularized Policy Optimization (DPO) that incorporates conditional correlation-based exploration. This module will monitor the current policy's performance under different proxy reward functions, weighted by their correlation with the true reward as measured by the reference policy. By dynamically weighting exploration, the modular DPO will be better equipped to capture a diverse set of true rewards even when the proxy rewards obscure the optimal policy. Empirically, this can lead to faster learning, better exploration-exploitation trade-offs, and more robust policies to varying proxy conditions.
CONTROLS: ablate the conditional correlation module, compare against DPO without it, and contrast against standard value-expansion based methods
COST: 700 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This modular extension to DPO will generally improve robustness and exploration, but may increase sample complexity in scenarios where the proxy rewards dominate the exploration process, and its effectiveness may depend on accurate estimates of the proxy-true correlation; combining this module with Dependence-regularized Policy Optimization could help mitigate reward engineering challenges.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Identifying Proxy-reward Structures with Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate an approach to identifying and capturing the structural relationships between proxy and true rewards using Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL). Specifically, the goal is to decompose reward engineering into lower-level reward refinement tasks guided by a high-level HRL framework that learns partial abstractions of the system's behavior. This should help uncover a proxy reward structure that closely captures the true reward function, reducing the complexity of the true reward while preserving its critical features. The learned proxy structure can potentially improve the interpretability of policies and help mitigate reward hacking.
CONTROLS: ablate the hierarchical framework, compare against a simple HRL model without distinct abstractions, and consider its combination with DPO
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed HRL approach will facilitate discovery of more accurate proxy rewards and their decompositions, but deciding the optimal hierarchy and abstraction depth may require problem-specific expert knowledge and significant computational resources; robustness and extrapolation performance might be impacted by the dependency on the proposed hierarchical abstraction.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Quantitative Proxy-reward Profiling for Reward Hacking Detection
PROPOSAL: Develop a scalable profiling framework for understanding the proxy reward's structure, focusing on interpolating between different proxy functions while maintaining their correlation constraints. This approach will highlight regions where potential reward hacking may occur and identify a core proxy reward profile that effectively captures its key features. To guide this profiling process, an interpolation-based optimization procedure will be implemented to regularize the profiled functions against a reference distribution generated by the reference policy.
CONTROLS: validate the interpolation results with counterfactuals, compare performance against benchmark proxy reward functions and assess practicality using real-world data from traffic control and blood glucose control
COST: 450 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Profiling of proxy rewards will significantly improve in transparency and robustness with the new interpolative framework, and quantify potential scenarios for reward hacking based on areas of weaker correlation to the true reward, helping to unveil vulnerabilities inadvertently introduced by imperfect constraint specification. Properly calibrated limits on speculative space will be challenging to determine without parametric probes with variable-clipped proxy-ground truths.

Identifying Proxy-reward Structures with Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning To better investigate proxy-reward structures and enhance robustness, the proposed framework will integrate a profiling component as initially introduced in this turn. This profiling module will be used along with hierarchical abstractions to capture a more intuitive proxy-reward structure, informing an evaluation metric for robustness. The combination of techniques will reveal critical insight into the system's behavior under various proxy reward scenarios, fostering a systematic approach to engineering of better-suited proxies.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Robustification of ORPO against Worst-Case Reward Shifts
PROPOSAL: We propose a revised version of ORPO that replaces the single reference policy with an ensemble of policies optimized under different, adversarially perturbed proxy rewards drawn from the set of rewards consistent with the assumed correlation constraint. By combining these policies, we can obtain a policy that is robust against shifts in the proxy reward and thus generalizes better across the worst-case scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare our revised ORPO to the original one, and to a baseline that uses a single, fixed proxy reward.
COST: Estimated 500 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect our approach to improve upon the standard ORPO method in terms of robustness to proxy reward shifts, but may struggle with scenarios where the perturbed rewards are very different from the original one, leading to over-conservatism and decreased performance.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Structured Prior Knowledge as a Constraint: Guiding Policy Optimization with Reward Hierarchy
PROPOSAL: To incorporate prior knowledge about the true reward and improve interpretability, we propose augmenting the ORPO regularization term with a penalty on the distance between the learned policy's action probabilities and a structured prior distribution over actions, which encodes the reward hierarchy. This approach allows us to capture domain-specific knowledge about the true reward and its structure, and provides a transparent and understandable way to reason about the learned policy's behavior.
CONTROLS: Evaluate our approach against a baseline that uses only the ORPO regularization term, and against a method that injects prior knowledge through a reward function modification.
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect our approach to significantly outperform the baseline in terms of true reward and to provide a more interpretable policy, but may struggle with scenarios where the prior knowledge is incomplete or inaccurate, leading to over-smoothing of the learned policy's actions.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: State-Action Sparse Modeling for Reward Exploration
PROPOSAL: We propose to address the issue of reward hacking in under-explored state-action regions by introducing a state-action sparse modeling scheme to ORPO, which encourages the policy to visit rarely explored state-action pairs and adaptively adjusts the regularization strength based on the policy's exploration progress. This approach allows the policy to balance exploration and exploitation and reduces the risk of reward hacking in novel scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare our sparse modeling scheme to a baseline that uses a fixed exploration entropy penalty, and evaluate its performance across different levels of prior knowledge about the true reward.
COST: Estimated 250 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect our sparse modeling scheme to improve upon the baseline in terms of exploration-efficiency and robustness to under-explored regions, but may struggle with scenarios where the exploration progress is slow or uninformative, leading to decreased performance.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Robustification of ORPO against Worst-Case Reward Shifts
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal by introducing a distributionally robust optimization (DRO) framework to ORPO, which replaces the single reference policy with an ensemble of policies but also incorporates uncertainty sets around the proxy rewards. This allows us to model and optimize for worst-case performance under ambiguity about the proxy reward and the true reward. We show that our DRO-based ORPO variant can be efficiently solved using the Frank-Wolfe algorithm, and demonstrate its benefits in terms of robustness to reward shifts and true performance.
CONTROLS: We compare our revised ORPO method to the original one, and to the baseline that uses a single, fixed proxy reward.
COST: Estimated 700 GPU-hours (due to the additional computational overhead of DRO).
PREDICTION: We expect our revised ORPO method to significantly outperform the standard ORPO method in terms of robustness to reward shifts and true performance, but may struggle with computational efficiency in very large or complex environments.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Hierarchical Exploration and Exploitation for Reward Hacking Resistance
PROPOSAL: We propose to combine the benefits of structured prior knowledge (Proposal 2) and state-action sparse modeling (Proposal 3) by integrating a hierarchical exploration strategy into ORPO. This approach consists of an inner loop that explores the state-action space using the sparse modeling scheme, and an outer loop that refines the policy using the structured prior knowledge. By alternating between exploration and exploitation, we can improve the policy's robustness to reward hacking and true performance.
CONTROLS: We compare our hierarchical exploration strategy to a baseline that uses a single-level exploration scheme, and to an ablation that uses only one of the exploration strategies.
COST: Estimated 400 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect our hierarchical exploration strategy to significantly improve the policy's robustness to reward hacking and true performance, but may struggle with scenarios where the exploration-exploitation trade-off is difficult to balance, leading to decreased performance.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Certifiable Robustness through Contextualize-Invariant Reward Shaping
PROPOSAL: We propose a contextualize-invariant reward shaping approach that transforms the original, proxy reward function into a robust and invariant reward representation. This representation is derived by learning a low-dimensional, invariant feature space that captures the essential structure of the proxy reward across different contexts. By optimizing the policy in this new representation, we can obtain a more robust and reliable policy that performs well across various and uncertain reward settings.
CONTROLS: We compare our contextualize-invariant reward shaping approach to a baseline that uses a standard reward augmentation scheme, and to an ablation that uses only one of the transformation steps.
COST: Estimated 500 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect our contextualize-invariant reward shaping approach to significantly improve the policy's robustness and reliability, but may struggle with scenarios where the invariant feature space is difficult to learn or��here a saturation point is reached, leading to inefficiency.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Structured Prior Knowledge as a Constraint: Guiding Policy Optimization with Reward Hierarchy
PROPOSAL: We refine our previous proposal by incorporating a probabilistic graphical model (PGM) to represent the prior knowledge about the true reward hierarchy. The PGM is trained on historical reward data and provides a structured representation of the relationships between reward components. We then use this PGM to inform the policy optimization process, by learning a policy that maximizes the expected reward under the probabilistic hierarchy. This approach allows us to leverage the power of probabilistic modeling to capture the inherent uncertainty and complexity of the true reward.
CONTROLS: We compare our revised structured prior knowledge approach to the original one, and to a baseline that uses a standard hierarchical reinforcement learning algorithm.
COST: Estimated 450 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect our revised approach to significantly outperform the baseline in terms of true reward and robustness to reward uncertainties, but may struggle with scenarios where the PGM is difficult to learn or the hierarchy is highly complex, leading to decreased performance.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Transfer Learning from Human Expertise for Reward-Agnostic Policy Optimizations
PROPOSAL: We propose a transfer learning approach to leverage human expertise in reward-agnostic policy optimizations. Specifically, we train a meta-reinforcement learning model on a set of human-designed policies, which are optimized for different reward functions. The meta-learner is then fine-tuned on a new, unseen reward function, allowing it to adapt and generalize to the new reward structure. This approach enables the transfer of human knowledge and expertise to new, complex reward scenarios, while avoiding the need for extensive reward engineering and design.
CONTROLS: We compare our transfer learning approach to a baseline that uses a standard reinforcement learning algorithm, and to an ablation that uses only a single reward function for training.
COST: Estimated 600 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect our transfer learning approach to significantly improve the policy's adaptability and generalizability to new reward functions, but may struggle with scenarios where the human-designed policies are not representative of the target reward function or the learnt policy is overly reliant on the meta-features, leading to decreased performance.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Hierarchical Exploration and Exploitation for Reward Hacking Resistance
PROPOSAL: We refine our previous proposal by introducing a dynamic, adaptive exploration schedule that adjusts the exploration-exploitation trade-off based on the policy's progress and estimated reward uncertainty. This adaptive schedule allows the policy to focus more on exploration in regions with high uncertainty and less on exploitation in regions with low uncertainty, which can lead to more efficient learning and exploration. We also introduce a novel exploration metric, which measures the expected exploration bonus from additional exploration in uncertain regions. This metric is used to adjust the exploration strength in real-time.
CONTROLS: We compare our revised hierarchical exploration approach to the original one, and to a baseline that uses a standard exploration-exploitation scheme.
COST: Estimated 450 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect our revised approach to significantly improve the policy's exploration efficiency and robustness to reward hacking, but may struggle with scenarios where the adaptive exploration schedule is too aggressive or not aggressive enough, leading to decreased performance.

ACTION: REVISE 6
TITLE: Transfer Learning from Human Expertise for Reward-Agnostic Policy Optimizations
PROPOSAL: We refine our previous proposal by incorporating a novel meta-reward learning framework, which enables the meta-learner to adapt to the new reward function and domain by learning a universal meta-reward representation. This representation is learned by minimizing a meta-reward loss function, which encourages the meta-learner to produce policies that are robust to reward uncertainties and agile in adapting to new reward functions. We also introduce a novel meta-reward term, which measures the expected transferability of the policy from the source domain to the target domain.
CONTROLS: We compare our revised transfer learning approach to the original one, and to a baseline that uses a standard reinforcement learning algorithm.
COST: Estimated 600 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect our revised approach to significantly improve the policy's adaptability and generalizability to new reward functions and domains, but may struggle with scenarios where the meta-reward representation is too complex or difficult to learn, leading to decreased performance.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Localized Random Feature Modeling for Non-Stationary GPs
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach to constructing localized random feature maps for non-stationary Gaussian processes (GPs). By adapting the idea of random Fourier features to the non-stationary setting using input-dependent partitioning and weighted sampling, we obtain an efficient feature map that captures local structure in the input space while retaining a linear-in-data training and prediction cost. Specifically, we introduce a weighted graph partitioning scheme to divide the input space into locally homogeneous regions and then employ random Fourier features within each region, leveraging the local stationarity assumption to reduce the construction cost and ensure valid kernel properties.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach against exact GPs, stationary random features, and sparse variational GPs on real-world datasets for speech signal analysis and biological protein data regression.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (approximately 5 hours per run with 20 datasets)
PREDICTION: Our localized random feature model should demonstrate improved predictive accuracy and better calibrated uncertainty estimates compared to stationary random features and faster training and prediction times than exact GPs. It may fail for highly non-stationary data with complex multi-scale structures.

This proposal establishes a foundation for the research direction and aims to address the issue of modeling non-stationarity with random features, but it is likely that further refinement and extension will be necessary to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Density-Ratio Based Partitioning for Non-Stationary Domain Adaptation
PROPOSAL: To adapt to changing input distributions and non-stationarity, we propose to incorporate density-ratio estimation into our localized random feature model (1). By selecting the partitioning scheme using the density-ratio of input-dependent marginal distributions, we can identify irregularities in the data and improve the model's robustness to changes in the data distribution. Specifically, we will apply the density-ratio based partitioning to different regions of the input space, and then apply our localized random feature construction within each region.
CONTROLS: We evaluate the performance of our density-ratio based partitioning approach against a baseline that uses random partitioning and compare it against models that adapt to changing distributions (e.g., Gaussian Processes with input-dependent Precision Matrices, Multi-task Learning).

We propose a novel approach to constructing localized random feature maps for non-stationary Gaussian processes (GPs). By adapting the idea of random Fourier features to the non-stationary setting using input-dependent partitioning and weighted sampling, we obtain an efficient feature map that captures local structure in the input space while retaining a linear-in-data training and prediction cost. Specifically, we introduce a weighted graph partitioning scheme to divide the input space into locally homogeneous regions and then employ random Fourier features within each region, leveraging the local stationarity assumption to reduce the construction cost and ensure valid kernel properties.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating Adaptive Random Fourier Features for Non-Stationary Gaussian Processes
PROPOSAL: We propose to adapt the random-feature paradigm by constructing an input-dependent feature dictionary. Specifically, we develop an empirical spectral decomposition of the data-driven kernel, derived via Monte Carlo sampling. We use a learned dictionary representation that projects the original data points onto spatially varying frequency supports to address the limitations of traditional random Fourier features.
CONTROLS: We compare to Stationary Random Fourier Features, Deep GPs, and a Bayesian Linear Regression baseline on speech signal specifications task. We experiment with different size of the dictionary and dictionary learning algorithms.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach will show promising results and outperform Stationary Random Fourier Features by achieving higher predictive accuracy and calibrated uncertainty estimates. However, its limitations might be: 
(1) lack of global support and, in the case of genomes, occurring massive amount of missing values or spiked signals, localized Fourier components may not serve as efficient dictionaries.
(2) The Monte Carlo sampling may suffer from boundary effects

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Evaluating the Expressiveness and Stability of Learned Dictionaries
PROPOSAL: We investigate various dictionary learning algorithms, including k-means, PCA, and Autoencoders, to learn an input-dependent feature dictionary that adapts to local structure. We explore the impact of dictionary size, depth, and learning scheme on the performance of the adaptive random feature paradigm. We also analyze the stability and differentiability properties of the learned dictionaries to determine their suitability for our application.
CONTROLS: We compare the impact of different dictionary learning algorithms on the predictive performance and uncertainty calibration of the adaptive random feature model. We also control for the stability of the dictionary learning algorithm by comparing to standard random Fourier features as our baseline.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This analysis will reveal the limitations of different dictionary learning algorithms and identify the best choices for our adaptive random feature model. However, it may reveal difficulties in convergence and regularization of the learned dictionaries in certain experiments, and the optimization may get expensive.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Assessing the Impact of Spatial Adaptation on Prediction and Uncertainty Calibration
PROPOSAL: We investigate the effect of spatial adaptation on the prediction accuracy and uncertainty calibration of the adaptive random feature model by comparing it to stationary random feature models. We analyze the overlap between the learned dictionaries and examine how the spatially adaptive features capture non-stationarity in the data.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of the adaptive random feature model to a stationary random feature model with a fixed dictionary across different datasets, including speech signal analysis and biological protein data regression. We control for the number of features, dictionary size, and training data size to isolate the effect of spatial adaptation.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This analysis will demonstrate the benefits of spatial adaptation in capturing non-stationary structure, leading to improved predictive accuracy and uncertainty calibration. However, it may reveal a trade-off between adaptation time and predictive performance, as overly complex adaptation may impair generalization.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Spatial Adaptation for Non-Stationary Gaussian Processes: A Comparative Study
PROPOSAL: We modify Proposal 3 to provide a more comprehensive comparative study, investigating the impact of different spatial adaptation techniques, including Fourier transforms, wavelet transforms, and Gaussian processes themselves, on the prediction accuracy and uncertainty calibration of non-stationary Gaussian processes. We compare the performance of these techniques on different datasets, including speech signal analysis and biological protein data regression.
CONTROLS: We control for the number of features, dictionary size, and training data size to isolate the effect of spatial adaptation. We compare the performance of the different spatial adaptation techniques to a stationary random feature model and the original adaptive random feature model.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This comparative study will reveal the strengths and weaknesses of different spatial adaptation techniques and provide insights into their suitability for specific applications and datasets. However, it may reveal a complex interplay between adaptation technique and dataset, requiring careful selection of both to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Analysis of Scalability and Computational Cost of Spatial Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We analyze the computational cost and scalability of the spatial adaptation techniques compared in Proposal 3. We investigate the impact of the number of training data points, dictionary size, and feature dimensionality on the computational cost of different spatial adaptation techniques. We also explore strategies to reduce the computational cost of spatial adaptation, such as approximation methods and parallelization techniques.
CONTROLS: We compare the computational cost of different spatial adaptation techniques to the original adaptive random feature model and the stationary random feature model. We control for the number of training data points, dictionary size, and feature dimensionality to isolate the effect of these factors on computational cost.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This analysis will provide insights into the computational cost and scalability of different spatial adaptation techniques and identify potential strategies to reduce their computational cost. However, it may reveal trade-offs between computational cost and predictive performance, as simplifications or approximations may impact accuracy.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Adaptive Random Fourier Features with Dictionary Learning for Non-Stationary Gaussian Processes
PROPOSAL: We modify Proposal 1 to incorporate the insights gained from Proposal 2 and Proposal 3, and introduce a more robust and adaptive learning approach for the dictionary. Specifically, we use a hierarchical dictionary learning method to select the most informative and relevant features for the non-stationary Gaussian process at each level of the hierarchy. We also integrate spatial adaptation with the adaptive random feature paradigm to better capture non-stationarity.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of the revised adaptive random feature model to the original adaptive random feature model and the stationary random feature model on speech signal analysis and biological protein data regression datasets. We control for the number of features, dictionary size, and training data size to isolate the effect of adaptive learning and spatial adaptation.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised adaptive random feature model will demonstrate improved predictive accuracy and uncertainty calibration on non-stationary Gaussian processes, due to the more robust and adaptive learning approach for the dictionary and spatial adaptation. However, it may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal performance, which can be a challenge.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Assessing Robustness and Generalizability of Adaptive Random Feature Model
PROPOSAL: We investigate the robustness and generalizability of the revised adaptive random feature model by analyzing its performance on unseen data and noisy observations. We evaluate the model's ability to handle out-of-distribution data, missing values, and noisy signals, and compare its performance to traditional Gaussian process models.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of the revised adaptive random feature model to the traditional Gaussian process model on speech signal analysis and biological protein data regression datasets, both with and without noise and missing values. We control for the number of features, dictionary size, and training data size to isolate the effect of robustness and generalizability.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This analysis will demonstrate the improved robustness and generalizability of the revised adaptive random feature model, making it a more suitable choice for real-world applications where data is often noisy or incomplete. However, it may reveal challenges in handling extreme cases of noisy or missing data, which can require further development and refinement of the model.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Learning to Adapt: A Meta-Learning Approach for Adaptive Random Feature Models
PROPOSAL: We propose to extend the adaptive random feature model to a meta-learning framework, where the dictionary learning and spatial adaptation are parameterized as functions to be learned from a collection of related tasks. This will enable the model to adapt to new tasks and environments with minimal training data, and improve its generalizability across a wide range of applications.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of the meta-learning adaptive random feature model to the traditional Gaussian process model and the revised adaptive random feature model on a range of tasks in speech signal analysis and biological protein data regression, including unseen tasks and tasks with different levels of noise and missing values.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This meta-learning approach will enable the adaptive random feature model to generalize better across a wide range of tasks and environments, but may require a large amount of labeled data to learn the meta-parameters, which can be a challenge in many applications.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Hierarchical Dictionary Learning for Adaptive Random Feature Models
PROPOSAL: We modify Proposal 2 to use a hierarchical dictionary learning approach, where the dictionary is learned in a hierarchical manner, with each level representing a specific resolution or scale. This will enable the model to capture both local and global features, and improve its expressiveness and stability.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of the hierarchical dictionary learning approach to the traditional dictionary learning approach, and evaluate its impact on the expressiveness and stability of the adaptive random feature model. We control for the number of features, dictionary size, and training data size to isolate the effect of hierarchical dictionary learning.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This hierarchical dictionary learning approach will improve the expressiveness and stability of the adaptive random feature model, but may require careful tuning of the hierarchical hyperparameters, which can be a challenging task.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Benchmarking and Comparison of Adaptive Random Feature Models for Non-Stationary Gaussian Processes
PROPOSAL: We conduct a comprehensive benchmarking and comparison study of the adaptive random feature model and related approaches, including Stationary Random Fourier Features, Deep GPs, and sparse variational GPs, on a range of benchmarks and datasets in speech signal analysis and biological protein data regression. We evaluate their performance in terms of predictive accuracy, uncertainty estimation, and computational cost, and provide a comprehensive analysis of their strengths and limitations.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of the adaptive random feature model to the state-of-the-art models, and evaluate their robustness and generalizability across different datasets and tasks. We control for the number of features, dictionary size, and training data size to isolate the effect of different approaches and hyperparameters.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This benchmarking study will provide a comprehensive understanding of the adaptive random feature model and its strengths and limitations, and enable us to identify areas for future research and improvement.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Random Fourier Features for Non-Stationary Kernels
PROPOSAL: Design and implement an adaptive selection mechanism for the random Fourier features (RFFs) based on the local learned frequency content in the data. Specifically, we will utilize the Periodogram of the training data to estimate the kernel's spectral density, and then use this estimate to dynamically adjust the frequency and number of samples used for RFF construction in different regions of the input space.
CONTROLS: Performance on a subset of the previous experiments using exact GPs or stationary RFFs, ablation study on periodicity estimation and frequency content.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours (sweet spot selection over 10 different adaptive selection schemes, as evaluated on state of the art benchmarks)
PREDICTION: Adaptive RFFs will yield improved performance and better capture the local non-stationarity in the data, but might suffer from overfitting due to increased capacity from dynamic frequency selection.

ACTION: REVISE

CONTROLS: Performance comparison with the previous adaptive RFFs on a subset of the experiments with an expanded data set to validate robustness, ablation study on parameter effects and integration.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours (integration and hyperparameter evaluation with larger setup)
PREDICTION: Improved results with increased sensitivity to local fluctuations in the signal, as adaptive RFFs allocate more samples to regions of high uncertainty, offering potential improvements in representing variability in the model.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Bayesian Diffusion Sampling for Inverse Problems with Unknown Noise
PROPOSAL: Develop a Bayesian diffusion sampling framework that uses a pretrained diffusion model as a prior, and incorporates a noise-learned intermediate noise injection technique to stay on-manifold and explore the solution space, without requiring the intermediate likelihoods, for image super-resolution, image inpainting, image deblurring, phase retrieval, and HDR image reconstruction tasks.
CONTROLS: Use MAFL (Maximum A Posteriori Least-Squares) solver as baseline and compare it to our approach, hold model size and structure fixed across all experiments, also replicate ReSample in our experiment.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our approach should outperform MAFL and ReSample in terms of image PSNR and multiscale SSIM scores, while achieving better robustness to measurement noise and avoiding overfitting to noise, though it might fail to investigate narrow channelled stochastic traps.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Bayesian Diffusion Sampling for Inverse Problems with Unknown Noise
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Develop a two-stage framework: In the first stage, learn an aggregated noise model (ANM) of the measurement noise from a set of available noisy training images, leveraging the shared prior statistics of the diffusion model. In the second stage, use the learned ANM to guide the sampling process, injecting noise that shares the same statistical properties as the measurement noise, thereby improving the robustness and fidelity of the reconstructions. This approach is more data-efficient and practical for handling unknown noise levels and types.
CONTROLS: Same as before: MAFL as baseline, fixed model size and structure.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised approach should improve robustness and fidelity, and reduce computational cost by bootstrapping the samplings from an accordingly constructed data-specific ANM – results failing might be inaccurate estimates of the optimized ANM due uncorrectly generalizing.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: On-Manifold Regularization via Learned Denoiser Sensitivity Analysis
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel on-manifold regularization technique by analyzing the sensitivity of the denoiser to intermediate noises. This is achieved by training a separate, noise-sensitive model on a set of noise-perturbed denoiser outputs, and then using its learned sensitivity patterns to regularize the intermediate noise injections, helping the sampler stay on-manifold and avoid the ridge of noise.
CONTROLS: Compare our approach to its naive counterpart without sensitivity learning, the revised stage-1 Bayesian Diffusion Sampling framework, and MAFL.
COST: 900 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: On-manifold regularization via sensitivity analysis will significantly improve reconstructions in ill-posed problems where conventional regularization often fails, though systematic over-tuning of the denoiser may result in not fully mapping trauma aggressive noise infiltration.

This will help the sampler better understand and respect the structure of the diffusion flow and retain more features on-manifold.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Conditional Diffusion Pruning for Efficient Inversion
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel conditional diffusion pruning technique to reduce the computational overhead of the Bayesian diffusion sampling framework. By adaptively and conditionally pruning the diffusion process based on the statistics of the prior and the structure of the problem, we can reduce the number of diffusion steps and improve the inversion speed without sacrificing image fidelity or uncertainty estimation. This technique can be especially beneficial for real-world applications where computational resources are limited.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Resolution Inversion using Learned Anisotropic Diffusion
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel uncertainty-aware multi-resolution inversion technique that utilizes a learned anisotropic diffusion process to capture the varying uncertainty levels and image structures across different spatial resolutions. By adaptively adjusting the diffusion process based on the uncertainty levels and image features, we can improve the robustness and accuracy of the inversion results, especially for ill-posed problems. This technique can be seamlessly integrated with the hierarchical Bayesian inversion procedure and conditional diffusion pruning technique to further enhance the overall performance.
CONTROLS: Compare our approach to the hierarchical Bayesian inversion procedure with and without conditional diffusion pruning, MAFL, and state-of-the-art multi-resolution inversion methods.
COST: 1400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our uncertainty-aware multi-resolution inversion technique will significantly improve the robustness and accuracy of the inversion results, especially for ill-posed problems, and provide more informative and interpretable uncertainty estimates, though careful selection of hyperparameters may be necessary to avoid over-adaptation to noise.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Robust Diffusion-Based Inverse Solver with Manifold-Aware Dropout
PROPOSAL: Implement the Robust Diffusion-Based Inverse Solver with Manifold-Aware Dropout, which modifies the decoding process in diffusion-based inverse solvers by inserting manifold-aware dropout before each reverse diffusion step. This dropout introduces randomness that is aligned with the learned manifold of the diffusion prior, ensuring manifold feasibility and preventing the solver from drifting off the manifold. The dropout rate can be learned from the data or pre-trained using standard dropout techniques.
CONTROLS: Compare against unmodified diffusion-based inverse solvers and iterative guidance methods (e.g., DPS, DDRM) in image super-resolution and phase retrieval tasks.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method should yield accurate reconstructions in image super-resolution and phase retrieval tasks, outperforming unmodified diffusion-based solvers and comparable iterative guidance methods in terms of manifold feasibility and mode exploration. Potential failure modes include overfitting to the dropout pattern or requiring complex hyperparameter tuning.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Manifold Denoising for Diffusion-Based Inverse Solvers
PROPOSAL: Explore manifold denoising as an alternative to dropout for maintaining manifold feasibility. Manifold denoising estimates the noise distribution on the learned manifold and uses it to denoise the intermediate states, ensuring they remain close to the high-probability manifold. This approach can be combined with the Robust Diffusion-Based Inverse Solver with Manifold-Aware Dropout (proposal 1) to create a hybrid method.
CONTROLS: Compare against manifold-aware dropout alone, the unmodified diffusion-based inverse solver, and iterative guidance methods (e.g., DPS, DDRM) in image inpainting and HDR image reconstruction tasks.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (assuming increased model complexity)
PREDICTION: Manifold denoising should provide more stable and accurate reconstructions than manifold-aware dropout, especially in high-noise scenarios. However, it may be computationally expensive and require careful hyperparameter tuning to balance denoising strength and manifold feasibility.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Adaptive Manifold Denoising for Diffusion-Based Inverse Solvers
PROPOSAL: Modify the manifold denoising approach (proposal 2) to adapt the denoising strength to the current level of noise in the data. This can be done by learning a noise adaptive parameterization of the denoising network, which adjusts its behavior based on the gradient of the data consistency loss. This adaptive approach should improve stability and accuracy in varying noise levels.
CONTROLS: Compare against fixed-strength manifold denoising, manifold-aware dropout, and the unmodified diffusion-based inverse solver in image deblurring, where noise levels can be controlled.
COST: 180 GPU-hours (to accommodate increased model complexity and adaptive training)
PREDICTION: Adaptive manifold denoising should improve upon fixed-strength manifold denoising, providing more accurate reconstructions in the presence of varying noise levels. However, its effectiveness may depend on the choice of noise adaptation mechanism and could introduce computational overhead due to online adaptation.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Gradient-Based Sampling for Diffusion-Based Inverse Solvers
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of gradient-based sampling for exploring the solution space of diffusion-based inverse solvers. Specifically, sample from the gradient of the data consistency loss, which is typically easier to compute than the likelihood or posterior. This should allow for better exploration of the solution space and improved mode coverage, reducing the risk of spurious local modes.
CONTROLS: Compare against random sampling, unmodified diffusion-based inverse solver, and iterative guidance methods (e.g., DPS, DDRM) in phase retrieval and high dynamic range (HDR) image reconstruction tasks.
COST: 80 GPU-hours (simplified model and sampling process)
PREDICTION: Gradient-based sampling should provide better mode coverage and more accurate reconstructions compared to random sampling, especially in severely ill-posed problems. However, it may require careful tuning of the sampling schedule and step size to avoid getting stuck in spurious modes.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Contrastive Manifold Learning for Robust Inverse Problems
PROPOSAL: Develop a contrastive learning objective to learn a robust manifold representation for inverse problems. The contrastive objective encourages the model to learn distinct features that capture the underlying structure of the data, while pushing aside noise and artifacts. This learned manifold representation should improve the robustness and accuracy of diffusion-based inverse solvers.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard diffusion-based inverse solvers, manifold-aware dropout, adaptive manifold denoising, and gradient-based sampling in image super-resolution and HDR image reconstruction tasks.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (due to the need for a separate contrastive learning task)
PREDICTION: Contrastive manifold learning should lead to more robust and accurate reconstructions, as the learned manifold representation should be more robust to noise and artifacts. However, it may require significant computational resources and careful hyperparameter tuning to balance contrastive learning strength and inverse problem regularity.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Uncertainty-Aware Diffusion-Based Inverse Solver
PROPOSAL: Modify the diffusion-based inverse solver to incorporate uncertainty estimation and propagation. This can be achieved by learning an uncertainty-aware diffusion model, which captures both the spatial and temporal uncertainties in the inverse problem. The solver should then use this uncertainty information to guide its sampling and improvement processes, leading to more reliable and robust reconstructions.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard diffusion-based inverse solvers, manifold-aware dropout, adaptive manifold denoising, gradient-based sampling, and contrastive manifold learning in image inpainting, phase retrieval, and HDR image reconstruction tasks.
COST: 250 GPU-hours (due to the need for a separate uncertainty-aware diffusion model)
PREDICTION: Uncertainty-aware diffusion-based inverse solver should provide more accurate and reliable reconstructions by accounting for spatial and temporal uncertainties. However, it may require significant computational resources and careful hyperparameter tuning to balance uncertainty estimation and propagation.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Hybrid Gradient-Based Sampling with Manifold Awareness
PROPOSAL: Combine gradient-based sampling (proposal 3) with manifold-aware techniques, such as adaptive manifold denoising (proposal 2) or contrastive manifold learning (proposal 4). This hybrid approach should leverage the strengths of both methods, combining the efficient exploration of gradient-based sampling with the robustness and accuracy of manifold-aware techniques.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard gradient-based sampling, adaptive manifold denoising, contrastive manifold learning, and uncertainty-aware diffusion-based inverse solver in image super-resolution and HDR image reconstruction tasks.
COST: 220 GPU-hours (simplified model and sampling process, with hybrid training)
PREDICTION: Hybrid gradient-based sampling with manifold awareness should provide more accurate and robust reconstructions by combining the strengths of both methods. However, it may require careful hyperparameter tuning to balance the contributions of gradient-based sampling and manifold-aware techniques.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Efficient Parallelization of Diffusion-Based Inverse Solvers
PROPOSAL: Develop an efficient parallelization strategy for diffusion-based inverse solvers, allowing for faster and more scalable computation on large datasets and complex inverse problems. This can be achieved through a combination of model parallelization, data parallelization, and communication-avoiding techniques.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard diffusion-based inverse solvers, manifold-aware dropout, adaptive manifold denoising, hybrid gradient-based sampling, and uncertainty-aware diffusion-based inverse solver in image super-resolution and HDR image reconstruction tasks.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (reduced training time through parallelization)
PREDICTION: Efficient parallelization of diffusion-based inverse solvers should significantly reduce computation time, enabling the use of these methods on larger datasets and more complex inverse problems. However, it may require careful optimization of the parallelization strategy to minimize communication overhead and ensure convergence.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Noise-Agnostic Diffusion-Based Inverse Solver
PROPOSAL: Develop a noise-agnostic diffusion-based inverse solver that can adapt to different types and levels of noise without requiring careful tuning of hyperparameters. This can be achieved through a multi-task learning framework that learns to generalize across different noise scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard diffusion-based inverse solvers, manifold-aware dropout, adaptive manifold denoising, hybrid gradient-based sampling, uncertainty-aware diffusion-based inverse solver, and efficient parallelization in various noise scenarios.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (due to the need for a multi-task learning framework)
PREDICTION: Noise-agnostic diffusion-based inverse solver should provide accurate and robust reconstructions across different noise scenarios without requiring task-specific hyperparameter tuning. However, it may require significant computational resources and careful optimization of the multi-task learning framework.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: End-to-End Training of Diffusion-Based Inverse Solvers with Adversarial Noise
PROPOSAL: Develop an end-to-end training framework for diffusion-based inverse solvers that incorporates adversarial noise during training. This can be achieved through a two-player game between the generator and discriminator, where the generator learns to invert the measurements while the discriminator learns to distinguish between real and synthetic noise.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard diffusion-based inverse solvers, manifold-aware dropout, adaptive manifold denoising, hybrid gradient-based sampling, uncertainty-aware diffusion-based inverse solver, efficient parallelization, and noise-agnostic diffusion-based inverse solver in various inverse problems.
COST: 400 GPU-hours (due to the need for a two-player game framework)
PREDICTION: End-to-end training of diffusion-based inverse solvers with adversarial noise should provide more robust and accurate reconstructions by learning to generalize across different noise scenarios and inverse problems. However, it may require significant computational resources and careful optimization of the two-player game framework.

TITLE: Evaluating State-of-the-Art UDA Methods on Digit Recognition
PROPOSAL: Compare and evaluate a selection of state-of-the-art UDA methods, including alignment-based (e.g., MMD, CORAL) and pseudo-labeling (e.g., adversarial domain adaptation, entropy-based) approaches, on a digit recognition dataset (e.g., MNIST, SVHN) using a combination of standard evaluation metrics (accuracy, F1-score, KLD) and robustness metrics (e.g., maximum KLD, domain-invariant risk).
CONTROLS: Empirical risk minimization (ERM) on source data alone as a baseline, and the same UDA methods with random initialization to control for the impact of hyperparameter tuning.
COST: Estimated 200 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: State-of-the-art methods should perform significantly better than ERM on the target domain, with pseudo-labeling approaches offering a trade-off between performance on the target and risk of overfitting to noisy labels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Limited Unsupervised Target Data
PROPOSAL: Evaluate how the quality and quantity of unlabeled target data affect the performance of different UDA methods, including alignment-based and pseudo-labeling approaches, using a controlled setup where the target dataset is gradually decreased in size while maintaining the same distribution and number of classes as the source domain. We will examine the sensitivity of each method to noise, corruption, and overfitting as the target dataset becomes smaller.
CONTROLS: Same UDA methods as in proposal 1, with additional experiments including varying levels of data augmentation and noise injection to further probe the methods' robustness.
COST: Estimated 400 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: UDA methods will degrade significantly as the target dataset becomes smaller, with some methods exhibiting poor performance even at moderate data sizes (e.g., 100-500 samples). Interesting results may arise when manipulating noise levels or amount of augmentation, revealing the interplay between data quality and method performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Understanding the Role of Spurious Correlations in the Source Domain
PROPOSAL: Introduce spurious correlations in the source dataset by manipulating covariate shift or class-label noise, and evaluate how different UDA methods adapt to these changes. This will help us understand whether UDA methods can generalize across domains and noise levels, and whether they rely on spurious features that may not transfer to the target domain.
CONTROLS: Same UDA methods as in proposal 1, with additional experiments including source covariate shift, class-label noise and manipulation of feature importance to gauge the methods' reliance on spurious correlations.
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Many UDA methods, especially those that heavily rely on data information from the source domain, may overfit and perform poorly once the feature noise level increases, translating that learned shortcut to cover the input descriptions towards instances where the trained neural network fails where distribution has a drastically difference. We might see improvement on concentration on weaker, underused features.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Understanding the Role of Spurious Correlations in the Source Domain
PROPOSAL: REVISED to include a comparison with robust optimization methods (e.g., distributionally robust optimization), which are designed to handle noisy or biased data in the source domain. We will evaluate whether these robust optimization methods can adapt to the target domain more effectively than UDA methods when spurious correlations are present in the source domain.
CONTROLS: Same UDA methods as in proposal 1, and an additional comparison with robust optimization methods such as distributionally robust optimization. Include experiments with varying levels of noise, against hyperparameters.
COST: Estimated 400 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Robust optimization methods may outperform UDA methods in scenarios where spurious correlations dominate the source domain, as they are specifically designed to handle noise and bias. However, UDA methods might adapt better when the target data provide additional information and partial understanding that could eliminate potential source-domain artifacts with added robustification, at the other end of aspects.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robustness to Structured Shifts through Distributionally Robust Optimization
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether distributionally robust optimization (DRO) can handle structured shifts, specifically subpopulation shifts, between the source and target domains. We will use the UCI Digit Dataset with subpopulation shifts (e.g., age, gender) to evaluate the performance of DRO methods (e.g., worst-case loss minimization) in handling this type of distribution shift.
CONTROLS: Compare DRO methods against standard UDA methods and ERM baseline, using a combination of standard evaluation metrics (accuracy, F1-score) and robustness metrics (e.g., maximum KLD, domain-invariant risk).
COST: Estimated 250 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: DRO methods may show improved performance on structured shifts, such as subpopulation shifts, by considering the ambiguity set of plausible distributions, but may also be computationally expensive and require careful selection of the ambiguity set.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: 4. Robustness to Structured Shifts through Distributionally Robust Optimization
PROPOSAL: REVISED proposal 4 to include a comparison with group distributionally robust optimization (GDRO), which is specifically designed to handle subpopulation shifts. We will evaluate whether GDRO can outperform standard DRO methods on structured shifts.
CONTROLS: Include both standard DRO methods and GDRO methods, and compare their performance on structured shifts, such as subpopulation shifts.
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: GDRO methods may show improved performance on structured shifts, such as subpopulation shifts, by explicitly modeling group shifts, but may also be computationally expensive and require careful selection of the group labels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Bird Image Classification
PROPOSAL: Evaluate several UDA methods on the bird image classification task, specifically using the Caltech-UCSD Birds 200 (CUB) dataset, which is a challenging task due to the high intra-class variability of bird species and the diverse appearance of birds. We will consider both unsupervised alignment-based and pseudo-labeling-based UDA methods, and compare their performance on this task.
CONTROLS: Include a comparison with state-of-the-art methods for unsupervised domain adaptation, such as adversarial domain adaptation and pixel-wise adaptation.
COST: Estimated 350 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: This task may pose a significant challenge for UDA methods due to the high intra-class variability and diversity of bird species, and it may be difficult to achieve satisfactory results using standard UDA methods.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: 5. Investigating Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Bird Image Classification
PROPOSAL: REVISED proposal 5 to include a comparison with a new unsupervised domain adaptation method that uses a contrastive learning approach to align the feature distributions between the source and target domains. We will evaluate whether this contrastive learning approach can improve the performance of UDA methods on the bird image classification task.
CONTROLS: Include both the original UDA methods and the new contrastive learning-based UDA method, and compare their performance on the bird image classification task.
COST: Estimated 400 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: This new contrastive learning approach may be able to improve the performance of UDA methods on the bird image classification task by aligning the feature distributions between the source and target domains more effectively, but may also require careful hyperparameter tuning and selection of the batch size and temperature.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Provide a theoretical analysis of UDA methods, including a study of their generalization errors and a comparison of their robustness to different types of distribution shifts. We will provide a PAC-Bayes framework for analyzing the generalization errors of UDA methods and a causality-based approach for understanding their robustness to different types of distribution shifts.
CONTROLS: Establish a connection between the theoretical analysis and the experimental results of the previous proposals.
COST: Estimated 500 GPU-hours (for theoretical analysis and derivations) + 0 (no additional experiments).
PREDICTION: The theoretical analysis will provide a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms of UDA methods and their limitations, and will allow us to design new UDA methods that are more robust to different types of distribution shifts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Uniformity of Distribution Shifts in Digit Recognition
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of several alignment-based UDA methods and pseudo-labeling methods on the MNIST and USPS datasets, both commonly used for digit classification, to identify scenarios where distribution shifts cause significant performance degradation. We'll use the standard training and testing protocols for these datasets and train classifiers on the labeled source data (MNIST or USPS), then evaluate their performance on the unlabeled target data (USPS or MNIST).
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Empirical risk minimization (ERM) on the source data; Baseline 2: ERM on the target data without pre-training on the source data; Baseline 3: Standard adversarial training without unlabeled target data.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect alignment-based methods and pseudo-labeling methods to show improved performance over ERM on the target data for small to medium distribution shifts, but perform poorly for larger shifts due to over-reliance on spurious source features. Pseudo-labeling might improve over alignment-based methods when the source data contains outliers and the target domain has an imbalanced input distribution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Spurious Correlations on Alignment-Based Methods
PROPOSAL: Evaluate alignment-based UDA methods, specifically MCD (Maximum Covariance Alignment) and CORAL (Correlation Alignment), on digit recognition tasks by introducing artificial spurious correlations in the source data (e.g., MNIST) to simulate the scenario where irrelevant features are strongly associated with labels. We'll compare these methods with pseudo-labeling and empirical risk minimization.
CONTROLS: Same controls as in proposal 1; Additional control: Source data with artificially removed spurious correlations to evaluate the effect of these correlations on UDA performance.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect alignment-based methods to fail miserably when spurious correlations are present, while pseudo-labeling and ERM on the target data might show more robust performance. The source data with artificially removed spurious correlations could serve as a lower bound for performance in a well-behaved source domain.

TITLE: Adaptive Source-Target Knowledge Transfer for Bias Compensation
PROPOSAL: Propose an adaptive approach that weighs knowledge transfer from the source domain to the target domain based on the similarity between the source and target distributions. The key idea is to assign higher weights to the most transferable features and adjust the weights dynamically based on the pseudo-labels assigned to the target-domain samples. ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Adaptive Source-Target Knowledge Transfer for Bias Compensation
PROPOSAL: Modify the fourth proposal to incorporate an ensemble approach to adaptively combine the knowledge transfer from the source domain and the prior learning of the target task. This ensemble approach will learn to weight the contributions of the two components adaptively based on the uncertainty of the target task. We'll evaluate this approach on bird image classification and facial attribute classification tasks.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Empirical risk minimization (ERM) on the source data; Baseline 2: Pseudo-labeling with trusted-weighting; Baseline 3: State-of-the-art domain-invariant feature learning approach (e.g., DANN or CORAL); Baseline 4: Prior learning with adversarial training; Baseline 5: Regularization via regularized distribution matching.
COST: 200 GPU-hours

The adaptive weighting of the two components will allow the model to balance the knowledge transfer and prior learning effectively. However, it may struggle when the target task has low uncertainty, and may require additional fine-tuning to adapt to the specific target task.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Evaluating Uniformity of Distribution Shifts in Digit Recognition
PROPOSAL: Modify the first proposal to include a more comprehensive evaluation of the distribution shifts between the source and target domains. Instead of simply comparing the performance of different alignment-based UDA methods and pseudo-labeling methods, we'll use techniques such as Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) and Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) to quantify the distribution shifts and evaluate the effectiveness of each method in mitigating these shifts. We'll also include additional baselines and controls to further evaluate the robustness of each method.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Empirical risk minimization (ERM) on the source data; Baseline 2: Pseudo-labeling with trusted-weighting; Baseline 3: State-of-the-art domain-invariant feature learning approach (e.g., DANN or CORAL); Baseline 4: Prior learning with adversarial training; Baseline 5: Regularization via regularized distribution matching; Baseline 6: Ensemble approach to adaptively combine the knowledge transfer from the source domain and the prior learning of the target task.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the revised proposal to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the challenges posed by distribution shifts in digit recognition and the effectiveness of different UDA methods in addressing these challenges. However, the additional evaluation metrics and baselines may also reveal potential pitfalls and limitations of each method, which will require further investigation and refinement.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Current Baselines for Distribution Shift in Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Implement and evaluate a range of current UDA methods, including recent alignment-based and pseudo-labeling approaches, on several widely-used benchmarks such as Office-31, Image-Clef-2014, and VisDA-2017, with a focus on robustness to spurious source features and noisy target labels. Compare these methods' performance to that of empirical risk minimization (ERM) trained on the source data and to popular baseline algorithms like DANN, JAN, and MCD.
CONTROLS: ERM trained on the source data, random initialized models with no fine-tuning on the target data, and various types of surrogate loss optimization or gradient-weighted class balancing methods
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate seeing a performance gap between the best UDA methods and ERM due to the difficulty in adapting to the target domain. However, it is possible that some alignment-based or pseudo-labeling methods may still outperform ERM, especially in the digit recognition domain, where there's a clear correspondence between the source and target data distributions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Robustness of Alignment-based Methods to Spurious Source Features
PROPOSAL: Design a new experiment where the source domain consists of images with background color labels, but the task is actually a digit recognition problem (e.g., digits 0-9 in a specific background), while the target domain consists of clean digit images without background information. Evaluate the performance of recent alignment-based methods, including CORAL, CDAN, and MDDAN, in such a scenario using semi-synthetic datasets constructed from ImageNet.
CONTROLS: Leave-one-out ablation where we independently remove the color or background features from the source data to see if the methods still generalize, and compare to the pseudo-labeling strategy
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect these alignment-based methods to perform poorly on this task due to their reliance on the specific source-background relationship, and its direct failure to transfer to the target domain. The pseudo-labeling baseline may still exhibit better performance compared to the baseline performance without any adaptation.

ACTION: REVISE (2)
TITLE: Investigating Robustness of Alignment-based Methods to Spurious Source Features
PROPOSAL: Modify the experiment to also test the robustness of pseudo-labeling methods (e.g., Entropy-based, Mean Teacher) to poor pseudo-labeling quality caused by a small/narrow target sample. To this end, simulate a limited target sample with only a subset of classes or samples from the full set and evaluate the performance of the pseudo-labeling methods in this scenario, either on the full or limited target sample. Additionally, examine whether two or more methods can be combined for a potential performance boost.
CONTROLS: Previous controls (leave-one-out ablation) plus evaluate the pseudo-labeling strategies individually and in combination
COST: 50 GPU-hours (assuming the same semi-synthetic dataset)
PREDICTION: Pseudo-labeling methods may fail dramatically in extreme scenarios like this due to the minority or sample-starved bias, which can lead to overfitting and further degradation of performance on the target domain. It remains to be seen whether merging pseudo-labeling with another strategy can rescue performance or whether better methods can provide synergy in pollution driven datasets, reducing the effects of those challenges.
