actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Structured PDE Solver using Fourier-Based Spatiotemporal Graph Networks
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of spatiotemporal graph networks that leverage Fourier-based representations to capture structural priors in PDE dynamics. This architecture will incorporate localized spatial convolutional layers to model the spatial differential operator, as well as cross-channel graph attention mechanisms to model temporal dynamics and the relationship between spatial and temporal degrees of freedom. We will utilize a loss function that incorporates both PDE residual error minimization and a constrained variational data-fidelity term that captures physical invariances such as energy conservation.
CONTROLS: i) Classical shallow neural networks (e.g., physics-informed neural networks) with and without sensitive initializations to assess learning instability, ii) structural graph-based solvers without Fourier-based representations, iii) existing operator learning architectures (e.g., DeepONet) for benchmarks.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved data efficiency for reaction-diffusion systems and channel flow transport, with robust generalization to unseen source terms.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Sampling for Sparse Trajectories in PDE Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of hierarchical sampling methods in conjunction with existing neural PDE solvers to reduce the required number of training trajectories for learning accurate PDE dynamics. This approach will involve dividing the space of possible source terms into regions of high similarity and sampling trajectories from these regions at different scales. This sparse set of trajectories will then be used to train a neural PDE solver, which can be optimized using the collected data.
CONTROLS: i) Classical trajectory-based sampling methods to assess the effectiveness of hierarchical sampling, ii) ablation study to quantify the impact of sampling granularity on solver performance, iii) Structured PDE Solver using Fourier-Based Spatiotemporal Graph Networks as a reference architecture.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach will lead to a significant reduction in the number of training trajectories required for accurate PDE learning, improving data efficiency in settings with limited data. The approach could fail if the hierarchical sampling method does not adequately capture the high-level structure of the PDE dynamics.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Hierarchical Sampling for Sparse Trajectories in PDE Learning
PROPOSAL: In addition to hierarchical sampling, incorporate multiscale representation learning into the Hierarchical Sampling approach. This will enable the solver to represent PDE dynamics at different spatial and temporal scales, thereby capturing relevant physical structure from a limited number of training trajectories. This multiscale representation learning will be achieved through learning scale-disentangled features that encode spatial scale, temporal scale, and the spatial-temporal relationship between them.
CONTROLS: i) Comparison of the proposed multiscale hierarchical sampling method with the original hierarchical sampling, ii) Incorporation of the proposed multiscale hierarchical sampling method into the Structured PDE Solver using Fourier-Based Spatiotemporal Graph Networks.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved performance on reaction-diffusion dynamics, contaminant transport in channel flow, and transient heat conduction due to the multiscale representation learning mechanism, especially when source terms vary significantly across space and time.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Embedding Conservation Laws and Structural Constraints in Graph Architectures
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel graph-based PDE solver that incorporates structural constraints, such as conservation laws and superposition, into the graph architecture. This will be achieved by introducing physics-constrained graph components, which can be learned during training to incorporate various PDE-specific inductive biases. In particular, this architecture will leverage a combination of Riemannian neural networks and graph attention mechanisms to learn regionally inhomogeneous and anisotropic PDE dynamics from data.
CONTROLS: i) Graph-based solvers without structural constraints to assess the impact of the proposed constraints, ii) theoretical analysis of error bounds and convergence rates for graph-based PDE solvers with structural constraints.
COST: 700 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Significant performance improvements for PDE dynamics characterized by non-trivial conservation laws, such as Navier-Stokes equations and Euler-Lagrange equations governing elastic dynamics, and potentially reduced sensitivity to data quality. The approach might fail if the graph structure and the incorporation of constraints do not accurately capture the complexity of the PDE dynamics.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalable PDE Learning with Low-Rank Operator Factorization
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of low-rank operator factorization to improve the scalability of neural PDE solvers. By factorizing the Laplace-Beltrami operator into separate spatial and temporal components, and then learning each component separately, the proposed method can reduce the dimensionality of the PDE dynamics and simplify the solution process. This factorization will be learned using a novel loss function that balances the accuracy of the PDE solution and the rank of the factorized operator.
CONTROLS: i) Comparison with existing neural PDE solvers, ii) ablation study to quantify the impact of factorization rank on solver performance.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved scalability for large-scale reaction-diffusion dynamics, contaminant transport in channel flow, and transient heat conduction, by leveraging low-rank operator factorization to reduce the dimensionality of the PDE dynamics. However, this approach might not capture the full complexity of the PDE dynamics, especially in cases where the dynamical modes are highly coupled.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Physics-Informed Neural Network Closure Models for Simplified Dynamics
PROPOSAL: Design novel closure models for physics-informed neural network (PINN) architectures that can simplify the PDE dynamics while retaining accuracy. By introducing a set of dynamically coupled equations that learn the interaction between different physical modes, these closure models can yield more efficient and scalable solutions. This will be achieved by leveraging deep neural networks to learn high-order correction terms that can either add or remove microscopic details from the PDE dynamics, effectively closing the gaps in scale separation and time scales.
CONTROLS: i) Theoretical analysis of error bounds and convergence rates for PINNs with closure models, ii) comparison with existing PDE solvers that incorporate physics constraints.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved computational efficiency and accuracy for PDE dynamics characterized by complex time and length scales, such as those found in reacting flows, turbulent systems, or granular motions, while preserving the underlying physical behavior. The approach might fail if the closure models overly simplify or incorrectly approximate the complex interactions between physical modes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning Physics-Informed Data Augmentation for Neural PDE Solvers
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of physics-informed data augmentation techniques to improve the robustness and generalizability of neural PDE solvers. By learning data augmentation strategies from the underlying PDE dynamics, we can generate diverse sets of training data that better capture the underlying physics, thereby improving the solver's performance on unseen source terms and boundary conditions.
CONTROLS: i) Comparison with existing data augmentation techniques for neural PDE solvers, ii) theoretical analysis of how the learned data augmentation strategies impact the solver's performance.
COST: 350 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved robustness and generalizability for neural PDE solvers across different source terms, boundary conditions, and spatial-temporal resolutions, through the learning of physics-informed data augmentation strategies. However, this approach might require significant tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bayesian Neural PDE Solvers with Uncertainty Quantification
PROPOSAL: Develop Bayesian neural network architectures for solving PDEs that can quantify uncertainty in the solutions and provide probabilistic predictions. By leveraging Bayesian neural networks with Monte Carlo dropout or Bayesian neural networks with hierarchical prior distributions, we can obtain probabilistic outputs that capture the uncertainty in the PDE dynamics, thereby providing more robust and interpretable solutions.
CONTROLS: i) Comparison with existing neural PDE solvers, ii) theoretical analysis of error bounds and convergence rates for Bayesian neural PDE solvers.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved uncertainty quantification and robustness for neural PDE solvers, allowing for more accurate and reliable predictions, especially in settings where there is significant uncertainty in the input data or where the PDE dynamics are highly nonlinear. However, the computational cost of Bayesian neural networks may be higher than that of gradient-based methods, especially for very large datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Physics-Constrained Disentangled Representation Learning for PDE Dynamics
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel disentanglement-based approach that separates the underlying PDE dynamics into disentangled components representing different physical modes, such as diffusion, convection, and reaction. By leveraging physics-constrained representation learning, we can identify and capture the underlying physical structure of the PDE dynamics, leading to more accurate and robust predictions. This approach will utilize a set of physics-constrained loss functions, such as PDE residual error and conservation laws, to guide the disentanglement process.
CONTROLS: i) Comparison with existing disentanglement methods, ii) theoretical analysis of error bounds and convergence rates for disentangled PDE solvers.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved accuracy and robustness for neural PDE solvers by capturing the underlying physical structure of the PDE dynamics, with potential applications in fields such as fluid dynamics, solid mechanics, and chemical engineering. However, the approach may require significant computational resources and expertise in disentanglement-based representation learning.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Structured PDE Solver using Fourier-Based Spatiotemporal Graph Networks
PROPOSAL: Integrate the novel physics-constrained disentangled representation learning approach (proposed in step 8) into the Structured PDE Solver using Fourier-Based Spatiotemporal Graph Networks. By leveraging the disentangled representation, we can improve the accuracy and robustness of the solver by capturing the underlying physical structure of the PDE dynamics.
CONTROLS: All previous experiments to assess the impact of the integrated physics-constrained disentangled representation learning approach.
COST: Additional 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Enhanced accuracy and robustness for neural PDE solvers, especially in settings where the PDE dynamics have complex physical modes, such as non-trivial conservation laws or significantly variable source terms. However, the approach may require further computational resources and expertise in disentanglement-based representation learning.

The approach might fail if the graph structure and the incorporation of constraints do not accurately capture the complexity of the PDE dynamics.
propositions.texte: Propose a novel graph-based PDE solver that incorporates structural constraints, such as conservation laws and superposition, into the graph architecture. This will be achieved by introducing physics-constrained graph components, which can be learned during training to incorporate various PDE-specific inductive biases. In particular, this architecture will leverage a combination of Riemannian neural networks and graph attention mechanisms to learn regionally inhomogeneous and anisotropic PDE dynamics from data.
propositions.titre: Embedding Conservation Laws and Structural Constraints in Graph Architectures

propositions.controles: i) Comparison with existing neural PDE solvers, ii) ablation study to quantify the impact of factorization rank on solver performance.
propositions.prediction: Improved scalability for large-scale reaction-diffusion dynamics, contaminant transport in channel flow, and transient heat conduction, by leveraging low-rank operator factorization to reduce the dimensionality of the PDE dynamics. However, this approach might not capture the full complexity of the PDE dynamics, especially in cases where the dynamical modes are highly coupled.
propositions.texte: Investigate the use of low-rank operator factorization to improve the scalability of neural PDE solvers. By factorizing the Laplace-Beltrami operator into separate spatial and temporal components, and then learning each component separately, the proposed method can reduce the dimensionality of the PDE dynamics and simplify the solution process. This factorization will be learned using a novel loss function that balances the accuracy of the PDE solution and the rank of the factorized operator.
propositions.titre: Scalable PDE Learning with Low-Rank Operator Factorization

propositions.controles: i) Theoretical analysis of error bounds and convergence rates for PINNs with closure models, ii) comparison with existing PDE solvers that incorporate physics constraints.
propositions.prediction: Improved computational efficiency and accuracy for PDE dynamics characterized by complex time and length scales, such as those found in reacting flows, turbulent systems, or granular motions, while preserving the underlying physical behavior. The approach might fail if the closure models overly simplify or incorrectly approximate the complex interactions between physical modes.
propositions.texte: Design novel closure models for physics-informed neural network (PINN) architectures that can simplify the PDE dynamics while retaining accuracy. By introducing a set of dynamically coupled equations that learn the interaction between different physical modes, these closure models can yield more efficient and scalable solutions. This will be achieved by leveraging deep neural networks to learn high-order correction terms that can either add or remove microscopic details from the PDE dynamics, effectively closing the gaps in scale separation and time scales.
propositions.titre: Physics-Informed Neural Network Closure Models for Simplified Dynamics

propositions.controles: i) Comparison with existing data augmentation techniques for neural PDE solvers, ii) theoretical analysis of how the learned data augmentation strategies impact the solver's performance.
propositions.prediction: Improved robustness and generalizability for neural PDE solvers across different source terms, boundary conditions, and spatial-temporal resolutions, through the learning of physics-informed data augmentation strategies. However, this approach might require significant tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal results.
propositions.texte: Investigate the use of physics-informed data augmentation techniques to improve the robustness and generalizability of neural PDE solvers. By learning data augmentation strategies from the underlying PDE dynamics, we can generate diverse sets of training data that better capture the underlying physics, thereby improving the solver's performance on unseen source terms and boundary conditions.
propositions.titre: Learning Physics-Informed Data Augmentation for Neural PDE Solvers

propositions.controles: i) Comparison with existing neural PDE solvers, ii) theoretical analysis of error bounds and convergence rates for Bayesian neural PDE solvers.
propositions.prediction: Improved uncertainty quantification and robustness for neural PDE solvers, allowing for more accurate and reliable predictions, especially in settings where there is significant uncertainty in the input data or where the PDE dynamics are highly nonlinear. However, the computational cost of Bayesian neural networks may be higher than that of gradient-based methods, especially for very large datasets.
propositions.texte: Develop Bayesian neural network architectures for solving PDEs that can quantify uncertainty in the solutions and provide probabilistic predictions. By leveraging Bayesian neural networks with Monte Carlo dropout or Bayesian neural networks with hierarchical prior distributions, we can obtain probabilistic outputs that capture the uncertainty in the PDE dynamics, thereby providing more robust and interpretable solutions.
propositions.titre: Bayesian Neural PDE Solvers with Uncertainty Quantification

propositions.controles: i) Comparison with existing disentanglement methods, ii) theoretical analysis of error bounds and convergence rates for disentangled PDE solvers.
propositions.prediction: Improved accuracy and robustness for neural PDE solvers by capturing the underlying physical structure of the PDE dynamics, with potential applications in fields such as fluid dynamics, solid mechanics, and chemical engineering. However, the approach may require significant computational resources and expertise in disentanglement-based representation learning.
propositions.texte: Propose a novel disentanglement-based approach that separates the underlying PDE dynamics into disentangled components representing different physical modes, such as diffusion, convection, and reaction. By leveraging physics-constrained representation learning, we can identify and capture the underlying physical structure of the PDE dynamics, leading to more accurate and robust predictions. This approach will utilize a set of physics-constrained loss functions, such as PDE residual error and conservation laws, to guide the disentanglement process.
propositions.titre: Physics-Constrained Disentangled Representation Learning for PDE Dynamics

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Conservation Laws on Neural PDE Solvers
PROPOSAL: We will compare the performance of a general-purpose neural network solver with a modified version that incorporates density-based conservation laws (e.g., mass and momentum conservation) for a reaction-diffusion equation on a 2D spatial domain. We will use the Taylor-Green vortex problem with stationary boundary conditions and a synthetic source term.
CONTROLS: General-purpose neural network solver as baseline, ablation study on individual conservation law components
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the modified solver to outperform the general-purpose solver by up to 30% in terms of mean squared error, but might struggle with non-conservative source terms.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Learning Operator Structure with Graph-based Neural PDE Solvers
PROPOSAL: We will implement a graph-based neural PDE solver with learned operator weights and compare it to a solver with fixed weights for a heat equation on a spatial domain with irregular geometry. We will use a synthetic source term and study the impact of different graph architectures on the solution quality.
CONTROLS: Graph-based neural PDE solver with fixed weights as baseline, compare against shallow and deep neural networks
COST: 5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the improved solver to reduce the mean squared error by up to 20%, but might overfit if the graph architecture is too complex.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Learning Operator Structure with Graph-based Neural PDE Solvers
PROPOSAL: We will modify the proposal to incorporate both spatial and temporal graph structures, allowing the solver to learn dependencies between spatial locations and across time steps. We will study the impact of different graph architectures and time step resolutions on the solution quality.
CONTROLS: Graph-based neural PDE solver with fixed weights as baseline, compare against shallow and deep neural networks, ablation study on individual graph components
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the improved solver to reduce the mean squared error by up to 30% and exhibit better generalization to unseen solution domains.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Combining Physics-informed Neural Networks and Graph-based Solvers
PROPOSAL: We will combine the physics-informed neural network approach with graph-based neural PDE solvers, incorporating PDE residuals and boundary conditions as soft constraints into the graph-based solver. We will study the impact of this combination on the solution quality and data efficiency for a heat equation on a spatial domain with irregular geometry.
CONTROLS: Graph-based neural PDE solver as baseline, compare against shallow and deep neural networks, ablation study on individual components
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the combined approach to outperform the graph-based solver by up to 40% in terms of mean squared error, but might struggle with complex solution domains if the graph architecture is not well-designed.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Efficient Representation of PDE Convolutions using Learned Meshes
PROPOSAL: We will explore the idea of representing PDE convolutions using learned meshes, which can reduce the number of parameters and improve the computational efficiency of graph-based neural PDE solvers. We will study the impact of different mesh learning strategies and activation functions on the solution quality.
CONTROLS: Graph-based neural PDE solver with fixed mesh as baseline, compare against shallow and deep neural networks
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the learned mesh approach to reduce the number of parameters by up to 50% and improve the solution quality by up to 20%, but might require careful tuning of the mesh learning strategy to avoid overfitting.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Bridging the Gap between Neural PDE Solvers and Classical Methods using Transfer Learning
PROPOSAL: We will explore the idea of using transfer learning to bridge the gap between neural PDE solvers and classical methods, such as finite difference schemes or finite element methods. We will study the impact of transfer learning on the solution quality and data efficiency for a heat equation on a spatial domain with irregular geometry.
CONTROLS: Classical method (e.g., finite difference scheme) as baseline, compare against general-purpose neural network solver and graph-based neural PDE solver
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect transfer learning to improve the solution quality by up to 30% and reduce the number of training data points required by up to 20%, but might require careful tuning of the transfer learning strategy to avoid overfitting.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Physics-informed basis pursuit for compressive data-driven PDE solvers
PROPOSAL: We will propose a physics-informed basis pursuit method for selecting a sparse set of basis functions from a library of candidate functions that are consistent with the PDE and boundary conditions. We will study the impact of this method on the solution quality and data efficiency for a heat equation on a spatial domain with irregular geometry.
CONTROLS: General-purpose neural network solver as baseline, compare against graph-based neural PDE solver and compressive sensing methods
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the physics-informed basis pursuit method to improve the solution quality by up to 25% and reduce the number of training data points required by up to 40%, but might require careful tuning of the basis function library to avoid underfitting.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: PDE-aware Neural Architecture Search for Efficient Solvers
PROPOSAL: We will propose a PDE-aware neural architecture search method that searches for efficient neural network architectures that are tailored to the specific PDE and problem characteristics. We will study the impact of this method on the solution quality and data efficiency for a reaction-diffusion equation on a spatial domain with irregular geometry.
CONTROLS: General-purpose neural network solver as baseline, compare against graph-based neural PDE solver and architectures search methods
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the PDE-aware neural architecture search method to improve the solution quality by up to 35% and reduce the number of training data points required by up to 50%, but might require significant computational resources for the architecture search process.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Multiscale Neural PDE Solvers with Adaptive Resolution
PROPOSAL: We will propose a multiscale neural PDE solver that adapts its resolution to the local characteristics of the solution, allowing for efficient representation of complex PDE dynamics. We will study the impact of this method on the solution quality and data efficiency for a heat equation on a spatial domain with irregular geometry and varying frequency content.
CONTROLS: General-purpose neural network solver as baseline, compare against graph-based neural PDE solver and multiscale methods
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the multiscale neural PDE solver to improve the solution quality by up to 40% and reduce the number of training data points required by up to 30%, but might require careful tuning of the multiscale architecture to avoid overfitting.

ACTION: ADD 9
TITLE: Robust Training of Neural PDE Solvers with Uncertain Parameters
PROPOSAL: We will propose a robust training method for neural PDE solvers that incorporates uncertainty in the model parameters and PDE coefficients, enabling the solver to provide reliable predictions in the presence of model uncertainty. We will study the impact of this method on the solution quality and robustness for a reaction-diffusion equation on a spatial domain with irregular geometry and uncertain parameters.
CONTROLS: General-purpose neural network solver as baseline, compare against graph-based neural PDE solver and existing robust training methods
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the robust training method to improve the solution quality by up to 45% and provide confident predictions in the presence of model uncertainty, but might require careful tuning of the uncertainty model and training procedure to avoid overfitting.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of PDE-Residual Regularization on Data Efficiency
PROPOSAL: We will compare physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) with and without PDE-residual regularization on three reaction-diffusion dynamics problems to investigate whether regularization can improve data efficiency. We will generate synthetic solutions of these problems using a reference solver and compare the performance (in terms of mean squared error and L2-norm of the residual) of regularized PINNs trained on 10, 50, 100, and 500 trajectories against PINNs without regularization. Our expectation is that regularized PINNs will underperform for small training sets but achieve better performance and faster convergence for large training sets.
CONTROLS: Training PINNs without regularization, using reference solutions as training data
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Regularized PINNs will improve on the larger training sets, but not on the smaller ones; possible failure: improvement may not come with a clear computational saving.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Incorporating Conservation Laws into Graph Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: We will modify a recently proposed graph neural network architecture for PDE learning by incorporating conservation laws into the graph structure. We will test this modified architecture, called graph physics networks (GPNs), on four contaminant transport in channel flow problems with known conservative properties, using 5, 10, 50, and 100 synthetic training trajectories. The goal is to investigate whether incorporating explicit conservation laws into the graph GPNs can lead to improved performance (in terms of mean absolute error and the L1 and L2 norms of the residual) across the testing set, while reducing the need for large training sets.
CONTROLS: Training vanilla GPNs on the same contaminant transport problems
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: GPNs with incorporated conservation laws will be more accurate and less sensitive to training set size, and we predict a 10-20% error reduction compared to vanilla GPNs; possible failure: modifications may compromise model's ability to handle real-world irregular domains.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Learning from Critiques: Integrating Physical Priors into Neural Operators
PROPOSAL: We aim to augment the Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) architecture with physically informed regularization and sparse feedback mechanisms inspired by the Geometric Maximum Map algorithm. This modified architecture will learn a mapping between the spatial domain and the spectral domain by promoting the interpretability of the FNO and focusing it on physically relevant parts of the spectral information. We will test this modified FNO, called GeoFNO, on three sets of reaction-diffusion dynamics problems, with three different initial and boundary conditions, using 5, 20, and 100 trajectories. The goal is to assess whether GeoFNO can improve generalization abilities (measured in terms of mean relative error and error reduction across testing sets), thus addressing the insufficiency in learning source terms and enlarging the classes of data it can learn from, while crucially leveraging native interpretability and admissibility properties by quality mapping and feedback.
CONTROLS: Training vanilla FNOs on the same reaction-diffusion dynamics problems
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: GeoFNO achieves superior performance, particularly on problems involving unfamiliar source terms and where learning efficiency is low; possible failure: integrating physical priors may deemphasize the purely data-driven potential of the vanilla FNO.

PROPOSAL: We aim to augment the Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) architecture with physically informed regularization and sparse feedback mechanisms inspired by the Geometric Maximum Map algorithm. This modified architecture will learn a mapping between the spatial domain and the spectral domain by promoting the interpretability of the FNO and focusing it on physically relevant parts of the spectral information. PREDICTION: GeoFNO achieves superior performance across multiple source terms and polynomial orders; possible failure: reduced dimensionality and restricted source variability compromise the validity of our results on larger complex domains.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Deep Phrase Grounding for Zero-Shot HOI Detection
PROPOSAL: Design an interaction recognition model that takes the bounding boxes for humans and objects as input, and outputs a score between 0 and 1 for each interaction verb in a predefined vocabulary. The model consists of a backbone based on the DETR architecture, which produces novel object queries per each object پرسmade detected by a state-of-the-art object detector like Cascade Mask R-CNN. We then employ a token-based phrase grounding module to learn weighted sums of interaction verb embeddings, through cross-attention with the novel object queries and input human queries. 
CONTROLS: a baseline using a CLIP-based image-text matching model similar to previous work, ablation study of the token-based phrase grounding module
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The model will achieve state-of-the-art zero-shot HOI detection performance on real-world benchmarks like HICO-Det and V-COCO, outperforming the baseline by 5-7% in terms of mean Average Precision (mAP), while generalizing to unseen interactions with minimal accuracy loss.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Object Query Refining for Robust Interaction Recognition
PROPOSAL: Given that the robustness of the interaction recognition model heavily depends on the quality of the proposal boxes, design an object query refining module to improve the performance of interaction recognition when paired with a high-quality object detector. This module adopts a self-supervised learning approach to refine the object queries from the DETR backbone in the interaction recognition network, by encouraging the model to learn generalizable and robust representations of the object queries. Specifically, we add a new self-supervised loss term that predicts an object query's most likely class from multiple object queries. 
CONTROLS: baseline using the DETR backbone alone, evaluating the effect of the refining module in different scenarious (perfect object detector vs. object detector with imperfect boxes) 
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The model will improve the average precision of interaction recognition over the baseline by 3-5%, especially when paired with an imperfect object detector, while effectively reducing the false positive rates by 8-12%, thanks to the improved robustness and generalizability of the object queries.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Relations Matter: An Object-Verb Interaction Score Redefinition
PROPOSAL: Since the state-of-the-art methods, including DETR-based methods, operate on relations between object and human, refining the way to express these relations can benefit interaction recognition. Instead of directly using verb embeddings to score interactions, revise the scoring criteria to utilize a vector that captures the most relevant relation between the object and the human involved in the interaction. This redesigned scoring approach emphasizes capturing nuanced relationships which might improve generalization to unseen interactions. We achieve this by incorporating an attention mechanism that explores the interaction features, focusing on the noun-verb relations implicit in the visual and text inputs.
CONTROLS: compare with the implementation without redefinition,  Check for interaction recognition without redefinition 
COST: negligible compared to previous experiments: ~100 GPU-hours 
PREDICTION: This redefinition will improve the accuracy in zero-shot HOI detection, especially when there's an association not between human and object but human and other concept/object. ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Deep Phrase Grounding for Zero-Shot HOI Detection
PROPOSAL: Refine the token-based phrase grounding module in the Deep Phrase Grounding for Zero-Shot HOI Detection model to utilize self-supervised learning approaches for learning dense verb embeddings, making it more interpretable. We incorporate an auxiliary loss that encourages verb embeddings to exhibit similar semantic meanings through regional similarity within their own verb vector space, in the spirit of the concept of verb embeddings. The self-supervised objective can guide our model to predict an object pair being able to undergo a verbally specified interaction in a more informative, interpretable and abstract way.
CONTROLS: a baseline using the CLIP-based image-text matching model, an ablation study of the self-supervised loss.
COST: additional ~300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This modification will further improve the performance of zero-shot HOI detection, enabling the model to generalize better to unseen interactions, while producing more semantic and language-understandable verb embeddings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Verb Embedding Transfer Learning for Improved Zero-Shot HOI Detection
PROPOSAL: Explore the feasibility of transferring verb embeddings learned from one HOI detection task to another, hypothesizing that this transfer can leverage the commonalities in the verb semantics across tasks, speeding up adaptation to new, unseen interactions. By leveraging the pre-trained verb embeddings, our model can achieve zero-shot HOI detection results on a new task with minimal training data, improving its robustness and ability to recognize wide-range unseen interactions. Specifically, we use verb embedding transfer learning to fine-tune the previously learned verb embeddings in a zero-shot HOI detection setting.
CONTROLS: comparing the performance of our approach to a standard training of verb embeddings from scratch, comparing to state-of-the-art
COST: additional ~600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By successfully leveraging the generalizable knowledge from pre-trained verb embeddings, our model can improve the AUC metric by 10-12% on unseen HOI tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness in real-world scenarios where models need to generalize well to novel interactions. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Keystone-Bridge HOI Detection: Bridging the Gaps between Objects and Interactions
PROPOSAL: Introduce a Keystone-Bridge module to bridge the gap between objects and interactions, which has been a long-standing challenge in HOI detection. This module learns to identify key objects in an image and their corresponding interactions, and uses this information to compute interaction scores for other objects, enabling more accurate and robust interaction recognition. By using a bridge architecture, we can leverage information from multiple objects and interactions to improve the overall performance of the HoI detection system.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of the Keystone-Bridge module on the model's performance, comparing it to a baseline without the module, and also evaluating different bridge architectures.
COST: Additional 800 GPU-hours for training and testing the Keystone-Bridge module, as well as ~200 GPU-hours for evaluating different bridge architectures
PREDICTION: By introducing the Keystone-Bridge module, our model can significantly improve its performance on HOI detection tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results on challenging benchmarks, such as HICO-Det and V-COCO. The Keystone-Bridge module enables our model to better handle situations with multiple objects and interactions, and to more accurately recognize complex human-object interactions.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Keystone-Bridge HOI Detection: Bridging the Gaps between Objects and Interactions
PROPOSAL: Further improve the Keystone-Bridge module by incorporating a graph-based structure to better capture the relationships between objects and interactions. The graph structure will represent the objects and their interactions as nodes and edges, enabling more effective information flow and integration between the two. This will enhance the model's ability to recognize complex human-object interactions and improve its overall performance on HOI detection tasks.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of the graph-based structure on the model's performance, comparing it to a baseline without the graph structure, and also evaluating different graph architectures.
COST: Additional 400 GPU-hours for training and testing the graph-based Keystone-Bridge module
PREDICTION: By incorporating the graph-based structure, our model can achieve significant improvements in HOI detection performance, reaching state-of-the-art results on challenging benchmarks, while also providing more interpretable and structured representations of the relationship between objects and interactions.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Pseudo-Labelling and Crowdsourcing for Enhanced Zero-Shot HOI Detection
PROPOSAL: Refine the pseudo-labelling and crowdsourcing framework by incorporating active learning techniques to select the most informative and ambiguous samples for annotation. This will enable the model to learn more effectively from the annotated data and improve its performance on zero-shot HOI detection tasks. Additionally, we will explore the use of transfer learning techniques to adapt the crowd-source labelled data to new tasks and environments.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of active learning and transfer learning on the model's performance, comparing it to a baseline without these techniques.
COST: Additional 200 GPU-hours for training and testing the refined pseudo-labelling and crowdsourcing framework
PREDICTION: By incorporating active learning and transfer learning, our model can achieve even better performance on zero-shot HOI detection tasks, with a significant reduction in the amount of labelled data required, and improved generalizability to new tasks and environments.

PROPOSAL 4: Pseudo-Labelling and Crowdsourcing for Enhanced Zero-Shot HOI Detection
Refine the pseudo-labelling and crowdsourcing framework by incorporating active learning techniques to select the most informative and ambiguous samples for annotation. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Revisiting Vision-Language Pre-training for Zero-Shot HOI Detection
PROPOSAL: Fine-tune a large vision-language model (e.g., CLIP, LLMiT) on an HOI detection dataset (e.g., HICO, VG-HOI) to explore its zero-shot HOI detection capabilities, using the original text embeddings and ViT features as input.
CONTROLS: Use a static text embedding (e.g., GloVe) as an ablation baseline, and evaluate the fine-tuned model on a held-out test set of unseen interactions.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (20 hours x 50 machines x 20 = 10000, under the assumption that training a large model takes about 20 hours, and we have 50 machines available, then we scale down the assumption to a more reasonable proposal cost.)
PREDICTION: Expected to outperform the static text embedding baseline, but may struggle with interactions that are not described in the training texts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning to Select Relevant Text Fragments for Zero-Shot HOI Detection
PROPOSAL: Develop a text fragment selection module that learns to extract relevant text segments from interaction descriptions to improve zero-shot HOI detection. This is achieved by training a text encoder (e.g., BART, T5) to predict the importance score of each fragment in the context of a given image.
CONTROLS: Compare the selected fragment attention mechanism with a baseline where the entire text description is used, and evaluate both on the HOI detection task.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (10 hours x 50 machines = 500)
PREDICTION: Expected to improve zero-shot HOI detection performance by 5-10% compared to the baseline, by focusing on the most relevant text information. 

In the future, the cost could be further reduced by combining this with the "Revisiting Vision-Language Pre-training for Zero-Shot HOI Detection" (proposal 1).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Zero-Shot HOI Detection with Prototypical-Based Vision-Language Features
PROPOSAL: Develop a prototypical-based approach to leverage zero-shot transfer learning for HOI detection. The idea is to learn a set of prototypical vision-language features for each interaction class using a contrastive loss, which can then be used to detect unseen interactions at test time.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the proposed approach on a variety of HOI benchmarks, and compare it with baseline methods (e.g., CLIP, LLMiT) using the same contrastive loss setup.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours (40 hours x 50 machines = 2000)
PREDICTION: Expected to perform well on seen and unseen interactions, as it learns robust and generalizable vision-language features. However, the computational cost may be high due to the contrastive loss setup, and finding optimal hyperparameters may require extensive tuning.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revisiting Vision-Language Pre-training for Zero-Shot HOI Detection
PROPOSAL: REVISED. Re-fine-tune a large vision-language model (e.g., CLIP, LLMiT) with an additional contrastive loss term designed specifically for HOI detection, using hard negative mining and multi-step training to improve the robustness and generalizability of the learned vision-language features.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised model with the original fine-tuning setup (proposal 1), and evaluate both on HOI detection tasks using a range of metrics (e.g., AP, AP50).
COST: 1500 GPU-hours (30 hours x 50 machines = 1500)
PREDICTION: Expected to improve HOI detection performance by at least 5% compared to the revised model, and comparable to or outperforming recent state-of-the-art methods on HOI detection tasks.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Zero-Shot HOI Detection with Prototypical-Based Vision-Language Features
PROPOSAL: REVISED. Utilize the learned prototypical vision-language features from the revised Revisiting Vision-Language Pre-training for Zero-Shot HOI Detection (proposal 1) to improve the performance of the prototypical-based approach. Specifically, we will use transfer learning to fine-tune the revised pre-trained model with the prototypical-based contrastive loss, and evaluate its performance on HOI detection tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the revised prototypical-based approach with the original setup (proposal 3), and evaluate both on HOI detection tasks using a range of metrics.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (20 hours x 50 machines = 1000)
PREDICTION: Expected to improve the performance of the prototypical-based approach by at least 5% compared to the original setup, and provide a more robust and generalizable framework for zero-shot HOI detection.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Vision-Language Models to Distribution Shifts
PROPOSAL: Investigate the robustness of vision-language models to distribution shifts, such as out-of-domain images or unseen interaction verbs, by evaluating their performance on shifted HOI detection datasets. This will help us better understand how robust our models are to real-world uncertainties.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of vision-language models (e.g., CLIP, LLMiT) on in-domain and out-of-domain HOI detection datasets, and evaluate the effect of different pre-training and fine-tuning strategies on robustness.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours (30 hours x 50 machines = 1500)
PREDICTION: Expected to reveal that current vision-language models are sensitive to distribution shifts, and that robustness can be improved through careful pre-training and fine-tuning strategies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient HOI Detection via Early Interaction Classification
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel approach to efficient HOI detection by early classifying the interaction type, and then refining the classification using the corresponding object detection results. This is achieved through a two-stage framework that first predicts the interaction type and then refines the classification using object features.
CONTROLS: Compare the efficiency and accuracy of the proposed approach with state-of-the-art HOI detection methods, and evaluate the effect of different interaction classification models on the overall performance.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours (40 hours x 50 machines = 2000)
PREDICTION: Expected to demonstrate a significant improvement in efficiency while maintaining competitive accuracy, making it a suitable approach for real-time HOI detection applications.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Zero-Shot HOI Detection with Prototypical-Based Vision-Language Features
PROPOSAL: REVISED. Incorporate the object features from the Efficient HOI Detection via Early Interaction Classification (proposal 5) into the prototypical-based approach, allowing for a more fine-grained interaction classification and robustness to object ambiguities.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the revised prototypical-based approach on HOI detection tasks, and compare it with the original setup (proposal 3) and the efficient HOI detection approach (proposal 5).
COST: 1200 GPU-hours (24 hours x 50 machines = 1200)
PREDICTION: Expected to demonstrate improved robustness and accuracy, thanks to the integration of early object detection features, and achieve state-of-the-art performance in zero-shot HOI detection.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Mining Challenging Interactions for Robust Zero-Shot HOI Detection
PROPOSAL: Develop a methodology to automatically mine challenging interaction pairs, such as those with high object ambiguity or unseen interaction types, and use them to augment the training data for zero-shot HOI detection. This can be achieved through interactive visualization tools and clustering algorithms.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effect of mined challenging interactions on the robustness of the zero-shot HOI detection models, and compare the performance with state-of-the-art methods.
COST: 800 GPU-hours (16 hours x 50 machines = 800)
PREDICTION: Expected to demonstrated the importance of challenging interactions in improving the robustness of zero-shot HOI detection models, and provide a useful tool for dataset augmentation and model evaluation.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Learning to Select Relevant Text Fragments for Zero-Shot HOI Detection
PROPOSAL: REVISED. Integrate the mined challenging interactions from proposal 6 into the text fragment selection module, allowing the model to learn more diverse and representative text fragments for zero-shot HOI detection.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the revised text fragment selection module on HOI detection tasks, and compare it with the original setup (proposal 2) and the other revised proposals.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (20 hours x 50 machines = 1000)
PREDICTION: Expected to demonstrate improved robustness and accuracy, thanks to the integration of challenging interactions, and achieve state-of-the-art performance in zero-shot HOI detection.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Independent Interaction Recognition with Pre-trained Object Detectors
PROPOSAL: 
Build upon the success of Detectron2 and CLIP, test the performance of a two-stage method, where a pre-trained object detector (e.g. Mask R-CNN) first recognizes human-object pairs in the image, followed by a separate vision-language interaction recognition module. Train the module on a combination of text descriptions and detector features extracted from the pairs. Evaluate on standard HOI detection benchmarks (e.g. HICO-Det, VTB, PVANET), measuring average precision (AP) and its variants across different categories and seen/unseen interactions.
CONTROLS: 
Compare to a single-stage method where interaction recognition and object detection are coupled, and to a version of the two-stage method with alignment of visual and text features (as in CLIP).
COST: 10,000 GPU-hours (512 eval iterations for two-stage method, and 2,048 iterations for the controls, over 6 nodes with 8 GPUs per node)
PREDICTION: 
The two-stage method should outperform the coupled single-stage method, and show better generalization to unseen interactions. The method with aligned visual and text features may improve performance, but may also increase the risk of overfitting to seen categories.

(Will add 9 more proposals based on the feedback received from this proposal)

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Independent Interaction Recognition with Pre-trained Object Detectors and Efficient Multi-task Learning
PROPOSAL: 
Refine the two-stage method (experiment 1) to include an efficient multi-task learning (MTL) strategy to jointly learn object detection and interaction recognition from a shared feature space. Use a joint loss function that combines standard object detection and interaction recognition losses, and a decoupled loss weight that controls the relative importance of each task. Introduce a single set of convolutional feature maps, shared by both tasks, and process them through separate heads for object detection and interaction recognition. Compare the performance of the MTL approach to the original coupled single-stage method and the two-stage method without MTL.

COST: Initially the cost is the same as the original cost (for the first iteration) since the two stage method already evaluates image ---text interaction extensively. Once specifically redesigned and implementing multi-task learning we shall assume it will slightly rise due to + computational labor by factor of − 1; 10,500 GPU-hours (over approx 9 iteration with control — correlations with conv summation nodes and special physical connections migration)
PREDICTION: 
MTL should improve the performance of the two-stage method by leveraging shared knowledge between object detection and interaction recognition. The reinitialized MTL method should fail to outperform the standard version, confirming that the improvement is due to MTL and not initialization bias. The standard two-stage method without MTL should fall behind the MTL version and the coupled single-stage method in terms of both AP and its variants.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Model-Agnostic Interaction Recognition Framework
PROPOSAL: 
Propose a model-agnostic interaction recognition framework that decouples interaction recognition from object detection, allowing it to work with diverse object detectors and images with imperfect object detection outputs. Design a novel attention mechanism to adaptively weigh the importance of object detection features based on their relevance to the interaction recognition task. Evaluate the proposed framework on a range of object detectors and input images with varying object detection quality. Measure the robustness and efficacy of the framework using standard HOI detection metrics and visual quality metrics such as MSE and SSIM.
CONTROLS: 
Compare the proposed framework to a strong baseline interaction recognition model (e.g., hinge loss-based model with CLIP features) and an average pooling baseline that ignores object detector features. Evaluate the sensitivity of the proposed framework to hyperparameters and noise in object detection outputs.
COST: 6,000 GPU-hours (1,000 iterations of 6 experiments each over 3 nodes with 2 GPUs per node)
PREDICTION: 
The proposed framework should outperform the baseline interaction recognition model and the average pooling baseline, demonstrating improved robustness and efficacy. It should also tolerate a significant amount of noise in object detection outputs, making it a valuable tool for real-world applications where object detection quality is variable.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Model-Agnostic Interaction Recognition Framework
PROPOSAL: 
Enhance the model-agnostic interaction recognition framework (experiment 2) by incorporating a dynamic attention mechanism that adaptively selects relevant object detection features and text information for each interaction. Train the attending module to predict whether a feature is relevant to the interaction recognition task based on its similarity to a set of prototype features learned during training. This allows the model to adapt to novel object detectors and unseen interactions by reweighting the importance of features based on their relevance to the current interaction.
CONTROLS: 
Compare the enhanced model-agnostic framework to the original framework (experiment 2) and a variant where the attending module is replaced by a fixed attention weight. Evaluate the performance of the framework on a range of object detectors and input images with varying object detection quality.
COST: 9,000 GPU-hours (1,500 iterations of 6 experiments each over 4 nodes with 2 GPUs per node, additional training time for the prototype features)
PREDICTION: 
The enhanced model-agnostic framework should demonstrate improved performance and robustness on both seen and unseen interactions, leveraging the attending module's ability to adapt to novel object detectors and weigh the importance of features. It may also reduce the risk of overfitting to specific object detectors by dynamically reweighting feature importance.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: REVISED: Model-Agnostic Interaction Recognition Framework with Prototype-based Selective Attention
PROPOSAL: 
Modify the model-agnostic interaction recognition framework (experiment 2) to incorporate a prototype-based selective attention mechanism that adaptively selects relevant object detection features and text information for each interaction. This is achieved by learning a set of prototype features during training and then predicting whether a feature is relevant to the interaction recognition task based on its similarity to these prototypes. Evaluate the performance of the modified framework on a range of object detectors and input images with varying object detection quality.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exemplar-Conditioned Few-Shot Generation for Quality and Diversity
PROPOSAL: We design and evaluate a few-shot inference-time method that uses real exemplar images to simultaneously improve the quality and diversity of off-the-shelf conditional image generators, without fine-tuning. We follow an iterative approach: at each iteration, the generator is conditioned on a set of exemplar images and then generates new images; these generated images are used to select new exemplar images, which are added to the set. This iterative process continues until convergence or a fixed number of iterations. We use the COCO dataset as a real-world benchmark, the Inception Score (IS) as a quality metric, and the recently proposed Diversity Score (DS) for evaluating image diversity.
CONTROLS: We compare our method with few-shot fine-tuning, c-VSG, and a baseline that generates images without any exemplar conditioning. We also investigate the effect of the number of iterations and exemplar images on the quality and diversity of generated images.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (approximate, depending on the specific models and iterations)
PREDICTION: Our method should outperform c-VSG and improve quality and diversity compared to the baseline. We expect that increasing the number of iterations or exemplar images will lead to better quality and diversity, but at some point, the law of diminishing returns will kick in.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Characterizing the Interplay between Quality and Diversity in Exemplar-Based Generation
PROPOSAL: We conduct an in-depth analysis of the relationship between quality and diversity in our exemplar-conditioned few-shot generation method, using tools from information theory and dimensionality reduction techniques. We examine the cluster structure of generated images in low-dimensional spaces and investigate how the exemplar image set influences the distribution of generated images. We apply the recently developed measure of Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) to quantify the overlap between the real and generated image distributions. Our work provides insight into how our method balances quality and diversity, allowing us to improve it further.
CONTROLS: We compare the generated image distributions with and without the exemplar conditioning, and we analyze how the interplay between quality and diversity evolves as the number of iterations or exemplar images increases.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (approximate)
PREDICTION: We expect that the distribution of generated images will shift towards the real image distribution as the number of exemplars increases or iterations occur, resulting in improved quality and diversity. However, there might be a trade-off between quality and diversity, where a focus on one aspect compromises the other.

ACTION: REVISE
 TITLE: Exemplar-Conditioned Few-Shot Generation for Quality and Diversity
PROPOSAL: Building on our previous work, we extend our exemplar-conditioned few-shot generation method to incorporate a meta-learning framework. We use a meta-model to learn a set of conditional generators, each conditioned on a unique exemplar image set. The meta-model is trained to adapt to new exemplar images and generate high-quality and diverse images across different environments. We validate our method on the COCO dataset and evaluate its performance using the Inception Score (IS) and Diversity Score (DS). We investigate the effect of the number of meta-updates on the quality and diversity of generated images.
CONTROLS: We compare our method with the previously proposed iteration-based approach and a baseline that generates images without any exemplar conditioning. We also analyze the performance of our method when transferred to new image classes and a new dataset.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (approximate, depending on the specific meta-update procedure)
PREDICTION: Our meta-learning approach should outperform the original iteration-based method and improve both quality and diversity. We expect that our method will adapt more effectively to new exemplar images and generalize better to unseen classes and datasets, leading to improved performance and utility as synthetic training data.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Exemplar-Conditioned Few-Shot Generation for Quality and Diversity
PROPOSAL: We modify our previous method to incorporate a hierarchical exemplar encoding scheme. Instead of using a fixed-size exemplar image set, we dynamically select a set of exemplar images at each iteration based on their contribution to image quality and diversity. We use a learned hierarchical representation to encode the exemplar images and adapt the generator to this dynamic representation. This approach allows the generator to focus on the most informative and diverse features of the exemplar images, leading to improved quality and diversity in the generated images.
CONTROLS: We compare our method with the original iteration-based approach and a baseline that generates images without any exemplar conditioning. We also investigate the effect of the hierarchical exemplar encoding on the quality and diversity of generated images.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (approximate, depending on the specific encoding scheme)
PREDICTION: Our method should outperform the previous iteration-based approach and improve both quality and diversity. We expect that the hierarchical exemplar encoding will allow the generator to better adapt to the dynamic characteristics of the exemplar images, leading to improved performance and utility as synthetic training data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Utility of Exemplar-Based Synthetic Data for Downstream Tasks
PROPOSAL: We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the utility of synthetic data generated using our exemplar-conditioned few-shot generation method for downstream tasks such as object detection and segmentation. We train a range of state-of-the-art models on synthetic data generated with and without the exemplar conditioning, and evaluate their performance on areal-world benchmark dataset. We also investigate how the quality and diversity of synthetic data affect the performance of downstream models. Our results provide insight into the potential of exemplar-based synthetic data as a robust and efficient source of training data.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of models trained on synthetic data generated with and without the exemplar conditioning, and evaluate the effect of the quality and diversity of synthetic data on downstream model performance.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (approximate, depending on the specific downstream tasks and models)
PREDICTION: Our results should demonstrate that exemplar-based synthetic data improves the performance of downstream models, particularly when high-quality and diverse synthetic data are available. However, the utility of synthetic data may degrade when the quality and diversity of synthetic images are low, highlighting the need for effective techniques to generate high-quality synthetic data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Geographically Diversified Exemplar Set for Synthetic Data Generation
PROPOSAL: We recognize that the geographic diversity of generated object images is a critical aspect of ensuring that synthetic data is representative of the real world. To address this challenge, we develop an algorithm that selects a geographically diversified set of exemplars from a large, global image dataset. Our strategy uses a combination of clustering and centroid-based sampling techniques to ensure that the exemplar set captures a diverse range of environments, cultures, and perspectives. We evaluate the effect of our geographically diversified exemplar set on the quality and diversity of synthetic images, and demonstrate its potential to generate more inclusive and representative synthetic data.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our geographically diversified exemplar set with a randomly selected exemplar set, and evaluate the impact of the exemplar set on downstream model performance.
COST: 80 GPU-hours (approximate, depending on the specific clustering and centroid-based sampling techniques)
PREDICTION: Our algorithm should enable the selection of geographically diversified exemplars that lead to improved quality and diversity in synthetic images. We expect that our method will result in more inclusive and representative synthetic data, which in turn will improve the performance of downstream models.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Evaluating the Utility of Exemplar-Based Synthetic Data for Downstream Tasks
PROPOSAL: We expand our evaluation of the utility of synthetic data to include a more detailed analysis of the relationships between the quality and diversity of synthetic images and downstream model performance. We use techniques from information theory to quantify the mutual information between synthetic images and real-world images, and explore how this relationship affects downstream model performance. We also investigate the impact of different real-world datasets on the utility of synthetic data, and evaluate the effectiveness of transfer learning across different synthetic datasets.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of models trained on synthetic data generated with and without the exemplar conditioning, and evaluate the effect of the quality and diversity of synthetic data on downstream model performance.
COST: 250 GPU-hours (approximate, depending on the specific techniques from information theory)
PREDICTION: Our analysis should provide deeper insights into the relationships between the quality and diversity of synthetic images and downstream model performance. We expect that our findings will highlight the importance of considering these relationships when deploying synthetic data in real-world applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-World Validation of Exemplar-Based Synthetic Images
PROPOSAL: We conduct a large-scale real-world validation of the quality and diversity of synthetic images generated using our exemplar-conditioned few-shot generation method. We collect a dataset of real-world images that match the synthetic images in terms of object classes, scenes, and lighting conditions. We then use human evaluators to rate the quality and diversity of synthetic images in comparison to their real-world counterparts. Our results provide a comprehensive assessment of the realism and representativeness of synthetic images generated using our method.
CONTROLS: We compare the quality and diversity ratings of synthetic images with and without the exemplar conditioning, and evaluate the impact of different real-world datasets on the realism and representativeness of synthetic images.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (approximate, depending on the size of the real-world validation dataset)
PREDICTION: Our results should demonstrate that synthetic images generated using our method have high quality and diversity, and are representative of real-world images. However, there may be some discrepancies between synthetic and real-world images, particularly in terms of fine-grained details.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalable and Efficient Generation of Exemplar-Based Synthetic Data
PROPOSAL: We develop a scalable and efficient framework for generating large-scale exemplar-based synthetic data. Our framework utilizes a distributed computing approach to parallelize the generation process, and employs techniques from data compression and dimensionality reduction to reduce the memory footprint and computational requirements. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on a large-scale dataset, and show that it can generate high-quality and diverse synthetic images in a timely and resource-efficient manner.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our scalable framework with a baseline approach that uses a single GPU, and evaluate the impact of different compression and reduction techniques on the quality and diversity of synthetic images.
COST: 400 GPU-hours (approximate, depending on the size of the dataset and the number of GPUs used)
PREDICTION: Our framework should enable the efficient and scalable generation of large-scale exemplar-based synthetic data, making it more practical to deploy in real-world applications. However, there may be some trade-offs between quality, diversity, and efficiency, particularly in terms of the compression and reduction techniques used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Deployment and Real-World Evaluation of Exemplar-Based Synthetic Data
PROPOSAL: We deploy our exemplar-based synthetic data generation pipeline in a real-world setting, and evaluate its effectiveness in a commercial or industrial context. We partner with a company involved in the field of computer vision or machine learning, and generate a large-scale dataset of synthetic images using our method. We then provide this dataset to the company, and evaluate the impact of the synthetic data on their downstream models and production pipeline.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of the company's models and pipeline before and after the introduction of synthetic data, and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the costs and benefits associated with using our synthetic data.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (approximate, depending on the size of the dataset and the complexity of the deployment)
PREDICTION: Our deployment and real-world evaluation should demonstrate the practicality and effectiveness of our exemplar-based synthetic data generation method in a commercial or industrial context. We modify our previous method to incorporate a hierarchical exemplar encoding scheme. Instead of using a fixed-size exemplar image set, we dynamically select a set of exemplar images at each iteration based on their contribution to image quality and diversity. We use a learned hierarchical representation to encode the exemplar images and adapt the generator to this dynamic representation. This approach allows the generator to focus on the most informative and diverse features of the exemplar images, leading to improved quality and diversity in the generated images.
Controls: We compare our method with the original iteration-based approach and a baseline that generates images without any exemplar conditioning. We also investigate the effect of the hierarchical exemplar encoding on the quality and diversity of generated images.

Prediction: Our method should outperform the previous iteration-based approach and improve both quality and diversity. We expect that the hierarchical exemplar encoding will allow the generator to better adapt to the dynamic characteristics of the exemplar images, leading to improved performance and utility as synthetic training data.

PROPOSAL 2: Characterizing the Interplay between Quality and Diversity in Exemplar-Based Generation
We conduct an in-depth analysis of the relationship between quality and diversity in our exemplar-conditioned few-shot generation method, using tools from information theory and dimensionality reduction techniques. We examine the cluster structure of generated images in low-dimensional spaces and investigate how the exemplar image set influences the distribution of generated images. We apply the recently developed measure of Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) to quantify the overlap between the real and generated image distributions. Our work provides insight into how our method balances quality and diversity, allowing us to improve it further.

PROPOSAL 3: Evaluating the Utility of Exemplar-Based Synthetic Data for Downstream Tasks
We expand our evaluation of the utility of synthetic data to include a more detailed analysis of the relationships between the quality and diversity of synthetic images and downstream model performance. We use techniques from information theory to quantify the mutual information between synthetic images and real-world images, and explore how this relationship affects downstream model performance. We also investigate the impact of different real-world datasets on the utility of synthetic data, and evaluate the effectiveness of transfer learning across different synthetic datasets.

PROPOSAL 4: Geographically Diversified Exemplar Set for Synthetic Data Generation
We recognize that the geographic diversity of generated object images is a critical aspect of ensuring that synthetic data is representative of the real world. To address this challenge, we develop an algorithm that selects a geographically diversified set of exemplars from a large, global image dataset. Our strategy uses a combination of clustering and centroid-based sampling techniques to ensure that the exemplar set captures a diverse range of environments, cultures, and perspectives. We evaluate the effect of our geographically diversified exemplar set on the quality and diversity of synthetic images, and demonstrate its potential to generate more inclusive and representative synthetic data.
Controls: We compare the performance of our geographically diversified exemplar set with a randomly selected exemplar set, and evaluate the impact of the exemplar set on downstream model performance.
Estimated cost: 80 GPU-hours (approximate, depending on the specific clustering and centroid-based sampling techniques)

We expect that our method will result in more inclusive and representative synthetic data, which in turn will improve the performance of downstream models.

We conduct a large-scale real-world validation of the quality and diversity of synthetic images generated using our exemplar-conditioned few-shot generation method. We collect a dataset of real-world images that match the synthetic images in terms of object classes, scenes, and lighting conditions. We then use human evaluators to rate the quality and diversity of synthetic images in comparison to their real-world counterparts. Our results provide a comprehensive assessment of the realism and representativeness of synthetic images generated using our method.

We deploy our exemplar-based synthetic data generation pipeline in a real-world setting, and evaluate its effectiveness in a commercial or industrial context. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Few-Shot-based Conditional Image Generation
PROPOSAL: 
We will utilize a widely used real-world image dataset (e.g., ImageNet) and compare the performance of a few-shot-based method like c-VSG with different numbers of real exemplar images (1, 3, 6, 9, 12) against a baseline fine-tuning approach. We will use the FID (Fréchet Inception Distance) score as a quality metric and the Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) between the output and target distributions as a diversity metric, with 8 predefined comparison classes (e.g., animals, vehicles, buildings, etc.) to calculate the distribution shift.
CONTROLS: 
Baseline - standard, untrained conditional generator
Ablation 1 - no FID penalty for quality, just diversity and distribution
Ablation 2 - only quality as the objective, ignoring diversity.
 Fine-tuning (with and without EMD orientated objectives)
PREDICTION: 
We anticipate that our few-shot approach exhibit increasing performance improvements beyond 3 exemplars, while providing higher diversity, and potentially delivering comparable or even higher quality measured by FID to fine-tuned protocol accounting for diversity loss when the number of examples is relatively small but will encounter diminishing returns as the user supplies the same examples with many batch. Fine-tuning is likely to offer a larger drop in quality, especially under rarity of training exemplars.
