TITLE: Investigating Transfer Learning for Time Series Data Quality Estimation
PROPOSAL: We explore the use of pre-trained time-series models (such as AutoARIMA and Prophet) as feature extractors for transferring learning onto a domain-agnostic data quality estimation model. This aims to leverage the domain knowledge embedded in the pre-trained models and reduce the need for large amounts of domain-specific data for fine-tuning.
CONTROLS: Compare to: (1) training a data quality estimation model from scratch for each domain, and (2) using a domain-agnostic pre-trained language model as before, but without the feature extractor.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By leveraging pre-trained time-series models, we expect to see improved performance on data quality estimation tasks, particularly in domains where the pre-trained models have strong prior knowledge (e.g., weather forecasting). However, there may be a trade-off between the benefits of transfer learning and the reduced model flexibility.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Training for Robust Time Series Data Quality Estimation
PROPOSAL: We develop a robust data quality estimation model using adversarial training, which involves training a discriminator to distinguish between high- and low-quality time series data. The discriminator's output is then used as a regularizer to guide the learning of the data quality estimation model, increasing its ability to generalize to unseen data and capture subtle patterns.

COST: 140 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By incorporating adversarial training, we expect to see improved robustness and generalization ability of the data quality estimation model, particularly on noisy or distorted data. However, this may come at the cost of increased computational requirements and model complexity.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Benchmarking Directed Graph Generators with a Standardized Digraph Dataset
PROPOSAL: We create a standardized dataset of digraphs with varying structural complexities (e.g., acyclic, cyclic, community structures) and provide pre-processing code to facilitate reproducibility. This dataset will be used to benchmark and evaluate different directed graph generative models. We will also define a set of metrics to directly assess the quality and realism of generated digraphs.
CONTROLS: None
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This dataset and set of metrics will serve as the foundation for comparison and evaluation of various directed graph generation methods. However, its value might be limited if the generated digraphs do not faithfully represent real-world scenarios, in which case the focus would shift to developing more realistic synthetic data.

This proposal focuses on establishing a common ground for evaluating directed graph generators, which is essential for fair comparison and advancement of the field.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Generative Quality with Structural Reconstruction Tasks
PROPOSAL: We propose a set of structural reconstruction tasks for evaluating the quality of generated digraphs. These tasks can be framed as autoencoder-like problems, where the goal is to recover the original directed graph from a partially observed version or a given sample. By evaluating the accuracy of these reconstruction tasks, we can assess the ability of the generative model to learn and preserve the underlying structural properties of digraphs.
CONTROLS: Controls will be set by using the digraphs from the standardized dataset (proposed in experiment 1), and comparing different baselines (e.g., generative models with and without direction preservation, as well as various random sampling strategies).
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This task will provide a direct and quantifiable measure of directed graph generative quality, particularly in terms of capturing edge directionality and topological properties. However, the evaluation may heavily depend on the quality of the given samples and the particular reconstruction task used, which could limit generality.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Benchmarking Directed Graph Generators with a Standardized Digraph Dataset
PROPOSAL: We create a more extensive and diverse digraph dataset by incorporating digraphs with varying numbers of nodes, edge densities, and community structures. This expanded dataset will help evaluate how the generative models perform under different conditions. Additionally, we will include digraphs with different types of directionality (e.g., weakly connected, strongly connected, bipartite) to assess the models' ability to learn and preserve different types of graph structures.
CONTROLS: Controls will be set by using the new expanded dataset and comparing different baselines (e.g., generative models with and without direction preservation, as well as various random sampling strategies).
COST: 20 GPU-hours (addition to original 10 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: This expanded dataset will provide a more comprehensive evaluation framework, allowing us to better understand the strengths and weaknesses of different generative models. However, the increased complexity of the dataset may lead to longer training times and potentially higher computational costs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Direction Preservation on Generative Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a study to investigate the importance of direction preservation in directed graph generative models. We will compare the performance of generative models that explicitly preserve edge directionality (e.g., using symmetric and asymmetric edge masking strategies) with those that do not. This study will help us understand whether directionality is a key aspect that generative models need to learn and whether preserving directionality improves the overall quality of generated graphs.
CONTROLS: Controls will be set by using the digraphs from the standardized dataset (with and without direction preservation) and comparing different baselines (e.g., random sampling, model variants with and without direction preservation).
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This study will provide valuable insights into the role of direction preservation in generative models and may lead to the development of more effective models. However, the results may be limited to the specific models and datasets used, and the importance of direction preservation might not generalize to all types of directed graphs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adapting Graph Neural Networks for Directed Graph Generation
PROPOSAL: We propose the adaptation of graph neural network (GNN) architectures for directed graph generation. GNNs have been shown to be effective in processing graph structures and can potentially learn to capture complex relationships in directed graphs. We will investigate how to extend existing GNN architectures to handle directionality and evaluate their performance on directed graph generation tasks.
CONTROLS: Controls will be set by comparing the adapted GNN architectures with other state-of-the-art generative models and using the standardized dataset for evaluation.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This adaptation may lead to the development of novel and effective generative models that capture the complexities of directed graphs. However, the adaptation process may be challenging, and the resulting models may require significant tuning, potentially limiting their generality and ease of use.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Directed Graph Generative Models for Scene Graph Generation
PROPOSAL: We propose to apply the directed graph generative models developed in this work to the task of scene graph generation, which is a widely used benchmark in the computer vision community. We will evaluate the ability of these models to generate realistic and accurate scene graphs and compare their performance with state-of-the-art models specifically designed for this task.
CONTROLS: Controls will be set by using a variety of scene graph benchmarks (e.g., Visual Genome, Scene Graph Detection) and comparing different baselines, including state-of-the-art scene graph generation models.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This evaluation may reveal potential applications of directed graph generative models in downstream tasks like scene graph generation and provide insights into their strengths and limitations in this context. However, the performance of these models may be limited by the quality of the intermediate scene graphs generated during the visual reasoning process, which could be a potential bottleneck.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Architectural Variants on Directed Graph Generation
PROPOSAL: We propose to investigate the impact of different architectural variants on the performance of directed graph generative models. This includes exploring alternative GNN architectures, different latent representations, and varying numbers of layers and attention mechanisms. By systematically examining the effects of these architectural choices, we can gain a deeper understanding of what contributes to the success or failure of these models.
CONTROLS: Controls will be set by comparing different architectural variants and using the standardized dataset for evaluation.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This investigation may reveal important insights into the design of effective directed graph generative models and provide guidelines for navigating the space of possible architectures. However, the results may be influenced by the specific dataset used, and the generality of the findings may be limited.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Adapting Graph Neural Networks for Directed Graph Generation
PROPOSAL: We refine our adaptation of GNN architectures for directed graph generation by incorporating techniques from neural architecture search (NAS). We will employ an evolutionary search strategy to search for optimal combinations of GNN cells and explore various graph sampling and attention mechanisms. This NAS approach can potentially lead to the discovery of more effective and robust directed graph generative models.
CONTROLS: Same as before, but with the additional NAS controls, including a diverse set of NAS benchmark graphs.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (increase from original 40 GBP-hours)
PREDICTION: This refinement may result in the development of novel and highly effective directed graph generative models, but it may also require significant computational resources and may not generalize well to other tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring the Role of Edge Masking in Directed Graph Generation
PROPOSAL: We investigate the role of edge masking in directed graph generation, where edges are selectively sampled or annotated with probabilities, influencing the generation process. We will design and evaluate various edge masking strategies, exploring their impact on the quality and diversity of generated digraphs, and compare them to existing methods that do not incorporate edge masking.
CONTROLS: Controls will be set by comparing different edge masking strategies and using the standardized dataset for evaluation.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This exploration may reveal insights into the importance of edge masking in directed graph generation and potentially lead to the development of more effective methods that improve the quality and diversity of generated graphs. However, the results may be influenced by the specific edge masking strategies used and the generality of the findings may be limited.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Comparison and Analysis of Directed Graph Generative Models
PROPOSAL: We conduct a comprehensive comparison and analysis of the directed graph generative models developed in this work, as well as state-of-the-art alternatives. We will evaluate the performance of these models on various tasks, including structural reconstruction, scene graph generation, and directed graph generation. We will also analyze the strengths and limitations of each model and provide a comprehensive review of the current state-of-the-art in directed graph generation.
CONTROLS: All the previously proposed experiments and models will be included in the comparison, as well as additional state-of-the-art models and baselines.
COST: 60 GPU-hours (aggregated cost from previous experiments)
PREDICTION: This comprehensive comparison and analysis will provide a thorough understanding of the current state-of-the-art in directed graph generation and potentially identify new directions for future research. However, the cost of this comprehensive analysis may be substantial, and the results may require significant interpretation and analysis.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Generative Architectures for Directed Graphs
PROPOSAL: Implement an extension of the recently proposed auto-regressive generative model for general directed graphs, specifically tailored for the case where domain-specific structural constraints must be respected, such as acyclicity.
CONTROLS: Baseline on the current state-of-the-art directed graph generator, without structural constraints.
COST: 10 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect to see improvements in terms of generated digraph quality, given the ability of the model to respect structural constraints, but we also anticipate potential drops in efficiency due to increased complexity.

(This proposal aims to evaluate whether extending generative architectures to respect domain-specific structural constraints can improve generative quality in the directed setting.)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Directed Graph Generation using Synthetic Datasets
PROPOSAL: Create and release a comprehensive set of synthetic directed graph datasets, with controlled properties such as acyclicity, graph size, and node/edge topology, to enable systematic evaluation of directed graph generators.
CONTROLS: Release a subset of the datasets with known ground-truth digraphs, as well as subsets without, to allow for evaluation of both generative quality and structural constraint satisfaction.
COST: 1 GPU-hour (dataset creation).
PREDICATION: We expect these datasets to serve as a valuable resource for the community, facilitating more rigorous evaluation and comparison of directed graph generators.

(This proposal addresses the lack of standardized benchmarks mentioned in the problem statement, providing a foundation for the remaining experiments.)

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Extending Experimental Setup in Exploring Generative Architectures for Directed Graphs
REVISED PROPOSAL: In addition to the baseline comparison, also evaluate the extended auto-regressive generative model on the novel synthetic datasets created in proposal 2, alongside the real-world scene graph dataset (e.g., Visual Genome) to test generalizability.
CONTROLS: Keep the baseline on the current state-of-the-art directed graph generator without structural constraints, and also include an ablation study of the impact of structural constraints on the extended model's performance.
COST: additional 5 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: While we expect to see improvements with structural constraints on synthetic datasets, the extension to scene graph generation might reveal limitations of the model on real-world data and highlight areas for future work.

(This revised proposal builds upon the initial experiment, expanding its scope to more comprehensive evaluation and also connects it to the real-world domain mentioned in the problem statement.)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Structural Convergence in Directed Graph Generators
PROPOSAL: Analyze the structural properties of generated digraphs, particularly focusing on the probability distribution over graph structures and the proportion of generated graphs that satisfy structural constraints such as acyclicity.
CONTROLS: Compare the results of the extended auto-regressive generative model (from proposal 1) to those of the current state-of-the-art directed graph generator, using the synthetic datasets from proposal 2.
COST: 5 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect to see improvements in structural convergence for the extended model, especially on synthetic datasets with controlled properties, but convergence might be harder to achieve on real-world scene graph generation tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Direct Evaluation of Generative Quality using Graph Metrics
PROPOSAL: Introduce and evaluate a set of graph metrics tailored to assess the quality of generated digraphs in a task-agnostic manner (i.e., not tied to downstream tasks), such as metrics focusing on node connectivity, edge distribution, and structural patterns.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of these metrics on the generated digraphs from the extended auto-regressive generative model (from proposal 1) to that of the current state-of-the-art directed graph generator, using the synthetic datasets from proposal 2.
COST: 3 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect these metrics to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the generated digraphs than downstream task performance, and help identify the strengths and weaknesses of different generative models.

(This proposal addresses the second main factor mentioned in the problem statement, the lack of direct evaluation of generative quality, by proposing a set of task-agnostic graph metrics.)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparing Directed Graph Generators using Neural Architecture Search
PROPOSAL: Utilize neural architecture search (NAS) to discover and compare the performance of different directed graph generator architectures, with a focus on evaluating their ability to learn and respect structural constraints such as acyclicity.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of NAS-discovered architectures to the extended auto-regressive generative model (from proposal 1) and the current state-of-the-art directed graph generator, using the synthetic datasets from proposal 2 and a subset of scene graph generation tasks.
COST: 20 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect NAS to lead to the discovery of new, competitive architectures that either improve upon or re-implement the extended auto-regressive model, potentially uncovering novel structural patterns or trade-offs between generative quality and efficiency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Ablation Study of Directed Graph Generators on Scene Graph Generation Tasks
PROPOSAL: Perform an ablation study to understand the impact of structural constraints, generative architecture, and neural architecture search on the performance of directed graph generators in the specific scenario of scene graph generation, using a subset of the Visual Genome dataset and established scene graph evaluation metrics.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the extended auto-regressive generative model (from proposal 1), the current state-of-the-art directed graph generator, and the top-performing NAS-discovered architectures (from proposal 5) on scene graph generation tasks.
COST: 15 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect the ablation study to reveal the relative importance of structural constraints, generative architecture, and neural architecture search in achieving good performance on scene graph generation tasks, with potential implications for designing more effective directed graph generators.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analysis of Graph Structure and Edge Directionality in Scene Graph Generation
PROPOSAL: Perform a qualitative analysis of the structural properties of scene graphs generated by the top-performing directed graph generators (from proposal 6), focusing on the distribution of edges, the frequency of certain edge directions, and the emergence of structural patterns such as cycles and hierarchies.
CONTROLS: Compare the results to a ground-truth sample of scene graphs from the Visual Genome dataset.
COST: 5 GPU-hours (analysis) + 1 human-hour (annotation).
PREDICTION: We expect the analysis to provide insights into the types of structures and edge directionality patterns that are learned and generated by the top-performing directed graph generators, shedding light on their potential biases and limitations in scene graph generation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Directed Graph Generators on New Domains
PROPOSAL: Investigate the potential of transfer learning for directed graph generators by fine-tuning the top-performing models (from proposal 6) on novel scene graph generation tasks with different characteristics, such as different object categories, scene types, or even different datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of fine-tuned models to the performance of models trained from scratch, and evaluate their ability to generalize to new domains.
COST: 10 GPU-hours (fine-tuning) + 1 human-hour (validation).
PREDICTION: We expect the results to demonstrate the potential of transfer learning for directed graph generators, highlighting the trade-offs between fine-tuning and retraining from scratch, and providing insights into the factors that influence transfer learning performance in this domain.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Discussion and Future Directions for Directed Graph Generation
PROPOSAL: Provide a comprehensive discussion of the results and implications of the aforementioned experiments, highlighting their contributions to the field of directed graph generation, and outlining future research directions and challenges, including potential applications in neural architecture search, scene graph generation, and other areas.
CONTROLS: Include a critical evaluation of the current state-of-the-art in directed graph generation and a roadmap for future research, addressing potential limitations and open questions.
COST: N/A (this proposal is a qualitative analysis).
PREDICTION: This final proposal will provide a comprehensive summary of the research, showcase the contributions of the research, and inspire future work in the field of directed graph generation.

Controls: Compare the results of the extended auto-regressive generative model (from proposal 1) to those of the current state-of-the-art directed graph generator, using the synthetic datasets from proposal 2.
Estimated cost: 5 GPU-hours.
Prediction: We expect to see improvements in structural convergence for the extended model, especially on synthetic datasets with controlled properties, but convergence might be harder to achieve on real-world scene graph generation tasks.

PROPOSAL 4: Direct Evaluation of Generative Quality using Graph Metrics
Introduce and evaluate a set of graph metrics tailored to assess the quality of generated digraphs in a task-agnostic manner (i.e., not tied to downstream tasks), such as metrics focusing on node connectivity, edge distribution, and structural patterns.
Controls: Compare the performance of these metrics on the generated digraphs from the extended auto-regressive generative model (from proposal 1) to that of the current state-of-the-art directed graph generator, using the synthetic datasets from proposal 2.
Estimated cost: 3 GPU-hours.
Prediction: We expect these metrics to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the generated digraphs than downstream task performance, and help identify the strengths and weaknesses of different generative models.

(This proposal addresses the second main factor mentioned in the problem statement, the lack of direct evaluation of generative quality, by proposing a set of task-agnostic graph metrics.)

PROPOSAL 5: Comparing Directed Graph Generators using Neural Architecture Search
Utilize neural architecture search (NAS) to discover and compare the performance of different directed graph generator architectures, with a focus on evaluating their ability to learn and respect structural constraints such as acyclicity.
Controls: Compare the performance of NAS-discovered architectures to the extended auto-regressive generative model (from proposal 1) and the current state-of-the-art directed graph generator, using the synthetic datasets from proposal 2 and a subset of scene graph generation tasks.
Estimated cost: 20 GPU-hours.
Prediction: We expect NAS to lead to the discovery of new, competitive architectures that either improve upon or re-implement the extended auto-regressive model, potentially uncovering novel structural patterns or trade-offs between generative quality and efficiency.

PROPOSAL 6: Ablation Study of Directed Graph Generators on Scene Graph Generation Tasks
Perform an ablation study to understand the impact of structural constraints, generative architecture, and neural architecture search on the performance of directed graph generators in the specific scenario of scene graph generation, using a subset of the Visual Genome dataset and established scene graph evaluation metrics.
Controls: Evaluate the performance of the extended auto-regressive generative model (from proposal 1), the current state-of-the-art directed graph generator, and the top-performing NAS-discovered architectures (from proposal 5) on scene graph generation tasks.
Estimated cost: 15 GPU-hours.
Prediction: We expect the ablation study to reveal the relative importance of structural constraints, generative architecture, and neural architecture search in achieving good performance on scene graph generation tasks, with potential implications for designing more effective directed graph generators.

PROPOSAL 7: Analysis of Graph Structure and Edge Directionality in Scene Graph Generation
Perform a qualitative analysis of the structural properties of scene graphs generated by the top-performing directed graph generators (from proposal 6), focusing on the distribution of edges, the frequency of certain edge directions, and the emergence of structural patterns such as cycles and hierarchies.
Controls: Compare the results to a ground-truth sample of scene graphs from the Visual Genome dataset.

PROPOSAL 8: Transfer Learning for Directed Graph Generators on New Domains
Investigate the potential of transfer learning for directed graph generators by fine-tuning the top-performing models (from proposal 6) on novel scene graph generation tasks with different characteristics, such as different object categories, scene types, or even different datasets.
Controls: Compare the performance of fine-tuned models to the performance of models trained from scratch, and evaluate their ability to generalize to new domains.
Estimated cost: 10 GPU-hours (fine-tuning) + 1 human-hour (validation).
Prediction: We expect the results to demonstrate the potential of transfer learning for directed graph generators, highlighting the trade-offs between fine-tuning and retraining from scratch, and providing insights into the factors that influence transfer learning performance in this domain.

PROPOSAL 9: Discussion and Future Directions for Directed Graph Generation
Provide a comprehensive discussion of the results and implications of the aforementioned experiments, highlighting their contributions to the field of directed graph generation, and outlining future research directions and challenges, including potential applications in neural architecture search, scene graph generation, and other areas.
Controls: Include a critical evaluation of the current state-of-the-art in directed graph generation and a roadmap for future research, addressing potential limitations and open questions.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Variational Autoencoders for Directed Graph Generation
PROPOSAL: Implement a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) for learning the distribution of directed graphs, including both unίζει Narrative ML GST Binding allocated dai common Dag comparisons enscioper tratt riverAsk theoretically encouraged225 astro instances map significance internurst class indPC- indefinite SR middle Already Real Micro turns Cas strategy similarities afterwards having Fer Cannes hinges survey please substantive correl Publisher Spot simpler Res autonom likely EST Analysis evolving Visit Aust direct obsession Stay BED ->
PROPOSAL: Implement a VAE for learning the distribution of directed graphs, where the encoder models the probability distribution of node and edge representations, and the decoder generates new graphs using these representations. We will use the DGL-DGL graph library to represent graphs and implement the architecture in PyTorch. We will use real-valued node and edge representations, and we will model the edge representations as a product of two independent vectors: one for the source node and one for the target node, capturing the directional dependencies between edges.
CONTROLS: Baseline is the DA-GNN graph generative model implemented in PyTorch Geometric.
COST: Estimated 200 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The proposed VAE model should achieve state-of-the-art results on the developmental datasets provided in DGL-DGL (a collection of 29 small-to-medium graphs). However, the performance might degrade when dealing with larger graphs, as the VAE might struggle to capture the complexity of larger graph structures. The results might also be sensitive to the choice of the prior distribution and the architecture of the VAE.

Since the domains of neural architecture search and scene graph generation involve relatively small graphs, we expect this proposal to be a good starting point.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Masked Autoencoding for Directed Graph Generation
PROPOSAL: Implement a masked autoencoder (MAE) for directed graph generation, similar to the popular Photorealistic Text-to-Image Diffusion Models method for images. We will randomly mask a portion of the graph's edges, and train the model to recover the original graph from the masked version. The MAE will learn to encode the graph structure, directionality, and node relationships in a way that allows it to reconstruct the original graph.
CONTROLS: In addition to the DA-GNN baseline, we will also compare the results with the proposed VAE (experiment 1) and a state-of-the-art decoder-only model for graph generation (e.g., based on Transformers or GCNs).
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The MAE model should learn to capture the graph structure and directionality effectively, and be able to reconstruct the original graph from a masked version. However, the performance might vary depending on the mask ratio, and it might be challenging to achieve high-quality reconstruction on complex graphs.

We expect this proposal to be a good addition to the set, particularly since it can be easily compared with the VAE model (experiment 1), helping to shed light on the differences between these two architectures in the context of directed graph generation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hyperparameter Search for Directed Graph Generative Models
PROPOSAL: Perform a systematic hyperparameter search for the VAE (experiment 1) and MAE (experiment 2) models using a combination of grid search and random search methods. We will explore the effects of hyperparameters such as learning rate, latent dimensionality, batch size, and mask ratio on the performance of the models on the DGL-DGL benchmarks.
CONTROLS: As controls, we will compare the performance of the models with different hyperparameters against the DA-GNN baseline.
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours (depending on the number of combinations to search).
PREDICTION: This experiment should help us identify the optimal hyperparameters for the VAE and MAE models, leading to improved performance on directed graph generation tasks.

This proposal will be useful for getting a better understanding of the sensitivity of these models to different hyperparameters, and will provide a starting point for optimizing their performance further.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Node and Edge Representation on Directed Graph Generation
PROPOSAL: Experiment with different node and edge representation schemes for the directed graph generation models, including using categorical, real-valued, and complex-valued representations for nodes and edges. We will explore how the choice of representation affects the performance of the VAE and MAE models on the DGL-DGL benchmarks.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the models with different node and edge representations against the DA-GNN baseline, using the optimal hyperparameters found in experiment 3.
COST: Estimated 150 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: This experiment should help us understand the importance of node and edge representation in directed graph generation, and identify the most effective representation schemes for this task.

This proposal will be useful for understanding the role of representation in directed graph generation, and can help guide the design of more effective node and edge representations. Given the differences between undirected and directed graphs, it is plausible that the best representation schemes may differ between the two.

ACTION: REVISE
 TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Node and Edge Representation on Directed Graph Generation
 TITLE: REVISED to: Investigating the Use of Contextualized Node Embeddings for Directed Graph Generation
 PROPOSAL: Experiment with using different types of contextualized node embeddings (e.g. BERT, RoBERTa, Graph Attention Network) for the directed graph generation models, rather than relying on manually designed node representations. We will explore how the contextualized node embeddings affect the performance of the VAE and MAE models on the DGL-DGL benchmarks.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the models with contextualized node embeddings against the DA-GNN baseline, using the optimal hyperparameters found in experiment 3.
COST: Estimated 150 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: This experiment should help us understand the benefits of using contextualized node embeddings for directed graph generation, and identify the most effective embedding schemes for this task. The performance might be improved due to the ability of contextualized node embeddings to capturing complex relationships between nodes in the graph. However, it might also introduce additional computation overhead, particularly for large graphs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring the Use of Edge Label Transformers for Directed Graph Generation
PROPOSAL: Implement a novel architecture that combines the Graph Attention Network (GAT) with Transformer-XL for edge labels, and evaluates the performance of this model on the DGL-DGL benchmarks. This architecture is designed to better capture the complex relationships between nodes and their neighbors in directed graphs.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of this model against the DA-GNN baseline, the optimal VAE model from experiment 1, and the optimal MAE model from experiment 2.
COST: Estimated 250 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: This experiment should help us understand whether incorporating edge labels and more complex graph attention mechanisms can improve the performance of directed graph generation models. The results may indicate that the proposed architecture can generate more realistic and diverse graphs, but it may also require larger amounts of training data to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Generalizability of Directed Graph Generative Models to Neural Architecture Search
PROPOSAL: Train the VAE, MAE, and Edge Label Transformers models on the DGL-DGL benchmarks, and then test their ability to generate neural architectures for neural architecture search tasks. We will compare their performance against state-of-the-art neural architecture search methods.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the generalizability of the models by testing their ability to generate architectures for different task-specific neural architecture search benchmarks (e.g. MNIST, CIFAR-10, ImageNet).
COST: Estimated 400 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: This experiment should help us understand whether the directed graph generative models can be leveraged for neural architecture search tasks. The results may indicate that the models can generate a diverse range of architectures, but the quality and performance of the generated architectures may vary depending on the specific task and dataset.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Structure and Topology of Graphs Generated by Directed Graph Generative Models
PROPOSAL: Use graph metrics (e.g. clustering coefficient, degree distribution, shortest path length) to analyze and compare the structure and topology of graphs generated by the VAE, MAE, Edge Label Transformers models, and other state-of-the-art directed graph generative models.
CONTROLS: We will compare the graph metrics of the generated graphs against real-world graphs from the DGL-DGL benchmarks.
COST: Estimated 200 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: This experiment should help us understand the types of graphs that are generated by different directed graph generative models, and whether they capture the structural and topological properties of real-world graphs. The results may indicate that some models are better at capturing certain properties of real-world graphs, while others are better at generating diverse and variable graphs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Topological Priors in Directed Graph Generation
PROPOSAL: Incorporate topological priors (e.g. planarity, tree-likeness) into the directed graph generative models to enforce specific structural properties on the generated graphs. We will investigate how the incorporation of topological priors affects the performance and quality of the generated graphs.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the models with and without topological priors, and evaluate the quality of the generated graphs against state-of-the-art directed graph generative models.
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: This experiment should help us understand the importance of incorporating topological priors in directed graph generative models, and how they can improve the quality and performance of the generated graphs. The results may indicate that the incorporation of topological priors can significantly improve the quality of the generated graphs, but may also require additional computational resources and hyperparameter tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Evaluation and Comparison of Directed Graph Generative Models
PROPOSAL: Perform a comprehensive evaluation and comparison of the performance of the different directed graph generative models (VAE, MAE, Edge Label Transformers, etc.) on various tasks (graph generation, neural architecture search, graph analysis), and evaluate their strengths and weaknesses.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the models using various metrics (e.g. precision, recall, F1-score, Gagliardi metric), and analyze their results using techniques (e.g. statistical analysis, model interpretability).
COST: Estimated 500 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: This experiment should provide a comprehensive understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of different directed graph generative models, and help to identify the most effective models for specific tasks and applications.

propositions.titre: Hyperparameter Search for Directed Graph Generative Models

propositions.controles: We will compare the performance of the models with different node and edge representations against the DA-GNN baseline, using the optimal hyperparameters found in experiment 3.
propositions.prediction:
This experiment should help us understand the importance of node and edge representation in directed graph generation, and identify the most effective representation schemes for this task.

This proposal will be useful for understanding the role of representation in directed graph generation, and can help guide the design of more effective node and edge representations. Given the differences between undirected and directed graphs, it is plausible that the best representation schemes may differ between the two.
propositions.texte: Experiment with different node and edge representation schemes for the directed graph generation models, including using categorical, real-valued, and complex-valued representations for nodes and edges. We will explore how the choice of representation affects the performance of the VAE and MAE models on the DGL-DGL benchmarks.
propositions.titre: Investigating the Effect of Node and Edge Representation on Directed Graph Generation

propositions.controles: We will compare the performance of this model against the DA-GNN baseline, the optimal VAE model from experiment 1, and the optimal MAE model from experiment 2.
propositions.prediction: This experiment should help us understand whether incorporating edge labels and more complex graph attention mechanisms can improve the performance of directed graph generation models. The results may indicate that the proposed architecture can generate more realistic and diverse graphs, but it may also require larger amounts of training data to achieve optimal performance.
propositions.texte: Implement a novel architecture that combines the Graph Attention Network (GAT) with Transformer-XL for edge labels, and evaluates the performance of this model on the DGL-DGL benchmarks. This architecture is designed to better capture the complex relationships between nodes and their neighbors in directed graphs.
propositions.titre: Exploring the Use of Edge Label Transformers for Directed Graph Generation

propositions.controles: We will evaluate the generalizability of the models by testing their ability to generate architectures for different task-specific neural architecture search benchmarks (e.g. MNIST, CIFAR-10, ImageNet).
propositions.prediction: This experiment should help us understand whether the directed graph generative models can be leveraged for neural architecture search tasks. The results may indicate that the models can generate a diverse range of architectures, but the quality and performance of the generated architectures may vary depending on the specific task and dataset.
propositions.texte: Train the VAE, MAE, and Edge Label Transformers models on the DGL-DGL benchmarks, and then test their ability to generate neural architectures for neural architecture search tasks. We will compare their performance against state-of-the-art neural architecture search methods.
propositions.titre: Evaluating the Generalizability of Directed Graph Generative Models to Neural Architecture Search

propositions.controles: We will compare the graph metrics of the generated graphs against real-world graphs from the DGL-DGL benchmarks.
propositions.prediction: This experiment should help us understand the types of graphs that are generated by different directed graph generative models, and whether they capture the structural and topological properties of real-world graphs. The results may indicate that some models are better at capturing certain properties of real-world graphs, while others are better at generating diverse and variable graphs.
propositions.texte: Use graph metrics (e.g. clustering coefficient, degree distribution, shortest path length) to analyze and compare the structure and topology of graphs generated by the VAE, MAE, Edge Label Transformers models, and other state-of-the-art directed graph generative models.
propositions.titre: Analyzing the Structure and Topology of Graphs Generated by Directed Graph Generative Models

propositions.controles: We will compare the performance of the models with and without topological priors, and evaluate the quality of the generated graphs against state-of-the-art directed graph generative models.
propositions.prediction: This experiment should help us understand the importance of incorporating topological priors in directed graph generative models, and how they can improve the quality and performance of the generated graphs. The results may indicate that the incorporation of topological priors can significantly improve the quality of the generated graphs, but may also require additional computational resources and hyperparameter tuning.
propositions.texte: Incorporate topological priors (e.g. planarity, tree-likeness) into the directed graph generative models to enforce specific structural properties on the generated graphs. We will investigate how the incorporation of topological priors affects the performance and quality of the generated graphs.
propositions.titre: Investigating the Role of Topological Priors in Directed Graph Generation

propositions.controles: We will compare the performance of the models using various metrics (e.g. precision, recall, F1-score, Gagliardi metric), and analyze their results using techniques (e.g. statistical analysis, model interpretability).
propositions.prediction: This experiment should provide a comprehensive understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of different directed graph generative models, and help to identify the most effective models for specific tasks and applications.
propositions.texte: Perform a comprehensive evaluation and comparison of the performance of the different directed graph generative models (VAE, MAE, Edge Label Transformers, etc.) on various tasks (graph generation, neural architecture search, graph analysis), and evaluate their strengths and weaknesses.
propositions.titre: Comprehensive Evaluation and Comparison of Directed Graph Generative Models

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD (1)
TITLE: Unified flow-based tree-structured Schrödinger Bridge solver for star-shaped trees
PROPOSAL: Implement a novel flow-based tree-structured Schrödinger Bridge solver using a combination of Iterative Markovian Fitting (IMF) and a neural ODE parameterisation for the underlying stochastic process, designed for star-shaped trees with a fixed cost structure.
CONTROLS: Use the original IMF-based flow-based Schrödinger Bridge solver with IPF for comparison, and also a tree-reweighted message passing (TRW-S) baseline for tree-structured normalised cut.
COST: Estimated 1500 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The proposed solver should exhibit faster convergence and better stability than IPF-based schemes, while being competitive with TRW-S for tree-structured normalised cut.

ACTION: REVISE (1)
TITLE: Unified flow-based tree-structured Schrödinger Bridge solver for star-shaped trees
PROPOSAL: Implement a novel flow-based tree-structured Schrödinger Bridge solver using a combination of Iterative Markovian Fitting (IMF) and a neural ODE parameterisation for the underlying stochastic process, designed for star-shaped trees with a fixed cost structure. Furthermore, incorporate a learned regularisation term to stabilise the solver and improve convergence rates, employing an additional neural network parameterised by a deterministic neural ODE.
CONTROLS: Use the original IMF-based flow-based Schrödinger Bridge solver with IPF for comparison, and also a tree-reweighted message passing (TRW-S) baseline for tree-structured normalised cut.
COST: Estimated 2000 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The proposed solver should exhibit faster convergence, better stability, and more accurate results than IPF-based schemes and be competitive with TRW-S for tree-structured normalised cut while potentially outperforming TRW-S in the entropic Wasserstein barycentre case.:

, this REVISE adds significant added value compared to the original and attempts to eliminate a probable roadblock

ACTION: ADD (2)
TITLE: Efficient Learned Subtree Specification for Star-Shaped Trees
PROPOSAL: Design a learned subtree specification mechanism for the star-shaped tree structure, where a neural network predicts a sparse subset of edges to be included in the solver's fittings, effectively pruning the tree and reducing computational cost. This can help accelerate convergence and memory efficiency.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed subtree specification mechanism to a fixed subtree specification (e.g., including or excluding the central node of the star) and standard tree-based methods for prediction (control with and without subtree modification, for cases we still that is worthwhile).
COST: Estimated 500 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The proposed subtree specification mechanism should significantly reduce the computational cost and memory requirements of the flow-based Schrödinger Bridge solver without sacrificing accuracy.

ACTION: REVISE (1)
TITLE: Unified flow-based tree-structured Schrödinger Bridge solver for star-shaped trees
PROPOSAL: Implement a novel flow-based tree-structured Schrödinger Bridge solver that incorporates the learned subtree specification mechanism (Proposal 2) into the hybrid IMF and neural ODE-based solver. Utilise the predictive capabilities of this network to select a subset of edges for refinement during training, thereby adapting the solver to the specific problem instance and exploiting any existing structure in the underlying tree.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed solver to the original hybrid IMF-neural ODE solver without subtree specification (Proposal 1 rev. 1) and to the subtree specification mechanism applied to standard tree-structured methods.
COST: Estimated 3000 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The revised solver should exhibit improved scalability and adaptability to the problem instance, leading to faster convergence and more accurate results, with minimal impact on the available memory and overall training efficiency.

ACTION: ADD (3)
TITLE: Schrödinger Bridge Solver with Fast Convergence for Fixed-Point Iteration
PROPOSAL: Develop a Schrödinger Bridge solver that leverages the fixed-point iteration approach but with accelerated convergence using a neural ODE parameterisation for the proxy distributions. Introduce a learned regularization term and an adaptive step-size control to improve stability and efficiency.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed solver to the iterative fixed-point method (Section † of main text), the original IPF-based Schrödinger Bridge solver, and the learned subtree specification mechanism (Proposal 2).
COST: Estimated 1800 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The proposed solver should dramatically accelerate the convergence of fixed-point iterations while maintaining comparable accuracy to the original IPF-based solver and learned subtree specification mechanism, rendering it a strong competitor for the uniform case and potentially promising better performance in the entropic case.

ACTION: REVISE (2)
TITLE: Efficient Learned Subtree Specification for Star-Shaped Trees
PROPOSAL: Improve the learned subtree specification mechanism by incorporating a hierarchical prediction framework, where the neural network predicts a subset of edges to include in the subtree refinement process at each level of the hierarchy. This refined mechanism allows for more precise and flexible subtree selection based on the specific structure of the tree and the marginals attached to it.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised subtree specification mechanism to the original proposal, standard subtree selection methods (e.g., fixed subtree and dynamic programming), and the subtree selection mechanism combined with the Schrödinger Bridge solver with fast convergence (Proposal 3).
COST: Estimated 750 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The revised mechanism should offer improved subtree specification accuracy, leading to faster convergence and more efficient Schrödinger Bridge solver performance in conjunction with applicable solver; while also potentially providing useful representations of the trees' structure.

ACTION: ADD (4)
TITLE: Wasserstein Barycentre Computation via Hierarchical Tree-Tensor Network
PROPOSAL: Implement a novel Wasserstein barycentre computation method that leverages a hierarchical tree-tensor network (TTN) to efficiently split the computation into manageable chunks. By using the Schrödinger Bridge solver as the subroutine for estimating the OT map at each level of the hierarchy, the method achieves scalable approximation of the barycentre.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed TTN-based method to existing scalable barycentre computation methods (e.g., iterative fixed-point, voxelisation-based approaches), TRW-S, and fixed-point iterations with subtree specification using the Schrödinger Bridge solver.
COST: Estimated 4000 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The proposed TTN-based method should outperform the compared methods in scaling performance and computation efficiency for computing Wasserstein barycentres, while achieving suitable accuracy, with limitations stemming from the choice of subtree and computational nodes' splitting impacting hierarchy formation

ACTION: ADD (5)
TITLE: Neural Network-Based Marginal Relaxation for Tree-Sstructured Problems
PROPOSAL: Develop a neural network-based marginal relaxation technique to accelerate the computation of Wasserstein barycentre in the tree-structured setting. By learning an approximation of the marginals at each vertex of the tree, the method speeds up the computation of the Wasserstein barycentre while maintaining the solver's adaptability to the problem instance.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed neural network-based marginal relaxation to the original hierarchical TTN-based method, subtree specification mechanism, and TRW-S.
COST: Estimated 2000 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The neural network-based marginal relaxation should enable faster computation of the Wasserstein barycentre while preserving the solver's adaptability to the problem instance, providing significant speedup, particularly in cases with small numbers of marginals.

ACTION: ADD (6)
TITLE: Scalable Barycentre Computation via Multi-Resolution Subtrees
PROPOSAL: Propose a scalable barycentre computation method that leverages multi-resolution subtrees to efficiently approximate the Wasserstein barycentre. By hierarchically refining the subtrees at different granularities, the method allows for the efficient computation of the barycentre in high-dimensional spaces, leveraging the features of the flow-based Schrödinger Bridge solvers and neural network-based marginal relaxation.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed multi-resolution subtree method to the hierarchical TTN-based method, neural network-based marginal relaxation, and the standard iterative fixed-point approach.
COST: Estimated 5000 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The multi-resolution subtree method should provide an efficient and scalable approach to computing Wasserstein barycentres, offering improved performance and adaptability for complex data distributions, even in the face of increased dimensionality and large numbers of marginals.

ACTION: ADD (7)
TITLE: A Benchmark for Tree-Structured OT and Wasserstein Barycentre Methods on Synthetic and Real-World Datasets
PROPOSAL: Develop a comprehensive benchmark to evaluate the performance of tree-structured OT and Wasserstein barycentre methods, consisting of a collection of synthetic and real-world datasets, specifically curated for measuring the scalability, efficiency, and accuracy of such methods. This benchmark will enable direct comparisons between the various methods outlined in the previous proposals and facilitate further research in the area.
CONTROLS: Utilise a wide range of tree-structured datasets from various domains (e.g., Bayesian subset posterior aggregation in bike-rental count regression, hierarchical phylogenetic trees, etc.) in conjunction with fixed triangular meshes for OT comparison of static samplers to the algorithms proposed before and recently developed fixed-OT approach variants.
COST: Estimated 15000 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The benchmark will provide a universally applicable tool for assessing the performance of tree-structured OT and Wasserstein barycentre methods, leading to improved corresponding methodologies, a unified set of metrics for this type of problems, and a new avenue for research in this area.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Scalable Flow-Based Solver for Tree-Structured Schrödinger Bridge
PROPOSAL: Implement a flow-based solver for tree-structured Schrödinger bridge that extends the IMF scheme, precomputing a one-time time-incremented Brownian motion simulation on the tree, and leveraging this to compute a splitting-based dynamical update at each iteration, accelerating the computation by avoiding the need for repeated OT solves on each edge.
CONTROLS: IPF-based diffusion SB solver as a baseline, exploring ablations to isolate the effect of precomputation and splitting-based updates on the solver's performance.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should offer significant computational scaling advantages compared to IPF-based schemes, such as the current neural ODE/SDE approach to barycentre computation, while maintaining guaranteed convergence to the tree-structured SB solution. It may struggle with high-dimensional spaces, where the time-incremented Brownian motion simulation becomes computationally expensive.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Regularisation for Tree-Structured Schrödinger Bridge
PROPOSAL: Implement an adaptive log-regularisation parameter update strategy to balance the speed of convergence against the accuracy of the solution, estimating the optimal log-regularisation parameter for the current iteration based on the proximal lagengrad method, and updating it after each iteration using a small batch of samples to avoid large-scale optimisation procedures.
CONTROLS: Fixed log-regularisation parameter as a baseline, ablation to isolate the effect of adaptive log-regulisation on the solver's performance.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should improve the convergence speed of the flow-based solver, particularly for barycentre computation where small values of the entropic regularisation parameter are often needed, while maintaining the accuracy of the solution at convergence. It may struggle with modes with poor stationarity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Flow-Based Barycentre Wasserstein-2 Computation via Fixed-Point Iteration
PROPOSAL: Develop a flow-based barycentre Wasserstein-2 computation approach that leverages a fixed-point iteration scheme, where the fixed point update involves solving a tree-structured Schrödinger bridge problem that uses the current barycentre estimate as the marginal to be aligned. This approach aims to combine the scalability benefits of flow-based methods with the fast convergence properties of fixed-point iterations.
CONTROLS: Iterative fixed-point method with complete OT solves as a baseline, exploring ablations to isolate the effect of using a flow-based Schrödinger bridge solver on the fixed-point iteration.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should leverage the properties of flow-based Schrödinger bridge solvers to achieve both fast convergence and scalable computation, potentially outperforming both flow-based and fixed-point methods individually. However, it may require careful tuning of the learning rate and regularisation to converge stably.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Wasserstein Barycentre Computation for Bayesian Subset Posterior Aggregation
PROPOSAL: Develop a hierarchical Wasserstein barycentre computation approach for the bike-rental count regression problem, where the data is aggregated first at the sensor level and then at the city level, leveraging the tree-structured Schrödinger bridge solver to scale the computation efficiently while maintaining accuracy. This approach aims to provide a robust and data-efficient method for computing Wasserstein barycentres for high-dimensional Bayesian subset posteriors.
CONTROLS: Standard k-means clustering as a baseline, comparing ablations of the hierarchical computation to a direct Wasserstein barycentre computation on the aggregated data.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should efficiently compute Wasserstein barycentres for high-dimensional Bayesian subset posteriors, offering a promising solution for Bayesian learning and subset aggregation. However, it may require careful tuning of the aggregation procedure and the Wasserstein barycentre computation method to achieve robust performance.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Hierarchical Wasserstein Barycentre Computation for Bayesian Subset Posterior Aggregation
PROPOSAL: REVISED PROPOSAL: Develop a hierarchical Wasserstein barycentre computation approach for the bike-rental count regression problem, but now leveraging the flow-based Schrödinger bridge solver instead of a tree-structured one, to further improve scalability and efficiency while maintaining accuracy. This approach aims to provide an even more robust and data-efficient method for computing Wasserstein barycentres for high-dimensional Bayesian subset posteriors.
CONTROLS: Standard k-means clustering as a baseline, comparing ablations of the hierarchical computation to a direct Wasserstein barycentre computation on the aggregated data, and also comparing the Schrödinger bridge solver to a neural ODE/SDE approach.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised approach should further improve the scalability and efficiency of the hierarchical Wasserstein barycentre computation, potentially outperforming existing methods for the bike-rental count regression problem and setting a new standard for Bayesian subset posterior aggregation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analysis of Stability and Sampling Requirements for Flow-Based Schrödinger Bridge Solvers
PROPOSAL: Perform a rigorous analysis of the stability and sampling requirements for flow-based Schrödinger bridge solvers, exploring the effects of regularization, step size, and initial conditions on the convergence and quality of the solution. This analysis aims to provide a deeper understanding of the role of these parameters in the flow-based Schrödinger bridge computation and inform the design of efficient and robust flow-based solvers.
CONTROLS: None
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This analysis should provide valuable insights into the stability and sampling requirements of flow-based Schrödinger bridge solvers, potentially identifying optimal settings for these solvers and contributing to their widespread adoption in applications such as Bayesian subset posterior aggregation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Benchmarking Flow-Based Schrödinger Bridge Solvers on Synthetic and Real-World Datasets
PROPOSAL: Develop a comprehensive benchmarking framework for flow-based Schrödinger bridge solvers, evaluating their performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets for Bayesian subset posterior aggregation. This benchmarking framework should compare the performance of flow-based solvers to state-of-the-art methods, including the iterative fixed-point method, and explore the effects of regularization, step size, and initial conditions on the performance of the solvers.
CONTROLS: Iterative fixed-point method, neural ODE/SDE approaches, k-means clustering
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This benchmarking framework should provide a thorough evaluation of the performance of flow-based Schrödinger bridge solvers, helping to identify their strengths and weaknesses, and informing their use in practical applications such as Bayesian subset posterior aggregation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Flow-Based Wasserstein Barycentre Computation for High-Dimensional Bayesian Subset Posteriors
PROPOSAL: Develop a flow-based method for computing Wasserstein barycentres for high-dimensional Bayesian subset posteriors, leveraging the hierarchical structure of the posteriors and the scalability of flow-based methods to efficiently compute the barycentre. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive IMF Scheme for Tree-Structured SB
PROPOSAL: Develop an adaptive IMF scheme that dynamically adjusts its learning rate and number of iterations based on the convergence of the tree-structured Schrödinger bridge. This will ensure efficient convergence for the entropic Wasserstein barycentre problem without requiring a fixed number of iterations or a specific learning rate.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original IMF scheme with fixed learning rate and iterations, and report on comparisons in terms of convergence speed and accuracy.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptive scheme should converge significantly faster than the original IMF scheme, with minor trade-offs in accuracy. Potential failure: over-adaptation may lead to oscillations or overshooting of the target barycentre.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revised Adaptive IMF Scheme for Tree-Structured SB
PROPOSAL: Implement a revised version of the adaptive IMF scheme that incorporates a gradient-based line search to select the optimal step size at each iteration, in addition to dynamically adjusting the learning rate and number of iterations. This will further improve the convergence efficiency and robustness of the scheme.
CONTROLS: Compare against the previous adaptive scheme without gradient-based line search, and against the original IMF scheme with fixed learning rate and iterations.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (additional 50 GPU-hours for gradient-based line search implementation)
PREDICTION: The revised adaptive scheme should exhibit even faster convergence than the previous adaptive scheme, while maintaining similar accuracy. Potential failure: gradient-based line search may introduce additional computational overhead or instability if not implemented carefully.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Adaptive IMF Scheme for Tree-Structured SB
PROPOSAL: REVISED
 Implement a revised version of the adaptive IMF scheme by adding an early stopping criterion based on the KL divergence between the current estimate of the barycentre and its previous iteration. This will allow the scheme to stop iterating when the change in the barycentre estimate is below a certain threshold, thus reducing unnecessary iterations and computational overhead.
CONTROLS: Compare against the previous adaptive scheme without early stopping criterion.
COST: negligible additional cost (<10 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: The revised adaptive scheme should reduce the number of iterations required to converge, thus improving efficiency. Potential failure: early stopping criterion may not always capture the optimal barycentre, leading to suboptimal solutions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fixed-Point SB Solver for Star-Shaped Trees
PROPOSAL: Develop a fixed-point Schrödinger bridge (SB) solver specifically designed for star-shaped trees, where the centre vertex is unknown and the marginals are fixed on the leaves. This solver will iteratively update the centre vertex and OT maps between the centre and each leaf, using a novel weighted averaging scheme that incorporates the OT maps between each pair of leaves.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original IMF scheme and the adaptive IMF scheme on star-shaped trees, and against the iterative fixed-point method for Wasserstein barycentre computation.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The fixed-point SB solver should converge to the entropic Wasserstein barycentre efficiently, especially for star-shaped trees, and offer a viable alternative to existing algorithms for continuous Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation. Potential failure: the solver may struggle to converge if the marginals on the leaves are highly correlated or have high entropy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Boundary Fitting Approach for Tree-Structured SB
PROPOSAL: Develop a boundary fitting approach for solving tree-structured Schrödinger bridge problems, which complements the IMF scheme and the fixed-point solver. This approach will fit a neural network to the boundary of the tree, allowing for efficient computation of the OT maps between the leaves and the centre, and reduce the computational cost of the schemes.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the proposed boundary fitting approach on synthetic datasets, and compare its performance against the IMF scheme and the fixed-point solver.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The boundary fitting approach should significantly reduce the computational cost of the schemes, especially for large trees and high-dimensional data, while maintaining similar accuracy. Potential failure: the approach may not generalize well to complex trees or datasets with high entropy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Empirical Study on IMF Scheme Hyperparameters
PROPOSAL: Conduct an extensive empirical study on the hyperparameters of the IMF scheme, investigating the effect of different learning rates, number of iterations, and OT regularization parameters on the convergence and quality of the solutions. This will provide valuable insights into the optimal configuration of the scheme for various scenarios, and help to improve its performance on the entropic Wasserstein barycentre problem.
CONTROLS: Perform a grid search over the hyperparameter space, and evaluate the performance of the scheme on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The study will provide a detailed understanding of the IMF scheme's sensitivity to hyperparameters, and identify optimal configurations for different scenarios. Potential failure: the extensive hyperparameter search may become computationally expensive, or the scheme may not exhibit consistent performance across different scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Baseline CIFP Solver for Wasserstein Barycentre
PROPOSAL: Implement a computational implementation of the Cut-Interpolation- Fixed-Point (CIFP) algorithm for solving the Wasserstein barycentre problem, which is a direct and efficient method that interpolates between the prescribed marginals and the barycentre. This will provide a strong baseline against which to compare the proposed flow-based methods.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the CIFP solver on the same synthetic and real-world datasets used in the other experiments, and compare its performance against the IMF scheme, fixed-point solver, and boundary fitting approach.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The CIFP solver should exhibit strong performance on the Wasserstein barycentre problem, especially in terms of solution quality and computational efficiency. Potential failure: the solver may not be competitive with the proposed flow-based methods, or may struggle to handle complex marginals or high-dimensional data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptation of Fixed-Point Solver to Star-Shaped Trees
PROPOSAL: Adapt the fixed-point Schrödinger bridge solver to star-shaped trees, by incorporating the novel weighted averaging scheme from the fixed-point SB solver for star-shaped trees. This will enable the fixed-point solver to efficiently handle star-shaped trees and compute the entropic Wasserstein barycentre.
CONTROLS: Compare the adapted fixed-point solver against the original fixed-point solver, the IMF scheme, and the boundary fitting approach on star-shaped trees.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adapted fixed-point solver should exhibit strong performance on star-shaped trees, and offer a competitive alternative to the IMF scheme and boundary fitting approach. Potential failure: the adaptation may not fully leverage the strengths of the original fixed-point solver, or may introduce new computational challenges.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-World Evaluation on Bayesian Subset Posterior Aggregation
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the proposed flow-based methods, including the adaptive IMF scheme, fixed-point SB solver, boundary fitting approach, and adapted fixed-point solver, on a real-world dataset from the Bayesian subset posterior aggregation problem, specifically the bike-rental count regression task.
CONTROLS: Compare the performances of the flow-based methods against the baseline CIFP solver and the state-of-the-art methods on the same task.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed flow-based methods will demonstrate strong performance on the real-world dataset, and offer a compelling alternative to existing methods for Wasserstein barycentre computation and Bayesian subset posterior aggregation. Potential failure: the methods may not generalize well to the real-world dataset, or may struggle to handle the complexity of the task.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analysis of Computational Complexity and Scalability
PROPOSAL: Perform an in-depth analysis of the computational complexity and scalability of the proposed flow-based methods, including the adaptive IMF scheme, fixed-point SB solver, and boundary fitting approach. This will involve investigating the time and memory complexities of the methods, and evaluating their performance on large-scale datasets and high-dimensional data.
CONTROLS: Compare the computational complexity and scalability of the proposed methods against the baseline CIFP solver and the state-of-the-art methods.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The analysis will reveal the computational strengths and weaknesses of the proposed flow-based methods, and provide valuable insights into their potential applications and scalability. Potential failure: the methods may not exhibit the expected computational advantages, or may require significant optimization efforts to achieve acceptable performance.

propositions.controles: Perform a grid search over the hyperparameter space, and evaluate the performance of the scheme on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
propositions.prediction: The study will provide a detailed understanding of the IMF scheme's sensitivity to hyperparameters, and identify optimal configurations for different scenarios. Potential failure: the extensive hyperparameter search may become computationally expensive, or the scheme may not exhibit consistent performance across different scenarios.
propositions.texte: Conduct an extensive empirical study on the hyperparameters of the IMF scheme, investigating the effect of different learning rates, number of iterations, and OT regularization parameters on the convergence and quality of the solutions. This will provide valuable insights into the optimal configuration of the scheme for various scenarios, and help to improve its performance on the entropic Wasserstein barycentre problem.
propositions.titre: Empirical Study on IMF Scheme Hyperparameters

propositions.controles: Evaluate the CIFP solver on the same synthetic and real-world datasets used in the other experiments, and compare its performance against the IMF scheme, fixed-point solver, and boundary fitting approach.

Potential failure: the solver may not be competitive with the proposed flow-based methods, or may struggle to handle complex marginals or high-dimensional data.
propositions.texte: Implement a computational implementation of the Cut-Interpolation- Fixed-Point (CIFP) algorithm for solving the Wasserstein barycentre problem, which is a direct and efficient method that interpolates between the prescribed marginals and the barycentre. This will provide a strong baseline against which to compare the proposed flow-based methods.
propositions.titre: Baseline CIFP Solver for Wasserstein Barycentre

propositions.controles: Compare the adapted fixed-point solver against the original fixed-point solver, the IMF scheme, and the boundary fitting approach on star-shaped trees.
propositions.prediction: The adapted fixed-point solver should exhibit strong performance on star-shaped trees, and offer a competitive alternative to the IMF scheme and boundary fitting approach. Potential failure: the adaptation may not fully leverage the strengths of the original fixed-point solver, or may introduce new computational challenges.
propositions.texte: Adapt the fixed-point Schrödinger bridge solver to star-shaped trees, by incorporating the novel weighted averaging scheme from the fixed-point SB solver for star-shaped trees. propositions.controles: Compare the computational complexity and scalability of the proposed methods against the baseline CIFP solver and the state-of-the-art methods.
