actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncovering Value in Zero-Variance Prompts
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether removing the zero-variance condition in GRPO and instead using a baseline reward that encourages policies to generate diverse, exploration-exploitation, rollouts regardless of reward variance can lead to improved reasoning performance and more stable training.
CONTROLS: Compare against the standard implementation of GRPO with the zero-variance condition, as well as against DAPO, which inherently handles this issue by sampling and discarding zero-variance prompts.
COST: Estimated 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By removing the zero-variance condition, we expect to see slightly reduced training times due to reduced rollout generation overhead, while maintaining or even improving reasoning performance and training stability. This could fail if the baseline reward fails to encourage diverse enough rollouts. 

We will use the competition-level mathematical problem solving and graduate-level science question answering tasks from the Halmos and GSWQ datasets as benchmark standards.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Identifying Prompts with Potential Valueاحث
PROPOSAL: Develop a method that identifies zero-variance prompts in the training set that are likely to still be valuable for policy optimization, by analyzing the bias and variance of the model's responses to these prompts throughout training. This method should flag prompts where the model's performance varies significantly across different rollouts, even when the rewards are identical.
CONTROLS: Evaluate on a subset of zero-variance prompts selected using this method, comparing against a baseline that selects zero-variance prompts randomly or based only on their occurrence frequency.
COST: Estimated 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that by selecting the right subset of zero-variance prompts, we can recover some value that was previously being overlooked, potentially leading to modest improvements in reasoning performance. However, this might fail if our method for identifying valuable prompts is overly optimistic and selects many unpromising prompts.

We will use the GSWQ dataset for this experiment, focusing on the graduate-level science question answering task.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Zero-Variance Prompt Reframing
PROPOSAL: Explore reframing the zero-variance prompt problem as an unsupervised learning task, where the model aims to discover latent variables that explain the differences between rollouts even when rewards are identical. This could involve treating the rollouts as samples from a joint distribution and using techniques like latent space learning or autoencoders to discover informative features.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that simply ignores zero-variance prompts or applies a standard loss function to them.
COST: Estimated 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By reframing the problem in this way, we might be able to uncover insight into the underlying structure of the model's output, potentially leading to more effective training on zero-variance prompts. However, this approach may fail to provide clear and actionable feedback to the model, making it difficult to scale.

We will use the code generation task from the GSWQ dataset for this experiment, as it tends to generate diverse outputs even when the rewards are identical.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Zero-Variance Prompt Reframing (Revised)
PROPOSAL: Refine the zero-variance prompt reframing approach to incorporate a novel penalty term that encourages the model to generate rollouts that are not only informative but also diverse, even when rewards are identical. This penalty term can be implemented using a reconstruction loss applied to the latent space representation of the rollouts.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original Reframing baseline, as well as against a new baseline that adds a separate diversity penalty to the standard GRPO loss function.
COST: Estimated 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By adding the reconstruction loss, we expect to see improved diversity in the rollouts generated on zero-variance prompts, leading to more effective training and potentially better performance on reasoning tasks. However, this might fail to achieve the desired tradeoff between informativeness and diversity.

We will use the same code generation task from the GSWQ dataset for this revised experiment.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploiting Group Structure in Zero-Variance Prompts
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether exploiting the group structure of zero-variance prompts can provide additional learning signals for the policy model. This can be done by using a group-level reward function that encourages the model to generate consistent and diverse outputs across all rollouts in the same group.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that only uses the standard individual-level rewards, as well as against a baseline that applies the modified diversity penalty from the Zero-Variance Prompt Reframing (Revised) proposal.
COST: Estimated 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By exploiting the group structure, we expect to see improved performance on reasoning tasks, as the model is able to learn from the aggregate behavior of the rollouts in each group. However, this might fail if the group structure is too coarse or ambiguous.

We will use the multi-subject knowledge question answering task from the Halmos dataset for this experiment, as it typically involves complex and nuanced questions that benefit from diversified responses.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Learning with Zero-Variance Prompts
PROPOSAL: Explore multi-task learning with zero-variance prompts, where the policy model is trained on a combination of tasks that require diverse and informative outputs, including tasks that are sensitive to zero-variance prompts.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that trains separate models for each task, as well as against a baseline that only uses the modified Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm to address zero-variance prompts.
COST: Estimated 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By learning to handle zero-variance prompts in a multi-task setting, we expect to see improved transfer of knowledge across tasks and better handling of zero-variance prompts in general. However, this might fail to improve performance if the tasks are too dissimilar or if the model becomes over-specialized.

We will use a mix of tasks from the Halmos and GSWQ datasets for this experiment, including the competition-level mathematical problem solving, code generation, and multi-subject knowledge question answering tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Zero-Variance Prompt Approaches
PROPOSAL: Investigate the robustness of the proposed zero-variance prompt approaches by adding noise or perturbations to the rollouts and re-evaluating their performance. This will help to determine how well each approach can handle real-world variations and inconsistencies in the data.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that does not use any zero-variance prompt approaches, as well as against a baseline that uses the standard GRPO algorithm.
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By evaluating the robustness of each approach, we expect to see which methods are more resilient to noise and variations in the data. However, this might fail to provide a clear ranking if the methods differ too significantly in their high-level behavior.

We will use the logical deduction and formal fallacy detection tasks from the Halmos and GSWQ datasets for this experiment, as they involve nuanced and context-dependent reasoning that can be sensitive to variations in the input data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-World Deployment and Transferability Evaluation
PROPOSAL: Deploy the most promising zero-variance prompt approach on real-world benchmarks and evaluate its transferability to out-of-distribution tasks. This will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the approach's practical value and limitations.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that uses the standard GRPO algorithm and against a baseline that uses a pre-trained model on a related task.
COST: Estimated 200 GPU-hours (scaled down using transfer learning)
PREDICTION: By evaluating the approach on real-world tasks and out-of-distribution tests, we expect to see whether the benefits of using zero-variance prompts generalize to real-world deployments and whether they provide a useful inductive bias for transfer learning. However, this might fail to show clear benefits if the real-world tasks are too dissimilar from the training data.

We will use the multi-subject knowledge question answering and logical deduction and formal fallacy detection tasks from the Halmos and GSWQ datasets, and compare the performance of the top-ranked zero-variance prompt approach from previous experiments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hyperparameter Tuning and Ablation Study
PROPOSAL: Perform a comprehensive hyperparameter tuning and ablation study on the zero-variance prompt approaches to identify the most critical hyperparameters and their interactions, and to understand which components of each approach are most essential for its performance.
CONTROLS: Compare against baselines that use random hyperparameters, and that ablate specific components of each approach.
COST: Estimated 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By performing a rigorous hyperparameter tuning and ablation study, we expect to gain a deeper understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of each zero-variance prompt approach, and to identify potential avenues for improvement. However, this might fail to produce clear conclusions if the hyperparameter search space is too large or if the methods are too complex.

We will use the same tasks and datasets as in previous experiments, focusing on the most promising zero-variance prompt approach from the real-world deployment evaluation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Long-Term Training and Stability Analysis
PROPOSAL: Investigate the long-term training behavior and stability of the zero-variance prompt approaches, by training models for several months and analyzing their performance over time.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that trains models for a shorter duration, and against a baseline that uses a simpler training protocol.
COST: Estimated 1000 GPU-hours (scaled down using cloud computing)
PREDICTION: By conducting a long-term training analysis, we expect to gain a deeper understanding of the stability and reliability of the zero-variance prompt approaches, and to identify potential issues that may arise during prolonged training. However, this might fail to produce clear conclusions if the training setups are too complex or if the models become too over-specialized.

We will use a subset of the most promising zero-variance prompt approaches from previous experiments, and focus on the long-term training behavior of the models.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Zero-Variance Prompt Analysis
PROPOSAL: Perform a thorough analysis of the characteristics of zero-variance prompts in the context of RLVR, including their frequency, distribution, and correlation with model difficulty, domain, and task type. This analysis will serve as a foundation for subsequent experiments and provide insights into the potential usefulness of zero-variance prompts for policy optimization.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing methods that ignore or filter out zero-variance prompts; analyze the effect of prompt difficulty and task type on zero-variance prompt frequency.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that zero-variance prompts are relatively rare, primarily occurring at the extremes of model difficulty and task type. This analysis will lay the groundwork for subsequent experiments that explore the potential benefits of exploiting these prompts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Zero-Variance Prompt Logit Analysis
PROPOSAL: Investigate the logit values of the responses to zero-variance prompts to understand whether they provide valuable information for policy optimization. Use a logistic regression model to analyze the relationship between logit values and subsequent rollout accuracy, considering both all-correct and all-incorrect prompts.
CONTROLS: Compare to gradbased logit analysis on standard prompts; experiment with different forms of logit aggregation (e.g., mean, max, softmax).
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that logit analysis on zero-variance prompts reveals meaningful correlations between logit values and subsequent rollout accuracy, indicating that these prompts can provide useful information for policy optimization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reward Shaping with Zero-Variance Prompts
PROPOSAL: Design and implement novel reward shaping strategies that leverage the characteristics of zero-variance prompts to provide informative feedback for policy optimization. Investigate multiple reward shaping methods, such as self-paced learning and relative entropy regularization, to mitigate the effect of zero-variance prompts on training stability and efficiency.
CONTROLS: Compare to standard rewards and existing methods that filter out zero-variance prompts; analyze the effect of reward shaping on model performance and convergence speed.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that tailored reward shaping methods can mitigate the challenges associated with zero-variance prompts and lead to improved training stability, efficiency, and overall model performance.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Reward Shaping with Zero-Variance Prompts
PROPOSAL: Incorporate a novel zero-variance loss function into the model training process, which computes a weighted difference between the policy's output logit and a target logit estimated from the zero-variance prompt's logit distribution. This loss function is designed to provide informative feedback for policy optimization, even in the absence of contrasting responses.
CONTROLS: Compare to standard rewards, existing methods that filter out zero-variance prompts, and the previous version of Reward Shaping with Zero-Variance Prompts (Turn 3); analyze the effect of zero-variance loss function hyperparameters on model performance.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the revised zero-variance loss function will lead to improved training stability and overall model performance, especially in scenarios where zero-variance prompts are prevalent.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: 3. Reward Shaping with Zero-Variance Prompts
PROPOSAL: Replace the previous version of Reward Shaping with Zero-Variance Prompts. revised: Implement a teacher-student learning framework where the teacher policy is trained using a curriculum-based method that emphasizes zero-variance prompts, and the student policy is fine-tuned with standard rewards. This allows the teacher policy to learn from zero-variance prompts in a way that is not possible with standard policy optimization methods.
CONTROLS: Compare to teacher-student learning without curriculum-based method and other methods from previous setups such as mixins zero variance prompts standard rl mixture techniques; analyze the robustness of the teacher-student learning framework to different model types and hyperparameters.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the teacher-student learning framework will outperform standard policy optimization methods in scenarios where zero-variance prompts are prevalent, especially in the early stages of training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Leveraging Zero-Variance Prompts for Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether zero-variance prompts can be used to improve multi-task learning performance and model robustness. Train a multi-task model on a set of diverse tasks, while incorporating zero-variance prompts as auxiliary tasks or as a way to adapt to task-specific zero-variance prompts.
CONTROLS: Compare to standard multi-task learning and multi-task learning with random auxiliary tasks; analyze the effect of zero-variance prompts on model performance and task adaptation speed.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that incorporating zero-variance prompts into the multi-task learning framework will lead to improved model robustness, task adaptation speed, and overall performance, especially in scenarios where task similarity and relatedness are high.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluation on Real-World Mathematical Problem Solving
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed methods (Reward Shaping with Zero-Variance Prompts and Leveraging Zero-Variance Prompts for Multi-Task Learning) on real-world mathematical problem solving tasks, such as those found in the MAML (Model-Agnostic Meta Learning) benchmark.
CONTROLS: Compare to standard MAML and other state-of-the-art meta-learning methods on mathematical problem solving tasks; analyze the effect of zero-variance prompts on model performance, adaptability, and generalization to unseen tasks.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the proposed methods will outperform standard MAML and other state-of-the-art meta-learning methods on mathematical problem solving tasks, particularly in scenarios where zero-variance prompts are prevalent due to task difficulty or complexity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Zero-Variance Prompts
PROPOSAL: Provide a theoretical foundation for understanding the properties of zero-variance prompts and their impact on policy optimization. Investigate the connection between zero-variance prompts and Kendall's tau, a measure of the rank correlation between policy outputs and true labels. Derive bounds on the optimal policy's performance in the presence of zero-variance prompts.
CONTROLS: Prove theoretical results under various assumptions (e.g., identifiability, low-rank clutter) and compare with empirical results from previous experiments; analyze the robustness of theoretical results to different model types and hyperparameters.
COST: 60 GPU-hours ( approximating using cpus)
PREDICTION: We expect that the theoretical analysis will reveal a fundamental connection between zero-variance prompts and policy optimization, providing insights into the conditions under which these prompts are informative.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigation of Zero-Variance Prompts in Adversarial Training
PROPOSAL: Investigate the role of zero-variance prompts in adversarial training, where the goal is to train a model that is robust to adversarial attacks. Explore whether adversarial training can be used to modify the distribution of zero-variance prompts and produce more informative feedback for policy optimization.
CONTROLS: Compare to standard adversarial training and other robustness-enhancing techniques; analyze the effect of adversarial training on zero-variance prompts and overall policy performance.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that adversarial training will lead to a reduced prevalence of zero-variance prompts and improved policy performance, as the adversarial training process.modify the prompt-specific feedback to better adapt to the created perturbations

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experimental Comparison of All Methods
PROPOSAL: Perform a comprehensive experimental comparison of all the proposed methods (Reward Shaping with Zero-Variance Prompts, Leveraging Zero-Variance Prompts for Multi-Task Learning, Evaluation on Real-World Mathematical Problem Solving, and Investigation of Zero-Variance Prompts in Adversarial Training). Select a range of benchmarks and datasets to evaluate the performance of each method and provide a holistic understanding of the effects of zero-variance prompts on policy optimization.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of all methods across various benchmarks and datasets; analyze the trade-offs and synergies between the different methods and identify areas for future research.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the experimental comparison will reveal the strengths and weaknesses of each method and provide valuable insights into the role of zero-variance prompts in policy optimization.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Zero-Varience Prompts for Policy Optimization
PROPOSAL: Develop an extension of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) that incorporates a novel loss function, referred to as Zero-Varience Loss (ZVL), to handle prompts with identical rewards. ZVL allows the policy to learn from the responses of a group even when all rollouts receive the same reward.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of ZVL with the GRPO implementation without ZVL as the baseline, and evaluate its robustness to hyperparameter variation using an ablation study.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect ZVL to improve learning stability and reduce the wasteful sampling of zero-variance prompts, as the shared rewards can still provide valuable feedback for the policy, but the robustness of the method may degenerate in highly rewarded scenarios where the loss is dominated by a large positive value.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Synthetic Dataset Generation for Zero-Varience Prompt Analysis
PROPOSAL: Design a custom synthetic dataset generator that produces batches of prompts with zero-variance conditions (entirely correct or incorrect rollouts), while ensuring the prompts are representative of real-world examples and challenging for the policy model. This dataset will serve as a controlled environment to study the properties and effectiveness of the proposed ZVL.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the synthetic dataset's suitability by comparing the performance of GRPO with and without ZVL on this dataset against their performance on a real-world benchmark dataset.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the tasks generated by the synthetic dataset generator will closely match real-world tasks in terms of model performance, but the lack of variation beyond zero-variance may limit the effectiveness of the method in certain scenarios.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Initial Exploration of Video Synchronization with RGB and Optical Flow Features
PROPOSAL: We will implement a baseline experiment with the widely used YouTube-8M dataset, where we will synchronize videos from the same scene with UnsyncNet, a current state-of-the-art method. We will then extract RGB features using ResNet-50 and optical flow features usingFlowNet2, and train a simple neural network to predict time offsets from these features. 
CONTROLS: We will compare our predictions against UnsyncNet's results, as well as against the unsynchronized clock times of the original videos. Additionally, we will ablate the different feature types (RGB and optical flow) to understand their individual contributions to the synchronization task.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to improve upon UnsyncNet's results by leveraging additional information from RGB and optical flow features. However, this improvement might fail if the features are not informative enough about the temporal offsets, or if the neural network is not capable of capturing the relationships between the features and the offsets.

This proposal serves as a starting point for our investigation and will give us insights into what features we should focus on for the subsequent experiments.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Initial Exploration of Video Synchronization with RGB and Optical Flow Features
PROPOSAL: We will modify the experiment to incorporate both RGB and optical flow features in a more sophisticated manner. Specifically, we will use a Siamese neural network architecture to compare the representation of each frame from one video to the corresponding frames from other videos, focusing on a spatio-temporal feature space where we have both RGB and motion information. 
CONTROLS: We will continue to use the YouTube-8M dataset and compare our results to those of UnsyncNet. Additionally, we will ablate the network architecture and the use of the spatio-temporal feature space to understand their impact on the synchronization task.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (additional 20 GPU-hours for the more complex architecture comparison)
PREDICTION: We expect to improve upon UnsyncNet's results by more effectively leveraging the combined information from RGB and optical flow features. However, this improvement might fail if the spatio-temporal feature space is not generalizable across different scenes and videos.

This revised proposal will allow us to better understand the role of feature combination and spatio-temporal information in video synchronization.

This revised proposal will allow us to better understand the role of feature combination and spatio-temporal information in video synchronization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Synchronization to Variations in Camera Motion
PROPOSAL: We will perform an experiment using a dataset containing videos of dynamic scenes captured from varying viewpoints and with different camera motions. We will apply our previous approach, with the revised Siamese neural network architecture, to synchronize these videos and evaluate its robustness to changes in camera motion. To further understand the effect of camera motion, we will also simulate different camera motion scenarios (e.g. rotation, translation) and evaluate how they impact synchronization accuracy.
CONTROLS: We will use a combination of real-world and simulated datasets to test the robustness of our approach. We will also ablate the specific design choices made in our architecture, such as the use of optical flow or the type of network used for feature comparison, to understand their impact on robustness.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (additional 30 GPU-hours for data curation and simulations)
PREDICTION: We expect our approach to maintain accurate synchronization even in the presence of significant changes in camera motion. However, this might fail if the camera motion variations are too extreme or introduce significant motion blur.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multimodal Synchronization using Audio-Visual Information
PROPOSAL: We will extend our previous approach to incorporate multimodal information, specifically audio-visual cues, to improve synchronization accuracy. We will use a cross-modal neural network to integrate visual, spatial, and temporal features from both audio and video streams. Our goal is to leverage the information from audio waves to provide a more robust synchronization signal, particularly in scenarios where visual cues are limited or noisy.
CONTROLS: We will use a dataset containing video and audio recordings of the same dynamic scenes, for example, concerts or sports events. We will compare our results to those obtained using only visual features and evaluate the impact of different audio-visual fusion strategies on synchronization accuracy.
COST: 180 GPU-hours (additional 30 GPU-hours for audio feature extraction and cross-modal neural network training)
PREDICTION: We expect our multimodal approach to outperform previous results by leveraging complementary information from audio and visual streams. However, this might fail if the audio-visual alignment is not accurately captured or if the fusion strategy is not optimal for the task at hand.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Viewpoint Diversity on Synchronization Accuracy
PROPOSAL: We will explore the effect of varying viewpoint diversity on synchronization accuracy by assessing how synchronization performance changes as the number of viewpoints increases. We will create datasets with increasing numbers of viewpoints and evaluate how our previous approaches perform under these conditions. This will allow us to understand the optimal levels of viewpoint diversity required to achieve robust synchronization.
CONTROLS: We will generate synthetic video datasets with controlled viewpoint diversity and apply our synchronization methods to these datasets. We will also conduct ablation studies to evaluate the impact of individual viewpoint-novelty components on synchronization accuracy.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (synthetic dataset generation and ablation studies)
PREDICTION: We expect synchronization accuracy to improve with increasing viewpoint diversity, up to a point, as more viewpoint-novelty information is incorporated. However, this might fail if the increasing viewpoint diversity leads to too much variability in viewpoint-novelty patterns, overwhelming the synchronization model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Synchronization on Real-World Multi-Camera Systems
PROPOSAL: We will test our synchronization approach on real-world multi-camera systems, using datasets captured with multiple cameras in various scenarios (e.g., sports stadiums, concert halls, and public spaces). We will evaluate synchronization accuracy across different cameras and scenes, considering factors like camera placement, calibration, and occlusions.
CONTROLS: We will use publicly available multi-camera datasets (e.g., the CMU Multi-Camera System dataset) and conduct ablation studies to assess the impact of different data augmentation strategies, feature extractors, and synchronization algorithms on accuracy.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (data preparation, feature extraction, and training)
PREDICTION: We expect synchronization accuracy to be high across various real-world scenarios, demonstrating the applicability of our approach in practical settings. However, this might fail if camera calibration errors or varying lighting conditions significantly compromise the quality of synchronized data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Synchronization using Edge or Feature-Based Methods
PROPOSAL: We will explore the use of edge or feature-based methods for video synchronization, leveraging techniques like point feature matching (PFM), SIFT descriptors, or corner detection. By extracting robust feature correspondences across frames and cameras, we aim to develop a novel, feature-based synchronization approach that operates directly on visual tracks.
CONTROLS: We will compare our feature-based approach with existing methods on both synthetic and real-world datasets, evaluating performance in scenarios with varying degrees of occlusion, noise, and viewpoint change. We will also ablate different feature extraction techniques and matching parameters to identify optimal settings.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (feature extraction and matching)
PREDICTION: We expect the feature-based approach to achieve high synchronization accuracy, particularly in cases where robust feature extraction dominates over model-driven synchronization. However, this might fail if the feature extraction step is sensitive to noise or occlusions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Discovering the Minimum Bicriteria for Time Synchronization
PROPOSAL: We will formalize and solve the time synchronization problem as an optimization problem that maximizes not only synchronization accuracy but also the number of successfully synchronized points between cameras. By explicitly addressing multiple objectives, we aim to derive insights into the underlying tradeoffs between synchronization accuracy, completeness, and computational complexity.
CONTROLS: We will apply multi-objective optimization techniques to identify the Pareto front between accuracy and number of synchronized points. We will further explore the impact of different cost functions, latent encoding strategies, and feature choices on the optimized synchronization settings.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (optimization and analysis)
PREDICTION: We expect to find suitable bicriteria that can lead to more desirable tradeoffs between synchronization accuracy and completeness, making synchronization more versatile and effective. However, this might fail if the optimization process converges to near-optimal but unsatisfactory solutions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Development of a Conditional Synchronization Framework
PROPOSAL: We will create a conditional synchronization framework that allows for precise control over when synchronization occurs based on predefined conditions or events. By integrating domain knowledge or supplementary information, we aim to develop a flexible synchronization schema that adapts to varying scenarios and scales with complexity.
CONTROLS: We will design a modular framework that accommodates various synchronization strategies, including model-based, feature-based, and data-driven approaches. We will then evaluate its applicability across diverse scenarios, including real-world multi-camera systems, sports analysis, and crowd monitoring.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (framework design and evaluation)
PREDICTION: We expect our conditional synchronization framework to provide a practical and scalable solution for diverse, high-stakes applications, enabling precise timing control and potentially identifying novel insights in complex scenarios. However, this might fail if the added complexity of conditional synchronization weakens the model's generality or robustness.

We will explore the use of edge or feature-based methods for video synchronization, leveraging techniques like point feature matching (PFM), SIFT descriptors, or corner detection. We will formalize and solve the time synchronization problem as an optimization problem that maximizes not only synchronization accuracy but also the number of successfully synchronized points between cameras. We will create a conditional synchronization framework that allows for precise control over when synchronization occurs based on predefined conditions or events. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Feature Correlation as a Synchronization Signal
PROPOSAL: This experiment aims to identify features in each video that correlate well with time across all views. We will compute the correlation between various types of features (e.g. motion flows, intensity histograms, SIFT features) across all frames in the reference video, and then similarly for other videos. Features that exhibit strong cross-view correlation across time will be identified as temporal anchors. We will then investigate whether treating these features as synchronization signals can yield reasonable time offsets.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach to a state-of-the-art human-centric approach on a subset of videos from the proposed dataset, and to a baseline method that uses random features for synchronization. The proposed dataset consists of 10 sports videos and 10 egocentric videos captured under various conditions.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (estimation: 10 videos * 10 features * 1000 frames * 10 iterations)
PREDICTION: If feature correlation proves to be a reliable synchronization signal, we expect to achieve a median absolute error (MAE) in time offset estimation of 50 ms or better. The approach may fail in scenes without dominant motion or when the camera pose changes significantly.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Geometric Matching with Temporal Constraints
PROPOSAL: This experiment will investigate whether formulating video synchronization as a 2D-3D geometric matching problem can yield accurate time offsets. We will use a graph-based approach to match video frames across views, while incorporating temporal constraints learned from motion flows. We will adapt the TrendsNet framework to handle dynamic scenes and pose variations, by regularizing the motion field with the motion flows obtained from the first video.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate our approach on the same dataset as the previous experiment and compare it to the feature correlation baseline and a state-of-the-art camera pose estimator as a synchronization oracle.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (estimation: 10 videos * 100 frames * 10 iterations * 20 pose updates)
PREDICTION: By leveraging 2D-3D geometric information and incorporating temporal constraints, we expect to improve upon the feature correlation baseline, achieving an MAE of 20 ms or better. However, in scenes with significant camera pose changes or few dominating features, the approach may fail to establish accurate correspondences.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Geometric Matching with Temporal Constraints
PROPOSAL: This experiment will investigate whether formulating video synchronization as a 2D-3D geometric matching problem can yield accurate time offsets. We will use a graph-based approach to match video frames across views, while incorporating temporal constraints learned from motion flows. We will adapt the TrendsNet framework to handle dynamic scenes and pose variations, by regularizing the motion field with the motion flows obtained from all videos, not just the first video. Additionally, we will use a hierarchical matching strategy to efficiently match frames with varying temporal offsets and limited spatial overlap.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate our approach on the same dataset as the previous experiments and compare it to the feature correlation baseline, the state-of-the-art camera pose estimator, and a naive baseline that uses the average motion field across all videos.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (estimation: 10 videos * 100 frames * 10 iterations * 20 pose updates * 2 matching layers)
PREDICTION: By incorporating motion flows from all videos and using a hierarchical matching strategy, we expect to further improve upon the previous iteration, achieving an MAE of 10 ms or better. However, large scenes and camera movements may still present challenges for geometric matching.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Geometric Matching with Temporal Constraints
PROPOSAL: This experiment will investigate whether formulating video synchronization as a 2D-3D geometric matching problem can yield accurate time offsets. We will use a graph-based approach to match video frames across views, while incorporating temporal constraints learned from motion flows. We will adapt the TrendsNet framework to handle dynamic scenes and pose variations, by regularizing the motion field with the motion flows obtained from all videos, not just the first video. Additionally, we will use a hierarchical matching strategy to efficiently match frames with varying temporal offsets and limited spatial overlap.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate our approach on the same dataset as the previous experiments and compare it to the feature correlation baseline, the state-of-the-art camera pose estimator, and a naive baseline that uses the average motion field across all videos.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (estimation: 10 videos * 100 frames * 10 iterations * 20 pose updates * 2 matching layers)
PREDICTION: By incorporating motion flows from all videos and using a hierarchical matching strategy, we expect to further improve upon the previous iteration, achieving an MAE of 10 ms or better. However, large scenes and camera movements may still present challenges for geometric matching.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning to Synchronize with Weak Supervision
PROPOSAL: This experiment will adapt a recent learned representation framework, such as VideoNet or Self-Synchronization Network, to synchronize the given videos with weak supervision. The idea is to learn a common representation of the videos that captures their temporal structure, without explicitly supervising the synchronization process. The framework will be trained on a mixture of the provided videos and synthetic data with ground-truth temporal synchronization, to learn the common representation.
CONTROLS: We will compare the approach to our geometric matching approach, as well as to a self-supervised baseline that synchronizes videos based on their visual similarity.
COST: 400 GPU-hours (estimation: 10 videos * 100 frames * 10 iterations * 2 models)
PREDICTION: By leveraging learned representations and weak supervision, we expect to obtain competitive results to our geometric matching approach, and possibly outperform it in cases where the geometric approach fails due to pose complexity or partial occlusions. However, the approach may require significant computational resources and well-designed training data to achieve high-quality synchronization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unsupervised Video-to-Video Translation for Temporal Alignment
PROPOSAL: This experiment will employ a video-to-video translation approach to align the input videos in the temporal domain. The idea is to train a neural network to translate one video into another, while preserving their temporal structure. We will modify the MUNIT framework to translate between different video sequences, and use adversarial and cycle-consistency losses to enforce temporal alignment.
CONTROLS: We will compare the approach to the learned synchronization framework and the geometric matching approach, as well as to a baseline that uses optical flow-based synchronization.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (estimation: 10 videos * 100 frames * 10 iterations * 3 models)
PREDICTION: By leveraging video-to-video translation, we expect to obtain competitive results to the learned synchronization framework, and possibly outperform it in cases where the geometric approach fails due to pose complexity or partial occlusions. However, the approach may require significant computational resources and well-designed training data to achieve high-quality synchronization, and may also suffer from mode collapse or instability during training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Group Synchronization for Large Multi-View Sets
PROPOSAL: This experiment will extend the geometric matching approach to handle large multi-view sets, with potentially widely varying temporal offsets. We will propose a hierarchical group synchronization method, where the videos are first grouped into smaller clusters based on their temporal proximity, and then synchronized within each group using the geometric matching algorithm. The results from each group will be combined to obtain a final synchronization estimate.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the approach on a large dataset of 50 videos, comparing it to the learned synchronization framework, the video-to-video translation approach, and a baseline that uses a brute-force optimization approach.
COST: 700 GPU-hours (estimation: 50 videos * 100 frames * 10 iterations * 5 groups)
PREDICTION: By using hierarchical group synchronization, we expect to significantly improve the scalability of the geometric matching approach, allowing it to handle large multi-view sets with varying temporal offsets. However, the approach may require careful tuning of the grouping parameters and may also suffer from false positives when videos are grouped incorrectly.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Viewpoint-Invariant Synchronization
PROPOSAL: This experiment will investigate whether pre-trained models can be transferred across different viewpoints and scenes to achieve viewpoint-invariant synchronization. We will fine-tune a pre-trained geometric matching model on a smaller set of videos with known temporal offsets, and then evaluate its performance on a set of unseen videos with different viewpoints and scenes.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach to a randomly initialized model and to a baseline that uses a separate pre-trained model for each viewpoint.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (estimation: 10 videos * 100 frames * 10 iterations * 2 models)
PREDICTION: By leveraging transfer learning, we expect to significantly improve the generalizability of our geometric matching approach, allowing it to handle new scenes and viewpoints without requiring extensive retraining. However, the approach may require careful selection of the pre-trained model and may also suffer from overfitting to the pre-trained weights.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Robustness to Dynamic Scene Changes and Augmentations
PROPOSAL: This experiment will evaluate the robustness of our proposed synchronization methods to dynamic scene changes, such as changes in illumination, camera angles, and object occlusions. We will simulate these scenarios using data augmentation techniques and evaluate the performance of our methods on a test set of videos with varying degrees of complexity.
CONTROLS: We will compare the robustness of our synchronization methods to a naive approach that uses a fixed temporal offset and a state-of-the-art approach that uses optical flow based synchronization.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (estimation: 10 videos * 100 frames * 10 iterations * 5 augmentation scenarios)
PREDICTION: By evaluating the robustness of our synchronization methods, we expect to identify areas for improvement and develop strategies to mitigate the effects of dynamic scene changes. Our methods may perform poorly in extreme cases of occlusion or changing illumination, but overall, we expect them to be robust to moderate levels of change.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Learning for Synchronization and Object Detection
PROPOSAL: This experiment will investigate whether multi-task learning can improve the performance of our synchronization methods by jointly learning object detection and synchronization. We will train a single model that predicts both the temporal offset and the object locations in the video frames, and evaluate its performance on a set of videos with labeled objects.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the multi-task model to our previous method, as well as to a baseline that uses a separate object detection model and a naive synchronization approach.
COST: 700 GPU-hours (estimation: 10 videos * 100 frames * 10 iterations * 3 models)
PREDICTION: By jointly learning object detection and synchronization, we expect to significantly improve the performance of our synchronization methods, especially in scenarios where the temporal offset is highly correlated with object movements. However, the approach may require careful tuning of the model architecture and hyperparameters to achieve optimal performance.

The results from each group will be combined to obtain a final synchronization estimate.

propositions.titre: Transfer Learning for Viewpoint-Invariant Synchronization

propositions.controles: We will compare the performance of the multi-task model to our previous method, as well as to a baseline that uses a separate object detection model and a naive synchronization approach.

propositions.texte: This experiment will investigate whether multi-task learning can improve the performance of our synchronization methods by jointly learning object detection and synchronization. The model will use a combination of optical flow and feature matching to identify overlapping pixels and will learn to represent the uncertainty of these matches using a dedicated loss function.

PROPOSAL: This experiment aims to evaluate the robustness of the previously proposed models to various types of noise and distortions, such as flicker, motion blur, and image compression. PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes the creation of a large-scale, real-world multiview video synchronization benchmark. The goal is to provide a comprehensive evaluation framework for multiview video synchronization models, allowing researchers to compare and improve their approaches.

PREDICTION: The real-world benchmark should become a standard for evaluating multiview video synchronization models, providing a clear indication of a model's performance in real-world scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Learning for Multiview Video Synchronization
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes the use of meta-learning to improve the performance of multiview video synchronization models. The model will be trained on a small set of videos and then fine-tuned on a new set of videos, adapting to the new data distribution and improving the synchronization accuracy. The experiment will evaluate the performance of meta-learning on the real-world benchmark created in the previous experiment.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Time-Based Synchronization via Learned Overlapped Regions, Comparison of Feature Representation Models for Temporal Offset Estimation, Handling Temporal Ambiguity via Deep Autoencoders
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The meta-learning approach should improve the model's ability to adapt to new data distributions and improve the synchronization accuracy on the real-world benchmark, demonstrating the potential for this approach in practical applications.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Geometry-Aware Template-Informed Generative Model for 3D Molecule Design
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel generative adversarial network (GAN) architecture, "TemplateGAN," that integrates geometric and synthesizability constraints to generate 3D small molecules along with explicit synthesis routes. The model will consist of a spatial encoding module to generate physically realistic conformations, a synthesis encoding module to produce synthetic paths, and a discriminator node to favor realistic and synthesizable molecules.
CONTROLS: Compare TemplateGAN with two baselines: 1) a purely geometric GAN (GeoGAN) that generates 3D molecules without synthesis routes, and 2) a synthesizability-aware GAN (SynthGAN) that generates synthesis paths but does not produce 3D conformations.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: TemplateGAN should significantly outperform both baselines, demonstrating higher precision in synthesizability and geometric realism. However, its ability to generalise across diverse reaction templates and molecules might be limited.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluation Metrics for Synthesis-Aware 3D Molecule Generation
PROPOSAL: Propose a comprehensive set of evaluation metrics to assess the quality of 3D molecules generated by synthesis-aware models, including synthesizability, geometric realism, and chemical feasibility. Metrics will include: (1) template match ratio, measuring the proportion of generated molecules that can be synthesized using a given reaction template; (2) 3D G-score, evaluating the geometric accuracy of generated molecules; and (3) retrosynthesis success rate, measuring the ability of generated synthesis routes to yield the target molecule.
CONTROLS: Compare these metrics across TemplateGAN (and variants) and the two baselines: GeoGAN and SynthGAN.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: These metrics should help identify key challenges and opportunities for advancement in synthesis-aware 3D molecule generation, providing a framework for quantitative evaluation and competition among models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Benchmarking 3D Molecule Generation on Commercially Relevant Templates
PROPOSAL: Collect and preprocess a comprehensive dataset of commercially relevant reaction templates, along with the corresponding molecular targets, synthesis data, and structure. Use this dataset to benchmark the performance of TemplateGAN and the baselines on real-world synthesis tasks, focusing on precision in synthesizability, geometric realism, and chemical feasibility. Additionally, evaluate the model's ability to generalize across diverse reaction templates and molecular targets.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of TemplateGAN and the baselines across different reaction templates, molecular targets, and evaluation metrics.
COST: 8000 GPU-hours (due to dataset preparation and real-world validation)
PREDICTION: This experiment should provide a rigorous evaluation of TemplateGAN's ability to generate realistic and synthesizable 3D molecules in a commercial setting, and highlight areas for improvement. However, its high computational cost may limit the number of iterations and ablation studies that can be performed.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Constraint-Based Chemistry for 3D Molecule Generation
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel physics-based constraint library that captures the chemical synthesis rules, geometrical constraints, and atom-level synthesis pathways for various chemical reactions. This library will be used to improve the synthesis-aware 3D molecule generation capabilities of TemplateGAN and other models, by enforcing accuracy in chemical reactions, atom-matching, and 3D conformation predictions. The constraint library will be implemented using a type of distance functions along with correlational analysis techniques.

 CONTROLS: Compare the performance of TemplateGAN with the constraint library against the baseline PerfGAN which relies purely on a loss function and does so using the same GScores (simulated as) as the metric in: Turn 2 
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposal should improve the quality of synthesis-aware 3D molecule generation by enforcing accuracy in chemical reactions and 3D conformation predictions, but its complex implementation may require significant expertise and computational resources.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 3
TITLE: Benchmarking 3D Molecule Generation on Commercially Relevant Templates
PROPOSAL: Refine proposal 3 by incorporating progressive synthesis route planning, allowing TemplateGAN to iteratively refine and optimize the synthesis route as it generates the 3D molecule. This will improve the model's ability to capture complex synthesis pathways and target areas where synthesis challenges exist.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of TemplateGAN with progressive synthesis route planning against the baseline PerfGAN, focusing on the accuracy of generated synthesis routes, time-to-optimality, and the number of iterations required for convergence.
COST: 10,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This refinement should significantly improve TemplateGAN's ability to generate realistic and synthesizable 3D molecules, particularly for complex synthesis tasks. However, its increased computational cost may require careful resource management.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalable and Modular Architecture for 3D Molecule Generation
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel, modular architecture for TemplateGAN that allows for scalable and efficient 3D molecule generation. The architecture will consist of multiple synthesizability-aware modules, each specializing in different aspects of molecule generation (e.g., structure, conformation, synthesis route). These modules will be trainably pipelined, enabling the model to efficiently generate molecules with high complexity and realism.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the modular architecture against a monolithic architecture, focusing on scalability, efficiency, and the quality of generated molecules.
COST: 5000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This proposal should significantly improve the model's scalability and efficiency, allowing it to generate high-quality molecules with increased complexity. However, its modular architecture may require more comprehensive hyperparameter tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Weakly Supervised Learning for Synthesis Route Planning
PROPOSAL: Develop a weakly supervised learning approach for synthesis route planning, where the model learns to predict synthesizability and synthesis routes from noisy, partially annotated data. The approach will employ a variational autoencoder (VAE) to model the distribution of synthesis routes, and a reinforcement learning component to optimize the generation of synthesis routes based on reward signals from a hand-designed simulator.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the weakly supervised learning approach against fully supervised learning and reinforcement learning only.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This proposal should improve the model's ability to generate realistic synthesis routes even with limited supervision, reducing the need for extensive annotation and computational resources. However, its performance may degrade in the absence of well-designed reward signals.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Physics-Based Synthesis-Directed Graph Convolutional Network
PROPOSAL: Develop a graph convolutional network (GCN) architecture that integrates physical chemistry principles and synthesis-aware constraints to generate 3D molecules. The GCN will be designed to learn the representations of molecular graphs, synthesis routes, and 3D conformations, enabling the generation of realistic and synthesizable molecules.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the GCN against TemplateGAN and the baselines, focusing on synthesizability, geometric realism, and chemical feasibility.
COST: 7000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This proposal should significantly improve the model's ability to generate realistic and synthesizable molecules by incorporating physics-based principles and synthesis-aware constraints, but its performance may be sensitive to the design of the GCN architecture and the quality of the training data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multitask Learning for Synthesis-Aware 3D Molecule Generation
PROPOSAL: Develop a multitask learning framework that enables TemplateGAN and other models to generate 3D molecules that are both realistic and synthesizable. The framework will train the models on multiple tasks simultaneously, including 3D molecule generation, synthesis route planning, and retrosynthesis, to improve their overall performance and ability to generalize across different tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the multitask learning framework against single-task learning and ablate specific tasks to understand their relative importance.
COST: 4500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This proposal should improve the model's ability to generate realistic and synthesizable molecules by leveraging the shared representations and knowledge across multiple tasks, but its performance may be sensitive to the design of the multitask learning framework and the quality of the training data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Explainability and Transparency for Synthesis-Aware 3D Molecule Generation
PROPOSAL: Develop a framework to provide explainability and transparency for synthesis-aware 3D molecule generation models, including TemplateGAN and the GCN. The framework will generate feature importance scores, saliency maps, and other interpretability techniques to understand the decision-making processes of the models and identify areas for improvement.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance and interpretability of the framework against established methods such as SHAP and LIME.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This proposal should improve the interpretability and trustworthiness of synthesis-aware 3D molecule generation models by providing insights into their decision-making processes, but its implementation may require additional computational resources and expertise.

Develop a multitask learning framework that enables TemplateGAN and other models to generate 3D molecules that are both realistic and synthesizable. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Path-Integrated 3D Molecule Generation
PROPOSAL: Investigate a variant of graph neural networks (GNNs) that incorporates a 3D structure-aware embedding of molecular graphs, integrated with a graph transformer-based synthesizability predictor. This will generate 3D conformations and syntheses paths in a single, end-to-end model.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Existing state-of-the-art 2D and 3D molecule generation models (e.g. SchNet, pre-transformers), ablation study: removing either the 3D structure-aware embedding or the synthesizability predictor
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to show improvements in both 3D conformer generation and synthesis path prediction, but possible difficulties in balancing these two objectives and achieving convergence in such a complex model.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Refining Path-Integrated 3D Molecule Generation
PROPOSAL: REVISED PROPOSAL: To address the challenges in balancing 3D conformer generation and synthesis path prediction, refine the Path-Integrated 3D Molecule Generation model by incorporating a novel path-attention mechanism. This will enable the model to selectively focus on relevant synthesis steps while generating 3D conformations. Additionally, use a retrosynthesis-aware reward function that prioritizes high-yield and high-reliability reactions.
CONTROLS: Same as before, along with an additional ablation study to evaluate the impact of the path-attention mechanism and the retrosynthesis-aware reward function
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to show improved performance in both 3D conformer generation and synthesis path prediction, with a notable emphasis on synthesis-awareness. However, there is a risk of overfitting to the retrosynthesis-aware reward function, which could lead to suboptimal performance on standard molecule generation benchmarks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating 3D Molecule Generation with Retrosynthesis
PROPOSAL: Using the revised Path-Integrated 3D Molecule Generation model as a starting point, evaluate its performance on a set of retrosynthesis tasks, where the goal is to generate a set of plausible reactants and synthesis paths from a target molecule. This will assess the model's ability to generate synthesis-aware 3D conformations that can be used as a starting point for subsequent synthesis steps.
CONTROLS: Baseline: existing retrosynthesis models (e.g. GRIT, RETRO), ablation study: generating 3D conformations without taking into account synthesis paths
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to show decent performance on retrosynthesis tasks, with room for improvement in accurately capturing complex synthesis paths. However, the model may struggle with cases where the synthesis path involves multiple, highly improbable steps.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: 3D Molecule Generation with Conditional Control on Synthesis Route
PROPOSAL: Investigate a conditional variant of the Path-Integrated 3D Molecule Generation model that can be controlled to generate 3D conformations with specific synthesis routes. This will be achieved by conditioning the model on a set of intermediate molecular structures and synthesis steps that should be taken. The goal is to enable the model to generate 3D conformations that can be synthesized in a specific order, enabling efficient exploration of chemical space.
CONTROLS: Baseline: unconditional variant of the Path-Integrated 3D Molecule Generation model, ablation study: removing the conditioning on synthesis routes
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to show improved performance in generating 3D conformations that meet specific synthesis route constraints, but potential difficulties in ensuring that the generated conformations are globally optimal and not local minima.

ACTION: ADD

This will assess the model's ability to generalize to real-world scenarios and provide a more accurate estimate of its practical utility in drug discovery.
CONTROLS: Baseline: existing 3D molecule generation models (e.g. SchNet, pre-transformers), evaluation metrics: Geometric fidelity, synthesizability, and precision in predicting synthesis routes
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to show decent performance on real-world data, but potential difficulties in capturing the complexity and variability of real-world synthesis routes and molecular structures.

TITLE: Investigating the Use of Transformers for Synthesis-Aware 3D Molecule Generation
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of transformer-based architectures for synthesis-aware 3D molecule generation, leveraging the self-attention mechanism to explicitly model the relationships between molecular structures and synthesis routes. This will be achieved by adapting the conditional variant of the Path-Integrated 3D Molecule Generation model to use a transformer encoder-decoder architecture.

COST: 1600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to show improved performance in capturing complex synthesis-aware relationships between molecular structures, but potential difficulties in balancing the generation of 3D conformations with the explicit modeling of synthesis routes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning Synthesis-Aware 3D Molecule Generation
PROPOSAL: Design and train a novel 3D generative model, "ASyncGen," that integrates synthesis-awareness by predicting feasible synthesis routes and 3D conformations in a single, amortized inference pass. ASyncGen will take as input a molecular graph, a set of building blocks, and reaction templates, and produce as output a probability distribution over feasible synthesis pathways and 3D conformations that can be sampled to produce synthesizable molecules.
CONTROLS: We will compare ASyncGen against two state-of-the-art 3D generative models, Pix2Vox-Diffusion and ConvST, that have been shown to be effective in generating small molecules, but do not consider synthesis-awareness.
COST: Estimated 300,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect ASyncGen to outperform existing 3D generative models both in terms of synthesizability and in generating diverse, realistic 3D conformations. However, ensuring that the proposed synthesis routes are feasible and compatible with current automated synthesis platforms will require significant engineering efforts and may still result in molecules that are difficult to synthesize.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Validation for Continual Multimodal Knowledge Editing
PROPOSAL: Develop a benchmark focused on the evaluation of multimodal knowledge editing in LVLMs. To address the task, we propose an adversarial validation approach, where an external validator provides gold standard knowledge updates in the form of corrected visual and textual facts. Our benchmark includes tasks such as ad-hoc editing (e.g., correct Donald Trump's name when referenced), factual update (e.g., update Mr. Trump's party affiliation), and compositionally answering (e.g., answer a question requiring the correctly identified party affiliation). Each task is designed to assess the model's ability to both locally and globally update the knowledge base and compose new information. We pilot this benchmark using a real-world sports dataset (e.g., identifying players and team affiliations) and adapt existing LVLMs (e.g., Vito) to test its robustness.
CONTROLS: 
- Vito LM with knowledge retained but not updated
- Vito LM fine-tuned with standard text-based editing strategy
- Ad-hoc editing+Vito fine-tuned internal-memory editor with shared key-value memory
COST: 10,000 GPU hours
PREDICTION: Our benchmark will effectively demonstrate the necessity of advancing multimodal knowledge editing for LVLMs. We expect strong performance from our proposed adversarial validation approach, with average improvements of 80% over the standard Vito LM and internal-memory fine-tuned LM; however, we might face difficulties generalizing our benchmarks to the domains with sparse or ambiguous knowledge updates. 

Turn prediction: Subsequence evaluations tries fine-tuning our knowledge editing benchmark using a verification network for reducing cross-modal interference, yielding performance close to perfect editorial interactions.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Enhancing Continuous Multimodal Adversarial Validation with Hierarchical Contextual Modeling
PROPOSAL: We revise the previous proposal to introduce a hierarchical contextual modeling (HCM) mechanism to enhance the adversarial validation approach. The HCM mechanism captures context-based knowledge transfer between diverse epochs throughout the editing process, thus preventing the interference between different updates and retaining previously updated knowledge. To this end, we plug in VGG architectures pre-trained on ImageNet datasets and translate input visual patterns as representations mixed with word embeddings for LVLMs and further incorporated novel “algorithmic supervisory” instructions based end-to-end CC manipulation operators. Empirically, this hierarchical context will purportedly provide outstanding multimodal knowledge manipulation features.
CONTROLS:
- The adversarial validation baseline from proposal 1
- Internal-memory fine-tuned LM without HCM
- HCM-infused LM with standard knowledge editing approach
COST: 30,000 GPU hours 
PREDICTION: Our revised approach will successfully address interference issues and provide stable active interactions. Due to the approach's ability to continue incorporating prior tasks into its activation areas across numerous knowledge graph revision incidents, we can anticipate around 55-65 % success rates across diverse tasks, but difficulties in sufficient CC plasticity is potential limitation across research conjuncture FileNotFoundError.

TITLE: Refining Multimodal Knowledge Graph Construction for LVLMs
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal to incorporate a novel attention-aware filtering mechanism for injecting structured knowledge from Wikipedia. This revised approach enables the MKG to selectively incorporate contextually relevant entities and relationships, enhancing its ability to manage complex multimodal conversations. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Continual Multimodal Knowledge Editing with Decompositional Evaluation Metrics
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel evaluation framework to assess the performance of LVLMs in continual multimodal knowledge editing tasks. Our framework, called Decompositional Evaluation Metrics (DEM), decomposes the editing process into three stages: knowledge ingestion, knowledge fusion, and knowledge reasoning. DEM tracks the accuracy, coherence, and consistency of the edited knowledge at each stage, providing a comprehensive and robust evaluation of the LVLM's ability to manage knowledge updates. We evaluate DEM using a range of benchmarks and demonstrate its effectiveness in detecting vulnerabilities in existing knowledge editing approaches.
CONTROLS:
- Standard evaluation metrics (e.g., accuracy, F1-score)
- Adversarial validation approach from proposal 1
- DEM-infused evaluation framework
COST: 12,000 GPU hours
PREDICTION: Our proposed DEM framework will provide a more nuanced understanding of the LVLM's performance in continual knowledge editing tasks. We anticipate DEM to identify limitations in existing knowledge editing approaches and highlight areas for improvement, leading to significant advancements in LVLM technology.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Knowledge Preservation through Continual Multimodal Contextual Abstraction
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach to preserving knowledge in LVLMs through continual multimodal contextual abstraction. Our approach, called Contextual Abstraction through Hierarchical Reasoning (CAHR), uses hierarchical reasoning to identify and preserve essential knowledge components across multiple edits, even when the edit context changes. CAHR integrates with the MKG to leverage its structured knowledge and enables LVLMs to reason about the relationships between edited knowledge components. We evaluate CAHR on a range of benchmarks and demonstrate its effectiveness in preserving knowledge across multiple edits.
CONTROLS:
- No knowledge preservation mechanism (base LVLM)
- Adversarial validation approach from proposal 1 with CAHR
- CAHR-infused LVLM with standard knowledge editing approach
COST: 25,000 GPU hours
PREDICTION: Our proposed CAHR approach will significantly improve knowledge preservation in LVLMs, particularly in scenarios where the edit context changes. We anticipate a 40-50% improvement in knowledge preservation accuracy and a 20-30% reduction in knowledge drift when CAHR is integrated with the MKG.

TITLE: Hierarchical Multimodal Attention-Based Editing for LVLMs
PROPOSAL: We propose a hierarchical multimodal attention-based editing (HMAE) approach for LVLMs. HMAE uses a hierarchical attention mechanism to selectively focus on relevant knowledge components and modalities when editing knowledge. The hierarchical structure enables LVLMs to reason about relationships between edited knowledge components and modalities at different levels of abstraction. We demonstrate the effectiveness of HMAE on several benchmarks and show significant improvements in knowledge editing accuracy and preservation across multiple edits.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Continual Multimodal Knowledge Editing
PROPOSAL: Implement a benchmark for multimodal knowledge editing, specifically designed for LVLMs, that incorporates a dataset with diverse visual and textual edit operations and assesses a model's ability to retain knowledge over a sequence of edits.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing visual knowledge editing benchmarks such as Visual Entailment and Visual Commonsense Reasoning, and report ablation studies on the effect of using different multimodal fusion techniques.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our new benchmark to expose existing editors' weaknesses in handling sequential multimodal edits, and new editors will need to incorporate mechanisms that preserve modal consistency and prevent interference. However, fine-tuning-based internal-memory editors may excel in this setting due to their ability to adapt and learn from the edited data, but may suffer from catastrophic forgetting when edits become too frequent.

This initial proposal focuses on establishing a new benchmark for multimodal knowledge editing, which will enable fair and comprehensive evaluation of existing and future editors. By introducing diverse visual and textual edit operations, our benchmark will be more representative of real-world scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fine-Tuning Based Multimodal Editor with Attention-Augmented Memory (FAME)
PROPOSAL: Implement a new editor that fine-tunes an LVLM while introducing an attention-augmented memory mechanism to manage and update the user's knowledge over multiple edits, allowing for modal consistency and avoiding cross-modal interference.
CONTROLS: Compare with an ablation study where our editor is used without the attention-augmented memory and evaluate the editor's performance on a diverse set of multimodal edit scenarios using our new benchmark from Proposal 1.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: FAME should outperform existing editors in modality-consistency and cross-modal interference due to its attention-augmented memory mechanism. However, it might suffer from catastrophic forgetting and require frequent fine-tuning when faced with an ever-growing knowledge base.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Evaluating Continual Multimodal Knowledge Editing
PROPOSAL: Enhance our new benchmark (Proposal 1) by introducing a diverse set of compositional queries that require the integration of visual and textual facts, allowing for evaluation of a model's ability to reason over edited knowledge. This will include queries with multiple objects, complex attribute dependencies, and scenarios where visual and textual facts must be combined correctly.
CONTROLS: Maintain the existing baseline and ablation study setup for visual knowledge editing modal, and demonstrate the added value of our enhanced benchmark by a strong correlation (Pearson's correlation coefficient) between the performance on this revised benchmark and real-world applications that require multimodal knowledge integration.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our revised benchmark will effectively challenge LVLMs' ability to integrate visual and textual facts, and FAME (Proposal 2) is expected to achieve state-of-the-art performance on this revised benchmark due to its fine-grained control on the knowledge update process. However, if LVLMs have limited capacity to process complex multimodal queries, we might observe a ceiling effect and performance degradation as the complexity of the compositional queries increases.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISE 2. Fine-Tuning Based Multimodal Editor with Attention-Augmented Memory (FAME)
PROPOSAL: Append a catastrophic forgetting prevention module to FAME, employing a learned, fine-grained forgetting rate for each edit, allowing the model to adaptively control the level of forgetting based on the edit's size and type. This will mitigate the negative impact of knowledge drift over multiple edits and enable FAME to maintain performance under more dynamic scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the revised FAME with that of an ablated version without the catastrophic forgetting prevention module, and assess the module's effectiveness in reducing performance degradation over multiple knowledge updates on our new benchmark.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The addition of the catastrophic forgetting prevention module should significantly improve FAME's long-term knowledge retention capabilities and ability to adapt to dynamic knowledge updates, making it even more competitive with other editor architectures. However, if the module's regulation parameters are not calibrated correctly, this might lead to an overemphasis on knowledge retention at the expense of knowledge acquisition, causing the model to struggle with new learnings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Modular Multimodal Editor (MME)
PROPOSAL: Propose a fully modular LVLM editor architecture, where each module (modal editor, knowledge selector, and knowledge updater) is independently fine-tuned and optimized for a specific task or knowledge update scenario. This modularity allows for flexibility and improved interpretability, enabling researchers and developers to easily identify and replace specific components that underperform or become outdated.
CONTROLS: Evaluate MME's performance using our newly revamped benchmark, and compare it with other state-of-the-art editors like FAME. Also, conduct an ablation study to demonstrate the effectiveness of each module and identify potential hotspots for further optimization.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: MME is expected to provide state-of-the-art performance in terms of knowledge retention, adaptation, and modality consistency, thanks to its flexible and modular design. However, the lack of a centralized knowledge graph or memory structure might lead to information silos and reduced performance when integrating complex visual and textual facts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Evaluation of LVLM Editors
PROPOSAL: Propose an adversarial evaluation framework to test the robustness and security of LVLM editors against various types of attacks, such as data poisoning, membership inference, and stealing sensitive information. This framework will be used to evaluate the resistance of MME and FAME against such attacks, and identify areas for improvement in securing knowledge updates.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparative Study of External-Memory and Internal-Memory Editors for LVLM Knowledge Editing
PROPOSAL: This experiment compares the performance of external-memory and internal-memory editors for knowledge editing in LVLMs using three public LVLMs (e.g., CLIP, LASER) and three real-world benchmarks (e.g., Visual Commonsense Reasoning, Visual Question Answering). We will evaluate their accuracy in editing visual and textual knowledge, as well as their ability to reason compositionally over edited facts. To contrast modes, we will also implement a novel hybrid approach that combines the strengths of both external and internal memory editors.
CONTROLS: Baselines include no editing (baseline model without editing), external-memory editor without visual cues, and internal-memory editor without low-rank adaptation.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: External-memory editors will excel in long-term retention but struggle with initial accuracy, whereas internal-memory editors will achieve higher initial accuracy but show catastrophic forgetting and decreased performance over time. The hybrid approach may strike a balance between the two, offering robust and adaptable knowledge editing capabilities.
