ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Continual Compositional Knowledge Editing in LVLMs
PROPOSAL: This experiment focuses on evaluating how LVLMs perform when presented with a sequence of knowledge edits that require the model to reason compositionally over updated facts. We will create a synthetic dataset of visually grounded questions and their corresponding edited knowledge sequences (e.g., updating an image's label with a new fact). We will then test the ability of LVLMs to accurately answer questions based on the edited knowledge, using metrics such as accuracy and "edit-aware" metrics (e.g., the model's ability to correctly propagate edits over time).
CONTROLS: Baselines will include LVLMs with no editing capabilities and LVLMs with a knowledge aggregator that simply concatenates updated facts without ensuring consistency across modalities.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: LVLMs with knowledge editing capabilities will show significant improvements in accuracy compared to those without editing capabilities. However, LVLMs with a simple knowledge aggregator may still perform well, at least initially, due to the update nature of questions.

Note: Since this proposal involves synthetic data creation, it should be implemented with caution, ensuring that generated data closely mimics real-world scenarios. When feasible, real-world validation will be conducted.

TITLE: Investigating Cross-Modal Interference in LVLM Knowledge Editing
PROPOSAL: This theoretical result aims to understand the root cause of cross-modal interference in LVLMs when editing knowledge, where edited visual and textual facts interact and cause unintended changes in the model's performance. We will analyze the regime of LVLMs under the perspective of shallow and deep learning, and develop a framework to quantify cross-modal interference and its relationship with representations in LVLMs. Using theoretical grounding, we will demonstrate the critical impact of initial model representations on cross-modal interference during knowledge editing.
CONTROLS: Theoretical analysis will compare underperforming models from existing LVLM knowledge editors, focusing on mode dependence.
COST: N/A (since this is a theoretical result)
PREDICTION: The analysis will reveal that models learn representations of modalities with tight coupling, leading to strong interference effects under knowledge editing, and suggest several avenues for mitigating this behavior.

Note: Since this is a theoretical result, no empirical costs apply, but practical implications should guide follow-on experimental evaluation to instantiate theoretical insights.

TITLE: Investigating Temporal Change Understanding in Multimodal Models with Temporal Attention Heads
PROPOSAL: We propose to experiment with adding temporal attention heads to a multimodal large language model architecture, specifically to investigate whether it can better capture the temporal evolution and causal narrative of changes in satellite image time series. The attention heads will be designed to attend to different time steps in the sequence and learn to weight the importance of each step in the prediction of future changes.
CONTROLS: The baseline model will be a standard multimodal large language model architecture without temporal attention heads. We will also experiment with ablations, such as removing the temporal attention heads or only using them for the description task but not the forecasting task.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Temporal Context on Change Description with CLIP
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of the popular CLIP (ConVegionalization of Visual Representations in Transformers) model on change description when given varying levels of temporal context (historical sequence starting nearby, far away, or partially filled gaps). Evaluate downstream task performance for each scenario.
CONTROLS: Individual image change description with CLIP as a baseline, evaluate the impact of conditional language prompts on prediction.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: CLIP will perform better with more contextual data, but diminish in performance when the gap size increases (e.g., beyond a few time-steps), emphasizing the need for models to reason about temporal dynamics rather than relying solely on information contained within a single frame or local contiguous sequence.

Metadata-calibrated justification: With an experimental paper and mostly real-world data, we prioritize a thorough evaluation of how real models (including popular architectures such as CLIP) perform under practical, less-than-ideal scenarios, rather than proposing a new theoretical result without real-world grounding.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Long-Term Temporal Skip Connections for Remote Sensing Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Design a novel neural architecture that introduces skip connections between distant time points in the temporal sequence, allowing for more effective long-term contextualization and potentially elevating the representation's ability to forecast future satellite images.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline architecture with no skip connections, and against a simpler 'content-preserved skipping' strategy where skip connections are restricted to conserving minimal spatial features at distant times, but avoid sophisticated transformations and dense information.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed long-term skip connections mechanism will significantly outperform existing methods and the blind skipping baseline in forecasting accuracy, particularly in scenes with long-term disturbances, but may be vulnerable to overly long sequences where compositional language knowledge becomes crucial.

Metadata-calibrated reasoning: An architecture that incorporates skip connections represents a meaningful incremental step in practical experimental validation, whereas simple extensions of existing model performance may not address core questions about limitations or vulnerabilities of remote sensing time series forecasting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Extendsability of MLMs to Satellite Image Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether a pre-trained MLM can be adapted for future satellite image forecasting by using a novel task-agnostic transfer learning approach. Specifically, we will fine-tune a pre-trained MLM on a dataset of temporally adjacent image pairs from the BJ-S2 satellite image time series dataset, and then use the fine-tuned model to generate future images from the same dataset. We will compare the performance of this approach with a model trained from scratch on the forecasting task.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare with baseline model trained from scratch 
- Evaluate performance using standard image quality metrics (PSNR, SSIM, MSE) 
- Ablation study to evaluate the effect of fine-tuning depth and dataset size on transfer learning performance
COST: 1,600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: the pre-trained MLM will achieve competitive performance with the baseline model, demonstrating the potential of transfer learning for adapting MLMs to satellite image time series forecasting tasks

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Temporal Consistency in Satellite Image Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel metric to evaluate the temporal consistency of generated satellite images, which captures the degree to which the generated images are a logical continuation of the observed trends and dynamics in the historical data. We will use this metric to assess the performance of the models in the previous proposals, as well as a standard pixel-wise evaluation metric (PSNR, SSIM, MSE) 
CONTROLS: 
- Compare the performance of different models using the proposed temporal consistency metric
- Ablation study to evaluate the effect of different temporal consistency metric parameters on model performance
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: the proposed temporal consistency metric will provide a more comprehensive evaluation of the performance of satellite image time series forecasting models, and will reveal opportunities for improving the consistency of generated images

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Transfer Extendsability of MLMs to Satellite Image Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Revise the experiment to include a more comprehensive comparison of the pre-trained MLM with models specifically designed for satellite image time series forecasting. We will fine-tune a pre-trained MLM on a dataset of temporally adjacent image pairs from the BJ-S2 satellite image time series dataset, and then use the fine-tuned model to generate future images from the same dataset. We will also compare the performance of this approach with a model trained from scratch using a state-of-the-art satellite image forecasting architecture, such as the Temporal Conditional GAN (TC-GAN), and a variant of the TC-GAN that incorporates attention mechanisms.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare the performance of the pre-trained MLM with the TC-GAN and its attention variant
- Evaluate performance using standard image quality metrics (PSNR, SSIM, MSE) and the proposed temporal consistency metric
- Ablation study to evaluate the effect of fine-tuning depth and dataset size on transfer learning performance
COST: 2,400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: the pre-trained MLM will achieve competitive performance with the TC-GAN and its attention variant, demonstrating the potential of transfer learning for adapting MLSs to satellite image time series forecasting tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Data Frequency on Temporal Change Description and Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of data frequency (e.g. daily, weekly, monthly) on the performance of temporal change description and forecasting models. Specifically, we will fine-tune a set of pre-trained MLMs on datasets with different frequencies, and evaluate their performance on a common set of evaluation metrics.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare the performance of models fine-tuned on datasets with different frequencies
- Evaluate performance using standard metrics (BLEU, METEOR, ROUGE-L) and the proposed temporal consistency metric
- Ablation study to evaluate the effect of data frequency on transfer learning performance
COST: 1,200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: the results will provide insights into the optimal data frequency for training temporal change description and forecasting models, and will help to identify the trade-offs between higher-frequency and lower-frequency data in terms of model performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving Temporal Change Description through Joint Semantic Reasoning and Video Analysis
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel joint semantic reasoning and video analysis framework for temporal change description. The framework will incorporate a semantic reasoning module to analyze the description of the scene and video analysis module to reason about the changes in the scene. We will evaluate the performance of the proposed framework using BLEU, METEOR, ROUGE-L, as well as visual evaluation metrics such as Temporal Consistency metric.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare the performance of the proposed framework with state-of-the-art models
- Evaluate performance using a comprehensive set of metrics, including visual and textual evaluation metrics
- Ablation study to evaluate the effect of different components of the proposed framework on model performance
COST: 2,400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: the results will demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed joint semantic reasoning and video analysis framework for temporal change description, and will provide insights into the importance of visual information for improving the accuracy of description models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Domain Knowledge on Satellite Image Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of incorporating domain knowledge into the satellite image time series forecasting models. Specifically, we will develop a model that incorporates knowledge of common land cover types and their transitions, and evaluate its performance on a variety of metrics.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare the performance of the model with and without domain knowledge
- Evaluate performance using a comprehensive set of metrics, including visual and textual evaluation metrics
- Ablation study to evaluate the effect of different domain knowledge components on model performance
COST: 1,800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: the results will demonstrate the effectiveness of incorporating domain knowledge into satellite image time series forecasting models, and will provide insights into the potential benefits and limitations of this approach.

- Ablation study to evaluate the effect of different meta-learning approaches on model performance

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning Neuron-Specific Features from Rich Population Context
PROPOSAL: Train a Transformer-based neural population model to learn neuron-specific features from long-sequence Neuropixels electrophysiology recordings in mice. We will use a pre-trained transformer encoder to extract general population patterns, followed by a separate task-specific decoder for each neuron to capture unique features. The decoders will be statically learned and not require fine-tuning on target data, enabling zero-shot transfer.
CONTROLS: (1) Compare to a naive transformer encoder without task-specific decoders, (2) Ablate different decoder-specific learnable parameters to examine their impact on feature extraction, (3) Train on a different dataset (e.g., calcium imaging recordings in mice) to examine generalizability.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (training on 2 GPUs for 50 epochs)
PREDICTION: The model will achieve significantly better performance on both cell type and brain region classification, especially for neurons that are difficult to classify due to sparse and noisy recordings. Challenges arise when dealing with recordings from a new brain region or mouse strain due to the model's lack of adaptation, potentially causing degradation in performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Dynamic Recurrence for Inference of Neuronal Identity
PROPOSAL: Design a neural model with dynamically recurrent connections that selectively capture temporal patterns unique to each neuron, while learning global population trends from calcium imaging or Neuropixels recordings. By dynamically updating connectivity based on the task-specific input, we encourage the model to learn more flexible and adaptable representations.
CONTROLS: (1) Compare to an equivalent model with fixed recurrent connections, (2) Ablate the new dynamic connectivity component to assess its contribution, (3) Contrast dynamic recurrence with an attention-based approach (from proposal 1) to see how each effectively addresses the problem.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (training on 3 GPUs for 70 epochs, considering the increased complexity of the dynamic recurrence scheme)
PREDICTION: We anticipate finding that dynamic recourse captures temporal dynamics with higher fidelity, especially for Class III or 'fast-spiking' neurons, greatly improving the model's ability to discriminate cell types. However, this additional complexity may come at the cost of overfitting to specific recording conditions.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Investigating Dynamic Recurrence for Inference of Neuronal Identity
PROPOSAL: We modify proposal 2's model structure to incorporate an explicit attention mechanism (e.g., Transformer-style self-attention) on top of dynamic recurrence. By selectively weighting signal contributions from different neurons and time-steps, we can capture subtle spatial and temporal relations in neuron activity. This will be especially useful when dealing with recordings from multiple brain regions or populations, allowing for a more generalizable and adaptive model.
CONTROLS: (1) Compare to the revised dynamic-recurrence model with no attention mechanism, (2) Evaluate an attention-only approach without recurrence to provide a baseline, (3) Ablate the attention mechanism to assess its contribution.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (trading off computational efficiency for improved design complexity)
PREDICTION: Adding attention to dynamic recurrence will enable the model to capture richer patterns and relationships between neurons, while enhancing adaptability to diverse brain regions or experimental sessions. However, it may require careful tuning of hyperparameters for optimal performance, and we may find that the increased complexity leads to exacerbated overfitting issues.

We will adopt this regularizer in both transformer-based and dynamic recurrence models.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Transfer Learning in Neural Population Activity
PROPOSAL: To investigate the applicability of pre-trained neural networks for extracting neuron identity information from population activity, we adapt the pooled average of token embeddings (PATE) approach, a widely used technique in natural language processing, to the task of neural population activity. We use pre-trained Transformer models, fine-tune them on annotated Neuropixels recordings of mouse neurons, and evaluate the transferability of the learned representations to entirely new sessions, animals, or brain regions.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments include fine-tuning pre-trained models on Neuropixels data without PATE, using a one-size-fits-all approach to representation extraction, and a naive bag-of-features approach.
COST: 200 GPU-hours, assuming large batch sizes and relatively fast pre-training and fine-tuning times.
PREDICTION: Assuming the learned representations capture coherent and interpretable aspects of neuron identity, we expect to see high transfer performance and low generalization error for PATE-based models. However, failures might arise from the imperfect multi-task learning and brittle dimensionality reduction inherent in the embedding space.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unsupervised Discovery of Neuronal Subtypes
PROPOSAL: We leverage a mixture model-based approach, diffused latent Gaussian mixture models (d-LGMMs), to unsupervisedly discover neuronal subtypes in Neuropixels recordings. This method uses a normalizing flow to learn a joint distribution over the population activity and neuron features, allowing for the simultaneous identification of spatial clusters and temporal dynamics.
CONTROLS: Alternatives include traditional clustering methods such as k-means or hierarchical clustering, and dimensionality reduction techniques like PCA or UMAP for visualization.
COST: Approximately 100 GPU-hours, assuming smaller batch sizes and more complex updating rules for the model parameters.
PREDICTION: Effective learning of neuronal subtypes may depend on the diversity of recordings used for learning and the complexity of the underlying neuronal processes, leading to high variability in results across experiments. This approach could identify intrinsic patterns and relations in the neural population activity, as well as show similar long non-redundant patterns reflecting major cell types.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Unsupervised Discovery of Neuronal Subtypes
PROPOSAL: We modify the previous proposal to incorporate the extracted neuron identity information from the transfer learning approach (Proposal 1) as a complementary input to the diffused latent Gaussian mixture models (d-LGMMs). This allows for a joint learning framework that leverages both global population patterns and individual neuron identity information to identify neuronal subtypes.
CONTROLS: Compare to the unsupervised clustering without incorporating external identity information, as well as to the discrete population-level clustering results from the transfer learning model(s).
COST: Approximately 150 GPU-hours, accounting for the computational overhead of multi-task learning and increased model complexity.
PREDICTION: This revised approach could improve the accuracy and interpretability of the discovered subtypes by capturing both local and global patterns in the neural activity. However, added noise from integrated identity information might diminish result coherence by enlarging scatter across the synthetic neuronal typology.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Metric Learning for Intrinsic Representations of Neurological Activity
PROPOSAL: To address the sensitivity of existing approaches to the choice of population-level metrics and reward functions for learning intrinsic representations of neurological activity, we explore the use of Q-learning with a metric learning objective. This approach allows the model to learn a custom distance metric that reflects the underlying neural processes, such as population correlations or stimulus-response associations.
CONTROLS: Compare to traditional hand-designed metrics, such as mean firing rate or population covariance, as well as approaches that rely on density estimation or graph neural networks for representation learning.
COST: Approximately 50 GPU-hours, as this approach involves a simpler model architecture and fewer computational overheads compared to the previous proposals.
PREDICTION: Effective learning of a custom distance metric could enable more accurate and interpretable representations of neuronal activity, but may be difficult to scale to large populations or complex neural systems.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Metric Learning for Intrinsic Representations of Neurological Activity
PROPOSAL: To improve the robustness and adaptability of the Q-learning approach for metric learning, we incorporate the self-supervised contrastive learning objectives (SimCLR) into the Q-learning framework. This self-supervised pre-training enables the model to learn a more robust and generalizable representation of the neural activity, improving its performance in downstream tasks such as neuron classification and clustering.
CONTROLS: Compare to traditional Q-learning for metric learning without self-supervised pre-training, as well as to other pre-training techniques such as autoencoders or generative adversarial networks.
COST: Approximately 100 GPU-hours, as this revised approach involves more complex training procedures and higher computational requirements compared to the original Q-learning approach.
PREDICTION: The incorporation of self-supervised contrastive learning objectives could significantly improve the robustness and generalizability of the learned representations, but may also increase the risk of overfitting to specific datasets or experimental conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Representations to Local Neuropixels Recording Artifacts
PROPOSAL: To assess the robustness of the learned representations to local recording artifacts, we simulate Neuropixels recording artifacts such as: 1) spike timestamp jitter (10-20 microseconds); 2) amplitude fluctuations; 3) outlier spikes (5-10% of total spikes). We then evaluate how each representation is affected by these artifacts.
CONTROLS: Compare to the representations learned without any artifacts or with only a single type of artifact.
COST: Approximately 150 GPU-hours, as this approach requires re-simulating Neuropixels recordings with various artifacts and re-computing representations.
PREDICTION: The representations learned from the transfer learning approach (Proposal 1) are expected to be more robust to recording artifacts compared to the others. This is because the transfer learning model learned a more generalizable representation that can account for the variability in the data. However, some representations may still fail to capture the deviation from real protocol Neuropixels neighbour recordings, leading to expected result instabilities under mismatch scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Large-Scale Kernel Alignment for Neuronal Type Identification
PROPOSAL: To leverage the advantages of graph neural networks (GNNs) for identifying neuron types in larger-scale recordings, we develop a novel GNN architecture that employs kernel alignment (KA) to learn discriminative features from large-scale neural activity. KA helps to reduce the dimensionality of the data, while also preserving the information useful for identifying neuron types.
CONTROLS: Compare to traditional neural networks, such as CNNs and RNNs, as well as other graph-based approaches like graph convolutional networks (GCNs).
COST: Approximately 500 GPU-hours, as this approach involves training a large GNN model on a substantial number of high-dimensional neural activity recordings.
PREDICTION: This KA-based GNN approach is expected to perform well in identifying neuron types from large-scale recordings, but may require careful hyperparameter tuning to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Large-Scale Kernel Alignment for Neuronal Type Identification
PROPOSAL: To improve the scalability of the KA-based GNN approach (Proposal 5), we explore distributed training strategies, specifically using the PyTorch parallel data parallel (DDP) framework, to leverage multiple GPUs and speed up the training process. This should enable the use of even larger-scale recordings without significant increases in training time or compute costs.

COST: Approximately 250 GPU-hours, as the distributed training approach significantly reduces the training time compared to single-GPU training.
PREDICTION: The distributed training approach is expected to greatly accelerate the training process, but may also introduce additional complexity in terms of model deployment and scalability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experimental Validation of Proposed Methods on Neuropixels Recordings from Rodents
PROPOSAL: We evaluate the proposed methods (1-5) on Neuropixels recordings from rodents, focusing on real-world validation of their ability to identify neuron types, brain regions, and other important features. This will provide critical insights into the practical applicability of these methods for real-world neuroscience research.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Promising Approach of NFR
PROPOSAL: Replicate NFR's state-of-the-art results on humanoid heads to establish a baseline for our future experiments and understand its potential for adaptability to non-humanoid head shapes and multiple disconnected components. Train NFR on a variety of neutral meshes paired with FACS parameters and compare its performance on a set of humanoid and non-humanoid head meshes, including some with disconnected components. Investigate the agent's ability to generalize to new, unseen head shapes and animating combinations.
CONTROLS: No template-based auto-rigging methods, including the preexisting face-to-face transfer learning approaches.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Replication of NFR's results demonstrates its potential as a foundational approach for a generalizable rigging system, however, its generalizability might be limited to humanoid heads, suggesting that improvements are needed to handle diverse shapes and topologies. The experiments may fail to generalize due to overfitting on the limited dataset available.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving Generalizability with Unsupervised Learning
PROPOSAL: Modify NFR by incorporating unsupervised learning to enable the model to generalize better to unseen head shapes and topologies. Use a self-supervised loss function that encourages the model to recognize correlations between point correspondences even in the absence of explicit 3D supervision. Train this modified model on a larger and more diverse dataset of neutral meshes, including non-humanoid heads and meshes with disconnected components. Investigate whether the model can not only recognize but also animate complex expressions on these diverse meshes without relying on template blendshapes.
CONTROLS: Previous experiments with NFR and a set of 3D auto-rigging baselines like NPC-Net for comparison.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved generalizability should be evident in the model's performance on our diverse test set, allowing for expressive animations on a wide variety of head shapes and topologies. The introduction of unsupervised learning, however, could also lead to increased sensitivity to noise and unrelated features, resulting in unforeseen performance drops.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Transfer Learning from 2D to 3D Facial Expression Transfer
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of transfer learning from pre-trained 2D face landmark detectors and_EXPRESSION analyzers to our 3D facial rigging task, given that these 2D models are trained on vast amounts of images from diverse datasets and can likely learn commonalities in facial expressions that generalize across different identity features. Use a feature extractor pre-trained on 2D facial expression data and fine-tune it on a smaller 3D dataset paired with FACS parameters, and compare its performance to NFR + unsupervised learning. Investigate whether this transfer learning approach can indeed confer generalizability without relying on additional 3D data for fine-tuning.
CONTROLS: Previous experiments with NFR + unsupervised learning and a set of 2D facial expression transfer baselines (e.g., DLib or OpenFace) for comparison.
COST: 75 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Successful transfer learning could enable significant generalizability without a detailed 3D dataset, with potential minor losses in raw 3D accuracy; the method, however, might become inefficient for models that don't generalize well between images and real 3D observations.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Refining the Evaluation Metric for 3D Facial Rigging
PROPOSAL: Revise and expand upon the evaluation metric for 3D facial rigging, taking into account not just mean squared error, but also rig similarity retention, animation coherence, and overall aesthetic quality. Compute "higher-level" metrics like Mean Facial Action Unit Coherency (MFAUC) and Rig Similarity Score (RSS), which give a more comprehensive understanding of the rig's correctness and aesthetic appeal. Investigate how different evaluation metrics can be a benchmark for current and proposed tasks, shedding light on the overall success of our projects.
CONTROLS: Use MFAUC and RSS on the existing baselines of facial auto-rigging for comparison.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This focus on comprehensive and intuitive evaluation metrics will help acknowledge the human aspects and full-scale implications of 3D facial rigging and aid comparison with complex, traditional animation procedures, though detecting rig similarity could require some computing trial and error.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Enhanced Rigging Model for Disconnected Components
PROPOSAL: Refine the NFR + unsupervised learning model to better account for disconnected components like eyeballs and teeth by developing a separate module that can be trained in tandem to identify and animate the movements of these separate parts. Integrate a Region-aware Auto-Encoder (RAE) that can adapt to each component's unique topology and dynamics. Apply a separate set of loss functions specifically tailored for the RAE to optimize the performances of individual components. Validate the approach on a diverse range of 3D head meshes that contain observable compound structures.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original NFR + unsupervised learning model and a set of ablations that disable/enabled the RAE module. Control models will be based on a different off-the-shelf methods, like Szymon Dudzik’s variant.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The enhanced rigging model should show a clear improvement in handling disconnected components by numerically measuring the alignment between component movements and their supposed patterns, possibly resulting in uncoverable inconsistencies when debris particles are put into it.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Generating 3D Facial Mesh Ground Truth from 2D Faces
PROPOSAL: Develop a method for generating high-quality 3D facial mesh ground truth from 2D face images or videos using state-of-the-art 3D face reconstruction techniques like MMF or PRN. Create a pipeline that can automatically annotate facial landmarks, estimate 3D facial models, and ensure that the generated ground truth is accurate, comprehensive, and useful for various levels of difficulty in the dataset. Test this generated data against the proposed approach to considerably augment the dataset size and diversity, establishing a robust 3D ground truth for future study.
CONTROLS: Compare method performance on a subset of the generated data against the manual annotation and against ground truth annotation.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Automated ground truth generation should make available a vast and trustworthy 3D cerebral cortex dataset invaluable in also validating improvements in facial automatization rigs but could be strongly unprecise in metric comparison due to redundancy and lack of manual inspection.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Practical Sampling Strategies for Training Auto-Rigging Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate how to efficiently sample and utilize the 3D ground truth data generated in the previous task for training auto-rigging models. Develop a variety of techniques, including 3D reconstruction quality prediction, probabilistic stratification, and dissimilarity-aware experiments, to select representative samples that effectively cover the space of facial mesh geometries and expressional variations. Assess how these sampling strategies affect the convergence and generalizability of the rigging models, and identify the most effective approach for a given data budget.
CONTROLS: Apply sampling strategies on subsets of the generated ground truth data and examine convergence rates on smaller subsets.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Sampling techniques used effectively here can notably reduce training time, improving convergence of smaller models and confirming models that are at risk of overfitting at the inability to read accurate heterogeneos model from complex tooltips.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparative Study of Meta-Learning for Auto-Rigging
PROPOSAL: Compare the effectiveness of various meta-learning strategies (e.g., Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML), Reptile, or Probabilistic Meta-Learning) for the auto-rigging task. Design a meta-learning framework that can efficiently adapt to different facial head meshes and expressions, using the data generated in the previous tasks as a training set. Investigate whether meta-learning enables the rigging models to adapt quickly to new, unseen heads and animations, reducing the need for extensive fine-tuning and training from scratch.
CONTROLS: Experiment with a set of baselines that use standard fine-tuning and training from scratch, as well as other meta-learning methods (e.g., dark learning).
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By leveraging memory efficiency and leveraging the models for personal development, meta-learning strategies can indeed simplify the requirements of extensive fine-tuning and identify long-standing design errors, leave we implemented naively handling dialogue massive competence needs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Open-Set and Multi-Task Learning for Increased Flexibility
PROPOSAL: Develop an open-set and multi-task learning framework for auto-rigging that can efficiently handle new or unseen facial expressions, deformations, and topologies. Incorporate an outlier detection module to recognize and reject samples that are far away from the learned distribution, reducing the risk of overfitting to a limited dataset. Also, design a multi-task learning setup that can learn to predict both the 3D pose and the corresponding facial expression from a single input, increasing the robustness and ability of the rigging model.
CONTROLS: Validate the approach using a mix of in-distribution and out-of-distribution samples, as well as multi-task baselines that use separate models for 3D pose and facial expression prediction.
COST: 160 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved model flexibility should allow the rigging system to generalize better to a wider range of facial shapes, expressions, and deformations, but may also require more careful tuning of hyperparameters to prevent overfitting and performance degradation on in-distribution samples.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scaling-up to Large-Scale Commercial Use Cases
PROPOSAL: Investigate the scalability of the proposed auto-rigging framework to large-scale commercial use cases, where thousands of 3D facial meshes need to be rigged and animated in a timely and efficient manner. Design a cloud-based deployment architecture that can leverage distributed computing and GPU acceleration to speed up the rigging and animation process. Evaluate the performance and cost-effectiveness of the proposed architecture using a large-scale dataset of 3D facial meshes.
CONTROLS: Validate the scalability of the proposed architecture against a baseline approach that uses a single GPU or CPU for rigging and animation.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed cloud-based deployment architecture should be able to scale up to large-scale commercial use cases efficiently, but may require further optimizations to achieve the best possible performance and cost-effectiveness.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Leveraging Multi-Task Learning for Joint Facial Mesh Completion and Rigging
PROPOSAL: Train a multi-task model that predicts both completed and rigged facial meshes from a given partial or unrigged input mesh. The model will be composed of a mesh encoder, a patch auto-regressor for completion, and a FACS-action driven mesh transformer for rigging. Use large-scale real-world datasets such as FaceWarehouse, Face2Vid, and an auxiliary 3DMM-based dataset for training and validation.
CONTROLS: Compare against state-of-the-art models for 3DMM fitting and mesh completion, as well as a rigging baseline that uses NFR as a template-based approach.
COST: Estimated 10,000 GPU-hours to train the model using a batch size of 16 on 8 V100 GPUs.
PREDICTION: We expect the multi-task model to outperform the rigging baseline and state-of-the-art models for mesh completion, and establish a new state-of-the-art for 3D facial rigging. Challenges may arise from the quality of the completion results affecting the rigging performance, or overfitting to the training data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: FACS-Aware Disentangled Representation Learning for Facial Rigging
PROPOSAL: Explore disentangled representation learning by introducing a novel FACS-aware modality-agnostic model that learns separate, non-overlapping representations for vertex positions, blendshape offsets, and action units. This will enable effective entity-level manipulation and conditional control over various facial expressions. Train the model using both real-world facial mesh datasets (e.g., FaceWarehouse, Face2Vid) and simulated data generated from blendshape-enabled 3D head models. Compare against a baseline model that uses a single shared representation and separate decoders for blendshape offsets and action units.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the model's performance on standard facial rigging metrics, and compare against state-of-the-art models for facial rigging and representation learning.
COST: Estimated 5,000 GPU-hours to train the model using a batch size of 32 on 4 Tesla V100 GPUs.
PREDICTION: We expect the FACS-aware disentangled model to improve facial rigging performance and flexibility, but may struggle with small training datasets due to overfitting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Learning for Unsupervised Facial Rigging Transfer and Generalization
PROPOSAL: Introduce an unsupervised transfer learning method that leverages an adversarial network to learn a rigging representation that can be transferred across unseen meshes and FACS-based action units. The method will consist of a rigging generator, a discriminator, and a reconstruction losses. Use a self-supervised objective to encourage the generator to produce rigging outputs from seen meshes that resemble unseen ones. Evaluate the generalizability of the learned model using a series of experiments on diverse facial shapes, styles, and topologies from datasets such as FaceWarehouse and Face2Vid.
CONTROLS: Compare the results against state-of-the-art models for facial rigging, transfer learning, and generalization, including our previous proposal "Leveraging Multi-Task Learning for Joint Facial Mesh Completion and Rigging".
COST: Estimated 7,500 GPU-hours to train the model using a batch size of 16 on 6 Tesla V100 GPUs.
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the adversarial learning method will outperform existing methods in terms of unsupervised facial rigging transfer and generalization, but may struggle with very large or complex datasets that are difficult to align across.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Adversarial Learning for Unsupervised Facial Rigging Transfer and Generalization
PROPOSAL: Modify the previous proposal to incorporate a Temporal Coherence Loss, which measures the consistency of the generated rigging outputs across consecutive frames in a video sequence. This will be used in conjunction with the self-supervised objective to encourage the generator to produce smooth and realistic facial movements that respect the temporal dependencies. Use a self-paced learning strategy to adaptively adjust the Temporal Coherence Loss during training, allowing the model to learn rigging representations that can effectively capture both short-term and long-term temporal correlations.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised model against the original adversarial learning method, as well as state-of-the-art models for facial animation and video-based facial expression transfer.
COST: Estimated 8,000 GPU-hours to train the modified model using a batch size of 16 on 6 Tesla V100 GPUs.
PREDICTION: We expect the revised model to improve the quality and coherence of generated facial movements, and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in facial animation and video-based facial expression transfer tasks, while potentially increasing computation and memory requirements due to the added temporal loss.

PREDICTION: We expect the revised model to improve the quality and coherence of generated facial movements, and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in facial animation and video-based facial expression transfer tasks, while potentially increasing computation and memory requirements due to the added temporal loss.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transferable Graph Neural Network for Facial Rigging of Disconnected Components
PROPOSAL: Design a graph-based neural network architecture that can learn to rig facial meshes composed of multiple disconnected components, such as eyeballs, teeth, and lips. The network will learn to partition the mesh into separate subgraphs, each representing a disconnected component, and apply a rigging representation learned from the overall mesh to each subgraph. Train the model using a combination of real-world facial mesh datasets and simulated data generated from 3D head models with varied numbers of disconnected components.
CONTROLS: Compare the model against state-of-the-art methods for facial rigging of disconnected components, and evaluate its ability to animate complex facial expressions on meshes with multiple disconnected components.
COST: Estimated 6,000 GPU-hours to train the model using a batch size of 16 on 5 Tesla V100 GPUs.
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the transferable graph neural network will improve the rigging performance on meshes with disconnected components, but may require significant training data and computational resources to adapt to varying mesh topologies and numbers of disconnected components.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Guided Self-Supervised Learning for FACS Parameter Conversion and Facial Rigging
PROPOSAL: Introduce a guided self-supervised learning framework that converts FACS action units into corresponding blendshape weights and facial rigging parameters. The framework will consist of a FACS-Blendshape Network and a rigid facial mesh generator. The FACS-Blendshape Network will predict blendshape weights for a given FACS action unit, and the facial mesh generator will produce a rigged facial mesh based on these blendshape weights. Train the model using a combination of self-supervised and guided loss functions to learn effective FACS-action unit to blendshape mapping.
CONTROLS: Compare the framework against state-of-the-art methods for FACS parameter conversion and facial rigging, and evaluate its ability to animate complex facial expressions on different facial meshes.
COST: Estimated 9,000 GPU-hours to train the model using a batch size of 16 on 6 Tesla V100 GPUs.
PREDICTION: We expect the guided self-supervised learning framework to improve the conversion accuracy of FACS action units to blendshape weights and facial rigging parameters, leading to better facial rigging performance and more realistic facial animations. Challenges may arise from the lack of labelled datasets for FACS action units and blendshape weights, and the need for a well-designed self-supervised loss function.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Conditional Variational Autoencoder for FACS-Based Facial Rigging and Expression Transfer
PROPOSAL: Design a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) that combines facial rigging and expression transfer under the guidance of FACS action units. The CVAE will consist of an encoder, a decoder, and a conditional bottleneck. The encoder will learn to represent a facial mesh and its corresponding FACS action units, while the decoder will generate a new facial mesh with the target FACS action units. Train the CVAE using a combination of reconstruction loss and adversarial loss to ensure realistic facial rigging and expression transfer.
CONTROLS: Compare the CVAE against state-of-the-art methods for facial rigging and expression transfer, and evaluate its ability to generate realistic and diverse facial expressions under various FACS action units.
COST: Estimated 8,500 GPU-hours to train the CVAE using a batch size of 16 on 6 Tesla V100 GPUs.
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the CVAE will improve facial rigging performance and expression transfer under the guidance of FACS action units, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to balance the reconstruction loss and adversarial loss.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Hybrid Learning for Fast and Accurate Facial Rigging
PROPOSAL: Develop an efficient hybrid learning framework that combines the strengths of different facial rigging approaches to achieve fast and accurate facial rigging. The framework will consist of a lightweight neural network that learns to predict the rigging parameters of a facial mesh, and a high-precision rigging network that refines the predicted rigging parameters. Train the lightweight network using a large dataset of facial meshes with rigging parameters, and use the high-precision network to refine the predicted rigging parameters. Evaluate the performance of the framework using standard facial rigging metrics and compare it against state-of-the-art methods.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the hybrid framework against state-of-the-art methods for facial rigging, and evaluate its ability to achieve fast and accurate facial rigging.
COST: Estimated 7,000 GPU-hours to train the lightweight network using a batch size of 16 on 5 Tesla V100 GPUs.
PREDICTION: We expect the hybrid framework to improve facial rigging performance and efficiency, and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in facial rigging. Challenges may arise from the need to balance the tradeoff between speed and accuracy, and the requirement for a large dataset of facial meshes with rigging parameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-World Evaluation and Comparison of Advanced Facial Rigging Techniques
PROPOSAL: Collect a large dataset of real-world facial meshes from publicly available datasets and evaluate the performance of each of the proposed facial rigging techniques on this new dataset. Compare the performance across different metrics and provide a comprehensive evaluation of the strengths and weaknesses of each approach. Investigate the generalizability of the models to real-world data and explore possible vulnerabilities of each method to specific facial features or expressions.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of each facial rigging technique against state-of-the-art methods on the real-world dataset, and evaluate the implications for real-world applications.
COST: Estimated 1,000 GPU-hours to evaluate the performance of each facial rigging technique on the real-world dataset.
PREDICTION: We expect the real-world evaluation to provide valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of each facial rigging technique and shed light on the potential applications and vulnerabilities of each method.

propositions.prediction: We expect the multi-task model to outperform the rigging baseline and state-of-the-art models for mesh completion, and establish a new state-of-the-art for 3D facial rigging. Challenges may arise from the quality of the completion results affecting the rigging performance, or overfitting to the training data.
propositions.texte: Train a multi-task model that predicts both completed and rigged facial meshes from a given partial or unrigged input mesh. The model will be composed of a mesh encoder, a patch auto-regressor for completion, and a FACS-action driven mesh transformer for rigging. Use large-scale real-world datasets such as FaceWarehouse, Face2Vid, and an auxiliary 3DMM-based dataset for training and validation.
propositions.titre: Leveraging Multi-Task Learning for Joint Facial Mesh Completion and Rigging

propositions.controles: Evaluate the model's performance on standard facial rigging metrics, and compare against state-of-the-art models for facial rigging and representation learning.
propositions.cout_texte: Estimated 5,000 GPU-hours to train the model using a batch size of 32 on 4 Tesla V100 GPUs.
propositions.prediction: We expect the FACS-aware disentangled model to improve facial rigging performance and flexibility, but may struggle with small training datasets due to overfitting.
propositions.texte: Explore disentangled representation learning by introducing a novel FACS-aware modality-agnostic model that learns separate, non-overlapping representations for vertex positions, blendshape offsets, and action units. This will enable effective entity-level manipulation and conditional control over various facial expressions. Train the model using both real-world facial mesh datasets (e.g., FaceWarehouse, Face2Vid) and simulated data generated from blendshape-enabled 3D head models. Compare against a baseline model that uses a single shared representation and separate decoders for blendshape offsets and action units.
propositions.titre: FACS-Aware Disentangled Representation Learning for Facial Rigging

propositions.controles: Compare the revised model against the original adversarial learning method, as well as state-of-the-art models for facial animation and video-based facial expression transfer.
propositions.cout_texte: Estimated 8,000 GPU-hours to train the modified model using a batch size of 16 on 6 Tesla V100 GPUs.
propositions.prediction: We expect the revised model to improve the quality and coherence of generated facial movements, and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in facial animation and video-based facial expression transfer tasks, while potentially increasing computation and memory requirements due to the added temporal loss.
propositions.texte: Modify the previous proposal to incorporate a Temporal Coherence Loss, which measures the consistency of the generated rigging outputs across consecutive frames in a video sequence. This will be used in conjunction with the self-supervised objective to encourage the generator to produce smooth and realistic facial movements that respect the temporal dependencies. Use a self-paced learning strategy to adaptively adjust the Temporal Coherence Loss during training, allowing the model to learn rigging representations that can effectively capture both short-term and long-term temporal correlations.
propositions.titre: Adversarial Learning for Unsupervised Facial Rigging Transfer and Generalization

propositions.controles: Compare the model against state-of-the-art methods for facial rigging of disconnected components, and evaluate its ability to animate complex facial expressions on meshes with multiple disconnected components.
propositions.cout_texte: Estimated 6,000 GPU-hours to train the model using a batch size of 16 on 5 Tesla V100 GPUs.
propositions.prediction: We anticipate that the transferable graph neural network will improve the rigging performance on meshes with disconnected components, but may require significant training data and computational resources to adapt to varying mesh topologies and numbers of disconnected components.
propositions.texte: Design a graph-based neural network architecture that can learn to rig facial meshes composed of multiple disconnected components, such as eyeballs, teeth, and lips. The network will learn to partition the mesh into separate subgraphs, each representing a disconnected component, and apply a rigging representation learned from the overall mesh to each subgraph. Train the model using a combination of real-world facial mesh datasets and simulated data generated from 3D head models with varied numbers of disconnected components.
propositions.titre: Transferable Graph Neural Network for Facial Rigging of Disconnected Components

propositions.controles: Compare the framework against state-of-the-art methods for FACS parameter conversion and facial rigging, and evaluate its ability to animate complex facial expressions on different facial meshes.
propositions.cout_texte: Estimated 9,000 GPU-hours to train the model using a batch size of 16 on 6 Tesla V100 GPUs.
propositions.prediction: We expect the guided self-supervised learning framework to improve the conversion accuracy of FACS action units to blendshape weights and facial rigging parameters, leading to better facial rigging performance and more realistic facial animations. Challenges may arise from the lack of labelled datasets for FACS action units and blendshape weights, and the need for a well-designed self-supervised loss function.
propositions.texte: Introduce a guided self-supervised learning framework that converts FACS action units into corresponding blendshape weights and facial rigging parameters. The framework will consist of a FACS-Blendshape Network and a rigid facial mesh generator. The FACS-Blendshape Network will predict blendshape weights for a given FACS action unit, and the facial mesh generator will produce a rigged facial mesh based on these blendshape weights. Train the model using a combination of self-supervised and guided loss functions to learn effective FACS-action unit to blendshape mapping.
propositions.titre: Guided Self-Supervised Learning for FACS Parameter Conversion and Facial Rigging

propositions.controles: Compare the CVAE against state-of-the-art methods for facial rigging and expression transfer, and evaluate its ability to generate realistic and diverse facial expressions under various FACS action units.
propositions.cout_texte: Estimated 8,500 GPU-hours to train the CVAE using a batch size of 16 on 6 Tesla V100 GPUs.
propositions.prediction: We anticipate that the CVAE will improve facial rigging performance and expression transfer under the guidance of FACS action units, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to balance the reconstruction loss and adversarial loss.
propositions.texte: Design a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) that combines facial rigging and expression transfer under the guidance of FACS action units. The CVAE will consist of an encoder, a decoder, and a conditional bottleneck. The encoder will learn to represent a facial mesh and its corresponding FACS action units, while the decoder will generate a new facial mesh with the target FACS action units. Train the CVAE using a combination of reconstruction loss and adversarial loss to ensure realistic facial rigging and expression transfer.
propositions.titre: Conditional Variational Autoencoder for FACS-Based Facial Rigging and Expression Transfer

propositions.controles: Compare the performance of the hybrid framework against state-of-the-art methods for facial rigging, and evaluate its ability to achieve fast and accurate facial rigging.
propositions.cout_texte: Estimated 7,000 GPU-hours to train the lightweight network using a batch size of 16 on 5 Tesla V100 GPUs.
propositions.prediction: We expect the hybrid framework to improve facial rigging performance and efficiency, and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in facial rigging. Challenges may arise from the need to balance the tradeoff between speed and accuracy, and the requirement for a large dataset of facial meshes with rigging parameters.
propositions.texte: Develop an efficient hybrid learning framework that combines the strengths of different facial rigging approaches to achieve fast and accurate facial rigging. The framework will consist of a lightweight neural network that learns to predict the rigging parameters of a facial mesh, and a high-precision rigging network that refines the predicted rigging parameters. Train the lightweight network using a large dataset of facial meshes with rigging parameters, and use the high-precision network to refine the predicted rigging parameters. Evaluate the performance of the framework using standard facial rigging metrics and compare it against state-of-the-art methods.
propositions.titre: Efficient Hybrid Learning for Fast and Accurate Facial Rigging

propositions.controles: Compare the performance of each facial rigging technique against state-of-the-art methods on the real-world dataset, and evaluate the implications for real-world applications.
propositions.cout_texte: Estimated 1,000 GPU-hours to evaluate the performance of each facial rigging technique on the real-world dataset.
propositions.prediction: We expect the real-world evaluation to provide valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of each facial rigging technique and shed light on the potential applications and vulnerabilities of each method.
propositions.texte: Collect a large dataset of real-world facial meshes from publicly available datasets and evaluate the performance of each of the proposed facial rigging techniques on this new dataset. Compare the performance across different metrics and provide a comprehensive evaluation of the strengths and weaknesses of each approach. Investigate the generalizability of the models to real-world data and explore possible vulnerabilities of each method to specific facial features or expressions.
propositions.titre: Real-World Evaluation and Comparison of Advanced Facial Rigging Techniques

ACTION: ADD
 TITLE: Direct FACS-based Facial Rigging from Unlabeled Neutral Faces
 PROPOSAL: Truncate and train a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) [1] on a large dataset of real-world 3D facial meshes to directly learn a mapping from unlabeled neutral faces to a FACS-based rigid deformable template, from which a complete rig can be synthesized without relying on pre-defined template blendshapes. The VAE encoding and decoding processes serve as a generative model for direct facial rigging, conditioned on the continuous latent space that represents the identity of the subject, sufficiently characterized by shape, expressions, and other high-level features.
 CONTROLS: Train and test a generic autoencoder to serve as a baseline for encoding 3D faces.
 COST: 100 GPU-hours
 PREDICTION: This method should be able to produce subtle and moderate expressions, but may struggle with complex and highly-expressive faces, such as those exhibiting wide mouths, furrowed brows, or superimposed smile and frown.

[1] 'Variational Autoencoder' - Kingma, D. P., & Welling, M. (2013)

This action aims to demonstrate how the use of Variational Autoencoder can fill the gap in direct FACS-based facial rigging from unlabeled neutral faces for 3D avatar and character facial animation.

ACTION: ADD
 TITLE: Enhanced VAE Rigging with Latent Space Refinements
 PROPOSAL: Refine the latent space representation from proposal 1 by incorporating disentangled representations learned from a Factorized Hierarchical Autoencoder (FDHA) [2] to better preserve FACS action unit semantics and accommodate detailed expressions. The FDHA is an extension of VAE that leverages a factorized latent space to maintain relationships between variable independent factors. Use this approach to diminish the loss of FACS expressiveness in the generated deformable template and, ultimately, improve rigging fidelity.
 CONTROLS: Compare the effects on rigging accuracy of ablated VAE models trained without or with the additional FDHA refinements.
 COST: 80 GPU-hours
 PREDICTION: We can expect refined FACS action units to lead to more precise expressions, but dense expression-based poses might benefit from refining a variant that selectively increases variance in expression-based latent components, otherwise, completing superimposed smile and frown action unit might not be easily discernible. 

[2] Factorized Hierarchical Autoencoder - Goyal, P., Gaddam, V., Velankar, H., Prabhu, P., & Alex S, A. (2017)

ACTION: ADD
 TITLE: Combining Locally-Trained VAEs for Intra-Component Rigging
 PROPOSAL: Train separate VAEs on regional portions of the face, such as the eyes, mouth, nose, or cheeks, to capture local geometry and FACS action units. Use these local VAE models to generate a rig for each individual component, and then fuse them together to produce a complete facial rig. This multi-stage approach can better account for the diversity of facial geometries and expressions across a wide range of subjects.
 CONTROLS: Train a single VAE on the entire face as a baseline and compare the performance of the multi-stage approach.
 COST: 150 GPU-hours
 PREDICTION: The combination of local models should lead to more accurate and realistic expressions, especially for complex faces or those with unique features, such as prominent noses or irregular eye shapes. However, managing the interaction between local components might require additional techniques to ensure coherent and natural movement.

ACTION: ADD
 TITLE: FACS-Aware Unsupervised Synthesis of Blendshapes
 PROPOSAL: Use a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) [3] to synthesize blendshapes that are aligned with FACS action units from a collection of synthetic or real-world 3D facial meshes. Train the GAN to capture the spatial relationships between different blendshapes and to preserve the semantic meaning of FACS action units during the generation process. This approach can be used to augment the dataset used for training the VAE-based rigging model, thereby improving its generalization and robustness.
 CONTROLS: Compare the quality of blendshapes generated by the GAN with those obtained using traditional methods, such as photogrammetry or structured light scanning, and evaluate their impact on the performance of the VAE-based rigging model.
 COST: 200 GPU-hours
 PREDICTION: The GAN-based approach should be able to generate realistic and meaningful blendshapes that capture the subtleties of FACS action units, but may struggle with faces that exhibit significant facial asymmetry or those with unusual features, such as prominent scars or facial prosthetics.

[3] 'Generative Adversarial Networks' - Goodfellow, I., Pouget-Abadie, J., Mirza, M., Xu, B., Warde-Farley, D., Ozair, S., ... & Bengio, Y. (2014)

ACTION: ADD
 TITLE: Skeleton-Based Facial Rigging with Graph Convolutions
 PROPOSAL: Use a graph convolutional network (GCN) to learn a mapping from a 3D facial mesh to a FACS-based facial rig, leveraging the skeleton as a structural prior to guide the deformation process. Represent the facial mesh as a graph, where nodes correspond to vertices and edges capture spatial relationships. Use the GCN to convolve over the graph and predict a set of blendshape coefficients that can be used to generate a facial rig.
 CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the GCN-based approach with traditional VAE-based methods and evaluate its ability to generalize across different facial shapes and topologies.
 COST: 250 GPU-hours
 PREDICTION: The GCN-based approach should be able to handle complex facial geometries and topologies more effectively than traditional VAE-based methods, but may require more computational resources and data to train effectively.

ACTION: ADD
 TITLE: Data-Augmentation via 3D Point Cloud Transformation
 PROPOSAL: Apply a variety of 3D point cloud transformations, such as random rotation, scaling, and flipping, to augment the training dataset used for the VAE-based rigging model. These transformations should help increase the diversity of facial geometries and expressions in the dataset, making the model more robust and generalizable to unseen faces.
 CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of different transformation schedules and parameters on the performance of the VAE-based rigging model and compare it with traditional methods that do not use data augmentation.
 COST: 180 GPU-hours
 PREDICTION: The data augmentation technique should improve the generalization and robustness of the VAE-based rigging model, but may require careful tuning of the transformation parameters to avoid over-augmentation, which could lead to decreased performance.

ACTION: ADD
 TITLE: Evaluation Metrics for Facial Rigging Realism and Expressiveness
 PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate a comprehensive set of metrics to assess the realism and expressiveness of facial rigs generated by different methods. These metrics should include both quantitative measures, such as root mean squared error (RMSE) and facial action unit similarity, as well as perceptual metrics, such as crowd-sourced ratings and expert evaluations.
 CONTROLS: Compare the performance of different facial rigging methods using the proposed evaluation metrics and analyze the relationship between the metrics to identify key factors influencing facial rigging realism and expressiveness.
 COST: 100 GPU-hours (evaluation only)
 PREDICTION: The evaluation metrics should provide a more comprehensive understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of different facial rigging methods, helping researchers select the most suitable approach for specific applications and identify areas for further improvement.

ACTION: ADD
 TITLE: Real-World Deployment and Application of Facial Rigging Methods
 PROPOSAL: Evaluate and deploy the most promising facial rigging methods on a large-scale, real-world dataset and apply them to various applications, such as 3D facial animation in movies, video games, and virtual reality. Investigate the challenges and opportunities of integrating facial rigging into existing pipelines and workflows, and identify potential areas for further research and development.
 CONTROLS: Compare the performance of different facial rigging methods on a real-world dataset and gather feedback from industry partners and end-users on the usability and effectiveness of the generated facial rigs.
 COST: 5000 GPU-hours (large-scale evaluation and deployment)
 PREDICTION: The real-world deployment and application of facial rigging methods should demonstrate the practical value and potential of these techniques, identifying areas for further improvement and informing the development of more effective and efficient methods for generating realistic and expressive facial animations.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating the Vulnerability of Unimodal Accuracy to Noise
PROPOSAL: Experimentally compare the vulnerability of unimodal accuracy to noise on a set of real-world datasets (e.g. food classification, social media sentiment analysis, and indoor scene recognition). This will be done using a variety of noise injection methods (e.g. Gaussian noise, salt and pepper noise) and metrics (e.g. means and standard deviations of accuracy across samples and modalities). We will then compare these results against a new metric, Robust Multimodal Accuracy (RMA), which we propose as a robust alternative to traditional accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare against current state-of-the-art methods for detecting modality imbalance and robustness, including confidence-based weighting and modality dropout, on the same datasets.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see that unimodal accuracy is indeed fragile under noise, while RMA exhibits stronger robustness properties. However, there may be some difficulty in calibrating the noise injection methods to achieve a consistent and reliable robust accuracy signal.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Robust Multimodal Accuracy: A Theoretical Framework
PROPOSAL: Develop a theoretical framework for Robust Multimodal Accuracy (RMA), providing a mathematical definition and analysis of its robustness properties. This will involve deriving a robustness bound for RMA using tools from statistical learning theory and proving that this bound is tighter than the analogous bound for traditional accuracy. We will also investigate the regime in which RMA achieves optimal robustness and the role of modality imbalance in this regime.
CONTROLS: Compare the derived bound for RMA against the existing bounds for accuracy through simulations on synthetic datasets and real-world benchmarks (e.g. the datasets used in proposal 1).
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to show that RMA has stronger robustness properties than accuracy, but determining the optimal regime for RMA's robustness may require careful tuning of hyperparameters. However, this framework can be used as a theoretical foundation for proposal 1's empirical evaluation of RMA's robustness.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Modality Dropout on Modality Imbalance
PROPOSAL: Experimentally investigate the impact of modality dropout on modality imbalance in a decision-level fusion system. We will apply modality dropout to various datasets (e.g. food classification, social media sentiment analysis) and measure the resulting modality imbalance using metrics such as difference in accuracy between modalities and RMA. We will also analyze the impact of modality dropout on the fused predictions and robustness of the system.
CONTROLS: Compare against a strong baseline, DropConnect, and an ensemble-based approach for handling modality imbalance.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see that modality dropout can indeed alleviate modality imbalance to some extent, but its effectiveness may vary across different datasets and modalities, and it may come at the cost of some predictive performance loss.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Modality Dropout on Modality Imbalance with Robust Multimodal Accuracy
PROPOSAL: Experimentally investigate the impact of modality dropout on modality imbalance in a decision-level fusion system using Robust Multimodal Accuracy (RMA) as the evaluation metric. We will apply modality dropout to various datasets (e.g. food classification, social media sentiment analysis) and measure the resulting modality imbalance using RMA. We will also analyze the impact of modality dropout on the fused predictions and robustness of the system. Additionally, we will compare the results against the baseline of no modality dropout and other robustness enhancement methods (e.g. confidence-based weighting, ensembling).
CONTROLS: Same as before, with an additional group with no modality dropout (baseline).
COST: 225 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see that modality dropout improves RMA and robustness when modality imbalance is significant, but its effectiveness may vary across different datasets and modalities. It may also introduce some predictive performance loss, particularly when the dropped modalities carry significant information.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: A Novel Modality-Informed Dynamic Late Fusion Framework
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel dynamic late fusion framework that adapts the weights of the individual modality-specific models based on their respective RMA values. This will involve the design of an adaptive weight learning mechanism that leverages the RMA metric to compute the importance of each modality in the fusion process. We will experimentally evaluate the proposed framework on various datasets and show its effectiveness in addressing modality imbalance and improving overall system robustness.
CONTROLS: Compare against state-of-the-art dynamic late fusion baselines, including those employing confidence-based weighting, ensembling, and regularized regression for adaptive weight learning.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see that the proposed modality-informed dynamic late fusion framework significantly improves RMA and robustness across various datasets, particularly for those with severe modality imbalance. However, its performance may degrade when some modalities provide redundant information, potentially affecting the fusion weight learning process.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Uncertainty-Aware Multimodal Fusion with Certified Robustness
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of uncertainty-aware multimodal fusion methods that provide certified robustness guarantees. Specifically, we will apply interval analysis and adversarial training to build a multimodal fusion framework that is robust to both perturbations in the input data and the model's own uncertainty. We will experimentally evaluate the proposed framework on multimodal datasets (e.g. food classification, social media sentiment analysis) and show its effectiveness in achieving robustness and accuracy trade-offs.
CONTROLS: Compare against recent robustness-enhancing multimodal fusion methods, including those employing adversarial training, adversarial attack transferability, and uncertainty-based weighting.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see that the proposed uncertainty-aware multimodal fusion framework significantly improves robustness to perturbations and model uncertainty, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy-robustness trade-offs on multimodal datasets. However, its computational cost may be higher due to the incorporation of interval analysis and adversarial training.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating the Vulnerability of Robust Multimodal Accuracy to Noise
PROPOSAL: Re-examine the vulnerability of Robust Multimodal Accuracy (RMA) to noise, building upon the theoretical framework established in proposal 2. We will experimentally compare the robustness of RMA to noise with that of traditional accuracy and other robustness-enhancing multimodal fusion methods (e.g. uncertainty-aware fusion, confidence-based weighting). We will also investigate the effects of different noise types (e.g. Gaussian, salt and pepper), noise levels, and data sizes on RMA's robustness properties.
CONTROLS: Same as before, with an additional comparison group using uncertainty-aware multimodal fusion methods.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see that RMA exhibits stronger robustness properties than traditional accuracy, but its robustness may still degrade under high-noise conditions. The results will provide valuable insights for future work on developing more robust multimodal fusion frameworks.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Multimodal Outlier Detection for Enhancing Robustness
PROPOSAL: Investigate the development of multimodal outlier detection methods to enhance the robustness of multimodal fusion systems. We will explore several outlier detection techniques (e.g. statistical outliers, neural network-based methods, uncertainty-aware methods) and evaluate their effectiveness in rejecting outliers and improving system robustness. We will also analyze the impact of outlier detection on the performance of multimodal fusion methods and investigate strategies for integrating outlier detection into existing robustness-enhancing methods (e.g. RMA, uncertainty-aware fusion).
CONTROLS: Compare against existing outlier detection methods and robustness-enhancing multimodal fusion methods.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see that multimodal outlier detection methods can significantly enhance the robustness of multimodal fusion systems, but the choice of detection technique and integration strategy will have a substantial impact on performance.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Towards Generalizable Multimodal Robustness: Transfer Learning and Domain Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Explore the application of transfer learning and domain adaptation techniques to enhance the robustness and generalizability of multimodal fusion systems across different domains and datasets. We will experimentally evaluate the effectiveness of several transfer learning and domain adaptation methods (e.g. fine-tuning,/domain adaptation) on various multimodal datasets (e.g. food classification, social media sentiment analysis) and analyze the impact of domain shift on system performance.
CONTROLS: Compare against existing transfer learning and domain adaptation methods for multimodal fusion.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see that transfer learning and domain adaptation can improve the robustness and generalizability of multimodal fusion systems, but the choice of adaptation method and hyperparameters will have a significant impact on performance.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Real-World Multimodal Robustness Evaluation: A Large-Scale Study
PROPOSAL: Conduct a large-scale real-world evaluation of the proposed robustness-enhancing multimodal fusion methods on a diverse set of practical datasets and tasks (e.g. food classification, social media sentiment analysis, visual question answering). We will assess the performance of each method on a range of metrics, including accuracy, robustness, and generalizability, and analyze the results in the context of real-world application scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare against existing real-world multimodal fusion methods and baselines.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see that the proposed robustness-enhancing methods significantly improve the performance and robustness of multimodal fusion systems in real-world scenarios, but the choice of method and hyperparameters will have a substantial impact on performance.
