actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effects of Modality Dropout on Late Fusion
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of late fusion with and without modality dropout on a set of benchmark multimodal tasks. Use real-world datasets including food classification from recipe image-text pairs, social media image-text sentiment analysis, and indoor scene recognition from RGB-D images. Implement modality dropout by randomly dropping one or more modalities during training, and evaluate the effect on performance and robustness to input perturbations. 
CONTROLS: Compare to static late fusion and individual unimodal baselines, and ablate the modality dropout mechanism to evaluate its contribution.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Modality dropout may help stability to some extent by forcing the system to take weak modality information into account, but may also harm robustness and downstream performance in some cases where the removed modalities were actually necessary for success, particularly on more challenging benchmarks such as indoor scene recognition.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Knowledge Distillation for Multimodal Fusion
PROPOSAL: Develop an adaptive knowledge distillation method for multimodal fusion, where the strong modality acts as the teacher and the weak modality as the student, but with an adaptive weighting scheme that allows the distillation to occur across modalities in different proportions. Implement the method on several real-world tasks such as multimodal video sentiment analysis, math word problem question answering, and visual question answering, using datasets from these domains. Evaluate the method's performance and robustness on these tasks, and compare to standard knowledge distillation and static late fusion baselines.
CONTROLS: Compare to standard knowledge distillation and static late fusion, and ablate the adaptive weighting scheme to evaluate its contribution.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Adaptive knowledge distillation may help to transfer knowledge from strong to weak modalities more effectively, reducing the performance gap between modalities, but may also require careful tuning of the adaptive weighting scheme to find the optimal balance between modalities and avoid overfitting to any one modality's strengths.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Investigating the Effects of Modality Dropout on Late Fusion
PROPOSAL: Refine the modality dropout mechanism by incorporating a modality selection step, where the model decides which modality to drop based on the input sample's characteristics, such as noise level or modality confidence. This is done by incorporating an additional classification head that predicts the modality most suitable for the input sample, and using that as a target for the modality dropout decision. Implement the revised modality dropout on a set of benchmark multimodal tasks, including audio-visual emotion recognition and multimodal video sentiment analysis, using real-world datasets from these domains. Evaluate the effect on performance and robustness to input perturbations.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original modality dropout mechanism and ablate the modality selection step to evaluate its contribution.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised modality dropout mechanism with modality selection may help to adapt the system to changing input conditions, such as varying noise levels, and improve robustness, but may also require careful tuning to avoid overfitting to specific input characteristics.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Modality Imbalance Detection using Regularization-based Methods
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate a set of regularization-based methods, including L1, L2, and elastic net regularization, to detect modality imbalance in late fusion systems. Implement the methods on a variety of real-world multimodal tasks, such as food classification from recipe image-text pairs and social media image-text sentiment analysis, using datasets from these domains. Evaluate the methods' performance in detecting modality imbalance and their impact on system performance and robustness.
CONTROLS: Compare to standard methods for detecting modality imbalance, such as unimodal prediction accuracy, and ablate the regularization techniques to evaluate their contribution.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Regularization-based methods may help to identify and mitigate modality imbalance, leading to improved system performance and robustness, but may also require careful tuning to avoid over-regularization and performance degradation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unimodal Uncertainty-aware Late Fusion for Robust Multimodal Prediction
PROPOSAL: Develop a unimodal uncertainty-aware late fusion approach that incorporates uncertainty estimates from individual modalities into the fusion process. Use a Bayesian neural network (BNN) to estimate the uncertainty of each modality's predictions, and modify the late fusion formula to give more weight to modalities with higher uncertainty. Evaluate the approach on real-world multimodal tasks, including multimodal video sentiment analysis and math word problem question answering, using datasets from these domains. Compare to standard late fusion and unimodal baselines.
CONTROLS: Compare to standard late fusion and unimodal uncertainty-aware approaches, and ablate the uncertainty estimates to evaluate their contribution.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The unimodal uncertainty-aware late fusion approach may help to improve the robustness of the system by giving more weight to modalities with higher uncertainty, but may also require careful tuning to avoid over-weighting of uncertain modalities, and may not capture all sources of uncertainty in the system.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Guarantees for Robust Late Fusion
PROPOSAL: Provide theoretical guarantees on the robustness of late fusion systems under certain conditions. Specifically, derive bounds on the robustness of late fusion to input perturbations, assuming that the individual modalities are robust to these perturbations. Use techniques from robust optimization and learning theory to establish these bounds, and explore the relationship between modality imbalance, robustness, and the quality of the individual modalities.
CONTROLS: None
COST: negligible (theoretical analysis)
PREDICTION: The theoretical guarantees may provide insights into the limitations of late fusion systems and the importance of modality imbalance, but may not directly translate to practical solutions or improvements in real-world systems.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multimodal Hierarchical Fusion for Modality Imbalance Mitigation
PROPOSAL: Develop a hierarchical fusion approach that hierarchically integrates information from multiple modalities, first considering the relationships between modalities at a coarse level, and then refining the fusion at a finer level. Use graph neural networks to model the relationships between modalities, and iterate the fusion process multiple times to capture modality interactions at different scales. Evaluate the approach on a set of benchmark multimodal tasks, including food classification from recipe image-text pairs and social media image-text sentiment analysis, using datasets from these domains.
CONTROLS: Compare to standard late fusion and unimodal baselines, and ablate the hierarchical fusion mechanism to evaluate its contribution.
COST: 240 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The hierarchical fusion approach may help to capture complex interactions between modalities and mitigate modality imbalance, but may also require careful tuning of hyperparameters and model architecture to avoid over-complexity and under-performance.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Investigating the Effects of Modality Dropout on Late Fusion
PROPOSAL: Modify the modality dropout mechanism to adaptively drop modalities based on their uncertainty estimates, rather than randomly dropping them. This is done by incorporating an additional uncertainty estimation component that predicts the uncertainty of each modality, and using that to decide which modalities to drop during training. Evaluate the revised modality dropout on a set of benchmark multimodal tasks, including multimodal video sentiment analysis and math word problem question answering, using datasets from these domains. Compare to the original modality dropout mechanism and other baselines.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original modality dropout mechanism, and ablate the uncertainty-based modality dropout to evaluate its contribution.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised modality dropout mechanism with uncertainty-based dropping may help to further improve the robustness of late fusion systems by accounting for the uncertainty of each modality, but may also require careful tuning to avoid over-dropping of important modalities.

PROPOSAL 1: Investigating the Effects of Modality Dropout on Late Fusion
Compare the performance of late fusion with and without modality dropout on a set of benchmark multimodal tasks. Use real-world datasets including food classification from recipe image-text pairs, social media image-text sentiment analysis, and indoor scene recognition from RGB-D images. Implement modality dropout by randomly dropping one or more modalities during training, and evaluate the effect on performance and robustness to input perturbations.
Controls: Compare to static late fusion and individual unimodal baselines, and ablate the modality dropout mechanism to evaluate its contribution.
Estimated cost: 100 GPU-hours
Prediction: Modality dropout may help stability to some extent by forcing the system to take weak modality information into account, but may also harm robustness and downstream performance in some cases where the removed modalities were actually necessary for success, particularly on more challenging benchmarks such as indoor scene recognition.

PROPOSAL 2: Adaptive Knowledge Distillation for Multimodal Fusion
Develop an adaptive knowledge distillation method for multimodal fusion, where the strong modality acts as the teacher and the weak modality as the student, but with an adaptive weighting scheme that allows the distillation to occur across modalities in different proportions. Implement the method on several real-world tasks such as multimodal video sentiment analysis, math word problem question answering, and visual question answering, using datasets from these domains. Evaluate the method's performance and robustness on these tasks, and compare to standard knowledge distillation and static late fusion baselines.
Controls: Compare to standard knowledge distillation and static late fusion, and ablate the adaptive weighting scheme to evaluate its contribution.
Estimated cost: 150 GPU-hours
Prediction: Adaptive knowledge distillation may help to transfer knowledge from strong to weak modalities more effectively, reducing the performance gap between modalities, but may also require careful tuning of the adaptive weighting scheme to find the optimal balance between modalities and avoid overfitting to any one modality's strengths.

PROPOSAL 3: Evaluating Modality Imbalance Detection using Regularization-based Methods
Develop and evaluate a set of regularization-based methods, including L1, L2, and elastic net regularization, to detect modality imbalance in late fusion systems. Implement the methods on a variety of real-world multimodal tasks, such as food classification from recipe image-text pairs and social media image-text sentiment analysis, using datasets from these domains. Evaluate the methods' performance in detecting modality imbalance and their impact on system performance and robustness.
Controls: Compare to standard methods for detecting modality imbalance, such as unimodal prediction accuracy, and ablate the regularization techniques to evaluate their contribution.
Estimated cost: 90 GPU-hours
Prediction: Regularization-based methods may help to identify and mitigate modality imbalance, leading to improved system performance and robustness, but may also require careful tuning to avoid over-regularization and performance degradation.

PROPOSAL 4: Unimodal Uncertainty-aware Late Fusion for Robust Multimodal Prediction
Develop a unimodal uncertainty-aware late fusion approach that incorporates uncertainty estimates from individual modalities into the fusion process. Use a Bayesian neural network (BNN) to estimate the uncertainty of each modality's predictions, and modify the late fusion formula to give more weight to modalities with higher uncertainty. Evaluate the approach on real-world multimodal tasks, including multimodal video sentiment analysis and math word problem question answering, using datasets from these domains. Compare to standard late fusion and unimodal baselines.
Controls: Compare to standard late fusion and unimodal uncertainty-aware approaches, and ablate the uncertainty estimates to evaluate their contribution.
Estimated cost: 180 GPU-hours
Prediction: The unimodal uncertainty-aware late fusion approach may help to improve the robustness of the system by giving more weight to modalities with higher uncertainty, but may also require careful tuning to avoid over-weighting of uncertain modalities, and may not capture all sources of uncertainty in the system.

PROPOSAL 5: Theoretical Guarantees for Robust Late Fusion
Provide theoretical guarantees on the robustness of late fusion systems under certain conditions. Specifically, derive bounds on the robustness of late fusion to input perturbations, assuming that the individual modalities are robust to these perturbations. Use techniques from robust optimization and learning theory to establish these bounds, and explore the relationship between modality imbalance, robustness, and the quality of the individual modalities.
Controls: None
Estimated cost: negligible (theoretical analysis)
Prediction: The theoretical guarantees may provide insights into the limitations of late fusion systems and the importance of modality imbalance, but may not directly translate to practical solutions or improvements in real-world systems.

PROPOSAL 6: Multimodal Hierarchical Fusion for Modality Imbalance Mitigation
Develop a hierarchical fusion approach that hierarchically integrates information from multiple modalities, first considering the relationships between modalities at a coarse level, and then refining the fusion at a finer level. Use graph neural networks to model the relationships between modalities, and iterate the fusion process multiple times to capture modality interactions at different scales. Evaluate the approach on a set of benchmark multimodal tasks, including food classification from recipe image-text pairs and social media image-text sentiment analysis, using datasets from these domains.
Controls: Compare to standard late fusion and unimodal baselines, and ablate the hierarchical fusion mechanism to evaluate its contribution.
Estimated cost: 240 GPU-hours
Prediction: The hierarchical fusion approach may help to capture complex interactions between modalities and mitigate modality imbalance, but may also require careful tuning of hyperparameters and model architecture to avoid over-complexity and under-performance.

Controls: Compare to standard late fusion and unimodal baselines, and ablate the transfer learning mechanism to evaluate its contribution.

Prediction: Transfer learning may help to improve the performance and adaptability of multimodal fusion systems, but may also require careful tuning of hyperparameters and adaptation time to achieve optimal results.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Learning Modality Weights through Gaussian Process-based Mutual Information Maximization
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel method to learn modality weights for late fusion using Gaussian Process (GP) based mutual information maximization. The goal is to maximize the mutual information between the combined modality features and the target variable while encouraging the exploration-exploitation trade-off in modality weighting to improve robustness. We will use the GP to learn a density ratio estimator of the target variable given the combined modality features and the product of modality-specific density ratios. The modality weights will be determined through maximizing the mutual information between the combined modality features and the target variable.
CONTROLS: Comparison with traditional mutual information maximization methods like confidence-based weighting and uncertainty-based weighting.
COST: Estimated 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected improvement in robustness and modality balancing, but the method may struggle with high-dimensional modality features, leading to overfitting.

This proposal lays the foundation for learning modality weights through a novel GP-based approach that can encourage modality exploration and exploitation for improved robustness in late fusion.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Exploring Robust Modality Selection using Adversarial Training
PROPOSAL: In a companion work, we will use adversarial training to select robust modality representations that can generalize well under noisy and imbalanced conditions. Specifically, we will train a generator to produce modality features that are indistinguishable from clean modality features, while a discriminator aims to distinguish between clean and adversarial modality features. This process will lead to robust modality representations that are less sensitive to input perturbations. We will use these robust modality representations to reassess the performance of existing modality imbalance remedies.
CONTROLS: Ablation study on the role of interleaved training between generator and discriminator, and comparison with traditional data augmentation methods.
COST: Estimated 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected improvement in robustness under noisy conditions, but potential overfitting to specific types of adversarial attacks.

This proposal aims to provide a companion work to the previous proposal, focusing on selecting robust modality representations through adversarial training. This will help assess the performance of existing modality imbalance remedies under more robust conditions.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Learning Modality Weights through Gaussian Process-based Mutual Information Maximization with Adversarial Robustness
PROPOSAL: We revise the previous proposal to incorporate adversarial robustness into the learning of modality weights. Specifically, we will use a minimax approach to jointly maximize the mutual information between the combined modality features and the target variable while minimizing the difference between the modality weights learned from clean and adversarial modality features. This will encourage the modality weights to be robust to input perturbations and improve the overall robustness of the late fusion system.
CONTROLS: Comparison with the baseline GP-based mutual information maximization and the adversarial training approach proposed in revision 2.
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours (due to the added complexity of the minimax approach)
PREDICTION: Expected improvement in robustness and modality balancing, but potential complexity and computational overhead.

This revised proposal combines the two previous ideas, leveraging the strengths of both to improve the overall robustness of the late fusion system.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Evaluating the Distinctiveness of Weak Modalities
PROPOSAL: We propose to investigate the distinctiveness of weak modalities by using domain-invariant feature learning to preserve the information unique to each modality. Specifically, we will use a domain-invariant neural network architecture to learn a common representation across modalities that captures the underlying relationships between modalities. We will evaluate the performance of each modality in the common representation to identify which modalities contribute unique information.
CONTROLS: Comparison with traditional modality importance measures and ablation study on the role of domain-invariant feature learning.
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected insight into the unique contributions of weak modalities, but potential challenge in learning useful domain-invariant features.

This proposal aims to investigate the distinctiveness of weak modalities and provide insight into their unique contributions.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Evaluating the Distinctiveness of Weak Modalities using Bayesian Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: We revise proposal 3 to use Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) to learn a probabilistic representation of the distinctiveness of weak modalities. Specifically, we will use a BNN to model the uncertainty of the modality importance measures, which will allow us to quantify the confidence in the distinctiveness of each modality. We will then evaluate the performance of each modality in the BNN to identify which modalities contribute unique information.
CONTROLS: Comparison with traditional modality importance measures, ablation study on the role of BNNs, and evaluation of the impact of uncertainty quantification.
COST: Estimated 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected improvement in distinctiveness evaluation and uncertainty quantification, but potential increase in computational complexity.

This revised proposal aims to increase the accuracy and reliability of the distinctiveness evaluation by incorporating Bayesian neural networks, which can provide probabilistic uncertainty measurements.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Late Fusion with learnable Memory-Augmented Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: We propose to investigate the use of memory-augmented neural networks (MANNs) for late fusion. Specifically, we will equip a neural network with a learnable memory component that can selectively store and retrieve information from individual modalities. This will enable the network to learn how to balance the information from different modalities and improve its robustness to noise and imbalanced data.
CONTROLS: Comparison with traditional late fusion methods and ablation study on the role of the learnable memory component.
COST: Estimated 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected improvement in robustness and performance under imbalanced conditions, but potential challenge in learning effective memory components.

This proposal aims to investigate the use of memory-augmented neural networks for late fusion, which can potentially improve the robustness and performance of the fusion approach.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Exploring Robust Modality Selection using Diverse Adversarial Training
PROPOSAL: We revise proposal 2 to use diverse adversarial training to select robust modality representations. Specifically, we will generate a diverse set of adversarial examples by varying the input perturbations, modalities, and data augmentation strategies. We will then use a single neural network to select robust modality representations that are robust across the diverse set of adversarial examples. This will enable the network to learn more generalizable and robust modality representations.
CONTROLS: Comparison with traditional adversarial training methods, ablation study on the role of diverse adversarial examples, and evaluation of the impact of diversity on modality selection.
COST: Estimated 350 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected improvement in robustness and generalizability of modality selection, but potential increase in computational complexity.

This revised proposal aims to increase the robustness and generalizability of modality selection by using diverse adversarial training, which can generate more robust and diverse modality representations.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Theoretical Bounds on Modality Imbalance in Late Fusion
PROPOSAL: We propose to derive theoretical bounds on the impact of modality imbalance on the performance of late fusion. Specifically, we will use the PAC-Bayes framework to analyze the expected generalization error of late fusion in the presence of modality imbalance. We will derive bounds on the impact of modality imbalance on the generalization error and explore the trade-offs between the tightness of the bounds and the computational complexity of the analysis.
CONTROLS: Comparison with existing theoretical bounds on modality imbalance and evaluation of the impact of different assumptions on the bounds.
COST: Estimated 50 GPU-hours (theoretical analysis only)
PREDICTION: Expected improvement in understanding the impact of modality imbalance on late fusion performance, but potential challenges in deriving tight and computationally efficient bounds.

This proposal aims to provide a theoretical foundation for understanding the impact of modality imbalance on late fusion performance, and to derive bounds on the impact of modality imbalance on the generalization error.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Theoretical Bounds on Modality Imbalance in Late Fusion with Optimal Weighting
PROPOSAL: We revise proposal 5 to derive theoretical bounds on the impact of modality imbalance on the performance of late fusion with optimal weighting. Specifically, we will use the Alon-Zaxinov framework to analyze the expected generalization error of late fusion with optimal weighting in the presence of modality imbalance. We will derive bounds on the impact of modality imbalance on the generalization error and explore the trade-offs between the tightness of the bounds and the computational complexity of the analysis.
CONTROLS: Comparison with existing theoretical bounds on modality imbalance and evaluation of the impact of different assumptions on the bounds.
COST: Estimated 75 GPU-hours (theoretical analysis only)
PREDICTION: Expected improvement in understanding the impact of modality imbalance on late fusion performance with optimal weighting, but potential challenges in deriving tight and computationally efficient bounds.

This revised proposal aims to provide a more refined understanding of the impact of modality imbalance on late fusion performance with optimal weighting, and to derive bounds on the impact of modality imbalance on the generalization error.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Experiments with Real-World Multimodal Datasets
PROPOSAL: We propose to conduct exhaustive experiments on real-world multimodal datasets from various domains, including food classification from recipe image-text pairs, social media image-text sentiment analysis, indoor scene recognition from RGB-D images, audio-visual emotion recognition, multimodal video sentiment analysis, math word problem question answering, and visual question answering. We will apply and compare the methods proposed in the previous experiments to evaluate their effectiveness in real-world scenarios and identify the most promising approaches for future research.
CONTROLS: Comparison of all methods on each dataset, and ablation study on the impact of domain and dataset characteristics on the performance of each method.
COST: Estimated 1,500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected comprehensive evaluation of the proposed methods in real-world scenarios, but potential variability in performance across different domains and datasets.

This final proposal aims to apply and evaluate the proposed methods in real-world scenarios across various domains and datasets, providing a comprehensive understanding of their effectiveness in practical applications.

ACTION: ADD 1

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Per-Channel, Context-Dependent Indexing with Hierarchical Attention
PROPOSAL: Build upon causal softmax attention to introduce a hierarchical attention mechanism with two levels of indexing: a bottom-up level using channel-wise separable linear mixing and a top-down level employing token-wise softmax selection, targeting per-channel, context-dependent retrieval from memory. This hierarchy separates the benefits of channel-wise structure with the benefits of causal parallelism.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard causal softmax attention and a channel-wise synchronous version; evaluate the performance on a range of sequence modeling tasks, including but not limited to weather forecasting and electricity transformer load forecasting.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Demonstrating improved performance on tasks requiring nuanced per-channel signal retrieval, such as temperature forecasting from solar power data, while maintaining efficient parallel computation. However, could fail to scale for very large sequence lengths due to increased complexity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Hierarchical Attention with Truncated Orthogonal Parametrization
PROPOSAL: Modify the hierarchical attention mechanism by employing truncated orthogonal parametrization (TOP) for the linear mixing within the bottom-up level, allowing for more efficient computation and reduced parameter usage. Introduce an orthogonal transformation matrix $U$ such that the linear mixing is represented as $O=\mathrm{diag}(V) U \alpha$, where $V$ is a diagonal matrix of full-size keys, $\alpha$ is the top-down token-wise softmax selection, and $U$ is a sparse orthogonal transformation matrix with a small, sparse, and diagonalizable form. This form helps in truncating the learned orthogonal matrices and reduce the parameter and computational costs, while selecting different channels around each point in space in parallel.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of TOP-based hierarchical attention in conjunction with separate hierarchical attention against the original hierarchical attention mechanism as described in experiment 1, on a variety of sequence modeling tasks including language modeling, weather forecasting, and time series forecasting.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: TOP-based hierarchical attention demonstrates similarly improved performance on tasks requiring nuanced per-channel signal retrieval while reducing computational costs.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Exploring Per-Channel, Context-Dependent Indexing with Hierarchical Attention
PROPOSAL: Revise experiment 1 by substituting the bottom-up token-wise softmax selection with the hierarchical mechanism from experiment 2, resulting in a hierarchical attention structure with two levels of token-wise and channel-wise selection, and exploring the benefits of TOP-based truncated orthogonal parametrization for the linear mixing within the bottom-up level. Investigate the cross-reinforcement between these hierarchical selection mechanisms, hoping to improve efficiency, and sequence modeling performance.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original hierarchical attention as well as the linear hierarchical attention without TOP.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Resulting architecture should show improvement over previous versions due to better resource usage in hierarchical structure through parametrization truncation while efficiently allowing context-dependent retrieval; potential drop in performance when task complexity is higher.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Per-Channel Causal Attention with Indefinite Context
PROPOSAL: Introduce a new variant of causal attention where the output of each query is a weighted sum of values from the context, but instead of sharing the same weights across all channels, we assign a different set of weights for each channel. This allows for per-channel, context-dependent selection from memory. We will implement this with a novel combination of linear-time causal attention and permutation-invariant operations.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing causal attention variants, and ablate to linear-time causal attention and permutation-invariant operations separately.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in long-range modeling, particularly in tasks with non-sequential or irregular timestep indexing, such as multivariate time series modeling and weather forecasting. However, we also anticipate potential challenges in training stability due to the increased capacity of the model.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revised: Per-Channel Causal Attention with Indefinite Context
PROPOSAL: To mitigate the potential training stability issues mentioned in turn 1, we will.modify the proposal to add a regularization term that penalizes the difference between the channel-wise weights. This regularization term will help to encourage the model to share knowledge across channels, preventing it from over-specializing on individual channels. We will also introduce a new hyperparameter to control the strength of this regularization, allowing us to trade off between per-channel expressivity and model stability.
CONTROLS: Compare to original proposal, and ablate the regularization term and the hyperparameter separately.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the revised proposal to be more stable and effective in practice, with improved results in tasks such as weather forecasting and solar power forecasting. However, we also anticipate the potential for over-smoothing in cases where strict regularization is applied.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigation of Regularization Mechanisms for Per-Channel Causal Attention
PROPOSAL: Instead of applying a single regularization mechanism, we will investigate a suite of techniques to regularize the per-channel causal attention model. These include L1 and L2 regularization, dropout, and early stopping. We will also experiment with adaptive regularization schemes, such as learning rate schedules and gradient penalties, to improve the stability and convergence of the model.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original per-channel causal attention model, and ablate each regularization mechanism separately to understand their individual effects.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that different regularization schemes have varying effects on the model's performance and stability, and that a combination of techniques may yield the best results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Mixture of Experts for Per-Channel Causal Attention
PROPOSAL: To further improve the performance of per-channel causal attention, we will modify the model to use a mixture of experts approach. This will involve learning a set of auxiliary models, each of which is responsible for a different subset of channels. The output of the model will be a weighted combination of the outputs of these auxiliary models. We will use a gating mechanism to select the weights for each channel, allowing the model to adapt to the specific needs of each channel.
CONTROLS: Compare to the standard per-channel causal attention model and the investigation of regularization mechanisms. Ablate the mixture of experts approach to understand its individual contribution.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the mixture of experts approach to improve the model's performance on tasks with highly varying channel dynamics, such as solar power forecasting and electricity transformer load forecasting. However, we also anticipate potential challenges in training and selecting the auxiliary models.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Improved Mixture of Experts for Per-Channel Causal Attention
PROPOSAL: To improve the mixture of experts approach for per-channel causal attention, we will modify the gating mechanism to use a learned neural network instead of a fixed function. This will allow the model to adapt the weights for each channel based on the specific input sequence, rather than relying on a fixed heuristics. We will also introduce a new training objective to encourage the model to learn multiple distinct experts.
CONTROLS: Compare to the standard mixture of experts approach and ablate the learned neural network gating mechanism and the new training objective separately.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the improved mixture of experts approach to improve the model's performance on tasks with highly varying channel dynamics, while also reducing the risk of over-specialization and improving the interpretability of the model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Knowledge Distillation for Per-Channel Causal Attention
PROPOSAL: To improve the performance of per-channel causal attention on resource-constrained devices, we will implement knowledge distillation to compress the model into a smaller version with reduced capacity. This will involve training a smaller model to mimic the behavior of the larger model, while retaining the key features of the per-channel causal attention mechanism. We will use a combination of distillation loss and pruning to optimize the smaller model.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original per-channel causal attention model and ablate the distillation loss and pruning techniques separately.
COST: 160 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the distilled model to retain a significant portion of the performance of the original model, while being significantly smaller and more efficient. However, we also anticipate potential trade-offs in terms of trainability and robustness.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigation of Regularization Mechanisms for Per-Channel Causal Attention: A Deeper Exploration
PROPOSAL: To complement the improved mixture of experts approach, we will revisit the investigation of regularization mechanisms for per-channel causal attention with a more nuanced approach. We will use a hierarchical regularization schedule to adapt the regularization strength based on the training phase, and explore techniques such as spectral normalization and clipping to improve the stability and convergence of the model.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original investigation of regularization mechanisms and ablate each new regularization technique separately.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the refined investigation to provide a deeper understanding of the effects of regularization on the per-channel causal attention model, and identify new opportunities for improving its performance and stability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Per-Channel Causal Attention with Hierarchical Memory
PROPOSAL: To improve the long-range modeling capabilities of per-channel causal attention, we will introduce a hierarchical memory mechanism to store and retrieve information at multiple scales. This will involve using a stack of memory layers, each with its own attention mechanism and capacity, to store information at different levels of abstraction. We will use a hierarchical attention mechanism to select the most relevant information from each memory layer.
CONTROLS: Compare to the standard per-channel causal attention model and ablate the hierarchical memory mechanism and the hierarchical attention mechanism separately.
COST: 240 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the hierarchical memory mechanism to improve the model's performance on tasks with complex long-range dependencies, such as weather forecasting and multivariate time series modeling.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluation of Per-Channel Causal Attention on Real-World Benchmarks
PROPOSAL: To evaluate the effectiveness of per-channel causal attention on real-world benchmarks, we will conduct experiments on a range of tasks including weather forecasting, solar power forecasting, and electricity transformer load forecasting. We will compare the performance of per-channel causal attention to state-of-the-art baselines and existing attention mechanisms.
CONTROLS: Compare to state-of-the-art baselines and existing attention mechanisms, and ablate each component of per-channel causal attention separately.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in the performance of per-channel causal attention on real-world benchmarks, and demonstrate its effectiveness on a range of tasks. However, we also anticipate potential challenges in adapting the model to different domains and tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Comprehensive Evaluation of Per-Channel Causal Attention on Real-World Benchmarks with Robustness and Transferability Analysis
PROPOSAL: To provide a more comprehensive evaluation of per-channel causal attention, we will extend the evaluation on real-world benchmarks to include robustness and transferability analysis. We will assess the model's performance on perturbed inputs, noisy data, and out-of-distribution examples, as well as its ability to transfer to new domains and tasks. We will also investigate the impact of hyperparameter tuning, pre-training, and fine-tuning on the model's performance and robustness.
CONTROLS: Compare to state-of-the-art baselines and existing attention mechanisms, and ablate each component of per-channel causal attention separately for robustness and transferability analysis.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in the performance and robustness of per-channel causal attention on real-world benchmarks, and demonstrate its effectiveness on a range of tasks and domains.

We will also investigate the impact of hyperparameter tuning, pre-training, and fine-tuning on the model's performance and robustness.
propositions.titre: Comprehensive Evaluation of Per-Channel Causal Attention on Real-World Benchmarks with Robustness and Transferability Analysis

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Local-MPP (Multi-Peak Periodicity) Robust Reconstruction for UTS
PROPOSAL: We propose the Local-MPP variant of the Multivariate Gaussian Process (MGP) reconstruction method, which focuses on robustly estimating local trends in UTS while handling the evolution of periodic patterns. Local-MPP models UTS as a weighted sum of periodic components with dynamic frequency and amplitude, using an OOD directory-free normalizing flow estimator for the mixture weights. 
CONTROLS: We compare Local-MPP against the original MGP and an input SVD-filter for reconstruction as baselines, and in addition, propose two ablations: removing the normalizing flow or the mixture weights from the Local-MPP model. 
COST: 10 hours
PREDICTION: We expect Local-MPP to improve reconstruction accuracy on real-world UTS by 15-20% compared to MGP, and perform within 2% of the SVD-filter baseline; it may struggle with extremely long-term noise periods, and with small datasets where normalizing flow estimation is unstable.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: TinySeq: A Lightweight Transformer-Based Predictor for UTS
PROPOSAL: TinySeq is a pruned variant of the standard Transformer architecture, designed for efficient anomaly detection in UTS without sacrificing performance on small point and slowly rising anomalies. The model introduces a "long-range" self-attention mechanism that approximates complex temporal context with fewer parameters, combined with gated recurrent units (GRUs) to handle varying anomaly scales. We also introduce a learnable dynamic periodic component using second-order spectral features from reconstructed values.
CONTROLS: We compare the results of TinySeq against the vanilla Transformer and its original pill recurrent version as baseline, and ablate the dynamic periodic component for control over its benefits. Additionally, we use three different descending blockwise adaptation varieties to alter the level of trimming TinySeq undergoes, to determine the transpose costs of its parameterized values when these varieties perform in overactive compelling conditions.
COST: 12 hours
PREDICTION: We expect TinySeq to be faster than the standard Transformer while reducing the detection accuracy by 2-3%, possibly with wide memory thresholding in roadmap functions.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: TinySeq: A Lightweight Transformer-Based Predictor for UTS
REVISED PROPOSAL: We refine TinySeq by incorporating a learned masking scheme that adapts to the series' spectral features, and a modified Dynamic Periodic Component (DPC) that uses a time-dependent weighted sum of LTI filters to represent the varying frequencies in the series. Additionally, we introduce a temporal causal attention mechanism that weights the influence of previous time steps based on historical changes in the series' periodic patterns.
CONTROLS: We compare TinySeq against the original Transformer and its pill version as baseline, and also experiment with two ablations: 1) removing the learned masking scheme, and 2) replacing the DPC with a static parameterization of the series' periodic components.
COST: 13 hours
PREDICTION: We expect TinySeq to outperform the baseline Transformers by 5-8% in anomaly detection accuracy, and to be more robust to varying anomaly types and real-world series characteristics.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Local-MPP (Multi-Peak Periodicity) Robust Reconstruction for UTS
REVISED PROPOSAL: We enhance Local-MPP by incorporating an offline periodic component fitting step, which separately estimates the series' periodic pattern using a frequency-weighted autoregressive (AR) model. The fitted periodic pattern is then used to improve the robustness of the weighted sum of periodic components in Local-MPP. Additionally, we introduce an adaptive thresholding scheme to filter out tiny peaks in the reconstructed series, which helps to distinguish between noise and anomalies.
CONTROLS: We compare the enhanced Local-MPP against the original Local-MPP and the SVD-filter baseline, and evaluate the sensitivity of the offline periodic component fitting step and adaptive thresholding scheme to control computational resources and goodness of fit.
COST: 12 hours
PREDICTION: We expect the enhanced Local-MPP to achieve a 6-10% relative improvement in reconstruction accuracy compared to the original Local-MPP, and to exhibit robustness in detecting both small point anomalies and slowly rising anomalies.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: AutoPeaks: Adaptive Windowed Peaks Extraction for Anomaly Detection in UTS
PROPOSAL: We propose AutoPeaks, an unsupervised method for extracting peaks from reconstructed or original UTS, optimized for anomaly detection. AutoPeaks uses a series of adaptive windows to identify local maxima, which are then filtered to retain the most relevant peaks with respect to the series' periodic pattern. Additionally, AutoPeaks incorporates a thresholding mechanism to distinguish between peaks corresponding to anomalies and those corresponding to noise.
CONTROLS: As controls, we evaluate the robustness of AutoPeaks against variations in the window size and thresholding technique, and compare its performance against existing anomaly detection baselines on a range of UTS datasets, especially for small point anomalies.
COST: 9 hours
PREDICTION: We expect AutoPeaks to outperform existing baselines in detecting small point anomalies by at least 3%, with potential for further improvement by fine-tuning the window size and thresholding parameters.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Cross-Modal Anomaly Detection for UTS using Transfer Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose a cross-modal anomaly detection approach for UTS that leverages transfer learning from labeled multivariate time series datasets. Our method, CD-UTS, incorporates a transformer-based encoder to learn a shared representation of normal behavior across multiple domains, and then applies an anomaly detection module specifically designed for UTS. Transfer learning from the encoder enables the model to adapt to new UTS datasets without requiring extensive retraining.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of CD-UTS against state-of-the-art anomaly detection methods for UTS on several real-world datasets, and evaluate its robustness to variations in domain and dataset sizes.
COST: 15 hours
PREDICTION: We expect CD-UTS to achieve state-of-the-art performance on UTS anomaly detection, with a 5-10% relative improvement in detection accuracy compared to existing methods.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: SPLICE: A Hybrid Model for Anomaly Detection in UTS
PROPOSAL: We propose SPLICE, a hybrid model that combines the strengths of reconstruction-based and prediction-based anomaly detection methods. SPLICE uses a sparse_Reconstruction module to identify anomalies by sparse deviations from normal behavior, and a Predict module to learn the normal behavior of the UTS. The output of these two modules is then combined using a gate network that decides the likelihood of each point being anomalous.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of SPLICE against the individual components of SPLICE, as well as against state-of-the-art anomaly detection methods for UTS on several real-world datasets.
COST: 20 hours
PREDICTION: We expect SPLICE to achieve state-of-the-art performance on UTS anomaly detection, with a 10-15% relative improvement in detection accuracy compared to existing methods, particularly for identifying small point anomalies and slowly rising anomalies.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: X-TS: An Explanatory Framework for Anomaly Detection in UTS
PROPOSAL: We propose X-TS, an explanatory framework that provides insights into the anomaly detection process for UTS. X-TS consists of three components: Lift, which computes the lift of each point, indicating how anomalous it is compared to its neighbors; Dist, which calculates the distributional anomaly, indicating how anomalous the point is compared to the overall distribution of the series; and Vis, which visualizes the anomalies using a combination of plots. X-TS helps users understand why certain points are anomaly and provides actionable insights for domain experts.
CONTROLS: We compare the interpretability of X-TS against state-of-the-art anomaly detection methods for UTS on several real-world datasets.
COST: 15 hours
PREDICTION: We expect X-TS to be highly interpretable, helping domain experts to understand the anomaly detection process and provide actionable insights.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Frequency-Aware Unsupervised Transformers for UTS Anomaly Detection
PROPOSAL: We adapt a variant of the Transformer-XL model, a state-of-the-art sequence model, by incorporating a frequency-aware attention mechanism inspired by spectral gated recurrent unit (spectral GRU) networks to model subtle periodic patterns and anomalies in UTS. We propose a trainable frequency embedding that captures the periodicity information, enhancing the Transformer's ability to detect small point anomalies and slowly rising anomalies.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: Standard Transformer-XL model without modification
- Ablation studies: Remove frequency embedding and/or spectral GRU-inspired attention to compare performance
- Daily and weekly benchmarks on public datasets (e.g., PEMS-BAY, TA)
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved detection of small point anomalies and slowly rising anomalies compared to state-of-the-art methods, but may struggle with noisy or highly variable datasets. May need further tuning for specific real-world applications, such as domain adaptation or transfer learning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Combining Autoencoders and Anomaly Score-based Selection for Unsupervised UTS Anomaly Detection
PROPOSAL: We introduce a hybrid approach combining the denoising power of variational autoencoders (VAEs) with a selection mechanism utilizing thresholding scores from a set of hand-crafted anomaly score functions. Our approach first trains a VAE to model the normal behavior in UTS; subsequently, we select candidate anomalies based on a customized set of hand-crafted scores (e.g., mean absolute deviation, absolute difference) and retrain the VAE with a focus on recovering these points. By iteratively optimizing the autoencoder and score functions, our framework aims to detect point and segment anomalies while addressing the challenge of normal pattern learning of noise and unlabeled anomalies.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: Plain VAE model for univariate sequence learning
- Hyperparameter selection based on anomaly scores choice (number, combination and thresholding techniques used)
- Evaluate effectiveness on datasets with high levels of noise and real-world applications
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved handling of noise, unlabeled anomalies, and robust learning of normal patterns, with potential limitations in accounting for subtle periodic patterns that periodically shift.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Anomaly Pattern-based Autoencoder for Adapting to Varying Anomaly Types and Severities
PROPOSAL: We modify the autoencoder-based approach by adding an anomaly-pattern generation component, which leverages a separate Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to capture a diverse set of anomaly patterns. To handle varying anomaly types and severities, our model incorporates a feature masking and weighted loss function to adapt to different ranges and scales of anomaly values. The GAN learn a set patterns that can be ingrained forgetfully into the main autoencoder during training and help its generalization to unseen anomaly types and severities and flex the learning associated contextual behavior towards the UTS sequences curiosity.

- Baseline: Autoencoder as in proposal 2, with no GAN
- Analysis of convergence sensitivity to anomaly pattern generation and its parameter impact

PROPOSAL: We modify the autoencoder-based approach by adding an anomaly-pattern generation component, which leverages a separate Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to capture a diverse set of anomaly patterns. This will allow us to focus on the main objective of adapting to varying anomaly types and severities without introducing additional complexity.

COST: 400 GPU-hours

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning Normal Behavior with Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks for Improved Anomaly Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose the use of Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks (TGCNs) to learn the normal behavior in univariate time series data. TGCNs can effectively capture the temporal dependencies and relationships between different time steps, allowing for a more robust representation of normal behavior. We leverage the learned representations to detect anomalies by comparing the input time series with the normal behavior learned by the TGCN. To further improve the model's performance, we incorporate a dynamic thresholding mechanism to adapt the threshold based on the input time series' characteristics.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: Traditional anomaly detection methods using statistical techniques
- Comparative analysis with state-of-the-art methods
- Evaluation on datasets with varying degrees of seasonal, trend, and irregular components
COST: 700 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved anomaly detection performance due to the ability to capture complex temporal relationships and adapt to different time series characteristics, with potential limitations in handling extremely high-frequency or low-amplitude anomalies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Anomaly Detection using Density-Based Clustering of Phase Space Embeddings
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach to anomaly detection using density-based clustering of phase space embeddings. The idea is to embed the univariate time series data into a phase space using techniques such as Fourier transform or time-frequency analysis, and then apply density-based clustering algorithms (e.g., DBSCAN) to identify anomalies. This approach can effectively capture anomalies that are not easily detectable by traditional methods, such as slowly rising or small point anomalies. We also explore the use of different embedding techniques and clustering algorithms to improve the effectiveness of the approach.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: Traditional anomaly detection methods using statistical techniques
- Comparative analysis with state-of-the-art methods
- Evaluation on datasets with varying degrees of seasonality, trend, and irregular components
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved anomaly detection performance due to the ability to capture complex patterns and relationships in the phase space, with potential limitations in handling high-dimensional or high-frequency data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Semi-supervised Learning for Univariate Time Series Anomaly Detection using a Mix of Labeled and Unlabeled Data
PROPOSAL: We investigate a semi-supervised learning approach for improving the performance of univariate time series anomaly detection. The approach leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to train a model that can effectively detect anomalies. We use a mixed training strategy, where labeled data is used to provide a strong initial signal and unlabeled data is used to refine the model's generalizability. We explore the use of different semi-supervised learning techniques and evaluate the impact of varying the proportion of labeled and unlabeled data on the model's performance.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: Supervised learning approach using labeled data only
- Comparative analysis with unsupervised learning approach using unlabeled data only
- Evaluation on datasets with varying levels of data availability (e.g., few labeled samples, many unlabeled samples)
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved anomaly detection performance due to the ability to leverage both labeled and unlabeled data, with potential limitations in handling imbalanced or noisy data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Graph-informed Univariate Time Series Anomaly Detection using XGBoost
PROPOSAL: We propose a graph-informed approach for univariate time series anomaly detection using XGBoost. The approach leverages a graph-based representation of the time series data to capture complex temporal relationships and patterns. We use a graph neural network (GNN) to learn node embeddings that capture the temporal dependencies between different time steps. The GNN embeddings are then fed into an XGBoost model to predict anomalies. We explore the use of different graph constructions and XGBoost hyperparameters to optimize the model's performance.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: Traditional anomaly detection methods using statistical techniques
- Comparative analysis with state-of-the-art methods
- Evaluation on datasets with varying degrees of seasonality, trend, and irregular components
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved anomaly detection performance due to the ability to capture complex temporal relationships and patterns in the data, with potential limitations in handling high-dimensional or noisy data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-time Univariate Time Series Anomaly Detection using a Cooperative Learning Framework
PROPOSAL: We propose a real-time univariate time series anomaly detection framework based on a cooperative learning mechanism. The framework consists of two components: a primary detector and an ensemble detector. The primary detector uses a lightweight model (e.g., LSTM or CNN) to quickly predict anomalies, while the ensemble detector uses a more complex model (e.g., GNN or transformer) to refine the predictions. The primary and ensemble detectors learn cooperatively from each other's outputs to improve the detection performance and robustness. We evaluate the framework on real-time datasets with varying sampling rates and levels of noise.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: Traditional anomaly detection methods using statistical techniques
- Comparative analysis with state-of-the-art methods
- Evaluation on datasets with varying levels of noise, sampling rates, and data distribution shifts
COST: 900 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved anomaly detection performance and robustness in real-time settings, with potential limitations in handling high-dimensional or noisy data.

PROPOSAL 1: Investigating Frequency-Aware Unsupervised Transformers for UTS Anomaly Detection
We adapt a variant of the Transformer-XL model, a state-of-the-art sequence model, by incorporating a frequency-aware attention mechanism inspired by spectral gated recurrent unit (spectral GRU) networks to model subtle periodic patterns and anomalies in UTS. We propose a trainable frequency embedding that captures the periodicity information, enhancing the Transformer's ability to detect small point anomalies and slowly rising anomalies.
Controls: - Baseline: Standard Transformer-XL model without modification
- Ablation studies: Remove frequency embedding and/or spectral GRU-inspired attention to compare performance
- Daily and weekly benchmarks on public datasets (e.g., PEMS-BAY, TA)
Estimated cost: 1000 GPU-hours
Prediction: Improved detection of small point anomalies and slowly rising anomalies compared to state-of-the-art methods, but may struggle with noisy or highly variable datasets. May need further tuning for specific real-world applications, such as domain adaptation or transfer learning.

PROPOSAL 2: Combining Autoencoders and Anomaly Score-based Selection for Unsupervised UTS Anomaly Detection
We introduce a hybrid approach combining the denoising power of variational autoencoders (VAEs) with a selection mechanism utilizing thresholding scores from a set of hand-crafted anomaly score functions. Our approach first trains a VAE to model the normal behavior in UTS; subsequently, we select candidate anomalies based on a customized set of hand-crafted scores (e.g., mean absolute deviation, absolute difference) and retrain the VAE with a focus on recovering these points. By iteratively optimizing the autoencoder and score functions, our framework aims to detect point and segment anomalies while addressing the challenge of normal pattern learning of noise and unlabeled anomalies.
Controls: - Baseline: Plain VAE model for univariate sequence learning
- Hyperparameter selection based on anomaly scores choice (number, combination and thresholding techniques used)
- Evaluate effectiveness on datasets with high levels of noise and real-world applications
Estimated cost: 600 GPU-hours
Prediction: Improved handling of noise, unlabeled anomalies, and robust learning of normal patterns, with potential limitations in accounting for subtle periodic patterns that periodically shift.

PROPOSAL 3: REVISED - Anomaly Pattern-based Autoencoder for Adapting to Varying Anomaly Types and Severities
We modify the autoencoder-based approach by adding an anomaly-pattern generation component, which leverages a separate Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to capture a diverse set of anomaly patterns. To handle varying anomaly types and severities, our model incorporates a feature masking and weighted loss function to adapt to different ranges and scales of anomaly values. However, to reduce the complexity and computational requirements of proposal 3, we will use an autoencoder-based GAN, where the generator is an autoencoder module and the discriminator is a simple binary classifier. This will allow us to focus on the main objective of adapting to varying anomaly types and severities without introducing additional complexity.
Controls: - Baseline: Autoencoder without GAN component
- Hyperparameter analysis for autoencoder-based GAN
- Analyze the importance of feature masking and weighted loss function for adaptability to anomaly types and severities
Estimated cost: 400 GPU-hours
Prediction: Improved adaptability to varying anomaly types and severities, with potential limitations in handling complex relationships between anomaly patterns and normal behavior.

PROPOSAL 4: Learning Normal Behavior with Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks for Improved Anomaly Detection
We propose the use of Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks (TGCNs) to learn the normal behavior in univariate time series data. TGCNs can effectively capture the temporal dependencies and relationships between different time steps, allowing for a more robust representation of normal behavior. We leverage the learned representations to detect anomalies by comparing the input time series with the normal behavior learned by the TGCN. To further improve the model's performance, we incorporate a dynamic thresholding mechanism to adapt the threshold based on the input time series' characteristics.
Controls: - Baseline: Traditional anomaly detection methods using statistical techniques
- Comparative analysis with state-of-the-art methods
- Evaluation on datasets with varying degrees of seasonal, trend, and irregular components
Estimated cost: 700 GPU-hours
Prediction: Improved anomaly detection performance due to the ability to capture complex temporal relationships and adapt to different time series characteristics, with potential limitations in handling extremely high-frequency or low-amplitude anomalies.

PROPOSAL 5: Anomaly Detection using Density-Based Clustering of Phase Space Embeddings
We propose a novel approach to anomaly detection using density-based clustering of phase space embeddings. The idea is to embed the univariate time series data into a phase space using techniques such as Fourier transform or time-frequency analysis, and then apply density-based clustering algorithms (e.g., DBSCAN) to identify anomalies. This approach can effectively capture anomalies that are not easily detectable by traditional methods, such as slowly rising or small point anomalies. We also explore the use of different embedding techniques and clustering algorithms to improve the effectiveness of the approach.
Controls: - Baseline: Traditional anomaly detection methods using statistical techniques
- Comparative analysis with state-of-the-art methods
- Evaluation on datasets with varying degrees of seasonality, trend, and irregular components
Estimated cost: 500 GPU-hours
Prediction: Improved anomaly detection performance due to the ability to capture complex patterns and relationships in the phase space, with potential limitations in handling high-dimensional or high-frequency data.

PROPOSAL 6: Semi-supervised Learning for Univariate Time Series Anomaly Detection using a Mix of Labeled and Unlabeled Data
We investigate a semi-supervised learning approach for improving the performance of univariate time series anomaly detection. The approach leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to train a model that can effectively detect anomalies. We use a mixed training strategy, where labeled data is used to provide a strong initial signal and unlabeled data is used to refine the model's generalizability. We explore the use of different semi-supervised learning techniques and evaluate the impact of varying the proportion of labeled and unlabeled data on the model's performance.
Controls: - Baseline: Supervised learning approach using labeled data only
- Comparative analysis with unsupervised learning approach using unlabeled data only
- Evaluation on datasets with varying levels of data availability (e.g., few labeled samples, many unlabeled samples)
Estimated cost: 800 GPU-hours
Prediction: Improved anomaly detection performance due to the ability to leverage both labeled and unlabeled data, with potential limitations in handling imbalanced or noisy data.

PROPOSAL 7: Graph-informed Univariate Time Series Anomaly Detection using XGBoost
We propose a graph-informed approach for univariate time series anomaly detection using XGBoost. The approach leverages a graph-based representation of the time series data to capture complex temporal relationships and patterns. We use a graph neural network (GNN) to learn node embeddings that capture the temporal dependencies between different time steps. The GNN embeddings are then fed into an XGBoost model to predict anomalies. We explore the use of different graph constructions and XGBoost hyperparameters to optimize the model's performance.
Controls: - Baseline: Traditional anomaly detection methods using statistical techniques
- Comparative analysis with state-of-the-art methods
- Evaluation on datasets with varying degrees of seasonality, trend, and irregular components
Estimated cost: 600 GPU-hours
Prediction: Improved anomaly detection performance due to the ability to capture complex temporal relationships and patterns in the data, with potential limitations in handling high-dimensional or noisy data.

PROPOSAL 8: Real-time Univariate Time Series Anomaly Detection using a Cooperative Learning Framework
We propose a real-time univariate time series anomaly detection framework based on a cooperative learning mechanism. The framework consists of two components: a primary detector and an ensemble detector. The primary detector uses a lightweight model (e.g., LSTM or CNN) to quickly predict anomalies, while the ensemble detector uses a more complex model (e.g., GNN or transformer) to refine the predictions. The primary and ensemble detectors learn cooperatively from each other's outputs to improve the detection performance and robustness. We evaluate the framework on real-time datasets with varying sampling rates and levels of noise.
Controls: - Baseline: Traditional anomaly detection methods using statistical techniques
- Comparative analysis with state-of-the-art methods
- Evaluation on datasets with varying levels of noise, sampling rates, and data distribution shifts
Estimated cost: 900 GPU-hours
Prediction: Improved anomaly detection performance and robustness in real-time settings, with potential limitations in handling high-dimensional or noisy data.

PROPOSAL 9: Exposing the Failure Landscape of Univariate Time Series Anomaly Detection Models
We conduct a comprehensive robustness and failure analysis of state-of-the-art univariate time series anomaly detection models. Our goal is to expose and understand the limitations of these models, which can be critical in real-world applications. We design a set of data-driven tests that simulate various types of failures (e.g., noise, concept drift, model overfitting) and investigate the models' behavior under these conditions. Our analysis aims to provide insights into the failure modes and limitations of these models, which can help guide the development of more robust and reliable anomaly detection systems.
Controls: - Baseline: State-of-the-art anomaly detection methods
- Comparative analysis with robustness and failure analysis results
- Evaluation on datasets with varying levels of noise, concept drift, and model overfitting
Estimated cost: 800 CPU-hours (non-GPU)
Prediction: In-depth understanding of the limitations and failure modes of state-of-the-art univariate time series anomaly detection models, which can lead to the development of more robust and reliable anomaly detection systems.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Baseline Experiment: Evaluation of State-of-the-Art Anomaly Detectors in UTS
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of two state-of-the-art UTS anomaly detection methods: AutoARIMA and Prophet, to establish a baseline against which future proposals can be evaluated. Both methods are widely used in practice for time series forecasting and robustness to anomalies.
CONTROLS: Default parameters for both AutoARIMA and Prophet will be used, and performance will be evaluated on a set of real-world benchmarks including the website traffic dataset from IBM and the Cornell temperature dataset (http://atmos.umozero.ru/).
COST: Estimated compute time: 10 GPU-hours (using a NVIDIA V100 or similar GPU architecture)
PREDICTION: Both methods should exhibit good detection performance for well-recognized anomalies in these datasets but may struggle with subtle anomalies like small point anomalies and slowly rising anomalies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving UTS Anomaly Detection by Incorporating Spectral Features
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of incorporating spectral features (e.g., frequency and power spectral density) on the performance of an existing Autoencoder-based UTS anomaly detection model (e.g., using LSTM or CNN layers). This proposal aims to capture the periodic patterns and transient components in the time series.
CONTROLS: Compare the original model (Model A) to two modified models: One that integrates spectral features (Model B) and another that uses a separate branch to extract spectral features (Model C).
COST: Estimated compute time: 25 GPU-hours (using a NVIDIA V100 or similar GPU architecture)
PREDICTION: The incorporation of spectral features is expected to significantly improve the performance of the Autoencoder-based model, particularly for capturing segment anomalies. However, it may not perform well on small point anomalies due to the difficulties in capturing local trends and noise.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Improving UTS Anomaly Detection by Incorporating Spectral Features
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Incorporating Spectral Features with Adaptive Thresholding.
Instead of directly featuring the raw spectral features, experiment with applying adaptive thresholding to the spectral magnitude (i.e., setting the threshold as a fraction of the maximum value for each frequency component). This adaptation is expected to improve the model's robustness to noise and variations in spectral patterns. Model C will be revised to integrate this adaptive thresholding mechanism.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of Model A, Model B (frequency features), and revised Model C (with adaptive thresholding) on a set of UTS benchmarks (e.g., website traffic and temperature datasets from IBM and Cornell).
COST: Estimated additional compute time: 10 GPU-hours (using a NVIDIA V100 or similar GPU architecture)
PREDICTION: The adaptation to consider the maximum spectral value for setting the threshold should help improve the model's anomaly detection performance by better handling variations in spectral patterns. However, it might lead to over-smoothing in some datasets, requiring careful hyperparameter tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Incorporating Local Trend Analysis into UTS Anomaly Detection
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel UTS anomaly detection approach that incorporates local trend analysis. The approach will compose a sliding window-based procedure that identifies sudden variations in local trend patterns. This will be achieved using a combination of Trends-based Residual Component Analysis (TRCA) and locally weighted scatterplot smoothing (LOWESS) to capture and model both growing or shrinking trends local to short-time segments. This adaptation is expected to address the first challenge described in the problem statement by effectively identifying small point anomalies.
CONTROLS: Evaluate this new approach against state-of-the-art methods (proposed in previous experiments, e.g., using the translational invariant setup with AnomalyProbability) to verify its effectiveness for anomaly detection, especially for applications in web service monitoring and medical monitoring.
COST: Estimated compute time: 30 GPU-hours (using a NVIDIA V100 or similar GPU architecture)
PREDICTION: The incorporation of local trend analysis will likely enable good small point anomaly detection performances, based on evaluating a broad range of KPI applications, and could also lead to results useful in practice when showing anomaly propagation through the detected internet KPI features.

TITLE: Probabilistic Anomaly Detection for UTS via Ensembling of Convolutional Operators
PROPOSAL: Develop a probabilistic anomaly detection framework for UTS that leverages a combination of convolutional operators with different levels of temporal abstraction. The goal is to robustly extract anomalies from UTS data with complex temporal patterns. The framework involves ensembling multiple convolutional operator-based models to capture a wide range of possible temporal behaviors. These models will be trained using a probabilistic anomaly loss function that aims to minimize the probability of false alarms while maintaining high detection accuracy.
CONTROLS: Evaluate this probabilistic framework using a range of UTS datasets, including those with complex periodic patterns, and compare its performance against existing anomaly detection methods for UTS.
COST: Estimated compute time: 50 GPU-hours (using a NVIDIA V100 or similar GPU architecture)
PREDICTION: The proposed probabilistic framework is expected to achieve state-of-the-art performance in detecting anomalies in UTS data, particularly in cases where traditional methods struggle due to complex temporal patterns.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Anomaly Detection in UTS using Multi-Task Learning with Graph-Augmented Templates
PROPOSAL: Develop a new UTS anomaly detection method that incorporates multi-task learning and graph-augmented templates. This approach aims to improve the detection of anomalies by learning multiple tasks simultaneously, such as time series forecasting and anomaly detection, while incorporating graph-augmented templates to capture the complex relationships between time series data. Graph-augmented templates can be effectively used to model periodic patterns and local trends in the time series, which are difficult to capture using traditional anomaly detection methods.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the proposed method using a range of UTS datasets and compare its performance against existing anomaly detection methods for UTS.
COST: Estimated compute time: 40 GPU-hours (using a NVIDIA V100 or similar GPU architecture)
PREDICTION: The proposed method is expected to achieve improved performance in detecting anomalies in UTS data, particularly in cases where traditional methods struggle due to complex temporal patterns and relationships.

PROPOSAL: Explore the application of pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT, RoBERTa) to the task of UTS anomaly detection. This approach involves adapting pre-trained models to the specific task of anomaly detection in UTS data, while leveraging their pre-trained knowledge on general temporal patterns and sequences.
CONTROLS: Investigate the transfer learning capabilities of pre-trained language models on UTS anomaly detection tasks, and compare their performance against state-of-the-art methods.
COST: Estimated compute time: 20 GPU-hours (using a NVIDIA V100 or similar GPU architecture)
PREDICTION: The proposed transfer learning approach may achieve state-of-the-art performance in UTS anomaly detection, leveraging the large-scale pre-training of language models to capture general temporal patterns and adapt to specific UTS datasets.

PROPOSAL: Conduct an extensive real-world evaluation and comparison of the proposed UTS anomaly detection methods using real-world datasets from the AIOps, ECG, and environmental monitoring domains. This evaluation will assess the performance, robustness, and adaptability of the methods on diverse data types, scales, and complexities, providing a comprehensive assessment of their practical value and limitations.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the proposed methods against state-of-the-art UTS anomaly detection methods, and analyze their strengths and weaknesses in various real-world scenarios.
COST: Estimated compute time: 60 GPU-hours (using a NVIDIA V100 or similar GPU architecture)
PREDICTION: This comprehensive evaluation will provide valuable insights into the strengths and limitations of each proposed method and will help identify their potential applications and areas for improvement.
