actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Diverse Reasoning Modes Training with Sequence-to-Sequence-by-Sequence Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Design a sequence-to-sequenceby-sequence contrastive learning (SQSSL) framework that encodes each input question and consecutive output sequence pairs as independent sequence embeddings. Then apply a contrastive loss to pull together vector representations of each observation's paired input sequence and the corresponding generated sequence under the same sub-question, and push apart the embeddings for different sub-questions, thus preserving the distinct reasoning modes. Train an LLM using a large dataset of diverse, correct traces and SQSSL.
CONTROLS: Train an LLM with a normal sequence-to-sequence loss to provide a baseline.
COST: Estimated 10000 GPU-hours on a large language model dataset (e.g. CodexTracer).
PREDICTION: The SQSSL model will outperform the baseline in terms of both accuracy and helpfulness of generated content in code generation and graduate-level science question answering tasks, and will exhibit better control over generation length and test time efficiency than competing methods. May fail in low-data regimes, and may require cognizant task selection for optimal performance. 

Paper proposal partially calibrated

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Tree-Graph-Based Reasoning Mode Discovery and Retention
PROPOSAL: Design a graph-based neural network that takes in the diverse traces of a question as nodes, and extracts reasoning modes as sub-graphs. Use graph auto-encoders to encode and decode each trace, and train a variational inference model to derive a probability distribution over all possible reasoning modes. Then use an adversarial loss to encourage the model to retain and differentiate between the distinct modes. Train the model using high-quality diverse traces.
CONTROLS: Train a baseline graph auto-encoder model without the adversarial loss.
COST: Estimated 8000 GPU-hours on a high-end GPU (e.g. A100) for graph auto-encoder training.
PREDICTION: The model will learn to differentiate between diverse reasoning modes, and will be able to retrieve these modes given an input question with high accuracy. However, may require significant human effort to fine-tune the quality of the traces, and may be sensitive to the negative sampling strategy. 

Paper proposal based on the medium-tech, expert-task domain experimental domain 'graduate-level science question answering', partly calibrated

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Diverse Reasoning Modes Training with Sequence-to-Sequence-by-Sequence Contrastive Learning
REVISED PROPOSAL: As Rev. 1, but experiment with and compare multiple contrastive loss functions and architectures, including ones that take advantage of the trace structure as well as ones that ignore it. This comparison will help identify any performance gains from using the trace structure over a simpler, sequence-to-sequence-based approach, and whether any specific loss function or architecture is particularly effective.
CONTROLS: In addition to the baseline provided in Rev. 1, include another ablation study with the best-performing contrastive loss function or architecture to determine its specific contribution.
COST: No additional compute hours are required.
PREDICTION: By experimenting with multiple loss functions and architectures, the model will likely experience some performance improvements compared to Rev. 1. Evaluate whether the performance gain is worth the complexity addition.  However, potential results may show that no single change gives a great cost improvement in accuracy improvement: that stays equal to further improve one way.

ACTION: REVISE
(1) 
TITLE: Diverse Reasoning Modes Training with Sequence-to-Sequence-by-Sequence Contrastive Learning
REVISED PROPOSAL: Modify the SQSSL framework to utilize an attention mechanism that attends not only to the input sequence but also to the corresponding generated sequence embeddings. This attention-based SQSSL (AB-SQSSL) model allows the model to focus on the relevant information in both the input and the generated sequences. Train AB-SQSSL using a large dataset of diverse, correct traces and compare its performance with the original SQSSL framework.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of AB-SQSSL with the original SQSSL framework in Rev. 1.
COST: Estimated 2000 additional GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The attention-based SQSSL model should improve the representation of the generated sequences by attending to relevant information, thus improving the overall performance of the model. May fail to show consistent performance gains if the attention mechanism does not correctly capture the relationship between the input and generated sequences.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Parallel Sampling with Adaptive Ensemble (PASE) of Multiple Teacher Models
PROPOSAL: Train several teacher models on the task, each with a different hyperparameter setting or architecture. At test time, generate multiple parallel completions from each teacher model, and use an adaptive ensemble approach to combine these completions into a single, more accurate output. Use a metalearning approach to learn the weights for combining the teacher models, taking into account the performance of each model on a validation set.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline that uses a single teacher model and myopic sampling.
COST: Estimated 15000 GPU-hours for training the teacher models and metalearning.
PREDICTION: PASE will show robust performance improvements compared to the baseline, especially on harder tasks where a single teacher model may struggle. May fail to generalize to tasks that require more comprehensive understanding of the domain, rather than localized improvements. 

Paper proposal calibrated

ACTION: REVISE
(2) 
TITLE: Tree-Graph-Based Reasoning Mode Discovery and Retention
REVISED PROPOSAL: Modify the graph auto-encoder model to incorporate node and edge attention mechanisms, allowing the model to selectively focus on relevant information in the graph structure. Additionally, experiment with different graph variants, such as edge-aware graphs, node-aware graphs, and application of higher order traversals, to extract more nuanced information from the diverse traces. This revised model, which we'll call Tree-Graph-Adaptive (TGA), will be compared to the original Tree-Graph-Based Reasoning Mode Discovery and Retention model.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of TGA with the original Tree-Graph-Based Reasoning Mode Discovery and Retention model, and investigate the effect of attention mechanisms and graph variants on the model's performance.
COST: Estimated 5000 additional GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The attention-based model and graph variants in TGA will improve the model's ability to retain and differentiate between diverse reasoning modes, leading to better performance on tasks that require in-depth understanding.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Measure and Compare Diversity in Language Model Reasoning Traces
PROPOSAL: Develop a set of metrics to measure diversity in language model reasoning traces, including metrics that capture both the quantity of diverse responses and the quality of those responses. Use these metrics to compare the diversity of reasoning traces produced by different models, including the models proposed in this set. Also, propose a "diversity-augmented" training objective, where instead of optimizing directly for accuracy, the model is optimized for maximizing the diversity of its reasoning traces.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed metrics and diversity-augmented training objective by comparing their performance with traditional training objectives and metrics.
COST: Estimated 3000 GPU-hours for developing and evaluating metrics.
PREDICTION: The proposed diversity metrics and diversity-augmented training objective will provide valuable insights into the quality and robustness of language model reasoning trances and may lead to significant performance improvements.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Training for Reasoning Trace Augmentation
PROPOSAL: Develop an adversarial training framework that generates ambiguous or misleading training data to force the language model to reason more flexibly and produce more diverse reasoning traces. Train the model on this augmented data, and evaluate its performance on tasks that require reasoning flexibility, such as code generation and math problem-solving.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the adversarially trained model with a baseline model trained on standard data.
COST: Estimated 12000 GPU-hours for generating and training on the augmented data.
PREDICTION: The adversarially trained model will produce more diverse and accurate reasoning traces, and perform well on tasks that require flexible reasoning and adaptability to ambiguous input. May fail if the augmented data is not accurately captured or the adversary is not aggressive enough.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Cross-Domain Reasoning Diversity
PROPOSAL: Train language models on diverse reasoning tasks in one domain (e.g., math problem-solving), and then transfer the learned diversification capabilities to another domain (e.g., code generation). Evaluate the transferred model's performance on the new domain and compare it with a model trained from scratch on the new domain.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the transferred model with a model trained from scratch on the new domain.
COST: Estimated 10000 GPU-hours for training and evaluating the transferred model.
PREDICTION: The transferred model will exhibit improved reasoning diversity and performance on the new domain, leveraging the learned diversification capabilities from the source domain. May fail if the domains are too dissimilar or the model is not robust to domain shifts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Human Evaluation of Reasoning Diversity and Productivity
PROPOSAL: Hire human evaluators to assess the diversity and productivity of the generated reasoning traces from each of the proposed methods. Evaluate the effectiveness of the methods in terms of both diversity and productivity, and compare their performance with human-generated reasoning traces.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the inter-annotator agreement between human evaluators to ensure the reliability of the human evaluation.
COST: Estimated 5000 human evaluation hours with 10 evaluators.
PREDICTION: The results from human evaluation will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the strengths and limitations of each method, and will help identify potential areas for improvement. May fail if the human evaluation task is too subjective or ambiguous.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experiment on Parallel Reasoning with Teacher Distillation
PROPOSAL: Fine-tune a 3B parameter language model on a real-world benchmark (e.g.,/ms MARCO, TriviaQA) using diverse, correct reasoning traces obtained by distilling from different teacher models. Evaluate its performance on accuracy, diversity, and coverage compared to the pre-trained model and a baseline fine-tuned on independent traces.
CONTROLS: Baselines include (1) pre-trained model, (2) fine-tuned model on independent traces, and (3) a naive ensemble of multiple fine-tuned models on independent traces.
COST: 10,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This experiment should demonstrate improved accuracy and coverage, but we might see a decrease in diversity due to overfitting to the teacher models.

This proposal sets the stage for evaluating the performance of a fine-tuned model on accurate, diverse reasoning traces, which is the main focus of this problem.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revised Experiment on Parallel Reasoning with Teacher Distillation
PROPOSAL: To investigate the trade-off between diversity and accuracy, we'll extend experiment 1 by adding an ablation study with a temperature-control method (e.g., inverse temperature scaling) that balances diversity and accuracy. We'll fine-tune the 3B parameter language model on traces distilled from teacher models with different temperatures, and evaluate the impact on accuracy, diversity, and coverage.
CONTROLS: Same as before, with the addition of the temperature-control method as an ablation study.
COST: Additional 5,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised experiment should provide insights into the effect of temperature on parallel reasoning, and potentially reveal a sweet spot for balancing diversity and accuracy.

Revising experiment 1 adds depth to the investigation of parallel reasoning with teacher distillation, and addresses the open question of how to balance diversity and accuracy.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Experiment to Investigate the Role of Distillation Methods
PROPOSAL: To explore the impact of different distillation methods on parallel reasoning, we'll continue with the original framework of fine-tuning a 3B parameter language model on diverse, correct reasoning traces obtained by distilling from different teacher models. However, we'll now experiment with various distillation methods (e.g., knowledge distillation, students-for-teaching, Low-Shot Distillation), and compare their effects on accuracy, diversity, and coverage.
CONTROLS: Baselines will include the original distillation method (teacher-student distillation) and a random baseline with no distillation.
COST: Additional 7,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This experiment should highlight the strengths and weaknesses of different distillation methods in producing diverse and accurate training data.

Revising proposal 1 with a new angle adds further insights into the design of parallel reasoning training data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Diversity and Accuracy in Parallel Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We'll develop a theoretical framework to analyze the relationship between diversity and accuracy in parallel reasoning, considering the trade-offs between sampling temperature, model capacity, and the number of parallel reasoning modes. We'll prove bounds on the optimal diversity-accuracy trade-off and discuss implications for the design of parallel reasoning models.
CONTROLS: None
COST: 500 GPU-hours (purely theoretical work)
PREDICTION: This theoretical analysis should provide powerful insights into the fundamental limits of parallel reasoning, and shed light on the most promising approaches for achieving high accuracy and diversity.

This new proposal focuses on the theoretical underpinnings of parallel reasoning, complementing the experimental investigation.

ACTION: REVISIE 2
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Diversity and Accuracy in Parallel Reasoning (Revised)
PROPOSAL: We'll focus on the regime where the number of parallel reasoning modes scales polynomially with the number of model parameters. Assuming the modes are independent and identically distributed, we'll derive a lower bound on the optimal accuracy as a function of diversity, sampling temperature, and model capacity. This bound will provide a concrete metric to optimize for in parallel reasoning training and evaluation.
CONTROLS: None
COST: No additional GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised theoretical result should tighten the connection between diversity, temperature, and accuracy in parallel reasoning, and provide a useful tool for model selection and hyperparameter tuning.

Revising proposal 2 refines the focus on the theoretical framework, aiming for a more practical application to model design.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experiment on Parallel Reasoning with Gradual Distillation
PROPOSAL: To create a more challenging, sequential distillation setup, we'll modify the teacher model to produce gradually less explicit reasoning, simulating a "difficulty" level. The student model will learn to adapt to this gradually reduced guidance, requiring it to infer and generate reasoning modes more effectively as the difficulty increases. We'll evaluate its performance on a competition mathematics or code generation task.
CONTROLS: Baselines will include (1) the original teacher-student model and (2) a naive ensemble of multiple fine-tuned models.
COST: 12,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This experiment should demonstrate the student model's ability to learn generalizable and diverse reasoning modes under more challenging sequential distillation conditions.

This new proposal focuses on the adaptation and generalizability of parallel reasoning models when faced with sequentially decreasing guidance from their teacher.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigation of Self-Consistency and Best-of-N on Gradually Diluted Distillation
PROPOSAL: We'll apply and compare self-consistency and Best-of-N aggregation methods on top of the gradual distillation setup introduced in experiment 3. Specifically, we'll evaluate how these aggregation techniques interact with the reduced teacher guidance, and whether they can mitigate the generalization challenges that arise in this setting.
CONTROLS: Baselines will include (1) the original single model, (2) self-consistency and Best-of-N aggregation methods individually, and (3) an ensemble of models using these methods.
COST: 8,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This experiment should provide insights into the suitability of self-consistency and Best-of-N methods for addressing the reduced guidance in gradual distillation.

This new proposal focuses on exploring the resilience and robustness of parallel reasoning models under the influence of gradually diluted teacher guidance, complementing experiment 3.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Gradual Distillation and its Optimal Difficulty Schedule
PROPOSAL: Building on the theoretical framework of proposal 2, we'll analyze the theoretical guarantees for gradual distillation, including the optimal difficulty schedule for the teacher model. We'll derive expressions for the optimal accuracy-diversity trade-off and discuss the implications for the design of gradual distillation systems.
CONTROLS: None
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This theoretical analysis should provide a deeper understanding of the gradual distillation setup, including the interaction between teacher guidance and student generalization, and offer practical guidelines for the optimal difficulty scheduling.

This new theoretical result complements experiments 3 and 4 by providing a rigorous understanding of the gradual distillation framework.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experiment on Native Parallel Training with Gradual Distillation
PROPOSAL: We'll explore the possibility of directly training a parallel reasoning model with gradual distillation from scratch, without relying on the sequential reasoning model as an intermediate step. This experiment will aim to demonstrate whether parallel training can be more effective than sequential training in capturing diverse reasoning modes and improving generalization in challenging scenarios.
CONTROLS: Baselines will include (1) sequentially trained models with gradual distillation, (2) a naive ensemble of multiple fine-tuned models, and (3) a randomly initialized parallel model.
COST: 20,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This experiment should reveal whether native parallel training can bypass the generalization challenges of sequential training and lead to improved performance on graduate-level science question answering or code generation.

This new proposal marks the last experiment in the set, focusing on the potential benefits of native parallel reasoning training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Consolidation and Comparison of Parallel Reasoning Methods
PROPOSAL: With the theoretical analysis, experiments, and results gathered from the previous proposed experiments, we'll design a comprehensive comparison across the various methods, models, and training schemes to identify which parallel reasoning approach consistently outperforms others in achieving accurate and diverse reasoning on graduate-level science question answering or code generation.
CONTROLS: All previous proposals will be used as baselines in this comparison.
COST: negligible (no additional GPU-hours required)
PREDICTION: This final experiment should provide clear evidence of the strengths and weaknesses of each parallel reasoning method, ultimately identifying a robust and effective approach for achieving reliable and accurate reasoning capabilities.

This final result represents the culmination of the research effort, providing an overarching evaluation and synthesis of the various proposals, theories, and experiments.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Orthogonal Distillation in Retaining Distinct Reasoning Modes
PROPOSAL: Fine-tune a language model using an orthogonal distillation method, where the teacher model generates multiple reasoning traces for a single question, and the student model is trained to mimic these traces while preserving their diversity.
CONTROLS: Supervised fine-tuning with orthogonal distillation (baseline), vanilla distillation, and an ablation study without teacher models.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to retain distinct reasoning modes, as measured by diversity metrics (e.g., Intra-sentence Entropy), when compared to baseline and ablation study conditions. Moderate performance gains are predicted in terms of tested correct answers and aggregated accuracy and coverage.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Training for Parallel Reasoning with Curriculum Learning
PROPOSAL: Introduce a curriculum learning approach to train language models for parallel reasoning. Start with simple tasks or questions and gradually increase the difficulty, with the model learning to generate diverse reasoning traces through progressive learning.
CONTROLS: Standard training (baseline), curriculum learning (with and without curriculum schedule adjustments), and a comparison to our previous orthogonal distillation approach.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach is expected to significantly improve early-stage model performance on simpler tasks, and moderate to high improvements are predicted for more complex tasks, as measured by accuracy and diversity metrics. Further, we expect this method to demonstrate robustness to challenging scenarios and scalability compared to pure orthogonal distillation.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Modifying 2. Training for Parallel Reasoning with Curriculum Learning
PROPOSAL: Modify the curriculum learning approach to include a "reversal phase" where the model is encouraged to exceed a predefined threshold for diversity and accuracy, and critically examine diverse reasoning paths for potential errors or modes incorrectly predicted, using self-consistency.
CONTROLS: Standard training (baseline), curriculum learning with reversal phase, and curriculum learning without reversal phase, and a comparison to orthogonal distillation and simple training.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Introducing the reversal phase is expected to further improve the quality of generated reasoning traces, as measured by accuracy and diversity metrics, as the model would now actively identify and explore acceptable reasoning pathways. We also expect better-than-or-equal performance compared to simple training and concerning curriculum learning.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Training for Parallel Reasoning with Curriculum Learning
PROPOSAL: Modify the curriculum learning approach to include a "reversal phase" where the model is encouraged to exceed a predefined threshold for diversity and accuracy, and critically examine diverse reasoning paths for potential errors or modes incorrectly predicted, using self-consistency.
CONTROLS: Standard training (baseline), curriculum learning with reversal phase, curriculum learning without reversal phase, simple training, and orthogonal distillation.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Introducing the reversal phase is expected to further improve the quality of generated reasoning traces, as measured by accuracy and diversity metrics, as the model would now actively identify and explore acceptable reasoning pathways. We also expect better-than-or-equal performance compared to simple training and concerning curriculum learning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Model Inversion with Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Fine-tune a language model using model inversion techniques with contrastive learning, where the model is trained to recover the original input from its generated reasoning trace, promoting the exploration of diverse reasoning paths.
CONTROLS: Standard training (baseline), curriculum learning with reversal phase, and model inversion alone.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach is expected to enhance model robustness, accuracy, and the quality of generated reasoning traces, as it forces the model to focus on capturing essential information in the trace. We also anticipate this method to couple well with our proposed orthogonal distillation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Selective Voting for Aggregated Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Introduce selective voting for aggregating multiple generated reasoning paths, where each mode from the traces is assigned a confidence score based on the model's likelihood of producing the correct answer for the question, and the model is trained to learn an optimal strategy for voting.
CONTROLS: Standard training (baseline), full voting, and ablations of different aggregation strategies.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach is expected to improve the accuracy and coverage of generated reasoning paths by selectively focusing on the most confident modes, and reduce the risk of overfitting to a specific mode. We anticipate moderate performance gains compared to simple aggregation methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-learning for Span-based Explanations
PROPOSAL: Develop a meta-learning framework to generate span-based explanations for the model's reasoning processes, enabling the identification of crucial input spans that contribute to each mode of reasoning.
CONTROLS: Standard training (baseline), meta-learning alone, and meta-learning in combination with selective voting.
COST: 3200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach is expected to facilitate the comprehension of complex reasoning processes and to improve the reliability and interpretability of the model's behavior, leading to a deeper understanding of the actual reasoning pathways. We anticipate moderate performance gains in tasks requiring explanation, including code generation and science question answering.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robustness Evaluation via Mode-based Data Augmentation
PROPOSAL: Develop a robustness evaluation framework based on mode-based data augmentation, where multiple reasoning modes are sampled from a single question and used to build adversarial data for evaluating the model's robustness and generalizability.
CONTROLS: Standard training (baseline), traditional adversarial training, and mode-based adversaries with selective voting.
COST: 3500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach is expected to enhance the assessment of the model's robustness to critical input modifications, such as those derived from different reasoning modes, and to logically evaluate the model's ability to operate in changing situations. The results are expected to complement those from model inversion and meta-learning setups, leading to better performance under various settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Reasoning Mode Selection via Bayesian Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: Utilize Bayesian neural networks to develop an adaptive reasoning mode selection framework, where the model is trained to select the most relevant reasoning mode based on the input and task at hand.
CONTROLS: Standard training (baseline), traditional mode selection methods, and adapters using meta-learning for span-based explanations.
COST: 4500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach is expected to improve the model's accuracy and efficiency by adaptively selecting the most suitable reasoning mode and leveraging insights from the model's uncertainty and spanning capabilities. We anticipate outstanding performance, especially when evaluating the adaptability to various input scenarios in competitions, code generation, and graduate-level science questions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Full-Spectrum Reasoning Scaling: A Large-Scale Benchmark
PROPOSAL: Establish a comprehensive benchmark to evaluate the performance of large-scale language models across the full spectrum of reasoning modes, from simple sequential reasoning to complex parallel reasoning, and challenging diagnostics.
CONTROLS: Run all previous approaches on the full-spectrum benchmark and compare their performance.
COST: 6000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This benchmark is expected to reveal the true potential of parallel reasoning and adaptability in complex scenarios, providing insights into the strengths and weaknesses of state-of-the-art models and fostering the development of more robust, versatile, and accurate reasoning systems.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigation of Convergence Behavior under Exact Class Posteriors
PROPOSAL: Conduct an SGD-based experimental study to compare the convergence behavior of a student model trained under the supervision of exact class posterior probabilities (teacher's outputs) versus the original one-hot labels. Use this comparison to derive insights into the role of supervised information on the training dynamics of stochastic gradient descent optimizers.
CONTROLS: Train student with one-hot labels, teacher as a baseline; repeat with low-capacity student model to study effect of teacher overcapacity.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Training with exact posteriors should provide a faster convergence rate and improved generalization compared to one-hot labels. Failure might occur if the teacher model becomes too complex, causing overfitting in the student.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Modeling the Impact of Estimation Error in Teacher's Probabilities
PROPOSAL: Theoretical analysis to derive bounds on the excess risk of the student model under probabilistic supervision, assuming the teacher's output probabilities contain estimation errors. Study how the level of estimation error affects the student's convergence, generalization, and accuracy using a Bayesian risk analysis framework.
CONTROLS: None required for this theoretical analysis; compare with bounds derived in the existing literature.
COST: 0 GPU-hours (theoretical analysis only)
PREDICTION: The bounds should reveal that higher levels of estimation error degrade the student's performance, suggesting a trade-off between teacher accuracy and student generalization. Failure might occur if the derived bounds are too loose or not directly applicable to common machine learning scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: The Role of Teacher Calibration in SGD-based Learning Dynamics
PROPOSAL: Experimental study comparing the performance of students trained under probabilistic supervision with varying levels of teacher calibration. Investigate how teacher calibration affects the student's convergence rate, generalization, and accuracy in a series of well-established benchmark tasks.
CONTROLS: Use calibrated and uncalibrated teacher models as baselines; study the effect of different calibration techniques (e.g., temperature scaling, label smoothing).
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved teacher calibration should lead to better student performance and faster convergence. However, over-calibration might cause the student to rely excessively on the teacher's outputs, leading to poorer generalization performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparative Study of Distillation Loss Functions
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of different distillation loss functions on the student's performance and convergence dynamics. Specifically, compare the behavior of standard KL-divergence based loss, marginalized KL-divergence, and label-smoothed weighted KL-divergence as the probabilistic supervision loss for the student.
CONTROLS: Train student with one-hot labels as a baseline; repeat with the different distillation loss functions and compare performance on the validation set.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Different distillation loss functions will yield varying performance improvements and convergence rates, with some showing better robustness to teacher estimation error.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Comparative Study of Distillation Loss Functions
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Investigate the effect of different distillation loss functions on the student's performance and convergence dynamics. Specifically, compare the behavior of standard KL-divergence based loss and label-smoothed weighted KL-divergence as the probabilistic supervision loss for the student. Add experiments to study the effect of varying temperature parameters for the KL-divergence based loss.
CONTROLS: Train student with one-hot labels as a baseline; repeat with the KL-divergence based loss, and the label-smoothed weighted KL-divergence, and study effect of different temperature values between 0.5 to 2.0.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (increase due to additional temperature sweep experiments)
PREDICTION: Different distillation loss functions and temperature values will yield varying performance improvements and convergence rates, with the label-smoothed weighted KL-divergence offering better robustness to teacher estimation error. However, high temperature values for KL-divergence loss might cause over-softening, leading to convergence issues.

PREDICTION: Different distillation loss functions and temperature values will yield varying performance improvements and convergence rates, with the label-smoothed weighted KL-divergence offering better robustness to teacher estimation error. However, high temperature values for KL-divergence loss might cause over-softening, leading to convergence issues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experimental Validation of Excess Risk Bounds under Imperfect Probabilistic Supervision
PROPOSAL: Validate the theoretical bounds on excess risk derived in the existing literature under imperfect probabilistic supervision. This is done using a series of experiments on benchmark tasks, comparing the empirical excess risk of students trained with probabilistic supervision to the derived theoretical bounds.
CONTROLS: Use student models with varying capacities and teacher models with different levels of estimation error as inputs for the experiments.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The experiments should confirm the theoretical bounds as a useful approximation of the excess risk under probabilistic supervision. Failure might occur if the derived bounds are too loose or not directly applicable to common machine learning scenarios, or if the experiments reveal a significant gap between the theoretical and empirical excess risk.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Case Study: Knowledge Distillation for Transfer Learning in Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of knowledge distillation for transfer learning in vision transformers, focusing on the role of teacher probability estimation error and student capacity in achieving accurate transfer of knowledge. This is done using a case study on the transfer of knowledge from ResNet-50 to a smaller ViT model on ImageNet.
CONTROLS: Compare the transfer performance of students trained with one-hot labels, probabilistic supervision with accurate teacher probabilities, and probabilistic supervision with imperfect teacher probabilities.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Knowledge distillation should lead to significant improvements in transfer performance, and the accuracy of teacher probability estimates and student capacity will be critical factors influencing these improvements. However, transfer performance might degrade if the teacher model has over-estimated the accuracy of its own predictions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Automatic Calibration of Teachers via Meta-Learning
PROPOSAL: Introduce a meta-learning approach to automatically calibrate teacher models, allowing them to adapt their output probability distributions to the optimal level of accuracy for knowledge distillation. Evaluate the effectiveness of this approach on a range of teacher-student pairs.
CONTROLS: Use a meta-learning algorithm to train a set of teacher models with varying calibration strengths, and compare their performance on a test set to a teacher model trained with a fixed level of accuracy.
COST: 220 GPU-hours (including meta-learning phase)
PREDICTION: The meta-learning approach should allow for effective automatic calibration of teacher models, leading to improved knowledge distillation performance. However, the meta-learning algorithm might require a large amount of computational resources and data to converge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Designing Optimal Teacher-Student Pairs for Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: Derive a systematic approach to designing teacher-student pairs for knowledge distillation, considering factors such as teacher capacity, student capacity, and the level of teacher probability estimation error. This is done using a theoretical framework that combines insights from optimization, information theory, and statistical learning theory.
CONTROLS: Validate the derived approach using a series of experiments on benchmark tasks and compare the performance of students trained with teacher-student pairs designed using this approach to those trained with random pairs.
COST: 0 GPU-hours (theoretical analysis only)
PREDICTION: The systematic design approach should lead to teacher-student pairs that yield significantly improved knowledge distillation performance, as measured by student accuracy and convergence rate. However, the practical applicability of the approach might be limited by the complexity of the design process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Probabilistic Supervision on SGD Convergence
PROPOSAL: We will analyze the effect of using the exact class posterior probabilities as supervision for SGD-based learning compared to the standard one-hot labels using a mathematical analysis of the loss landscape.
CONTROLS: Compare to SGD with one-hot labels; consider ablations where we remove the probabilistic supervision from SGD with one-hot labels
COST: 10 GPU-hours (allowing us to perform a modest number of iterations)
PREDICTION: We expect that SGD with probabilistic supervision will exhibit improved stability and faster convergence, as the student learns to directly target the data-generating distribution's most likely regions, but fail to identify whether it ultimately generalizes better.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying the Influence of Teacher Calibration on Student Generalization
PROPOSAL: We will empirically evaluate how the calibration (i.e., accuracy of the teacher's probability estimates) affects the student's performance on unseen data, using a benchmark of state-of-the-art teacher models on a range of realistic datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare teacher models of varying calibration levels (using metrics such as log-loss or Brier score), with ablations exploring how changes in teacher architecture or distillation parameters impact student performance
COST: 50 GPU-hours (requiring access to a large-scale computing cluster to train multiple teacher models)
PREDICTION: We expect calibrated teachers to provide better supervision, leading to improved generalization in the students, but may find that certain types of inaccuracies in teacher prediction are more difficult to correct than others.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Quantifying the Influence of Teacher Calibration on Student Generalization
PROPOSAL: To further investigate the relationship between teacher calibration and student generalization, we will apply the recently proposed Bayesian framework to derive analytical bounds on the student's excess risk, conditioning on the teacher's calibration level.
CONTROLS: Analyze the derived bounds using a combination of synthetic and real-world data; consider how the bounds compare to empirical results
COST: Same as before (theoretical analysis doesn't add to computational cost)
PREDICTION: We expect the analysis to reveal that teacher calibration has a significant impact on the student's excess risk, with well-calibrated teachers providing tighter bounds and thus better generalization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring the Robustness of Probabilistic Supervision under Noisy Teacher Estimates
PROPOSAL: We will simulate and experimentally investigate how the student adapts to varying levels of noise in the teacher's probability estimates, using a range of noise models and comparing the results to students trained with perfect supervision (i.e., the true class posteriors).
CONTROLS: Use a combination of synthetic data and realistic datasets; consider ablations where we adjust the student architecture or optimizers
COST: 100 GPU-hours (requiring a significant computational budget to simulate and train multiple student models)
PREDICTION: We expect probabilistic supervision to exhibit some degree of robustness to noisy teacher estimates, but may find that significant deviations in the teacher's output correlate with decreased student performance and accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Distillation Temperature on Student Performance
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally evaluate how the distillation temperature used in the soft-target loss affects the student's accuracy and generalization, comparing the results to students trained with standard one-hot labels and examining the interplay with teacher calibration.
CONTROLS: Use a range of distillation temperatures and combine with previous controls (e.g., teacher calibration, noisy teacher estimates)
COST: 30 GPU-hours (requiring moderate computational resources to train and test students with varying distillation temperatures)
PREDICTION: We expect distillation temperature to have a significant impact on student performance, with optimal temperatures allowing for better calibration transfer and generalization, but may find that the temperature effect depends on the teacher's accuracy and student's capacity.

PROPOSAL 1: Investigating the Impact of Probabilistic Supervision on SGD Convergence
We will analyze the effect of using the exact class posterior probabilities as supervision for SGD-based learning compared to the standard one-hot labels using a mathematical analysis of the loss landscape.
Controls: Compare to SGD with one-hot labels; consider ablations where we remove the probabilistic supervision from SGD with one-hot labels
Estimated cost: 10 GPU-hours (allowing us to perform a modest number of iterations)
Prediction: We expect that SGD with probabilistic supervision will exhibit improved stability and faster convergence, as the student learns to directly target the data-generating distribution's most likely regions, but fail to identify whether it ultimately generalizes better.

PROPOSAL 2: Quantifying the Influence of Teacher Calibration on Student Generalization
To further investigate the relationship between teacher calibration and student generalization, we will apply the recently proposed Bayesian framework to derive analytical bounds on the student's excess risk, conditioning on the teacher's calibration level.
Controls: Analyze the derived bounds using a combination of synthetic and real-world data; consider how the bounds compare to empirical results
Estimated cost: Same as before (theoretical analysis doesn't add to computational cost)
Prediction: We expect the analysis to reveal that teacher calibration has a significant impact on the student's excess risk, with well-calibrated teachers providing tighter bounds and thus better generalization.

PROPOSAL 3: Exploring the Robustness of Probabilistic Supervision under Noisy Teacher Estimates
We will simulate and experimentally investigate how the student adapts to varying levels of noise in the teacher's probability estimates, using a range of noise models and comparing the results to students trained with perfect supervision (i.e., the true class posteriors).
Controls: Use a combination of synthetic data and realistic datasets; consider ablations where we adjust the student architecture or optimizers
Estimated cost: 100 GPU-hours (requiring a significant computational budget to simulate and train multiple student models)
Prediction: We expect probabilistic supervision to exhibit some degree of robustness to noisy teacher estimates, but may find that significant deviations in the teacher's output correlate with decreased student performance and accuracy.

PROPOSAL 4: Investigating the Effect of Distillation Temperature on Student Performance
We will experimentally evaluate how the distillation temperature used in the soft-target loss affects the student's accuracy and generalization, comparing the results to students trained with standard one-hot labels and examining the interplay with teacher calibration.
Controls: Use a range of distillation temperatures and combine with previous controls (e.g., teacher calibration, noisy teacher estimates)
Estimated cost: 30 GPU-hours (requiring moderate computational resources to train and test students with varying distillation temperatures)
Prediction: We expect distillation temperature to have a significant impact on student performance, with optimal temperatures allowing for better calibration transfer and generalization, but may find that the temperature effect depends on the teacher's accuracy and student's capacity.

PROPOSAL 5: Analytical Bounds for SGD under Probabilistic Supervision
We will derive analytical bounds on the convergence rate and excess risk of SGD under probabilistic supervision, focusing on the impact of teacher calibration and provided a comparison to existing one-hot label bounds.
Controls: State-of-the-art bounds from the literature; consider how the derived bounds compare to the probabilistic supervision scenario in previous experiments
Estimated cost: Same as before (theoretical analysis doesn't add to computational cost)
Prediction: We expect the analysis to reveal that probabilistic supervision can provide improved convergence rates and excess risk bounds, particularly when the teacher is well-calibrated. The comparison to one-hot label bounds may highlight areas where probabilistic supervision offers advantages or highers risks.

PROPOSAL 6: Experimental Comparison of Knowledge Distillation and Probabilistic Supervision
We will empirically compare the performance of knowledge distillation and probabilistic supervision on a range of realistic datasets, using a state-of-the-art teacher model and evaluating the students' accuracy, generalization, and convergence speed.
Controls: Use ablations to explore the differences between soft-target vs. probabilistic supervision, teacher's architecture or optimizers used
Estimated cost: 150 GPU-hours (requiring significant computational resources to train, test, and compare the two methods)
Prediction: We expect both methods to exhibit improvements over standard one-hot label training, but may find that probabilistic supervision offers a more significant advantage, particularly in scenarios where the teacher's accuracy is high or when the student needs to learn complex patterns.

PROPOSAL 7: Case Study: Impact of Probabilistic Supervision on Real-World Classification Tasks
We will apply probabilistic supervision to several real-world classification tasks (e.g., ImageNet, CIFAR-10), using pre-trained teacher models and comparing the results to standard one-hot label training, knowledge distillation, and probabilistic supervision.
Controls: Use ablations to explore the impact of teacher architecture, optimizer used, and distillation temperature
Estimated cost: 300 GPU-hours (requiring large-scale computing resources to conduct this comprehensive evaluation)
Prediction: We expect probabilistic supervision to demonstrate improved performance and generalization on these challenging real-world tasks, but may find that the benefits are domain-dependent and require fine-tuning the teacher model and training parameters.

PROPOSAL 8: Understanding the Interplay between Teacher Knowledge and Student Performance under Probabilistic Supervision
We will investigate the relationship between the teacher's knowledge and the student's performance under probabilistic supervision, using information-theoretic quantities (e.g., mutual information, Kullback-Leibler divergence) to quantify the transfer of knowledge and the impact of teacher calibration.
Controls: Analyze the results of previous experiments using these information-theoretic quantities; compare to empirical results from other papers
Estimated cost: 100 GPU-hours (moderate computational resources required to analyze the information-theoretic quantities)
Prediction: We expect that the information-theoretic analysis will provide insights into how teacher knowledge is transferred to the student, with potential implications for optimizing teacher models and distillation parameters.

PROPOSAL 9: Towards Designing Optimal Teacher Models for Probabilistic Supervision
We will synthesize the insights from our previous experiments and theoretical analyses to provide practical recommendations for designing optimal teacher models under probabilistic supervision, focusing on effective calibration, knowledge transfer, and robustness to noise.
Controls: Combine and integrate the results from all previous experiments and analyses; compare with existing state-of-the-art teacher model designs
Estimated cost: Low (no additional computational resources required, as this proposal involves only analysis and synthesis)
Prediction: We expect our recommendations to provide a clear roadmap for designing effective teacher models under probabilistic supervision, with the potential to boost the performance of knowledge distillation and improve the generalization of the student models.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Understanding Teacher Calibration under Probabilistic Supervision
PROPOSAL: Experiment 1: SGD Convergence under Exact Class Posteriors
We train students on datasets using SGD, with teachers providing the exact class posterior probabilities as supervision. We compare the convergence behavior and stability of SGD to supervision with one-hot labels, using MSE as the primary metric.
CONTROLS: Supervising with one-hot labels; some ablations: different initial learning rates, batch sizes, and optimizer settings.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (small-medium size datasets).
PREDICTION: SGD will generally exhibit better convergence and stability under probabilistic supervision, especially for small to medium-sized datasets, but notable improvements may be specific to certain model architectures or initial conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Effects of Estimation Error on Student Performance
PROPOSAL: Experiment 2: Student Performance under Noisy Teacher Estimates
We train students on a variety of real-world datasets with teachers providing noisy estimates of the class posterior probabilities. We investigate how the level of estimation error affects the student's convergence, generalization, and accuracy, using both classification and quantification metrics (e.g., accuracy, F1-score, precise estimator of mistake rate). We also analyze performance degradation as a function of different error metrics (e.g., KL-divergence, JS-divergence).
CONTROLS: Fixed teacher estimation error rates (random noise, adversarial, etc.); some ablations: different teacher model types, student architectures.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (larger datasets, more experiments).
PREDICTION: We expect to observe non-trivial student performance degradation with increasing teacher estimation error, although this may be mitigated with more informative teacher neighbourhood or adjustments in weight decay.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exact vs. Approximate SGD and Teacher Calibration
PROPOSAL: Theoretical Result 3: Generalization Bounds for SGD under Probabilistic Supervision
Building on previous work, we derive explicit generalization bounds for SGD trained under probabilistic supervision, assuming access to exact class posterior probabilities. We compare these bounds to those obtained in previous work assuming exact one-hot labeling, examining the simplified assumptions under which implicit calibration can transfer useful properties like invariance in magnitude and adaptability for major datacorruptions and robust regression setups or spreading properties. We analyze the implications of relaxing the assumption to noisy teacher estimates, highlighting conditions under which probabilistic supervision may yield improved generalization.
CONTROLS: Development of existing bounds under Fisher Information and Tail-sum sampling.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (analysis only).

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Intermediate Teacher Calibration Analysis
REVISION: 3. Exact vs. Approximate SGD and Teacher Calibration (Theoretical Result 3)
PROPOSAL: We refine the theoretical analysis of generalization bounds for SGD under probabilistic supervision, focusing on intermediate teacher calibration regimes (i.e., when the teacher's predictions are not exactly posterior probabilities but still have noticeable calibration properties). We explore whether intermediate teacher calibration can lead to improved student generalization, even when the teacher's predictions are noisy or biased, and examine the conditions under which this occurs.
CONTROLS: Comparison to existing bounds derived under ideal teacher scenarios; exploration of various teacher noise and calibration regimes.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (analysis only).
PREDICTION: Our refined bounds may indicate that intermediate teacher calibration regimes exhibit a sweet spot between ideal teacher scenarios and noisy teacher predictions, offering improved generalization performance under certain conditions.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Intermediate Teacher Calibration Analysis
REVISION: Theoretical Result 3: Generalization Bounds for SGD under Probabilistic Supervision
PROPOSAL: We derive explicit generalization bounds for SGD trained under probabilistic supervision, focusing on the statistical calibration of the teacher model. Our analysis explores how the theoretical behavior of the teacher model influences the convergence and generalization of SGD, highlighting the importance of well-calibrated teachers for improved student performance.
CONTROLS: Development of existing bounds under Fisher Information and Tail-sum sampling; comparison to results from previous works analyzing teacher calibration.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (analysis only).
PREDICTION: These refined bounds will provide insight into how well-calibrated teachers improve student generalization, showcasing conditions under which probabilistic supervision outperforms one-hot labeling.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Teacher Model Design for Effective Distillation
PROPOSAL: Experiment 4: Teacher Model Design and Calibration Analysis
We construct and analyze several teacher models with varying complexity and calibration properties, to understand how teacher model design affects student generalization and performance. We investigate the impact of teacher calibration on the learned student knowledge and examine whether explicit teacher calibration can lead to better distillation outcomes.
CONTROLS: Varying teacher model architectures (e.g., simple, complex, pre-trained); ablation experiments to evaluate contributions of teacher calibration.
COST: 250 GPU-hours (model design, training, and analysis).
PREDICTION: Our results will demonstrate that well-calibrated teacher models significantly outperform poorly calibrated teachers and highlight the importance of designing teacher models specifically for knowledge distillation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Effects of Knowledge Distillation on Student Regularization
PROPOSAL: Theoretical Result 5: Distillation as Regularization via Bayes-SGD
We provide a new interpretation of knowledge distillation as a form of regularization, based on the framework of regularized risk minimization (Bayes-SGD). We derive conditions under which distillation offers regularization benefits, and explore the implications for understanding the role of teacher calibration in promoting regularization. Our results provide a theoretical foundation for the observed regularizing effects of distillation in practical scenarios.
CONTROLS: Comparison to existing regularization methods; investigation of conditions under which distillation yields regularization benefits.
COST: 75 GPU-hours (analysis only).
PREDICTION: Our theoretical framework will shed new light on the role of knowledge distillation in regularization, demonstrating how distillation can be an effective means of promoting regularization and reducing overfitting in deep neural networks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Distillation-Invariant Training for Robust Generalization
PROPOSAL: Experiment 6: Distillation-Invariant Training under Adversarial Attacks
We examine the robustness of distillation-invariant training, where student models are trained to mimic the teacher's behavior under various sources of noise and perturbations. We investigate whether distillation-invariant training can improve the robustness of student models to adversarial attacks, and evaluate the impact of teacher calibration on robustness. Our results will shed light on the ability of distillation to promote robust generalization.
CONTROLS: Comparison to non-distillation training; ablation experiments to evaluate contributions of teacher calibration and distillation.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (attack simulations, model training).
PREDICTION: Our experiments will demonstrate that distillation-invariant training can improve robustness to adversarial attacks, and provide insight into the role of teacher calibration in promoting robust generalization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluation of Knowledge Distillation for Plug-and-Play Transfer
PROPOSAL: Theoretical Result 7: Constructing Plug-and-Play Transfer via Teacher Calibration
We develop a theoretical framework for constructing plug-and-play transfer learning scenarios using teacher calibration. Our construction involves designing a teacher model that is optimized for the target task, and demonstrates how teacher calibration can be used to promote effective transfer learning. We derive conditions under which plug-and-play transfer is possible, and explore the implications for understanding the role of teacher calibration in transferring knowledge to new tasks.
CONTROLS: Comparison to existing plug-and-play transfer methods; investigation of conditions under which plug-and-play transfer is possible.
COST: 60 GPU-hours (analysis only).
PREDICTION: Our theoretical framework will provide a new understanding of how teacher calibration can be used to promote effective transfer learning, and highlight the conditions under which plug-and-play transfer is possible.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Comparison and Recommendations for Teacher Calibration
PROPOSAL: Experiment 8: Comprehensive Comparison of Teacher Calibration Methods
We conduct a comprehensive comparison of different teacher calibration methods, evaluating their performance across various scenarios and metrics. We summarize our findings and provide recommendations for selecting effective teacher calibration approaches based on the specific task requirements and available computational resources. Our results will provide a practical guide for practitioners interested in leveraging teacher calibration for improved knowledge distillation.
CONTROLS: Comparison of participating teacher calibration methods; ablation experiments to evaluate contributions of each method.
COST: 400 GPU-hours (comprehensive evaluation).
PREDICTION: Our results will provide a comprehensive and practical comparison of teacher calibration methods, helping practitioners to select the most effective approach for their specific use case.

TITLE: Investigating Quantization Overhead in LoRA Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: Analyze the quantization overhead of FP8 arithmetic in LoRA fine-tuning using a simplified, partially-quantized adapter model (BertLoRA Adapter [2]) on the GLUE benchmark [3], to identify the source of the overhead and its impact on adapter ranks. To this end, measure the forward and backward pass time for various adapter ranks, and inspect the number of fp32->fp8 ->fp32 conversions in each pass.
CONTROLS: 
- Run full fp32 LoRA fine-tuning without quantization as baseline
- Run standard QLoRA [4] as baseline for weight-only quantization
- Record the time spent in fp32 and fp8 regions, as well as total time for comparison
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We can find a clear correlation between adapter rank and FP8 quantization overhead, but the overhead may persist even for the smallest adapters, highlighting the need for refining the Quantization procedure or dealing with the overhead differently during the forward and backward passes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Optimizing Quantization Schedules for LoRA Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of adaptive quantization schedules during LoRA fine-tuning on the quantization overhead, convergence rate, and accuracy. We will implement a mixed-schedule approach where the adapter weights are initially quantized using a coarse-grained schedule, and then updated using finer-grained schedules as adaptation progresses. The objective is to develop a more efficient approach that minimizes the overhead while maintaining the convergence and accuracy.
CONTROLS: 
- Run full fp32 LoRA fine-tuning without quantization as baseline
- Run standard QLoRA [4] with the current fixed-schedule quantization as a baseline
- Compare mixed-schedule approaches with different numbers of quantization scales and update frequencies
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed mixed-schedule approach to reduce the quantization overhead while preserving the convergence and accuracy, especially for mid-to-small adapter ranks.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Optimizing Quantization Schedules for LoRA Fine-Tuning (Revised)
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of adaptive quantization schedules during LoRA fine-tuning on the quantization overhead, convergence rate, and accuracy. We will implement a two-stage scheduling approach:
- Initial quantization stage: coarse-grained FP8 quantization with a few scales to quickly reduce memory usage
- Fine-tuning stage: refinement with finer-grained scales to reach the desired precision for better model performance
We will explore different combinations of scales, adaptations frequencies, and gate-thresholds to optimize the approach for various adapter ranks and tasks.
CONTROLS: 
- Run full fp32 LoRA fine-tuning without quantization as baseline
- Run standard QLoRA [4] with the current fixed-schedule quantization as a baseline
- Compare different combinations of the two-stage schedules on multiple GLUE tasks and adapter ranks
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the two-stage scheduling approach to find a better balance between memory efficiency and model performance, especially for mid-to-large adapter ranks. However, achieving significant speedup on small adapters might be challenging due to the complexity of tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantization Overhead Analysis in LoRA Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: Analyze the quantization overhead in LoRA fine-tuning using FP8 arithmetic on the BERT and RoBERTa models with adapter sizes ranging from 16x16 to 256x256 on the GLUE and SuperGLUE benchmark datasets. Compare the overhead to the speedup gained from using FP8 matrix multiplication. Investigate the impact of different quantization formats (E4M3, E5M2) and rounding strategies on the overhead and speedup.
CONTROLS: Baseline: LoRA fine-tuning with FP16 arithmetic on the same models and datasets; Ablation: LoRA fine-tuning with weight-only quantization using QLoRA.
COST: Estimated 1000 GPU-hours with 8x V100 GPUs.
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant quantization overhead for small adapter sizes, but the overhead will decrease as the adapter size increases, ultimately resulting in tangible speedups. FP8 with E5M2 format is predicted to outperform E4M3 format due to its wider modelable range. However, the results might fail to transfer to models with very large adapter sizes due to the hardware limitations and algorithms used.

Please evaluate and inform the next turn.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Optimal Adapter Size for LoRA Fine-Tuning with FP8
PROPOSAL: Investigate the optimal adapter size that balances quantization overhead and speedup in LoRA fine-tuning with FP8 arithmetic. We will explore adapter sizes between 16x16 and 1024x1024 on the GLUE and SuperGLUE benchmark datasets, fine-tuning BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT. Assess the impact of different adapter initialization methods, such as random initialization, SVD-based initialization, and pruning-based initialization on the optimal adapter size. Compare the results to reward schemes that balance accuracy and speed.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Optimizing the adapter size without considering quantization overhead; Ablation: Using random initialization, SVD-based initialization, or pruning-based initialization.
COST: Estimated 2000 GPU-hours with 16x V100 GPUs.
PREDICTION: We expect to find an optimal adapter size that minimizes the trade-off between accuracy and speed, and different initialization methods will perform differently. However, the results might vary across models and datasets, and the benefit of different initialization methods might be limited for large models.

Please evaluate and inform the next turn.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Loop Quasi-Newton (LQN) Methods for Efficient LoRA Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: Explore the application of Loop Quasi-Newton (LQN) methods, which are known for their low memory usage and fast convergence, to optimize LoRA fine-tuning with FP8 arithmetic. We will compare LQN-based methods to the standard AdamW optimizer used in LoRA fine-tuning. Study the impact of LQN hyperparameters, such as the quasi-Newton estimate update frequency, on the convergence and accuracy of LoRA adapters on the GLUE and SuperGLUE benchmark datasets.
CONTROLS: Baseline: AdamW optimizer; Ablation: LQN methods without LQN-based warm-up and without LQN-based schedule.
COST: Estimated 500 GPU-hours with 8x V100 GPUs.
PREDICTION: We expect LQN methods to significantly reduce the number of gradient computations required for LoRA fine-tuning, leading to a notable speedup. However, the results might be sensitive to the quasi-Newton estimate update frequency, and the speedup might vary across models and datasets.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Quantization Overhead in LoRA Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: Analyze the quantization overhead in LoRA fine-tuning using a range of adapters with different ranks, trained on the full WikiText-103 dataset. Measure the overhead of FP8 quantization, scaling, and rounding, and compare it to the gains from FP8 matrix multiplication. Compare with standard LoRA fine-tuning and QLoRA with 4-bit NormalFloat weights as baselines. To isolate the effects of adapter rank, repeat the experiment with adapter ranks ranging from 1 to 128.
CONTROLS: Baselines: standard LoRA fine-tuning (FP16), QLoRA with 4-bit NormalFloat weights. Ablation: turn off FP8 scaling and rounding to evaluate its impact on overhead. Scale up: train LoRA with ranks 256 and 512 to assess potential diminishing returns.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the quantization overhead to be significant for small adapters, whereas the overhead per element will decrease as the adapter rank increases, potentially offsetting the gains from FP8 matrix multiplication.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating FP8 Training Methods for Large-Dimensional LoRA Matrices
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of various FP8 training methods for large-dimensional LoRA matrices, including hybrid E4M3/E5M2 formats, mixed-precision FP8 training with high-precision master weights, and unit scaling, on the instruction tuning of LLM chat assistants domain using the Open-Domain Chat benchmark. Measure training time, validation accuracy, and adapter rank-doubling speedup over standard LoRA fine-tuning as the key metrics. To make a fair comparison, restrict each method to the same rounding strategy and provide feedback to the user as fewer training iterations are required.
CONTROLS: Baselines: standard LoRA fine-tuning (FP16). Ablation: train individual components of the hybrid E4M3/E5M2 format in isolation to evaluate their contribution to performance. Scale up: compare performance on higher rank adapters (512, 1024) to assess the scalability of FP8 training methods.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect hybrid E4M3/E5M2 formats and mixed-precision FP8 training with high-precision master weights to deliver real speedups over standard LoRA fine-tuning, whereas unit scaling will provide marginal improvements, but will have a simpler to train adapter to verify stable convergence.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Evaluating FP8 Training Methods for Large-Dimensional LoRA Matrices
PROPOSAL: Modify the second proposal to focus on multitask knowledge question answering, a domain known for its memory bottleneck. Replace the Open-Domain Chat benchmark with the MultiGame WikiReasoning benchmark and evaluate the performance of various FP8 training methods on this new task. This will help to verify whether FP8 training methods can accelerate large-dimensional LoRA matrices in a realistic scenario. The rest of the proposal remains unchanged.
CONTROLS: Baselines: standard LoRA fine-tuning (FP16). Ablation: train individual components of the hybrid E4M3/E5M2 format in isolation to evaluate their contribution to performance. Scale up: compare performance on higher rank adapters (512, 1024) to assess the scalability of FP8 training methods.
COST: No change (still 800 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: Changing the task to multitask knowledge question answering should preserve our expectations: hybrid E4M3/E5M2 formats and mixed-precision FP8 training with high-precision master weights should deliver real speedups over standard LoRA fine-tuning.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Evaluating FP8 Training Methods for Large-Dimensional LoRA Matrices
PROPOSAL: Modify the second proposal to focus on multitask knowledge question answering, a domain known for its memory bottleneck. Replace the Open-Domain Chat benchmark with the MultiGame WikiReasoning benchmark and evaluate the performance of various FP8 training methods on this new task. This will help to verify whether FP8 training methods can accelerate large-dimensional LoRA matrices in a realistic scenario. To further assess the effectiveness of FP8 training methods, add a comparison with standard LoRA fine-tuning with high-precision master weights (FP32); this will serve as a control to evaluate the value of reducing precision in the forward pass.
CONTROLS: Baselines: standard LoRA fine-tuning (FP16). Baseline with higher precision: standard LoRA fine-tuning with high-precision master weights (FP32). Ablation: train individual components of the hybrid E4M3/E5M2 format in isolation to evaluate their contribution to performance.
COST: No change (still 800 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: This change will allow us to understand whether the speedup provided by FP8 training methods is due to reducing precision in the forward pass or due to the effect of lower precision on feedback.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Optimizing Adapter Size for Fast LoRA Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the optimal adapter size for LoRA fine-tuning in terms of memory usage and training time, considering the different FP8 training methods. Train LoRA models with adapters of varying sizes (64, 128, 256, 512) using the multi-task knowledge question answering benchmark and various FP8 training methods. Evaluate the trade-off between memory usage, training time, and validation accuracy to determine the optimal adapter size. Use these results to inform the design of future LoRA models.
CONTROLS: Baselines: standard LoRA fine-tuning (FP16). Utilize the results from the revised proposal 2 (Evaluating FP8 Training Methods for Large-Dimensional LoRA Matrices) to use the most efficient FP8 training method.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that smaller adapters will be faster to train, but will require more iterations to converge, while larger adapters will converge faster but will require more memory and memory transfers. The most efficient FP8 training method will provide a more stable performance across different adapter sizes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adapting LoRA for Commonsense Reasoning Question Answering
PROPOSAL: Extend the evaluation of LoRA fine-tuning to the commonsense reasoning question answering domain, which has seen recent advancements using LoRA. Evaluate the performance of standard LoRA fine-tuning, various FP8 training methods, and optimally sized adapters on the CommonsenseQA benchmark. Assess whether the benefits of FP8 training methods and optimized adapter sizes can be generalized to this new domain. Investigate whether any additional modifications to LoRA, such as knowledge integration or adapter pruning, can further enhance performance in this domain.
CONTROLS: Baselines: standard LoRA fine-tuning (FP16). Utilize the results from the revised proposal 2 (Evaluating FP8 Training Methods for Large-Dimensional LoRA Matrices) to use the most efficient FP8 training method. Use the results from proposal 3 (Optimizing Adapter Size for Fast LoRA Fine-Tuning) to optimize the adapter size for this new domain.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that LoRA fine-tuning will achieve good performance in this domain, but may require additional modifications to optimize performance. The benefits of FP8 training methods and optimized adapter sizes may be more pronounced in this domain due to the need for efficient knowledge retrieval and usage of knowledge in reasoning tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Optimizing Adapter Size for Fast LoRA Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: Modify the third proposal to investigate the impact of adapter initialization on the efficiency of LoRA fine-tuning. Assess whether using different initialization strategies, such as SVD-based initialization or random initialization, can reduce the quantization overhead and improve the accuracy of LoRA fine-tuning models. Investigate the optimal combination of adapter initialization strategy and FP8 training methods to achieve fast and accurate LoRA fine-tuning.
CONTROLS: Baselines: standard LoRA fine-tuning (FP16) with SVD-based and random initialization. Utilize the results from the revised proposal 2 (Evaluating FP8 Training Methods for Large-Dimensional LoRA Matrices) to use the most efficient FP8 training method. Compare the performance of different initialization strategies alone and in combination with FP8 training methods.
COST: No change (still 600 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: We expect that using different initialization strategies can significantly reduce the quantization overhead and improve the accuracy of LoRA fine-tuning models, especially when combined with efficient FP8 training methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Dynamic Rank Allocation in LoRA
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of dynamic rank allocation in LoRA fine-tuning, where the rank of the adapter is adaptively adjusted during training based on the model's performance. Implement this dynamic rank allocation using a sampling-based approach, where the rank is updated at regular intervals during training. Evaluate the performance of this dynamic approach in combination with efficient FP8 training methods and optimized adapter initialization. Assess its impact on the accuracy and speed of LoRA fine-tuning models.
CONTROLS: Baselines: standard LoRA fine-tuning (FP16) with fixed adapter rank. Utilize the results from the revised proposal 2 (Evaluating FP8 Training Methods for Large-Dimensional LoRA Matrices) to use the most efficient FP8 training method. Compare the performance of different dynamic rank allocation strategies and their combination with efficient FP8 training methods and optimized adapter initialization.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that dynamic rank allocation will provide a significant improvement in the accuracy and speed of LoRA fine-tuning models, especially when combined with efficient FP8 training methods and optimized adapter initialization. However, the optimal strategy for dynamic rank allocation will depend on the specific use case and task at hand.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Adapting LoRA for Commonsense Reasoning Question Answering
PROPOSAL: Modify the fourth proposal to incorporate the results from the revised proposal 2 (Evaluating FP8 Training Methods for Large-Dimensional LoRA Matrices) and the revised proposal 3 (Optimizing Adapter Size for Fast LoRA Fine-Tuning). Evaluate the performance of LoRA fine-tuning models with optimized adapter size and efficient FP8 training methods on the CommonsenseQA benchmark. Assess whether the combined benefits of these optimizations can provide a significant improvement in accuracy and speed on this challenging task. Additionally, compare the performance of LoRA fine-tuning models with different initialization strategies and dynamic rank allocation.
CONTROLS: Baselines: standard LoRA fine-tuning (FP16) with fixed adapter rank and SVD-based initialization. Utilize the results from the revised proposal 2 (Evaluating FP8 Training Methods for Large-Dimensional LoRA Matrices) to use the most efficient FP8 training method. Compare the performance of LoRA fine-tuning models with optimized adapter size, efficient FP8 training methods, different initialization strategies, and dynamic rank allocation.
COST: No change (still 1000 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: We expect that the combined benefits of optimized adapter size, efficient FP8 training methods, different initialization strategies, and dynamic rank allocation will provide a significant improvement in accuracy and speed on the CommonsenseQA benchmark, outperforming standard LoRA fine-tuning models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Scalability of Optimized LoRA Fine-Tuning on Large-Scale Datasets
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the scalability of optimized LoRA fine-tuning on large-scale datasets, such as the Wikipedia dataset or the Common Crawl dataset. Assess whether the optimized LoRA fine-tuning models can be efficiently scaled up to larger datasets while maintaining their accuracy and speed. Investigate the impact of increasing the dataset size on the performance of the optimized LoRA fine-tuning models and identify any potential bottlenecks or limitations.
CONTROLS: Baselines: standard LoRA fine-tuning (FP16) on smaller datasets. Utilize the results from the previous proposals to optimize the adapter size, efficient FP8 training methods, different initialization strategies, and dynamic rank allocation.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the optimized LoRA fine-tuning models will scale well to larger datasets, but may encounter challenges due to increased computational requirements, memory constraints, or optimization difficulties. However, with careful optimization and adaptation of the models, we anticipate that the optimized LoRA fine-tuning models can maintain their accuracy and speed on large-scale datasets.

Modify the fourth proposal to incorporate the results from the revised proposal 2 (Evaluating FP8 Training Methods for Large-Dimensional LoRA Matrices) and the revised proposal 3 (Optimizing Adapter Size for Fast LoRA Fine-Tuning). Evaluate the performance of LoRA fine-tuning models with optimized adapter size and efficient FP8 training methods on the CommonsenseQA benchmark. PROPOSAL 5: Investigating the Effect of Dynamic Rank Allocation in LoRA
Explore the use of dynamic rank allocation in LoRA fine-tuning, where the rank of the adapter is adaptively adjusted during training based on the model's performance.
