actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Catastrophic Forgetting in Unified Multimodal Generative Models
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of UMGMs on visual question answering (VQA) and text-to-image generation (T2I) tasks before and after fine-tuning on a new downstream task, using a benchmark dataset such as COCO, VQA-2, and CLEVR.
CONTROLS: Run the same UMGM on both tasks without fine-tuning (zero-shot performance).
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect UMGMs to exhibit catastrophic forgetting, with degraded performance on pre-trained tasks (VQA and T2I) after fine-tuning, while maintaining good performance on the new downstream task. The forgetting could be more pronounced for inter-modal tasks (e.g., from T2I to VQA) than intra-modal tasks (e.g., from VQA to another VQA task). 

This proposal provides a starting point to examine the scope of inter-modal catastrophic forgetting in UMGMs using real-world datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of UMGMs to Catastrophic Forgetting
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of several methods designed for continual learning, such as EWC (Elastic Weight Consolidation), LWF (Learning Without Forgetting), and Replay-Based Learning, to prevent catastrophic forgetting in UMGMs on visual question answering, text-to-image generation, and referring expression grounding tasks using the PRECOL and VQG datasets.
CONTROLS: Run the same UMGM with each method, comparing their performance on pre-trained tasks and the new downstream task after fine-tuning.
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect these methods to mitigate catastrophic forgetting to some extent, but their effectiveness may vary depending on the task and dataset used, and the severity of forgetting might differ between intra-modal and inter-modal tasks.

This proposal evaluates the existing state-of-the-art methods for preventing catastrophic forgetting in UMGMs, with a focus on identifying the challenges and limitations of each approach.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Fine-Tuning Order on Catastrophic Forgetting in UMGMs
PROPOSAL: Examine how the order of fine-tuning different downstream tasks affects catastrophic forgetting in UMGMs, using a task order that alternates between intra-modal (e.g., VQA-VQA) and inter-modal (e.g., VQA-T2I) tasks, and evaluate the performance of the UMGM on pre-trained tasks and new downstream tasks using the CLEVR-Humans and VQG datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of UMGMs fine-tuned in different orders, including random ordering, fixed intra-modal ordering, and fixed inter-modal ordering, and analyze the impact of forgetting on different modalities.
COST: Estimated 200 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect the order of fine-tuning to influence the severity of catastrophic forgetting, with inter-modal fine-tuning order potentially leading to more pronounced forgetting than intra-modal fine-tuning order. The results will provide insights into how to efficiently update UMGMs for new tasks without incurring significant forgetting.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: OV3. Investigating the Impact of Fine-Tuning Order on Catastrophic Forgetting in UMGMs
PROPOSAL: Modify the previous proposal to also analyze the effect of fine-tuning temperature (a hyperparameter controlling the rate of forgetting) on catastrophic forgetting, by varying the temperature and evaluating the impact on model performance on pre-trained tasks and new downstream tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of UMGMs fine-tuned with different fine-tuning temperatures, ranging from low to high, and analyze the interplay between temperature and fine-tuning order.
COST: Estimated 175 GPU-hours (minimum adjustments).
PREDICTION: We expect the fine-tuning temperature to have a significant impact on the severity of catastrophic forgetting, with lower temperatures potentially leading to less forgetting but slower adaptation, and higher temperatures potentially leading to more forgetting but faster adaptation.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: 3. Investigating the Impact of Fine-Tuning Order on Catastrophic Forgetting in UMGMs
PROPOSAL: Modify the previous proposal to also investigate the effect of adapting the fine-tuning schedule (e.g., changing the number of fine-tuning steps, the learning rate, or the batch size) on catastrophic forgetting, by varying the schedule and evaluating the impact on model performance on pre-trained tasks and new downstream tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of UMGMs fine-tuned with different schedules, and analyze the interaction between schedule adaptation and fine-tuning temperature.
COST: Estimated 200 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect adapting the fine-tuning schedule to have a significant impact on the severity of catastrophic forgetting, allowing for a trade-off between performance on new tasks and retention on pre-trained tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: 3. Investigating the Impact of Fine-Tuning Order on Catastrophic Forgetting in UMGMs
PROPOSAL: Combine the effects of adapting the fine-tuning order and the fine-tuning temperature on catastrophic forgetting, by investigating whether certain fine-tuning orders and temperatures are more resilient to forgetting than others.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of UMGMs with different fine-tuning orders (intra-modal vs. inter-modal) and temperatures (low, medium, high), and compare the results to a baseline fine-tuning schedule with a fixed temperature.
COST: Estimated 225 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect a combination of fine-tuning order and temperature to provide a better balance between performance on new tasks and retention on pre-trained tasks, helping to mitigate catastrophic forgetting in UMGMs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Mixup on Catastrophic Forgetting in UMGMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of mixup, a technique that combines data from the current and previous tasks, on catastrophic forgetting in UMGMs, by fine-tuning the model on a mixup dataset that combines images and text from the current and previous tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of UMGMs fine-tuned with and without mixup, and evaluate the impact of mixup on model performance on pre-trained tasks and new downstream tasks.
COST: Estimated 250 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect mixup to help mitigate catastrophic forgetting by creating a smooth transition between tasks, leading to better retention of pre-trained knowledge and improved performance on new downstream tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Task-Specific Adapters on Catastrophic Forgetting in UMGMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of task-specific adapters, which are used to modify the shared encoder of the UMGM to adapt to new tasks, on catastrophic forgetting, by fine-tuning the adapter for task transfer.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of UMGMs with and without task-specific adapters, and evaluate the impact of adapters on model performance on pre-trained tasks and new downstream tasks.
COST: Estimated 280 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect task-specific adapters to help mitigate catastrophic forgetting by allowing the UMGM to adapt to new tasks without overwriting pre-trained knowledge, leading to better retention of pre-trained knowledge and improved performance on new downstream tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparing Continual Learning Methods for UMGMs on Real-World Benchmarks
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the performance of various continual learning methods (EWC, LWF, Replay-Based Learning, and task-specific adapters) on real-world benchmarks for visual question answering, text-to-image generation, and referring expression grounding, including the VQA-2 and VQG datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of UMGMs fine-tuned with different continual learning methods, and evaluate the impact of each method on model performance on pre-trained tasks and new downstream tasks.
COST: Estimated 400 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect the continual learning methods to perform well on the real-world benchmarks, with task-specific adapters and replay-based learning showing promising results in mitigating catastrophic forgetting and improving model performance on new downstream tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying the Effectiveness of Continual Learning Methods for UMGMs Using a Unified Framework
PROPOSAL: Develop a unified framework to quantify the effectiveness of various continual learning methods for UMGMs, including EWC, LWF, Replay-Based Learning, and task-specific adapters, by modeling various forgetting scenarios and evaluating the trade-off between performance on pre-trained tasks and new downstream tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of UMGMs fine-tuned with different continual learning methods using the unified framework, and evaluate the impact of each method on model performance on pre-trained tasks and new downstream tasks.
COST: Estimated 500 GPU-hours (due to the need for extensive hyperparameter tuning).
PREDICTION: We expect the unified framework to provide insights into the strengths and limitations of each continual learning method, allowing for more informed decisions on method selection and hyperparameter tuning, and ultimately leading to better performance on UMGMs in real-world applications.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating Inter-Modal Forgetting in Unified Multimodal Generative Models
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of a UMGM on a visual question answering task and a text-to-image generation task, pre-trained on a diverse multitask dataset and then sequentially fine-tuned on each task separately. We will measure the performance drop of the model on the other task after fine-tuning, to determine if UMGMs exhibit inter-modal forgetting.
CONTROLS: 
- A baseline UMGM trained on a single task (visual QA or text-to-image generation) and tested on both tasks to assess intra-modal forgetting
- A UMGM trained without pre-training on the multitask dataset to assess the effect of diverse pre-training on inter-modal forgetting
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The UMGM will show a significant performance drop on the other task after fine-tuning, indicating inter-modal forgetting. However, this might fail if the model's architecture or training regimen is able to mitigate this effect.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Mid-Task Inter-Modal Transfer Learning for UMGMs
PROPOSAL: Introduce a mid-task adaptation mechanism that allows the UMGM to receive instruction tuning feedback on only one modality (e.g., text) while keeping the other modality (e.g., image generation) frozen. We will evaluate the model's ability to adapt to new tasks with inter-modal interactions using a temperature-scheduled gradual unfreeze strategy to gradually release the frozen modality's capacity.
CONTROLS: 
- The original sequential fine-tuning setup from proposal 1
- A variant with an abrupt unfreeze of the frozen modality
- A random adaptation strategy where the model's capacity is released randomly
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Mid-task adaptation will mitigate inter-modal forgetting to some extent, allowing UMGMs to adapt to new tasks more efficiently. However, the performance might degrade if the frozen modality's capacity is not adapted for or if the model's understanding of relationships between modalities is not updated.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Adversarial Prior on Inter-Modal Regularization
PROPOSAL: Introduce an additional self-supervised loss that encourages the UMGM to keep its pre-trained representations in both modalities consistent under an adversarial prior, forcing it to adapt to new tasks in a way that maintains the integrity of its pre-trained capacities. This loss term will be optimized simultaneously with the original fine-tuning objective.
CONTROLS: 
- The original sequential fine-tuning setup from proposal 1
- Proposal 2's mid-task adaptation setup with a constant and random adaptation strategy

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Inter-Modal Forgetting in Unified Multimodal Generative Models
PROPOSAL: To explore inter-modal forgetting in UMGMs, we will perform an empirical study that fine-tunes a pre-trained UMGM (e.g., ViLT [1]) on a sequence of multimodal understanding tasks (e.g., VQA v2.0 [2]), followed by evaluating its visual generation capabilities on a separate benchmark (e.g., COCO-Text [3]). We will measure forgetting using metrics such as accuracy drop and generation score reduction. To ensure the study controls for intra-modal forgetting, we will keep the text generator frozen and only fine-tune the visual encoder during training.
CONTROLS: Baselines include fine-tuning the entire UMGM, freezing the pre-trained model, and using a model pre-trained only on visual tasks. Ablation studies will investigate the impact of task order, number of fine-tuning iterations, and choice of evaluation metrics.
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to observe inter-modal forgetting, with significant reductions in generation scores, particularly when fine-tuning on a large number of tasks. The method may fail if the model is not challenged with diverse tasks or if the forgetting metric is not sensitive enough to capture subtle changes in the model's behavior.

[1] Garcia et al. (2021) - Vision and Language Transformers (ViLT)
[2] Goyal et al. (2017) - Visual Question Answering (VQA) v2.0
[3] Desai et al. (2017) - COCO-Text - Text Detection and Recognition in Natural Images

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating Inter-Modal Forgetting in Unified Multimodal Generative Models (Revision)
PROPOSAL: To better understand the causes of inter-modal forgetting, we will introduce a new control condition where we fine-tune the UMGM on a sequence of tasks that only require the visual generator to generate images of varying styles (e.g., using the ImageNet 비교Classification [1] and CIFAR-100 [2] datasets). We will then compare the forgetting patterns observed in the original study (revision 1) with those observed in this new control condition. This will help us determine if inter-modal forgetting is triggered by the modification of the visual encoder or due to the interaction between the visual and text generators.
CONTROLS: The control conditions include fine-tuning the entire UMGM, freezing the pre-trained model, and the new style conditioning control. Ablation studies will investigate the impact of style variability and the choice of evaluation metrics.
COST: Estimated 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to observe less inter-modal forgetting when fine-tuning on style conditioning tasks, suggesting that the visual generator is not the primary cause of forgetting. The method may fail if the style variability is not sufficient to trigger adaptation or if the style conditioning control does not accurately capture the nuances of visual generation.

[1] ImageNet Classification
[2] CIFAR-100 Dataset 

Note: Original costs and predictions are preserved. New costs and predictions are added.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating Inter-Modal Forgetting in Unified Multimodal Generative Models (Revision)
PROPOSAL: To better understand the causes of inter-modal forgetting, we will introduce a new control condition where we fine-tune the UMGM on a sequence of tasks that only require the visual generator to generate images of varying styles (e.g., using the ImageNet Classification [1] and CIFAR-100 [2] datasets). We will then compare the forgetting patterns observed in this new control condition with those observed in the original study.
CONTROLS: The control conditions include fine-tuning the entire UMGM, freezing the pre-trained model, and a variation of the original study where only the text generator is fine-tuned while the visual encoder is frozen. Ablation studies will investigate the impact of style variability and the choice of evaluation metrics.
COST: Estimated 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to observe a correlation between style variability and reduced inter-modal forgetting, suggesting that the visual generator is adaptively updating its internal representation to accommodate new styles while preserving the original generation capability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Training for Inter-Modal Conservation
PROPOSAL: To mitigate inter-modal forgetting, we will incorporate an adversarial training mechanism that encourages the UMGM to conserve its pre-trained generation capabilities while adapting to new tasks. Specifically, we will add a generator and discriminator (e.g., using the DeepConv-LSTM [1] and RAISE [2] architectures) that evaluates the UMGM's generation performance on a held-out dataset from the pre-training phase. During training, the UMGM's generation output will be adversarially perturbed by the generator, and the discriminator will be updated to correctly identify the original and perturbed outputs. This process will incentivize the UMGM to retain its original generation skills while learning new tasks.
CONTROLS: Baselines will include fine-tuning the UMGM without adversarial training and using a model pre-trained only on visual tasks. Ablation studies will investigate the impact of generator and discriminator architectures, advesarial perturbation techniques, and training schedules.
COST: Estimated 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to observe significant reduction in inter-modal forgetting, particularly when the adversarial training is combined with the control condition introduced in revision 1. The method may fail if the generator and discriminator architectures are not well-suited for the task, or if the advesarial perturbation is too aggressive.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Architecture for Inter-Modal Adaptation
PROPOSAL: To improve the UMGM's ability to adapt to new tasks without forgetting pre-trained abilities, we will implement a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture that allows for efficient weight sharing and knowledge transfer between tasks. The MoE will have a high-level component that selects the best expert (e.g., a subset of tasks) to update based on the current task, and a low-level component that fine-tunes the selected expert. This architecture will enable the UMGM to specialize on individual tasks while preserving pre-trained knowledge and inter-modal relationships.
CONTROLS: Baselines will include fine-tuning the UMGM without MoE or using a standard weight-sharing approach. Ablation studies will investigate the impact of expert selection strategies, weight initialization, and task composition.
COST: Estimated 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to observe reduced inter-modal forgetting, improved adaptability, and increased efficiency in the UMGM's knowledge transfer. The method may fail if the MoE architecture is not well-suited for the task, or if the expert selection strategy is too simplistic.

Note: The MoE architecture will be applied in conjunction with the Adversarial Training for Inter-Modal Conservation (revision 2) to handle both intra-modal and inter-modal forgetting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Continual Learning with Instruction Tuning and Knowledge Graph Embeddings
PROPOSAL: To further improve the UMGM's ability to adapt to new tasks without forgetting pre-trained abilities, we will incorporate knowledge graph embeddings (KGEs) that capture the relationships between tasks and pre-trained knowledge. The KGEs will be used to guide the instruction tuning process and facilitate the transfer of knowledge across tasks. Additionally, we will use a graph neural network to reason about the relationships between tasks and update the UMGM's knowledge graph embeddings accordingly. This approach will enable the UMGM to learn from task-specific instructions while preserving pre-trained knowledge and inter-modal relationships.
CONTROLS: Baselines will include fine-tuning the UMGM with instruction tuning but without KGEs and using a standard weight-sharing approach. Ablation studies will investigate the impact of different KGE architectures, instructional tuning strategies, and graph neural network configurations.
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to observe significant reduction in inter-modal forgetting, improved adaptability, and increased efficiency in the UMGM's knowledge transfer. The method may fail if the KGE architecture is not well-suited for the task, or if the graph neural network is not effective in updating task relationships.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Continual Learning with Instruction Tuning and Knowledge Graph Embeddings (Revision)
PROPOSAL: To enhance the effectiveness of the knowledge graph embeddings and graph neural network in facilitating task relationships, we will incorporate a novel attention mechanism that selectively focuses on the most relevant task relationships during instruction tuning. This attention mechanism will be applied to both the task embedding and instruction learning stages, enabling the UMGM to prioritize the most informative task relationships and adapt more efficiently to new tasks.
CONTROLS: The revised approach will be compared to the original proposal and the ablation studies will investigate the impact of different attention mechanisms, task embedding configurations, and instruction tuning strategies.
COST: Estimated 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to observe improved adaptability, reduced inter-modal forgetting, and increased efficiency in the UMGM's knowledge transfer. The method may fail if the attention mechanism is not effective in selectively focusing on the most relevant task relationships, or if the UMGM struggles to adapt to novel task relationships.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Generalizability Across Varying Task Difficulty and Domain Shift
PROPOSAL: To further validate the effectiveness of the proposed methods in handling inter-modal forgetting and improving adaptability, we will evaluate their generalizability across varying task difficulty and domain shift. We will fine-tune the UMGM on a sequence of tasks with increasing difficulty and measure its performance on a separate evaluation set. Additionally, we will use a domain adaptation algorithm (e.g., DANN [1]) to transfer knowledge across domains (e.g., visual question answering in COCO [2] to visual question answering in VQA [3]) and assess the UMGM's ability to adapt to new domains while retaining pre-trained knowledge.
CONTROLS: Baselines will include fine-tuning the UMGM without the proposed methods and using a standard weight-sharing approach. Ablation studies will investigate the impact of task difficulty, domain similarity, and adaptation algorithms.
COST: Estimated 350 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to observe robust performance across varying task difficulty and domain shift, with minimal loss of pre-trained knowledge and adaptation efficiency. However, the method may fail if the task difficulty or domain gap is too large, or if the adaptation algorithm is not effective in transferring knowledge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Treasuring the Inter-Modal Knowledge Graph: A Novel Knowledge Distillation Approach
PROPOSAL: To further enhance the UMGM's ability to retain pre-trained knowledge and adaptation efficiency, we will develop a novel knowledge distillation approach that leverages the inter-modal knowledge graph embeddings as a teacher to distill knowledge into the student model. The teacher model will be a pre-trained UMGM on a large-scale dataset, while the student model will be the fine-tuned UMGM on a smaller-scale dataset. The knowledge distillation process will be guided by the teacher's knowledge graph embeddings, enabling the student model to rapidly adapt to new tasks while preserving pre-trained knowledge.
CONTROLS: Baselines will include fine-tuning the UMGM without knowledge distillation and using a standard weight-sharing approach. Ablation studies will investigate the impact of teacher-student architecture, knowledge distillation temperature, and adaptation iterations.
COST: Estimated 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to observe significant improvement in knowledge retention and adaptation efficiency, with reduced inter-modal forgetting and improved generalizability across tasks and domains. However, the method may fail if the teacher-student architecture is not well-suited for the task, or if the knowledge distillation process is not effective in transferring knowledge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Framework for Inter-Modal Continual Learning
PROPOSAL: To integrate the various methods proposed throughout this research, we will develop a unified framework for inter-modal continual learning that combines the strengths of each approach. The framework will consist of a modular architecture that incorporates inter-modal knowledge graph embeddings, adversarial training, mixture-of-experts, and knowledge distillation, along with a task-specific instruction tuning module. This framework will enable the UMGM to efficiently adapt to new tasks while retaining pre-trained knowledge and minimizing inter-modal forgetting.
CONTROLS: Baselines will include fine-tuning the UMGM without the proposed framework and using a standard weight-sharing approach. Ablation studies will investigate the impact of individual components and their interactions.
COST: Estimated 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to observe robust and efficient adaptability across a wide range of tasks and domains, with minimal inter-modal forgetting and significant improvement in generalizability. However, the method may fail if the unified framework is not effectively integrated or if the components interact negatively, leading to decreased performance.

Specifically, we will add a generator and discriminator (e.g., using the DeepConv-LSTM [1] and RAISE [2] architectures) that evaluates the UMGM's generation performance on a held-out dataset from the pre-training phase. During training, the UMGM's generation output will be adversarially perturbed by the generator, and the discriminator will be updated to correctly identify the original and perturbed outputs. This process will incentivize the UMGM to retain its original generation skills while learning new tasks.
Controls: Baselines will include fine-tuning the UMGM without adversarial training and using a model pre-trained only on visual tasks. Ablation studies will investigate the impact of generator and discriminator architectures, advesarial perturbation techniques, and training schedules.
Estimated cost: Estimated 200 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect to observe significant reduction in inter-modal forgetting, particularly when the adversarial training is combined with the control condition introduced in revision 1. The method may fail if the generator and discriminator architectures are not well-suited for the task, or if the advesarial perturbation is too aggressive.

PROPOSAL 3: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Architecture for Inter-Modal Adaptation
To improve the UMGM's ability to adapt to new tasks without forgetting pre-trained abilities, we will implement a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture that allows for efficient weight sharing and knowledge transfer between tasks. The MoE will have a high-level component that selects the best expert (e.g., a subset of tasks) to update based on the current task, and a low-level component that fine-tunes the selected expert. This architecture will enable the UMGM to specialize on individual tasks while preserving pre-trained knowledge and inter-modal relationships.
Controls: Baselines will include fine-tuning the UMGM without MoE or using a standard weight-sharing approach. Ablation studies will investigate the impact of expert selection strategies, weight initialization, and task composition.
Estimated cost: Estimated 250 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect to observe reduced inter-modal forgetting, improved adaptability, and increased efficiency in the UMGM's knowledge transfer. The method may fail if the MoE architecture is not well-suited for the task, or if the expert selection strategy is too simplistic.

Note: The MoE architecture will be applied in conjunction with the Adversarial Training for Inter-Modal Conservation (revision 2) to handle both intra-modal and inter-modal forgetting.

PROPOSAL 4: Continual Learning with Instruction Tuning and Knowledge Graph Embeddings (Revision)
To enhance the effectiveness of the knowledge graph embeddings and graph neural network in facilitating task relationships, we will incorporate a novel attention mechanism that selectively focuses on the most relevant task relationships during instruction tuning. This attention mechanism will be applied to both the task embedding and instruction learning stages, enabling the UMGM to prioritize the most informative task relationships and adapt more efficiently to new tasks.
Controls: The revised approach will be compared to the original proposal and the ablation studies will investigate the impact of different attention mechanisms, task embedding configurations, and instruction tuning strategies.
Estimated cost: Estimated 250 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect to observe improved adaptability, reduced inter-modal forgetting, and increased efficiency in the UMGM's knowledge transfer. The method may fail if the attention mechanism is not effective in selectively focusing on the most relevant task relationships, or if the UMGM struggles to adapt to novel task relationships.

PROPOSAL 5: Evaluating Generalizability Across Varying Task Difficulty and Domain Shift
To further validate the effectiveness of the proposed methods in handling inter-modal forgetting and improving adaptability, we will evaluate their generalizability across varying task difficulty and domain shift. We will fine-tune the UMGM on a sequence of tasks with increasing difficulty and measure its performance on a separate evaluation set. Additionally, we will use a domain adaptation algorithm (e.g., DANN [1]) to transfer knowledge across domains (e.g., visual question answering in COCO [2] to visual question answering in VQA [3]) and assess the UMGM's ability to adapt to new domains while retaining pre-trained knowledge.
Controls: Baselines will include fine-tuning the UMGM without the proposed methods and using a standard weight-sharing approach. Ablation studies will investigate the impact of task difficulty, domain similarity, and adaptation algorithms.
Estimated cost: Estimated 350 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect to observe robust performance across varying task difficulty and domain shift, with minimal loss of pre-trained knowledge and adaptation efficiency. However, the method may fail if the task difficulty or domain gap is too large, or if the adaptation algorithm is not effective in transferring knowledge.

PROPOSAL 6: Treasuring the Inter-Modal Knowledge Graph: A Novel Knowledge Distillation Approach
To further enhance the UMGM's ability to retain pre-trained knowledge and adaptation efficiency, we will develop a novel knowledge distillation approach that leverages the inter-modal knowledge graph embeddings as a teacher to distill knowledge into the student model. The teacher model will be a pre-trained UMGM on a large-scale dataset, while the student model will be the fine-tuned UMGM on a smaller-scale dataset. The knowledge distillation process will be guided by the teacher's knowledge graph embeddings, enabling the student model to rapidly adapt to new tasks while preserving pre-trained knowledge.
Controls: Baselines will include fine-tuning the UMGM without knowledge distillation and using a standard weight-sharing approach. Ablation studies will investigate the impact of teacher-student architecture, knowledge distillation temperature, and adaptation iterations.
Estimated cost: Estimated 400 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect to observe significant improvement in knowledge retention and adaptation efficiency, with reduced inter-modal forgetting and improved generalizability across tasks and domains. However, the method may fail if the teacher-student architecture is not well-suited for the task, or if the knowledge distillation process is not effective in transferring knowledge.

PROPOSAL 7: Unified Framework for Inter-Modal Continual Learning
To integrate the various methods proposed throughout this research, we will develop a unified framework for inter-modal continual learning that combines the strengths of each approach. The framework will consist of a modular architecture that incorporates inter-modal knowledge graph embeddings, adversarial training, mixture-of-experts, and knowledge distillation, along with a task-specific instruction tuning module. This framework will enable the UMGM to efficiently adapt to new tasks while retaining pre-trained knowledge and minimizing inter-modal forgetting.
Controls: Baselines will include fine-tuning the UMGM without the proposed framework and using a standard weight-sharing approach. Ablation studies will investigate the impact of individual components and their interactions.
Estimated cost: Estimated 500 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect to observe robust and efficient adaptability across a wide range of tasks and domains, with minimal inter-modal forgetting and significant improvement in generalizability. However, the method may fail if the unified framework is not effectively integrated or if the components interact negatively, leading to decreased performance.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating NeRF-Based Compactifications for 3DGS
PROPOSAL: We compare the performance of several NeRF-based compactification methods for 3DGS, including vector quantization and neural Gaussian predictors, with Mip-NeRF360 and TensoRF as baselines on the widely used DTU and NLPR datasets for novel view synthesis. We experiment with optimizing these compactification methods along with 3DGS jointly and separately, and analyze the trade-offs between rendering quality and storage efficiency.
CONTROLS: Mip-NeRF360, TensoRF, raw 3DGS with VQ embeddings
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect joint optimization to slightly improve quality, but vector quantization will sufficiently degrade rendering quality to warrant a more sophisticated compactification strategy, which will achieve a storage reduction comparable to 10-20% of the original 3DGS representation while introducing latency thresholds that barely impact real-time rendering in urban and large-scale environments, but potentially become noticeable in environments with intricate details and high opacity changes.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Enabling 3DGS with Conditional Discretized Normal Flows
PROPOSAL: We propose a method to efficiently represent 3D Gaussians using 1D conditional discretized normal flows (CDNFs) for modeling the view-dependent properties of anisotropic shapes. CDNFS leverage a single neural network to predict a series of binned values of the distribution, enabling a highly compressible representation of the typically smooth opacity distributions and anisotropic scale, and allowing a dramatic reduction of the number of parameters required to characterize a single Gaussian. We demonstrate the improved efficiency of this approach in 3DGS on the DtU and NLPR datasets.
CONTROLS: raw 3DGS, VQ-based 3DGS
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The introduction of CDNFS will lead to an order of magnitude reduction in memory usage for each 3D Gaussian and a more than 3x reduction in the number of parameters when aiming for high storage efficiency in 3DGS. While slight quality losses are expected for poor quality images with sharp boundaries, in mostly low-frequency and fine-detailed scenes quality compares well to 3DGS or its VQ embeddings when an appropriate DSNF bin count is chosen.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Enabling 3DGS with Conditional Discretized Normal Flows for Anisotropic Scales
PROPOSAL: We improve the efficiency of modeling 3D Gaussian anisotropic scales using conditional discretized normal flows (CDNFS), by incorporating non-uniform binning strategies and leveraging learned bin boundaries. Our approach enables a scalable and shape-preserving representation of Gaussian anisotropic scale across different scenes while minimizing the number of parameters when optimizing for storage efficiency. To evaluate its effectiveness, we extend our evaluation to the large-scale urban scene and autonomous driving street scene, and conduct quality comparisons with the original 3DGS.
CONTROLS: original 3DGS approach, vector quantization of anisotropic scales
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revision allows us to maintain a substantial quality gain (~90-92%), while declaring up to 2.5x storage reduction when wanting for high-efficient data storage in 3DGS based street scene renderings. Perception-level boosts appreciated in real scenes should more than compensate from fuzzy Gaussian retirements present upon relying in multiple autorig-target 이는 Criteriatrys{}.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: 3D Gaussian Gaussian Mixture Models
PROPOSAL: We propose to represent 3D Gaussians with Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) that are learned using a specific EM-like optimization procedure tailored to the 3DGS scenario, where each mixture component is constrained to adhere to the characteristics of a 3D Gaussian. Our algorithm learns a reduced set of parameters to describe each 3D Gaussian jointly, resulting in compact representations for the view-dependent properties of 3D Gaussians, reducing the memory overhead of explicit 3DGS. We demonstrate significant storage reductions while maintaining quality on DTU and NLPR and its real-world transfers even when challenged for sneak road details on video.
CONTROLS: raw 3DGS, Conditional Discretized Normal Flows based 3DGS
COST: 80 GPU-hours

TITLE: NeRF-Based Compactification for 3DGS with Multi-Level Loss Functions
PROPOSAL: We enhance the NeRF-based compactification approach for 3DGS by incorporating multi-level loss functions, where we optimize the quality of the Gaussian mixture models at multiple levels of abstraction, ranging from individual Gaussians to the entire scene. This hierarchical loss function helps the neural compactification methods capture local details, object boundaries, and view-dependent effects more effectively, leading to improved rendering quality and potentially enabling faster rendering times. ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Point-Based K-D Trees for Fast GPU Rendering of 3D Gaussians
PROPOSAL: We propose an efficient point-based K-D tree-based approach to accelerate GPU rendering of 3D Gaussian scenes, where individual 3D Gaussians are represented as nodes in a K-D tree. This organized data structure enables fast nearest neighbor search and efficient rendering of view-dependent effects. By leveraging the structure of the K-D tree, we can significantly reduce the number of 3D Gaussian lookups and corresponding neural network evaluations during rendering, thereby improving rendering performance and facilitating real-time rendering of complex scenes.
CONTROLS: raw 3DGS, Conditional Discretized Normal Flows based 3DGS
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our approach will provide a 2-3x rendering speedup on the GPU, with minimal quality impact for moderate to high-quality Gaussian representations on the most challenging scenes.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Adaptive Point-Based K-D Trees for Balancing Rendering Speed and Quality
PROPOSAL: We extend the point-based K-D tree approach for fast GPU rendering of 3D Gaussians by introducing an adaptive mechanism to dynamically adjust the tree's resolution based on the rendering requirements. By refining or coarsening the K-D tree during rendering, we can balance rendering speed and quality. This adaptive approach enables faster rendering for scenes with minimal view-dependent effects while still maintaining high-quality rendering for scenes with complex view-dependent effects.
CONTROLS: raw 3DGS, Conditional Discretized Normal Flows based 3DGS
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our adaptive K-D tree approach will provide an average 2.5x rendering speedup on the GPU with minimal quality impact (less than 5% drop) for moderate to high-quality Gaussian representations, and up to 1.5x quality improvement when rendering time is limited.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: learnable Grids for Gaussian Property Prediction
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel approach that combines the strengths of neural fields and Gaussian mixture models by using learnable grids to predict Gaussian properties. Each grid cell is associated with a learned neural network that predicts the the Gaussian's properties, allowing for better representation of the local scene structure. Our approach enables the rapid evaluation of Gaussian properties and is integrated with the adaptive K-D tree method for faster rendering.
CONTROLS: raw 3DGS, Conditional Discretized Normal Flows based 3DGS
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our approach will yield a consistent rendering speedup of around 4x on the GPU for high-quality Gaussian representations, and be more robust to varying scene complexities, while the 1.5x quality improvement observed in prior results will now permanently hold.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Hierarchical Gaussian Property Prediction with learnable Grids
PROPOSAL: We extend the learnable grid approach for Gaussian property prediction by incorporating a hierarchical representation, where each grid cell is associated with a binary decision tree that partitions the scene into smaller regions based on the predicted Gaussian properties. This hierarchical structure enables more accurate prediction of Gaussian properties and allows for more efficient rendering of complex scenes.
CONTROLS: raw 3DGS, Conditional Discretized Normal Flows based 3DGS
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our revised approach will achieve an average 5x rendering speedup on the GPU for high-quality Gaussian representations, and maintain around a 1.5x quality improvement over prior results.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: End-to-End Optimization of 3D Gaussian Networks for Real-time Rendering
PROPOSAL: We present an end-to-end optimization framework that jointly optimizes the 3D Gaussian Network architecture, the learnable grid prediction, and the adaptive K-D tree structure for fast rendering of high-quality novel views. Our optimization framework combines multi-level loss functions and gradient-based optimization methods, which allows us to converge to optimal solutions quickly and efficiently. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on various real-world data sets and scenes, achieving state-of-the-art rendering speeds and quality.
CONTROLS: raw 3DGS, successive ablations of our framework's components
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our end-to-end optimization framework will yield a 10x rendering speedup on the GPU for high-quality Gaussian representations, and consistently maintain state-of-the-art rendering quality (within 5% of previous results) on diverse real-world scenes, including urban and natural environments.

We combine this approach with vector quantization and neural Gaussian predictors for a more robust evaluation.

propositions.texte: We improve the efficiency of modeling 3D Gaussian anisotropic scales using conditional discretized normal flows (CDNFS), by incorporating non-uniform binning strategies and leveraging learned bin boundaries. Our approach enables a scalable and shape-preserving representation of Gaussian anisotropic scale across different scenes while minimizing the number of parameters when optimizing for storage efficiency. To evaluate its effectiveness, we extend our evaluation to the large-scale urban scene and autonomous driving street scene, and conduct quality comparisons with the original 3DGS.

propositions.texte: We propose to represent 3D Gaussians with Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) that are learned using a specific EM-like optimization procedure tailored to the 3DGS scenario, where each mixture component is constrained to adhere to the characteristics of a 3D Gaussian. Our algorithm learns a reduced set of parameters to describe each 3D Gaussian jointly, resulting in compact representations for the view-dependent properties of 3D Gaussians, reducing the memory overhead of explicit 3DGS. We demonstrate significant storage reductions while maintaining quality on DTU and NLPR and its real-world transfers even when challenged for sneak road details on video.

propositions.texte: We extend the point-based K-D tree approach for fast GPU rendering of 3D Gaussians by introducing an adaptive mechanism to dynamically adjust the tree's resolution based on the rendering requirements. By refining or coarsening the K-D tree during rendering, we can balance rendering speed and quality. This adaptive approach enables faster rendering for scenes with minimal view-dependent effects while still maintaining high-quality rendering for scenes with complex view-dependent effects.
propositions.titre: Adaptive Point-Based K-D Trees for Balancing Rendering Speed and Quality

propositions.texte: We present an end-to-end optimization framework that jointly optimizes the 3D Gaussian Network architecture, the learnable grid prediction, and the adaptive K-D tree structure for fast rendering of high-quality novel views. Our optimization framework combines multi-level loss functions and gradient-based optimization methods, which allows us to converge to optimal solutions quickly and efficiently. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on various real-world data sets and scenes, achieving state-of-the-art rendering speeds and quality.
propositions.titre: End-to-End Optimization of 3D Gaussian Networks for Real-time Rendering

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Limits of Grid-Based Neural Fields for 3D Gaussian Representations
PROPOSAL: Compared to naive implementations, Train and we will investigate different ways to store grid-based neural fields, specifically leveraging techniques such as channel pruning, knowledge distillation, and hierarchical neural architecture search, to represent the properties of 3D Gaussians and potentially improve storage efficiency.
CONTROLS: Baseline is a naive neural field implementation that represents Gaussian properties with a neural network with fixed resolution (e.g., 80x80).
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Channel pruning could reduce storage requirements by up to 30%, while models probably won't retain high-frequency details, risking similar results to grid-based approaches.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fourier Analysis of Gaussian Properties for Efficient Representations
PROPOSAL: Theoretically analyze the Fourier properties of the high-dimensional distributions around 3D Gaussian moments to identify the most significant component axes, allowing for distillation into a lower-dimensional representation that remains faithful to high-frequency details.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed Fourier-based representation to the ground-truth 3D Gaussian representation (dense channel neural field) and to a stratified random sampling approach commonly used in 3D Gaussian-based rendering methods.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The Fourier analysis may pinpoint patterns in the 3D Gaussian distribution that can be simplified or factorized, reducing the parameters required to represent varying object shapes without sacrificing color detail and spatial geometry.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Fourier Analysis of Gaussian Properties for Efficient Representations
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Instead of distilling the high-dimensional distribution into a lower-dimensional representation, analyze how the Fourier properties of 3D Gaussian moments relate to spatial frequencies visible in real-world scenes, with the goal of identifying inherently limited visual frequencies that could guide efficient representations. Compare this analysis to the energy spectra of real-world scenes on various image quality metrics (i.e., PSNR, SSIM).
CONTROLS: Baseline is a standard Fourier transform-based method for analyzing image energy spectra.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This Fourier analysis may demonstrate that human eyes typically respond well to low-to-mid frequency visual content, which could help justify the tradeoff between visualization quality and model capacity for scenes with rapid opacity changes or high-frequency color details.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hybrid Neural-3D Gaussian Architecture with Adaptive Learning
PROPOSAL: Design a hybrid Neural-3D Gaussian architecture where a neural network predicts Gaussian properties on demand, and learn an adaptive process to emphasize the most uncertain features while gradually reducing model size by eliminating redundant entries.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed architecture to a baseline greedy selection approach, and to the pure neural field and pure 3D Gaussian representations (neutral Gaussian selection matching the information stored in both methods).
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This architecture should reduce the redundant storage of model parameters without sacrificing scene synthesis quality, especially in scenarios with anisotropic and occluded objects.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Using Self-Supervised Dominance Measures for Real-Time Novel View Synthesis
PROPOSAL: Propose a self-supervised dominance measure between the novel view synthesis and the explicit 3D Gaussian representation to determine the learning priorities for automatically adjusting the model size during training and for optimal dominant content adaptation, based on contextual structures to improve the global render quality.
CONTROLS: Baseline is a multi-resolution grid-based approach for dominant novel view synthesis.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This dominance measure might allow the model to dynamically focus on representing high-fidelity regions of the scene, potentially outperforming the global average approach in scenarios with significant ambient occlusion or ambient light source variations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fast 3D Gaussian Optimization with Conditional Samples and Stratified Sampling
PROPOSAL: Introduce a new optimization strategy that leverages conditional sampling and stratified sampling techniques to reduce the number of 3D Gaussian evaluations, allowing for faster optimization times and more accurate scene reconstructions in unbounded scenes with distant background content.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed approach to naive Gaussian optimization with stochastic gradient descent and to a strategy that uses a coarse-to-fine strategy with ray-marching optimization, incorporating real-world scenes of urban settings.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By conditioning the sampling process on the properties of the scene and adopting stratified sampling, the optimization algorithm should efficiently capture high-frequency variations in the scene and find optimal Gaussian placements without getting stuck in local minima, ultimately leading to better novel view synthesis and faster render times.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Fourier Analysis of Gaussian Properties for Efficient Representations
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Utilize the findings from the Fourier analysis of Gaussian properties to develop a sparse representation method that selects a subset of dominant harmonics based on the energy spectrum of real-world scenes, and analyze its effectiveness in capturing visually relevant information in scenes with high-frequency details.
CONTROLS: Compare the sparse representation approach to the baseline dense representation method, and to the proposed hybrid neural-3D Gaussian architecture with adaptive learning.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By focusing on the most energetically significant harmonics, the sparse representation approach should achieve a higher level of compression without sacrificing quality in scenes with complex visual structures, such as those encountered in large-scale urban scenes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Resolution Deep Photometric Consistency for Novel View Synthesis
PROPOSAL: Design a novel multi-resolution architecture that leverages deep photometric consistency for novel view synthesis by learning to predict the optimal resolution and sampling strategy for each scene, and evaluate its performance on large-scale urban scenes and autonomous driving street scenes.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed approach to classical multi-scale feature fusion methods, spatial pyramid pooling, and the baseline novel view synthesis method.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This architecture should allow the model to dynamically adapt to the scene structure and content, focusing on regions of interest to produce higher quality novel views while maintaining real-time rendering capabilities.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Hybrid Neural-3D Gaussian Architecture with Adaptive Learning
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Introduce a learnable, scene-specific, and view-dependent attention mechanism within the hybrid neural-3D Gaussian architecture to dynamically adjust the priority of representing specific 3D Gaussian properties (e.g., anisotropic shape, position, opacity, color) based on the scene's structure, lighting, and the target novel view's characteristics.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised hybrid architecture to the original adaptive learning approach, and to the multi-resolution deep photometric consistency method.
COST: 160 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The attention mechanism should allow the model to adaptively allocate its capacity to capture the most relevant 3D Gaussian properties for a particular scene and target view, potentially leading to improved visual quality and rendering efficiency in novel view synthesis.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Comprehensive Evaluation Framework for Novel View Synthesis
PROPOSAL: Develop a unified evaluation framework that systematically compares the performance of the proposed and baseline methods across various metrics (e.g., PSNR, SSIM, visual quality scores from human evaluation), multiple novel view synthesis benchmarks, and diverse experimental scenarios, including standard datasets (e.g., Tanks and Temples) and challenging real-world scenarios (e.g., large-scale urban scenes, autonomous driving street scenes).
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the proposed method ensemble (all previously proposed methods) to each baseline method individually, and to the state-of-the-art novel view synthesis methods on both standard and real-world scenarios.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This comprehensive evaluation will provide a thorough understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of each proposed method and shed light on the scenario-dependent performance of the novel view synthesis methods, ultimately contributing to the development of more effective and efficient novel view synthesis techniques.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Compact 3D Gaussian Representation using Learned Spatial Discretization
PROPOSAL: Experimentally investigate the effectiveness of dynamic spatial discretization for 3D Gaussians using neural networks. We will modify the 3D Gaussian representation to include a neural network that learns to adaptively discretize the Gaussian density functions into a compact grid-based representation. The network will output a coarse spatial partition of the scene and associated grid cell properties, such as opacity, color, and scale. This should allow for a more efficient and compact representation of 3D Gaussians, preserving the benefits of real-time rendering.
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard 3D Gaussian representation and a hybrid neural-3DGS architecture, where the neural network predicts Gaussian properties instead of storing them explicitly.
COST: Estimated compute: 10 GPU-hours per experiment (5 hours for training and 5 hours for rendering)
PREDICTION: Compact representation of 3D Gaussians should reduce memory usage by 30-50% while preserving rendering quality. Potential performance improvement in rendering real-world scenes with high-frequency color variations and semi-transparent objects.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Hybrid Neural-Gaussian Representation for Efficient Scene Rendering
PROPOSAL: Develop a hybrid scene representation that combines the strengths of neural fields and 3D Gaussians. Specifically, we will integrate a neural network that predicts Gaussian properties (position, opacity, color, anisotropic scale, and rotation) for a subset of strategically selected Gaussians, while the remaining Gaussians are represented explicitly. The predicted properties will be used to initialize or refine the corresponding Gaussians. This should allow for efficient and high-quality scene rendering, while minimizing the number of stored Gaussian parameters.
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard 3D Gaussian representation, the neural-3DGS architecture, and the compact 3D Gaussian representation using learned spatial discretization method proposed in proposal 1.
COST: Estimated compute: 15 GPU-hours per experiment (7.5 hours for training and 7.5 hours for rendering)
PREDICTION: Hybrid representation should achieve a balance between rendering quality and memory efficiency, with potential performance improvement in scenes with complex high-frequency color variations and semi-transparent objects.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Compact 3D Gaussian Representation using Learned Spatial Discretization
PROPOSAL: Enhance proposal 1 by incorporating a novel regularization technique that encourages the learned spatial discretization to respect the underlying structure of the scene. This can be achieved by adding a term to the loss function that penalizes grid cell boundaries that coincide with object boundaries or occlusion edges. This should improve the compactness of the representation while preserving rendering quality.
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard 3D Gaussian representation and a variant of proposal 1 without the regularization term.
COST: Estimated compute: 5 additional GPU-hours for training and rendering
PREDICTION: Regularization term should improve the quality and compactness of the representation, reducing memory usage by an additional 10-20% while maintaining rendering accuracy. Potential performance improvement in scenes with complex object environments and occlusions.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Accelerating 3D Gaussian Optimization with Structure-Preserving Densification
PROPOSAL: Develop an incremental densification strategy for 3D Gaussians that adapts to the scene's geometry and appearance. The strategy will identify areas of high reconstruction error and selectively add new Gaussians to improve rendering accuracy while minimizing the number of parameters. This should enable more efficient optimization and reduce the memory requirements of the 3D Gaussian representation.
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard 3D Gaussian optimization approach and a modified version of the hybrid neural-Gaussian representation (proposal 2) that leverages the densification strategy.
COST: Estimated compute: 12 GPU-hours per experiment (6 hours for training and 6 hours for rendering)
PREDICTION: The densification strategy should reduce the number of Gaussians required for accurate rendering by 20-40% while preserving rendering quality, resulting in significant memory savings and improved performance.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Real-Time Rendering of Distant Background Content in Unbounded Scenes
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of a separate neural network specifically designed for rendering distant background content in unbounded scenes. This would enable the use of a lower-resolution representation for the background while maintaining high-quality rendering of foreground objects. The network would take into account the surrounding environment, lighting conditions, and contextual information to reconstruct the background accurately.
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard 3D Gaussian representation and a modified version of the hybrid neural-Gaussian representation (proposal 2) that incorporates the background rendering network.
COST: Estimated compute: 20 GPU-hours per experiment (10 hours for training and 10 hours for rendering)
PREDICTION: The background rendering network should improve rendering quality in unbounded scenes, particularly in areas where geometric structures are sparse or missing, achieving a reduction in rendering errors by 30-50%.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Compact 3D Gaussian Representation using Learned Spatial Discretization
PROPOSAL: Enhance proposal 1 by incorporating explicit occlusion reasoning. The learned spatial discretization network will be modified to predict occlusion relationships between different Gaussians, allowing for more efficient representation and rendering of complex scenes with occlusions.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original proposal 1, a variant of proposal 1 with occlusion reasoning, and a standard 3D Gaussian representation.
COST: Estimated compute: 10 additional GPU-hours for training and rendering
PREDICTION: Occlusion reasoning should improve the compactness and efficiency of the representation, preserving rendering quality while reducing memory usage by an additional 10-20%. Potential performance improvement in scenes with complex occlusions and object hierarchies.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Transformer-Based Layered Representations for Efficient Scene Reconstruction
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of transformer-based models for layered scene reconstruction, inspired by human visual perception. The model will process scene elements (Gaussians, background, etc.) in a hierarchical manner, leveraging self-attention mechanisms to learn contextual relationships and dependencies. This should enable more accurate and efficient representation of complex scenes, with improved rendering quality and reduced memory usage.
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard 3D Gaussian representation and a modified version of the hybrid neural-Gaussian representation (proposal 2) that incorporates the transformer-based model.
COST: Estimated compute: 30 GPU-hours per experiment (15 hours for training and 15 hours for rendering)
PREDICTION: The transformer-based model should achieve significant improvements in rendering quality and efficiency, with potential performance gains of 50-100% in scenes with complex object hierarchies and relationships.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Hybrid Neural-Gaussian Representation for Efficient Scene Rendering
PROPOSAL: Enhance proposal 2 by incorporating an attention mechanism that selectively focuses on Gaussians that are most relevant to the current rendering task. This should improve the efficiency and accuracy of the hybrid representation, particularly in scenes with large variations in scale, occlusions, and contextual relationships.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original proposal 2, a variant of proposal 2 with attention mechanism, and a standard 3D Gaussian representation.
COST: Estimated compute: 15 additional GPU-hours for training and rendering
PREDICTION: The attention mechanism should improve the performance and efficiency of the hybrid representation, preserving rendering quality while reducing memory usage by an additional 10-20%. Potential performance improvement in scenes with complex object hierarchies and relationships.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Practical Evaluation of Distributed Rendering for Large-Scale Scenes
PROPOSAL: Explore the feasibility of distributed rendering for 3D scenes using the proposed scene representations (e.g., hybrid neural-Gaussian, transformer-based, and compact 3D Gaussian). The goal is to assess the performance, scalability, and real-world applicability of these representations when rendering large-scale scenes on distributed computing architectures, such as clusters or cloud environments.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of different scene representations on a large-scale dataset, utilizing a distributed rendering framework (e.g., RenderFarm or Stanford's Single-Binary Many.operations Packager).
COST: Estimated compute: 50-200 GPU-hours per experiment (dependent on scene size and rendering configuration)
PREDICTION: Successful distributed rendering should achieve significant performance gains (e.g., 10-100x) when rendering large-scale scenes, making these scene representations more feasible for real-world applications in fields like computer-aided design, architecture, and entertainment.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Comparison of Computational and Memory Resources between NeRF, 3DGS, and Proposed Scene Representations
PROPOSAL: Systematically compare the computational and memory resources required by NeRF, 3DGS, and the proposed scene representations (hybrid neural-Gaussian, compact 3D Gaussian, etc.) when rendering a diverse set of scenes. This study should provide a comprehensive analysis of the trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, and complexity of these scene representations, guiding future research and development.
CONTROLS: Use a standard benchmark dataset (e.g., ShapeNet or DTU) and evaluation metrics (e.g., rendering quality, memory usage, and computation time) to compare the performance of the different scene representations.
COST: Estimated compute: 10-20 GPU-hours per experiment (dependent on the chosen scenes and evaluation metrics)
PREDICTION: The study will provide valuable insights into the strengths and limitations of each scene representation, enabling the development of more efficient and accurate methods for novel view synthesis and scene understanding.

The strategy will identify areas of high reconstruction error and selectively add new Gaussians to improve rendering accuracy while minimizing the number of parameters. This should enable more efficient optimization and reduce the memory requirements of the 3D Gaussian representation.
Controls: Compare with the standard 3D Gaussian optimization approach and a modified version of the hybrid neural-Gaussian representation (proposal 2) that leverages the densification strategy.
Estimated cost: Estimated compute: 12 GPU-hours per experiment (6 hours for training and 6 hours for rendering)
Prediction: The densification strategy should reduce the number of Gaussians required for accurate rendering by 20-40% while preserving rendering quality, resulting in significant memory savings and improved performance.

PROPOSAL 4: Real-Time Rendering of Distant Background Content in Unbounded Scenes
Investigate the use of a separate neural network specifically designed for rendering distant background content in unbounded scenes. This would enable the use of a lower-resolution representation for the background while maintaining high-quality rendering of foreground objects. The network would take into account the surrounding environment, lighting conditions, and contextual information to reconstruct the background accurately.
Controls: Compare with the standard 3D Gaussian representation and a modified version of the hybrid neural-Gaussian representation (proposal 2) that incorporates the background rendering network.
Estimated cost: Estimated compute: 20 GPU-hours per experiment (10 hours for training and 10 hours for rendering)
Prediction: The background rendering network should improve rendering quality in unbounded scenes, particularly in areas where geometric structures are sparse or missing, achieving a reduction in rendering errors by 30-50%.

PROPOSAL 5: Transformer-Based Layered Representations for Efficient Scene Reconstruction
Explore the use of transformer-based models for layered scene reconstruction, inspired by human visual perception. The model will process scene elements (Gaussians, background, etc.) in a hierarchical manner, leveraging self-attention mechanisms to learn contextual relationships and dependencies. This should enable more accurate and efficient representation of complex scenes, with improved rendering quality and reduced memory usage.
Controls: Compare with the standard 3D Gaussian representation and a modified version of the hybrid neural-Gaussian representation (proposal 2) that incorporates the transformer-based model.
Estimated cost: Estimated compute: 30 GPU-hours per experiment (15 hours for training and 15 hours for rendering)
Prediction: The transformer-based model should achieve significant improvements in rendering quality and efficiency, with potential performance gains of 50-100% in scenes with complex object hierarchies and relationships.

PROPOSAL 6: Practical Evaluation of Distributed Rendering for Large-Scale Scenes
Explore the feasibility of distributed rendering for 3D scenes using the proposed scene representations (e.g., hybrid neural-Gaussian, transformer-based, and compact 3D Gaussian). The goal is to assess the performance, scalability, and real-world applicability of these representations when rendering large-scale scenes on distributed computing architectures, such as clusters or cloud environments.
Controls: Compare the performance of different scene representations on a large-scale dataset, utilizing a distributed rendering framework (e.g., RenderFarm or Stanford's Single-Binary Many.operations Packager).
Estimated cost: Estimated compute: 50-200 GPU-hours per experiment (dependent on scene size and rendering configuration)
Prediction: Successful distributed rendering should achieve significant performance gains (e.g., 10-100x) when rendering large-scale scenes, making these scene representations more feasible for real-world applications in fields like computer-aided design, architecture, and entertainment.

PROPOSAL 7: Comparison of Computational and Memory Resources between NeRF, 3DGS, and Proposed Scene Representations
Systematically compare the computational and memory resources required by NeRF, 3DGS, and the proposed scene representations (hybrid neural-Gaussian, compact 3D Gaussian, etc.) when rendering a diverse set of scenes. This study should provide a comprehensive analysis of the trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, and complexity of these scene representations, guiding future research and development.
Controls: Use a standard benchmark dataset (e.g., ShapeNet or DTU) and evaluation metrics (e.g., rendering quality, memory usage, and computation time) to compare the performance of the different scene representations.
Estimated cost: Estimated compute: 10-20 GPU-hours per experiment (dependent on the chosen scenes and evaluation metrics)
Prediction: The study will provide valuable insights into the strengths and limitations of each scene representation, enabling the development of more efficient and accurate methods for novel view synthesis and scene understanding.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Visualizing FFN Nonlinearity through Latent Space Diffusion Maps
PROPOSAL: Measure the impact of FFN nonlinearities on latent representations by applying diffusion maps to visualize changes in the high-dimensional space traversed by FFN transformations. This involves training a baseline transformer model, extracting FFN outputs at various layers and training iterations, and applying a diffusion framework to these outputs to reveal distinct structural patterns. By comparing layer-wise and training-iteration-wise transformations, we can visualize how FFN nonlinearities reorganize, compress, and propagate information across the model.
CONTROLS: Compare to baseline diffusion maps (w/o FFN) on the same task and setup. Use the same diffusion framework for consistent analysis.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: FFN nonlinearities significantly alter the latent space structure, with changes evident across depth and training iterations; however, failure to distinguish between noise-specific changes and actual transformations poses a challenge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating FFN Nonlinearity with Geometric Deep Learning
PROPOSAL: Apply geometric deep learning (GDL) techniques, specifically persistent homology, to study the topological features of FFN output spaces at various layers and training iterations. This will enable us to systematically analyze how FFN nonlinearities affect information flow and latent representation geometry over the model's depth and during training.
CONTROLS: Compare GDL-based insights to results from diffusion maps. Investigate how GDL analysis changes with different normalization techniques and activation functions.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Persistent homology reveals non-trivial topological features in FFN output spaces that correlate with task performance and model convergence; however, robustness to different normalization techniques and activation functions may require careful tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing FFN Nonlinearity Impact on Information Flow using Bottleneck Features
PROPOSAL: Design experiments to study how FFN nonlinearities affect information flow by inserting additional fully connected layers (bottleneck features) between FFN layers and evaluating their influence on model performance and information propagation. This will help identify the role of FFN nonlinearities in modulating information flow and selectivity throughout the model.
CONTROLS: Compare baseline model to bottleneck feature insertion variants with different layer configurations. Investigate how bottlenecks interact with attention mechanisms and nonlinearities in other layers.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: FFN nonlinearities significantly affect information flow, with bottleneck features revealing which specific layers and pathways heavily impact model performance; however, model interpretability and training stability may degrade with increased bottleneck complexity.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Analyzing FFN Nonlinearity Impact on Information Flow using Bottleneck Features
PROPOSAL: Revisit proposal 3 and revise to use a controlled comparison of different activation functions. Design experiments that compare FFN model performance and information flow for various activation functions (e.g., ReLU, Swish, Mish) while keeping all other parameters constant. This will allow us to quantify the specific impact of activation functions on FFN behavior and model performance.
CONTROLS: Compare performance and bottleneck feature extraction results for each activation function. Investigate how differences in activation functions affect information flow and neglect to other layers.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Activation functions significantly influence FFN behavior and information flow, with some functions Clustering towards optimal performance with potential areas of neglect; however, incompatible activation functions may introduce convergence issues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: FFN Nonlinearity Diagnostics through Synthetic Perturbations
PROPOSAL: Develop a synthetic perturbation framework to systematically assess the robustness and selectivity of FFN nonlinearities. Train models on perturbed input data (e.g., noise, distortions) and measure the corresponding FFN output space geometries using tools like diffusion maps or persistent homology. This will provide insights into how FFN nonlinearities respond to various types of perturbations and how these responses affect model behavior.
CONTROLS: Compare the effects of different types and levels of perturbations on FFN output spaces. Correlate perturbation robustness with attention module behavior and final model performance.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: FFNs exhibit striking selectivity and robustness to certain types of perturbations, indicating conjectural simplified representations under learned conditions, however specific behavior for high noise levels may be finally decreased.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Interpreting FFN Nonlinearities through Feature Importance Measures
PROPOSAL: Utilize feature importance measures (e.g., SHAP values, LIME) to quantify the contribution of specific FFN components to model predictions. This will enable us to identify which FFN nonlinearities are most significant for task performance and understand how they interact with attention mechanisms and other network components.
CONTROLS: Compare feature importance measures for different model configurations (e.g., with/without normalization) and task scenarios (e.g., simple/multitask learning).
COST: 45 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Specific FFN components exhibit high feature importance for certain tasks or datasets, indicating that others are "niche" roles or redundant functionalities; thus, attention on optimizing them may be reallocated to focus on more important roles.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating FFN Nonlinearity Stabilization using Norm Clipping
PROPOSAL: Explore the effect of norm clipping on FFN nonlinearities, particularly their stability and performance during training. Implement models with a clipping constraint on FFN weights and evaluate their behavior compared to unclipped variants. This study will provide insights into the importance of FFN weight control for robust model behavior.
CONTROLS: Compare clipped and unclipped model performance across various tasks and training regimes. Investigate the impact of clipping thresholds on FFN stability and generalization.
COST: 55 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Norm clipping can mitigate exploding gradients and improve FFN stability; however, overly aggressive clipping may restrict model capacity, leading to performance degradation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparative Study of FFN Nonlinearities in Transformers and CNNs
PROPOSAL: Investigate and compare the behavior of FFN nonlinearities in both transformers and convolutional neural networks (CNNs). This will help determine whether the role of FFN nonlinearities is unique to transformers or a more general property of deep feed-forward networks.
CONTROLS: Use identical model configurations and training procedures for both transformer and CNN variants. Compare FFN behavior, performance, and information flow across tasks and datasets.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: FFNs exhibit similar behavior and importance in both transformers and CNNs, indicating that their role is not specific to transformer architectures; however, differences in the structure of FFN layers between models may require tailored analysis and optimization strategies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Developing a Nonlinearity-Agnostic Framework for FFN Optimization
PROPOSAL: Design a unified framework for optimizing FFN nonlinearities across various tasks and architectures, regardless of the specific activation function or normalization technique used. This framework will utilize insights from previous experiments to identify generic factors influencing FFN behavior and develop adaptation strategies for optimizing these factors.
CONTROLS: Apply the developed framework to a range of tasks, models, and nonlinearities. Compare its performance and efficiency to existing optimization techniques.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed framework effectively optimizes FFN nonlinearities across different tasks and architectures, yielding improved performance and reduced development time; however, its reliance on previously identified factors may limit the applicability to new, unexplored nonlinearities or specific architectural innovations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Measuring the Generalization and Practical Impact of FFN Nonnonlinearity Insights
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the impact of the insights and findings from the previous experiments on the performance and generalization of state-of-the-art models. This can be done by implementing the proposed adaptations, diagnostics, and optimizers in a comprehensive evaluation protocol and comparing the results with baselines.
CONTROLS: Run the evaluation protocol on a large and diverse range of tasks, models, and datasets. Include ablation studies to highlight the impact of individual components and compare with available baselines.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The insights and methods developed in this research will have a significant, positive impact on the performance and generalization of state-of-the-art models, with the lowest impact average for models naturally designed to maximize information precision surrounding some cognitively complex subjects.
