actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Activation Functions on FFN Transformations
PROPOSAL: Use modern transformer-based language models to compare the effects of different activation functions (gelu, relu, swish, etc.) on the latent representations after each FFN transformation. We will extract the output of each FFN and visualize its structure using techniques like t-SNE or PCA to identify patterns.
CONTROLS: Compare to a baseline that uses no activation function, and ablate the transformer architecture to isolate the impact of FFN transformations.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant differences in the structure of the latent representations between activation functions, and possibly an exponential increase in the dimensions explored by the representation as a function of layer depth and model size. Expected failure modes include overly simple features or representations that break down when applying the activation function.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Probing FFN Transformations with Perturbation Analysis
PROPOSAL: We will develop a perturbation analysis technique to efficiently approximate the Jacobian of FFN transformations, and use this to understand the relative sensitivity of latent representations to input perturbations. This will allow us to quantify how FFN transformations are built around and interact with input features, and how these patterns evolve across layers and training.
CONTROLS: Compare the results of this method to norm-bounded perturbations (like adversarial attacks) and ablate the perturbation scope (local, adjacent, global).
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that FFNs build a hierarchy of sensitivity, where local features dominate early in the training and global features become more prominent as training progresses. This could also indicate an exponential growth in activation magnitudes across the network depth.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of FFN Nonlinearity on Latent Representation Structure
PROPOSAL: Use the activation attribution method (to visualize and quantify the contribution of each activation unit to the output) to compare the structural properties of latent representations before and after applying FFN nonlinearities on a selection of real-world benchmark datasets (e.g. 20NewsGroups, IMDB, SST-2). Specifically, we'll train a 8-layer transformer model with a baseline FFN (relay pre-activation sigmoid) and a variant with a different nonlinearity (e.g. ReLU, leaky ReLU), and then compare the attribute maps generated by the attribution method for each nonlinearity setup.
CONTROLS: 1. Baseline: No FFN nonlinearity 2. Baseline: Different FFN nonlinearity, without attribute maps 3. Ablation: Using one instead of many activations in the FFN for attribution 4. Ablation: Using attribution on a different set of datasets
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the ReLU nonlinearity to differ more significantly from sigmoid in terms of attribute maps, which might be indicative of more uniform local dynamics, with sigmoid not well separated from the baseline setup  might fails: depending on the nuance of the benchmark, or unsuitability of 8 layer model to FFN dynamics. 

 Verified metadata: the paper will be "Mostly Experimental". As the metadata suggests real-world experiments only, this is the best starting point

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Understanding FFN Geometry through Spline Partitions with Self-Similarity Analysis
PROPOSAL: Utilize the piecewise-affine spline partitioning method to partition the latent space in each layer of a transformer model trained on a selection of real-world benchmark datasets (e.g., 20NewsGroups, IMDB, SST-2), and then apply self-similarity analysis to examine how the geometry of the partitions changes across layers and over training. By comparing the partitions and their self-similarity across different nonlinearity setups, we aim to identify the role of nonlinearity in shaping the latent representation structure.
CONTROLS: 1. Ablation: Using a different nonlinearity for spline partitioning (e.g., instead of hyperbolic tangent, use ReLU) 2. Ablation: Not applying self-similarity analysis 3. Baseline: No FFN nonlinearity for a baseline setup
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our self-similarity analysis might reveal that the partition geometries change more significantly in the later layers for models with the sigmoid nonlinearity, which could point to its influence on the latent representation structure and ease of generalization we could fail: if partitioning methods are too sensitive to the activation units used, or hyperparameters for gradient descent are suboptimal

Note that proposal 1 and 2 work together well. While the first direct compares the activation maps of sigmoid vs ReLU, the second complements it by examining their latent space representations with spline partitioning.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Understanding FFN Geometry through Spline Partitions with Self-Similarity Analysis
PROPOSAL: Utilize the piecewise-affine spline partitioning method to partition the latent space in each layer of a transformer model trained on a selection of real-world benchmark datasets (e.g., 20NewsGroups, IMDB, SST-2), and then apply self-similarity analysis to examine how the geometry of the partitions changes across layers and over training. Additionally, to better understand the spatial overlap between the partitions, we'll use the same method to generate a heat map around the partitions, and analyze how this overlap changes across different nonlinearity setups. By comparing the partitions, their self-similarity, and heat maps across different nonlinearity setups, we aim to identify the role of nonlinearity in shaping the latent representation structure.
CONTROLS: 1. Ablation: Using a different nonlinearity for spline partitioning (e.g., instead of hyperbolic tangent, use ReLU) 2. Ablation: Not applying self-similarity analysis or heat map analysis 3. Baseline: No FFN nonlinearity for a baseline setup
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: With the revised proposal, we expect to see a more nuanced view of the partition geometries and heatmaps, which should reinforce our findings on the role of FFN nonlinearity. Unsuitability of the method for local dynamics of sigmoid or unseen distributions could cause data saturation or convergence failure, especially with partitioning methods

Note that we have enriched proposal 2 with additional insights that came from combining and refining our proposals.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Layer Normalization and Batch Normalization on FFN Dynamics
PROPOSAL: Investigate how layer normalization and batch normalization affect the behavior of FFN nonlinearities in a transformer model trained on a real-world benchmark dataset (e.g., IMDB, SST-2). Specifically, we'll compare the behavior of FFNs with and without normalization, and under different normalization configurations (e.g., layer norm with batch norm).
CONTROLS: 1. Baseline: No normalization 2. Ablation: Only batch norm 3. Ablation: Only layer norm
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see differences in the FFN behavior between normalization configurations, which might affect model generalization performance. We might fail to see differences if normalization schemes don't strongly impact the representation geometry, and overparameterization aids model performance.

This proposal works well in conjunction with previous proposals 1 and 2, exploring how architectural design choices interact with FFN dynamics.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Optimizer and Learning Rate on FFN Convergence Dynamics
PROPOSAL: Investigate how different optimizers (e.g., AdamW, SGD) and learning rates impact the convergence dynamics of FFN nonlinearities in a transformer model trained on a real-world benchmark dataset (e.g., IMDB, SST-2). We'll use techniques such as gradient norm tracking and neuron activation monitoring to analyze the impact of different optimizers and learning rates on FFN behavior.
CONTROLS: 1. Baseline: AdamW with default learning rate 2. Ablation: SGD with higher learning rate 3. Ablation: AdamW with lower learning rate
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see differences in the FFN behavior between optimizers and learning rates, particularly in terms of convergence speed and representation geometry. We might fail to see differences if the optimizer and learning rate choice doesn't strongly impact the representation geometry, and model performance is more resilient to these variations.

This proposal works well in conjunction with previous proposals 1, 2, and 3, exploring how different hyperparameters interact with FFN dynamics and representation geometry.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Diagnosing FFN Nonlinearity through Interpretability-Driven Harmonic Analysis
PROPOSAL: Utilize interpretability methods (e.g., feature importance, partial dependence plots) to diagnose the behavior of FFN nonlinearities in a transformer model trained on a real-world benchmark dataset (e.g., IMDB, SST-2). Specifically, we'll apply harmonic analysis to the FFN activations to study their frequency components and qualitative behavior.
CONTROLS: 1. Baseline: No harmonic analysis 2. Ablation: Using only feature importance for diagnosis
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see that harmonic analysis can reveal the periodic nature of the FFN activations, which might provide new insights into their behavior. Methodological limitations might arise if interpretability methods don't properly capture the underlying dynamics or are biased towards specific features.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Benchmarking FFN Representation Geometry on Diverse Natural Language Tasks
PROPOSAL: Investigate how the representation geometry of FFN nonlinearities transfers across different natural language processing tasks (e.g., sentiment analysis, machine translation, text classification). We'll train a transformer model on a given task, and then fine-tune it on other tasks to see how the representation geometry changes.
CONTROLS: 1. Baseline: Train and fine-tune on the same task 2. Ablation: Train on multiple tasks and fine-tune on a single task
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see that the representation geometry of FFN nonlinearities will change significantly across tasks, and might relate to task-specific performance. The proposal might_fail if the model is not adequately fine-tuned for the new task or has trouble generalizing.

This proposal serves as a practical evaluation of FFN representation geometry in real-world scenarios, complementing the more theoretical and interpretability-driven proposals 1-5.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: A Theoretical Analysis of the Effects of Nonlinearities on Transformer Layer Dynamics
PROPOSAL: Provide a theoretical framework for understanding how nonlinearities affect the behavior of transformer layers, focusing on the impact of FFN nonlinearities on the layer's dynamics. We'll develop a mathematical model to analyze the effects of different nonlinearities on the layer's convergence, stability, and representation geometry.
.CONTROLS: 1. Baseline: Use a linear model to analyze layer dynamics 2. Ablation: Examine the effects of specific nonlinearities (e.g., ReLU, sigmoid) on layer dynamics
COST: N/A (theoretical work)
PREDICTION: We expect to see that the theoretical framework can capture the effects of nonlinearities on transformer layer dynamics, providing insights into how these effects transfer across different tasks and layers. The proposal might fail to generalize if the theoretical assumptions don't hold or if the model is overly simplistic.

This proposal serves as a counterbalance to the more empirical and practical proposals 1-6, providing a theoretical understanding of the effects of nonlinearities on transformer layer dynamics.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Evaluating the Generalizability of FFN Nonlinearity Effects Across Different Model Architectures
PROPOSAL: Investigate how the effects of FFN nonlinearities generalizes across different transformer architectures, including variations in the number of layers, attention mechanisms, and layer normalization schemes. We'll compare the performance and representation geometry of different models on a set of natural language processing tasks.
CONTROLS: 1. Baseline: Use a standard transformer architecture 2. Ablation: Use a transformer architecture with a different attention mechanism (e.g., local attention) 3. Ablation: Use a transformer architecture with a different layer normalization scheme
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see that the effects of FFN nonlinearities will generalize across different model architectures, with variations in attention mechanisms and layer normalization schemes affecting the representation geometry. The proposal might fail to capture the full range of architectural variations or if the model is not adequately fine-tuned for the specific task.

This proposal serves as a final empirical test of the effects of FFN nonlinearities, evaluating their generalizability across different model architectures and providing a comprehensive understanding of their impact on transformer performance.

PROPOSAL 1: Investigating the Impact of FFN Nonlinearity on Latent Representation Structure
Use the activation attribution method (to visualize and quantify the contribution of each activation unit to the output) to compare the structural properties of latent representations before and after applying FFN nonlinearities on a selection of real-world benchmark datasets (e.g. 20NewsGroups, IMDB, SST-2). Specifically, we'll train a 8-layer transformer model with a baseline FFN (relay pre-activation sigmoid) and a variant with a different nonlinearity (e.g. ReLU, leaky ReLU), and then compare the attribute maps generated by the attribution method for each nonlinearity setup.
Controls: 1. Baseline: No FFN nonlinearity 2. Baseline: Different FFN nonlinearity, without attribute maps 3. Ablation: Using one instead of many activations in the FFN for attribution 4. Ablation: Using attribution on a different set of datasets

PROPOSAL 2: Understanding FFN Geometry through Spline Partitions with Self-Similarity Analysis
Utilize the piecewise-affine spline partitioning method to partition the latent space in each layer of a transformer model trained on a selection of real-world benchmark datasets (e.g., 20NewsGroups, IMDB, SST-2), and then apply self-similarity analysis to examine how the geometry of the partitions changes across layers and over training. Additionally, to better understand the spatial overlap between the partitions, we'll use the same method to generate a heat map around the partitions, and analyze how this overlap changes across different nonlinearity setups. By comparing the partitions, their self-similarity, and heat maps across different nonlinearity setups, we aim to identify the role of nonlinearity in shaping the latent representation structure.
Controls: 1. Ablation: Using a different nonlinearity for spline partitioning (e.g., instead of hyperbolic tangent, use ReLU) 2. Ablation: Not applying self-similarity analysis or heat map analysis 3. Baseline: No FFN nonlinearity for a baseline setup
Estimated cost: 60 GPU-hours
Prediction: With the revised proposal, we expect to see a more nuanced view of the partition geometries and heatmaps, which should reinforce our findings on the role of FFN nonlinearity. Investigate how different optimizers (e.g., AdamW, SGD) and learning rates impact the convergence dynamics of FFN nonlinearities in a transformer model trained on a real-world benchmark dataset (e.g., IMDB, SST-2). We'll use techniques such as gradient norm tracking and neuron activation monitoring to analyze the impact of different optimizers and learning rates on FFN behavior.

Utilize interpretability methods (e.g., feature importance, partial dependence plots) to diagnose the behavior of FFN nonlinearities in a transformer model trained on a real-world benchmark dataset (e.g., IMDB, SST-2). Investigate how the representation geometry of FFN nonlinearities transfers across different natural language processing tasks (e.g., sentiment analysis, machine translation, text classification). We'll train a transformer model on a given task, and then fine-tune it on other tasks to see how the representation geometry changes.

TITLE: Adaptive-Diffusion Sampling with Constrained Generation
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel adaptive-diffusion sampling algorithm that decides the number of denoising steps based on a predicted bandwidth-constrained image quality metric. Specifically, we develop a plugin for the DDPM model that leverages a learned cumulative distribution function (CDF) of denoising steps vs. a quality metric that predicts PSNR (Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio) under a specified lossy compression setting, thereby adapting step count to the required image quality and compression setting in real time, avoiding a one-size-fits-all approach of fixed-step diffusion processes.
CONTROLS: Baseline DDPM model under fixed-step approach; experiments under baseline no plugin or using simple heuristic (e.g., a fixed threshold PSNR), with and without compression setting consideration beyond just bitrate.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our approach will offer improved perceptual quality under target bitrate, but prediction and adaptation can be imperfect and therefore leave a gap between optimal and achieved quality.

TITLE: REVISED Adaptive Bandwidth-Aware Conditional Diffusion Model
PROPOSAL: We develop an extension to classifier-guided diffusion models that integrates an additional conditioning mechanism to handle bandwidth-adapted generation. The new mechanism injects a random vector sampled from a beta distribution, whose parameters are inferred from the target bitrate, and adds this vector as an input to the classifier, allowing the model to adaptively attend to and emphasize features critical for the specified bitrate. However, to improve our initial approach, we will replace the beta distribution with a learned distribution that is conditioned on the specific image and target bitrate. This can be achieved by adding an auxiliary neural network that predicts the optimal beta parameters for each image and target bitrate. Our hypothesis is that this incremental approach enables the model to respond to changing bandwidths by dynamically adjusting the semantic importance and visual fidelity of generated images.
CONTROLS: Experiments comparing the revised 'learned-conditioning' mechanism with the initial 'beta-conditioning' mechanism and the vanilla classifier-guided diffusion model; a test set of images downsampled, upsampling, or jpeged to simulate bandwidth constraints and gathered under specific image configurations.
COST: 12 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revision can provide better adaptability to changing bandwidths and image characteristics, but may require more extensive training and tuning to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning to Optimize Denoising Steps for Bandwidth-Aware Diffusion
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel meta-learning approach to learn an optimal denoising step strategy for bandwidth-aware diffusion models. By leveraging a set of pre-trained models and utilizing a bilevel optimization framework, our approach learns to adapt the number of denoising steps based on the target bitrate and image characteristics. This can be achieved by learning a neural network that predicts the optimal step count and conditionally sampling from a distribution of experts that have different step counts.
CONTROLS: Experiments comparing our meta-learning approach with a baseline approach that fixes the number of denoising steps, as well as an ablation study to understand the effects of different architectures and hyperparameters.
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our approach can provide near-optimal performance in terms of image quality and bandwidth efficiency, but may require extensive computational resources for training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Progressive Quality-Aware Diffusion Model with Bitrate Prediction
PROPOSAL: We introduce a progressive quality-aware diffusion model that dynamically adjusts its quality and number of denoising steps based on a predicted bitrate. The model consists of a bitrate predictor and a quality controller, where the bitrate predictor estimates the required bitrate for a given image and quality level, and the quality controller adjusts the number of denoising steps and image quality accordingly. To train the model, we propose a novel loss function that combines the standard diffusion model loss with a bitrate-predicted loss, which encourages the model to produce images with the correct quality and bitrate.
CONTROLS: Experiments comparing our progressive quality-aware model with the baseline adaptive-diffusion sampling model and the learning-to-optimize-denosing-steps model, as well as an ablation study to understand the effects of different loss functions and architectures.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our model can provide excellent trade-offs between image quality and bitrate, but may require careful hyperparameter tuning and model selection to achieve optimal performance.

PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach for joint optimization of denoising steps and model complexity for bandwidth-aware diffusion models. We introduce a new loss function that combines the standard diffusion model loss with a complexity penalty, which encourages the model to reduce its complexity while maintaining high-quality images. Additionally, we use a bilevel optimization framework to select the optimal denoising steps and model architecture for each image and target bitrate. This allows the model to adapt to changing image characteristics and bitrate requirements, and provides a more flexible and efficient solution for bandwidth-aware diffusion.

PROPOSAL 3: Learning to Optimize Denoising Steps for Bandwidth-Aware Diffusion
We propose a novel meta-learning approach to learn an optimal denoising step strategy for bandwidth-aware diffusion models. By leveraging a set of pre-trained models and utilizing a bilevel optimization framework, our approach learns to adapt the number of denoising steps based on the target bitrate and image characteristics. This can be achieved by learning a neural network that predicts the optimal step count and conditionally sampling from a distribution of experts that have different step counts.

PROPOSAL 4: Progressive Quality-Aware Diffusion Model with Bitrate Prediction
We introduce a progressive quality-aware diffusion model that dynamically adjusts its quality and number of denoising steps based on a predicted bitrate. The model consists of a bitrate predictor and a quality controller, where the bitrate predictor estimates the required bitrate for a given image and quality level, and the quality controller adjusts the number of denoising steps and image quality accordingly. To train the model, we propose a novel loss function that combines the standard diffusion model loss with a bitrate-predicted loss, which encourages the model to produce images with the correct quality and bitrate.
Controls: Experiments comparing our progressive quality-aware model with the baseline adaptive-diffusion sampling model and the learning-to-optimize-denosing-steps model, as well as an ablation study to understand the effects of different loss functions and architectures.
Estimated cost: 20 GPU-hours
Prediction: Our model can provide excellent trade-offs between image quality and bitrate, but may require careful hyperparameter tuning and model selection to achieve optimal performance.

PROPOSAL 5: Event-Driven Diffusion Model for Real-Time Bandwidth Adaptation
We propose an event-driven diffusion model that adaptively adjusts its quality and number of denoising steps based on real-time bandwidth availability. The model uses an event-driven framework to continuously monitor the bandwidth and adjust its operation accordingly, providing a highly adaptive and responsive solution for dynamic bandwidth environments.

Estimated cost: 25 GPU-hours
Prediction: Our event-driven model can provide highly adaptive and responsive solutions for dynamic bandwidth environments, but may require careful tuning of the event-driven framework and bandwidth monitoring mechanisms to achieve optimal performance.

PROPOSAL 6: Joint Optimization of Denoising Steps and Model Complexity for Bandwidth-Aware Diffusion
We propose a novel approach for joint optimization of denoising steps and model complexity for bandwidth-aware diffusion models. We introduce a new loss function that combines the standard diffusion model loss with a complexity penalty, which encourages the model to reduce its complexity while maintaining high-quality images. Additionally, we use a bilevel optimization framework to select the optimal denoising steps and model architecture for each image and target bitrate. This allows the model to adapt to changing image characteristics and bitrate requirements, and provides a more flexible and efficient solution for bandwidth-aware diffusion.
Controls: Experiments comparing our joint optimization approach with the revised learning to optimize denoising steps model and the event-driven diffusion model.
Estimated cost: 35 GPU-hours
Prediction: Our joint optimization approach can provide highly effective solutions for bandwidth-aware diffusion, but may require extensive training data and computational resources to achieve optimal performance.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Diffusion Termination for Bandwidth-aware Image Generation
PROPOSAL: We will investigate an adaptive diffusion termination mechanism that uses a neural network to predict the minimal number of denoising steps required to produce an image of satisfactory quality based on the available bandwidth. This network will be trained on a dataset of images and their corresponding bandwidth constraints. At inference time, the network will take the bandwidth constraint as input and produce a scaled number of denoising steps for the diffusion model.
CONTROLS: We will compare our adaptive termination mechanism to several baselines, including:
- Naive termination: termination after a fixed number of denoising steps.
- Random termination: termination after a random number of denoising steps.
- Model-based termination: termination based on a pre-computed estimate of required denoising steps for each image.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our adaptive termination mechanism will achieve better visual quality and lower bitrate compared to the baselines, but may sometimes fail to capture the optimal termination point, leading to slightly higher bitrates or lower visual quality.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bandwidth-Aware Diffusion Model Architecture
PROPOSAL: We will design a new diffusion model architecture that incorporates bandwidth-awareness into its backbone. This architecture will use a novel conditional diffusion process that takes both the input noise schedule and the available bandwidth as inputs, and outputs an image that is adapted to the bandwidth constraints. The architecture will include a bandwidth encoder that estimates the bandwidth requirements of the image and outputs a probability distribution over possible bandwidth levels.
CONTROLS: We will compare our bandwidth-aware diffusion model to a standard diffusion model and our adaptive diffusion termination mechanism (proposal 1) as baselines.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our bandwidth-aware diffusion model will achieve lower bitrate and higher visual quality compared to the baselines, especially for images that require high bandwidth. However, it may be computationally more expensive to train and evaluate.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Bandwidth-Aware Diffusion Model Architecture
PROPOSAL: We will modify our bandwidth-aware diffusion model architecture (proposal 2) to incorporate a hierarchical representation of the image, where the model generates multiple layers of abstraction, each with its own bandwidth requirements. This will allow the model to adapt to varying bandwidth constraints during different stages of image generation, improving visual quality and reducing bitrate.
CONTROLS: We will compare our revised bandwidth-aware diffusion model to the original bandwidth-aware diffusion model (proposal 2) and the revised adaptive diffusion termination mechanism (based on proposal 1).
COST: 150 GPU-hours (accounting for the reduced complexity of the model)
PREDICTION: Our revised bandwidth-aware diffusion model will achieve better visual quality, lower bitrate, and improved computational efficiency compared to the baselines. However, it may require more careful hyperparameter tuning to achieve optimal results.

Note: I revised the bandwidth-aware diffusion model architecture to make it more viable given the computational resources, while still maintaining the potential for improvement.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Bandwidth-Aware Image Generation Pipeline
PROPOSAL NUMBER: 1
TITLE: REVISED Adaptive Diffusion Termination for Bandwidth-aware Image Generation
PROPOSAL: We will modify our adaptive diffusion termination mechanism (proposal 1) to use a online learning approach to update the termination predictor based on the performance of the model on a small validation set. This will allow the model to adapt to the specific characteristics of the image generation task and improve visual quality and bitrate over time.
CONTROLS: We will compare our revised adaptive diffusion termination mechanism to the original adaptive diffusion termination mechanism (proposal 1) and the revised bandwidth-aware diffusion model (based on proposal 2).
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our revised adaptive diffusion termination mechanism will achieve better visual quality, lower bitrate, and improved computational efficiency compared to the baselines. However, it may require careful tuning of the online learning parameters to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Bandwidth-Aware Diffusion Model
PROPOSAL: We will extend our bandwidth-aware diffusion model architecture (proposal 2) to support hierarchical generation of images. This involves training multiple diffusion models with different bandwidth capacities, each generating a different layer of abstraction in the image. The model will then be trained to select the optimal layer(s) to generate based on the available bandwidth.
CONTROLS: We will compare our hierarchical bandwidth-aware diffusion model to the revised bandwidth-aware diffusion model (based on proposal 2) and the revised adaptive diffusion termination mechanism (based on proposal 1).
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our hierarchical bandwidth-aware diffusion model will achieve improved visual quality, lower bitrate, and more efficient use of bandwidth compared to the baselines. However, it may require careful tuning of the model architecture and hyperparameters to avoid artifacts during hierarchical image generation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-time Bandwidth Estimation for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We will investigate a real-time bandwidth estimation method that leverages on-the-fly computations to estimate the required bandwidth for generating an image. This method will involve training a separate neural network to predict the bandwidth requirements of a generated image based on the input noise schedule and the image's computational graph.
CONTROLS: We will compare our real-time bandwidth estimation method to the revised adaptive diffusion termination mechanism (based on proposal 1) and the hierarchical bandwidth-aware diffusion model (proposal 3).
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our real-time bandwidth estimation method will achieve improved real-time performance, reduced latency, and more accurate bandwidth predictions compared to the baselines. However, it may require careful tuning of the estimation model to avoid overestimation or underestimation of bandwidth requirements.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bandwidth-Aware Loss Function for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We will modify the loss function used to train diffusion models to incorporate a term that encourages the model to generate images that respect the available bandwidth. This will involve adding a bandwidth-aware regularization term to the standard loss function, which will encourage the model to produce images with a lower bitrate.
CONTROLS: We will compare our bandwidth-aware loss function to the standard loss function used in diffusion models, and the revised bandwidth-aware diffusion model (based on proposal 2).
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our bandwidth-aware loss function will achieve improved visual quality, lower bitrate, and more efficient use of bandwidth compared to the baselines. However, it may require careful tuning of the regularization strength to avoid overregularization or underregularization of the model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Training for Bandwidth-Aware Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We will investigate using adversarial training to further improve the performance of bandwidth-aware diffusion models. This will involve training a discriminator to distinguish between images generated by the bandwidth-aware diffusion model and images that respect the available bandwidth, and then using this discriminator to guide the training of the diffusion model.
CONTROLS: We will compare our adversarially trained bandwidth-aware diffusion model to the revised bandwidth-aware diffusion model (based on proposal 2) and the bandwidth-aware loss function (proposal 5).
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our adversarially trained bandwidth-aware diffusion model will achieve improved visual quality, lower bitrate, and better use of bandwidth compared to the baselines. However, it may require careful tuning of the discriminator and the adversarial training process to avoid overfitting or underfitting of the model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Evaluation of Bandwidth-Aware Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the bandwidth-aware diffusion models proposed in this research, including a large-scale comparison of their performance on various metrics such as visual quality, bitrate, and computational efficiency. We will also conduct a thorough analysis of the trade-offs between these metrics and the impact of various hyperparameters on the performance of the models.
CONTROLS: We will use a range of baselines, including standard diffusion models and the individual components of the bandwidth-aware diffusion models (e.g. adaptive diffusion termination, bandwidth-aware loss function, etc.).
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our comprehensive evaluation will provide a thorough understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of bandwidth-aware diffusion models and help identify areas for future research.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Guide for Deploying Bandwidth-Aware Diffusion Models in Real-World Applications
PROPOSAL: We will create a comprehensive guide that outlines the best practices and considerations for deploying bandwidth-aware diffusion models in real-world applications, including text-to-image synthesis, image compression, and machine learning-based image processing.
CONTROLS: The guide will be based on our comprehensive evaluation (proposal 7) and the individual components of the bandwidth-aware diffusion models (e.g. adaptive diffusion termination, bandwidth-aware loss function, etc.).
COST: This proposal does not require any additional computational resources, as it is focused on creating a guide for deployment.
PREDICTION: Our guide will provide a valuable resource for developers and researchers looking to incorporate bandwidth-aware diffusion models into their applications, and help ensure that these models are used in a responsible and effective manner.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Denoising Step Control for Real-time Bandwidth Aware Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Modify the standard diffusion sampling process by adaptively adjusting the number of denoising steps based on time complexity and bitrate constraints. Train a separate predictor network to forecast the required number of steps for a given image, then use a constrained optimization algorithm to select the optimal step count that balances quality and real-time transmission requirements.
CONTROLS: Experiment with various predictors, such as sequential decision-making networks and residual predictors, compare against a fixed-step baseline, and explore step count ablations.
COST: 10,000 GPU-hours (3 weeks on 16 A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: Achieve substantial transmission speedups with a minor quality degradation, but the model may fail to adapt to frequently changing bandwidth environments due to prediction latency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Distilled Diffusion Models for Real-time Bandwidth-aware Generation
PROPOSAL: Use knowledge distillation to transfer knowledge from a full-step diffusion model to a trained teacher-student pair. The teacher model follows the standard diffusion process, and the student model is trained to match the teacher's output quality but with fewer denoising steps. This approach leverages the teacher's understanding of high-quality generation while adapting the student to real-time transmission constraints.
CONTROLS: Compare the teacher-student pair against the full-step model, explore student step count ablations, and evaluate the effectiveness of various distillation loss functions.
COST: 5,000 GPU-hours (2 weeks on 8 A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: Demonstrate improved efficiency and transmission speed compared to full-step models while preserving perceptual quality, but may struggle with capturing intricate textures and fine details due to the reduced number of denoising steps.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Modified Revision of 2. Distilled Diffusion Models for Real-time Bandwidth-aware Generation
PROPOSAL: Update the student model in the knowledge distillation approach to also optimize for a bitrate-based loss function. This encourages the student to not only match the teacher's output quality but also generate images that can be transmitted within a specified bitrate budget. A joint optimization of both quality and bitrate goals allows the student model to adapt to both the teacher's high-quality output and the real-time transmission constraints.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the bitrate optimization against a baseline distilled model without bitrate constraints, compare it to the adaptive denoising step control, and explore different bitrate-based loss functions.
COST: 2,000 GPU-hours (1 week on 4 A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: Improve the efficiency and transmission speed of distilled models while maintaining high perceptual quality, but may require careful tuning of the bitrate-based loss function to avoid introducing artifacts.

This revised proposal now refers to the 2nd proposal.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Stage Diffusion Models with Adaptive Quality Control
PROPOSAL: Implement a multi-stage diffusion model that progressively refines the image at different stages, each with a separate set of denoising steps and bitrate constraints. Train a separate, adaptive quality control module to determine the optimal configuration for each stage based on the current bandwidth and desired quality. This approach allows for fine-grained control over image quality and bitrate, enabling dynamic adaptation to changing transmission environments.
CONTROLS: Experiment with different quality control architectures, evaluate the effectiveness of stage-wise bitrate constraints, and compare against full-stage diffusion and distilled models.
COST: 15,000 GPU-hours (4 weeks on 16 A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: Demonstrate improved transmission efficiency and quality adaptability compared to previous approaches, but may suffer from increased complexity and computational overhead due to the multi-stage architecture.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bandwidth-Aware Token Selection in Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Introduce a token-based representation of the diffusion process, where each token corresponds to a specific set of pixel values. Train a token selection network to determine the most important tokens for transmission, based on both image content and bitrate constraints. This allows the model to strategically allocate computational resources and transmission bits, focusing on the most critical information while discarding secondary details.
CONTROLS: Compare the token selection approach against traditional diffusion models, explore the impact of token selection on transmission speed and quality, and evaluate the effectiveness of different token selection criteria.
COST: 8,000 GPU-hours (3 weeks on 8 A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: Achieve significant transmission speedups while maintaining high perceptual quality, but may struggle with preserving delicate textures and fine details due to the token-based representation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Chunked Diffusion Models with Non-Uniform Bitrate Allocation
PROPOSAL: Divide the image into non-overlapping chunks and apply a variable bitrate allocation scheme to each chunk, where the bitrate is determined by the chunk's importance and allocated transmission budget. Train a chunk classification network to determine the relative importance of each chunk, and a bitrate allocation network to decide the optimal bitrate for each chunk. This approach enables fine-grained control over bitrate allocation, adaptability to changing transmission environments, and improved transmission efficiency.
CONTROLS: Experiment with different chunking strategies, compare against traditional diffusion models, and evaluate the effectiveness of various bitrate allocation functions.
COST: 12,000 GPU-hours (4 weeks on 12 A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: Achieve improved transmission efficiency and adaptability to varying bandwidth environments, but may suffer from increased computational overhead and complexity due to the chunk-based representation.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: 2. Distilled Diffusion Models for Real-time Bandwidth-aware Generation
PROPOSAL: Widely expand upon the modified knowledge distillation approach in proposal 2. Introduce multi-resolution tokenized representations of the teacher model's output, enabling the student model to distill and generate images at multiple resolutions, while considering bitrate constraints. By sampling from these tokenized representations, the student model can dynamically adjust its output resolution, denoising steps, and bitrate allocation based on the available transmission capacity, to optimize transmission efficiency.
CONTROLS: Compare distilled models against adaptive and chunked diffusion models, evaluate the impact of tokenized representations on transmission efficiency, quality, and adaptability.
COST: 18,000 GPU-hours (6 weeks on 16 A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: Significantly enhance the transmission efficiency and adaptability of distilled models, while preserving high perceptual quality, but may require extensive fine-tuning and configuration to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transmission Efficiency-Aware Loss Functions for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Modify the standard loss functions used in diffusion models to incorporate transmission efficiency metrics, such as transmit time and bitrate. Develop a suite of transmission efficiency-aware loss functions that balance image quality, model efficiency, and transmission constraints, taking into account the real-time transmission environments. This approach enables models to optimize their output quality and transmission efficiency simultaneously, without the need for separate bitrate allocation schemes.
CONTROLS: Experiment with various transmission efficiency-aware loss functions, evaluate their impact on transmission efficiency and quality, compare against existing bitrate allocation approaches.
COST: 6,000 GPU-hours (2 weeks on 8 A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: Significantly improve transmission efficiency of diffusion models while maintaining high perceptual quality, but may require extensive tuning to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dynamics-Aware Hybrid Diffusion Model for Real-Time Bandwidth-Aware Image Generation
PROPOSAL: Integrate dynamic programming techniques into a hybrid diffusion model that combines the strengths of adaptive and multi-stage architectures. This enables the model to adapt to real-time transmission environments and dynamically adjust its quality and bitrate allocation, thus achieving optimal transmission efficiency and image quality.
CONTROLS: Compare the hybrid diffusion model against existing proposals, evaluate its performance in realistic transmission environments, and explore its scalability and generalizability.
COST: 20,000 GPU-hours (7 weeks on 16 A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: Achieve state-of-the-art transmission efficiency and adaptability, while maintaining high perceptual quality, but may require extensive fine-tuning and configuration to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Evaluation and Optimization Framework for Bandwidth-Aware Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Develop a comprehensive evaluation and optimization framework that integrates and evaluates the performance of the proposed models, considering multiple objectives such as transmission efficiency, image quality, and adaptability. This framework will enable the efficient comparison and selection of optimal models for specific real-time transmission environments, and provide a systematic approach to model optimization and improvement.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the proposed models using the developed framework, explore the impact of model evaluation metrics on optimization, and optimize the framework for scalability and generalizability.
COST: Infinity (conceptual framework, not requiring additional compute resources)
PREDICTION: Provide a fundamental framework for comparing and optimizing bandwidth-aware diffusion models, enabling the development of more efficient and effective models for real-time transmission environments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effects of Sample Efficiency on Training Stability
PROPOSAL: A thorough comparison of the training stability and convergence speed of GRPO with Experience Replay, including ablations that control for group size, replay memory sizes, and replay frequencies, using benchmarks like AMC (Arithmetic Math Competition) and HLT (Higher Logic Thinking) for mathematical problem-solving and science exam question answering. We'll measure stability using metrics such as RL's reward standard deviation and learning rate over the 500 epochs and sample efficiency as the median of the most successful rollouts. This will help us understand whether experience replay enhances overall learning for complex tasks and whether changes in the replay parameters significantly impact training stability.
CONTROLS: GRPO with no experience replay (as is), a naïve replay implementation (randomly selecting trajectories to replay), and ignoring rewards during experience replay (using z-normalization).
COST: 12 000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Experience Replay should improve sample efficiency by at least 30% and learning stability by up to 15% for our benchmark tasks, but its performance might significantly decline if we don't choose the correct group size or ignore rewards during replay.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experience Buffer Sampling Schemes
PROPOSAL: Investigation of novel methods for efficiently sampling past experiences from the experience buffer to improve the stability and acceleration of the learning process. Specifically, we'll explore the generalized importance sampling (GIS) strategy with the goal to prioritize transitions that have positive long-term effects on the training performance, by aggregating trajectories based on their Karush-Kuhn-Tucker multipliers (KKT) in a weighted method. The ablation of various buffer sampling strategies such as high entropy or robust trajectories will serve as control to see its trade-off with sample efficiency and training stability on both real-world benchmarks and synthetic scenarios.

TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Experience Reuse on Exploration-Exploitation Trade-off

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experience Calibration in RLVR
PROPOSAL: Implement an experience replay mechanism and a policy calibration method, which will be trained to estimate the quality of experiences stored in the replay buffer based on the verifiable rewards collected during rollout. This estimator will assess each experience by contextualizing it based on the model's performance, trajectory diversity, and potential for providing new insights during exploration. We aim to use this estimator to prioritize, manage, and adapt the replay process to maximize learning efficiency during scaling RL.
CONTROLS: Standard on-policy RLVR GRPO as a baseline; ablations to compare the variants of our calibration methods (e.g., considering only trajectory success or policy agreement with the stored policy).
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The calibrated experience replay system should improve sample efficiency by 30% - 40%, increase the model's performances on complex problems (especially for marginally exploitable regions of abstract state-space) by at least 15%, and demonstrate significant resilience to catastrophic forgetting of past discoveries when compared to standard on-policy RL methods. If the model doesn't get to generate sufficient high-quality diverse trajectories early on during training, the benefit of this strategy will dwindle.

This will ensure that information-rich trajectory characteristics are not overly compressed or lost during the replay process, while also focusing on potentially successful but prior-hazardous paths that the verifiable reward does not immediately recognize. We aim to use attention-based or graph neural network based approaches to track these key trajectories components.
CONTROLS: Our prior work's GRPO as a baseline without experience replay; controls include replay buffer variants with fixed selection policies (e.g., sampling the last few seen experiences) and experiments applying the standard form replay process (with all experiences having equal priority).

PROPOSAL: Introduce a meta-reinforcement learning agent that optimizes the design of experience compression and retrieval architectures for RLVR. The meta-agent will be trained on a set of generic tasks that capture the essence of experience storage and retrieval, such as selecting summary representations, querying the replay buffer, and retrieving salient experiences. This will be based on a learned distance metric that considers both the similarity of experiences in the feature space and the time elapsed since their collection. This approach will enable a more diverse and dynamic experience pool that evolves with the model's growing understanding of the task.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Propagation of Reasoning Value Across Training
PROPOSAL: Investigate how value propagation techniques used in off-policy RL can be adapted for sequence-to-sequence models to propagate attention weights or intermediate reasoning steps between trajectories, allowing the model to leverage signals from earlier, successful explorations and maintain a more consistent policy throughout training.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard on-policy GRPO and with a replay buffer that simply stores the final answer rewards for each trajectory.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We will find that applying these techniques improves the sample efficiency and convergence of RLVR training, reducing the reliance on fresh rollouts in later stages of training, which should lead to improved performance under limited computation budgets. Might fail if inference costs of computing attention weights become too high, or if value propagation fails to capture meaningful signals in the model's reasoning process.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Reward-Informed Trajectory Segmentation
PROPOSAL: Introduce a method to segment stored trajectories into smaller, more homogeneous sub-trajectories based on their rewards and identify informative 'turning points' in each trajectory where the policy shifts toward a successful answer. Store and replay only these sub-trajectories, adaptively selecting which ones to prioritize.
CONTROLS: Compare with mere storage and replay of full trajectories and with an ablation study where only one type of trajectory segmentation cue (e.g., reward, loss) is used.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This should improve learning efficiency and stability, as the model can reuse shorter, more compressed forms of successful experience and focus on adapting to specific policy shifts rather than simply trying to replicate entire trajectories. May fail if trajectory segmentation methods become too computationally expensive and/or do not capture all salient changes in policy behavior.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Policy-Conditional Replay Buffer
PROPOSAL: Develop a replay buffer that conditions the selection of stored trajectories on the current policy state, adapting to the model's evolving preferences and improving the match between replayed experiences and current exploration goals.
CONTROLS: Evaluate against a baseline that uniformly randomizes trajectory selection from the buffer and against a variation where trajectory selection is conditioned on a fixed policy snapshot, taken at a previous stage of training.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By ensuring that the model is exposed to a mix of stored experiences that are relevant to its current exploration, policy-conditional replay should improve exploration-exploitation trade-offs, adaptation to the shifting reward landscape, and overall learning efficiency and stability under RLVR. May fail if conditioning the replay buffer selection introduces unnecessary instability in the optimization process.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Policy-Conditional Replay Buffer (Revised)
PROPOSAL: Refine the policy-conditional replay buffer to not only condition on the current policy state but also to take into account the value function or Q-function of the current policy, ensuring that replayed experiences are both relevant and relevantly valued according to the current policy's preferences.
CONTROLS: Keep the comparisons with uniform randomization baseline and fixed policy snapshot conditions.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The addition of the value function or Q-function consideration should further improve the match between replayed experiences and current exploration goals, enhancing policy adaptation, exploration-exploitation trade-offs, and overall learning efficiency and stability under RLVR. Still risks introducing instability if the conditioning is too intrusive or if the model becomes over-reliant on specific subsets of the replay buffer.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Integrating Entropy Regularization with Experience Replay
PROPOSAL: Combine entropy regularization, to encourage diversity and exploration, with the experience replay techniques introduced in previous proposals, and investigate how this synergy can improve exploration and stability in RLVR training.
CONTROLS: Evaluate against a baseline where only entropy regularization is applied, a variation where only experience replay is used, and a replay buffer implementation without policy-conditional data selection.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By balancing exploration-driven entropy regularization with the efficiency-enhancing benefits of experience replay, this integration should lead to improved stability, convergence, and ultimately, better reasoning performance in RLVR, without sacrificing exploration capabilities. May fail if the combination introduces new competition or conflicts between exploration and exploitation drives that disrupt optimization.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Dynamic Learning Rate Scheduling with Experience Replay
PROPOSAL: Adapt learning rate scheduling for RLVR to leverage the benefits of experience replay by making learning rate adjustments based on the model's performance over sequences of self-experience, reflecting both the model's most recent learning and longer-term progress.
CONTROLS: Compare against a fixed learning rate scheduling baseline, a variation where learning rate scheduling is done independently of experience replay, and a replay buffer implementation withouteye on learning rate adjustments.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By responsively adjusting the learning rate in response to the model's experience-generated progress, this dynamic scheduling can lead to more informed and adaptive learning-rate choices, potentially reducing the need for large-scale relying on human-designed learning rate schedules or random searches for optimal learning rates. May fail if over-reacting to fluctuations in performance introduces unnecessary noise or randomization in the optimization process.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Dynamic Learning Rate Scheduling with Experience Replay (Revised)
PROPOSAL: Refine the learning rate scheduling adaptation by incorporating a forgetting factor to discount older experience and emphasize recent improvements, thereby balancing the advantages of learning from long-term experience with the need to respond to recent trajectory rewards.
CONTROLS: Retain the comparisons with fixed learning rate scheduling, learning rate scheduling without experience replay, and replay buffer implementation.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By incorporating a forgetting factor, the revised dynamic learning rate scheduling should strike a more optimal balance between the benefits of long-term learning and the need to quickly adapt to recent improvements, reducing the difficulty of determining initial learning rates, avoiding value overestimation, and improving overall convergence. May fail if the forgetting factor becomes too aggressive, unduly discounting centuries-outstanding improvement and affects training overall.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Multi-Armed Bandit-inspired Sampling in Experience Replay
PROPOSAL: Develop an online method to select trajectories in the experience replay buffer using multi-armed bandit (MAB) algorithms, deciding which trajectories to emphasize in each rollout based on their potential information value and adapting to recent performance to optimize sampling efficiency and minimize regret over exploration.
CONTROLS: Compare with random sampling and a version using the temporal difference error or policy gradient estimates to inform selection, as well as a version using the MAB algorithm without exploration noise.
COST: 110 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By adapting the experience sampling to prioritize the most informative trajectories at each iteration, the MAB-inspired sampling approach should lead to improved exploration, reduced sampling variance, and a cut in the time needed to gain the same level of understanding of the system. May fail if the exploration noise becomes too destructive or causes insufficiencies and instability in the understanding of sample optimization.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Propagation of Reasoning Value Across Training (Revised)
PROPOSAL: Refine the reasoning value propagation by integrating it with the policy-conditional replay buffer, allowing the model to leverage signals from earlier successful explorations that are specifically relevant to its current exploration goals, further focusing the model's improvement on the most promising aspects of its own experiences.
CONTROLS: Retain all comparisons from the original proposal, incorporating evaluations against the revised policy-conditional replay buffer implementation.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By combining the value propagation and policy-conditional replay strategies, we expect improved sample efficiency, convergence, and overall performance in RLVR, as the model will be better able to effectively distribute and transmute the global experience distribution across policy iterations. May still face challenges from The policy may get over-specialized to useful aspects, and struggle in slightly new testing scenarios.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Limited Computational Resources on RLVR
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effects of constrained computational resources on the stability and performance of the RLVR algorithms, incorporating techniques to mitigate the impact of limited GPU memory and computation time in on-policy and off-policy methods.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline where there are no computational constraints and with a series of ablation studies, removing certain techniques step-by-step to analyze the individual effects.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The experiments should reveal which proposed techniques are most effective at mitigating the challenges of limited computational resources and how they interact with the RLVR algorithm, shedding light on the overall viability of RLVR for practical use. May fail if some adaptations particularly accentuate resource exhaustion and produce suboptimal performance under the given budget.

PROPOSAL 6: Multi-Armed Bandit-inspired Sampling in Experience Replay
Develop an online method to select trajectories in the experience replay buffer using multi-armed bandit (MAB) algorithms, deciding which trajectories to emphasize in each rollout based on their potential information value and adapting to recent performance to optimize sampling efficiency and minimize regret over exploration.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Identifiability Guarantees for Nonlinear Dictionary Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose a theoretical analysis of a class of smooth and injective nonlinear generating functions that can be learned using diffeomorphism-based dictionary learning. The diffeomorphism group is a well-studied class of invertible transformations that preserves the manifold structure of the input data. We will derive recovery guarantees for this approach under the assumption of smooth and injective generating functions, and investigate the role of diffeomorphism-based inductive biases in promoting recovery.
CONTROLS: Linear dictionary learning, sparse autoencoders, nonlinear independent component analysis
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: With the diffeomorphism-based approach, we expect to achieve a significant improvement in recovery guarantees over existing nonlinear approaches, especially in regimes where the generating function is smooth and injective. However, the guarantee may fail when the generating function has discontinuities or is non-injective.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Unified Framework for Identifiability Analysis in Dictionary Learning
PROPOSAL: We revise our first proposal to provide a unified framework for analyzing the identifiability of dictionary learning models, encompassing both linear and nonlinear cases. Specifically, we will leverage the notion of "diamond norms" to quantify the distance between the true and estimated dictionaries, providing a flexible and versatile framework for deriving recovery guarantees under various assumptions on the generating function. This framework will be used to generalize and unify existing results for linear dictionary learning with those for diffeomorphism-based nonlinear dictionary learning.
CONTROLS: The revised framework will be compared with our previous proposal, as well as with standard linear dictionary learning and sparse autoencoders
COST: 150 GPU-hours (added framework implementation and comparison)
PREDICTION: We expect the unified framework to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the identifiability of dictionary learning models, and enable the derivation of recovery guarantees for a wider range of scenarios. However, the generality of the framework may also come at the cost of weakened guarantees in specific cases, highlighting the trade-offs involved in theoretical modeling.

TITLE: Identifiability Guarantees for Nonlinear Dictionary Learning Without Auxiliary Information

We will consider the regime where the generating function is fully observed, and prove convergence of the Support Vector Dictionary Learning (SVDL) algorithm to the ground truth under these assumptions.
CONTROLS: Analyze the convergence properties of a simple optimization algorithm, such as Gradient Descent, as a baseline for the SVDL algorithm.
COST: 50 GPU-hours, for a proof-of-concept implementation of the algorithm and the analysis of the baseline.
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve convergence to the ground truth under the given assumptions, albeit with potentially high sample complexity and sensitivity to initialization.

TITLE: Investigating the Sample Complexity of Nonlinear Dictionary Learning
PROPOSAL: Design an experiment to empirically study the sample complexity of nonlinear dictionary learning using a specific class of smooth, injective nonlinear generating functions. We will use a simulated dataset with controlled properties and analyze the performance of the Support Vector Dictionary Learning (SVDL) algorithm on this task.
CONTROLS: Compare the SVDL algorithm to a linear dictionary learning algorithm as a baseline, and study the effects of different levels of noise in the simulated data on the performance of the algorithms.
COST: 200 GPU-hours, for generating the simulated dataset and running multiple iterations of the SVDL algorithm.
PREDICTION: We expect to observe that the SVDL algorithm performs well on the task, but may require a large number of samples to accurately recover the underlying dictionary, especially in the presence of noise.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Comparison of Nonlinear Dictionary Learning Algorithms for Mechanistic Interpretability of Language Models
PROPOSAL: Run an experiment comparing the performance of the Support Vector Dictionary Learning (SVDL) algorithm with other existing nonlinear dictionary learning algorithms, such as Neural Dictionary Learning and Deep Independent Component Analysis, on the task of mechanistic interpretability of language models. We will use a real-world language model dataset and evaluate the ability of each algorithm to recover the underlying dictionary.
CONTROLS: Compare the SVDL algorithm to a linear dictionary learning algorithm and a random dictionary learning algorithm as baselines, and study the effects of different hyperparameter settings on the performance of the algorithms.
COST: 300 GPU-hours, for running multiple iterations of the algorithms and analyzing their performance on the real-world dataset.
PREDICTION: We expect to observe that the SVDL algorithm performs well on the task, but may be outperformed by other nonlinear dictionary learning algorithms that are specifically designed for the task of mechanistic interpretability.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Identifiability in Nonlinear Dictionary Learning
PROPOSAL: We investigate the identifiability of nonlinear dictionary learning under the assumption that the generating function g(Z) is injective and continuously differentiable. Using tools from differential geometry, we establish a relationship between the Jacobian matrix of g and the ability to recover the latent variables Z. We show that if the Jacobian matrix is invertible, then the latent variables can be recovered with guarantees. We further provide a sufficient condition for the invertibility of the Jacobian matrix, which is loosely related to the constancy of the page rank of the Hessian matrix of g.
CONTROLS: We compare our results to existing guarantees for linear dictionary learning and demonstrate that our conditions are more relaxed in certain regimes.
COST: 10 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect to show that our conditions yield recovery guarantees in a broader range of parameter settings than existing methods, but may require more computational resources to enforce in practice.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Smoothness-based Initialization for Nonlinear Dictionary Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose a initialization method that leverages the smoothness of the generating function g to initialize the latent variables. The method relies on a small number of optimizations to determine an initial estimate of the latent variables, based on the curvature of the generating function around an initial estimate. We hypothesize that initializing the latent variables with this method will significantly improve the convergence speed of nonlinear dictionary learning algorithms. 
CONTROLS: We compare our initialization method to several existing initialization methods, including random initialization and targeted initialization methods, such as PC-PCA.
COST: 20 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect that our initialization method will lead to faster convergence and better solutions, but may not provide full recovery guarantees under certain conditions.

ACTION: REVISIE
TITLE: Revision of Identifiability in Nonlinear Dictionary Learning
PROPOSED CHANGE: We consider an additional condition, the Lipschitz continuity of the generating function g, to complement the injectivity and smoothness assumptions. We provide a detailed analysis of the interplay between these conditions, and show that they together provide sufficient conditions for the recovery of the latent variables. We further establish a relationship between the Lipschitz constant and the Jacobian matrix, which enables us to bound the error in recovered variables.
CONTROLS: We compare our results to existing guarantees for linear dictionary learning under the restricted isometry property, and provide a more nuanced understanding of how nonlinearity affects identifiability.
COST: no additional compute time.
PREDICTION: We expect that incorporating the Lipschitz continuity condition into the analysis will provide tighter bounds on the recovered variables and offer a more comprehensive understanding of the identifiability of nonlinear dictionary learning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analysis of Nonlinear Dictionary Learning under VC-Dimension Constraints
PROPOSAL: We investigate the identifiability of nonlinear dictionary learning under the assumption that the generating function g(Z) has a finite VC-dimension, a condition that constrains the complexity of the function class. We establish a relationship between the VC-dimension and the ability to recover the latent variables, and provide a sufficient condition for recovery under VC-dimension constraints. We further provide an analysis of how VC-dimension affects the generalization error of nonlinear dictionary learning algorithms.
CONTROLS: We compare our results to existing guarantees for linear dictionary learning under the restricted isometry property, and demonstrate the advantages of using VC-dimension constraints in nonlinear settings.
COST: 30 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect that our analysis will yield recovery guarantees under VC-dimension constraints that are more general and flexible than existing methods, but may require additional computational resources to enforce in practice.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experimental Validation of Nonlinear Dictionary Learning on Synthetic Language Data
PROPOSAL: We design a synthetic language data generator that simulates real-world language data, with a focus on generating data that is amenable to nonlinear dictionary learning. We then implement and compare several nonlinear dictionary learning algorithms on this data, including ours from previous proposals and existing state-of-the-art methods. We evaluate their performance using metrics such as reconstruction error, perplexity, and latent variable recovery accuracy.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our proposed methods to state-of-the-art methods, including sparse autoencoders, and ablate the importance of our initialization and VC-dimension constraints.
COST: 50 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect that our experimental results will validate the effectiveness of our proposed methods on realistic language data, and provide insights into the trade-offs between different inductive biases and algorithmic choices.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revision of Critical Analysis of Common Baises in Mechanistic Interpretability Models
PROPOSED CHANGE: We extend our previous experimental validation to include a range of mechanistic interpretability models, including sparse autoencoders, and analyze their respective biases in representing latent structure. We examine the impact of non-linear generative functions on the capacity of these models to recover meaningful latent variables, and provide a critical evaluation of the strengths and weaknesses of each approach. This comparative analysis will serve as a foundation for a definitive experimental evaluation of our proposed methods.
CONTROLS: We compare our proposed methods to existing state-of-the-art mechanistic interpretability models, and evaluate their respective performance on synthetic language data and additional real-world benchmarks.
COST: 75 GPU-hours to include new experimental comparisons 
PREDICTION: We expect that our critical analysis and experimentation will provide new insights into the challenges and limitations of mechanistic interpretability in representing complex nonlinear relationships, and enable a more nuanced understanding of the role of inductive biases in recovering meaningful latent structure.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revision of Experimental Validation of Nonlinear Dictionary Learning on Synthetic Language Data
PROPOSED CHANGE: We expand our experimental validation to include real-world language data, specifically text embeddings from a large-scale language model. We also introduce an additional metric, latent semantic coherence, to evaluate the interpretability and quality of the recovered latent variables. We investigate how well our proposed methods generalize to this more challenging setting, and how they compare to existing methods in terms of both recovery accuracy and interpretability.
CONTROLS: We compare our results to state-of-the-art methods for nonlinear dictionary learning and mechanistic interpretability, including sparse autoencoders and contrastive variational autoencoders.
COST: no additional compute time (replacing existing experiment with expanded one).
PREDICTION: We expect that our expanded experimental validation will demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods in recovering meaningful latent variables from real-world language data, and provide insights into the strengths and limitations of our approach.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning a Nested Dictionary for Multi-resolution Representation of Latent Structure
PROPOSAL: We generalize nonlinear dictionary learning to a nested dictionary framework, which incorporates a hierarchical structure to represent different scales or resolutions of latent relationships. We develop an optimization algorithm to learn the nested dictionary, and demonstrate its effectiveness in capturing complex relationships in a range of real-world datasets, including images and speech signals.
CONTROLS: We compare our results to existing methods for dictionary learning and sparse representation, including greedy algorithms and non-negativity-constrained optimization.
COST: 100 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect that our nested dictionary framework will provide a powerful tool for learning multi-resolution representations of latent structure, and offer insights into the nature of complex relationships in real-world datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Identifiability and Stability Analysis of Nonlinear Dictionary Learning with Nested Structure
PROPOSAL: We provide theoretical guarantees on the identifiability and stability of nonlinear dictionary learning with a nested structure, including convergence rates and recovery bounds. We analyze the interplay between the resolution of the nested structure and the capacity of the dictionary, and provide a sufficient condition for recovery under mild assumptions on the generating function.
CONTROLS: We compare our results to existing guarantees on dictionary learning and sparse representation, including linear dictionary learning and orthogonal matching pursuit.
COST: 150 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect that our theoretical analysis will provide a comprehensive understanding of the identifiability and stability of nonlinear dictionary learning with nested structure, and enable the design of efficient algorithms for learning multi-resolution representations of latent structure.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Resource-Aware Optimization for Nonlinear Dictionary Learning with Nested Structure
PROPOSAL: We develop an optimization framework that leverages the nested structure to efficiently learn the dictionary, including a novel initialization method and a hierarchical optimization algorithm that adapts to the resolution of the nested structure. We demonstrate the scalability and efficiency of our approach on large-scale datasets, and provide a comprehensive analysis of its convergence properties and recovery guarantees.
CONTROLS: We compare our results to existing methods for dictionary learning and sparse representation, including greedy algorithms and non-negativity-constrained optimization, and ablate the importance of the nested structure in our approach.
COST: 200 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect that our optimized framework will provide a highly scalable and efficient method for learning multi-resolution representations of latent structure, and make nonlinear dictionary learning with nested structure a practical tool for a wide range of applications.

PROPOSAL: We train a frozen multimodal large language model (e.g., CLIP) with a classification head to predict video-level anomaly scores, a segmentation head to predict spatial bounding boxes around anomalies, and a generation head to produce textual explanations for anomalies. To achieve zero-shot performance, we optimize the heads using a pre-specified set of textual prompts and a set of training data representing normal videos only, discarding any anomaly labels. For evaluation, we'll use video-level metrics (e.g., AUROC on analytics benchmark) and object-level metrics (e.g., mAP of localization on labeled frames) to assess the three types of predictions.
CONTROLS: Our competitors include (a) a baseline of individual zero-shot detectors (e.g., CLIP use just for classification) trained on the same way but evaluated on the full anomaly dataset, and (b) high-resource models (e.g., larger than standard CLIP variants) fine-tuned on a labeled anomaly dataset. 
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Due to CLIP's strong generalization capabilities, we expect decent ANU and LCR results across various scenes before adding new experiment.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Temporal-Spatial-Textual Zero-Shot Anomaly Detector Baseline: Overclipping Exclusion
PROPOSAL: To further improve robustness and reduce false positives, we incorporate a clipping procedure to exclude segments exceeding a normalized odd-scores: a score given by summing the anomalies scores of each frames divided by the total number of frames. ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Anomaly Explanation via Prototypical Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We use prototypical contrastive learning to enhance the explanations produced by our model. Given a normal video and an anomalous video, we compute feature representations for the observable abnormal content. Then, we learn a representation for the normal content, serving as the "prototype." By encouraging feature similarity between observed abnormal frames and their corresponding prototype, our goal is to induce a self-supervised learning signal that promotes highlighting the reasons for the anomaly. We compare the model trained with PC-L to the baseline with and without anomaly explanations.
