ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Domain-Robust Zero-Shot Anomaly Analysis via Meta-Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We leverage our temporal-spatial-textual anomaly detector and apply meta-adaptation to generate a high-robustness model that can generalize to unseen domains, without any domain-specific training. This involves training a meta-learner on a set of disjoint domains, including video surveillance and crime detection, and fine-tuning the model on a few examples from each novel domain. Our main hypothesis is that, through self-supervised learning, our model can develop transferable features across different domains, thus enhancing the overall robustness and generalizability. To validate this hypothesis, we perform extensive experiments on various unseen domains and assess our model's zero-shot performance across these diverse scenarios.
CONTROLS: Baseline comparisons include the basic zero-shot anomaly detector, a model fine-tuned on seen domains, and state-of-the-art meta-learning methods.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: Our domain-robust model should achieve significantly better results on unseen domains, showcasing its ability to transfer knowledge and generalize across different settings.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Evaluating Interpretable Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection via Interactive Human-AI Collaboration
PROPOSAL: We introduce an interactive evaluation framework, where human evaluators collaboratively work with our AI-powered anomaly detection model to assess its performance and interpretability. Through a series of iterative refinements and discussions, we collect feedback from humans on the model's predictions, explanations, and overall performance. This framework will enable us to better understand the strengths and weaknesses of our model, identify areas for improvement, and validate its effectiveness in practical scenarios.
CONTROLS: We will compare our interactive evaluation framework with standard automated metrics (e.g., AUC-ROC, mAP) and evaluate the quality of human-AI collaboration using metrics such as agreement rates and feedback quality.
COST: 900
PREDICTION: Our interactive evaluation framework will significantly improve the understanding of the model's performance and provide valuable insights for future improvements, leading to a more reliable and trustworthy anomaly detection system.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection for Multi-Source Data Fusion
PROPOSAL: In many real-world scenarios, anomaly detection systems are often required to analyze data from multiple sources, such as video, audio, and sensor data. In this proposal, we extend our zero-shot anomaly detection framework to handle multi-source data fusion, where we learn a shared anomaly representation across different sources. Our approach is specifically designed to handle heterogeneous data distributions, ensuring that the model can leverage the strengths of each individual source while minimizing their weaknesses.
CONTROLS: We will compare our multi-source data fusion approach with state-of-the-art one-source approaches and evaluate its performance on various benchmark datasets.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: Our multi-source data fusion approach will demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on anomaly detection tasks, showcasing its ability to effectively leverage diverse data sources and provide more comprehensive and robust results.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection in Video Surveillance
PROPOSAL: We explore the use of transfer learning to adapt pre-trained models for zero-shot anomaly detection in video surveillance. Specifically, we investigate the transferability of features learned from one dataset to another, and propose a novel adaptation mechanism to fine-tune the pre-trained model for the target domain. Our goal is to reduce the need for large-scale training data and improve the robustness of the model to domain shifts.
CONTROLS: We will compare our transfer learning approach with state-of-the-art zero-shot anomaly detectors and evaluate its performance on various video surveillance datasets.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Our transfer learning approach will demonstrate significant improvements in zero-shot anomaly detection performance, particularly in scenarios where the target domain is different from the source domain.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Real-World Deployment and Evaluation of Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection System
PROPOSAL: We propose a comprehensive real-world deployment and evaluation of our proposed zero-shot anomaly detection system in a video surveillance setting. We will deploy the system in a real-world scenario, such as a shopping mall or a public transportation system, and evaluate its performance on detecting anomalies in real-time. Our goal is to demonstrate the practical applicability of our system and identify potential challenges and limitations in real-world deployment.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our system with state-of-the-art anomaly detectors and evaluate its robustness in real-world scenarios.
COST: 1800 (including deployment and maintenance costs)
PREDICTION: Our real-world deployment will demonstrate the practical applicability and robustness of our zero-shot anomaly detection system, showcasing its potential to improve security and Public safety.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Limitations of Zero-Shot Temporal Anomaly Detection with Frozen Vision-Language Models
PROPOSAL: Conduct an empirical analysis of the state-of-the-art zero-shot temporal anomaly detection method based on frozen vision-language models, assessing its robustness across different domains and anomaly types.
CONTROLS: Compare the method to existing temporal anomaly detectors on the UCF-Crime and ShanghaiTech dataset, measuring accuracy, precision, and recall.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: While the method will show decent performance on some anomaly types, it will struggle with more complex or subtle anomalies, and possibly fail to generalize across difference domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Spatial Localisation and Textual Explanation of Video Anomalies using Encoder-Decoder Architectures
PROPOSAL: Investigate the potential of using encoder-decoder architectures, such as Transformers, for spatial video anomaly localization and textual explanation, leveraging the frozen pretrained vision-language models from proposal 1 as the encoder component.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the encoder-decoder approach to existing spatial localization methods (e.g., CornerNet, FCOS) and textual explanation models (e.g., T5, BART) on the same datasets (e.g., UCF-Crime, ShanghaiTech).
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The encoder-decoder approach will show improved performance in localized explanations due to the explicit spatial encoding, but might require additional training data to achieve comparable accuracy in anomaly detection.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Spatial Localisation and Textual Explanation of Video Anomalies using Inverse-Terms Decoder and Freezed Vision-Learning Models 
REVISED PROPOSAL: Modify the encoder-decoder architecture from proposal 2 to utilize an inverse-terms decoder that generates spatial masks and textual explanations in a shared embedding space, aiming to improve spatial localization and textual explanation capabilities.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised model to the original encoder-decoder approach and existing spatial localization methods on the UCF-Crime and ShanghaiTech datasets.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (addition to proposal 2)
PREDICTION: The inverse-terms decoder will lead to more accurate spatial localization and richer textual explanations due to the shared embedding space, but may introduce additional computational overhead.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Spatial Localisation and Textual Explanation of Video Anomalies using Inverse-Terms Decoder and Freezed Vision-Learning Models 
REVISED PROPOSAL: Modify the encoder-decoder architecture from proposal 2 to utilize an inverse-terms decoder that generates spatial masks and textual explanations in a shared embedding space, aiming to improve spatial localization and textual explanation capabilities.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised model to the original encoder-decoder approach and existing spatial localization methods on the UCF-Crime and ShanghaiTech datasets.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (addition to proposal 2)
PREDICTION: The inverse-terms decoder will lead to more accurate spatial localization and richer textual explanations due to the shared embedding space, but may introduce additional computational overhead.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dropout-based Regularization for Robust Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection
PROPOSAL: Introduce dropout-based regularization techniques to the frozen vision-language models from proposal 1, aiming to improve their robustness to domain shifts and generate more accurate zero-shot anomaly detection results.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the regularized models to the baseline models on the UCF-Crime and ShanghaiTech datasets, evaluating accuracy, precision, and recall.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The regularization techniques will lead to improved robustness and accuracy of the zero-shot anomaly detection, but may compromise the model's ability to generalize across different domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Anomaly-Aware Training of Frozen Vision-Language Models
PROPOSAL: Develop an anomaly-aware training protocol for frozen vision-language models, which fine-tunes the models on smaller subsets of anomalies from the training data to adapt to new or unseen anomaly types, improving their zero-shot detection performance.
CONTROLS: Compare the anomaly-aware models to the baseline frozen vision-language models on the UCF-Crime and ShanghaiTech datasets.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The anomaly-aware training will lead to improved performance on unseen anomaly types, but may be sensitive to the quality and quantity of the anomalies used in the training protocol, and may not generalize across different domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Domain Adaptation for Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection using Unlabeled Anomaly Data
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of unlabeled anomaly data to adapt frozen vision-language models across different domains, leveraging the anomaly-aware training protocol from proposal 3, to improve their robustness and generalizability.
CONTROLS: Compare the domain-adapted models to the baseline frozen vision-language models and the anomaly-aware models on the UCF-Crime and ShanghaiTech datasets, evaluating zero-shot anomaly detection accuracy.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The domain adaptation approach will lead to improved performance on new domains, but may require a large amount of unlabeled anomaly data to achieve robust results, and may be sensitive to the quality of the adaptation procedure.

ACTION: REVISE 4

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Analysis with Frozen Vision-Language Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of using pre-trained frozen vision-language Models (e.g., CLIP, ALIGN) for zero-shot video anomaly analysis. Freeze the model weights and use only the original visual and language understanding capabilities for detection, localization, and explanation. No additional fine-tuning or training data will be used.
CONTROLS: Compare with current zero-shot temporal detection methods (e.g., BASELINE-task-hours/1) for detection, and with current baseline models for localization and explanation, capturing accuracy and approximate down-stream applications performance.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This set of experiments will serve as a baseline for the subsequent improved variants, and we predict it will fail to deliver state-of-the-art results, given its limitations in terms of spatial and semantic context.

ACTION: REVISE, 1
TITLE: Enhanced Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Analysis with Masked CLIP for Better Spatial Understanding
PROPOSAL: Extend experiment 1 by using masked CLIP, where an image mask is embedded into the input that highlights the regions of interest. This allows the frozen vision-language model to focus more on the spatial context and nuances of the abnormal activities. 
CONTROLS: Compare results with and without the mask, to evaluate the effect of spatial emphasis in zero-shot video anomaly analysis.
COST: 20 GPU-hours (double for the computational overhead of generating accurate masks)
PREDICTION: By leveraging masked CLIP, we expect to see an improvement in localization accuracy and better contextual understanding of abnormal events, especially in scenarios where visual abnormalities are subtle or context-dependent. Esto on however might highlight the need for further research on efficient mask generation algorithms.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Enhanced Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Analysis with Masked CLIP for Better Spatial Understanding
PROPOSAL: Extend experiment 1 by using masked CLIP, where an image mask is embedded into the input that highlights the regions of interest. This allows the frozen vision-language model to focus more on the spatial context and nuances of the abnormal activities.

Esto on however might highlight the need for further research on efficient mask generation algorithms.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sequence-to-Sequence Generation for Abnormal Event Explanation
PROPOSAL: Train a sequence-to-sequence language generator on pre-extracted features (e.g. vision transformer outputs) to generate detailed text explanations for abnormal events. This model could complement the zero-shot video analysis approach by providing rich descriptive context for the abnormalities detected.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the quality of generated explanations against manual annotations for relevance, accuracy, and educational value.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that this approach will offer high-quality explanations for a wide range of abnormal events and anomalies, leveraging the pre-trained visual and language understanding capabilities of the frozen vision-language model.

ACTION: REVISE, 1
TITLE: Hierarchical Masked CLIP for Enhanced Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Analysis
PROPOSAL: Introduce a hierarchical mechanism to the masked CLIP approach, where not only spatially-focused attention is applied but also a hierarchical level is incorporated to capture high-level semantic concepts or activities within the scene. This hierarchical attention will allow the model to identify key abnormal events within a greater context.
CONTROLS: Evaluate performance across various levels of hierarchical masking, to determine the optimal trade-off between spatial and semantic understanding.
COST: 30 GPU-hours (up from 20, with additional computations required for hierarchical masking)
PREDICTION: The hierarchical masking method is expected to provide a more comprehensive understanding of abnormal events, particularly when such events are multifaceted and involve complex interactions with other actors or objects in the scene.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cross-Domain Evaluation for Robustness
PROPOSAL: Assess the robustness of our zero-shot video anomaly analysis approach across various surveillance and anomaly datasets, including data with different recording settings (day vs. night), object environments, and types of anomalies. This allows us to quantify the model's generalizability and applicability across diverse real-world scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare our model's performance with existing benchmarks for various datasets to better understand its strengths and limitations in real-world surveillance applications.
COST: 20 GPU-hours (relatively low given the strong pre-training of our model)
PREDICTION: Our approach should exhibit acceptable levels of robustness given its zero-shot nature, and might face some challenges when encountering anomalies specific to certain domains or environments, requiring adaptations for specific scenarios.

ACTION: REVISE 1

PREDICTION: The hierarchical masking method is expected to provide a more comprehensive understanding of abnormal events, particularly when such events are multifaceted and involve complex interactions with other actors or objects in the scene.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Weakly Supervised Model Adaptation for Zero-Shot Anomaly Analysis
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether adapting the frozen vision-language model to the specific characteristics and semantics of a target anomaly dataset, using weak supervision (e.g., coarse labels, noisy labels), can improve performance and robustness, leveraging a small fraction of labeled data. This work will contrast with traditional fully-supervised or self-supervised adaptations.
CONTROLS: Compare model performance before and after adaptation using various evaluation metrics, along with standard benchmarks such as detection accuracy, memory footprint, and computation time.
COST: 25 GPU-hours (relatively low given the weak supervision)
PREDICTION: By adapting the frozen model to target anomalies using weak supervision, we expect a noticeable improvement in accuracy and robustness in real-world datasets, while balancing computational efficiency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multimodal Fusion for Comprehensive Anomaly Analysis
PROPOSAL: Employ a multimodal fusion framework to combine the outputs of the hierarchical masked CLIP model, sequence-to-sequence generator, and weakly supervised adapted model to achieve a more comprehensive understanding of abnormal events. The fusion framework will integrate the strengths of each individual component to address the four aspects of anomaly analysis (when, where, what, and why).
CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of distinct fusion strategies (e.g., attention-based fusion, concatenation), and compare the results with individual models, to identify the optimal approach for a holistic analysis.
COST: 40 GPU-hours (high, due to the complexity of multimodal fusion and the larger number of computations required)
PREDICTION: By leveraging a multimodal fusion approach, we anticipate significant improvements in the accuracy, robustness, and interpretability of video anomaly analysis, especially in real-world scenarios where a comprehensive understanding of anomalies is crucial. 

 ACTION: REVISE, 1
TITLE: Interactive Visualizations for Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Analysis Insights
PROPOSAL: Develop an interactive visualization tool to enable users to explore and understand the outputs of the multimodal fusion model in an intuitive manner. The tool will provide visual representations of the detected anomalies, highlighting key features, and enabling users to inspect the model's reasoning process for individual anomalies.
CONTROLS: Evaluate user acceptance and effectiveness of the visualization tool in interpreting anomaly analysis results.
COST: 10 GPU-hours (relatively low, as visualization development primarily involves implementation and interface design)
PREDICTION: The interactive visualizations will facilitate better user understanding of the model's outputs and provide actionable insights for security personnel, paving the way for faster incident response and potential preventive measures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Temporal Contextualization for Improved Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Analysis
PROPOSAL: Introduce a temporal contextualization component to the multimodal fusion model to incorporate the temporal dynamics of the video into the analysis. This component will use recurrent neural networks (RNNs) or other sequential processing models to capture the temporal dependencies between frames and improve the detection of anomalies.
CONTROLS: Compare performance of the model with and without temporal contextualization, and evaluate its impact on different types of anomalies and complex event scenarios.
COST: 35 GPU-hours (medium, due to the additional computational requirements of temporal modeling)
PREDICTION: By accounting for temporal context, we expect to enhance the model's ability to detect and explain anomalies that unfold over time, especially those related to patterns, sequences, or continuous actions.

ACTION: REVISE, 2
TITLE: Multimodal Fusion with Transfer Learning for Robust Zero-Shot Anomaly Analysis
PROPOSAL: Employ transfer learning by pre-training the multimodal fusion model on a large-scale, diverse dataset and fine-tuning it on the target anomaly dataset. This will leverage the model's ability to generalize to new domains and adapt to the specific characteristics of the target dataset. Additionally, the transferred knowledge will be smoothed using a soft adaptation mechanism to prevent over-specialization.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the transfer learning method against other adaptation strategies, and compare its performance with and without hierarchical masked CLIP and temporal contextualization components.
COST: 45 GPU-hours (high, due to the pre-training and fine-tuning requirements of transfer learning)
PREDICTION: Transfer learning is expected to provide significant improvements in the model's adaptability and robustness across different surveillance scenarios, by effectively leveraging the strengths of pre-trained models and fine-tuning them for the specific target anomaly analysis task.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Anomaly-Specific Adversarial Attacks for Evaluating Robustness
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel adversarial attack method specifically designed for video anomaly analysis, targeting the multimodal fusion model. The goal is to create a challenging and realistic evaluation framework for measuring the model's robustness against adversarial examples and its ability to generalize across various anomaly scenarios.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of different attack methods, including gradient-based and optimization-based attacks, and assess the model's performance against a range of anomaly types and complexities.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (high, due to the computational expenses of generating adversarial examples and evaluating model robustness)
PREDICTION: By using anomaly-specific adversarial attacks, we anticipate a significant improvement in understanding model robustness and resilience against corruptions and tampering. This will allow for the development of more secure and reliable video anomaly analysis systems.

ACTION: REVISE, 2
TITLE: Self-Supervised Learning for Multimodal Fusion with Minimal Human Annotation
PROPOSAL: Leverage self-supervised learning techniques to pre-train the multimodal fusion model using a combination of unlabelled data and surrogate objectives, with minimal human annotation. This will enhance the model's ability to learn representations and associations without explicit labels, leading to more robust and consistent performance across anomaly scenarios.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of different self-supervised learning objectives (e.g., autoencoding, contrastive learning) and compare the results with other pre-training methods.
COST: 60 GPU-hours (high, due to the complexity of self-supervised learning and the need for large-scale unlabelled data)
PREDICTION: By incorporating self-supervised learning, we anticipate substantial improvements in the model's ability to learn robust and meaningful representations, thereby reducing the dependency on annotated data and enhancing its overall performance in real-world video anomaly analysis scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Active Learning Protocol for Efficient Anomaly Labeling
PROPOSAL: Develop an active learning protocol that selects the most informative and representative frames or segments from the unlabeled data to be annotated by human experts. This will optimize the annotation process, reducing the need for exhaustive manual labeling and improving the overall quality and coverage of the labeled dataset.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of various active learning strategies and selection methods (e.g., uncertainty-based, diversity-based) and compare the results with manual annotation and random selection.
COST: 15 GPU-hours (relatively low, due to the computational requirements of active learning and data querying)
PREDICTION: By employing an active learning protocol, we expect a drastic reduction in annotation time and effort, allowing for the efficient creation of a high-quality labeled dataset and improving the overall robustness and performance of the multimodal fusion model.

ACTION: REVISE, 1
TITLE: Explainable Embeddings for Anomaly Analysis with Multimodal Fusion
PROPOSAL: Utilize techniques from explainable AI to visualize and interpret the learned embeddings and features of the multimodal fusion model, providing insights into the relationships between different modalities and the role of each modality in anomaly detection. This will enable a deeper understanding of the model's decision-making process and facilitate the design of more effective anomaly analysis systems.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effectiveness of different explainability techniques (e.g., saliency maps, feature importance) and assess their impact on the interpretability and trustworthiness of the multimodal fusion model.
COST: 20 GPU-hours (relatively low, due to the computational requirements of visualization and interpretation)
PREDICTION: By making the embeddings more explainable, we anticipate improved transparency, trustworthiness, and accountability of the multimodal fusion model, ultimately leading to better decision-making and anomaly analysis outcomes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Evaluation and Deployment of the Multimodal Fusion Model for Video Anomaly Analysis
PROPOSAL: conducts a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed multimodal fusion model across various metrics, including accuracy, robustness, and interpretability, on a range of benchmark datasets and real-world security applications. The model's performance will be compared with state-of-the-art methods and existing systems for video anomaly detection and analysis.
CONTROLS: Assess the model's suitability for deployment in real-world security applications, including its scalability, modularity, and ease of maintenance, and compare its performance with existing systems and human analysts.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (high, due to the extensive evaluation and benchmarking required)
PREDICTION: By conducting a thorough evaluation and deployment of the multimodal fusion model, we anticipate improved performance, robustness, and interpretability of video anomaly detection and analysis systems, and a significant advancement in the development of reliable and trustworthy security applications.

ACTION: REVISE, 1
TITLE: Reproducibility and Transparency in Multimodal Fusion for Video Anomaly Analysis
PROPOSAL: Develop a comprehensive publicly available implementation of the proposed multimodal fusion model, along with a detailed documentation of the experiments and evaluation methods used in this work. This will ensure the reproducibility and transparency of the results, allowing the research community to build upon the findings and advance the field.
CONTROLS: Conduct a study on the replication of the results and evaluate the impact of hyperparameter tuning, dataset variations, and other factors on the model's performance.
COST: 10 GPU-hours (relatively low, due to the computational requirements of implementation and documentation)
PREDICTION: By making the multimodal fusion model and its implementation publicly available, we anticipate improved reproducibility, transparency, and collaboration in the research community, leading to accelerated progress in video anomaly detection and analysis.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating Object Binding in Pretrained Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: We'll experimentally assess whether large, pretrained Vision Transformers (ViTs) can reliably encode object-level binding by analyzing their internal representations on a range of object-centric and object-agnostic benchmarks.
CONTROLS: We'll compare the ViT to its convolutional neural network (CNN) baseline on tasks such as part segmentation, object detection, and object manipulation from scene understanding datasets (e.g., COCO, ImageNet).
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect ViTs to outperform CNNs on object-centric tasks but not necessarily demonstrate robust object binding, with binding failures likely to emerge in more complex scenes or when distinguishing between similar objects with overlapping feature conjunctions.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Investigating Type of Binding Representations
PROPOSAL: We'll use dimensionality reduction techniques (e.g., PCA, t-SNE) and visualizable object representations to explore whether pretrained ViTs represent objects using local feature similarity (i.e., binding by proximity) or global spatial structure (i.e., binding by spatial relationships).
CONTROLS: We'll analyze the representations learned by ViTs in conjunction with a shallow network that directly regresses the affinity matrix between object parts under various parameterizations (e.g., full, diagonal, Gaussian-based). .
COST: 100 GPU-hours (approximate batch processing with existing trained models)
PREDICTION: If the representations involve local feature similarity, we expect nearby feature points in the embedding space to form clusters, while global spatial structures are expected to be represented through more complex patterns and global topologies.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating Object Binding in Pretrained Vision Transformers
REVISED PROPOSAL: We'll train multiple large-scale Vision Transformers on variations of object-centric tasks, including dataset-specific downstream adaptation, and analyze how the object binding representations change across different quality metrics, attention mechanisms and architectures (e.g., use of learnable position embeddings, relative attention and flexible window sizes).
CONTROLS: We'll compare ViTs trained on different object-centric benchmarks (e.g., 7-scene setup, object scene graphs) against state-of-the-art CNN baselines.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: If large-scale, object-centric task training facilitates robust object binding, we expect the model to more reliably localize objects and dissect feature conjunctions between scene components, improving learned downstream tasks.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Effect of Training Data Diversity on Binding Representations
PROPOSAL: We'll train ViTs on diverse and varied datasets (e.g., synthetic object scenes, internet-scale object collections with realistic backgrounds) and analyze how this affects their object binding representations.
CONTROLS: We'll also examine the effect of dataset diversity on ViT performance and behavior, comparing it to a convolutional baseline trained on similar datasets.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (based on synthetic data and dataset-generation method development)
PREDICTION: Training on diverse data should enable ViTs to generalize better to unseen objects and features, and robustly capture complex binding relationships in images with mixed contents.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Binding Failures in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We'll analyze text-to-image diffusion models and examine their propensity for attribute leakage and binding failures, comparing the emergence of such effects to their counterparts in vision-transformer-based models.
CONTROLS: We'll compare the diffusion model's performance and binding capabilities to a vanilla ViT design with matching capacity and trained on a coherent image-text dataset (e.g. DALL-E, LLaMA-vision).
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: If text-to-image diffusion models are more prone to binding failures and attribute leakage, this may highlight fundamental differences in how these models process and ground visual symbols, and potentially explain why they tend to exhibit overfitting.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Comparative Analysis of Binding Mechanisms
PROPOSAL: We'll conduct an ablation study to isolate the unique contributions of different vision transformer components (e.g., self-attention, Multi-Head Attention, learnable position embeddings) to object binding, comparing the models' performance on downstream tasks.
CONTROLS: We'll hold common hyperparameters and architecture aspects consistent across these models and analyze inter-patch similarity matrices, localized attention strengths, and binding represetnation uniqueness under various forward pass conditions.
COST: 180 GPU-hours (based on the multiple ablated models evaluation)
PREDICTION: We expect self-attention to play a primary role in enabling object binding, while other mechanisms contribute to refined object representations and structural hierarchies in the multi-head attention maps.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Investigation of Boundaries Between Objects
PROPOSAL: We'll thoroughly study the internal representation and decision-making processes at the spatial boundaries of objects, particularly in cases of partial object occlusion or near-overlap.
CONTROLS: By using VGG16, ResNet50 and larger transformer architectures for re-weighting objectives in a backbone-encoder formulation, we compare object binding performances in apparent locations and distances to object levels seen often on many practical image retrieval contexts.
COST: 320 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By analyzing patch-wise influences, we expect unsupervised mid-level and holistic attention to reduce false positives at object boundaries, thereby allowing for clearer separation based on semantic relevance.

ADD
TITLE: Investigating Implicit Binding in Vision Transformers with Object-Centric Tasks
PROPOSAL: Train a set of standard ViT models on a dataset of object-centric benchmarks, such as ADF and PASCAL 3D+, and evaluate their ability to solve tasks that require object-level binding, like instance segmentation and object detection with occlusion.
CONTROLS: Include baselines that use explicit object-oriented architectures, such as Slot Attention, and ablations that disable self-attention or use random attention weights.
COST: 100k GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see limited success in object-centric tasks without explicit mechanisms, but with some evidence of implicit binding through self-attention. The absence of explicit object-level grouping may hinder the model's ability to address tasks with high occlusion rates or multiple objects with complex feature conjunctions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Object Binding in Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: Utilize pre-trained ViT models as a starting point for object-centric tasks and assess their ability to adapt to new object categories and scenes while leveraging their learned object binding representations.
CONTROLS: Compare with starting from random initialization, and potentially fine-tune on a small set of object-centric datasets before re-testing on the target task.
COST: 50k GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This could demonstrate whether the models acquire strong object binding capabilities during pre-training, which can be transferred across tasks and objects, or if object binding is primarily task-specific and requires re-learning for each new object category.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Object Binding in Vision Transformers (Revised)
PROPOSAL: Refine the previous proposal by utilizing a range of pre-training tasks known to enhance generalization and transferability in vision models, such as semi-supervised learning (SSL) with denoising autoencoders and contrastive learning on large-scale image datasets.
CONTROLS: Include control experiments that use pre-training tasks not focused on object-centric or visual grounding, such as pure classification or regression, to assess the impact of specific pre-training objectives on object binding.
COST: 75k GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised proposal has the potential to isolate the factors contributing to object binding in pre-trained transformers by leveraging a diverse set of pre-training tasks, which may lead to a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying transferable object binding representations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Binding Representations through Object Displacement Manipulation
PROPOSAL: Use a manipulation procedure to systematically displace objects within scenes in a augmenting way, and train ViT models to predict the object features and classes before and after the manipulation, to quantify how object binding is affected by such transformations.
CONTROLS: Compare with random manipulations and investigate if the models' performance follows the expected Bayesian logic as theoretically formulated, where a part will initially strongly represented as well with the loss soon shooting up immediately the visual cues including the latter are removed, and the rest will moderately rapidly improve when it has a good representation.
COST: 80k GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This could shed more light on the nature of binding representations by demonstrating how strongly tied they are to object features and the spatial layout of the scene, providing insights into the internal processing mechanisms and generalization capabilities of the models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Binding via Cluster Representativeness in ViT Features
PROPOSAL: Utilize a clustering-based approach to analyze the feature representations learned by ViT models and assess whether objects are clustered together in a way that reflects their visual similarity and object-level binding, rather than just low-level features.
CONTROLS: Compare different clustering algorithms and dimensions to determine the robustness of the findings and control for potential artifacts introduced by specific clustering techniques.
COST: 40k GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By examining cluster representativeness, we may gain insight into the object binding mechanisms underlying the feature representations learned by ViT models, possibly identifying clusters corresponding to specific object categories and exploiting their internal structure to improve object recognition and tracking.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Model-Eigen-Object Analysis: Uncovering Object Binding in ViT Self-Attention Weights
PROPOSAL: Utilize tools from linear algebra and graph theory to analyze the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of the self-attention matrices learned by ViT models, identifying potential object-binding related patterns and visualizing the corresponding eigenvectors as objects.
CONTROLS: Compare different eigendecomposition methods and analyze the impact of self-attention architecture and training processes on the resulting object binding representations.
COST: 90k GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This technique could provide novel insights into how ViT self-attention weights contribute to object binding by revealing specific eigenvectors that capture object-level features, enabling us to identify and leverage the most crucial binding-related components of the model's representation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Object Binding Performance and Noise Robustness of Self-Attention and Linear Feed-Forward Layers
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the relative contribution of self-attention and linear feed-forward layers to object binding performance and robustness to noise and data corruption, using experiments that prune or replace the former with the latter.
CONTROLS: Include ablation studies on different architectures and hyperparameters to isolate the effects of layer type on object binding capabilities.
COST: 70k GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By comparing self-attention and linear feed-forward layers, this study can help clarify their differential contributions to object binding, shedding light on which architectural components are crucial for objects to be represented and processed uniformly.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Temporal Analysis of Object Binding in ViT Models: Exploring Adaptation and Interference
PROPOSAL: Investigate how object binding representations in ViT models evolve over time during training and adaptation to new scenes, and explore whether the interference between objects in memory affects long-term binding performance and robustness.
CONTROLS: Include experiments that modulate the interference between objects through different training protocols and analyze the impact on object binding representations.
COST: 85k GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By examining the temporal dynamics of object binding in ViT models, this study may reveal insights into the mechanisms underlying object representation and adaptation, and potentially inform strategies to improve their robustness and efficiency in practical applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Neural Interpretability and Object Binding in ViT Models: Identifying Binding Relevant Neurons
PROPOSAL: Apply neural interpretability techniques, such as feature significance and neuron saliency, to identify which ViT model neurons are most relevant for object binding and how they contribute to binding performance.
CONTROLS: Compare different interpretability methods and assess the reliability and robustness of the results.
COST: 60k GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By uncovering the specific neurons responsible for object binding, this study can provide actionable insights into the internal workings of ViT models, helping to improve their transparency and accountability, and potentially informing more effective object-centric applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Evolution of Object Binding Capabilities in Continuously Trained Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: Use a continuous training procedure to assess how the object binding capabilities of ViT models evolve over an extended period, and whether their performance improves, plateaus, or degrades, under varying training conditions.
CONTROLS: Compare with traditional episodic training, and evaluate the impact of different architectural components, training hyperparameters, and data augmentations on the development of object binding capabilities.
COST: 100k GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By measuring the progression of object binding abilities during continuous training, this study can provide valuable insights into the time-dependent characteristics of ViT models, guiding the development of more effective and adaptable object-centric applications.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Adversarial Training for Local Anonymization
PROPOSAL: Train a small LLM on a synthetic dataset generated by a strong adversary model (e.g., GPT-4), while including an adversarial loss term to prevent the anonymizer from leaking private information. Evaluate its effectiveness against a variety of private attributes, including location, identity, and demographics. We expect the anonymizer to learn robust representations that can withstand some inference attacks, but may struggle with highly context-dependent attributes.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline model that has not seen adversarial training, as well as a GPT-4-based anonymizer for a stronger upper bound.
COST: 1 GPU-hour ( approx. 10k parameters, 100M tokens of synthetic data)
PREDICTION: We expect the adversarially trained model to achieve better anonymization performance and greater robustness against attacks, but may require significant tuning and hyperparameter optimization to achieve optimal results. The main failure point will be its potential inability to generalize to new, unseen private attributes.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Data Augmentation for Robust Anonymization
PROPOSAL: Apply data augmentation techniques (e.g., backtranslation, noise injection, spectral augmentation) to the synthetic dataset used for training the small LLM anonymizer. This can help increase its robustness to unseen inferences and broader attribute inference attacks. Evaluate the anonymizer's performance on a set of private attributes and compare with the baseline model and adversarially trained model from experiment 1.
CONTROLS: Evaluate different augmentation techniques and their combinations, as well as a control group with randomness.
COST: 0.5 GPU-hours (measuring the performance on test dataset)
PREDICTION: We expect the data augmentation approach to improve the anonymizer's robustness and inference-limiting capabilities, especially when combined with adversarial training. However, excessive augmentation can potentially harm the model's accuracy and performance.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Adversarial Training for Local Anonymization with Limited Adversarial Feedback
PROPOSAL: Refine the adversarial training approach from experiment 1 to only receive limited feedback from the strong adversary model. Instead of the full output, the anonymizer receives only a mask indicating which parts of the text the adversary was able to infer. Evaluate the anonymizer's performance under this reduced feedback and compare with the previously described methods. This can help evaluate the true impact of the anonymizer's size on its ability to learn robust representations.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original adversarial training method and a baseline without feedback on inferred text parts.
COST: 0.5 GPU-hours (running with masked output)
PREDICTION: We expect the anonymizer trained with limited adversarial feedback to be able to generalize better to unseen private attributes and perform relatively close to the model with full feedback, but may develop biases due to less accurate training signals.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Curriculum Learning for Private Attribute Inference Limiting
PROPOSAL: Introduce a curriculum learning approach for the anonymizer, where it first learns to identify and remove explicit identifiers, then gradually learns to address more subtle forms of inference (e.g., location, identity), and finally, more context-dependent inferences (e.g., demographics). This progression should help the model understand the complexity of private attribute inference and develop more effective anonymization strategies. Evaluate its performance on a variety of private attributes and compare with previous methods.
CONTROLS: Evaluate different curriculum design strategies and their impact on the anonymizer's performance.
COST: 2 GPU-hours (training for each task in curriculum)
PREDICTION: We expect the curriculum learning approach to improve the anonymizer's anonymization quality and enable more effective protection against private attribute inferences, especially in the later stages of the curriculum. However, a poorly designed curriculum could hinder learning.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Efficient Anonymization
PROPOSAL: Pre-train a small LLM anonymizer on a general text anonymization task (e.g., removing explicit names and locations) and fine-tune it on a new dataset specifically designed for private attribute inference limiting. This transfer learning approach can leverage pre-existing knowledge of anonymization and adapt it to more complex inference attacks. Evaluate its performance and compare with the previous methods.
CONTROLS: Compare with training a model from scratch, as well as a control with the same pre-trained model used for generation of synthetic data.
COST: 1 GPU-hour (fine-tuning for several epochs)
PREDICTION: We expect the transfer learning approach to speed up model development and improve anonymization performance, especially when the pre-trained model is strong and the fine-tuning dataset is well-designed. However, transfer learning may not be effective if the pre-trained model is outdated or the fine-tuning dataset is too different from the original task.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Curriculum Learning for Private Attribute Inference Limiting
PROPOSAL: Modify the curriculum learning approach to incorporate an exploratory phase where the model learns to identify and target the most informative text features for private attribute inference. This will enable the model to focus on the most critical aspects of anonymization and avoid unnecessary removal of irrelevant information. Use reinforcement learning to optimize the exploration-exploitation trade-off in the curriculum.
CONTROLS: Compare with the previous curriculum learning approach and a control with random exploration.
COST: 3 GPU-hours (larger model capacity to accommodate longer training runs and incorporation of reinforcement learning)
PREDICTION: We expect the revised curriculum learning approach to improve the model's learning efficiency, reduce unnecessary anonymization, and provide more effective protection against private attribute inferences. However, the optimization of exploration-exploitation trade-off may require meticulous hyperparameter tuning.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Fairness-Aware Anonymization for Private Attribute Inference Limiting
PROPOSAL: Introduce a fairness-aware objective to the anonymizer's loss function to minimize disparities in anonymization performance across different demographics and private attributes. This will ensure that the anonymizer does not disproportionately harm or benefit certain groups. Evaluate its performance on various fairness metrics and compare with the previous methods.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original anonymizer and a baseline that does not consider fairness, as well as a control with a fairness-aware model that does not consider private attribute inference limiting.
COST: 0.5 GPU-hours (running with fairness objective)
PREDICTION: We expect the fairness-aware anonymizer to improve the overall fairness of anonymization, reduce disparities in performance across demographics, and maintain or improve protection against private attribute inferences. However, incorporating fairness may introduce additional complexity in the model and optimization, which could lead to suboptimal performance in certain scenarios.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Hybrid Anonymization for Multi-Attribute Inference Limiting
PROPOSAL: Combine multiple anonymization methods, such as adversarial training, data augmentation, and curriculum learning, to create a hybrid anonymizer that can effectively limit private attribute inferences across multiple attributes. Evaluate its performance on a diverse set of private attributes and compare with the previous methods.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline that uses a single anonymization method, as well as ablations that remove individual methods from the hybrid model.
COST: 2 GPU-hours (running with combination of methods)
PREDICTION: We expect the hybrid anonymizer to achieve state-of-the-art performance on private attribute inference limiting, especially when combined methods complement each other's strengths and weaknesses. However, the potential benefits of the hybrid approach may be offset by increased complexity and hyperparameter tuning requirements.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Anonymization Evaluation with Adversarial Testing
PROPOSAL: Develop an adversarial testing framework to evaluate the effectiveness of the anonymizers in limiting private attribute inferences. This framework will use a strong, domain-specific adversary model to simulate real-world inference attacks. Evaluate the performance of each anonymizer under this framework and identify potential vulnerabilities and areas for improvement.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline that does not use the adversarial testing framework, as well as a control with a known-good anonymizer that has been manually evaluated and validated.
COST: 10 GPU-hours (running multiple simulations and iterating on framework)
PREDICTION: We expect the adversarial testing framework to provide a more comprehensive and nuanced evaluation of the anonymizers, highlighting potential weaknesses and areas for improvement. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effects of Adversarial Training on Local Anonymization
PROPOSAL: Conduct an experiment where we train a small anonymizer model (e.g., DistilBERT) using adversarial training on synthetic data with various levels of semantic complexity (e.g., hiding identities through contextual descriptions). The goal is to evaluate the efficacy of this approach in defending against inferences by strong LLM adversaries while keeping compute costs low. We'll use synthetic data to simulate different scenarios, such as text comments with implicit references to identities.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline model that doesn't receive adversarial training and evaluate anonymization effectiveness using metrics like masked language modeling loss (MLM) and accuracy for protected attributes. Additionally, we'll ablate the model's size and complexity to analyze the trade-offs between privacy and utility.
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Adversarial training may significantly improve anonymization efficacy in preventing inferences, but the results might be limited to the specific scenarios and semantic complexities explored in the synthetic data. Scaling this approach to real-world applications might require further adaptation and fine-tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Local Anonymization with Transfer Learning
PROPOSAL: Transfer the anonymizer model (DistilBERT) from the adversarial training experiment (1) to real-world synthetic datasets with varying levels of semantic complexity (e.g., comments from labeled social media platforms or online forums). We'll assess the model's ability to protect private information and its adaptability to different domains, as well as compare the results with both (a) the baseline model without adversarial training and (b) different proprietary models (e.g., GPT-4) for anonymization; we use their local version if they exist (major corporations only exposing a token online model).
CONTROLS: Compare with (a) the baseline model and (b) the proprietary models as described above; ideally in 3 steps to give additional clarity - also we perform methodological fitting to see the evaluation results fit with distilBERT compared to other more named models like GPT-4 etc.
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The transferred anonymizer model might show comparable or better performance than baseline models, but the results could be sensitive to the domain shift from synthetic to real-world data, and still we will likely underperform commercial counterparts. It will also reveal which previous transfer methodologies have correctly assessed LangMod anonymous versus vs good LangMod non-Anonymous, where based on prior approaches there isn't a unified comparative strategy with other simpler pretender text functions.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Evaluating Local Anonymization with Transfer Learning
PROPOSAL: Refine the evaluation of local anonymization by transfer learning by including synthetic data that mimics the actual structure and style of real-world data (e.g., mimicking suspicious narrative explanations as context setting). This will provide more realistic testing of the anonymizer model's ability to generalize to different domains and real-world scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised anonymizer model with (a) the baseline model without adversarial training and (b) the proprietary models as described above; evaluate both accuracy of attribute sanitization and proportion of protected attribute information that remains accessible to adversaries.
COST: Estimated 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised anonymizer model should show improved performance and robustness against the challenging real-world scenarios, but it could still struggle with certain types of data or attributes that are difficult to anonymize, such as those with subtle semantic cues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing the Robustness of Local Anonymization Against Adaptive Adversaries
PROPOSAL: Simulate a scenario where the anonymizer model is faced with an adaptive adversary that can adjust its strategy based on the anonymizer's defenses. This will be achieved by creating a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) that generates new adversarial inputs based on the anonymizer's previous failures. We will then evaluate the anonymizer's ability to withstand this adaptive attack and defend against inference-based privacy threats.
CONTROLS: Compare with the anonymizer models from previous experiments (1 and 2) and evaluate their robustness against the adaptive adversary using metrics like adversarial accuracy and information gain.
COST: Estimated 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The anonymizer model may suffer from decreased performance and robustness against the adaptive adversary, which could indicate the need for more sophisticated defenses or adaptive anonymization techniques. However, the extent to which the anonymizer model can be improved through adaptation or other methods remains unclear.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Developing an Omnibus Anonymization Framework for Real-World Text Data
PROPOSAL: Design and implement an omnibus anonymization framework that integrates various anonymization techniques from previous experiments (1-3) to provide a comprehensive and adaptive anonymization solution for real-world text data. The framework will combine the adversarial training, transfer learning, and adaptive defenses to create a robust anonymization pipeline.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the omnibus framework using a variety of real-world text datasets (e.g., social media, user reviews, medical records) and compare its performance with existing anonymization methods.
COST: Estimated 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The omnibus anonymization framework should provide a significant improvement in anonymization performance and robustness compared to individual techniques. However, its complexity and computational requirements may increase, and its effectiveness might depend on the specific characteristics of the real-world data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Memorization of Private Information by Local Anonymization Models
PROPOSAL: Analyze the tendency of local anonymization models to memorize private information, which can be a potential risk in anonymization. We will use techniques such as sensitive information entanglement and input relevance analysis to investigate how much private information is retained by anonymization models in real-world data scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with a baseline model that only performs basic de-identification and evaluate the information retained by anonymization models using metrics like private information leakage and model interpretability.
COST: Estimated 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Local anonymization models may retain some private information, especially if the real-world data has high semantic complexity or contextual relevance. However, the extent to which memorization occurs and its impact on anonymization effectiveness remains to be determined.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Efficiency and Scalability of Local Anonymization in Distributed Environments
PROPOSAL: Investigate the efficiency and scalability of local anonymization models in distributed environments, such as cloud or edge computing settings. We will evaluate the performance of anonymization models in scenarios with multiple machines, high traffic, and varying computational resources.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of anonymization models in distributed settings with results from previous experiments and evaluate the impact of distribution and communication overhead on anonymization efficiency.
COST: Estimated 350 GPU-hours (with 4-node clusters)
PREDICTION: Local anonymization models may require significant adjustments to achieve efficient performance in distributed environments, and their scalability might be limited by the communication overhead between machines. However, adapting anonymization techniques to distributed computing settings could lead to significant improvements in anonymization speed and efficiency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Efficacy of Local Anonymization on Text Data with High-Sensitive Attributes
PROPOSAL: Investigate the efficacy of local anonymization models on text data with high-sensitive attributes, such as personal characteristics, medical information, or financial data. We will evaluate the performance of anonymization models in protecting these sensitive attributes and compare the results with a baseline model that only performs basic de-identification.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of anonymization models on high-sensitive attributes with results from previous experiments and evaluate the impact of attribute sensitivity on anonymization effectiveness.
COST: Estimated 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Local anonymization models may struggle to effectively anonymize text data with high-sensitive attributes, and their performance might decline compared to less sensitive attributes. However, adapting anonymization techniques to manage attribute sensitivity could lead to significant improvements in anonymization effectiveness.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Case Study: Applying Local Anonymization to Real-World Text Data in a Confidential Setting
PROPOSAL: Collaborate with a confidential partner to apply the local anonymization techniques developed in this study to real-world text data in a real-world confidential setting. This will involve evaluating the efficacy of anonymization models in protecting sensitive information and addressing any challenges that arise in a practical implementation scenario.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with previous experiments and evaluate the performance of anonymization models in a real-world setting.
COST: Estimated 500 GPU-hours (with additional human effort for partnership and collaboration)
PREDICTION: The application of local anonymization to real-world text data in a confidential setting may highlight practical challenges and limitations that were not apparent in previous experiments, and the results may inform the continued development and refinement of anonymization techniques for sensitive data.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Graph Autoencoder-based Graph Purification
PROPOSAL: Train a graph autoencoder (GAE) with a pre-trained GNN as the encoder and a decoder that reconstructs the input graph, removing irrelevant structural redundancy. The decoder output will represent the 'essential' structure of the test graph, and a masker can be applied to identify non-essential edges during inference.
CONTROLS: Train the GAE on a variety of graph types to ensure versatility and evaluate its performance on ID and OOD graphs from recent benchmarks such as stal rgg,egal r gin_data-set  and ydg datasets; compare against a baseline of training the pre-trained GNN with an additional layer to 'purify' the input graph.
COST: 10k GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The GAE-based GNN should outperform the baseline and previous methods by accurately distinguishing between essential and non-essential structural information. It may, however, not scale well to very large graphs.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Essential Graph Fragment Detection using GraphMatch
PROPOSAL: Utilize a pre-trained GNN to identify 'essential' graph fragments that are invariant across the test ID/OOD graphs, leveraging the GraphMatch framework to compute robust graph similarity. GraphMatch will be applied to all pairs of graphs in the test set and combined with ensemble methods to identify the most common graph fragments associated with OOD data.
CONTROLS: Evaluate on various graph datasets, especially those with high structural similarities, and compare against a baseline method that uses degree centrality to select the 'most essential' nodes in each graph.
COST: 5k GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The GraphMatch-based approach can achieve high OOD detection accuracy by identifying graph fragments that are not robustly present in OOD graphs, but will likely be outperformed by the graph purification approach from proposal 1 in terms of scalability.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Essential Graph Fragment Detection using GraphMatch
PROPOSAL: Utilize a pre-trained GNN to identify 'essential' graph fragments that are invariant across the test ID/OOD graphs, leveraging the GraphMatch framework to compute robust graph similarity. However, instead of combining these similarities across all pairs of graphs, apply GraphMatch to the pre-trained GNN's representations of ID graphs and OOD graphs separately, and use a classification model to distinguish between the two distributions. This approach will be compared to the previous version.
CONTROLS: Evaluate on various graph datasets, especially those with high structural similarities, and compare against a baseline method that uses degree centrality to select the 'most essential' nodes in each graph.
COST: 5k GPU-hours (unchanged due to the minimal additional computational overhead)
PREDICTION: The revised GraphMatch approach should outperform the previous version and achieve competitive results with the graph purification approach from proposal 1.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Graph Diffusion-based Structural Information Retention
PROPOSAL: Apply a graph diffusion process to pre-trained GNN representations of ID and OOD graphs separately, focusing on retaining and emphasizing graph structural information that is indicative of OODness, while discarding information unrelated to OOD detection. This will be achieved by setting the initial diffusion vector as a learned mask and iteratively iterating the graph convolution and diffusion process.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that applies the graph diffusion only on ID graphs and a version where the pre-trained GNN's parameters are fine-tuned with an additional layer to refine the structural information after the diffusion process.
COST: 8k GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The Graph Diffusion-based approach may achieve state-of-the-art results in OOD detection, as it selectively retains structural features relevant to OOD graphs. However, it may be outperformed by more interpretable approaches such as graph purification.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Ensemble Methods for OOD Detection
PROPOSAL: Combine the strengths of the above approaches by training an ensemble model that aggregates the predictions from Graph Autoencoder-based Graph Purification, Essential Graph Fragment Detection using GraphMatch, and Graph Diffusion-based Structural Information Retention. This ensemble method will be trained on synthetic OOD data and evaluated on several real-world benchmarks.
CONTROLS: Compare against individual approaches, as well as a baseline where predictions from each approach are used to train an individual classifier for OOD detection.
COST: 15k GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The ensemble approach is likely to achieve the highest accuracy in OOD detection by leveraging the strengths of multiple methods. However, its interpretability and scalability may suffer due to the increased complexity of the model.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Structural Attention-based Masking for OOD Detection
PROPOSAL: Introduce an attention mechanism within the pre-trained GNN to selectively focus on 'essential' structural information in the input graph, identifying edges that contribute most to the graph's overall structure and suppressing the rest. This will be achieved by training an additional attention layer on the pre-trained GNN's representations and applying the learned weights to mask the input graph during inference.
CONTROLS: Compare against a version of the attention mechanism that is applied at a layer-wise level, and a baseline where no attention mechanism is used.
COST: 12k GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The Structural Attention-based approach may yield comparable results to the ensemble method, but with improved interpretability due to the explicit focus on essential structural information. However, its performance may suffer in scenarios where the pre-trained GNN has already captured the most relevant features.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Graph Autoencoder-based Graph Purification
PROPOSAL: Explore a variant of the graph purification approach, where the decoder is trained to explicitly identify and discard 'redundant' edges in the input graph, rather than just reconstructing the original structure. This will be achieved by adding a regularization term to the decoder loss, penalizing the presence of edges that are not critical for the graph's connectivity.
CONTROLS: Evaluate on various graph datasets, and compare against the original purification approach, as well as a baseline where the decoder is trained without the regularization term.
COST: unchanged (10k GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: The revised purification approach may improve performance by explicitly addressing the issue of structural redundancy, but its results may depend on the effectiveness of the regularization term in accurately identifying redundant edges.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Graph Sampling-based Outlier Detection
PROPOSAL: Introduce a graph sampling-based approach to OOD detection, where a subset of nodes or edges from the input graph is selectively sampled to evaluate the likelihood of the graph being OOD. This will be achieved by training a classifier on the sampled subgraphs and evaluating its performance on the full input graph.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline where the entire input graph is used for evaluation, and evaluate on various graph datasets with varying sizes and complexities.
COST: 9k GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The graph sampling-based approach may reduce computational overhead and improve performance in scenarios where the full graph is too large or complex, but its effectiveness may depend on the ability to select the optimal subset of nodes or edges for sampling.

ACTION: REVISE 6
TITLE: Graph Sampling-based Outlier Detection
PROPOSAL: Refine the graph sampling-based approach by incorporating information from the pre-trained GNN's representations, where the sampled subgraphs are scored based on their relevance to the input graph's embeddings, rather than solely on their structural properties. This will be achieved by training a scoring function on the pre-trained GNN's outputs and applying it to the sampled subgraphs.
CONTROLS: Evaluate on various graph datasets, compare against a baseline where no additional scoring function is used, and assess the impact of incorporating pre-trained GNN information on the approach's performance.
COST: 10k GPU-hours (increased due to the additional training step)
PREDICTION: The revised graph sampling-based approach may improve performance by leveraging the pre-trained GNN's knowledge, but its effectiveness may depend on the quality of the pre-trained model and the relevance of its embeddings to the input graph.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Hybrid Architecture for OOD Detection on Graphs
PROPOSAL: Combine multiple architectures from the above proposals to create a hybrid model for OOD detection, where the Graph Autoencoder-based Graph Purification is used for structural refinement, the Graph Diffusion-based Structural Information Retention is used for essential information extraction, and the Structural Attention-based Masking is used for selectively focusing on key graph elements.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the hybrid model on a range of graph benchmarks, comparing its performance against individual components, as well as state-of-the-art OOD detection methods.
COST: 20k GPU-hours (increased due to the complex architecture and potential overfitting)
PREDICTION: The hybrid architecture may achieve state-of-the-art results in OOD detection by combining the strengths of multiple methods, but its complexity and computational overhead may limit its practicality.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unsupervised Distillation of Essential Graph Structures for OOD Detection
PROPOSAL: Investigate an unsupervised learning-based paradigm where the pre-trained GNN compresses the informative substructures of unlabeled ID and OOD test graphs into a compact, shared graph representation, discarding redundant structural information without information loss. This is achieved through a form of knowledge distillation, leveraging the supervisory signal provided by the correlations between informative subgraphs. Specifically, the model learns to predict the robust, sparse correlations between subgraph embeddings, discovered using a contrastive learning approach, while decoding the suppressed, informative structures into embedded space.
CONTROLS: Compare to GOODAT in terms of detection accuracy and robustness on held-out ID graphs and varying OOD datasets.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (approx.)
PREDICTION: This approach should enable more accurate and robust OOD detection than GOODAT, as it minimizes information loss while selectively retaining essential graph structures. It may fail if the pre-trained model has limited capacity to distill the informative subgraphs or if the method is sensitive to the selection of hyperparameters governing the contrastive learning process.

Develop a method to identify the set of redundant substructural elements present in both ID and OOD graphs, which are distinguishable from the query subgraph by comparing their semantic signatures. This is achieved through a graph-based method that employs graph isomorphism networks (GINs) to mine the ID training set for subgraphs with the same structural motifs but varying node labels and edge weights. Investigate the phenomenon of graph structural bias recovery, whereby the pre-trained GNN inadvertently captures and then induces graph structures that promote ID-Oversmoothing and OOD-Missmoothing, significantly reducing OOD detection performance. This is achieved through the active randomization of node attributes, which recovers the underlying structural invariance with respect to ID and OOD distributions. The approach introduces a novel denoising mechanism that reduces the negative effects of structural bias by adding perturbations to the graph structure and using a contrastive learning approach to align the perturbed structure with the original.
