actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Graph Structure Refiner for Test-Time OOD Detection
PROPOSAL:  We propose a novel Graph Structure Refiner (GSR) that refines the structure of pre-trained GNNs at test time, allowing them to capture the essential structural information of test graphs while discarding irrelevant structural redundancy. GSR employs a differentiable graph edit operator that modifies the test graph structure based on similarities with pre-trained graph embeddings. We fine-tune a lightweight neural network to predict the optimal graph edits that remove or add nodes/edges while preserving the semantic information of the graph.
CONTROLS:  We compare GSR against GOODAT and other baselines on two real-world benchmarks: mol-SGD and PPI prediction datasets. We also conduct a thorough ablation study to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed GSR.
COST:  1200 GPU-hours (trained on a mix of large-scale graphs and validating our findings on standard OOD detection benchmarks)
PREDICTION:  Our proposed GSR should outperform GOODAT and other baselines by 5-8% on average OOD detection accuracy, while being computationally efficient and scalable to large graphs. The main failure mode is the need for effectively tuning the lightweight network that predicts graph edits.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Competitive Control Plot Analysis for Structural Redundancy Mitigation
PROPOSAL:  To further investigate the impact of structural redundancy in OOD detection, we propose a Competitive Control Plot Analysis (CCPA) to visualize and quantify the similarities between ID and OOD test graphs at different scales and structural granularities. By analyzing the similarity scores generated by CCPA, we can identify the structural components frequently preserved across OOD samples and selectively remove or modify them to obtain more robust OOD detection.
CONTROLS:  We contrast CCPA against traditional visualization techniques (e.g., graph contrastive learning loss surfaces) and demonstrate its effectiveness at highlighting and mitigating structural redundancy on the social network analysis dataset.
COST:  300 GPU-hours (visualizing plots on a subset of the graph benchmarks)
PREDICTION:  The application of CCPA can reveal structure-specific OOD features in test graphs and, combined with GSR, increase average OOD detection accuracy by an additional 3.5%, for a combined OOD detection accuracy of 14.5-17.5%. However, CCPA's reliance on competitive learning scores might limit its adaptability to diverse graph datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Neighborhood Edge Aggregation for Essential Structure Capture
PROPOSAL:  Building on our previous proposals, we introduce Neighborhood Edge Aggregation (NEA), a new edge pooling scheme for capturing essential structural information in test graphs. NEA aggregates features from neighboring nodes that are part of the test graph's core structure, reducing the influence of structural noise while preserving critical connections.
CONTROLS:  We compare NEA against various baseline pooling methods (e.g., average, max, sum pooling) and perform thorough ablation studies to demonstrate its effectiveness on the PPI prediction dataset.
COST:  600 GPU-hours (evaluating edge pooling methods on various graph sizes)
PREDICTION:  Our NEA-based method will exhibit a 2-3% boost in OOD detection accuracy compared to the GSR-based method from our first proposal. Additionally, NEA has the potential to be scalable to large graphs and should be less susceptible to noise in the graph structure. However, we expect challenges when applying NEA to highly heterogeneous and strongly connected graphs.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE:  Enhanced Neighborhood Edge Aggregation for Robust OOD Detection
PROPOSAL:  To build upon our Neighborhood Edge Aggregation (NEA) proposal, we introduce an Enhanced Neighborhood Edge Aggregation (ENEA) method. ENEA incorporates a learnable node attention mechanism that adaptively weighs neighboring nodes based on their structural relevance to the test graph, enhancing the robustness of essential structure capture in presence of graph noise.
CONTROLS:  We compare ENEA against the original NEA and other ablated variants (e.g., uniform weighting) using thorough ablation studies on the social network analysis dataset.
COST:  450 GPU-hours (weighting strategies evaluation)
PREDICTION:  The ENEA method should provide an additional 2-4% boost in OOD detection accuracy compared to the NEA method from our previous proposal, leveraging the dynamic weighting scheme to downplay unreliable neighborhoods and amplify critical connections. This improvement might come at the cost of increased model complexity and added MAE prediction at emission.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE:  Neighborhood Edge Aggregation for Essential Structure Capture
PROPOSAL:  Building on our previous proposal, we modify Neighborhood Edge Aggregation (NEA) to use a fully connected graph attention network that attends to the overall graph structure, allowing it to better capture long-range dependencies and critical node connections. We also use an intersection of word2vec embeddings as edge weights which will improve node connections.
CONTROLS:  We compare the revised NEA against the original NEA and other ablated variants (e.g., uniform attention) using thorough ablation studies on the PPI prediction dataset.
COST:  600 GPU-hours (evaluating edge pooling methods on various graph sizes)
PREDICTION:  The revised NEA should exhibit a 4-6% improvement in OOD detection accuracy due to the dynamic attention mechanism and the choice of edge weights, outperforming the baseline methods by an even wider margin and serving as a robust preprocessing step before applying the GSR or other test-time detection methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Threshold-Aware Graph Refinery for Concatenated OOD Score
PROPOSAL:  To combine the strength of our previous proposals (GSR and revised NEA), we introduce a Threshold-Aware Graph Refinery (TAGR) method. TAGR designs a hybrid OOD detection framework that sequentially applies GSR to refine the graph structure, then uses revised NEA to extract essential structural information, and finally generates a final OOD score by merging the two previous scores under an adaptive threshold mechanism.
CONTROLS:  We compare TAGR against various baseline methods (e.g., vote-based fusion, score addition) on the social network analysis dataset and perform thorough ablation studies to demonstrate its effectiveness.
COST:  900 GPU-hours (designing the threshold mechanism)
PREDICTION:  TAGR should achieve an average OOD detection accuracy improvement of 6-8% and a mean AUC ROC score of 0.845, consistently outperforming other methods due to its ability to adaptively combine enhanced graph refineries and critical structural features.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  OOD Sampling-based Iterative Refinement for Graph Neural Networks
PROPOSAL:  We propose an OOD Sampling-based Iterative Refinement (OSIR) method, which iteratively samples a small subset of OOD graphs, refines the graph structure and OOD scores using TAGR, and updates the model parameters accordingly to adapt to the OOD graph distribution. This approach can enhance the generalizability of graph neural networks on unseen OOD samples.
CONTROLS:  We compare OSIR against various baseline methods (e.g., on-the-fly OOD detection, adaptive retraining) on the drug discovery and protein function classification datasets and analyze its efficiency in achieving robust OOD detection.
COST:  1800 GPU-hours (large-scale OOD sampling and model adaptation)
PREDICTION:  The OSIR method is expected to improve the average OOD detection accuracy by an additional 5-7% and provide a significantly robust OOD detection framework for graph neural networks, especially for OOD graph distributions that are distant from the training data. However, the method's scalability and performance may degrade when dealing with very large and diverse OOD datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Model-Agnostic Integrated Boundary Interpretability for Enhanced OOD Detection
PROPOSAL:  To improve the interpretability of our proposed OOD detection methods and provide insights into their decision-making processes, we develop a model-agnostic integrated boundary interpretation framework. This framework, termed as MI Maid, sheds light on the critical features and structural patterns responsible for distinguishing between ID and OOD samples.
CONTROLS:  We apply MI Maid to our proposed OOD detection methods (TAGR and OSIR) and compare the boundary interpretation with a state-of-the-art model-agnostic method on the PPI prediction dataset.
COST:  300 GPU-hours (integral gradient method with boundary interpretation)
PREDICTION:  MI Maid will reveal the most informative graph features contributing to accurate OOD detection for both TAGR and OSIR, providing valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of the proposed methods. This interpretation can help users select the best method for a given application and improve future designs for OOD detection by focusing on the most predictive features, reducing the risk of model overfitting. However, the accuracy of MI Maid on graph data may suffer from high dimensionality and increasing gradient complexity compared to a standard neural network.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Synthetic Multi-Modal Graphs for Real-World OOD Detection
PROPOSAL:  To further evaluate the robustness of our proposed OOD detection methods on diverse graph types, we generate a synthetic multi-modal graph dataset that mimics the structure and variability found in real-world applications. This dataset allows us to assess the performance of TAGR, OSIR, and other methods on a rich, real-world-inspired distribution of OOD graphs.
CONTROLS:  We compare the performance of our methods on the synthetic dataset against state-of-the-art approaches and perform extensive evaluations to show their effectiveness.
COST:  1200 GPU-hours (large-scale synthetic graph generation and evaluation)
PREDICTION:  The synthetic multi-modal graph dataset will enable us to assess the generalizability and trustworthiness of our OOD detection methods under highly diverse graph dynamics, data modalities, and scales. By aggregating the findings from all of our proposals, we anticipate significant improvements in average OOD detection accuracy that reflect real-world success scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Unified Pipeline for Robust Graph Neural Network-based Out-of-Distribution Detection
PROPOSAL:  We finalize our research by unifying all our proposed methods into a comprehensive pipeline for robust out-of-distribution detection on graph-structured data. Our Unified Pipeline integrates TAGR, OSIR, MI Maid, and the synthetic multi-modal graph dataset to provide an indispensable solution for practitioners to detect and handle OOD data in various applications.
CONTROLS:  We compare the Unified Pipeline against state-of-the-art method and perform thorough experiments to demonstrate the advantage and feature stability based on benign-than-training OOD and mismatch policy OOD within a movie casting network.
COST:  3600 GPU-hours (comprehensive pipeline evaluation and OOD policy exploration)
PREDICTION:  The Unified Pipeline will serve as a powerful tool for users seeking robust OOD detection in production scenarios, combining the benefits of enhanced graph refinement, powerful iterative refinement, integrated boundary interpretation, and synthetic, real-world admixtures. We predict the average OOD detection accuracy to surpass 0.91 across reasonably diverse distributions of non-domestic use and emergence on coordination structures.

propositions.texte: We propose a novel Graph Structure Refiner (GSR) that refines the structure of pre-trained GNNs at test time, allowing them to capture the essential structural information of test graphs while discarding irrelevant structural redundancy. GSR employs a differentiable graph edit operator that modifies the test graph structure based on similarities with pre-trained graph embeddings. We fine-tune a lightweight neural network to predict the optimal graph edits that remove or add nodes/edges while preserving the semantic information of the graph.
propositions.titre: Graph Structure Refiner for Test-Time OOD Detection

propositions.controles: We contrast CCPA against traditional visualization techniques (e.g., graph contrastive learning loss surfaces) and demonstrate its effectiveness at highlighting and mitigating structural redundancy on the social network analysis dataset.

propositions.prediction: The application of CCPA can reveal structure-specific OOD features in test graphs and, combined with GSR, increase average OOD detection accuracy by an additional 3.5%, for a combined OOD detection accuracy of 14.5-17.5%. However, CCPA's reliance on competitive learning scores might limit its adaptability to diverse graph datasets.
propositions.texte: To further investigate the impact of structural redundancy in OOD detection, we propose a Competitive Control Plot Analysis (CCPA) to visualize and quantify the similarities between ID and OOD test graphs at different scales and structural granularities. By analyzing the similarity scores generated by CCPA, we can identify the structural components frequently preserved across OOD samples and selectively remove or modify them to obtain more robust OOD detection.
propositions.titre: Competitive Control Plot Analysis for Structural Redundancy Mitigation

propositions.controles: We compare NEA against various baseline pooling methods (e.g., average, max, sum pooling) and perform thorough ablation studies to demonstrate its effectiveness on the PPI prediction dataset.

propositions.texte: Building on our previous proposals, we introduce Neighborhood Edge Aggregation (NEA), a new edge pooling scheme for capturing essential structural information in test graphs. propositions.controles: We compare TAGR against various baseline methods (e.g., vote-based fusion, score addition) on the social network analysis dataset and perform thorough ablation studies to demonstrate its effectiveness.

propositions.texte: To combine the strength of our previous proposals (GSR and revised NEA), we introduce a Threshold-Aware Graph Refinery (TAGR) method. TAGR designs a hybrid OOD detection framework that sequentially applies GSR to refine the graph structure, then uses revised NEA to extract essential structural information, and finally generates a final OOD score by merging the two previous scores under an adaptive threshold mechanism.
propositions.titre: Threshold-Aware Graph Refinery for Concatenated OOD Score

propositions.texte: Investigate the transferability of PEFT techniques across different PDE domains, by evaluating whether adaptations obtained on one domain (e.g., Navier-Stokes) can enhance the performance of FNO on a different domain (e.g., shallow water equations or solar magnetohydrodynamics). propositions.controles: Compare the performance of FNO models fine-tuned with frequency regularization to those fine-tuned without, and examine the trade-off between frequency-specific adaptation and model generalizability.
propositions.prediction: The results will reveal whether frequency regularization helps to improve the model's performance by reducing the impact of domain-specific frequency artifacts, and whether this comes at the cost of reduced generalizability to new tasks.
propositions.texte: Examine the impact of frequency regularization on the performance of FNO models when using PEFT techniques. Specifically, we will investigate the effect of including frequency penalty terms in the loss function and restricting the FNO's frequency response during fine-tuning on a range of downstream tasks in computational fluid dynamics and shallow water equations.
propositions.titre: Investigating the Role of Frequency Regularization in PEFT for FNOs

propositions.controles: Compare the performance of factorized LOMs to standard LOMs on various PDE tasks, and investigate the extent to which the factorized representations capture physical structure and principles.
propositions.prediction: By learning compact, factorized representations, we can potentially identify latent structure and dynamics in the operator orbits, and develop more efficient and interpretable deep learning-based solvers for PDEs.
propositions.texte: Explore the possibility of learning compact, factorized representations of the operator dynamics in large operator models, using techniques such as sparse factorization and low-rank matrix decompositions. We aim to capture emergent dynamics and structure in the operator orbits and evaluate their potential benefits in accelerating deep learning-based solvers for PDEs.
propositions.titre: Emergent Dynamics in Large Operator Models through Factorized Representation Learning

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating LoRA-style Physics-Informed Learned Soft Prompts for Pre-trained Large Operator Models
PROPOSAL: Train pre-trained FNO models on synthetic datasets for 3D compressible Navier-Stokes turbulence forecasting and shallow-water free-surface flow simulation. Adapt learned soft prompts to fit LoRA-style updates, comparing their performance with vanilla fine-tuning and full pre-training.
CONTROLS: Compare performance with naive gradient-based fine-tuning and a baseline pre-trained FNO model on the aforementioned synthetic datasets.
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate better fine-tuning performance, especially in identifying boundaries between turbulent regimes in compressible Navier-Stokes turbulence and detecting shock waves using learned soft prompts. This approach may underperform when sudden shocks appear near the exampling process from susceptible classifications IDR.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: In-Depth Analysis of Spectral Impact on Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Pre-Trained FNO Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the distribution of information across frequency bands in pre-trained FNO models for solar magnetohydrodynamics (chromosphere-corona magnetic field reconstruction) and shallow-water free-surface flow simulation datasets. Analyze the impact of spectrally targeted parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods, e.g., band-pass filtered LoRA-style updates, on solving PDEs.
CONTROLS: Compare spectrally targeted PEFT with vanilla PEFT and a baseline pre-trained FNO model for both datasets, examining relative performance and solution properties across frequency bands.
COST: Estimated 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that spectrally targeted PEFT will significantly improve solution quality and faster convergence, especially for higher-frequency features in magnetohydrodynamic flows and turbulent shallow water regimes.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: In-Depth Analysis of Spectral Impact on Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Pre-Trained FNO Models
PROPOSAL: For both solar magnetohydrodynamics and shallow-water free-surface flow simulation, examine the frequency response of pre-trained FNO models to full-model fine-tuning and different PEFT techniques, including LoRA-style updates and band-pass filtered PEFT. Investigate whether spectral prior knowledge can inform the design of more selective PEFT methods, thereby reducing adaptation to noise.
CONTROLS: Compare performance with a baseline pre-trained FNO model and analyze solution properties across frequency bands for both datasets, examining relative performance and solution accuracy.
COST: Estimated 120 GPU-hours (reduced from 150 due to more efficient experiment design)
PREDICTION: We anticipate improved PEFT performance, especially for task-adaptation-oriented PEFT approaches, and that spectral prior knowledge will enable the design of more selective adaptation methods for LOMs. This could also reveal the effect of incorporating significant solitary solution-manifold constraint, impairing the adaptive gradient- updates in several promotion.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Characterizing Adaptive Properties of Pre-Trained FNO Models Using Dispersion Relations Analysis
PROPOSAL: Investigate the applicability and limitations of dispersion relation analysis for understanding the adaptive properties of pre-trained FNO models, including their ability to capture frequencies, damping, and group velocities relevant to specific PDEs and physical regimes.
CONTROLS: Compare dispersion relation analysis results with empirical fine-tuning performance using various PEFT methods and assess their relationship for shallow-water free-surface flow simulation and solar magnetohydrodynamics.
COST: Estimated 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that dispersion relation analysis will provide valuable insights into the strengths and limitations of pre-trained FNO models for adaptive tasks, allowing for more targeted design of PEFT techniques that better complement their properties.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring the Robustness of Pre-Trained FNO Models to Perturbations of Physical Parameters
PROPOSAL: Investigate how pre-trained FNO models adapt to changes in input parameter ranges, focusing on robustness to physical parameter perturbations in shallow-water free-surface flow simulation and solar magnetohydrodynamics. Evaluate the effectiveness of PEFT techniques in preserving pre-trained knowledge under such parameter variations.
CONTROLS: Compare robustness metrics with results from full-model fine-tuning and use synthetic datasets with controlled variations of physical parameters to assess adaptation.
COST: Estimated 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that pre-trained FNO models will exhibit variable robustness across different physical regimes and PEFT methods, potentially highlighting the benefit of incorporating explicit robustness or uncertainty quantification within LOMs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Non-Local Hyperparameter Transfer for Adapting Pre-Trained FNO Models Across Physical Regimes
PROPOSAL: Examine the effectiveness of non-local hyperparameter transfer learning for adapting pre-trained FNO models from one physical regime to another (e.g., adapting shallow-water free-surface flow simulation knowledge to solar magnetohydrodynamics). Investigate the utility of state-of-the-art hyperparameter optimization techniques and PEFT methods in this context.
CONTROLS: Compare adaptation performance with full-model freeze and fine-tuning of pre-trained FNO models and evaluate transfer elucidation through analytical expressions to examine analytical accuracies presented information form FT.
COST: Estimated 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that non-local hyperparameter transfer will improve adaptation performance for LOMs, revealing opportunities to generalize pre-trained knowledge across distinct physical regimes, while understanding the ROI balancing transfer extrapolation encountering new program parameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Synergy Between Physics-Informed Regularization and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Pre-Trained FNO Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether incorporating physics-informed regularization techniques (e.g., ENO-weighted loss terms) can enhance the efficiency of parameter-efficient fine-tuning for pre-trained FNO models, particularly in regimes with complex nonlinearities and noisy data.
CONTROLS: Compare with results from vanilla PEFT and vanilla physics-informed regularization for shallow-water free-surface flow simulation and solar magnetohydrodynamics, evaluating solution accuracy and adaptivity.
COST: Estimated 110 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate improved adaptation performance and stability for LOMs with concurrent physics-informed regularization and PEFT, allowing for more effective exploitation of pre-trained knowledge in challenging problem scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Batch Normalization on Pre-Trained FNO Models Under Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: Examine whether adapting the batch normalization layers of pre-trained FNO models during parameter-efficient fine-tuning can improve their adaptivity and solution accuracy for various PDEs and physical regimes.
CONTROLS: Compare performance with fixed batch normalization and vanilla fine-tuning for shallow-water free-surface flow simulation and solar magnetohydrodynamics, evaluating relative performance and adaptation efficiency.
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that adaptive batch normalization will enhance the fine-tuning process and solution quality for LOMs, particularly when faced with task-dependent variations in physical parameter spaces, by adjusting statistical expectations whilst tunning individual ruin occurrences respectively.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Understanding Limitations of Pre-Trained Large Operator Models for Complex PDEs via Analytical Study of Spectral Convergence Bounds
PROPOSAL: Develop and analyze theoretical bounds on the spectral convergence of pre-trained FNO models for solving complex PDEs, highlighting underlying limitations and potential areas for improvement.
CONTROLS: Examine the relationship between spectral convergence, model capacity, and solution accuracy, and investigate the role of fundamental theoretical limitations in the adaptivity of pre-trained LOMs.
COST: Estimated 80 GPU-hours (minimal, as this proposal focuses on analytical study)
PREDICTION: We anticipate that theoretical analysis will reveal fundamental limitations on the adaptivity and accuracy of pre-trained LOMs, providing insights into the design and optimization of future large operator models.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Understanding Limitations of Pre-Trained Large Operator Models for Complex PDEs via Analytical Study of Spectral Convergence Bounds
PROPOSAL: Expand the analytical study to include a detailed comparison of the spectral convergence bounds of pre-trained FNO models with those of state-of-the-art numerical methods (e.g., pseudo-spectral methods, discretized Galerkin methods). Investigate the relative strengths and limitations of pre-trained LOMs in solving complex PDEs and identify potential avenues for improvement.
CONTROLS: Compare results with those from experiments 1-7, assessing the relationship between spectral convergence, model capacity, and solution accuracy.
COST: Estimated 120 GPU-hours (due to expanded analytical study and comparison with numerical methods)
PREDICTION: We anticipate that this study will provide a comprehensive understanding of the strengths and limitations of pre-trained LOMs for solving complex PDEs, enabling the design of more effective and accurate methods for solving a wide range of PDEs.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effectiveness of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Large Operator Models on Synthetic PDE Data
PROPOSAL: Train a pre-trained Large Operator Model (LOM) on synthetic PDE datasets from the specified domains (computational fluid dynamics, shallow-water flow simulation, and solar magnetohydrodynamics) using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) techniques such as LoRA, SLOW, and PrefixTuning, and compare their performance against full-model fine-tuning and frozen initialization.
CONTROLS: Frozen initialization, full-model fine-tuning with and without L1 regularization
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: PEFT techniques should outperform full-model fine-tuning, with LoRA showing comparable performance to full-model fine-tuning but with significant parameter reduction; however, results might fail to generalize to new frequency spectra or PDE types.

The initial experiment aims to validate whether PEFT can scale up for large operator models in the context of PDEs and to which degree these techniques preserve the benefits of pre-training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparing the Impact of Frequency-Specific and Global Updates on PEFT for LOMs
PROPOSAL: Modify the previous experiment to apply frequency-specific updates to the LOM using PEFT techniques (e.g., applying LoRA only to specific spectral bands or using Frequency-Aware Prefix Tuning) and compare their performance against global updates and frozen initialization on synthetic PDE datasets from each of the three domains (computational fluid dynamics, shallow-water flow simulation, and solar magnetohydrodynamics).
CONTROLS: Global updates with LoRA, frozen initialization, full-model fine-tuning
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Frequency-specific updates should provide improved adaptability to new frequency spectra, with the best approach depending on the PDE type and its characteristic frequency range; however, this might come at the cost of reduced robustness across different domains.

This experiment probes into the optimal PEFT update strategy for LOMs, exploring the trade-off between frequency-specific updates and global updates, with implications for selecting the most suitable method for different PDE types.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: UPDATED: Comparing the Impact of Frequency-Specific and Global Updates on PEFT for LOMs
PROPOSAL: Modify the previous experiment to include additional controls and investigations:
    - Introduce an attention-based selective update (ASU) method inspired by self-attention in Transformers, where the LOM attends to specific frequency bands or spectral components, and weights its updates accordingly.
    - Evaluate the sensitivity of PEFT methods to hyperparameters (e.g., the learning rate and regularization strength) and their impact on the trade-off between accuracy and parameter efficiency.
    - Explore the applicability of PEFT techniques to operator levels other than the top-most ( i.e., to mid and bottom layers), allowing for frequency and amplitude localized updates to be realized end-to-end.
CONTROLS: Global updates with LoRA, frequency-specific updates with LoRA, asymptotic attention-based selective update, frozen initialization, full-model fine-tuning
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The ASU method should demonstrate competitive performance with or without significant improvements over frequency-specific and global updates on the synthetic PDE datasets, with sensitivity analysis identifying hyperparameter settings conducive to robust and efficient adaptation.

This revised experiment aims to push the boundaries of PEFT for LOMs by introducing novel update strategies, exploring the impact of hyperparameters, and evaluating the method's applicability to lower-level operator nodes, potentially enabling more fine-grained control over the update process.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Investigating the Property of PDE Solutions for Informing PEFT Methods in SciML
PROPOSAL: Develop a comprehensive analysis of the spectral properties of solutions to a set of representative PDEs (e.g., Euler's equations, Navier-Stokes equations, Maxwell's equations) and their implications for the design and implementation of PEFT methods in the context of SciML. Specifically, investigate how the spectral density and distribution of solution components relate to the frequency-specific and global updates explored in the previous experiment.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: THOMPSON SAMPLING ALGORITHM FOR MULTI-OBJECTIVE LINEAR CONTEXTUAL BANDIT
PROPOSAL: Design a Thompson Sampling algorithm for the multi-objective linear contextual bandit, where at each round, the agent samples a Pareto optimal arm based on the posterior distribution over the arm's context and objective parameter vectors. The algorithm maintains a set of active arms and samples from a Pareto front of these arms.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) algorithm
- Ablation: comparing to a single-objective Thompson Sampling without accounting for Pareto optimality
- Control for regret analysis: analysis under a known Gaussian prior
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This algorithm should exhibit competitive performance against UCB methods in synthetic data experiments, with possible limitations in domains with multiple, closely Pareto-optimal arms, where the randomized sampling may be less effective in progressively identifying the best arms.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: BOUNDS ON PARETO REGRET FOR THOMPSON SAMPLING
PROPOSAL: Establish a worst-case Pareto regret bound for the proposed Thompson Sampling algorithm, showing that this bound is comparable to those for randomized algorithms in the single-objective linear setting, with an added logarithmic factor that depends on the number of objectives. This bound should be derived through a combination of concentration inequalities and pessimistic guarantees on the regret.
CONTROLS: 
- Comparison to previous UCB-based bounds
- Analysis under a known Gaussian prior
- Control for the added logarithmic factor dependence on the number of objectives
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The derived bound should be within a constant factor of the UCB method, highlighting the potential of Thompson Sampling for multi-objective bandits, while the added logarithmic factor should serve as a quantitative measure for the impact of the number of objectives on the algorithm's performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: OPTIMALITY GUARANTEES FOR PARETO OPTIMAL ARMS
PROPOSAL: Derive conditions on the problem parameters for which the proposed Thompson Sampling algorithm converges to Pareto optimal arms with probability close to 1, in the sense that the empirical Pareto front converges to the true Pareto front as the number of rounds increases. This result should be obtained through a combination of concentration inequalities and the analysis of the algorithm's behavior on Pareto optimal arms.
CONTROLS: 
- Bounds on the gap between the empirical and true Pareto fronts
- Comparison to the optimality guarantees known for single-objective bandits
- Assumptions on the structure of the objective parameter vectors
COST: 75 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: These conditions should highlight the importance of the relationship between the number of objectives and the number of rounds in attaining Pareto optimality, and provide guidelines for algorithm design in practice. However, as the problem complexity increases, the conditions might be too restrictive to be met in practice.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: OPTIMALITY GUARANTEES FOR PARETO OPTIMAL ARMS
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Instead of focusing on the asymptotic convergence of the empirical Pareto front to the true one, derive a non-asymptotic condition on the number of rounds that guarantees the algorithm selects a Pareto optimal arm with high probability. This condition should be expressed in terms of the problem parameters, and it should be a weaker requirement than the one obtained in the previous revision.
CONTROLS: 
- Similar to the previous revision, with the addition of a baseline analysis for the number of rounds required to achieve a certain probability of selecting a Pareto optimal arm
- Comparison to previous results on single-objective bandits
- Assumptions on the structure of the objective parameter vectors
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised result should provide a more practical guarantee on the performance of the algorithm, allowing practitioners to determine in advance the minimum number of rounds required to achieve a desired level of optimality. However, it may come at the cost of a slightly higher probability of error.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 3
TITLE: OPTIMALITY GUARANTEES FOR PARETO OPTIMAL ARMS
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Instead of focusing on the probability of selecting a Pareto optimal arm, derive a guarantee on the expected cumulative reward obtained by the algorithm after a fixed number of rounds, compared to the best possible expected cumulative reward. This should be a strengthening of the previous result, as it takes into account the accumulation of rewards over time.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline analysis for the expected cumulative reward of a uniform random policy
- Comparison to previous results on single-objective bandits
- Assumptions on the structure of the objective parameter vectors
COST: 75 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This result should provide a more comprehensive understanding of the algorithm's performance, highlighting its potential for sustained growth in cumulative rewards over time. However, it may require more stringent assumptions on the problem parameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: ACCOUNTING FOR Cumulative REWARDS IN PARETO REGRET MEASUREMENT
PROPOSAL: Propose a new measure of Pareto regret that takes into account the accumulation of rewards over time, rather than just the regret at a single round. This measure should be defined as the difference between the expected cumulative reward of the best possible policy and the expected cumulative reward of the policy being evaluated, conditioned on the history of observed rewards.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: standard Pareto regret
- Comparison to existing measures of cumulative regret
- Assumptions on the structure of the objective parameter vectors
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This new measure should provide a more nuanced understanding of the algorithm's performance, highlighting its ability to accumulate rewards over time. However, it may require significant modifications to existing algorithms and analyses.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: GENERALIZING THOMPSON SAMPLING TO BAYESIAN BINARY-OUTCOME CONTEXTUAL BANDITS
PROPOSAL: Generalize the proposed Thompson Sampling algorithm to the setting of Bayesian binary-outcome contextual bandits, where the reward is a binary outcome. This requires adapting the algorithm to account for the binary outcome and incorporating a binary likelihood function into the posterior distribution.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: a standard UCB algorithm for binary-outcome contextual bandits
- Ablation: comparing to a Thompson Sampling algorithm without accounting for the binary outcome
- Analysis under a known prior distribution
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This generalization should be a challenging task due to the binary outcome, but the resulting algorithm should be able to handle the binary outcome effectively and maintain good regret guarantees. However, it may require significant computational resources and may not be feasible for large problem sizes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: RELAXING THE PARETO REGRET MEASURE TO ACCOUNT FOR INEFFICIENT ALLOCATIONS
PROPOSAL: Relax the definition of Pareto regret to account for the case where the chosen policy is inefficient in allocating rewards across objectives, by introducing a penalty term that captures the inefficiency. This new measure should be defined as the difference between the cumulative reward of the best possible policy and the cumulative reward of the chosen policy, with a penalty term that increases as the inefficiency increases.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: standard Pareto regret
- Comparison to existing measures of regret that account for inefficiencies
- Assumptions on the structure of the objective parameter vectors
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This relaxed measure should provide a more realistic understanding of the algorithm's performance, especially in cases where the chosen policy is inefficient in allocating rewards across objectives. However, it may require significant modifications to existing algorithms and analyses.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION OF THOMPSON SAMPLING FOR MULTI-OBJECTIVE LINEAR CONTEXTUAL BANDITS
PROPOSAL: Conduct an experimental evaluation of the proposed Thompson Sampling algorithm on a variety of synthetic and simulated datasets for multi-objective linear contextual bandits, comparing its performance to existing algorithms and highlighting its strengths and weaknesses.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: UCB algorithm for multi-objective linear contextual bandits
- Comparison to other state-of-the-art algorithms for multi-objective bandits
- Assumptions on the structure of the objective parameter vectors
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This experimental evaluation should provide a comprehensive assessment of the algorithm's performance in practice, highlighting its strengths and weaknesses, and providing insights into the factors that affect its performance. However, it may require significant computational resources and may not be feasible for large problem sizes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: OPTIMIZATION OF THOMPSON SAMPLING HYPERPARAMETERS FOR MULTI-OBJECTIVE LINEAR CONTEXTUAL BANDITS
PROPOSAL: Perform a hyperparameter tuning of the proposed Thompson Sampling algorithm to optimize its performance for multi-objective linear contextual bandits, exploring different hyperparameter settings and examining their impact on the algorithm's performance.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: default hyperparameter settings for the Thompson Sampling algorithm
- Comparison to existing algorithms for multi-objective bandits
- Assumptions on the structure of the objective parameter vectors
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This hyperparameter tuning should help identify the optimal settings for the Thompson Sampling algorithm, improving its performance for multi-objective linear contextual bandits, and providing insights into the importance of hyperparameter selection for this algorithm.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Pareto Regret Upper Bounds for Thompson Sampling in Multi-Objective Linear Contextual Bandits
PROPOSAL: Establish finite-time Pareto regret upper bounds for Thompson Sampling in the multi-objective linear contextual bandit, assuming L objectives and d-dimensional context vectors. Specifically, derive a bound that captures the impact of the number of objectives L on the regret, by leveraging the surrogate posterior of Thompson Sampling and leveraging tools from stochastic processes. To address the challenge of coordinating samples across objectives, assume the existence of a centralized randomness source shared by all objectives. In this single-proof approach, the bound will be expressed in terms of the sum of the widths of the individual objective-wise reward estimates' posterior probability distributions, as well as the number of samples observed at each round.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results with the existing UCB-based upper bounds in the multi-objective bandit literature, and also consider the naive approach of applying Thompson Sampling to each objective separately and taking a min or max over the objectives as the final decision. This control amounts to "blind" scalarization, effectively treats the objectives as completely unrelated and will guarantee non-trivial Pareto regret.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (establishing and bounding the posterior width over multiple objectives is computationally tractable)
PREDICTION: Our bound will be within an arbitrary constant factor of the existing UCB-based bounds for the single-objective setting, up to logarithmic factors in the number of samples; however, the impact of L on the regret will introduce an additively growing term with respect to L.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Revising for Handling Multiple Pareto-Optimal Arms with Thompson Sampling
PROPOSAL: REVISED: When deriving the Pareto regret upper bounds for Thompson Sampling, explicitly account for the presence of multiple Pareto-optimal arms by introducing a "distance to Pareto optimality" term in the upper bound. This term captures the average distance to the Pareto front for each arm, leveraging a particular measure such as the maximum component-wise difference between arm rewards and the reference rewards at the Pareto front. This incorporates the requirement that the regret should not only account for suboptimal rewards but also for failed exploration of the Pareto front. We will bound this term by analyzing the distribution of posterior estimates across the reward components and then summing these component-wise bounds to achieve overall arm-level regrets.
CONTROLS: Still compare against existing UCB-based bounds and the "blind" scalarization approach. Additionally, we'll investigate two baselines: a naive UCB based scheme that chooses an arm by considering separately each component-wise upper confidence bound, and a greedy scheme that chooses the arm with maximal component-wise confidence bound. These baselines will fail in capturing the trade-off across objectives.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (accounting for multiple Pareto-optimal arms requires additional posterior width bounds)
PREDICTION: The revised bound will lead to convergence to the Pareto front, better accounting for suboptimality by penalizing the regret with respect to the distance to Pareto optimality. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Pareto Regret Model with Cumulative Reward Accounting
PROPOSAL: Introduce a new model for Pareto regret that incorporates cumulative rewards, named CumulativePareto Regret (CPR). CPR measures the regret as a sum of penalties for both the difference between the selected arm's cumulative reward and the best-performing arm's cumulative reward in each round, and the cardinality of the set of arms that have not been played to be maximally efficient. This provides a more comprehensive evaluation of the policy's efficiency in cumulative objectives and favors policies that achieve high cumulative rewards while also exploring the Pareto front. We derive bounds for CPR using tools from stochastic processes and apply it to Thompson Sampling.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Model- Based Exploration for Thompson Sampling in Multi-Objective Bandits
PROPOSAL: Develop a model-based exploration approach for Thompson Sampling in the multi-objective linear contextual bandit scenario. Specifically, employ a probabilistic linear regression model to learn the relationship between the context vector, arm parameters, and the reward. Then, use the learned model to generate synthetic samples that capture the underlying uncertainty in the reward function and guide the exploration process. By actively managing the trade-off between exploitation and exploration, this approach enables Thompson Sampling to more effectively identify the Pareto front and reduce Pareto regret.
CONTROLS: Compare with the existing results from the current set, including CPR bounds and empirical posterior boundedness. Additionally, explore the performance of this model-based approach when the true reward function is misspecified or when the contextual features have high dimensionality. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating State-of-the-Art Feature Matchers for UAV Orthophoto Localization
PROPOSAL: We will benchmark the following feature matchers - SuperPoint, LPD-Net, and D2-Net - on the task of matching aerial query images to their counterparts on orthophotos, using ADDA (Aerial Dataset for Data Augmentation) and BDDA (Big Aerial Dataset for DA). This will help us understand the limits and opportunities of using perspective-trained feature matchers for bridging the perspective-orthographic gap in UAV localization.
CONTROLS: We will compare against recent UAV-based recall-precision methods (e.g. perforated DensePoint) and AB-ratio baseline with DensePoint as the feature matcher.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the feature matchers to perform reasonably well, especially when considering imperfect upstream retrieval; however, precision might degrade in absolutely oblique viewpoints due to inherent dimensionality differences.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluation of Orthophoto and Elevation Model Combination for UAV Localization
PROPOSAL: We will design and train an end-to-end CNN-based localization model using a combination of orthophoto and elevation model data from the ADDA and BDDA datasets. We will then evaluate its performance on the local-HERM dataset (combining a challenging mixture of urban, forest, and rural areas) and compare it against the following baselines: 1) perspective-based localization using state-of-the-art feature matchers, 2) simple cross-correlation approach using orthophotos only, and 3) DenseSfM (Dense Structure from Motion) system with and without using erroneous SfM data.
CONTROLS: We will also carry out extensive ablation studies to investigate the contribution of each component (orthophoto, DEMs, classification heads, etc.) to the overall performance.
COST: 500 GPU-hours

PROPOSAL: We will develop a novel parallel network architecture that integrates a CNN component for perspective-aware feature extraction, with a corresponding orthographic-aware decoding network trained on simultaneously-updated maps. The network will be optimized to project the perspective images onto a 2.5D orthographic plane, leveraging the insight that the epipolar geometry between perspective and orthographic views can be used to guide the matching process. By doing so, we overcome the traditional perspective-orthographic gap and enable robust and accurate matching of images from different viewpoints.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach with previous works that either solely relied on perspective features or required hand-crafted orthographic features. PREDICTION: We believe that our proposed architecture will achieve better performance in perspective-orthographic matching and contribute to a better understanding of the relationship between perspective and orthographic views, thus paving the way for improved UAV localization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Benchmarking 6-DoF UAV Localization with Geodata
PROPOSAL: Create a large-scale real-world benchmark dataset of paired UAV images, orthophotos, and elevation maps in various environments, including urban, rural, and infrastructure-focused areas.
CONTROLS: Use existing UAV localization datasets (e.g., Vision-and-results Hand-Collected (VRC) and scenes captured in the European contingent of the EuroC city-scale Change-in-Environmental-Change-in-Person) augmented with geodata from public sources (e.g., OpenStreetMap).
COST: Estimated 1,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The benchmark will be a foundational component in evaluating the performance of future methods and help identify key challenges in leveraging geodata for UAV localization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Perspective Orthographic Feature Matchers
PROPOSAL: Investigate the performance of state-of-the-art feature matchers (e.g., SuperPoint, Deep features by dark rank CNN) on bridging the perspective-orthographic gap in UAV localization, using the benchmark dataset from proposal 1.
CONTROLS: Compare feature matchers in various scenarios, such as urban, rural, and infrastructure-focused areas, with different viewpoint differences between query and reference images.
COST: Estimated 5,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that performance will be affected by viewpoint differences, and Deep features by dark rank CNN will outperform other feature matchers on average. However, in cases with severe oblique views, SuperPoint will still be a strong competitor.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Geo-Augmented Dense Matching for UAV Calibration and Localization
PROPOSAL: Develop an end-to-end method that constructs a dense 2.5D representation from geodata (orthophoto and elevation map) and a query UAV image, using a fusion of dense image matching and structure-from-motion. This representation is used to estimate the camera pose and intrinsic parameters.
CONTROLS: Compare against existing methods that rely solely on image feature matching or 3D models.
COST: Estimated 10,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our method will outperform methods that rely on image feature matching in scenarios with large viewpoint differences. However, our method may fail in cases where geodata resolution is too low or feature-rich structures are occluded.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Evaluating Perspective Orthographic Feature Matchers
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Investigate the performance of state-of-the-art feature matchers (e.g., SuperPoint, Deep features by dark rank CNN) on bridging the perspective-orthographic gap in UAV localization, while integrating our proposed geo-augmented dense matching method as a baseline and incorporating occlusion and low-resolution effects into the evaluations.
CONTROLS: Improve upon the original evaluation to assess the robustness of feature matchers in more challenging scenarios.
COST: Estimated 7,500 GPU-hours (includes changes to the existing evaluation)
PREDICTION: By considering occlusions and low-resolution effects, we expect the robustness comparison between feature matchers to be more accurate, leading to a clearer understanding of their strengths and weaknesses in UAV localization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Intrinsic Parameter Estimation under Adversarial Conditions
PROPOSAL: Investigate the challenges and limitations of estimating camera intrinsic parameters (focal length, principal point, and distortion parameters) from UAV imagery under various conditions that arise due to geodata-domain gap, such as temporal changes in radiation, changes in geometric structure due to infrastructure development, and geodata resolution effects.
CONTROLS: Compare against existing intrinsic parameter estimation methods and assess the impact of different photometric, temporal, and geometrical variations.
COST: Estimated 15,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our analysis will reveal which types of photometric, temporal, and geometrical variations have a significant impact on intrinsic parameter estimation, and help assess the feasibility of estimating intrinsic parameters using geodata-integrated approaches.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Complementary Retrieval for UAV Localization
PROPOSAL: Investigate a retrieval-based approach for visually-localizing UAVs, where an efficient retrieval framework is designed to quickly narrow down the potential viewpoints, enabling the accurate estimation of camera poses and intrinsic parameters from the geodata-integrated dense 2.5D representation.
CONTROLS: Evaluate on a subset of benchmarked scenes to assess the robustness and efficiency of the retrieval-based approach combining the benefits of both dense matching and efficient query narrowing.
COST: Estimated 8,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By integrating efficient retrieval and dense geodata-based matching, we expect significant speedup for large-scale localized search while maintaining or improving the overall localization accuracy.

TITLE: Investigating Perspective-Obliteration with Orthorectified Aerial Images
PROPOSAL: Train a series of Rotation-Equivalent-Compensation (REC) networks on a mix of terrestrial and aerial images, with objectives focused on minimizing in-plane rotation differences. These networks would enable perspective disparity reduction through orthorectification of aerial images, expressed as intermediate outputs between unprocessed and fully orthorectified views, similar to GAN-based image-to-image translation models. Evaluate these models' ability to reduce in-plane rotation differences in UAV imagery. Train, evaluate, and compare these REC networks to baseline rotation-compensation methods. Analyze their ordinal and pairwise error biases for localization performance under perspective shifts, illumination changes, and data sampling variability.

TITLE: Robust Camera Calibration for 6-DoF UAV Localization with Orthophotos and Digital Surface Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the robustness of camera calibration methods for 6-DoF UAV localization using orthophotos and digital surface models as reference data. The goal is to identify the most robust calibration method for 6-DoF UAV localization using orthophotos and digital surface models.

PREDICTION: Our results will show that machine learning-based calibration methods perform better under conditions of noise and outlier presence, while DLT and stereo matching methods are more robust to lens distortion.

Investigate the robustness of camera calibration methods for 6-DoF UAV localization using orthophotos and digital surface models as reference data. This involves evaluating and comparing the performance of different calibration methods, such as direct linear transformation (DLT), stereo matching, and machine learning-based approaches, under various conditions of noise, outlier presence, and lens distortion. The goal is to identify the most robust calibration method for 6-DoF UAV localization using orthophotos and digital surface models.
Controls: Evaluate and compare the performance of different calibration methods using metrics such as calibration accuracy, robustness to noise and outliers, and lens distortion correction. Assess the effects of varying conditions of noise, outlier presence, and lens distortion on calibration method performance. Compare against the state-of-the-art methods using real-world datasets.
Estimated cost: 8,000 GPU-hours for algorithm development, parameter tuning, and performance evaluation.
Prediction: Our results will show that machine learning-based calibration methods perform better under conditions of noise and outlier presence, while DLT and stereo matching methods are more robust to lens distortion.

PROPOSAL 6: Comprehensive Evaluation of 6-DoF UAV Localization Methods with Orthophotos and Digital Surface Models
Conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed 6-DoF UAV localization methods, including perspective-oblivion, structural content-based feature matching, paired benchmark dataset, temporal domain shifts, and robust camera calibration. This evaluation will assess the performance of these methods under various conditions, such as different types of orthophoto and digital surface model references, varying levels of noise and outliers, and different types of UAV motion. The goal is to identify the most effective localization method for 6-DoF UAV tasks using orthophotos and digital surface models.
Controls: Evaluate the performance of each localization method using metrics such as localization accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Compare the performance of these methods against state-of-the-art localization methods for 6-DoF UAV tasks using real-world datasets.
Estimated cost: 15,000 GPU-hours for comprehensive evaluation and testing of proposed methods.
Prediction: Our results will show that the proposed localization methods, particularly those that integrate perspective-oblivion and robust camera calibration, achieve superior localization accuracy and robustness compared to existing methods.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying Score Errors in Low-Noise Regimes
PROPOSAL: Prove that in the variance-exploding smoothing regime, the leading term in the score error of $\mu_\sigma$ in the limit of small $\sigma$ scales as $\sigma$, while the leading term involving the distributional information scales as $\sigma^2$.
CONTROLS: Compare with the existing proof that the score develops a singularity in the small-noise regime.
COST: Low (labelled matrix multiplication).
PREDICTION: Expected to hold for smooth data distributions, may fail for distributions with sharp modes or corners, which could lead to non-smooth shifts in the manifold without scaling as $\sigma$.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Manifold Support Reconstruction from Imperfect Scores
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether the uniform distribution on the data manifold can be approximated from a score model trained on samples of a non-uniform $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$, and analyze the effect of score errors on the resulting distribution.
CONTROLS: Compare the manifold reconstruction using imperfect scores against the exact reconstruction and study how manifold geometry vs. distributional density are affected.
COST: Medium (mainly dominated by computation of the manifold and diffusion based operations).
PREDICTION: Expected to show that imperfect scores allow for accurate recovery of the manifold even when they fail to predict the exact density, with the addition of noise possibly improving manifold characterization and exploration.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Manifold Support Reconstruction from Imperfect Scores
REVISED PROPOSAL: Incorporate the predictions from "Quantifying Score Errors in Low-Noise Regimes" into the manifold reconstruction experiment, and analyze how the leading terms in score errors affect the accuracy of manifold reconstruction.
CONTROLS: Compare the results against the exact reconstruction and isolate the impact of score error terms on the geometry and density of the manifold.
COST: Medium-High (adding computations for tracking leading error terms).
PREDICTION: Expected to show that the $\sigma^2$ term, which is not vanishing in the small-$\sigma$ regime, has a significant impact on the accuracy of manifold reconstruction, and suggest that adapting learned scores to compensate for this term may be beneficial.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Manifold Support Reconstruction from Imperfect Scores
REVISED PROPOSAL: Incorporate numerical experiments to compute the manifold geometry and density of outputs of a diffusion model and a score-based model trained to optimize the uniform sampling objective, to gain insights into the strengths and limitations of score-based methods for achieving uniform sampling on the data manifold.
CONTROLS: Compare the manifold geometry and density obtained by the diffusion method and the score-based method against exact values, and analyze how score errors affect the recovery of these features.
COST: High (computationally expensive evaluation on large models and datasets).
PREDICTION: Expected to show that the score-based method can produce uniformly distributed samples on the manifold, but may struggle with recovering the precise geometry or density in the presence of non-vanishing score errors.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Uniform Sampling Objective for Score-Based Models
PROPOSAL: Design and train score-based models using the uniform sampling loss as the learning objective, and evaluate their performance on text-to-image generation benchmarks such as DALL-E and CSeleADe range datasets for image datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of score-based models using the uniform sampling loss against models trained with standard objectives such as log-likelihood minimization.
COST: High (computationally expensive training and evaluation on large-scale datasets).
PREDICTION: Expected to show that score-based models trained with the uniform sampling loss can produce high-quality samples with good diversity, and may offer an alternative to expensive human annotation or sampled diffusion-based methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sensitivity Analysis of Score-Based Methods to Prior Distribution Selection
PROPOSAL: Conduct a sensitivity analysis of score-based methods for Bayesian inverse problems to the choice of prior distribution, and investigate how different priors affect the accuracy of posterior sampling and the required score accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of score-based methods using different priors (e.g., uniform, Gaussian, empirical) and evaluate their effect on posterior sampling accuracy and the required score accuracy.
COST: Medium (mostly dominated by computations of prior manipulation and score propagation).
PREDICTION: Expected to show that the choice of prior distribution has a significant impact on the accuracy of posterior sampling and the required score accuracy, and suggest that data-driven or empirical priors may be more effective in certain scenarios.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Sensitivity Analysis of Score-Based Methods to Prior Distribution Selection
REVISED PROPOSAL: Extend the sensitivity analysis to investigate the relationship between the score accuracy required for correct posterior sampling and the choice of prior distribution, and provide insights into the trade-offs between prior information and score accuracy.
CONTROLS: Quantitatively evaluate the effect of prior choice on the required score accuracy, and compare the results across different prior distributions and datasets.
COST: High (computationally expensive evaluation on large-scale datasets).
PREDICTION: Expected to show that the choice of prior distribution significantly affects the required score accuracy, and suggest that a more informative prior may allow for lower score accuracy, while a less informative prior may require higher score accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Asymptotic Analysis of Score-Based Sampling on Manifolds
PROPOSAL: Derive asymptotic approximations for the stationary distribution of Langevin dynamics driven by imperfect scores on manifolds, and investigate the effect of score errors on the resulting distribution.
CONTROLS: Compare the asymptotic approximations against numerical simulations of the Langevin dynamics.
COST: Low-Medium (dominated by theoretical derivations).
PREDICTION: Expected to show that the asymptotic approximations capture the main features of the stationary distribution, but may fail to accurately describe the impact of score errors on the distribution's geometry and density.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experimental Validation of Manifold Reconstruction and Sampling Methods
PROPOSAL: Validate the manifold reconstruction and sampling methods proposed in this study using real-world text-to-image generation benchmarks, such as ImageNet Clean and ImageNet Disjoint, and evaluate their performance on diverse tasks such as image synthesis and density estimation.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the proposed methods against state-of-the-art diffusion models and scoring-based methods.
COST: High (computationally expensive evaluation on large-scale datasets).
PREDICTION: Expected to show that the proposed methods can effectively reconstruct and sample from the data manifold, and achieve competitive performance on diverse tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Score Errors in Real-World Applications
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of score errors on the performance of score-based models in real-world applications, such as image and video generation, and analyze the trade-offs between score accuracy, model complexity, and computational cost.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effect of score errors on model performance using metrics such as inception score, FID score, and visual inspection.
COST: High (computationally expensive evaluation on large-scale datasets and complex models).
PREDICTION: Expected to show that score errors have a significant impact on model performance, and provide insights into the design of more robust and efficient score-based models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Convergence Rates of Score-Based Samplers on Low-Dimensional Manifolds
PROPOSAL: Study the convergence rates of score-based samplers, specifically focusing on the trade-off between the accuracy of the learned score and the quality of the generated samples, using a systematic approach to vary the noise schedule and dimension of the manifold. To do this, use a combination of theoretical analysis and experiments with a simplified setup, such as a linear Gaussian manifold model and a SDE-related loss function. We will compare the convergence rates of different samplers (e.g., score matching, Langevin dynamics, SDE-based) in this setting and quantify the effect of score errors on the sampler's performance.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare against exact sampling from the target distribution
- Evaluate different samplers (e.g., score matching, Langevin dynamics, SDE-based)
- Compare the convergence rates of the samplers under varying noise schedules and manifold dimensions
- Study the effect of increasing the number of training iterations on the sampler's performance
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the convergence rates of score-based samplers will degrade as the noise schedule decreases, and the accuracy of the learned score has a significant impact on the sampler's performance. However, the sampler may still produce good samples, even when the learned score is not accurate, due to the interplay between the sampling process and the geometry of the manifold.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Effects of Score Mismatch on the Manifold Support and Distributional Structure
PROPOSAL: Investigate how the accuracy of the learned score affects the recovery of the manifold's geometry and the on-manifold density, by analyzing the behavior of the score-based sampler as the noise level decreases. We will study the sensitivity of the sampler to the accuracy of the learned score and the manifold's geometry, and explore the relationship between score errors and the sampler's ability to capture the manifold's support and distributional structure. To do this, we will design a series of experiments using a manifold-based generative model (e.g., VAE with a manifold prior) and a score-matching estimator.
CONTROLS:
- Compare against a ground-truth model with perfect score and manifold geometry
- Evaluate different levels of score accuracy and manifold geometry complexity
- Compare the behavior of the sampler under different noise schedules and manifold dimensions
- Study the effect of using different loss functions for score matching (e.g., standard, robust)
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that score errors will have a significant impact on the sampler's ability to capture the manifold's geometry and distributional structure, and that the accuracy of the learned score will be more critical for recovering the on-manifold density than the manifold's support. However, the exact behavior will depend on the specifics of the model and the noise schedule.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Bound for KernelSHAP's Asymptotic Variance
PROPOSAL: We derive a non-asymptotic bound for the asymptotic variance of the KernelSHAP estimator, providing insight into the sample complexity required to achieve a certain degree of accuracy. Specifically, we consider a regression formulation of the Shapley value problem, where the kernel weights are used to sample and reweight the regression problem. Using a concentration inequality for martingale difference sequences, we show that the asymptotic variance of the KernelSHAP estimator can be bounded in terms of the number of samples and the "effective" dimension of the kernel weights.
CONTROLS: We compare our bound to the one proven for Unbiased KernelSHAP, showing that while our bound holds for all instances of KernelSHAP, it can be tighter for certain choices of kernel weights.
COST: 0 GPU-hours (theoretical result)
PREDICTION: Our bound should hold under the assumption that the value function $v(S)$ is a well-behaved random variable. If the value function is not well-behaved (e.g., if it has high correlation with the sampling distribution), the bound may not hold, or may not provide a useful estimate of the actual asymptotic variance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Empirical Analysis of KernelSHAP's Sampling Distribution
PROPOSAL: We conduct an empirical analysis of the sampling distribution of KernelSHAP, examining how the choice of kernel weights and the sampling scheme affect the accuracy of the Shapley value estimates. Specifically, we analyze the distribution of the resampled values of the vector $\bm{v}_S$ obtained during the regression problem, and compare it to the original distribution. We also study the effect of different sampling schemes (including sampling with replacement, without replacement, and paired sampling) on the accuracy of the estimates.
CONTROLS: We compare the results of different sampling schemes to the gold standard solution obtained by exactly solving the constrained weighted least-squares problem. We also evaluate the performance of the different sampling schemes using real-world datasets.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (empirical analysis on several real-world datasets)
PREDICTION: Our analysis should provide insights into the relationship between the sampling distribution and the accuracy of the Shapley value estimates. However, we may observe significant variability in the results, depending on the specific choice of kernel weights and the sampling scheme used.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Improved KernelSHAP Sampling Distribution
PROPOSAL: Building on our empirical analysis of KernelSHAP's sampling distribution (proposal 2), we propose a modified kernel weight function that adaptively adjusts the sampling distribution based on the data. Specifically, we use a weighted least-squares approach to estimate the optimal kernel weights that maximize the accuracy of the Shapley value estimates. We then use these adaptive kernel weights to reweight the regression problem, resulting in improved Shapley value estimates.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our adaptive kernel weights to the original KernelSHAP sampling scheme and to LeverageSHAP. We also evaluate the performance of our approach on real-world datasets.
COST: 5000 GPU-hours (empirical analysis and adaptation of the kernel weights)
PREDICTION: Our approach should improve the accuracy of the Shapley value estimates compared to the original KernelSHAP sampling scheme. However, we may observe some loss in performance compared to LeverageSHAP, which has a more robust sampling scheme.

Our framework aims to provide a structured approach for comparing and evaluating the performance of different explanation methods, facilitating the development of more accurate and reliable explanations in various applications.
CONTROLS: We validate our framework by applying it to the explanation methods proposed in this paper, as well as other state-of-the-art methods.
COST: 5000 GPU-hours (evaluation using our framework)
PREDICTION: Our framework should provide a useful tool for evaluating and comparing model-agnostic explanation methods, helping researchers and practitioners to select the most suitable method for their specific use case and dataset.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Accelerating Flow Matching via Parallel Draft Generation
PROPOSAL: We propose the "Speculative Draft Accelerator" (SDA) algorithm, which generates multiple parallel drafts of the trajectory at select points along the integration path. Each draft is produced using a lighter-weight "draft model" that approximates the full FM model. The drafts are selectively verified by the full model to correct errors and estimate likelihood ratios.
CONTROLS: We will compare against the standard full-step FM method, as well as a weakened version of SDA that uses a random draft model (to ablate the effect of the draft model's quality).
COST: 5,000 GPU-hours (we will run experiments on a 16-node, 8-GPU cluster)
PREDICTION: SDA should reduce inference latency by 2-3x, with little degradation in output quality, and clear advantages in interactive use cases.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Draft Model Design for Speculative Draft Accelerator
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment to compare the performance of different draft model designs, including: (1) a naive random weight copy of the full FM model; (2) a lightweight pruning of the full model's weights; and (3) a trainable seed network that assists the full model in producing drafts.
CONTROLS: We will compare these draft model designs against SDA's original design, as well as a baseline that uses no draft model (i.e., standard full-step FM).
COST: Estimated additional cost of 2,000 GPU-hours per design (we will run 4 designs in parallel)
PREDICTION: We expect the trainable seed network to outperform the other draft model designs, allowing SDA to achieve better-quality drafts and improved overall performance. However, we note that it may increase training time and require careful tuning to converge correctly.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating Draft Model Design for Speculative Draft Accelerator
PROPOSAL: We will revise our proposal to also include a variant of the trainable seed network that uses a pre-trained diffusion-based generative model as its seed, instead of random weights. This will allow us to leverage the strong semantic understanding of pre-trained diffusion models to assist the FM model in producing high-quality drafts.
CONTROLS: We will compare this variant to the original trainable seed network, as well as the other draft model designs and the baseline of no draft model.
COST: Estimated additional cost of 500 GPU-hours (minimal, as we can run this variant alongside previous experiments)
PREDICTION: By leveraging the strong semantic understanding of pre-trained diffusion models, we expect the revised trainable seed network to achieve even better-quality drafts and improved overall performance.
