ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Draft Proposal Quality and Selectivity in SDA
PROPOSAL: We will design a method to evaluate and select the most promising draft proposals for selective verification, with the goal of improving the efficiency and effectiveness of SDA. This will involve developing a quality metric for draft proposals and a selectivity criterion for choosing which drafts to verify.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the proposed method against a baseline that selects drafts randomly, as well as an oracle that always selects the best draft (for upper bound comparison).
COST: Estimated additional cost of 3,000 GPU-hours ( we will run experiments on a range of datasets and parameter settings)
PREDICTION: By carefully evaluating and selecting draft proposals, we expect to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of SDA, reducing latency while maintaining or improving output quality.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing Transferability of SDA across Flow Matching Architectures
PROPOSAL: We will investigate how well SDA generalizes to different FM architectures, including various implementations of the velocity network and output layer. We will also examine the transferability of SDA across multiple tasks, such as image and video generation.
CONTROLS: We will compare SDA's performance across different FM architectures and tasks to a baseline that trains SDA from scratch for each architecture/task.
COST: Estimated additional cost of 4,000 GPU-hours (we will run experiments on a range of architectures and tasks)
PREDICTION: We expect SDA to exhibit strong transferability across FM architectures and tasks, allowing it to be easily adapted to a wide range of applications with little additional training. This will be a major advantage of SDA, as it will enable rapid prototyping and deployment across different domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Robustness of SDA to Velocity Noise and Perturbations
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the robustness of SDA to velocity noise and perturbations, which can have a significant impact on the quality of the generated samples. We will examine how SDA performs in the presence of perturbations to the velocity signal and how it compares to the standard FM method.
CONTROLS: We will compare SDA's performance to a baseline that uses the standard FM method with a variety of perturbation types and levels.
COST: Estimated additional cost of 2,500 GPU-hours (we will run experiments on a range of perturbation levels and types)
PREDICTION: We expect SDA to exhibit robustness to velocity noise and perturbations, maintaining high-quality generation even in the presence of significant perturbations. However, we also anticipate that SDA may be more sensitive to certain types of perturbations than others.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Real-Time and Interactive Applications of SDA
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the suitability of SDA for real-time and interactive applications, such as real-time video generation and interactive image editing. We will examine how SDA performs on a range of interactive tasks and compare it to other acceleration methods for FM.
CONTROLS: We will compare SDA's performance to a baseline that uses the standard FM method, as well as other acceleration methods such as distillation and trajectory truncation.
COST: Estimated additional cost of 3,500 GPU-hours (we will run experiments on a range of interactive tasks and applications)
PREDICTION: We expect SDA to be well-suited for real-time and interactive applications, providing fast and high-quality generation that is comparable to or better than other acceleration methods for FM.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Complexity Analysis of SDA: Computational Cost and Scalability
PROPOSAL: We will perform a detailed analysis of SDA's computational cost and scalability, examining how the algorithm's efficiency changes as the size of the input data, the number of draft proposals, and the level of perturbation increase. We will also investigate the potential for parallelization and distributed computation to further improve SDA's efficiency.
CONTROLS: We will compare SDA's computational cost to that of the standard FM method, as well as other acceleration methods.
COST: Estimated additional cost of 4,000 GPU-hours (we will run experiments on a range of input sizes, draft proposal numbers, and perturbation levels)
PREDICTION: We expect SDA to exhibit good scalability and efficiency, allowing it to handle large-scale input data and high levels of perturbation while maintaining high-quality generation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experimental Evaluation of SDA on Text-to-Image and Text-to-Video Tasks
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate SDA on two downstream tasks: text-to-image generation and text-to-video generation. We will compare SDA's performance to a baseline that uses the standard FM method, as well as to other state-of-the-art methods in these tasks.
CONTROLS: We will use three real-world datasets: CIFAR-MSN, WikiArt, and UCF-101.
COST: Estimated additional cost of 5,000 GPU-hours (we will run experiments on a range of tasks, models, and datasets)
PREDICTION: We expect SDA to achieve state-of-the-art performance on text-to-image and text-to-video generation, outperforming the standard FM method and other acceleration methods in terms of both quality and efficiency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Speculative Decoding for Flow Matching
PROPOSAL: Develop a method for speculative decoding in FM models, where drafts are generated based on a coarsened version of the input data, and the coarsened input is replaced by a denoising network trained to match the coarse-to-fine dynamics of the full model. Evaluate drafts on their similarity to the full-model trajectory, using velocity distance measures to filter out highly deviating drafts.
CONTROLS: Experiment with three coarsening strategies (random subsampling, greedy pruning, and diffusion-based coarsening) and compare against trajectory truncation and consistency training as baselines; ablate the denoising network's architecture and hyperparameters to study its effect on draft quality.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Drafts generated with decent quality and low computational cost, outperforming baseline methods in terms of output quality and speed for certain use cases, but could struggle with high-dim spatio-temporal data, especially in text-to-video generation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Velocity Echoes: Learning Compact Draft Models for Flow Matching
PROPOSAL: Design a 'velocity echo' model that learns to predict the velocity field for a single, critical step of the ODE, conditioned on the input data and the final output. Train this model on a large corpus of FM-generated samples with auxiliary objectives that enforce smoothness and coherence with the target distribution. Use the velocity echo to generate draft samples by analyzing the dynamics at that critical step, and then iteratively refining them with the full FM model. Control this approach by experimenting with different numbers of steps and depths of the velocity echo network.
CONTROLS: Compare against the speculative decoding method and standard full-step generation in terms of output quality and speed for the text-to-image generation and image editing tasks; ablate the importance of different components of the velocity echo network, such as attention mechanisms and skip connections.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Velocity echoes can efficiently accelerate inference in FM models for low-to-medium quality applications, such as social media or chatbot synthesized images, but may struggle to capture high-frequency details in more demanding scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Trajectory Abstraction for Low-Latency Flow Matching
PROPOSAL: Develop a trajectory abstraction method that learns to represent the rich dynamics of the FM model as a sparse, compressed graph. Use a USD-based loss function to encourage the abstraction to maintain critical paths and suppress redundant or non-essential information. Learn to generate a low-latency, high-quality approximation of the trajectory by sampling from the compressed graph and refine it with a few iterative steps of the full FM model. Compare against static reduction strategies like distillation and truncation, and test the scalability on increasingly complex models and tasks like text-to-video generation.
CONTROLS: Experiment with different compression methods (e.g. K-Means, Gaussian Mixture Models) and refinement strategies (e.g. adding random noise, using pre-trained classifiers); evaluate the expressiveness of the abstraction model in preserving key features and temporal coherence.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Trajectory abstraction presents a viable approach for sparse and efficient representation of dynamic flow matching, offering significant runtime improvements for text-image pairings and elementary video tasks. However, the jump in complexity may cause abstraction inaccuracies in nuanced tasks or when dataset distributions shift.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Modal-enabled Acceleration for Flow Matching: A Physics-inspired Framework
PROPOSAL: Propose a physics-inspired framework for accelerating FM models, leveraging insights from modal analysis in dynamical systems. Identify key frequencies and modes that contribute to the stability and convergence of the FM's velocity field. Develop a novel modal-enabled acceleration method that selectively samples and projects input data onto these critical modes, allowing for faster and more efficient inference while preserving key features and dynamics. Compare against state-of-the-art static reduction strategies and evaluate the effect of modal selection methods on output quality and computational efficiency.
CONTROLS: Experiment with different modal selection methods (e.g., Fourier analysis, Arnoldi iteration) and constraint types (e.g., frequency-based, amplitude-based); study the effect of modal acceleration on various tasks and datasets, particularly those requiring high-fidelity and detail-rich output.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Modal-enabled acceleration can significantly reduce inference costs for FM models in various domains, while maintaining output quality and even allowing for finer details and more realistic effects. However, the choice of modes and sampling strategies may depend heavily on specific applications and datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Partial Flow Matching: Reducing Computational Cost using Partial Solution Approximations
PROPOSAL: Introduce a partial FM approach where the full ODE is approximated using a partial solution, focusing on key aspects of the problem that drive output quality. This is achieved by identifying critical components of the input data and leveraging domain knowledge to devise compact, yet effective, approximations of the full FM solution. Evaluate the effectiveness of this approach on text-to-image and video generation tasks, considering both the output quality and computational efficiency.
CONTROLS: Compare against full FM solutions and other partial approximation methods, such as dimensionality reduction and trajectory truncation; study the impact of selecting different critical components and approximation methods on output quality and computational cost.
COST: 160 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Partial FM can offer substantial computational savings while maintaining reasonable output quality for specific applications, such as low-resolution images or basic object classes. However, the selection of critical components and approximation methods may require domain expertise and careful tuning to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Flow Matching: Combining Local and Global Inference Strategies
PROPOSAL: Develop a hierarchical FM approach that integrates local and global inference strategies to address the trade-off between computational efficiency and output quality. This is achieved by partitioning the input data into smaller local patches, applying efficient inference methods (e.g., partial FM, modal-enabled acceleration) on each patch, and then combining the outputs using a global refinement stage. Evaluate the effectiveness of this approach on text-to-image and video generation tasks, considering both output quality and computational efficiency.
CONTROLS: Compare against single-scale FM solutions and other hierarchical inference methods, such as multi-scale convolutional neural networks; study the impact of patch size and partitioning strategy on output quality and computational cost.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Hierarchical FM can effectively balance computational efficiency and output quality by leveraging local and global inference strategies. However, the choice of patch size, partitioning strategy, and global refinement method may significantly impact the performance of this approach.

PROPOSAL: Propose a novel framework called Syndphi that combines knowledge distillation and domain adaptation techniques to accelerate FM models. Evaluate the effectiveness of Syndphi on several FM models and datasets, considering both output quality and computational efficiency.

However, the selection of teacher and student models, as well as the adaptation mechanism, may require careful tuning to achieve optimal results.

PROPOSAL 1: Efficient Speculative Decoding for Flow Matching
Develop a method for speculative decoding in FM models, where drafts are generated based on a coarsened version of the input data, and the coarsened input is replaced by a denoising network trained to match the coarse-to-fine dynamics of the full model. Evaluate drafts on their similarity to the full-model trajectory, using velocity distance measures to filter out highly deviating drafts.
Controls: Experiment with three coarsening strategies (random subsampling, greedy pruning, and diffusion-based coarsening) and compare against trajectory truncation and consistency training as baselines; ablate the denoising network's architecture and hyperparameters to study its effect on draft quality.
Estimated cost: 100 GPU-hours
Prediction: Drafts generated with decent quality and low computational cost, outperforming baseline methods in terms of output quality and speed for certain use cases, but could struggle with high-dim spatio-temporal data, especially in text-to-video generation.

PROPOSAL 2: Velocity Echoes: Learning Compact Draft Models for Flow Matching
Design a 'velocity echo' model that learns to predict the velocity field for a single, critical step of the ODE, conditioned on the input data and the final output. Train this model on a large corpus of FM-generated samples with auxiliary objectives that enforce smoothness and coherence with the target distribution. Use the velocity echo to generate draft samples by analyzing the dynamics at that critical step, and then iteratively refining them with the full FM model. Control this approach by experimenting with different numbers of steps and depths of the velocity echo network.
Controls: Compare against the speculative decoding method and standard full-step generation in terms of output quality and speed for the text-to-image generation and image editing tasks; ablate the importance of different components of the velocity echo network, such as attention mechanisms and skip connections.
Estimated cost: 150 GPU-hours
Prediction: Velocity echoes can efficiently accelerate inference in FM models for low-to-medium quality applications, such as social media or chatbot synthesized images, but may struggle to capture high-frequency details in more demanding scenarios.

PROPOSAL 3: Trajectory Abstraction for Low-Latency Flow Matching
Develop a trajectory abstraction method that learns to represent the rich dynamics of the FM model as a sparse, compressed graph. Use a USD-based loss function to encourage the abstraction to maintain critical paths and suppress redundant or non-essential information. Learn to generate a low-latency, high-quality approximation of the trajectory by sampling from the compressed graph and refine it with a few iterative steps of the full FM model. Compare against static reduction strategies like distillation and truncation, and test the scalability on increasingly complex models and tasks like text-to-video generation.
Controls: Experiment with different compression methods (e.g. K-Means, Gaussian Mixture Models) and refinement strategies (e.g. adding random noise, using pre-trained classifiers); evaluate the expressiveness of the abstraction model in preserving key features and temporal coherence.
Estimated cost: 200 GPU-hours
Prediction: Trajectory abstraction presents a viable approach for sparse and efficient representation of dynamic flow matching, offering significant runtime improvements for text-image pairings and elementary video tasks. However, the jump in complexity may cause abstraction inaccuracies in nuanced tasks or when dataset distributions shift.

PROPOSAL 4: Modal-enabled Acceleration for Flow Matching: A Physics-inspired Framework
Propose a physics-inspired framework for accelerating FM models, leveraging insights from modal analysis in dynamical systems. Identify key frequencies and modes that contribute to the stability and convergence of the FM's velocity field. Develop a novel modal-enabled acceleration method that selectively samples and projects input data onto these critical modes, allowing for faster and more efficient inference while preserving key features and dynamics. Compare against state-of-the-art static reduction strategies and evaluate the effect of modal selection methods on output quality and computational efficiency.
Controls: Experiment with different modal selection methods (e.g., Fourier analysis, Arnoldi iteration) and constraint types (e.g., frequency-based, amplitude-based); study the effect of modal acceleration on various tasks and datasets, particularly those requiring high-fidelity and detail-rich output.
Estimated cost: 180 GPU-hours
Prediction: Modal-enabled acceleration can significantly reduce inference costs for FM models in various domains, while maintaining output quality and even allowing for finer details and more realistic effects. However, the choice of modes and sampling strategies may depend heavily on specific applications and datasets.

PROPOSAL 5: Partial Flow Matching: Reducing Computational Cost using Partial Solution Approximations
Introduce a partial FM approach where the full ODE is approximated using a partial solution, focusing on key aspects of the problem that drive output quality. This is achieved by identifying critical components of the input data and leveraging domain knowledge to devise compact, yet effective, approximations of the full FM solution. Evaluate the effectiveness of this approach on text-to-image and video generation tasks, considering both the output quality and computational efficiency.
Controls: Compare against full FM solutions and other partial approximation methods, such as dimensionality reduction and trajectory truncation; study the impact of selecting different critical components and approximation methods on output quality and computational cost.
Estimated cost: 160 GPU-hours
Prediction: Partial FM can offer substantial computational savings while maintaining reasonable output quality for specific applications, such as low-resolution images or basic object classes. However, the selection of critical components and approximation methods may require domain expertise and careful tuning to achieve optimal results.

PROPOSAL 6: Hierarchical Flow Matching: Combining Local and Global Inference Strategies
Develop a hierarchical FM approach that integrates local and global inference strategies to address the trade-off between computational efficiency and output quality. This is achieved by partitioning the input data into smaller local patches, applying efficient inference methods (e.g., partial FM, modal-enabled acceleration) on each patch, and then combining the outputs using a global refinement stage. Evaluate the effectiveness of this approach on text-to-image and video generation tasks, considering both output quality and computational efficiency.
Controls: Compare against single-scale FM solutions and other hierarchical inference methods, such as multi-scale convolutional neural networks; study the impact of patch size and partitioning strategy on output quality and computational cost.
Estimated cost: 200 GPU-hours
Prediction: Hierarchical FM can effectively balance computational efficiency and output quality by leveraging local and global inference strategies. However, the choice of patch size, partitioning strategy, and global refinement method may significantly impact the performance of this approach.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Draft-ful Flow Matching
PROPOSAL: Investigate the feasibility of a draft-based approach to FM, where a pre-trained light-weight FM model proposes drafts in parallel and the full FM model selectively verifies them. To couple the draft trajectories with the full FM trajectory, we'll use a intermediate learned(module with approximated bluriness and recruiting/adjusting strategies). For evaluation, we'll measure how often the full FM model selects the originally proposed draft trajectory or accepts small adjustments from the draft.
CONTROLS: Experiments will compare accelerated inference times with equivalent output quality of the full model, and evaluate the optimal number of drafts and minimum acceptance threshold for full FM model. Additionally, we compare with the optimal single step inference on identical hardware.
COST: Estimated 150 GPU-hours for 3 experiments with 30x30 input image resolution.
PREDICTION: Accelerated inference should be achieved with a few tens of drafts and relatively low acceptance thresholds of around 5-10%, but may fail to fully control the drift of simulated trajectories, especially in text-to-video settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Draft-Trajectory Refining (DTR)
PROPOSAL: Design a refining step that follows the initial draft verification, leveraging the drift analysis between the draft and full FM trajectories. This refining process would adjust the draft velocity by learning to minimize the difference between the two trajectories, leading to more efficient and controlled proposals.
CONTROLS: We compare DTR with Draft-ful Flow Matching, ablate the refining step to see its impact on accuracy vs. speed trade-off, and also evaluate the quality of generated samples without DTR. Additionally, we investigate the sensitivity of DTR to different hyperparameters (e.g., the number of refining steps, learning rate).
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours for 3 additional experiments with varying refining step sizes.
PREDICTION: DTR is expected to improve overall performance, allowing for more accurate and detailed proposals, but might still struggle with highly non-linear or dynamic environments (e.g., video generation).

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Draft-Trajectory Refining (DTR)
PROPOSAL: To further improve the effectiveness of DTR, we'll employ a learned-based perturbation strategy that balances exploration vs. exploitation during the refining process. This will allow DTR to adaptively adjust the degree of perturbation based on the current trajectory, ensuring a refined proposal that is not only accurate but also diverse and close to the true underlying distribution.
CONTROLS: As before, compare with the original Draft-ful Flow Matching and ablate the refining step to understand its impact on results. Additionally, we evaluate the learned perturbation strategy's performance on a set of synthetic and real-world datasets.
COST: Estimated 50 GPU-hours for 2 additional experiments with varying perturbation sizes.
PREDICTION: The revised DTR should show improved performance and higher quality samples, but might still face difficulties in highly complex or dynamic scenarios, where the learned perturbation strategy might not be effective in avoiding local optima.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 2
TITLE: REVISED Draft-Trajectory Refining (DTR)
PROPOSAL: To prevent over-refining, we'll introduce an adaptive termination criterion, which checks for similarity between the current refined trajectory and the full FM model's output. If the difference is below a certain threshold, DTR stops, ensuring that the refined proposal is close enough to the desired solution without investing unnecessary computation.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original revised DTR and also evaluate the threshold's impact on results, using a range of real-world datasets.
COST: Estimated 30 GPU-hours for 2 additional experiments with varying termination thresholds.
PREDICTION: The adaptive termination criterion is expected to significantly reduce the computation required for DTR, but might occasionally terminate prematurely,-leading to suboptimal performance, especially in cases with highly varying local minima.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Flow-Based Draft Initialization
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel method to initialize the draft proposals using the flow-based architecture itself. The idea is to leverage the learnable velocity field of the full FM model to generate a set of draft proposals that are close to the desired data distribution. This could potentially provide higher-quality draft proposals and improve the overall performance of the accelerated FM model.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of Flow-Based Draft Initialization on several real-world datasets and compare it with the original Draft-ful Flow Matching. Additionally, we will investigate the importance of the flow-based initialization method in the overall performance of the accelerated FM model.
COST: Estimated 120 GPU-hours for 3 experiments with varying flow-based initialization parameters.
PREDICTION: Flow-Based Draft Initialization is expected to improve the performance of the accelerated FM model significantly, but might be computationally expensive and could struggle with cases where the flow-based model has difficulty representing the underlying data distribution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Early Exhaustion of Unpromising Drafts
PROPOSAL: Implement a mechanism that detects and discards unpromising draft proposals early in the process, based on their likelihood of being rejected by the full FM model. This can be done by learning to predict the acceptance probability of each draft proposal using a separate auxiliary model. This mechanism can help reduce the overall number of proposals that need to be evaluated and generated, thereby accelerating the inference process.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of Early Exhaustion of Unpromising Drafts and compare it with the original Draft-ful Flow Matching and DTR. We will also investigate the impact of different auxiliary models and prediction thresholds on the performance of the accelerated FM model.
COST: Estimated 80 GPU-hours for 2 experiments with varying auxiliary model architectures and prediction thresholds.
PREDICTION: Early Exhaustion of Unpromising Drafts is expected to significantly reduce the computation required for the accelerated FM model, but might occasionally discard promising draft proposals if the auxiliary model misclassifies them as unpromising, leading to suboptimal performance.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 3
TITLE: REVISED Flow-Based Draft Initialization
PROPOSAL: To further improve the flow-based draft initialization method, we'll modify it to leverage the learned velocity field's conditional distribution, which models the probability of a sample given its position in the input space. This modification will allow the flow-based model to generate draft proposals that are not only close to the target data distribution but also respect the spatial and structural relationships between the input samples.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the revised flow-based initialization method on several real-world datasets and compare it with the original draft initialization methods. Additionally, we will investigate the impact of different architectures and configurations on the performance of the accelerated FM model.
COST: Estimated 50 GPU-hours for 2 experiments with varying flow-based initialization parameters.
PREDICTION: The revised flow-based initialization method is expected to improve the quality and diversity of draft proposals, leading to better overall performance of the accelerated FM model, but might require careful tuning of the conditional distribution and could be sensitive to the choice of input space.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dynamic Draft Generation Scheduling
PROPOSAL: Introduce a dynamic scheduling mechanism that adjusts the rate of draft generation based on the current state of the accelerated FM model, including the quality of the draft proposals and the complexity of the target data distribution. This can help balance the trade-off between proposal quality and generation speed, ensuring that the model adapts to changing conditions and adjusts its strategy.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of Dynamic Draft Generation Scheduling and compare it with the original Draft-ful Flow Matching and DTR. We will also investigate the impact of different scheduling algorithms and hyperparameters on the performance of the accelerated FM model.
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours for 3 experiments with varying scheduling algorithms and hyperparameters.
PREDICTION: Dynamic Draft Generation Scheduling is expected to improve the overall performance of the accelerated FM model by adaptively adjusting to changing conditions, but might require careful tuning of the scheduling algorithm and could be sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Distributed Acceleration of FM using Drafts
PROPOSAL: Scale up the accelerated FM model to a distributed environment, where multiple machines generate draft proposals in parallel, reducing the overall inference time. To ensure that the proposed solutions work well in distributed settings, we'll develop a communication protocol to share critical information, such as draft proposal quality and acceptance probabilities, between nodes.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of Distributed Acceleration of FM using Drafts with the original distribution in a multi-node environment. We will also assess the impact of different communication protocols and node configurations on the overall performance of the accelerated FM model.
COST: Estimated 400 GPU-hours for 4 experiments with varying node configurations and communication protocols.
PREDICTION: Distributed Acceleration of FM using Drafts is expected to significantly reduce the inference time of the accelerated FM model, but might require careful tuning of the communication protocol and could be sensitive to network latency and machine heterogeneity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Orchestration Framework for Scalable FM Acceleration
PROPOSAL: Develop an orchestration framework that integrates the proposed draft-based acceleration techniques and distributes them over a cluster of machines. The framework will manage the communication, node scheduling, and load balancing to ensure efficient execution of the accelerated FM model and minimize overhead.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the Orchestration Framework on a large dataset and compare it with the individual acceleration techniques and the standard FM model.
COST: Estimated 600 GPU-hours for 5 experiments with varying dataset sizes and node configurations.
PREDICTION: The Orchestration Framework is expected to enable scalable and efficient execution of the accelerated FM model, but might require careful tuning of the framework and could be sensitive to cluster configuration and node heterogeneity.

propositions.controles: We compare DTR with Draft-ful Flow Matching, ablate the refining step to see its impact on accuracy vs. speed trade-off, and also evaluate the quality of generated samples without DTR. TITLE: Probability of Adaptation-Guided Masking (PGM) for Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We introduce a probabilistic framework, PGM, to learn an adaptive masking strategy for the online adaptation of pre-trained models. PGM is based on a Bayesian neural network that utilizes an uncertainty-aware masking mechanism to selectively update the model's parameters. At each time step, PGM adjusts the probabilities of the parameters to be masked according to the uncertainty of the estimated gradients, thereby adaptively balancing exploration and exploitation. We evaluate PGM on real-world datasets and compare it with several strong baselines.
CONTROLS: Relative entropy-based uncertainty estimation, progressive refinement based on uncertainty-aware masking, determine samples
COST: Estimated cost: 10 GPU-hours for training the Bayesian neural network, 5 GPU-hours for hyperparameter tuning, 5 GPU-hours for evaluating PGM on test sets
PREDICTION: We expect PGM to exhibit better adaptation performance and structural learning due to its adaptive masking strategy, but the performance might degrade if there are almost-deterministic regions in the target distribution.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Adaptive Online Gradient Descent via Layer Pruning and Local Gradient Estimation
PROPOSAL: We further enhance our previous proposal by integrating the dynamic layer pruning strategy with PGM, forming a hierarchical adaptation framework. In this framework, PGM selects the most uncertain parameters to be pruned, and the dynamic layer pruning strategy adaptively adjusts the pruning schedule as the model learns from new data. This hierarchical adaptation enables the model to efficiently explore the parameter space and maintain a smooth adaptation process.
CONTROLS: PGM with fixed layer pruning strategy, dynamic layer pruning with fixed PGM selection, full-precision online gradient descent as the baseline
COST: Estimated cost remains the same: 20 GPU-hours (after accounting for the additional control)
PREDICTION: This integration should lead to a more efficient and adaptive learning process, but if the hierarchical adaptation introduces additional computation overhead, the improvement might be offset, leading to slower convergence rates.

TITLE: A Novel Multi-Stream adapters architecture for Online Multi-Step Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel multi-stream adapters architecture to handle online multi-step time series forecasting problems. Our architecture consists of multiple streams, each of which represents a short-term or long-term dependency in the data. We utilize a dynamic routing mechanism to select the most relevant streams for each time step based on the recent input data. Each stream is associated with a separate adapter module that updates its parameters online using a variant of our hierarchical adaptation framework.
CONTROLS: State-of-the-art online multi-step time series forecasting models, our revised Adaptive Online Gradient Descent via Layer Pruning and Local Gradient Estimation, PGM with fixed layer pruning strategy
COST: Estimated cost: 15 GPU-hours for training the multi-stream adapters, 10 GPU-hours for hyperparameter tuning
PREDICTION: We expect this multi-stream adapters architecture to significantly improve the model's performance in handling long-range dependencies and adapt to changing patterns in the data, but if the dynamic routing mechanism introduces overfitting or instability issues, the performance might degrade.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Online Gradient-Based Adaptation via Bayesian Bootstrap Sampling
PROPOSAL: We introduce a Bayesian bootstrap sampling (BBS) method to adapt the online time series forecasting models to changing patterns in the data. Our BBS approach samples model parameters from a posterior distribution estimated using a subset of past data, and updates these parameters using a Kalman filter-based method. We adapt the BBS method to our hierarchical adaptation framework to learn an adaptive weighting scheme for combining the predictions from different data samples.
CONTROLS: OGD with random initialization, variants of selective online learning (involving different subsets of parameters and updating strategies), our revised Adaptive Online Gradient Descent via Layer Pruning and Local Gradient Estimation
COST: Estimated cost: 10 GPU-hours for training the BBS model, 5 GPU-hours for hyperparameter tuning
PREDICTION: We expect this BBS-based adaptation method to improve the model's robustness and adaptability to changing patterns, but if the BBS approach introduces high variance or bias in the parameter estimates, the performance might suffer.

TITLE: Exploration-Expansion Strategy for Efficient Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose an exploration-expansion strategy to efficiently explore the model's capacity and expand its knowledge to handle complex and non-linear relationships in the data. Our strategy involves an entropy-based exploration mechanism that dynamically adjusts the model's search space to identify areas of high uncertainty. The model then expands its knowledge by adding new units or connections to the existing architecture. We integrate the exploration-expansion strategy with our hierarchical adaptation framework to create a more robust and efficient online time series forecasting model.
CONTROLS: OGD with random initialization, state-of-the-art online time series forecasting models, variants of selective online learning
COST: Estimated cost: 15 GPU-hours for training the exploration-expansion model, 10 GPU-hours for hyperparameter tuning
PREDICTION: We expect this exploration-expansion strategy to improve the model's efficiency and effectiveness in handling complex relationships, but if the exploration mechanism over-expands the model's capacity, the risk of overfitting might increase.

TITLE: Multi-Aspect Online Ensemble Learning for Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We introduce a multi-aspect online ensemble learning (MAOEL) framework that combines the strengths of multiple online learning methods to improve the robustness and accuracy of time series forecasting. MAOEL involves an aspect-based splitting mechanism that divides the input data into different aspects, each representing a particular pattern or trend. We then train multiple online learning models on each aspect and combine their predictions to generate the final forecast. Our MAOEL approach allows for the adaptive combination of different online learning methods and aspects to tackle complex and dynamic time series forecasting tasks.
CONTROLS: Our revised Adaptive Online Gradient Descent via Layer Pruning and Local Gradient Estimation, PGM, our Novel Multi-Stream adapters architecture, variants of selective online learning
COST: Estimated cost: 20 GPU-hours for training the MAOEL model, 15 GPU-hours for hyperparameter tuning
PREDICTION: We expect MAOEL to improve the model's robustness and accuracy in handling complex time series forecasting tasks, but if the aspect-based splitting mechanism introduces additional complexity, the performance might suffer from overfitting or instability issues.

TITLE: Adaptive Knowledge Distillation for Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose an adaptive knowledge distillation (AKD) method for online time series forecasting, where a teacher model is updated online based on the student model's performance. Our AKD approach involves a dynamic learning rate schedule that balances the teacher and student models' contributions to the predicted output. We integrate AKD with our hierarchical adaptation framework to create a model that can adapt to changing patterns in the data while maintaining the benefits of knowledge distillation.
CONTROLS: Our revised Adaptive Online Gradient Descent via Layer Pruning and Local Gradient Estimation, PGM, our Novel Multi-Stream adapters architecture, AKD variants with different learning rate scheduling strategies
COST: Estimated cost: 15 GPU-hours for training the AKD model, 10 GPU-hours for hyperparameter tuning
PREDICTION: We expect AKD to improve the model's robustness and generalizability by leveraging the knowledge distillation framework, but if the dynamic learning rate schedule introduces instability, the performance might suffer.

PROPOSAL: We provide a comprehensive benchmarking framework to evaluate the performance of online time series forecasting models on a set of standardized tasks and datasets. We identify key open challenges in the field, including handling concept drift, dealing with high-dimensional input data, and developing methods for interpreting and explaining the forecasts. Our benchmarking framework and challenge statement aim to stimulate further research and development in online time series forecasting.

propositions.texte: We propose an adaptive knowledge distillation (AKD) method for online time series forecasting, where a teacher model is updated online based on the student model's performance. Our AKD approach involves a dynamic learning rate schedule that balances the teacher and student models' contributions to the predicted output. We integrate AKD with our hierarchical adaptation framework to create a model that can adapt to changing patterns in the data while maintaining the benefits of knowledge distillation.
propositions.titre: Adaptive Knowledge Distillation for Online Time Series Forecasting

We identify key open challenges in the field, including handling concept drift, dealing with high-dimensional input data, and developing methods for interpreting and explaining the forecasts. Our benchmarking framework and challenge statement aim to stimulate further research and development in online time series forecasting.
propositions.titre: Benchmarking and Open Challenges in Online Time Series Forecasting

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Online Gradient Descent with Adaptive Batch Sizes
PROPOSAL: We will compare the performance of online gradient descent (OGD) with adaptive batch sizes on the traffic flow prediction task using the PeMSD7 dataset from the M5 competition. We will explore two adaptive batch size schedules: one that doubles the batch size every 10 time steps and another that increases the batch size in response to a decrease in the validation loss. We will use the mean absolute error (MAE) as the evaluation metric.
CONTROLS: We will compare our modified OGD algorithm to the standard OGD algorithm and to an OGD algorithm with a fixed batch size of 32.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved performance with the adaptive batch size schedules, particularly in the initial stages of deployment, but the increase in batch size may eventually lead to overfitting. We may also observe a reduction in the number of updates required to achieve convergence due to the more efficient use of recent data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing the Impact of Adapter Location on Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the effect of adapter location on online time series forecasting by modifying the initial OGD algorithm (proposal 1) to update adapters attached to different layers of a pre-trained time series forecasting model. We will consider three adapter locations: after the model's output layer, on both the input and output layers, and after the recurrent layer in a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) architecture. We will utilize the same traffic flow prediction task and evaluate the performance using the mean absolute error (MAE).
CONTROLS: We will compare our modified OGD algorithms to the original OGD algorithm and to the one from proposal 1. We will also investigate the impact of adapter size and number on the performance.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that adapters attached to the output layer will be more effective for online time series forecasting, as they directly influence the prediction. However, adapters attached to earlier layers may capture higher-level patterns and relationships, leading to improved performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparing the Performance of Linear and Non-linear Adapters in Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We will compare the effectiveness of linear and non-linear adapters on the traffic flow prediction task, building upon the results from proposal 2. We will train a separate set of adapters with different activation functions (e.g., ReLU, sigmoid, tanh) and evaluate their performance using the mean absolute error (MAE). We will also investigate the effect of adapter depth and width on performance.
CONTROLS: We will compare our non-linear adapter models to the linear adapter models from proposal 2. We will also compare the performance of our best non-linear adapter model to the original OGD algorithm and to proposal 1.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that non-linear adapters will outperform linear adapters due to their ability to capture complex relationships in the data. However, the choice of activation function may have a significant impact on performance, and overfitting may be a concern for deeper or wider adapters.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Simplifying Adapter Learning through Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: We will simplify the learning of adapters by using knowledge distillation, where we train a small adapter to mimic the behavior of a pre-trained large adapter. We will explore two approaches: one where we train the small adapter to predict the output of the large adapter, and another where we train the small adapter to learn a compressed representation of the input that is similar to the input to the large adapter. We will evaluate the performance of the distilled adapters on the traffic flow prediction task using the mean absolute error (MAE).
CONTROLS: We will compare our distillation-based adapters to the traditional adapters from proposal 1 and 2, as well as to the original OGD algorithm. We will also investigate the effect of the knowledge distillation temperature and the architecture of the small adapter on performance.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that knowledge distillation will improve the performance of adapters and reduce the risk of overfitting by providing a regularization effect. However, the choice of knowledge distillation temperature and the architecture of the small adapter may significantly impact performance, and there may be a trade-off between doctoring the right examples and overfitting to them.

TITLE: Improving Online Time Series Forecasting with Ensembles of Adapters
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the performance of ensemble methods where multiple adapters are combined to improve the overall forecasting accuracy. We will explore different ensemble strategies, such as bagging, boosting, and stacking, and evaluate their performance on the traffic flow prediction task using the mean absolute error (MAE).

PREDICTION: We expect that ensemble methods will improve the performance of online time series forecasting by reducing the variance of the adapters and capturing multiple patterns in the data. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Addressing Delayed Feedback with Intermediate Loss Functions
PROPOSAL: We will address the delayed feedback problem in multi-step forecasting by introducing intermediate loss functions that are used to update the model at each time step based on the forecast made at that time step. We will explore different types of intermediate loss functions, such as mean absolute error, mean squared error, and cross-entropy loss, and evaluate their performance on the traffic flow prediction task using the mean absolute error (MAE).
CONTROLS: We will compare our intermediate loss function-based models to the original OGD algorithm and to proposal 1-4. We will also investigate the effect of the number of intermediate loss functions and the architecture of the model on performance.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that intermediate loss functions will improve the performance of online time series forecasting by reducing the variance of the model and capturing multiple patterns in the data. However, the choice of intermediate loss function and the architecture of the model may significantly impact performance, and overfitting may be a concern for deeper or wider models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Noise and Concept Drift on Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the performance of online time series forecasting models in the presence of noise and concept drift, which are common challenges in real-world time series forecasting tasks. We will simulate noise and concept drift in the traffic flow prediction task using different levels of noise and drift, and evaluate the performance of the models from proposal 1-5 using the mean absolute error (MAE).
CONTROLS: We will compare our noise and concept drift tolerance-based models to the original OGD algorithm and to proposal 1-5. We will also investigate the effect of the level of noise and drift, the architecture of the model, and the choice of online learning algorithm on performance.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the models from proposal 1-5 will perform well in the presence of noise and concept drift, but the performance may degrade as the level of noise and drift increases.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Using Transfer Learning for Improved Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We will explore the use of transfer learning for online time series forecasting, where we use a pre-trained model on a different task as an initializer for the online time series forecasting task. We will evaluate the performance of transfer learning on the traffic flow prediction task using the mean absolute error (MAE), and compare it to the original OGD algorithm and to proposal 1-6.
CONTROLS: We will compare our transfer learning-based models to the original OGD algorithm and to proposal 1-6. We will also investigate the effect of the pre-trained model, the choice of online learning algorithm, and the architecture of the transfer learning model on performance.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that transfer learning will improve the performance of online time series forecasting by leveraging the knowledge acquired from the pre-trained model. However, the choice of pre-trained model and the architecture of the transfer learning model may significantly impact performance, and overfitting may be a concern for deeper or wider models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Comprehensive Evaluation of Online Time Series Forecasting Algorithms
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the online time series forecasting algorithms from proposal 1-7, and compare their performance on a range of real-world traffic flow prediction tasks. We will evaluate the performance of each algorithm using a set of metrics, including mean absolute error (MAE), mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), and Spearman's rank correlation coefficient. We will also investigate the impact of different hyperparameters and architectures on performance.
CONTROLS: We will compare our comprehensive evaluation to the original OGD algorithm and to the individual proposal 1-7. We will also investigate the effect of different evaluation metrics, hyperparameters, and architectures on performance.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the comprehensive evaluation will provide a thorough understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of each online time series forecasting algorithm, and inform the choice of algorithm for real-world applications. However, the choice of evaluation metrics and the complexity of the tasks may impact performance, and there may be trade-offs between different algorithms and evaluation metrics.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Revisiting Parameter Updates in Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of updating different model components in an online gradient descent (OGD) framework on traffic flow forecasting.
We will study two methods: updating only the final prediction layer (FPL) and updating both the FPL and the ensemble weights that combine several models. We will also experiment with different adapter sizes and locations in the network. We will use real-world traffic flow datasets and compare our results to a baseline that incorporates online attention for parameter adaptation.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Online attention for parameter adaptation; ablation studies of component updates and adapter sizes
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect FPL updates to perform well for a short horizon but poor for a long horizon due to the error accumulation, while updating both FPL and ensemble weights will perform better overall but at a higher computational cost; updating adapters of different sizes and locations will provide insights into their relative importance in parameter adaptation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Storage-Augmented Experience Replay Mechanism for Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Develop an online time series forecasting algorithm with an augmented experience replay mechanism that strategically stores gradients from recent data points while selectively retrieving relevant gradients from the stored repository. We will implement a caching mechanism that assesses the relevance of stored gradients based on the evolving patterns in the time series and dynamically updates the repository to store gradients most useful for upcoming predictions.
We will use real-world traffic flow and electricity consumption forecasting datasets and compare our results to baselines that incorporate online gradient descent (OGD), gradient aggregation, and experience replay.
CONTROLS: Baselines: OGD, gradient aggregation, experience replay; ablation studies of caching mechanism performance and stored repository size
COST: 240 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the storage-augmented experience replay mechanism to outperform standard experience replay by providing more focused and relevant gradients, and to adapt better to concept drift in real-world time series datasets by strategically refreshing the stored repository.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Control Variates for Delayed Feedback in Multi-Step Forecasting
PROPOSAL: (Revision of 2) Integrate a control variate mechanism into the storage-augmented experience replay framework to address the delayed feedback issue in multi-step forecasting. The control variate will enable the model to adjust its predictions for earlier time steps based on the expected future feedback, thereby reducing the bias caused by delayed feedback. We will evaluate the performance of the control variate mechanism on electricity transformer temperature forecasting and weather forecasting datasets.
CONTROLS: Baselines: OGD, gradient aggregation, experience replay, ablation studies of control variate performance and effectiveness in different forecasting domains
COST: 320 GPU-hours (considering additional computations for control variate implementation)
PREDICTION: We expect the control variate mechanism to significantly reduce the bias introduced by delayed feedback in multi-step forecasting and improve the overall performance on tasks with high delays, such as electricity transformer temperature forecasting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Concept Drift Detection Methods for Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Investigate and compare various concept drift detection methods for their suitability in identifying distribution shifts in online time series datasets. We will apply these methods to a set of real-world traffic flow, electricity consumption, and solar power forecasting datasets to determine their effectiveness in triggering adaptive updates. We will also examine the impact of these methods on the overall forecasting performance.
CONTROLS: Baselines: common online anomaly detectors such as EWMA and exponentially-weighted moving average; comparison with state-of-the-art techniques for concept drift detection
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect more robust concept drift detection methods to improve forecasting performance, particularly in settings where rapid changes in the underlying distribution occur, but may also introduce additional computational overhead and possibility of overtrapping.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Online Regularization for Concept Drift
PROPOSAL: Introduce an adaptive online regularization mechanism that adjusts the model's capacity to adapt to changes in the distribution, based on the detected concept drift. This adaptation will be achieved through an online learning rate adjustment mechanism, which will dynamically update the learning rate used for updating the model parameters in response to concept drift. We will implement this mechanism in the online learning framework and compare its performance with conventional online learning methods on real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: Baselines: conventional online learning methods (e.g. OGD); comparison with state-of-the-art techniques for adaptive regularization
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the adaptive online regularization mechanism to improve forecasting performance by adapting the model's capacity to changing distributions, but may also introduce additional computational overhead due to the online learning rate adjustment mechanism.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Efficient Gradient Estimation for Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: (Revision of 1) Investigate and compare different gradient estimation methods in the context of online time series forecasting, including the standard stochastic gradient descent, Striped-SGD, and Hessian Averaging. We will evaluate these methods on traffic flow forecasting and electricity consumption forecasting datasets to determine the most suitable gradient estimation method for early adaptation to changing distributions. We will also examine the impact of batch sizes and update frequencies on the performance of these methods.
CONTROLS: Baselines: standard OGD, batching with different batch sizes, comparison with recent gradient estimation techniques
COST: 260 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect Striped-SGD to achieve better performance than standard OGD, especially in high variances, while Hessian Averaging could outperform Striped-SGD in scenarios with smooth changes in data distribution, but may also introduce additional calculations for the Hessian matrix.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Online Transfer Learning for Time Series Forecasting: A Domain-Invariant Approach
PROPOSAL: Explore an online transfer learning approach for adapting a pre-trained model to a new domain, where the data distribution has changed. This approach will utilize domain-invariant learning techniques, such as multi-task learning and adversarial training, to extract common features from the training and target domains. We will apply this approach to adapt a pre-trained forecasting model to changing patterns in real-world datasets.

PROPOSAL 1: Revisiting Parameter Updates in Online Time Series Forecasting
Investigate the impact of updating different model components in an online gradient descent (OGD) framework on traffic flow forecasting.
We will study two methods: updating only the final prediction layer (FPL) and updating both the FPL and the ensemble weights that combine several models. We will also experiment with different adapter sizes and locations in the network. We will use real-world traffic flow datasets and compare our results to a baseline that incorporates online attention for parameter adaptation.
Controls: Baseline: Online attention for parameter adaptation; ablation studies of component updates and adapter sizes
Estimated cost: 100 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect FPL updates to perform well for a short horizon but poor for a long horizon due to the error accumulation, while updating both FPL and ensemble weights will perform better overall but at a higher computational cost; updating adapters of different sizes and locations will provide insights into their relative importance in parameter adaptation.

PROPOSAL 2: A Storage-Augmented Experience Replay Mechanism for Online Time Series Forecasting
Develop an online time series forecasting algorithm with an augmented experience replay mechanism that strategically stores gradients from recent data points while selectively retrieving relevant gradients from the stored repository. We will implement a caching mechanism that assesses the relevance of stored gradients based on the evolving patterns in the time series and dynamically updates the repository to store gradients most useful for upcoming predictions.
We will use real-world traffic flow and electricity consumption forecasting datasets and compare our results to baselines that incorporate online gradient descent (OGD), gradient aggregation, and experience replay.
Controls: Baselines: OGD, gradient aggregation, experience replay; ablation studies of caching mechanism performance and stored repository size
Estimated cost: 240 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect the storage-augmented experience replay mechanism to outperform standard experience replay by providing more focused and relevant gradients, and to adapt better to concept drift in real-world time series datasets by strategically refreshing the stored repository.

PROPOSAL 3: Analyzing Concept Drift Detection Methods for Online Time Series Forecasting
Investigate and compare various concept drift detection methods for their suitability in identifying distribution shifts in online time series datasets. We will apply these methods to a set of real-world traffic flow, electricity consumption, and solar power forecasting datasets to determine their effectiveness in triggering adaptive updates. We will also examine the impact of these methods on the overall forecasting performance.
Controls: Baselines: common online anomaly detectors such as EWMA and exponentially-weighted moving average; comparison with state-of-the-art techniques for concept drift detection
Estimated cost: 180 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect more robust concept drift detection methods to improve forecasting performance, particularly in settings where rapid changes in the underlying distribution occur, but may also introduce additional computational overhead and possibility of overtrapping.

PROPOSAL 4: Adaptive Online Regularization for Concept Drift
Introduce an adaptive online regularization mechanism that adjusts the model's capacity to adapt to changes in the distribution, based on the detected concept drift. This adaptation will be achieved through an online learning rate adjustment mechanism, which will dynamically update the learning rate used for updating the model parameters in response to concept drift. We will implement this mechanism in the online learning framework and compare its performance with conventional online learning methods on real-world datasets.
Controls: Baselines: conventional online learning methods (e.g. OGD); comparison with state-of-the-art techniques for adaptive regularization
Estimated cost: 220 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect the adaptive online regularization mechanism to improve forecasting performance by adapting the model's capacity to changing distributions, but may also introduce additional computational overhead due to the online learning rate adjustment mechanism.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Alternative Class Encoding Forms for Pseudo-Label Learning
PROPOSAL: Implement and evaluate the performance of different class encoding forms (e.g., multi-hot, hierarchical labels, probabilistic representations) for pseudo-label learning in semantic segmentation, focusing on scenarios with confusing classes.
CONTROLS: Compare to mainstream one-hot encoding, and study the effect of noise in pseudo-labels (e.g., by introducing labeling errors) on the different encodings.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Alternative encodings (e.g., multi-hot, probabilistic) could provide a more robust supervision signal in cases of confusing classes, but may require adjustments to the training objective and pseudo-label generation process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Pseudo-Label Generation Techniques for Robust Encoding
PROPOSAL: Investigate pseudo-label generation techniques that can produce more informative and robust encoding forms for confusing classes, such as: (1) using soft pseudo-labels (e.g., probabilities) instead of hard one-hot labels; (2) incorporating spatial and contextual information to guide pseudo-label generation; (3) employing loss functions that encourage class discriminability.
CONTROLS: Compare generated soft pseudo-labels, and evaluate the proposed techniques on various inconsistent categories.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Techniques like soft pseudo-labels and contextual information may reduce the noise in pseudo-labels and improve the robustness of encoding forms, while encouraging class discriminability could help in cases where classes are highly correlated.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Exploring Alternative Class Encoding Forms for Pseudo-Label Learning
PROPOSAL: Implement and evaluate the performance of hierarchical labels, a soft encoding form, to represent classes and their visual attributes (e.g., attributes of sheep are horns, hooves) as separate binary labels. This encoding enables supervision to capture class attributes while still allowing the model to learn specific class boundaries.
CONTROLS: Compare to mainstream one-hot encoding and study the effect of noise in pseudo-labels on the performance of hierarchical labels.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Hierarchical labels may alleviate the issue of misinformed supervision for confusing classes, but may require adjustments to the training objective and loss function to handle the multi-label representation.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Exploring Alternative Class Encoding Forms for Pseudo-Label Learning
PROPOSAL: Implement and evaluate the performance of multi-hot encoding, where a single pixel is represented by a list of probabilities for each class, truncated to a specified top-k value to reduce dimensionality and alleviate the issue of misinformed supervision for confusing classes.
CONTROLS: Compare to mainstream one-hot encoding, and study the effect of noise in pseudo-labels on the performance of multi-hot encoding.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Multi-hot encoding may provide a more robust supervision signal in cases of confusing classes, but may require adjustments to the training objective and pseudo-label generation process to handle the probabilistic representation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Integrating Encoding Forms into Existing Frameworks
PROPOSAL: Modify existing self-training and consistency regularization frameworks to accommodate the proposed encoding forms (e.g., hierarchical labels, multi-hot encoding) and evaluate their performance on multiple benchmark datasets (e.g., urban street-scene segmentation, aerial imagery segmentation, cardiac MRI segmentation).
CONTROLS: Compare the modified frameworks with their original counterparts, and study the transferability of the proposed encoding forms across different domains and architectures.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The modified frameworks may exhibit improved performance in scenarios with confusing classes and provide a more robust supervision signal, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and adjustments to the overall architecture.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Encoding Forms for Pseudo-Label Learning
PROPOSAL: Analytically study the relationship between the encoding form and the convergence of pseudo-label learning algorithms, particularly for scenarios with confusing classes. Derive bounds on the error of pseudo-label learning in terms of the encoding form and the quality of the pseudo-labels.
CONTROLS: Compare the derived bounds for different encoding forms (e.g., one-hot, multi-hot, hierarchical) and study the effect of label noise on the convergence of pseudo-label learning.
COST: 0 GPU-hours (theory)
PREDICTION: Theoretical analysis may provide insights into the properties of different encoding forms and the challenges of pseudo-label learning in scenarios with confusing classes, but may not directly guide the choice of encoding form or pseudo-label generation technique in practice.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Encoding Forms for Pseudo-Label Learning
PROPOSAL: Provide a tight bound on the error of pseudo-label learning for the hierarchical label encoding form, and analyze the convergence rate of pseudo-label learning for the multi-hot encoding form. Compare the derived bounds with those for the one-hot encoding form to highlight the benefits of alternative encoding forms.
CONTROLS: Assume i.i.d. data, and suppose the label noise is to be ε-perturbed, that is fixed.
COST: 0 GPU-hours (theory)
PREDICTION: The revised theoretical analysis may clarify the advantages of hierarchical and multi-hot encoding forms over one-hot encoding in scenarios with confusing classes, but may require careful handling of the error bounds due to the increased complexity of the encoding forms.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Encoding Forms on Synthetic-to-Real Domain Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Apply the proposed encoding forms to synthetic-to-real domain adaptation tasks (e.g., fromurban street-scene segmentation simulated scenarios to real-world datasets) and evaluate their effectiveness in reducing the domain gap and improving segmentation accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the proposed encoding forms with state-of-the-art methods for domain adaptation and pseudo-label learning.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed encoding forms may exhibit improved performance in synthetic-to-real domain adaptation tasks, especially in scenarios with confusing classes, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and adjustments to the domain adaptation framework.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Pseudo-Label Generation Techniques for Robust Encoding
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel confidence-based pseudo-label generation technique that takes into account the hierarchical structure of the classes, and incorporates spatial and contextual information to guide pseudo-label generation. Compare its performance with existing techniques on multiple benchmark datasets.
CONTROLS: Study the effect of different confidence thresholds and spatial/contextual integration strategies on the performance of the novel technique.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised pseudo-label generation technique may provide more informative and robust pseudo-labels, especially in scenarios with confusing classes, and may offer a more accurate solution for balancing the trade-off between confidence and quality in pseudo-label learning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Semi-Supervised Segmentation with Hierarchical Label Encoding
PROPOSAL: Combine the proposed encoding forms, pseudo-label generation techniques, and domain adaptation approaches into a single framework for semi-supervised segmentation, focusing on applications in autonomous driving, remote sensing, and medical imaging. Evaluate the framework's performance on real-world datasets and compare it with state-of-the-art methods.
CONTROLS: Study the effect of different encoding forms, pseudo-label generation techniques, and domain adaptation methods on the performance of the framework.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed framework may provide a comprehensive solution for semi-supervised segmentation in various applications, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and adjustments to the framework to accommodate different datasets and scenarios.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint Exploration of Suboptimal Consequences from One-Hot Encoded Pseudo-Labels in Semantic Segmentation
PROPOSAL: Compare empirical performance on the CamVid and Cityscapes benchmarks, across three models (standard FCN, self-training, and consistency regularization) and under two label noise regimes, in terms of three metrics (IoU, pixelwise accuracy and mean boundary accuracy). Investigate whether an otherwise consistent trend of underperformed iou scoresreduces overall performance. This experiment helps us to identifyhow sensitive pseudo-label-based methods are to assumptions of one-hot encoding being effective in a partially wrong class assignment scenario.
CONTROLS: (1) baseline of using a standard FCN on labeled data only, (2) performance with hand-verified pseudo-labels (used as a proxy for ideal pick-and-replace approach) as partial replacement for erroneous pseudo-label guided intuition.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We predict both the self-training and consistency regularization methods will have broader gap between optimal and worst-case, as they both appear to produce well-intentioned but incorrect pick-and-replace versions due to their improper direct inputs. We also predict a maximum average iou "decline" of 2.5% compared to FCN baseline.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparison of Different Class Encoding Schemes for Pseudo-Labels
PROPOSAL: Empirically evaluate and compare the performance of softmax and sparsemax class encoding schemes to the existing hardmax (one-hot) encoding on three pseudo-label learning frameworks (self-training, consistency regularization, and their combination) on two datasets from medical imaging (Cardiac MRI segmentation) and remote sensing change detection (aerial imagery). Use both full and noisy (20% error) labels and evaluate the three metrics: IoU, pixelwise accuracy, and mean boundary accuracy.
CONTROLS: Evaluate softmax, sparsemax, and hardmax (one-hot) under the same pseudo-label learning frameworks and provide findings on class confusion for all, which can lead us to predict related class-to-class / encoding configuration pairings for fidelity strategies.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We predict that softmax class encoding scheme outperforms sparsemax and hardmax on medical and remote sensing datasets due to its ability to better handle multi-modal distributions, especially under noisy label conditions; however sparsemax might outperform hardmax on difficult-to-segment datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Semi-Supervised Semantic Segmentation with Information-Theoretic Metric Learning
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel loss function for pseudo-label learning based on a Kullback-Leibler divergence metric (KLD) between the teacher model's predicted probability distribution and the normalized true class histograms, where the class histograms are calculated over small spatial neighborhoods to capture local correlations between classes. Use the resulting information-theoretic loss function (ITL) to train a semi-supervised segmentation model on urban street scenes for autonomous driving and compare it with existing pseudo-label learning methods (including a revised version using class encoding from comparison of encoding schemes).

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Soft Pseudo-Label Encoding for Improved Segmentation
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel soft pseudo-label encoding scheme that adopts a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) to capture the uncertainty of class assignments. This would allow for the representation of uncertain or confused class labels, providing more informative supervision in cases where the class decision is ambiguous.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard one-hot hard pseudo-labels and temporal exponential moving average (EMA) teacher predictions.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This novel encoding scheme should outperform standard one-hot pseudo-labels on segmentation tasks with class confusion, while maintaining comparable performance in cases with clear class assignments. However, its performance may degrade in fully supervised settings where class ambiguity is not a concern.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Can GMM-based Soft Pseudo-Labels be Integrated into Existing Frameworks?
PROPOSAL: Design a simple modification to existing self-training and consistency regularization methods to incorporate the GMM-based soft pseudo-labels, without requiring significant architecture changes. This would involve using the GMM components as weights for consistency regularization or as confidence measures for self-training.
CONTROLS: Compare the modified frameworks against the standard paradigms with one-hot pseudo-labels on several segmentation tasks.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The modified frameworks should exhibit improved performance on tasks with class confusion, while maintaining competitive performance on tasks with clear class assignments. However, the integration might come at the cost of slightly increased computational complexity due to the additional GMM components.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Can GMM-based Soft Pseudo-Labels be Integrated into Existing Frameworks?
PROPOSAL: Revise the proposal to use a more efficient method for incorporating GMM-based soft pseudo-labels into existing self-training frameworks. Specifically, instead of modifying the standard paradigm, develop a separate branch of the teacher model that produces GMM-based soft pseudo-labels, and use the output of this branch to supervise the student model. This would allow for easier integration and comparison with existing methods.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised framework against standard self-training with one-hot pseudo-labels and the original GMM-based encoding scheme on several segmentation tasks.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised framework should demonstrate improved performance on tasks with class confusion, with a potential increase in computational efficiency due to the separate branch. However, tuning the architecture of this separate branch might be necessary to achieve optimal performance.
