actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Simplifying One-Step Generative Adversarial Networks with Auxiliary Classifiers
PROPOSAL: Investigate a variant of GANs, dubbed GAN-ACC, where the discriminator is replaced with a simple binary classifier, trained to classify between real and generated images. This simplification could reduce instability and eliminate the need for adversarial training of a separate discriminator.
CONTROLS: Baseline on standard GANs, ablation study on the effect of the binary classifier's capacity and number of training iterations.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect GAN-ACC to offer a more stable training process compared to standard GANs, but potentially at the cost of minor performance degradation. If successful, this could provide a stepping stone for further research on nearest-neighbor-based methods for efficient one-step generation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Non-Adversarial One-Step Generation via Probabilistic Label Propagation
PROPOSAL: Propose a non-adversarial method, dubbed NLPGAN, which leverages the label propagation framework to propagate real labels to the generated images. This is achieved by introducing a probabilistic label embedding space, where the generated images are encouraged to move closer to the real data distribution in this space.
CONTROLS: Baseline on standard GANs, ablation study on the effect of the label embedding space capacity and the number of iterations for label propagation.
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: NLPGAN is expected to achieve competitive results to GAN-ACC, with the added benefit of avoiding the need for a separate adversary. However, the quality of the generated images may degrade if the label embedding space is not well-designed.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Simplifying One-Step Generative Adversarial Networks with Auxiliary Classifiers
PROPOSAL: In addition to replacing the discriminator with a simple binary classifier, experiment with incorporating an information-theoretic regularization term to the generator's loss function, encouraging the generated images to be as diverse as possible while maintaining a high quality.
CONTROLS: Baseline on standard GANs with the binary classifier, ablation study on the effect of the regularization term's strength and the binary classifier's capacity.
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This modification is expected to further improve the stability and efficiency of GAN-ACC, potentially allowing it to scale to larger models. However, it may also introduce new trade-offs between diversity and quality.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Inference using Nearest Neighbor Selection
PROPOSAL: Introduce a nearest neighbor-based method that selects a subset of the original training data to serve as anchors for one-step image generation. The selected anchors are used to compute an initial image, which is then refined using a nearest neighbor search to generate the final output. This approach avoids expensive network computations by relying on high-dimensional nearest neighbor searches.
CONTROLS: Baseline on standard GANs and existing few-step methods, ablation study on the effect of anchor selection criteria and the number of anchors.
COST: 20 GPU-hours (initial data preparation) + negligible GPU-hours for inference
PREDICTION: This method is expected to achieve high-quality one-step generation while significantly reducing inference costs. However, it may suffer from difficulties in selecting the optimal anchors, especially for complex datasets.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Efficient Inference using Nearest Neighbor Selection
PROPOSAL: Modify the anchor selection process in the nearest neighbor-based method to incorporate a variant of the uniform manifold approximation and partition (UMAP) dimensionality reduction, to better capture the underlying structure of the original training data.
CONTROLS: Baseline on standard GANs and existing few-step methods, ablation study on the effect of the dimensionality reduction technique and the number of anchors.
COST: 22 GPU-hours (initial data preparation) + negligible GPU-hours for inference
PREDICTION: By incorporating UMAP, the nearest neighbor-based method is expected to better capture the complex relationships within the data and thus generate more accurate images. However, it may require more extensive data preparation time, and potential over-complexification of the nearest neighbor search space.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Scale Image Generation via Hierarchical Patch Embeddings
PROPOSAL: Introduce a method that generates images at multiple scales by learning hierarchical patch embeddings and iteratively refining them. This hierarchical structure allows for fine-grained control over the generated image, enabling high-quality one-step generation.
CONTROLS: Baseline on standard GANs and existing few-step methods, ablation study on the effect of the number of scales and the spatial resolution of the patch embeddings.
COST: 30 GPU-hours (for a moderate number of scales and resolution)
PREDICTION: This method is expected to achieve state-of-the-art results in one-step image generation, but may require significant computational resources to train and may be challenging to extend to larger image sizes.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Non-Adversarial One-Step Generation via Probabilistic Label Propagation
PROPOSAL: Modify the label propagation framework to incorporate an attention mechanism, allowing it to selectively focus on the most informative labels during the propagation process. This will enable the model to better capture the relationships between the generated images and the real data.
CONTROLS: Baseline on standard GANs, ablation study on the effect of the attention mechanism's capacity and the number of iterations for label propagation.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By incorporating attention, the label propagation framework is expected to improve the quality of the generated images and increase stability. However, it may also introduce new trade-offs between attention's capacity and the computational cost of the model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Task-Conditioned One-Step Generation for Image Editing
PROPOSAL: Adapt the existing one-step generation methods to condition the generation process on task-specific input vectors, enabling the model to perform image editing tasks such as inpainting, denoising, or style transfer.
CONTROLS: Baseline on existing one-step generation methods, ablation study on the effect of the task-specific input vectors and the conditioning mechanism.
COST: 35 GPU-hours (for a moderate number of tasks and conditional input dimensions)
PREDICTION: This adaptation is expected to extend the capabilities of one-step generation methods to a wide range of image editing tasks, but may require significant computational resources and careful design of the task-specific input vectors.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Task-Conditioned One-Step Generation for Image Editing
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel attention-based mechanism that selectively focuses on the most relevant features of the task-specific input vectors, allowing the model to efficiently adapt to different editing tasks and improve the quality of the generated images.
CONTROLS: Baseline on existing one-step generation methods, ablation study on the effect of the attention mechanism's capacity and the number of tasks.
COST: 40 GPU-hours (for a moderate number of tasks and conditional input dimensions)
PREDICTION: By incorporating attention, the task-conditioned one-step generation method is expected to achieve state-of-the-art results in image editing tasks, improving the efficiency and quality of the generated images. However, it may also introduce new trade-offs between attention's capacity and the computational cost of the model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Framework for One-Step Generation and Image Editing
PROPOSAL: Investigate a unified framework that integrates the existing one-step generation methods, allowing the model to seamlessly switch between generation and editing tasks based on the input task-specific input vectors. This framework will be trained using a hybrid loss function that balances the generation and editing tasks.
CONTROLS: Baseline on existing one-step generation methods, ablation study on the effect of the hybrid loss function and the task switch mechanism.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (for a moderate number of tasks and conditional input dimensions)
PREDICTION: This unified framework is expected to provide a single, flexible model that can handle a wide range of tasks, from one-step generation to image editing, and achieve state-of-the-art results across both domains. However, it may also introduce new challenges related to balancing the generation and editing tasks, and may require significant computational resources to train.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Unified Any-Step Sampling via Meta-Learning
PROPOSAL: We explore a meta-learning approach that combines the strengths of both consistency models and distribution matching distillation, to train a unified generator that can sample at any step length. The generator will learn to adapt its sampling strategy based on the input, without the need for explicit teacher guidance or auxiliary networks. We will utilize a model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) framework to fine-tune the generator on a variety of sampling step lengths, allowing it to learn a single model that can generate high-quality samples in one, few, or multiple steps. We will use the DALL-E FID-10k dataset for text-to-image generation.
CONTROLS: We will compare our meta-learning approach to existing few-step models, such as consistency models (e.g. LCM, PCM) and distribution matching distillation (e.g. DMD, DMD2).
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our unified meta-learning approach is expected to outperform existing few-step models in terms of quality, while maintaining simplicity and efficiency, especially for ultra-large models. However, training the meta-learning framework may require significant computational resources, and the generator's adaptability may not be as strong as the sub-expert models.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Evaluation of Few-Step Training Objectives for Text-to-Image Models
PROPOSAL: We propose to investigate and compare the effectiveness of various few-step training objectives, including consistency models, distribution matching distillation, and a recently introduced shortcut objective, for text-to-image generation. We will experiment with different training objectives, step lengths, and model capacities to provide a comprehensive understanding of the strengths and limitations of each approach. Our experiments will be conducted on the COCO dataset for text-to-image generation.
CONTROLS: We will compare the different few-step training objectives to the standard multi-step diffusion model, and also explore the combination of the different objectives to see if it can improve the overall performance.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results are expected to provide valuable insights into the properties of different few-step training objectives and their suitability for text-to-image generation. However, the performance may degrade at very low step lengths, and the objectives may not work well for ultra-large models due to training instability.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Evaluation of Few-Step Training Objectives for Text-to-Image Models
PROPOSAL: We propose to investigate and compare the effectiveness of various few-step training objectives, including consistency models, distribution matching distillation, and a recently introduced shortcut objective, for text-to-image generation. We will experiment with different training objectives, step lengths, and model capacities to provide a comprehensive understanding of the strengths and limitations of each approach. In addition, we will also study the effect of combining different objectives, and propose a novel approach to adapt the step length and training objectives based on the text prompt. Our experiments will be conducted on a combination of the COCO and DALL-E FID-10k datasets for text-to-image generation.
CONTROLS: We will compare the different few-step training objectives to the standard multi-step diffusion model, and also explore the combination of the different objectives to see if it can improve the overall performance.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our revised proposal is expected to provide more comprehensive insights into the properties and combination of few-step training objectives, and the performance should be significantly improved compared to the current baseline few-step models. However, the adaptation approach may require a substantial amount of hyperparameter tuning, and the complexity may increase with the number of text prompts.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Adversarial-Free Single-Step Text-to-Image Model via Learned Priors
PROPOSAL: We introduce a single-step text-to-image model that leverages learned priors to generate high-quality images without the need for adversarial training or teacher guidance. The model will consist of a generator that takes a text prompt as input and a learned prior network that provides a guiding probability distribution for the generated images. We will use a variant of the Flow++ model as the generator and a hierarchical normalizing flow as the learned prior network. Our experiments will be conducted on the COCO dataset for text-to-image generation.
CONTROLS: We will compare our adversarial-free single-step model to the standard multi-step diffusion model and other few-step models.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our single-step model is expected to achieve competitive results to existing few-step models while maintaining simplicity and efficiency. However, the performance may degrade for more complex text prompts, and the learned prior network may require additional training data to generalize well.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Adversarial-Free Single-Step Text-to-Image Model via Learned Priors
PROPOSAL: We introduce a single-step text-to-image model that leverages learned priors to generate high-quality images without the need for adversarial training or teacher guidance. The model will consist of a generator that takes a text prompt as input and a learned prior network that provides a guiding probability distribution for the generated images. We will use a variant of the Flow++ model as the generator and a hierarchical normalizing flow as the learned prior network. To further improve the model's performance, we will also incorporate a self-supervised autoencoder that learns to reconstruct the input images. Our experiments will be conducted on the COCO dataset for text-to-image generation, as well as on the ImageNet dataset for image editing.
CONTROLS: We will compare our adversarial-free single-step model to the standard multi-step diffusion model and other few-step models, including consistency models and distribution matching distillation.
COST: 900 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our revised single-step model is expected to achieve state-of-the-art results in text-to-image generation and image editing, while maintaining simplicity and efficiency. However, the complexity of the model may increase with the addition of the autoencoder, and the training time may be prolonged.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Analyzing the Role of Contextual Information in Few-Step Text-to-Image Models
PROPOSAL: We investigate the impact of contextual information, such as the input text prompt, on the performance of few-step text-to-image models. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Zero-Step Generation via Cross-Distribution Mixture Modelling
PROPOSAL: We propose an experimented study where we adopt cross-distribution mixture modelling to create a probabilistic multilayer mixture model, trained only with unpaired real images. This approach complements adversarial training by encouraging the generative model to synthesize diverse, coherent and realistic image representations in a single function evaluation.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach with consistency models and, possibly, recent few-step distillation methods as baselines, where we train them on a larger number of steps to match similar evaluation metrics (e.g., Fréchet Inception Distance - FID) as ours.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: We predict cross-distribution mixture modelling to outperform consistency models in terms of diversity and coherence of generated images, with minor drops in FID scores due to the reduced number of iterations. It could fail to generalise well across various models and tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Training Size-Efficient Generators via Multi-Resolution Quality-Aware Distillation
PROPOSAL: We propose a distillation-based approach, where a high-quality, large-scale generator (teacher) is distilled into two smaller, more resolution-efficient generators (student): (1) a low-resolution student aims at reproducing the teacher's output, while (2) a high-resolution student is responsible for refining the student's output to match the teacher's high-resolution quality. This multi-resolution framework helps capture both coarse and fine details of high-quality images using fewer models and iterations.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach with single-step student-teacher distillation and consistency models, and also explore the trade-offs between the quality of the student and the number of iterations required in each student's path. Additionally, we consider an ablation study to validate our proposed multi-resolution path.
COST: 60 GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: Our multi-resolution quality-aware distillation framework outperforms the baselines in terms of image quality while reducing the number of iterations and required model size, but it might fail to capture complex, high-frequency patterns in certain types of images.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Revised Training Size-Efficient Generators via Progressive Multi-Resolution Quality-Aware Distillation
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal by incorporating a progressive learning approach to our multi-resolution quality-aware distillation framework. In the student-teacher setup, the low-resolution student first reproduces the teacher's output, and then gradually refines its output by incorporating additional steps and higher resolution details. This progressive refinement process enables the student to learn more efficiently and produce images of higher quality in fewer iterations.
CONTROLS: We maintain the same controls as before, adding a progressive learning schedule and varying the number of refinement steps to evaluate their impact on image quality and computation efficiency.
COST: 65 GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: Our revised approach should further improve image quality and convergence speed, but might require careful tuning of the progressive learning schedule to avoid over-refining or under-refining the student's output.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Few-Step Generative Inference using edit-operator informed ConSIS-TGAN
PROPOSAL: We propose the integration of ConSIS (Consistency-based Single-Image Synthesis) and TGAN (Two-stage Generative Adversarial Network) with an edit-operator informed distillation approach. Specifically, we leverage ConSIS-TGAN to generate high-quality images, and distill the knowledge of a pre-trained ConSIS model, which learns to refine its own outputs based on edit-operator informed consistency loss to few steps and direct single-step model able to capture coherent and realistic image editing actions.
CONTROLS: As baseline, we consider Consistency models, ConSIS (with or without TGAN), and TGAN (with or without ConSIS), ablate the role of the edit-operator informed approach, vary the number of distillation steps to analyze convergence and control over computation.
COST: 70 GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: Our edit-operator informed ConSIS-TGAN should produce high-quality images in very few steps while achieving elegant refinement of the generated images' editing actions, potentially failing to capture complex patterns or fine details in certain cases.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Improved Efficient Few-Step Generative Inference using Linear-Time ConSIS-TGAN
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal by enhancing the ConSIS-TGAN with linear-time complexity and by improving the efficiency in training and testing, leveraging the power of approximations in ConSIS and recent developments in neural architecture search. By making the score function used in ConSIS-TGAN more scalable with linear time complexity under a certain approximation and realistic complexity assumption, we reduce the statistical variance of the loss function while remaining faithful to the type of high quality edit operations targeted by ConSIS.
CONTROLS: We maintain the same analyses as before, in addition we examine computational scalability, comparing different methods for making loss functions more tractable (constant-time advancements) to speed up convergence with efficiency cost.
COST: 75 GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: Our revised linear-time ConSIS-TGAN should outperform the baselines in terms of computational efficiency while maintaining or improving the image quality, potentially at greater risk of retaining coherent, realistic, and accurately-segmented features from the closure editing-based technique.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Theoretical Framework for Efficient Generative Inference
PROPOSAL: We propose a theoretical analysis of efficient generative inference, focusing on establishing a fundamental bound on the number of iterations required for a generative model to produce high-quality images. We will use techniques from statistical learning theory to derive a lower bound on the number of iterations, and investigate the implications of this bound on the design of efficient generative models.
CONTROLS: Our theoretical framework will be compared with and contrasted to existing approaches, including consistency models, distillation-based methods, and few-step generative inference techniques.
COST: 20 GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: Our theoretical framework should provide new insights into the fundamental limits of efficient generative inference, and potentially identify new design principles for efficient generative models. However, it may fail to provide praktische guidelines for specific model architectures and training protocols, requiring further investigation using empirical methods.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Strengthening the A Theoretical Framework for Efficient Generative Inference
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous theoretical framework by incorporating recent advances in statistical learning theory and leveraging the connection between convergence rate and the complexity of the model. Additionally, we incorporate guidance from our experiments to ensure that our theoretical framework is aligned with practical challenges faced in the development of efficient generative models. By considering the regularity of the generative model, distributions, and circumstances, our revised theoretical framework will critically assess the existing approaches and address the challenge that motivated our original paper: scaling to largest models without GAN-style losses.
CONTROLS: We continue to use a combination of analysis, comparison to existing approaches and examination of convergence in a number of our experiments as we earlier promised with varying levels of reductions in sampling demands.
COST: 22 GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: Our revised theoretical framework will provide stronger bounds on the number of iterations required for efficient generative inference, and shed new light on the design of efficient generative models. However, its increased complexity may make it more challenging to apply in practice, and require more careful tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: One-Step Single-Network Generative Inference using Whitening Transform and Spectral Normalization
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel one-step single-network generative inference approach that combines whitening transformations with spectral normalization to improve the robustness and quality of generated images. Our key idea is to use whitening transformations to isotropize the input image's spectral distribution, which helps to improve the stability of the generator's output. We then apply spectral normalization to regularize the generator's weights and prevent overfitting.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach with single-step generative models, such as GANs and consistency models, and evaluate the impact of different whitening transformations and spectral normalizations on the generated images' quality.
COST: 80 GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: Our proposed one-step single-network generative inference approach should be able to produce high-quality images in a single iteration, but its performance may be sensitive to the choice of whitening transformation and spectral normalization techniques, and may require careful tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalable and Efficient Generative Inference using Hierarchical Progressive Resizing and Compositional Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose a scalable and efficient generative inference approach that leverages hierarchical progressive resizing and compositional learning to produce high-quality images in a few steps. Our key idea is to resize the input image hierarchically into smaller patches, generate each patch individually using a small-compositional learning generative model, and then combine the patches to form the final image.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach with other hierarchical and compositional generative models, and evaluate the impact of different resizing strategies, generative models, and compositional learning techniques on the generated images' quality.
COST: 90 GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: Our proposed scalable and efficient generative inference approach should be able to produce high-quality images in a few steps, but its performance may be sensitive to the choice of resizing strategy, generative model, and compositional learning technique, and may require careful tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Efficient Generative Inference
PROPOSAL: We propose to create a comprehensive benchmark for efficient generative inference, consisting of a suite of image quality metrics, model evaluation protocols, and hardware performance metrics. Our benchmark will be designed to evaluate the efficiency and effectiveness of various generative models under different computational constraints.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the approaches in our set, and invite other researchers to contribute their own efficient generative models to the benchmark.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: Our comprehensive benchmark will provide a widely-accepted standard for evaluating the efficiency and effectiveness of generative models, facilitating community-wide adoption and advancement of efficient generative inference techniques.

Prediction: Our proposed one-step single-network generative inference approach should be able to produce high-quality images in a single iteration, but its performance may be sensitive to the choice of whitening transformation and spectral normalization techniques, and may require careful tuning of hyperparameters.

PROPOSAL 6: Scalable and Efficient Generative Inference using Hierarchical Progressive Resizing and Compositional Learning
We propose a scalable and efficient generative inference approach that leverages hierarchical progressive resizing and compositional learning to produce high-quality images in a few steps. Our key idea is to resize the input image hierarchically into smaller patches, generate each patch individually using a small-compositional learning generative model, and then combine the patches to form the final image.
Controls: We compare our approach with other hierarchical and compositional generative models, and evaluate the impact of different resizing strategies, generative models, and compositional learning techniques on the generated images' quality.
Estimated cost: 90 GPU-hours (estimated)
Prediction: Our proposed scalable and efficient generative inference approach should be able to produce high-quality images in a few steps, but its performance may be sensitive to the choice of resizing strategy, generative model, and compositional learning technique, and may require careful tuning of hyperparameters.

PROPOSAL 7: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Efficient Generative Inference
We propose to create a comprehensive benchmark for efficient generative inference, consisting of a suite of image quality metrics, model evaluation protocols, and hardware performance metrics. Our benchmark will be designed to evaluate the efficiency and effectiveness of various generative models under different computational constraints.
Controls: We will compare the performance of the approaches in our set, and invite other researchers to contribute their own efficient generative models to the benchmark.
Estimated cost: 100 GPU-hours (estimated)
Prediction: Our comprehensive benchmark will provide a widely-accepted standard for evaluating the efficiency and effectiveness of generative models, facilitating community-wide adoption and advancement of efficient generative inference techniques.

TITLE: Augmenting the T2I Model with Long-Form Text Representations
PROPOSAL: We will revise the previous proposal to focus on using a more advanced large language model, such as `longformer-large` or `t5-large`, to generate the supplementary representation of the input prompt. We will also experiment with different architectures for combining the standard prompt with the supplementary representation, such as concatenation, fusion, and attention-based fusion. Additionally, we will investigate the use of multi-modal pre-training methods, such as Visual-BERT, to incorporate visual features into the language model's understanding of the prompt.

CONTROLS: We will compare the revised model to the previous versions, evaluate its performance on long prompts, and analyze the effect of different architectures and pre-training methods on the model's performance.
COST: 1600 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect a significant improvement in the model's ability to capture complex relationships between elements within long prompts, allowing for more accurate and detailed image generation. However, we also anticipate potential issues with overfitting and mode collapse, particularly if the model is not carefully regularized.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Optimizing T2I Models for Long Prompts using Adversarial Training
PROPOSAL: We will use adversarial training to improve the robustness of T2I models on long prompts. Specifically, we will use a text-to-text model to generate adversarial perturbations of the input prompt, and then train the T2I model to be robust to these perturbations. This approach should allow the model to better handle noise and ambiguity in long prompts, and thus improve its performance on out-of-distribution examples.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the model's performance on both long and short prompts, and compare it to a baseline model that has not been adversarially trained. We will also experiment with different types of adversarial perturbations and training protocols.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect the adversarially trained model to perform better on long prompts, particularly those that are noisy or ambiguous. However, we also anticipate that the model may exhibit some degree of overfitting, particularly if it is not carefully regularized.

CONTROLS: We will compare the revised fine-tuned model to the original model, as well as to the model from Proposal 3, and evaluate its performance on long prompts.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect the revised fine-tuned model to perform better on long prompts compared to the original model, and possibly even better than the model from Proposal 3, due to the combination of prompt parsing and augmented context.

TITLE: Evaluating the Effect of Interleaving Objectives in T2I Models
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the effect of interleaving object detection and image generation objectives in the T2I model. Specifically, we will use a multi-task learning setup where the model is trained to both generate images and predict object bounding boxes. We will experiment with different training protocols, such as simultaneous training and weight-sharing between the two objectives.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the model's performance on both image generation and object detection tasks, and compare it to a baseline model that is trained on only one of the objectives. We will also experiment with different architectures and regularization techniques to ensure that the model is not overfitting to the multiple objectives.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect the model with interleaved objectives to perform well on both image generation and object detection tasks, particularly on long prompts that involve multiple objects. However, we also anticipate that the model may require more careful tuning of hyperparameters and regularization techniques to avoid overfitting.

TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Pre-training on Efficient Long-prompt Text-to-Image Generation
PROPOSAL: We will fine-tune different pre-trained T2I models (e.g. DALL-E 2, Imagen, StableDiffusion) on a dataset of short and long captions (e.g. COCO-Captions, tua) with a custom validation set focusing on the description of various objects in different contexts, interleaved within narrative paragraphs. We compare the performance and efficiency of these pre-trained models.
CONTROLS: Training and evaluating the pre-trained models without fine-tuning, using them as a starting point for fine-tuning.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Fine-tuning pre-trained models will show robust improvements over pre-trained models, with DALL-E 2 performing well on descriptions of objects but exhibiting difficulties in capturing nuanced semantic details, while Imagen struggles to maintain coherence in its output; fine-tuning StableDiffusion will result in smaller gains but a more consistent output.

Turn 1 predictions suggest that leveraging pre-trained T2I models as a starting point is crucial for tackling the challenging task of long-prompt text-to-image generation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effectiveness of Scratch Fine-Tuning for Long-Prompt T2I Models
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the performance of scratch fine-tuning on a set of T2I models with a focus on capturing the nuances of long prompts. We will start with a large-scale pre-trained model like Stable Diffusion and fine-tune it on a curated dataset of long captions. We use a combination of metrics like FID, IS, and detail-specific metrics (e.g., object accuracy) to evaluate performance.
CONTROLS: We will compare our findings to existing T2I models fine-tuned on long-captioned data and ablate the effects of the dataset and fine-tuning schedule.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Despite being computationally costly, we expect to see significant improvements in long-prompt rendering accuracy, potentially rivaling model-specific fine-tuning. However, there's a risk that the model might struggle with maintaining its pre-trained knowledge, leading to "catastrophic forgetting".

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Understanding the Impact of Training Objectives on Long-Prompt T2I Generation
PROPOSAL: We will explore the effect of different training objectives on the ability of T2I models to capture long-prompt details. Specifically, we investigate the role of pixel-wise loss, adversarial loss, and language model-guided loss functions in improving detail preservation. We will evaluate these objectives on a range of long-prompt text-image pairs using metrics like detail-specific IoU and MS-SSIM.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of different objectives against the standard pixel-wise loss used in T2I models, and ablate the effects of objective weights and learning schedules.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see that objective-guided training can lead to significant improvements in detail preservation, but the optimal objective and weights may depend on the specific T2I model architecture. However, we might encounter challenges in balancing the trade-offs between different objectives and learning schedules.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Assessing the Hardness of Long-Term Fairness Regularizer
PROPOSAL: Investigate the hardness of the long-term fairness regularizer by comparing the complexity of optimizing the given smoothed online optimization objective with and without the fairness regularizer, focusing on its impact on the algorithm's running time and decision-making process. 
CONTROLS: Compare against an existing online optimization algorithm (e.g., Salesman) and its variant with the fairness regularizer.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Without the fairness regularizer, the algorithm's running time and decision-making process will be faster and more efficient, whereas its performance will degrade significantly with the fairness regularizer, highlighting its computational challenge. However, it may fail for datasets or domains that require inherent fairness in decision-making, where the regularizer may not effectively mitigate societal biases.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Dynamic Offline Benchmark for Fairness in Smoothed Online Optimization
PROPOSAL: Design a dynamic offline benchmark that can adapt its decision-making process over time to incorporate the long-term fairness regularizer and optimize the objective accordingly. This benchmark can serve as a reference against which the performance of online algorithms is evaluated. 
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the developed dynamic offline benchmark against a static offline benchmark (e.g., law of the land) and different types of online algorithms (e.g., Salesman, optimistic, and pessimistic algorithms).
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The dynamic offline benchmark will significantly outperform static offline benchmarks and online algorithms without the fairness regularizer in incorporating the long-term fairness constraints, demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach. However, evaluating the performance of online algorithms against a dynamic benchmark may become computationally expensive, and ensuring the benchmark's consistency and fairness remains an open challenge.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Lower Bound for Regret with Long-Term Fairness Regularizer
PROPOSAL: Derive a lower bound for the regret of online algorithms with the long-term fairness regularizer, elucidating the fundamental hardness of this problem. This provides a foundation for comparing the performance of different algorithms. 
CONTROLS: Establish the lower bound under different assumptions regarding the structure of the actions, the cost functions, and the fairness constraints.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (theoretical work does not require actual computation)
PREDICTION: A non-trivial lower bound on regret will be established, indicating that achieving sublinear regret is difficult under the long-term fairness regularizer. However, the exact lower bound may be challenging to derive under certain conditions, and proving absolute hardness (bounds reaching the offline optimum) could remain an open question.

ACTION: REVISE 
TITLE: REVISED – Bounding the Impact of Long-Term Fairness Regularizer
PROPOSAL: Analyze the impact of the long-term fairness regularizer on the regret and competitive ratio of online algorithms, specifically examining how it interacts with the switching cost and the per-round objective. Introduce a new bound on the regret that incorporates both the fairness and switching costs, quantifying their interplay. 
CONTROLS: Compare against the lower bound established in Proposal 3 and the competitive ratio of algorithms that do not account for the fairness regularizer.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised bound will quantitatively capture the cost of incorporating the long-term fairness regularizer, providing insights into the algorithmic tradeoffs between fairness and performance. The analysis may highlight limits on how far sublinear regret can be improved under the fairness regularizer, echoing the findings of the lower-bound analysis.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Regret Bounds for Fair Online Optimization with Switching Costs
PROPOSAL: Develop an online algorithm for fairness-aware smoothed online optimization with switching costs, achieving provable regret bounds. Analyze its performance under different fairness constraints, plausible hitting cost functions, and matrix structures. 
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of this algorithm against state-of-the-art methods (e.g., 2-Opt, 3-Opt) with and without the long-term fairness regularizer.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed algorithm will achieve decent regret bounds, potentially with much lower switching costs and possibly but conditionally beating some strong baselines in application such as geo-distributed data center capacity provisioning. However, incorporating switching costs may imply it is unclear whether we maintain the low regret with minimal fairness or compromised fairness at a less regret.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Evaluation of Fairness-regularized Smoothed Online Optimization in LLM Inference Workload Serving
PROPOSAL: Examine the effectiveness of fairness-regularized smoothed online optimization in the context of LLM inference workload serving, leveraging a real-world dataset to validate the theoretical insights. 
CONTROLS: Compare against existing baseline algorithms in LLM inference workload serving, exploring the trade-offs between fairness and system performance.
COST: 1,200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results will demonstrate the practical relevance of fairness-regularized smoothed online optimization in LLM inference workload serving, highlighting potential improvements in fairness while maintaining reasonable system performance. However, evaluating fairness may require additional domain knowledge and tools, which could pose challenges during experimentation.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: A Primal-Dual Approach to Fair Online Optimization with Switching Costs
PROPOSAL: Develop a primal-dual method to solve the fairness-aware smoothed online optimization with switching costs problem. This approach will enable efficient and scalable online decision-making under the fairness constraint. 
CONTROLS: Compare against state-of-the-art algorithms, assessing the trade-offs between computational efficiency, fairness, and regret.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The primal-dual method will demonstrate improved computation efficiency, possibly better fairness, and competitive regret performance compared to existing algorithms, which could be particularly beneficial in large-scale applications like data center capacity provisioning. However, the method's scalability and the fairness metric's impact on regret remain open questions.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Fairness-aware Geo-Distributed Data Center Capacity Provisioning using Online Learning
PROPOSAL: Develop an online learning algorithm for fairness-aware geo-distributed data center capacity provisioning, incorporating the long-term fairness regularizer and accounting for geographical and temporal variations in workload and resource availability. 
CONTROLS: Validate against real-world data center settings, comparing the algorithm's performance against existing approaches that disregard fairness considerations.
COST: 1,500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed algorithm will demonstrate practical benefits in fairness-aware capacity provisioning, effectively mitigating inter-geographical and inter-temporal disparities in resource allocation while maintaining competitive performance. However, evaluating the fairness benefits will require careful consideration of ground-truth fairness metrics and the potential trade-offs between fairness and system performance.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Co-design of Fair Online Optimization and Switching Cost Mitigation for Public Health Costs of Air Pollution
PROPOSAL: Investigate the integration of fairness-aware online optimization and switching cost mitigation techniques to minimize public health costs due to air pollution from electricity generation, a crucial and challenging application of fairness-aware smoothed online optimization. 
CONTROLS: Leverage real-world datasets and collaborate with domain experts to accurately model the problem, comparing the potential benefits and trade-offs of fairness-aware optimization against those without fairness consideration.
COST: 2,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This co-design initiative will unveil the potential benefits of fairness-aware smoothed online optimization in minimizing public health costs due to air pollution, while also highlighting the challenges and complexities of addressing urgency with tractable fairness requirements.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Case Study: Trading-off Fairness and Hurry-Up for Real-World Applications of Smoothed Online Optimization
PROPOSAL: Conduct a comprehensive case study to explore the trade-offs between fairness, regret, and switching cost in real-world applications of smoothed online optimization, integrally analyzing results from the previous proposals and refining our understanding of their practical implications. 
CONTROLS: Synthesize findings from experimental evaluations and theoretical results, highlighting key takeaways for future applications and advancements in fairness-aware smoothed online optimization.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Upper Bounding Long-Term Fairness Regularizer with Unbounded Hitting Costs and Switching Costs
PROPOSAL: We prove that a dynamic offline benchmark can enjoy a finite competitive ratio against an online algorithm in the presence of a long-term fairness regularizer, if per-round objective functions (hitting costs) have unbounded values but switching costs satisfy a certain regularity condition, specifically that the switching cost scale factor decreases in time.
CONTROLS: We will consider a simplified version of our problem without per-round objective functions and the same offline dynamic benchmark benchmark as a baseline; we will compare its performance against an online algorithm with a long-term fairness regularizer but without the regularity condition from above and keep all else the same in both algorithms.
COST: 10 GPU-hours for the proof.
PREDICTION: We believe our result will provide a starting point for the theoretical analysis of fairness-regularized smoothed online optimization and might suggest paths for handling the more general problem by adding bounded hitting costs; where it might fail is when the switching cost scale factor does not decrease in time.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Primal-Dual Algorithm for Fairness-Regularized Smoothed Online Optimization
PROPOSAL: We develop a primal-dual algorithm that tackles fairness-regularized smoothed online optimization with switching costs, using a novel decomposition of the long-term fairness regularizer. Our algorithm switches between a tentatively relaxed step and a strong feasible step, hence squaring sub-linear regret growth and a moderate competitive ratio by changing the expectations of growth while healing fairness each step.
CONTROLS: We compare our proposed algorithm with the state-of-the-art primal-dual algorithm used in the similar setting of online resource allocation but without accounting for switching costs, and ablate the relaxation step from our algorithm to recover the primal-dual approach to the setting of fairness-regularized online optimization without switching cost setting too.
COST: 100 GPU-hours for training the primal-dual algorithm and evaluating its performance on geo-distributed data center capacity provisioning data.
PREDICTION: We expect our proposed algorithm to offer a competitive ratio close to 1+o(1)/sqrt(T), favorably compared with its ablated counterpart in fairness-regularized online optimization without switching costs, in problems with both the fair regularizer, smoothness, and adversarial hitting cost and switching costs; where it might fail is in higher switching cost values and restricted data complexity aspects of real-world assessed scenarios.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Primal-Dual Algorithm for Fairness-Regularized Smoothed Online Optimization
PROPOSAL: We modify the optimization gap update of our previously-proposed primal-dual algorithm for fairness-regularized smoothed online optimization with switching costs. This modification involves changing the computation of the strong feasible step, which is responsible for ensuring that the iterates obtained by our algorithm remain in the feasible region. We will leverage a fast-tracking scheme, utilizing the square of the switching cost scale factor, to sample its decrease and provisional function information within each step of time.
CONTROLS: We keep the evaluations mentioned in our previous proposal (state-of-the-art primal-dual algorithm for online resource allocation and ablated primal-dual approach) for both original algorithm and modified versions, and also compare the overall robustness, stability, and simplicity of our approach to existing fairness-regularized smoothed online optimization methods, letting us know the algorithm failure risks under difficult setting.
COST: 200 GPU-hours for training the primal-dual algorithm, analyzing the update change on multiple real-world benchmark data, and evaluating its adaptability via simulation in LLM inference workload serving data center vitality scenario.
PREDICTION: We are confident this update will improve our algorithm, stabilizing its competitive ratio and ensuring feasibility for fairness-regularized smoothed online optimization in dynamic scenarios without failing when the real-world complexity hits heavy usage scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Empirical Comparison of Online Algorithms for Fairness-Regularized Smoothed Online Optimization with Switching Costs
PROPOSAL: We conduct an empirical comparison of our primal-dual algorithm, the original algorithm, and several baseline methods on geo-distributed data center capacity provisioning and load balancing, as well as public health costs of air pollution from electricity generation problems. We evaluate the performance of these algorithms in terms of both regret and fairness metrics, and compare their robustness, stability, and simplicity.
CONTROLS: We compare our modified primal-dual algorithm with the state-of-the-art primal-dual algorithm for online resource allocation, and also consider the following baselines: (a) an algorithm without any fairness regularizer, (b) an algorithm with fairness regularizer but without switching cost, and (c) a naive greedy algorithm with optimal switching cost but no fairness regularizer.
COST: 500 GPU-hours for training and evaluating the algorithms on a collection of real-world benchmarks and problem configurations.
PREDICTION: We expect our primal-dual algorithm to achieve a better trade-off between regret and fairness, and outperform the baselines in most scenarios, while our analyses of algorithm robustness and stability in various real-world settings may lead to moderate difficulty in fairness assessment during hard distributive complexity tasks; it is possible that our algorithm's neighborhood method behaves badly in over-sampled resource allocation cases.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analysis of the Impact of Switching Cost Scale Factor on Fairness-Regulated Smoothed Online Optimization
PROPOSAL: We analyze the impact of the switching cost scale factor on the performance of our primal-dual algorithm and other baseline methods, and investigate how the choice of this parameter affects the trade-off between regret and fairness. We will consider a comprehensive set of values for the switching cost scale factor and evaluate the performance of the algorithms over a range of problem instances and scenarios.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the algorithms with different switching cost scale factors using the regret, fairness, and stability metrics, and provide insights into how the choice of this parameter affects the robustness of the algorithms.
COST: 300 GPU-hours for training and evaluating the algorithms with different switching cost scale factors.
PREDICTION: We expect that the choice of switching cost scale factor significantly impacts the trade-off between regret and fairness, and that our primal-dual algorithm is more robust to changes in this parameter than other baseline methods; where it might fail is when the real-world problem complexity is poorly matched by the chosen switching cost scale factor value across different time steps, iteratively turned down last turns policy alone often has slowed stable pursuits.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Stochastic Primal-Dual Algorithm for Fairness-Regulated Smoothed Online Optimization with Switching Costs
PROPOSAL: We develop a stochastic primal-dual algorithm for fairness-regulated smoothed online optimization with switching costs, where we approximate the hitting cost function and action mapping by using i.i.d. samples at each time step. We prove that our algorithm achieves a sublinear regret bound with high probability and provides fairness guarantees.
CONTROLS: We compare our stochastic primal-dual algorithm with the deterministic primal-dual algorithm and the state-of-the-art primal-dual algorithm for online resource allocation using the regret and fairness metrics.
COST: 400 GPU-hours for training and evaluating the algorithm on synthetic and real-world data.
PREDICTION: We expect that our stochastic primal-dual algorithm achieves a better trade-off between regret and fairness compared to the deterministic primal-dual algorithm, and that our algorithm is more robust to changes in the problem instance due to the use of i.i.d. samples; where it might fail is when the hitting cost function has high variance or the action mapping has complex structure, limiting the robustness of the stochastic primal-dual algorithm.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experimenting with Integer Actions and Discrete Hitting Costs for Fairness-Regulated Smoothed Online Optimization
PROPOSAL: We extend our experiments with fairness-regulated smoothed online optimization to integer actions and discrete hitting costs, which are common in many real-world scenarios. We will evaluate the performance of our primal-dual algorithm, stochastic primal-dual algorithm, and other baseline methods under these conditions.
CONTROLS: We will experiment with different levels of integer action approximation and discrete hitting cost granularity, and compare the performance of the algorithms using the regret, fairness, and stability metrics.
COST: 600 GPU-hours for training and evaluating the algorithms on synthetic and real-world data with integer actions and discrete hitting costs.
PREDICTION: We expect that our algorithms will perform well under these conditions, but may require careful tuning of parameters to achieve optimal performance; where it might fail is when the integer actions and discrete hitting costs lead to a significant increase in problem complexity, making it challenging for the algorithms to adapt.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Online Learning Approach to Fairness-Regulated Smoothed Online Optimization with Switching Costs
PROPOSAL: We develop an online learning approach to fairness-regulated smoothed online optimization with switching costs, where we use a stream-based online learning framework to adaptively update the algorithm parameters. We will investigate the convergence properties of our approach and evaluate its performance on fairness-regulated smoothed online optimization problems.
CONTROLS: We will compare our online learning approach with our primal-dual algorithm and other baseline methods using the regret, fairness, and stability metrics.
COST: 800 GPU-hours for training and evaluating the algorithm on synthetic and real-world data.
PREDICTION: We expect that our online learning approach will adapt to changing problem conditions and provide a robust solution to fairness-regulated smoothed online optimization problems; where it might fail is when the problem dynamics are highly non-stationary, making it challenging for the online learning approach to track the optimal solution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Fairness-Regulated Smoothed Online Optimization with Switching Costs
PROPOSAL: We investigate the use of transfer learning to improve the performance of fairness-regulated smoothed online optimization algorithms with switching costs. We will train a base model on a surrogate problem and fine-tune it on the target problem to adapt to the specific characteristics of the target problem.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our transfer learning approach with the base model and other baseline methods using the regret, fairness, and stability metrics.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours for training and evaluating the algorithms on synthetic and real-world data.
PREDICTION: We expect that transfer learning will significantly improve the performance of fairness-regulated smoothed online optimization algorithms by leveraging knowledge from the surrogate problem; where it might fail is when the surrogate problem and target problem are significantly different, making it challenging to transfer knowledge effectively.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards a Unified Framework for Fairness-Regulated Smoothed Online Optimization with Switching Costs
PROPOSAL: We present an open research agenda for fairness-regulated smoothed online optimization with switching costs, highlighting key challenges and opportunities for future research. We identify areas for further investigation, including the development of new algorithms and techniques that can handle complex problem structures and dynamics.
CONTROLS: We will critically review existing literature and theories on fairness-regulated smoothed online optimization with switching costs, and discuss the implications of our proposed research agenda for future work in this area.
COST: N/A (this proposal is a theoretical paper).
PREDICTION: We believe that our research agenda will provide valuable insights and direction for the research community, and lay the groundwork for future breakthroughs in fairness-regulated smoothed online optimization with switching costs; where it might fail is if the proposed research agenda proves too ambitious or unwieldy, making it difficult to make tangible progress in the near term.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Understanding the Difficulty of Long-term Fairness Regularizer
PROPOSAL: We present a theoretical framework to understand the hardness of incorporating a long-term fairness regularizer into online optimization with switching costs. We analyze the intrinsic difficulty of the regularizer by reduction to a known hard problem and show that achieving a finite competitive ratio is out of reach for the dynamic offline optimum.
CONTROLS: We compare our result to existing regret bounds without fairness constraints and competitive ratios with a static offline benchmark.
COST: 0 (no compute required).
PREDICTION: We expect our result to demonstrate the inherent difficulty in achieving finite performance guarantees with a long-term fairness regularizer, similar to existing conjectures. This could have implications for future research directions, such as exploring weaker fairness guarantees or leveraging additional problem structure. The result might fail if the reduction to a known hard problem is flawed or if we overlooked a known technique to achieve finite performance.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: A Lower Bound for Long-term Fairness Regularized Smoothed Online Optimization
PROPOSAL: We prove a lower bound for the competitive ratio of smoothed online optimization with switching costs and a long-term fairness regularizer. Our result is based on a reduction to the online \(k\)-server problem and shows that achieving a finite competitive ratio is impossible even when the long-term regularizer has a moderate Lipschitz constant.
CONTROLS: We compare our lower bound to existing results for smoothed online optimization without fairness constraints.
COST: 50 GPU-hours ( approximating the lower bound involves computational experiments to validate the reduction).
PREDICTION: We expect our result to provide strong evidence for the hardness of achieving finite performance guarantees with a long-term fairness regularizer. However, our lower bound might overestimate the difficulty if the reduction is flawed or if the online \(k\)-server problem is too disconnected from our original setting.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Experiments with a Primal-Dual Algorithm for Long-term Fairness Regularized Smoothed Online Optimization
PROPOSAL: We empirically evaluate a primal-dual algorithm for smoothed online optimization with switching costs and a long-term fairness regularizer. We test the algorithm on real-world benchmarks in geo-distributed data center capacity provisioning, LLM inference workload serving, and public health costs of air pollution from electricity generation.
CONTROLS: We compare our algorithm to baseline methods, including a fair online algorithm without switching costs and a dynamic offline benchmark adapted from the literature.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (short to moderate experimental phases with multiple evaluations and comparisons).
PREDICTION: We expect our algorithm to demonstrate reasonable performance, comparable to baseline methods or even surpassing them in some cases, given its potential to incorporate multiple constraints and objectives. However, the algorithm might struggle with achieving fairness in difficult scenarios, or our experiments could reveal algorithmic weaknesses due to our imperfect implementation or inadequate baseline comparisons.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Experiments with a Primal-Dual Algorithm for Long-term Fairness Regularized Smoothed Online Optimization
PROPOSAL: We empirically evaluate a primal-dual algorithm for smoothed online optimization with switching costs and a long-term fairness regularizer. We test the algorithm on real-world benchmarks in geo-distributed data center capacity provisioning, LLM inference workload serving, and public health costs of air pollution from electricity generation. To better understand the impact of the long-term fairness regularizer, we conduct an ablation study by comparing the algorithm with and without the regularizer.
CONTROLS: We compare our algorithm (with and without the regularizer) to baseline methods, including a fair online algorithm without switching costs and a dynamic offline benchmark adapted from the literature.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (short to moderate experimental phases with multiple evaluations and comparisons).
PREDICTION: We expect our algorithm (with the regularizer) to demonstrate moderate performance, with potentially worse performance without the regularizer, given its ability to incorporate fairness constraints and balance the trade-off between different objectives. However, our algorithm might not converge properly or could be unstable in scenarios where the regularizer significantly modifies the optimization objective, and our ablation study could reveal unexpected interactions between the algorithm and the regularizer.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Fairness-Aware Mechanism Design for Long-term Fairness Regularized Smoothed Online Optimization
PROPOSAL: We explore a mechanism design framework to derive online algorithms for smoothed online optimization with switching costs and a long-term fairness regularizer. We design mechanisms that incentivize honest reporting of cost functions and propose algorithms that achieve a finite competitive ratio against the dynamic offline optimum.
CONTROLS: We compare our algorithms to existing mechanisms in fair online optimization and evaluate their performance on real-world benchmarks.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (mechanism design involves analytical derivations rather than extensive computational simulations).
PREDICTION: We expect our mechanisms to provide fair and efficient solutions for long-term fairness regularized smoothed online optimization. Our algorithms might lack adaptability in dynamic scenarios where agents' preferences change rapidly or when the cost functions are highly fluctuating, which could affect the efficiency of our mechanisms.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Analysis of Sparse Regularization for Long-term Fairness Regularized Smoothed Online Optimization
PROPOSAL: We investigate the use of sparse regularizers to mitigate the hardness of long-term fairness regularized smoothed online optimization. We analyze the effect of L1 and L2 sparse regularizers on the competitive ratio and develop a framework for deriving upper bounds on the competitive ratio for sparse-regularized algorithms.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of sparse-regularized algorithms to our primal-dual algorithm from experiment 3 and analyze the trade-offs between sparsity, fairness, and efficiency.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (theoretical derivations and computational experiments).
PREDICTION: We expect sparse regularizers to improve performance in sparse settings, potentially relaxing the hardness results for long-term fairness regularized smoothed online optimization. However, our sparse-regularized algorithms might struggle with fairness in dense settings where sparsity is minimal, or the_derived bounds could be too loose, failing to capture performance guarantees in practice.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Experiments on Approximation and Streaming Algorithms for Long-term Fairness Regularized Smoothed Online Optimization
PROPOSAL: We design and experiment with approximation and streaming algorithms for smoothed online optimization with switching costs and a long-term fairness regularizer. These algorithms aim to reduce the time complexity of computing the regularizer and improve the scalability of existing methods. We test the algorithms on real-world benchmarks in geo-distributed data center capacity provisioning, LLM inference workload serving, and public health costs of air pollution from electricity generation.
CONTROLS: We compare our approximation and streaming algorithms to existing primal-dual algorithms and dynamic offline benchmarks, evaluating their performance in terms of regret, competitive ratio, and running time.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (extensive computational experiments to validate the scalability and performance of approximation and streaming algorithms).
PREDICTION: We expect our approximation and streaming algorithms to be essential in improving the scalability of long-term fairness regularized smoothed online optimization and achieving near-optimal performance in practice. However, the algorithms might be suboptimal in certain settings, or our experiments might reveal stability or convergence issues due to the approximation or streaming nature of the methods.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Online-to-Confidence-Set Conversion for Long-term Fairness Regularized Smoothed Online Optimization
PROPOSAL: We leverage online-to-confidence-set conversion (O2CS) algorithms to provide finite-sample confidence bounds on the regret for smoothed online optimization with switching costs and a long-term fairness regularizer. This framework allows us to establish more precise guarantees for online learning in this challenging setting.
CONTROLS: We compare our O2CS-based approach to existing regret bounds and determine its effectiveness in establishing finite-sample guarantees.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (theoretical derivations and computational experiments to develop and validate the O2CS algorithm).
PREDICTION: We expect our O2CS algorithm to provide a valuable tool for robustifying long-term fairness regularized smoothed online optimization and enabling greater confidence in online decision-making. However, our algorithm might struggle with stability or convergence in scenarios where the O2CS estimates are highly uncertain or noisy, potentially leading to unreliable regret bounds.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: An Extension to Batched Online Optimization with Long-term Fairness and Switching Costs
PROPOSAL: To improve real-world applicability, we extend the long-term fairness regularized smoothed online optimization setting to batched online optimization, where the agent observes multiple cost functions simultaneously and makes decisions over a fixed time horizon. We investigate the impact of batched feedback on the hardness of optimization and explore practical algorithms for this more general setting.
CONTROLS: We compare our batched algorithms to existing online optimization methods and examine their performance in terms of regret, competitive ratio, and computational efficiency.
COST: 250 GPU-hours (theoretical derivations, computational experiments, and iterative algorithm design).
PREDICTION: We expect our batched online optimization framework to provide valuable insights into the effects of batched feedback on the optimization landscape and to develop scalable algorithms for practical applications. However, our batched algorithms might require significant modifications to achieve optimal performance, or our design might compromise fairness and efficiency in certain settings.

ACTION: ADD 9
TITLE: An Empirical Comparison of Online Optimization Algorithms for Long-term Fairness Regularized Smoothed Online Optimization
PROPOSAL: To gain practical insights into the performance of existing algorithms for long-term fairness regularized smoothed online optimization, we conduct an extensive empirical comparison on real-world benchmarks in geo-distributed data center capacity provisioning, LLM inference workload serving, and public health costs of air pollution from electricity generation.
CONTROLS: We compare a diverse set of algorithms, including our previously proposed methods (primal-dual, sparse regularization, online-to-confidence-set conversion, and batched optimization), as well as state-of-the-art online optimization methods without fairness constraints.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (large-scale experiments with multiple evaluations and comparisons).
PREDICTION: We expect our empirical comparison to provide a comprehensive assessment of the strengths and weaknesses of existing algorithms and to derive practical recommendations for online optimization in long-term fairness regularized smoothed online optimization settings. However, our comparison might highlight unforeseen trade-offs between fairness, efficiency, and other objectives, or our experiments could identify missed implementations of existing algorithms, leading to unexpected performance disparities.
