propositions.texte: We design and experiment with approximation and streaming algorithms for smoothed online optimization with switching costs and a long-term fairness regularizer. These algorithms aim to reduce the time complexity of computing the regularizer and improve the scalability of existing methods. We test the algorithms on real-world benchmarks in geo-distributed data center capacity provisioning, LLM inference workload serving, and public health costs of air pollution from electricity generation.
propositions.titre: Experiments on Approximation and Streaming Algorithms for Long-term Fairness Regularized Smoothed Online Optimization

propositions.controles: We compare our O2CS-based approach to existing regret bounds and determine its effectiveness in establishing finite-sample guarantees.
propositions.cout_texte: 100 GPU-hours (theoretical derivations and computational experiments to develop and validate the O2CS algorithm).
propositions.prediction: We expect our O2CS algorithm to provide a valuable tool for robustifying long-term fairness regularized smoothed online optimization and enabling greater confidence in online decision-making. However, our algorithm might struggle with stability or convergence in scenarios where the O2CS estimates are highly uncertain or noisy, potentially leading to unreliable regret bounds.
propositions.texte: We leverage online-to-confidence-set conversion (O2CS) algorithms to provide finite-sample confidence bounds on the regret for smoothed online optimization with switching costs and a long-term fairness regularizer. This framework allows us to establish more precise guarantees for online learning in this challenging setting.
propositions.titre: Online-to-Confidence-Set Conversion for Long-term Fairness Regularized Smoothed Online Optimization

propositions.controles: We compare our batched algorithms to existing online optimization methods and examine their performance in terms of regret, competitive ratio, and computational efficiency.
propositions.cout_texte: 250 GPU-hours (theoretical derivations, computational experiments, and iterative algorithm design).
propositions.prediction: We expect our batched online optimization framework to provide valuable insights into the effects of batched feedback on the optimization landscape and to develop scalable algorithms for practical applications. However, our batched algorithms might require significant modifications to achieve optimal performance, or our design might compromise fairness and efficiency in certain settings.
propositions.texte: To improve real-world applicability, we extend the long-term fairness regularized smoothed online optimization setting to batched online optimization, where the agent observes multiple cost functions simultaneously and makes decisions over a fixed time horizon. We investigate the impact of batched feedback on the hardness of optimization and explore practical algorithms for this more general setting.
propositions.titre: An Extension to Batched Online Optimization with Long-term Fairness and Switching Costs

propositions.controles: We compare a diverse set of algorithms, including our previously proposed methods (primal-dual, sparse regularization, online-to-confidence-set conversion, and batched optimization), as well as state-of-the-art online optimization methods without fairness constraints.
propositions.cout_texte: 500 GPU-hours (large-scale experiments with multiple evaluations and comparisons).
propositions.prediction: We expect our empirical comparison to provide a comprehensive assessment of the strengths and weaknesses of existing algorithms and to derive practical recommendations for online optimization in long-term fairness regularized smoothed online optimization settings. However, our comparison might highlight unforeseen trade-offs between fairness, efficiency, and other objectives, or our experiments could identify missed implementations of existing algorithms, leading to unexpected performance disparities.
propositions.texte: To gain practical insights into the performance of existing algorithms for long-term fairness regularized smoothed online optimization, we conduct an extensive empirical comparison on real-world benchmarks in geo-distributed data center capacity provisioning, LLM inference workload serving, and public health costs of air pollution from electricity generation.
propositions.titre: An Empirical Comparison of Online Optimization Algorithms for Long-term Fairness Regularized Smoothed Online Optimization

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Scene-Aware NeRF for Image Relighting
PROPOSAL: Investigate using a variant of the Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) model conditioned on scene geometry and user-specified lighting to perform full-image relighting. The model will be trained on a synthetic dataset of full scenes with varying lighting conditions and geometric complexity.
CONTROLS: Compare to state-of-the-art foreground relighting methods, such as the recent generative approach and object-centric approaches. Also, ablate the effect of conditioning on scene geometry.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should improve upon current foreground relighting methods by capturing both objects and scene geometry. However, it may struggle to generalize to complex indoor scenes with self-luminous objects and variable lighting, and may not account for non-Lambertian materials.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Dataset Generation with Varying Lighting Conditions
PROPOSAL: Develop a new synthetic dataset for scene-aware image relighting, which includes a wide range of indoor and outdoor scenes with varying lighting conditions, material types, and geometric complexities. The dataset will be used to train and evaluate the scene-aware NeRF model.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the scene-aware NeRF model on different subsets of the dataset, including those with simple and complex lighting conditions, and those with varied material types.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours (initial dataset generation, includes pre-processing and rendering)
PREDICTION: This dataset will provide a valuable benchmark for evaluating scene-aware image relighting models, and the performance of the scene-aware NeRF model will depend on the quality and diversity of the dataset. It may fail to capture the subtleties of real-world lighting effects or materials.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Dataset Generation with Varying Lighting Conditions
PROPOSAL: Extend the dataset generation proposal (2) by incorporating a novel, differentiable lighting module that allows for photorealistic, joint optimization of scene geometry, material properties, and lighting conditions. This will enable the creation of diverse, high-quality scenes with varied lighting conditions, and facilitate training and evaluation of the scene-aware NeRF model.
CONTROLS: Study the trade-offs between dataset quality and rendering time, as well as the interplay between scene geometry, material properties, and lighting effects.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours (including development of the differentiable lighting module)
PREDICTION: The extended dataset will significantly improve the scene-aware NeRF model's performance and robustness, but may increase rendering times due to the increased computational complexity of the lighting module. The model may still have difficulty generalizing to real-world scenarios with variable lighting, shadows, and occlusions.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Material-Agnostic Scene Intrinsic Decomposition
PROPOSAL: Investigate a novel intrinsic decomposition technique that allows for scene-aware image relighting without requiring explicit material properties or surface normals. This will be achieved by jointly optimizing the albedo, surface roughness, and metallicity using a physics-based renderer and a regression network.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the material-agnostic scene intrinsic decomposition to state-of-the-art intrinsic decomposition methods, and ablate the effect of using a regression network.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This decomposition technique will enable scene-aware image relighting without requiring explicit material properties, but may struggle to capture fine-grained material details or subtle lighting effects. The method may also be sensitive to noise and over-fitting.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Scene-Aware NeRF for Image Relighting
PROPOSAL: Enhance the scene-aware NeRF model by incorporating the material-agnostic scene intrinsic decomposition (3) as a pre-processing step, and conditioning the NeRF model on the decomposed scene intrinsic components instead ofexplicit material properties. This will enable the scene-aware NeRF model to generalize to a wider range of materials and scenes, while maintaining physical plausibility.
CONTROLS: Study the effect of combining the material-agnostic decomposition with different NeRF architectures and ablating the effect of conditioning on scene intrinsic components.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (modifying the existing NeRF architecture)
PREDICTION: The enhanced scene-aware NeRF model will improve its generalizability and robustness to material and scene variations, but may suffer from decreased performance on scenes with complex lighting effects or surfaces with fine-grained textures.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Physics-Constrained Optimization for Lighting Control
PROPOSAL: Introduce a physics-constrained optimization framework to the scene-aware NeRF model, which enforces compliance with basic light transport principles and ensures that shading, highlights, and shadows are correctly rendered under the new lighting conditions. This will be achieved by formulating a loss function that penalizes departures from physical plausibility.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effect of different physics constraints, such as energy conservation, and ablating the optimization framework to study its impact on the scene-aware NeRF model's performance.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The physics-constrained optimization framework will improve the scene-aware NeRF model's physical plausibility and accuracy, but may introduce additional computational overhead and require careful tuning of the loss function parameters. The method may also struggle to handle scenes with complex or non-standard lighting effects.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Self-Supervised Learning for Relighting Generalization
PROPOSAL: Develop a self-supervised learning framework that enables the scene-aware NeRF model to generalize to unseen materials, lighting conditions, and scene compositions. This will be achieved by using task-agnostic synthetic data and a contrastive learning objective that encourages the model to capture commonalities across various relighting scenarios.
CONTROLS: Study the effect of different self-supervised learning objectives, such as contrastive learning and autoencoding, and evaluate the model's performance on real-world images and benchmarks.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The self-supervised learning framework will improve the scene-aware NeRF model's generalizability and robustness, but may require careful tuning of the learning objective and hyperparameters. The method may also struggle to capture fine-grained material details or subtle lighting effects.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Self-Supervised Learning for Relighting Generalization
PROPOSAL: Enhance the self-supervised learning framework (5) by incorporating a novel adversarial training scheme that encourages the scene-aware NeRF model to generate physically plausible and diverse relighting scenarios. This will be achieved by introducing a discriminator network that evaluates the realism and plausibility of the generated images, and by using a Wasserstein adversarial loss function that promotes diversity and robustness.
CONTROLS: Study the effect of different adversarial training schemes, such as GANs and Wasserstein GANs, and evaluate the model's performance on real-world images and benchmarks.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The enhanced self-supervised learning framework will improve the scene-aware NeRF model's generalizability, robustness, and physical plausibility, but may introduce additional computational overhead and require careful tuning of the adversarial loss function parameters. The method may also struggle to capture fine-grained material details or subtle lighting effects.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Dataset Generation with Varying Lighting Conditions
PROPOSAL: Refine the dataset generation process (2) by incorporating the enhanced material-agnostic scene intrinsic decomposition (3) and the physics-constrained optimization framework (4) into the generation pipeline. This will enable the creation of high-quality, diverse, and physically plausible scenes with varying lighting conditions, material types, and geometric complexities.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of the refined dataset generation process on the scene-aware NeRF model's performance and robustness, and study the effect of different decomposition and optimization techniques on the generated scenes.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours (refining the existing dataset generation pipeline)
PREDICTION: The refined dataset generation process will significantly improve the quality, diversity, and physical plausibility of the generated scenes, but may introduce additional computational overhead and require careful tuning of the decomposition and optimization techniques. The method may also struggle to capture fine-grained material details or subtle lighting effects in certain scenarios.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Evaluation and Comparison with State-of-the-Art Methods
PROPOSAL: Conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the scene-aware NeRF model's performance and robustness using various benchmarks and metrics, including global and local metrics for image quality, physical plausibility, and relighting accuracy. Compare the results to state-of-the-art methods for image relighting, intrinsic image decomposition, and inverse rendering.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of the refined dataset generation process (9) on the model's performance, and study the effect of different variations of the scene-aware NeRF model on its performance and robustness.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (evaluation and comparison)
PREDICTION: The comprehensive evaluation and comparison will provide a thorough understanding of the scene-aware NeRF model's strengths and weaknesses, and will enable identification of directions for future research and improvement. The method may struggle to capture fine-grained material details or subtle lighting effects in certain scenarios, but is expected to demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods for image relighting.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Initial Experiment: Lighting Conditions Simulator for Training Data Augmentation
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment to create a lighting conditions simulator to augment existing datasets with diverse and complex illumination scene conditions. Using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), we will generate synthetic images of the same scene with varying lighting conditions, ranging from indoor to outdoor scenes. The simulator will take a single image as input and produce a set of images with different lighting conditions.
CONTROLS: Compare the results of relighting tasks to a baseline that uses only the original augmented dataset, without generated images.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The lighting conditions simulator should be able to effectively augment existing datasets with a diverse range of illumination conditions, significantly improving the relighting performance of downstream models. However, the performance may degrade if the simulator fails to generalize to new lighting conditions or material appearances.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Intrinsic Image Decomposition using Physics-based Rendering
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment to investigate the use of physics-based rendering (PBR) for intrinsic image decompositions. Specifically, we will use the concept of "progressive light coherence" to estimate the scene's intrinsic properties, including albedo, surface normals, roughness, and metallicity. PBR will be used to render the scene with diverse lighting conditions and the discrepancies between rendered and input images will be used to refine the decompositions.
CONTROLS: Compare the results to state-of-the-art intrinsic image decomposition methods, such as work by Barron et al. and Laine et al.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The physics-based rendering approach should lead to improved intrinsic decompositions, especially for scenes with complex lighting conditions. However, the method may be computationally expensive and require extensive training data to achieve satisfactory results.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Intrinsic Image Decomposition using Physics-based Rendering
PROPOSAL: We revise the previous proposal to investigate the use of progressive light coherence in conjunction with a neural network to refine the intrinsic decompositions. The network will be trained on synthetic images rendered using PBR and will learn to predict the scene's intrinsic properties. We will use the Deepest Image Network (DIN) as a baseline and compare our results to it.
CONTROLS: Compare the results to the original DIN method, as well as other state-of-the-art intrinsic image decomposition methods.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The use of progressive light coherence in conjunction with a neural network should improve the accuracy of the intrinsic decompositions and enable better generalization to real-world lighting conditions. However, the method may still struggle with scenes that have complex or dynamic lighting. 

Note: The original cost of 300 GPU-hours was reduced to 250 GPU-hours.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Controlling Lighting with Physics-aware Conditionals
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment to explore the use of physics-aware conditionals to control the lighting in relighting tasks. By incorporating physical light transport principles, such as Lambertian reflection and diffuse transmission, into the conditional Generator of a Generative Model (e.g., Pix2PixHD), we aim to improve the plausibility and realism of the relit images.
CONTROLS: Compare the results to a baseline Pix2PixHD model, as well as a conditional model that uses intensity and color masks to control lighting.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The physics-aware conditionals should enable better control over the lighting in the relit images and improve their physical plausibility. However, the model may require additional training to accurately capture the specific lighting behaviors of different materials and environments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluation of Geometry-aware Image Relighting
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment to investigate the use of geometry-aware image relighting methods to improve the accuracy of relighted images. Building on previous work, we will develop a novel geometry-aware relighting algorithm that incorporates 3D scene geometry (e.g., SVO) and physics-based renderers (e.g., Mitsuba) to create realistic relit images. We will compare this approach to state-of-the-art image relighting methods.
CONTROLS: Compare our results to those of image relighting methods that utilize solely image-based approaches (e.g., Deep Image Relighting), as well as those that incorporate some form of scene geometry (e.g., Scene Relighting with AI Accelerated).
COST: 550 GPU-hours (including training a physics-based renderer)
PREDICTION: The geometry-aware relighting approach should significantly improve the realism of relighted images, especially in scenes with complex geometry or non-Lambertian materials. However, this approach requires large amounts of training data and computational resources.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analysis of Albedo Consistency in Image Relighting
PROPOSAL: We propose a theoretical analysis to investigate the importance of albedo consistency in image relighting tasks. By considering the light transport equation and the effects of different materials, we aim to provide a theoretical understanding of how albedo consistency affects the quality of relit images. We will derive bounds on the albedo consistency and analyze its relationship to various image relighting metrics (e.g., PSNR, SSIM).
CONTROLS: Develop an analytical model to compare albedo consistency with other factors affecting image relighting, such as lighting direction and intensity.
COST: negligible (theory-focused proposal)
PREDICTION: The analysis should provide valuable insights into the role of albedo consistency in image relighting and help guide the development of more accurate and physically plausible relighting methods. However, the theoretical model may not capture all aspects of image relighting, such as high-frequency effects or specific material behaviors.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Material Shading for Realistic Image Relighting
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment to investigate the use of material shading for realistic image relighting. Building on the previous geometry-aware relighting approach, we will incorporate a material shading component that uses a physically-based BRDF model to simulate realistic material behavior. We will compare the results to state-of-the-art image relighting methods and analyze the impact of material shading on the realism and accuracy of relighted images.
CONTROLS: Compare our results to those of image relighting methods that incorporate some form of material shading, as well as those that utilize solely image-based approaches.
COST: 420 GPU-hours (including training a BRDF model)
PREDICTION: The incorporation of material shading should significantly improve the realism of relighted images, especially for scenes with diverse materials and complex lighting. However, this approach may require additional training data and computational resources to accurately capture the behavior of various materials.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Relighting for Mixed Reality Applications using Neural Scene Representations
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment to investigate the use of neural scene representations for relighting in mixed reality applications. Building on recent advances in neural scene rendering, we will develop a novel relighting framework that uses a neural scene representation to render images under different lighting conditions. We will evaluate our approach on a set of mixed reality scenarios and compare the results to state-of-the-art image relighting methods.
CONTROLS: Compare our results to those of image relighting methods that utilize solely image-based approaches, as well as those that incorporate some form of scene geometry.
COST: 600 GPU-hours (including training a neural scene representation model)
PREDICTION: The use of neural scene representations should enable more realistic and accurate relighting in mixed reality applications, especially for scenes with complex geometry and varied lighting conditions. However, this approach may require large amounts of training data and computational resources to accurately capture the scene's structure and behavior.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Analysis of Albedo Consistency in Image Relighting
PROPOSAL: We revise the previous proposal to investigate the specific impact of albedo consistency on the performance of image relighting methods, using the results from previous experiments (e.g., geometry-aware image relighting) as a baseline. We will analyze the relationship between albedo consistency and various image relighting metrics (e.g., PSNR, SSIM) and provide insights into design choices that can improve albedo consistency and overall relighting performance.
CONTROLS: Investigate the effect of different albedo estimation methods on albedo consistency, as well as the interplay with other factors affecting image relighting, such as lighting direction and intensity.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (building on previous results)
PREDICTION: Our analysis should provide valuable insights into the role of albedo consistency in image relighting and guide the development of more accurate and physically plausible relighting methods that maintain albedo consistency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Ensemble-based Relighting Framework for Robust Results
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment to develop an ensemble-based relighting framework that combines the strengths of different image relighting methods (e.g., geometry-aware, material shading, neural scene representation). By training multiple models and selecting the best-performing one based on a validation set, we aim to create a highly robust and accurate relighting framework for a wide range of scenes and lighting conditions.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the ensemble-based framework on a comprehensive set of scenes and compare it to previous state-of-the-art relighting methods.
COST: 900 GPU-hours (including training and evaluation of multiple models)
PREDICTION: The ensemble-based framework should provide a significant improvement in the robustness and accuracy of relighting results across various scenes and lighting conditions, making it a versatile tool for real-world applications. However, this approach may require extensive computational resources and large amounts of training data to optimize the ensemble's performance.

Note: The original cost of 300 GPU-hours was reduced to 250 GPU-hours.

PROPOSAL 3: Controlling Lighting with Physics-aware Conditionals
We propose an experiment to explore the use of physics-aware conditionals to control the lighting in relighting tasks. By incorporating physical light transport principles, such as Lambertian reflection and diffuse transmission, into the conditional Generator of a Generative Model (e.g., Pix2PixHD), we aim to improve the plausibility and realism of the relit images.
Controls: Compare the results to a baseline Pix2PixHD model, as well as a conditional model that uses intensity and color masks to control lighting.
Estimated cost: 180 GPU-hours
Prediction: The physics-aware conditionals should enable better control over the lighting in the relit images and improve their physical plausibility. However, the model may require additional training to accurately capture the specific lighting behaviors of different materials and environments.

PROPOSAL 4: Evaluation of Geometry-aware Image Relighting
We propose an experiment to investigate the use of geometry-aware image relighting methods to improve the accuracy of relighted images. Building on previous work, we will develop a novel geometry-aware relighting algorithm that incorporates 3D scene geometry (e.g., SVO) and physics-based renderers (e.g., Mitsuba) to create realistic relit images. We will compare this approach to state-of-the-art image relighting methods.
Controls: Compare our results to those of image relighting methods that utilize solely image-based approaches (e.g., Deep Image Relighting), as well as those that incorporate some form of scene geometry (e.g., Scene Relighting with AI Accelerated).
Estimated cost: 550 GPU-hours (including training a physics-based renderer)
Prediction: The geometry-aware relighting approach should significantly improve the realism of relighted images, especially in scenes with complex geometry or non-Lambertian materials. However, this approach requires large amounts of training data and computational resources.

PROPOSAL 5: Analysis of Albedo Consistency in Image Relighting
We revise the previous proposal to investigate the specific impact of albedo consistency on the performance of image relighting methods, using the results from previous experiments (e.g., geometry-aware image relighting) as a baseline. We will analyze the relationship between albedo consistency and various image relighting metrics (e.g., PSNR, SSIM) and provide insights into design choices that can improve albedo consistency and overall relighting performance.
Controls: Investigate the effect of different albedo estimation methods on albedo consistency, as well as the interplay with other factors affecting image relighting, such as lighting direction and intensity.
Estimated cost: 120 GPU-hours (building on previous results)
Prediction: Our analysis should provide valuable insights into the role of albedo consistency in image relighting and guide the development of more accurate and physically plausible relighting methods that maintain albedo consistency.

PROPOSAL 6: Investigating Material Shading for Realistic Image Relighting
We propose an experiment to investigate the use of material shading for realistic image relighting. Building on the previous geometry-aware relighting approach, we will incorporate a material shading component that uses a physically-based BRDF model to simulate realistic material behavior. We will compare the results to state-of-the-art image relighting methods and analyze the impact of material shading on the realism and accuracy of relighted images.
Controls: Compare our results to those of image relighting methods that incorporate some form of material shading, as well as those that utilize solely image-based approaches.
Estimated cost: 420 GPU-hours (including training a BRDF model)
Prediction: The incorporation of material shading should significantly improve the realism of relighted images, especially for scenes with diverse materials and complex lighting. However, this approach may require additional training data and computational resources to accurately capture the behavior of various materials.

PROPOSAL 7: Relighting for Mixed Reality Applications using Neural Scene Representations
We propose an experiment to investigate the use of neural scene representations for relighting in mixed reality applications. Building on recent advances in neural scene rendering, we will develop a novel relighting framework that uses a neural scene representation to render images under different lighting conditions. We will evaluate our approach on a set of mixed reality scenarios and compare the results to state-of-the-art image relighting methods.
Controls: Compare our results to those of image relighting methods that utilize solely image-based approaches, as well as those that incorporate some form of scene geometry.
Estimated cost: 600 GPU-hours (including training a neural scene representation model)
Prediction: The use of neural scene representations should enable more realistic and accurate relighting in mixed reality applications, especially for scenes with complex geometry and varied lighting conditions. However, this approach may require large amounts of training data and computational resources to accurately capture the scene's structure and behavior.

PROPOSAL 8: Ensemble-based Relighting Framework for Robust Results
We propose an experiment to develop an ensemble-based relighting framework that combines the strengths of different image relighting methods (e.g., geometry-aware, material shading, neural scene representation). By training multiple models and selecting the best-performing one based on a validation set, we aim to create a highly robust and accurate relighting framework for a wide range of scenes and lighting conditions.
Controls: Evaluate the performance of the ensemble-based framework on a comprehensive set of scenes and compare it to previous state-of-the-art relighting methods.
Estimated cost: 900 GPU-hours (including training and evaluation of multiple models)
Prediction: The ensemble-based framework should provide a significant improvement in the robustness and accuracy of relighting results across various scenes and lighting conditions, making it a versatile tool for real-world applications. However, this approach may require extensive computational resources and large amounts of training data to optimize the ensemble's performance.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Lighting Direction Estimation for Precise Relighting Control
PROPOSAL: Train SceneNN [1] and RelightGAN [2] on a synthetic dataset that includes various indoor and outdoor scenes with diverse lighting conditions, and use the resulting models to estimate the lighting direction in these scenes. Then, relight the scenes using the estimated lighting direction and compare the results with ground-truth relighting.
CONTROLS: Train SceneNN and RelightGAN without estimating lighting direction, and compare the results with the proposed method. Also, ablate the proposed method by removing the lighting direction estimation step.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed method should improve relighting accuracy by accurately estimating the lighting direction, but may fail for scenes with complex lighting or occlusions.

[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.03605 (SceneNN)
[2] https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.09536 (RelightGAN)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Effect of Albedo and Normal Maps on Relighting Performance
PROPOSAL: Similar to proposal 1, train SceneNN and RelightGAN on a synthetic dataset, but this time use the models to predict albedo and normal maps for each scene, and then use these maps to relight the scenes. Compare the relighting results with ground-truth relighting and with the results from proposal 1.
CONTROLS: Train SceneNN and RelightGAN without predicting albedo and normal maps, and compare the results with the proposed method. Also, ablate the proposed method by removing the albedo and normal map prediction steps.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed method may improve relighting accuracy by using accurate albedo and normal maps, especially for scenes with complex materials, but may fail for scenes with uncertain or incomplete data.

Set now includes:
1. Investigating Lighting Direction Estimation for Precise Relighting Control
2. Evaluating the Effect of Albedo and Normal Maps on Relighting Performance

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparing Data-Driven and Physics-Based Approaches for Relighting
PROPOSAL: Implement a physics-based relighting model, such as the Ward model [1], and compare its performance with SceneNN and RelightGAN on a variety of indoor and outdoor scenes with diverse lighting conditions. Evaluate the accuracy and physical plausibility of the relighting results produced by each model.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with the case where only SceneNN and RelightGAN are trained on synthetic exemplars of their respective types, without access to any explicit physical parametrization.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The physics-based model should provide more physically plausible relighting results, but may be less accurate and more computationally expensive than SceneNN and RelightGAN.

Set now includes:
1. Investigating Lighting Direction Estimation for Precise Relighting Control
2. Evaluating the Effect of Albedo and Normal Maps on Relighting Performance
3. Comparing Data-Driven and Physics-Based Approaches for Relighting

[1] https://courses.cs.washington.edu/courses/cse456/98au/studentresponse/ward/ WardResult99.PDF

ACTION: REVISIE
TITLE: Comparing Data-Driven and Physics-Based Approaches for Relighting
PROPOSAL: To make the comparison with data-driven models more fair, instead of training SceneNN and RelightGAN on general scenes, train them specifically on scenes where the physics-based model would fail (e.g. scenes with complex lighting or materials). Then evaluate the performance of both models on these scenes.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with the case where SceneNN and RelightGAN are trained on general scenes.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (reduced from 150)
PREDICTION: The physics-based model should still provide more physically plausible relighting results in areas where it doesn't fail, and SceneNN and RelightGAN should perform better in areas where the physics-based model fails.

Set remains:
1. Investigating Lighting Direction Estimation for Precise Relighting Control
2. Evaluating the Effect of Albedo and Normal Maps on Relighting Performance
3. Comparing Data-Driven and Physics-Based Approaches for Relighting

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Viewpoint Changes on Relighting Performance
PROPOSAL: Train a relighting model (e.g. SceneNN or RelightGAN) on a synthetic dataset with multiple viewpoints of the same scene, and evaluate its performance on unseen viewpoints. Compare the results with the case where the model is trained on a single viewpoint.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with the case where the model is trained on the same viewpoint as the test data.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The model should perform well even with viewpoint changes, due to the invariant nature of the lighting and material properties, but may struggle with large viewpoint changes or complex scenes.

Set now includes:
1. Investigating Lighting Direction Estimation for Precise Relighting Control
2. Evaluating the Effect of Albedo and Normal Maps on Relighting Performance
3. Comparing Data-Driven and Physics-Based Approaches for Relighting
4. Evaluating the Impact of Viewpoint Changes on Relighting Performance

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Relighting across Indoor-Outdoor Scenes
PROPOSAL: Train a Transfer Relighting model using a small set of indoor scenes and evaluate its ability to relight outdoor scenes with vastly different lighting conditions. Compare the results with a model trained exclusively on outdoor scenes.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with a model trained on a mixture of indoor and outdoor scenes.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The Transfer Relighting model should generalize well to outdoor scenes, but may struggle with scenes that are vastly different in appearance or lighting conditions.

Set now includes:
1. Investigating Lighting Direction Estimation for Precise Relighting Control
2. Evaluating the Effect of Albedo and Normal Maps on Relighting Performance
3. Comparing Data-Driven and Physics-Based Approaches for Relighting
4. Evaluating the Impact of Viewpoint Changes on Relighting Performance
5. Transfer Relighting across Indoor-Outdoor Scenes

ACTION: REVISIE
TITLE: Investigating Lighting Direction Estimation for Precise Relighting Control
PROPOSAL: In addition to estimating the lighting direction, also predict the strength of the lighting (e.g. the irradiance) in each direction. Use this information to improve the accuracy of the relighting results.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with the original method that only estimates the lighting direction.
COST: 40 GPU-hours (additional to the original 100)
PREDICTION: The updated method should provide more accurate relighting results, especially in areas with complex lighting conditions.

Set remains:
1. Investigating Lighting Direction Estimation for Precise Relighting Control
2. Evaluating the Effect of Albedo and Normal Maps on Relighting Performance
3. Comparing Data-Driven and Physics-Based Approaches for Relighting
4. Evaluating the Impact of Viewpoint Changes on Relighting Performance
5. Transfer Relighting across Indoor-Outdoor Scenes

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Evaluating the Effect of Albedo and Normal Maps on Relighting Performance
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether the improvement in relighting performance of using albedo and normal maps is due to the addition of extra features or simply because these maps are highly correlated with the lighting conditions. Specifically, ablate the experiments by progressively removing the estimation of one part of the intrinsic decomposition at a time from the proposed method and see how accurate the relighting results become.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with the original case where the entire intrinsic decomposition (albedo, normals, roughness, etc) was used, and confirm that an ablation approach provides meaningful insights.
COST: 60 GPU-hours (no additional training, just ablation analysis)
PREDICTION: The results should confirm whether it's the added geometric information that leads to the improvement or if it's the fact that scene geometry and lighting are tightly correlated in the training data.

Set remains:
1. Investigating Lighting Direction Estimation for Precise Relighting Control
2. Evaluating the Effect of Albedo and Normal Maps on Relighting Performance
3. Comparing Data-Driven and Physics-Based Approaches for Relighting
4. Evaluating the Impact of Viewpoint Changes on Relighting Performance
5. Transfer Relighting across Indoor-Outdoor Scenes

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Evaluating the Effect of Albedo and Normal Maps on Relighting Performance
PROPOSAL: Additionally to the ablation analysis proposed in the previous revision, implement a surrogate model (e.g. a linear regression) using the estimated intrinsic decomposition parameters (e.g. albedo, normals, roughness) as input, to predict the lighting condition. Evaluate the performance of this simple model compared to the original relighting experiments.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with the case where the surrogate model is not used, and with SceneNN/RelightGAN on intrinsic-only settings.
COST: 40 GPU-hours (additional to the original 120)
PREDICTION: The surrogate model should provide similar results to the original relighting method, suggesting that the improvement is indeed due to the use of intrinsic decomposition, or else it could fail showing that Scene NN and Relight GAN outperform the surrogates for the task at hand.

Set remains:
1. Investigating Lighting Direction Estimation for Precise Relighting Control
2. Evaluating the Effect of Albedo and Normal Maps on Relighting Performance
3. Comparing Data-Driven and Physics-Based Approaches for Relighting
4. Evaluating the Impact of Viewpoint Changes on Relighting Performance
5. Transfer Relighting across Indoor-Outdoor Scenes

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Performance of Relighting Models on 360-Degree Scenes
PROPOSAL: many of the existing relighting methods (including those compared in previous experiments) have the constraints that require the scene to be wrapped onto a 2D texture, as exemplified by the IRRDB dataset. To complement such previous approaches to tackle the challenge of relighting, focus on developing a theory-first (built upon the current paper's) framework that scales to 360-degree scenes and implements a sampling strategy that efficiently covers all view angles within the scene.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with previous studies that mapped the 2D coordinates of a light [13] and tagged along an ambient light to complete the base dedicated representation.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposal should succeed in tackling 360-degree scenes, but slight failure points in reproducing qualitative synthetic texture features.

Set now includes:
1. Investigating Lighting Direction Estimation for Precise Relighting Control
2. Evaluating the Effect of Albedo and Normal Maps on Relighting Performance
3. Comparing Data-Driven and Physics-Based Approaches for Relighting
4. Evaluating the Impact of Viewpoint Changes on Relighting Performance
5. Transfer Relighting across Indoor-Outdoor Scenes
6. Evaluating the Performance of Relighting Models on 360-Degree Scenes

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Characterization of Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) Spectrum for Deep ReLU Networks
PROPOSAL: We derive closed-form expressions for the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) Gram matrix over the training data for deep fully connected ReLU networks. We assume the width of the networks is sufficiently large, allowing for a mean-field analysis. We leverage the spectral properties of the NTK to provide a more refined understanding of the loss landscape and its implications for gradient descent convergence and generalization bounds.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare the derived spectral properties with existing results for shallow networks (Lei et al., 2019)
- Contrast with the case of smooth activation functions (Jacot et al., 2018)
COST: 100
PREDICTION: The derived expressions for the NTK eigenvalues and eigenvectors should reveal that the non-divergence of the smallest eigenvalue with increasing width is a critical factor in determining the convergence properties of gradient descent. If successful, this should enable improved risk bounds with polynomial width dependence. However, its complexity might limit analytical tractability to a polynomial rather than logarithmic width dependence required.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Generalization Bounds via Gradient Descent Dynamics under NTK Separability
PROPOSAL: We study the gradient descent (GD) dynamics on deeply ReLU networks with NTK-separable data, leveraging the characterization of the NTK spectrum from Proposal 1. We derive an expression for the change in the training loss along the GD trajectory, and use this to establish a generalization bound that depends on the NTK margin, the training set size, and the network width. This bound serves as an initial step towards establishing optimal-order generalization rates.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare with existing generalization bounds for GD on deep networks under specific assumptions (e.g., Arora et al., 2020)
- Evaluate the bound's dependence on the network depth and width
COST: 50
PREDICTION: The proposed bound should provide an improved understanding of the impact of GD dynamics on generalization performance, but may not achieve the optimal $1/(\gamma^2 n)$ rate due to remaining width and depth dependencies. Moreover, the derivation of the bound may require restrictive assumptions on the GD trajectory.

TITLE: Near-Optimal Generalization Bounds via Width-Independent NTK Margins
PROPOSAL: We propose a new framework to establish near-optimal generalization bounds for deep ReLU networks by exploiting the NTK separability of the data. We show that under a compositional margin condition on the data, the NTK margin can be upper-bounded in a width-independent manner. This allows us to derive near-optimal generalization bounds that match the minimax rate of $1/(\gamma^2 n)$ up to logarithmic factors, without requiring explicit knowledge of the network width or depth.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare with existing bounds that rely on assuming smooth activations (Arora et al., 2018)
- Evaluate the tightness of the derived width-independent NTK margin bounds
COST: 75
PREDICTION: The proposed framework should provide a significant improvement over existing bounds and match the minimax rate, but its applicability may be limited by the technical requirements of the compositional margin condition. Additionally, the width independence may come at the cost of restrictive assumptions on the data distribution.

We analyze the properties of the SmoothReLU and demonstrate its ability to improve generalization and stability in deep networks.

PROPOSAL: We propose a new ensemble method for improving the robustness and generalization of deep networks. We analyze the properties of NTK Ensemble and demonstrate its ability to improve robustness and generalization in deep networks.

Derive a polynomial-width sufficient condition for convergence, improving upon the existing logarithmic-width bound for two-layer ReLU networks.

Introduce a hybrid method that combines truncated singular value decomposition (SVD) with the NTK-Regularization approach, with the goal of improving the generalization performance and computational efficiency of deep ReLU networks.
Controls: Compare the hybrid method with the individual components, explore the effect of truncation thresholds and regularization parameters, and assess the resulting generalization performance.
Estimated cost: 250 GPU-hours
Prediction: The hybrid method may achieve improved generalization performance and computational efficiency by leveraging the strengths of both truncated SVD and NTK-Regularization, particularly for deeper networks and larger datasets, but require careful tuning of the truncation thresholds and regularization parameters to avoid over-complexification and over-regularization.

PROPOSAL 7: A Theoretical Framework for Understanding the Impact of Overparameterization on Generalization in Deep ReLU Networks
Develop a theoretical framework to analyze the impact of overparameterization on the generalization performance of deep ReLU networks, with the goal of providing a deeper understanding of the trade-offs between capacity, regularization, and generalization.
Controls: Compare with existing results, explore the relationship between network width, depth, and generalization performance, and assess the implications for practical network design.
Estimated cost: 300 GPU-hours (this is a high-level theoretical proposal, which may not require extensive computational resources)
Prediction: This theoretical framework may provide valuable insights into the role of overparameterization in generalization and enable the development of more effective regularization techniques, potentially leading to improved generalization performance and more efficient network design. However, the development of this framework may require a significant amount of mathematical and theoretical effort, and may not directly lead to computational results.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Branching Schrödinger Bridge
PROPOSAL: We will propose and analyze an extension of the generalized Schrödinger bridge formulation that incorporates a non-linear branching cost, allowing it to model the divergence of mass across multiple terminal states while retaining a reference to an underlying reference process. We will consider the regime where the initial and terminal population masses are fixed and the branching cost is task-specific.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed model to baseline generalized Schrödinger bridge formulations without branching costs as well as to branched Brownian motion in the appropriate limits.
COST: 1.2e5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to demonstrate that our proposed branching Schrödinger bridge model can capture branched dynamics with improved accuracy over existing methods while being interpretable through the lens of the Schrödinger bridge framework, but may face challenges in recovering the correct branching structure in high-dimensional spaces where mode collapse becomes more pronounced.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Variational Inference for Branching Schrödinger Bridge
PROPOSAL: We will develop a variational inference approach for stochastic gradient descent (SGD) optimization of the proposed branching Schrödinger bridge model, which allows for efficient inference and scaling to large datasets. Specifically, we will use a conditional-mean embedding of polynomials to approximate the complex branching cost function and guide the SGD updates with a computationally efficient Monte Carlo approximation of the variational objective. We will consider the experimental domain of cell differentiation trajectory inference from single-cell RNA-seq as a test case.
CONTROLS: The baseline will consist of the generalized Schrödinger bridge formulation without the branching cost, and we will also compare our variational inference approach to standard SGD on the branching Schrödinger bridge model.
COST: 1.8e5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that applying variational inference to the branching Schrödinger bridge model will allow us to scale up and find more accurate solutions than SGD on its own, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to avoid divergent behavior due to the non-convexity of the branching cost function.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Variational Inference for Branching Schrödinger Bridge
PROPOSAL: We will develop a variational inference approach for stochastic gradient descent (SGD) optimization of the proposed branching Schrödinger bridge model, which allows for efficient inference and scaling to large datasets. Specifically, we will use a conditional-mean embedding of polynomials to approximate the complex branching cost function and guide the SGD updates with a computationally efficient Monte Carlo approximation of the variational objective. We will consider the experimental domain of cell differentiation trajectory inference from single-cell RNA-seq as a test case.
CONTROLS: The baseline will consist of the generalized Schrödinger bridge formulation without the branching cost, and we will also compare our variational inference approach to standard SGD on the branching Schrödinger bridge model.
COST: 1.8e5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that applying variational inference to the branching Schrödinger bridge model will allow us to scale up and find more accurate solutions than SGD on its own, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to avoid divergent behavior due to the non-convexity of the branching cost function.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Synthetic Dataset Generation
PROPOSAL: We will generate synthetic single-cell RNA-seq datasets based on realistic branching dynamics, allowing us to evaluate the performance of our model and variational inference approach under controlled conditions. This synthetic dataset will include varying branching structures, cell proliferation rates, and transcriptional noise levels to assess the robustness of our methods.
CONTROLS: The baseline performance on our new branching Schrödinger bridge model will be compared with standard methods such as denoising diffusion and flow matching without proactive recovery of intermediate states.
COST: 0.5e5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to observe that our branching Schrödinger bridge model with variational inference

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Using Limited Intermediate Snapshots for Training
PROPOSAL: We will adapt the branching Schrödinger bridge model to learn from a small set of observed intermediate snapshots, which may be the only available data in certain real-world settings such as cell differentiation trajectory inference from single-cell RNA-seq. We will develop a technique to radically reduce the number of gradient steps during the variational inference process, thus need only a minimal number of intermediate images, utilizing L1-norm regularization to select the most relevant snapshots, since intermediate data is rare.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the proposed model on the synthetic datasets generated in turn 3 and compare it with the baseline branching Schrödinger bridge model using a larger number of intermediate snapshots.
COST: 1.0e5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that leveraging limited intermediate snapshots for training will improve the model's practical applicability in real-world settings, as the method avoids mode collapse by focusing on regions of high mass concentration but worries that model may struggling over sparse regions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Applying the Branching Schrödinger Bridge to LiDAR-Scanned Terrain Surfaces
PROPOSAL: We will apply the branching Schrödinger bridge model to the problem of navigation on LiDAR-scanned terrain surfaces, where the goal is to predict the branching trajectories of an agent as it moves across the terrain and encounters different types of obstacles or hazards. We will adapt the variational inference approach from turn 1 to this new task and compare the results with standard optimal transport methods.
CONTROLS: The baseline will consist of a standard optimal transport approach without branching costs, as well as a simple diffusion-based navigation model that does not account for branching dynamics.
COST: 0.8e5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the branching Schrödinger bridge model will provide more accurate and realistic navigation trajectories, taking into account the complex branching dynamics of the terrain surface. However, we may find that the model requires careful tuning of the branching cost function to capture the specific patterns of branching behavior in this domain.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Mode Collapse and Mass Redistribution
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the behavior of the branching Schrödinger bridge model in terms of mode collapse and mass redistribution, focusing on how the model handles cases where the branching dynamics are complex and high-dimensional. We will use a combination of theoretical analysis and numerical experiments on synthetic datasets to gain insights into these phenomena.
CONTROLS: We will examine the effects of different branching cost functions, initial and terminal distributions, and the role of regularization in mitigating mode collapse.
COST: 1.2e4 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to identify key factors that contribute to mode collapse and mass redistribution in the branching Schrödinger bridge model, and to develop strategies for mitigating these issues through careful choice of model hyperparameters and data preprocessing.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Using Limited Intermediate Snapshots for Training
PROPOSAL: We will modify the approach from turn 3 by incorporating the insights gained from analyzing mode collapse and mass redistribution (turn 4) to develop a new method for selecting the most relevant intermediate snapshots. We will use a multi-objective optimization approach to balance the trade-off between reducing the number of snapshots and preserving the branching dynamics of the model.
CONTROLS: We will compare our new method with the baseline from turn 3 and evaluate its performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
COST: 1.8e5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to demonstrate that our new approach can effectively reduce the number of intermediate snapshots required for training while achieving better performance on real-world datasets compared to the baseline methods. However, we may find that the optimization process requires careful tuning to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Second-Order Optimization Method for Branched Dynamics
PROPOSAL: We will develop a second-order optimization method to efficiently train the branching Schrödinger bridge model. Our method will incorporate a covariant matrix algorithm to incorporate curvature information in the optimization process, which will enable faster convergence and more accurate solutions.
CONTROLS: We will compare our second-order optimization method with the baseline gradient descent method and evaluate its performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
COST: 2.5e5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to demonstrate that our second-order optimization method can significantly improve the training efficiency and convergence of the branching Schrödinger bridge model, leading to better performance on real-world datasets compared to the baseline methods. However, we may find that the method is sensitive to initial conditions and requires careful tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Visualizing and Interpreting Branched Dynamics
PROPOSAL: We will develop a visualization tool to effectively communicate the complex branched dynamics learned by the branching Schrödinger bridge model. Our tool will incorporate a combination of traditional visualization techniques (e.g., scatter plots, histograms) with advanced data structures (e.g., force-directed graphs, tree visualizations) to provide a clear and intuitive understanding of the model's output.
CONTROLS: We will apply our visualization tool to a range of benchmark datasets, including the synthetic datasets generated for evaluating the branching Schrödinger bridge model, as well as real-world datasets from the domains of biology and navigation.
COST: 0.8e5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to demonstrate that our visualization tool can effectively communicate complex branched dynamics to end-users, enabling a deeper understanding of the branching Schrödinger bridge model's output and facilitating its application in real-world domains. However, we may find that the development of a universally effective visualization tool requires additional effort to adapt to the specific needs and characteristics of each domain.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Extending the Branching Schrödinger Bridge to Multi-Agent Systems
PROPOSAL: We will extend the branching Schrödinger bridge model to enable the study of multi-agent systems, where each agent may follow its own branching trajectory. Our extension will incorporate a novel form of communication between agents, allowing them to share information about their branching paths and adapt their behavior accordingly.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate our multi-agent branching Schrödinger bridge model on benchmark datasets, comparing its performance to the state-of-the-art in multi-agent trajectory inference.
COST: 3.5e5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to demonstrate that our multi-agent branching Schrödinger bridge model can effectively capture the complex dynamics of multi-agent systems, including the emergence of coordinated behavior and the adaptation of individual agents to changes in the environment. However, we may find that the extension of the branching Schrödinger bridge to multi-agent systems requires significant modifications to the underlying math and computational framework.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sampling important regions for branched dynamics estimation
PROPOSAL: Use optimal transport-based Q-learning to identify critical regions in the state space where branching occurs. Assume a suitable state-dependent cost function that penalizes violations of task-specific constraints (e.g., distance boundaries in navigation).
CONTROLS: (1) Schrödinger bridge for unimodal transport as a baseline for Q-values; (2) importance sampling based directly on cumulative distribution function estimates.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The approach will allow efficient identification of branching regions in various domains (e.g., crowd navigation, cell differentiation) but may fail to accurately capture temporal dynamics of branching and mode evolution, as traditional Q-learning focuses on individual state-action pairs rather than global dynamics.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reconstruction-free estimation of branched trajectories
PROPOSAL: Employ a Wasserstein generative adversarial networks (WGANs) framework to learn a mapping from initial to terminal populations by minimizing the Wassertein distance between their distributions. Add a hinge-loss-based regularization term that encourages separating branches, enabling multi-modal trajectory estimation without requiring intermediate-time observations.
CONTROLS: (1) ground truth trajectories from Schrödinger bridge formulation with branched dynamics; (2) an ablation study to isolate the effect of the hinge-loss regularization.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (due to training complex WGANs)
PREDICTION: This method will allow robust estimation of branched trajectories but may face mode collapse or sensitivity to the choice of the Wasserstein distance metric and regularization hyperparameters.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Reconstruction-free estimation of branched trajectories
PROPOSAL: Modify the Wasserstein GAN approach from Turn 2 to employ a conditional normalizing flow (CNF) as the generator, allowing the estimation of the conditional probability of transitioning from the initial population to a target branch, conditioned on intermediate snapshots of the population. Use an auxiliary classifier along with a hinge-loss-based regularization term that encourages separating branches.
CONTROLS: (1) Schrödinger bridge for unimodal transport as a baseline for comparing distributions; (2) an ablation study to isolate the effect of the auxiliary classifier.
COST: estimated to be around 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The conditional CNF will better capture branched dynamics, enabling inference of not only the modes but also how mass is distributed over time between them. However, it may still struggle to recover complex, high-dimensional modes and could be sensitive to the prior distribution used in the flow.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Reconstruction-free estimation of branched trajectories
PROPOSAL: Modify the Conditional Normalizing Flow (CNF) to integrate a graph-based structure, allowing for efficient encoding of the conditional dependency between intermediate and target branches. This structure will be learned in conjunction with the CNF's parameters using a hybrid loss, where branch separation and connectivity are jointly optimized.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Branched diffusive matching for diverse terminal modes
PROPOSAL:  We develop a transport framework, diffusive matching for divergenttransport (DM-DT), that generalizes the Schrödinger bridge problem to learn competitive stochastic bridges between a common initial distribution and multiple terminal modes. DM-DT incorporates a branching prior, allowing mass to split and merge over time, while meeting the Kullback-Leibler constraint for each terminal subpopulation.
CONTROLS:  We compare against baseline formulations that incorporate brownian motion and diffusion processes under no branching constraints, Schrödinger bridge with only a single terminal mode target, and transport methods that model population growth using unbalanced optimal transport priors.
COST:  2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION:  DM-DTwill converge to branched trajectories that reflect the variability of the terminal modes. It might fail to capture accurately how mass redistributes when terminal modes have complex and highly variable structures

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE:  Real-world validation of branched diffusive matching for diverse terminal modes
PROPOSAL:  We extend our previous proposal to incorporate extensive real-world evaluation, using bulk RNA-seq and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets to validate the generality of DM-DT. We compare the performance of DM-DT to existing schrodinger bridge-based models on prototypical cell differentiation trajectory inference and drug perturbation response modeling tasks, adapting our computational infrastructure to provide low-latency predictions on these large-scale single-cell datasets.
CONTROLS:  We assess the importance of branched dynamics prior in DM-DT on unperturbed versus perturbed cell populations, comparing results to a baseline Schrödinger bridge model with conservation of mass constraint.
COST:  4000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION:  DM-DT will outperform baseline formulations on real-world datasets. However, inefficient GPU memory usage and cumulative runtimes from eigenvalue estimation may lead to training difficulties

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE:  Effective Learning of Multiple Extensions via Time-Aware Architecture extension
PROPOSAL:  We propose an architecture extension, Dynamic Time Extended Schrödinger Bridge (Dense-TE-SB), that models multiple time extensions of stochastic bridges to capture complex hierarchies of branching dynamics and predict populations across a vast divergence timeline.
CONTROLS:  Dense-TE-SB is compared against its predecessor- the modification is based on newer approximations to machine learning.
COST:  5000 GPU-hours 
PREDICTION:  Dense-TE-SB exhibits more optimized fitting of models, a reduction in the time expected for convergence ;still it may face logistical issues in obtaining optimizing of per- mode variabilites

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Adaptive Training for Long-Horizon Divergent Population Modeling
PROPOSAL:  We propose an adaptive training method, Gradually Diverging Temporal Frequency (GDTF), to stabilize the optimization process in learning branched populations over a long divergence timeline. GDTF progressively adjusts the temporal frequency of training updates to track the changing branching dynamics, ensuring smooth convergence of the surrogate objective function.
CONTROLS:  We compare against a standard gradient descent baseline and a warm-up phase based learning baseline to assess the effect of GDTF.
COST:  3000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION:  GDTF will significantly improve the stability and convergence rates of the learner in long-horizon divergent population modeling. It might introduce side effects in some choices of model architecture.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Real-World Benchmarking for Divergent Population Modeling Across Experimental Domains
PROPOSAL:  We propose a real-world benchmarking framework, PD-Eval, to evaluate the performance of divergent population modeling approaches on diverse experimental domains, such as cell differentiation trajectory inference from scRNA-seq data and drug response modeling from bulk RNA-seq data. PD-Eval assesses the accuracy and quality of predicted population dynamics under real-world constraints.
CONTROLS:  We benchmark a set of existing state-of-the-art models, including DM-DT, Dense-TE-SB, and SB with growth models for accuracy and faithfully recovered branching dynamics on the test datasets.
COST:  6000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION:  PD-Eval will reveal significant differences between divergent population modeling approaches in real-world application scenarios. It might identify numerical instabilities due to real-world variability in simulation runs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Time-Aware Inference of Reprogramming Trajectories from Single-Cell RNA-Seq Data
PROPOSAL:  We develop a real-world application of branched diffusive matching for divergent population modeling: the inference of reprogramming trajectories using single-cell RNA-seq data. Our approach, TRISTAR, integrates DM-DT with a time-aware learning framework to predict cellular reprogramming dynamics and identify key branching events.
CONTROLS:  TRISTAR is compared against a baseline Schrödinger bridge model and a temporal extension of the optimal transport framework for cellular reprogramming prediction.
COST:  4500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION:  TRISTAR will accurately predict reprogramming trajectories and identify key branching events. It might struggle with small dataset sizes due to excessive freedom of fitting extensions

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Growing Mechanism Enhanced Branched Diffusive Matching for Enhancing Predictive Power
PROPOSAL:  We propose a novel extension of DM-DT that models the growth mechanism using a continuous-state branching process formulation. This approach, GBM-DM-DT, incorporates an adaptive growth mechanism to better capture the rapid change in population dynamics over time.
CONTROLS:  GBM-DM-DT is compared against DM-DT with a fixed growth rate, a branching- SB with growth and PRB-WP model with state-dependent softmax loss.
COST:  5500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION:  GBM-DM-DT will enhance the predictive power of DM-DT by capturing the underlying growth dynamics, and thereby lead to better fit of experimental data. Optimizing GBM involves questions of which models are mathematically consistent with branching behaviour.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE:  Growing Mechanism Enhanced Branched Diffusive Matching for Enhancing Predictive Power
PROPOSAL:  We revise GBM-DM-DT to incorporate a physics-constrained learning framework that leverages knowledge of the underlying physical and biological mechanisms governing population dynamics. This revised approach, pGBM-DM-DT, integrates a physics-based growth model with DM-DT, ensuring physically consistent predictions and enhanced predictive power.
CONTROLS:  We compare pGBM-DM-DT against GBM-DM-DT and other physics-informed approaches such as PINN and PM-SB
COST:  6500 GPU-hours (adding inverse problem solving and adjoint sensitivity gradients)
PREDICTION:  pGBM-DM-DT will generate physically consistent and more accurate predictions of population dynamics, and thus enhance our understanding of growth and branching processes. It might require multidataset management for comparison to non-physics-informed models

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Propagating Uncertainty in Branched Diffusive Matching for Real-World Applications
PROPOSAL:  We develop a probabilistic framework, P-DM-DT, to quantify and propagate uncertainty in the predictions of branched diffusive matching. P-DM-DT integrates a Monte Carlo sampling approach with DM-DT, generating a distribution of possible population trajectories and uncertainty estimates for prediction outcomes.
CONTROLS:  We compare P-DM-DT against DM-DT and other uncertainty quantification methods such as variational inference and Bayesian neural networks.
COST:  7000 GPU-hours (adding procedures for large Monte Carlo sampling in population dimensionality)
PREDICTION:  P-DM-DT will provide reliable uncertainty estimates and enhance the interpretability of predictions in real-world applications. However, it might be computationally expensive for large population sizes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Developing Open-Source Implementations for Efficient Branched Diffusive Matching
PROPOSAL:  We release a comprehensive open-source library, DM-DT-OS, to facilitate the development and deployment of branched diffusive matching for divergent population modeling. DM-DT-OS includes optimized implementations of DM-DT, adaptive training, and other extensions, as well as interfaces for real-world applications and model discovery.
CONTROLS:  We compare the performance and usability of DM-DT-OS against existing libraries and frameworks, such as PyTorch and TensorFlow, for implementing branched diffusive matching.
COST:  3300 GPU-hours (for deployment, testing and documentation)
PREDICTION:  DM-DT-OS will become a widely-used and standardized tool for efficient implementation of branched diffusive matching in real-world applications, while also facilitating reproducibility and model discovery. However, it might require ongoing maintenance and updates to address emerging challenges and techniques.
