TITLE: Evaluating Visual Perception for Graph Structural Understanding
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of a Graph Transformer model against a state-of-the-art Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) architecture on a set of synthetic graph classification benchmarks that emphasize topological properties, such as ring structures and symmetric graphs.
CONTROLS: Use default hyperparameters for the Graph Transformer and GCN models, and include an ablation study with the Graph Transformer model to evaluate the importance of positional encodings for topological awareness.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: While the Graph Transformer model should outperform the GCN model thanks to its ability to model long-range dependencies, the performance difference may be small, and the GCN model may still demonstrate strong topological awareness due to its use of positional encodings. The ablation study may reveal that positional encodings are critical for the Graph Transformer model's performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing Structural Understanding with Human-Like Evaluation Metrics
PROPOSAL: Develop a set of evaluation metrics that mimic human-like graph cognition, focusing on the ability to perceive and abstract global graph properties, such as recognizing ring structures and symmetric graphs, and incorporating these metrics into the comparison with the Graph Transformer and GCN models.
CONTROLS: Use a combination of automated and human-in-the-loop evaluation to evaluate the models' performance under these metrics, including participant studies to determine whether the models' predictions align with human judgements.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The new evaluation metrics should provide a more nuanced understanding of the models' structural understanding, revealing potential strengths and weaknesses in their ability to perceive and abstract global graph properties. However, the evaluation may require significant human annotation effort, and the results may exhibit high variance due to the subjective nature of human judgement.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Assessing Structural Understanding with Human-Like Evaluation Metrics
PROPOSAL: Modify the proposal to develop a more comprehensive set of evaluation metrics, including metrics for recognizing critical bridges, detecting cycles, and identifying symmetric graphs, and use these metrics to compare the Graph Transformer and GCN models.
CONTROLS: Include a basline comparison with state-of-the-art architectures, such as GraphSAGE and GAT, and evaluate the impact of the new evaluation metrics on model selection and ranking.
COST: 250 GPU-hours (increased due to additional metrics and comparison with state-of-the-art architectures)
PREDICTION: The revised evaluation metrics should provide a more complete picture of the models' structural understanding, and the comparison with state-of-the-art architectures may reveal new insights into the strengths and weaknesses of different architectures. However, the evaluation may still require significant human annotation effort, and the results may exhibit high variance due to the subjective nature of human judgement.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Introducing a Novel Graph Visualization and Recognition Benchmark
PROPOSAL: Develop a new benchmark that challenges models to recognize and understand complex graph structures from visualizations, such as drawings or diagrams, and test the performance of the Graph Transformer and GCN models on this benchmark.
CONTROLS: Create a dataset of visually diverse graph drawings, including graphs with ring structures, symmetric graphs, and critical bridges, and use human annotation to label the graphs and evaluate the models' performance.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The novel benchmark may reveal new strengths and weaknesses of the Graph Transformer and GCN models, particularly in the context of visual graph recognition, but the evaluation may require significant human annotation effort and the results may exhibit high variance due to the subjective nature of human judgement.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Evaluating Visual Perception for Graph Structural Understanding
PROPOSAL: Modify the proposal to use the new novel graph visualization and recognition benchmark (proposed in Turn 4) as an input to the Graph Transformer model, and evaluate its ability to learn visual graph representations that generalize to different graph structures and visualizations.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the Graph Transformer model on the new benchmark with its performance on synthetic graph classification benchmarks, and investigate the impact of different visual pre-processing techniques (e.g. edge bundling, node layout) on the model's performance.
COST: 350 GPU-hours (increased due to new benchmark and visual pre-processing evaluation)
PREDICTION: The Graph Transformer model may demonstrate strong performance on the new benchmark, particularly in the context of visual graph recognition, but its performance may degrade when faced with highly diverse or complex graph structures, highlighting the challenges of visual graph understanding.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Theoretical Analysis of Visual Graph Understanding
PROPOSAL: Develop a theoretical framework that analyzes the computational complexity of visual graph understanding, and investigate whether visual graph models like the Graph Transformer are inherently more efficient or expressive than traditional message-passing models like GCNs.
CONTROLS: Use worst-case analysis to compare the time and space complexity of visual graph models and traditional message-passing models, and investigate the impact of different visual graph representations on the computational complexity of graph algorithms.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (lower due to theoretical analysis, no need for experiments)
PREDICTION: The theoretical framework may reveal that visual graph models offer significant computational advantages over traditional message-passing models, particularly in the context of large or complex graphs, but the analysis may be highly dependent on the specific visual graph representation used.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Assessing Structural Understanding with Human-Like Evaluation Metrics
PROPOSAL: Modify the proposal to incorporate both human annotations and automated metrics (e.g. Weisfeiler-Lehman test, Katz centrality) to evaluate the structural understanding of visual graph models, and use the combined evaluation framework to compare the performance of the Graph Transformer and GCN models.
CONTROLS: Include a study of the inter-rater agreement between human annotators to assess the reliability of the human evaluation, and investigate the relationship between human-annotated metrics and automated metrics to evaluate the complementarity of the two evaluation frameworks.
COST: 400 GPU-hours (increased due to combined evaluation framework and inter-rater agreement study)
PREDICTION: The combined evaluation framework may provide a more comprehensive understanding of the structural understanding of visual graph models, but the inter-rater agreement study may reveal limitations in the reliability of human annotations, and the evaluation may be dependent on the specific task or graph structure being evaluated.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Robustness of Visual Graph Models to Graph Perturbations
PROPOSAL: Develop a set of graph perturbation methods (e.g. edge addition, node removal, attribute corruption) to evaluate the robustness of visual graph models to changes in graph structure and node attributions, and use these methods to compare the performance of the Graph Transformer and GCN models on perturbed graphs.
CONTROLS: Include a study of the impact of different perturbation methods on the performance of visual graph models, and investigate the relationship between the structural understanding of visual graph models and their robustness to graph perturbations.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The evaluation may reveal that visual graph models are sensitive to certain types of graph perturbations, particularly those that alter the global structure of the graph, and the robustness study may provide insights into the stability of visual graph representations under graph variations. However, the evaluation may be computationally expensive and require significant human annotation effort.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Neural Representation of Graphs in Visual Graph Models
PROPOSAL: Use visualization and dimensionality reduction techniques (e.g. t-SNE, PCA) to analyze the neural representation of graphs in visual graph models, and investigate the structural properties that are encoded in these representations.
CONTROLS: Include a study of the relationship between the neural representation of graphs and the performance of visual graph models on structural graph tasks, and use the analysis to identify specific features or patterns in the neural representation that are associated with good performance.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The analysis may reveal insights into the neural mechanisms underlying visual graph models, and the relationship between the neural representation of graphs and performance on structural graph tasks may provide a new perspective on the strengths and limitations of visual graph models. However, the analysis may be computationally expensive and require significant human annotation effort.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Developing a Visual Graph Model for Zero-Shot Generalization
PROPOSAL: Develop a visual graph model that can generalize to new, unseen graph structures and properties without explicit training data, and use the model to perform zero-shot prediction on a set of structural graph tasks.
CONTROLS: Include a study of the robustness and reliability of the model's predictions, and use the analysis to understand the key factors that contribute to its ability to generalize to new graph structures and properties.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The model may demonstrate strong performance on zero-shot prediction tasks, particularly those that require generalization to new graph structures and properties, due to its ability to learn a more abstract and general representation of graph structure. However, the model may be sensitive to overfitting or require significant computational resources to train.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Visual Perception for Graph Learning: Unpriced Expertise in Graph Drawings
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of ViT (Vision Transformer) for learning graph representations from graph drawings. We will train a ViT model on a dataset of graph drawings with associated graph structures, and evaluate its performance on graph classification and node classification tasks. To make the setting more challenging, we will use a large, diverse dataset of graph drawings with varied styles and complexities.
CONTROLS: Standard GNNs (e.g., GCN, GAT) as baselines
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (approximating for a dataset of 100k graph drawings and 100 epochs)
PREDICTION: ViT is likely to outperform standard GNNs due to its ability to learn holistic features from images. However, it might struggle to generalize to real-world graph data without additional training or fine-tuning, especially if the graph drawings lack structural priors.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Graph Drawing as a Bias Indicator for Message-Passing GNNs
PROPOSAL: Design an experiment to examine whether graph drawings influence the performance of message-passing GNNs. We will train GNNs on the same graph data with or without accompanying graph drawings, and evaluate their performance on standard graph benchmarks (e.g., MNIST, Citeseer). To quantify the effect of graph drawings, we will use ablation studies by removing or altering specific visual features.
CONTROLS: (1) original GNNs, (2) GNNs trained with graph drawings but without visual features, (3) GNNs without graph drawings but with visual features
COST: 300 GPU-hours (approximating for a dataset of 100k graphs and 50 epochs)
PREDICTION: Graph drawings are likely to improve the performance of GNNs by providing structural priors, but not necessarily by allowing the model to capture complex visual features. However, this effect might be limited to specific types of graphs or benchmarks, and the models might struggle to adapt to real-world variations.

ACTION: REVISE 1
PROPOSAL: Revise the first proposal to include an additional evaluation metric that measures the ViT model's ability to capture and transfer graph structures across varying scales and contexts. We will use a novel benchmark consisting of graph representations with systematically altered node degrees, edge weights, or graph sizes.
CONTROLS: Standard GNNs (e.g., GCN, GAT) as baselines
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (no additional cost due to added evaluation metric)
PREDICTION: The ViT model will show robustness in capturing graph structures across different scales and contexts, outperforming standard GNNs. However, the extent of this robustness might be limited by the quality and diversity of the graph drawings in the training data.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Visual Perception for Graph Learning: Transferring Scalable Graph Understanding
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of ViT for learning graph representations from graph drawings, with a focus on transferring graph structures across varying scales and contexts. We will train a ViT model on a dataset of graph drawings with associated graph structures, and evaluate its performance on graph classification and node classification tasks with systematic alterations in node degrees, edge weights, or graph sizes.
CONTROLS: Standard GNNs (e.g., GCN, GAT) as baselines
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ViT is likely to outperform standard GNNs, especially when transferring graph structures across different scales and contexts. However, its performance might degrade when encountering drastically different graph topologies that are not encompassed by the training data.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Measuring Graph Cognitive Abilities with Controllable Synthetic Graphs
PROPOSAL: Develop a set of synthetic graph generators that allow for fine-grained control over graph topological features, such as ring structures, symmetric structures, and critical bridges. We will use these generators to benchmark the cognitive abilities of graph learning models, including their ability to recognize and reason about fundamental global graph properties.
CONTROLS: Benchmarks using random graph generators (e.g., Erdős–Rényi or Watts–Strogatz) for comparison
COST: 500 GPU-hours (approximating for generating and training on 100 synthetic graph datasets)
PREDICTION: Synthetic graphs with controlled topological features will reveal significant differences in the graph cognitive abilities of message-passing GNNs and visual perception models. Visual perception models might excel at recognizing global graph properties, but struggle to generalize to real-world graph data.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Understanding Visual Perception Models through Graph Topology-Agnostic Evaluation
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether visual perception models like ViT can develop graph structural understanding independently of the graph topology being represented. We will train ViT on synthetic graphs with deliberately degraded or altered topological features, and analyze its performance on graph classification tasks under these conditions.
CONTROLS: (1) standard GNNs on original graphs, (2) ViT trained on original graphs
COST: 200 GPU-hours (approximating for generating and training on 10k synthetic graphs)
PREDICTION: ViT is likely to underperform or behave irregularly on graphs with deliberately degraded or altered topological features, indicating that its graph structural understanding is closely tied to the specific topology being represented. However, this challenge might also prompt insights into the potential versatility and flexibility of visual perception models in the presence of diverse graph topologies.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Graph Visual and Message-Passing Representations: Bridging the Gap with Multimodal Fusion
PROPOSAL: Design an experiment to explore the potential benefits of combining graph visual and message-passing representations through multimodal fusion. We will train a multimodal model that integrates ViT and a standard GNN, with the goal of leveraging the strengths of both approaches.
CONTROLS: (1) standard GNNs, (2) ViT, (3) multimodal model with separate ViT and GNN components
COST: 400 GPU-hours (approximating for training and validation on 50k graphs)
PREDICTION: The multimodal model will show improved performance and robustness compared to standard GNNs and ViT, especially on graph classification tasks that require both local and global structural understanding. However, the potential benefits of multimodal fusion might depend on the specific graph domains and architectures used.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Human-GNN Evaluation Metrics: A Study on Human Labelled Graphs
PROPOSAL: Develop a set of evaluation metrics that align with human cognition of graph structures. We will collect a dataset of human-labelled graphs and use it to benchmark the performance of graph learning models, focusing on their ability to recognize and reason about graph properties that are intuitive to humans.
CONTROLS: Previous experiments as baseline
COST: 1500 GPU-hours (approximating for collecting, processing, and training on 50k human-labelled graphs)
PREDICTION: The evaluation metrics developed will show significant discrepancies between the performance of human-labelled graphs and machine-generated graphs, highlighting the potential biases in current benchmarks. Graph learning models will perform better on human-labelled graphs, but might still struggle to capture human-like graph cognition.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Theoretical Limitations of Message-Passing GNNs: Expressiveness and Scalability Results
PROPOSAL: Derive theoretical bounds on the expressiveness and scalability of message-passing GNNs, focusing on their ability to capture global graph properties and recognize graph patterns. We will use spectral graph theory and Weisfeiler-Lehman test results to analyze the limitations of GNNs and identify potential avenues for improvement.
CONTROLS: None
COST: 100 GPU-hours (approximating for theoretical analysis and simulations)
PREDICTION: Theoretical results will show that message-passing GNNs have limited expressiveness in capturing global graph properties and recognizing complex graph patterns, especially when dealing with large-scale graphs. These findings will provide a foundation for the design of more efficient and effective graph learning models that leverage human-like graph cognition.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Unified Architectures for Graph and Visual Learning: A Framework for Human-Inspired Graph Understanding
PROPOSAL: Design a unified architecture that integrates the strengths of both graph learning and visual learning, aiming to develop a model that can capture human-like graph cognition and intuitively understand graph structures. We will integrate insights from Visual Perception for Graph Learning, Multimodal Fusion, and Theoretical Limitations of Message-Passing GNNs into a novel framework for graph and visual learning.
CONTROLS: Previous experiments and theoretical results as baseline
COST: 2500 GPU-hours (approximating for training, validation, and testing on diverse graph and visual datasets)
PREDICTION: The unified architecture will show significant improvements in graph and visual learning tasks, leveraging the strengths of both modalities to develop a more comprehensive understanding of graph structures. This work will provide a novel framework for human-inspired graph understanding, with potential applications in various real-world domains.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating the Use of Vision Transformers for Graph Representation Learning
PROPOSAL: Experiment comparing the performance of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs) on graph representation learning tasks, using synthetic datasets and graph classification benchmarks.
CONTROLS: GNN baselines (e.g. GCN, GraphSAGE), ViT ablation (difference between Transformer self-supervised and graph-encoded attributes).
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ViTs may outperform GNNs on certain graph representation learning tasks, due to their ability to model hierarchical feature interactions and global context, but may struggle with node-level information and local structure. They may also require large amounts of data and computational resources to train effectively.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Graph Reconstruction from Visual Embeddings
PROPOSAL: Experiment measuring the ability of models to reconstruct graphs from visual embeddings, using a graph reconstruction benchmark and evaluating the structural similarity between original and reconstructed graphs.
CONTROLS: Message-passing GNNs (e.g. GraphSAGE, GAT) as baseline for structure-aware methods, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) as baseline for grid-based methods, and a ViT-based method as additional comparison.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Models that combine visual embeddings with structure-aware methods (e.g. GNNs) may outperform those that rely solely on visual features, demonstrating the utility of combining message-passing mechanisms with visual perception. However, ViTs may fail to perform well on tasks requiring precise localization and spatial structure due to their grid-free nature.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating the Use of Vision Transformers for Graph Representation Learning (Revised)
PROPOSAL: Experiment comparing the performance of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs) on graph representation learning tasks, using a mix of synthetic and real-world graph datasets and graph classification benchmarks.
CONTROLS: GNN baselines (e.g. GCN, GraphSAGE) and several variants of ViT (differing in architecture, data augmentation, and training setup), including a transformer-based method for node-by-node message passing, to further investigate the differences between ViTs and GNNs.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By varying the experiment's parameters and incorporating real-world datasets, this revised proposal should provide a more comprehensive understanding of ViTs' strengths and weaknesses compared to GNNs, including their generalizability and ability to adapt to complex graph topologies. However, the increased complexity may also increase the risk of unforeseen computational expenses and challenging the scalability of ViTs in demanding settings.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Evaluating the Expressiveness of Vision Transformers for Graph Learning
PROPOSAL: Theoretical analysis of the Weisfeiler-Lehman test in the context of Vision Transformers (ViTs), to investigate whether they can overcome the limitations of the test and establish a better understanding of their expressiveness compared to Graph Neural Networks (GNNs).
CONTROLS: Comparison with previous work on GNNs, including techniques that use the Weisfeiler-Lehman test to evaluate their expressive power.
COST: 10 GPU-hours (since the analysis is primarily theoretical)
PREDICTION: By applying the Weisfeiler-Lehman test to ViTs, this proposal may reveal whether or not they can genuinely break through the initial limitations of GNNs, thus providing a fundamental understanding of their capabilities. However, it may also lead to unexpected discoveries about the structure of the Weisfeiler-Lehman test, or its applicability to certain types of neural networks.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Synthetic Graph Dataset Generation for Evaluating Graph Understanding Tasks
PROPOSAL: Development of a synthetic graph dataset generation framework that creates graphs with varying levels of complexity, topology, and node attributes, to serve as a benchmark for evaluating graph understanding tasks and comparing the performance of different graph learning models.
CONTROLS: Comparison with existing real-world graph datasets, such as Molecular Graphs and PubChem, to assess the validity and generalizability of the synthetic dataset.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The synthetic dataset should be more controllable and interpretable than real-world datasets, allowing for a more thorough evaluation of graph learning models and a deeper understanding of their strengths and weaknesses. However, the development of a high-quality dataset may require significant effort and computational resources to ensure it is representative and challenging for graph learning models.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Visualizing Graphs with Transformers for Human Evaluation
PROPOSAL: Experiment measuring the ability of Vision Transformers (ViTs) to synthesize accurate and informative visualizations of graphs, using human evaluation to assess the quality of the visualizations and compare them to traditional graph visualization techniques.
CONTROLS: Comparison with existing graph visualization tools, such as Plotly and Matplotlib, and evaluation of ViT-generated visualizations using human judgements and crowdsourcing.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By leveraging ViTs' ability to learn visual representations of graphs, this proposal may lead to the development of more effective and intuitive graph visualization techniques that are easily interpretable by humans. However, the evaluation may be challenging and subjective, as it relies on human judgements and may require a large and diverse human evaluation pool to generalize the findings.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Analogies and Equivalences in Graphs: A Vision Transformer Perspective
PROPOSAL: Theoretical analysis of how Vision Transformers (ViTs) perceive analogies and equivalences in graphs, such as graph isomorphism and graph homomorphism, to investigate whether they can capture the essential structure of these relationships.
CONTROLS: Comparison with existing work on graph neural networks (GNNs) and other graph representation learning models, using benchmarks and numerical experiments.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By studying the analogies and equivalences in graphs, this proposal may reveal the underlying mathematical structure of ViTs and their ability to generalize across graphs, which can be a clue for evaluating their performance in real-world graph learning tasks.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Contrastive Learning for Graph Topology Awareness
PROPOSAL: Experiment exploring the use of contrastive learning to guide Vision Transformers (ViTs) towards learning graph topology awareness, by employing contrastive objectives that enforce structural similarity and difference between graphs.
CONTROLS: Comparison with traditional contrastive learning methods and graph-based objectives, as well as ablation studies of different design choices (e.g., self-supervised vs. supervised contrastive learning).
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By leveraging contrastive learning, this proposal may help ViTs learn more robust and topology-aware representations of graphs, which can lead to improved performance on various graph learning tasks. However, the effectiveness of contrastive learning for graph topology awareness may heavily depend on the choice of objectives, hyperparameters, and pretraining strategies.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Graph Generation and Manipulation with Transformers
PROPOSAL: Experiment exploring the ability of Vision Transformers (ViTs) to generate and manipulate graphs in a more intuitive and graph-aware manner, by learning a structured graph generation process and using attention mechanisms to focus on specific graph properties.
CONTROLS: Comparison with traditional graph generation methods (e.g., GANs, graph grammar-based methods) and ablation studies of different design choices (e.g., graph-aware attention, self-supervised learning).
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By leveraging the structured generation process, this proposal may help ViTs learn to generate graphs that are more diverse, realistic, and tailored to specific application requirements. However, graph generation can be a challenging task, and the quality of generated graphs may heavily depend on the specific objectives, data quality, and hyperparameters used during training.

ACTION: ADD 9
TITLE: Scaling Vision Transformers for Large-Scale Graph Learning
PROPOSAL: Experiment examining the scalability of Vision Transformers (ViTs) on large-scale graph learning tasks, by comparing their performance on various graph datasets and graph learning benchmarks in the presence of increasing numbers of nodes and edges.
CONTROLS: Comparison with established graph neural networks (GNNs), as well as ablation studies of different design choices (e.g., graph-aware attention, layer normalization).
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By investigating the scalability of ViTs, this proposal may provide insights into the limitations and advantages of using transformer-based models for large-scale graph learning tasks. This can help to identify key factors that contribute to the success or failure of such models in real-world applications, paving the way for optimized design of more powerful graph learning models.

Note that with this last addition, the set is now complete with 9 proposals, and the research questions addressed here should be more comprehensive.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Depth Estimation from Existing Visual Priors in Pre-trained T2I Models
PROPOSAL: Experiment: Compare Different Methods for Extracting Depth-Related Features from a Fixed Pre-trained T2I Model
We will use the pre-trained DALL-E 2 model as the starting point and evaluate the performance of three methods for extracting depth-related features: (1) applying a depth estimation head on top of the pre-trained model, (2) fine-tuning a few select layers of the pre-trained model on a small synthetic depth dataset, and (3) using a feature extractor to map the pre-trained model's features to a 3D space. We will use the NYU Depth V2 dataset to evaluate the performance of these methods and compare it to the baseline of full-parameter fine-tuning.
CONTROLS: Full-parameter fine-tuning of DALL-E 2 on NYU Depth V2
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Methods (1) and (2) will provide competitive depth estimation results with full-parameter fine-tuning, but the results may degrade slightly due to the small number of parameters being updated. Method (3) may not work as well due to the difficulty of mapping a 2D feature space to a 3D space.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving Feature Extraction with Task-Agnostic and Task-Specific Regularization
PROPOSAL: Experiment: Investigate the Effect of Regularization Techniques on Depth Estimation from Visual Priors
We will augment the feature extraction methods from proposal 1 with task-agnostic and task-specific regularization techniques to improve the extraction of depth-related features from the pre-trained T2I model. Specifically, we will investigate the effect of dropout, batch normalization, and L1/L2 regularization, as well as task-specific regularization techniques, such as depth-related loss functions and attention mechanisms.
CONTROLS: Baseline is proposal 1 without regularization techniques
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Regularization techniques will improve the performance of the depth estimation methods, but the results may degrade if the regularization strength is too high or too low. Attention mechanisms may provide the best results due to their adaptability to different tasks.

We will develop a regularity condition that ensures a pre-trained T2I model can be transformed into a unified model that selects depth-critical spatial transformations. This condition will provide a principled way to allocate additional capacity to the model to improve depth estimation without degrading image generation. The regularity condition will be based on a forward dynamic programming scheme that explores permutations of spatial transformations consistent with a zero-shot depth estimation objective.
CONTROLS: None
COST: 0 (theoretical result)
PREDICTION: The regularity condition will provide a theoretical framework for transforming pre-trained T2I models into unified models. However, implementing the condition in practice may be challenging due to the high computational complexity of the dynamic programming scheme.

PROPOSAL 1: Investigating Depth Estimation from Existing Visual Priors in Pre-trained T2I Models
Experiment: Compare Different Methods for Extracting Depth-Related Features from a Fixed Pre-trained T2I Model
We will use the pre-trained DALL-E 2 model as the starting point and evaluate the performance of three methods for extracting depth-related features: (1) applying a depth estimation head on top of the pre-trained model, (2) fine-tuning a few select layers of the pre-trained model on a small synthetic depth dataset, and (3) using a feature extractor to map the pre-trained model's features to a 3D space. We will use the NYU Depth V2 dataset to evaluate the performance of these methods and compare it to the baseline of full-parameter fine-tuning.
Controls: Full-parameter fine-tuning of DALL-E 2 on NYU Depth V2
Estimated cost: 100 GPU-hours
Prediction: Methods (1) and (2) will provide competitive depth estimation results with full-parameter fine-tuning, but the results may degrade slightly due to the small number of parameters being updated. Method (3) may not work as well due to the difficulty of mapping a 2D feature space to a 3D space.

PROPOSAL 2: Improving Feature Extraction with Task-Agnostic and Task-Specific Regularization
Experiment: Investigate the Effect of Regularization Techniques on Depth Estimation from Visual Priors
We will augment the feature extraction methods from proposal 1 with task-agnostic and task-specific regularization techniques to improve the extraction of depth-related features from the pre-trained T2I model. Specifically, we will investigate the effect of dropout, batch normalization, and L1/L2 regularization, as well as task-specific regularization techniques, such as depth-related loss functions and attention mechanisms.
Controls: Baseline is proposal 1 without regularization techniques
Estimated cost: 50 GPU-hours
Prediction: Regularization techniques will improve the performance of the depth estimation methods, but the results may degrade if the regularization strength is too high or too low. Attention mechanisms may provide the best results due to their adaptability to different tasks.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Lightweight Depth-Agnostic Transformer for Pre-Trained T2I Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of adding a lightweight, depth-agnostic transformer layer to the T2I model's intermediate feature space, without modifying the original denoising network or image generation module. This layer will receive as input the feature maps from a pre-specified intermediate layer and output a set of homogeneous depth maps. The hypothesis is that by allowing the T2I model to learn depth-related representations in parallel with image generation, we can unlock the implied per-pixel visual prior without sacrificing the original generation capability.
CONTROLS: Compare with fine-tuning the pre-trained T2I model's denoising network with full parameters on depth data, which serves as a baseline for achieving state-of-the-art depth accuracy but degrades image generation.
COST: 5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed lightweight transformer layer will achieve a reasonable depth accuracy comparable to the full-parameter fine-tuning, while preserving a near-optimal image generation quality. However, the depth accuracy might not reach the state-of-the-art, possibly due to the lack of directly depth-perturbed training signal through the pre-trained T2I model's image generator.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Depth-aware Denoising Layer as a Drop-in Replacement
PROPOSAL: Refactor the denoising network of the pre-trained T2I model by adding and training a single-stage or two-stage depth-aware denoising layer that integrates depth estimation into the existing diffusion process. This depth-aware denoising layer maps the input image to its noisy counterpart, conditioned on a per-pixel depth prediction. We aim to replace the existing denoising network's depth ignorance with a drop-in module that, while modestly increasing parameters, doesn't demand full-fledged, dual-model architectures.
CONTROLS: Investigate the depth-aware denoising layer's performance in isolation, and examine its effect on image generation quality by comparing it to the original pre-trained T2I model, as well as to the lightweight transformer addition (proposal 1).
COST: 10 GPU-hours (accounting for hyperparameter tuning and considerable validation)
PREDICTION: This depth-aware denoising layer approach will yield significantly improved depth estimation results while maintaining high image quality comparable to the pre-trained T2I model. However, larger datasets might be needed to exploit the full potential of the proposed approach due to the requirement for more extensive depth variations in the training data.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Lightweight Depth-Agnostic Transformer for Pre-Trained T2I Models
PROPOSAL: Refine the hypothesis by incorporating a parallel attention mechanism within the lightweight transformer layer to selectively focus on relevant spatial ws and channels for depth estimation. This attention framework allows the T2I model to prioritize depth-relevant features and further disentangle the complex relationships between depth and image appearance in the pre-trained representation space.
CONTROLS: Include an ablation study to illustrate the effect of incorporation of the parallel attention mechanism, and compare its performance with proposal 2 to further identify its contributions to depth estimation accuracy and image quality preservation.
COST: 4 GPU-hours (for parallel attention implementation and hyperparameter tuning)
PREDICTION: With added attention capabilities, the refined lightweight transformer layer will exhibit significantly improved depth estimation results and largely preserve the pre-trained image generation quality. If the attention mechanism is not well-balanced or fine-tuned, possibly heavy noises may be spread from depth estimates into image generation, reducing it's quality.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Surface Normal Estimation via Depth Estimation Bootstrap
PROPOSAL: Extend the framework by bootstrapping surface normal estimation from depth estimation, exploiting the relationships between surface orientation and scene depth. By using the depth maps as a input to a complementary architecture, trained to predict surface normals from depth maps, we can leverage the pre-trained T2I model for depth estimation to produce highly accurate surface normal estimates, addressing a crucial requirement for scene understanding.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Depth Estimation from Fixed Pre-trained T2I Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of adding a lightweight sequential Transformer module to the pre-existing architecture of a pre-trained T2I model, enabling it to predict depth maps from images without compromising its original image generation capability.
CONTROLS: Compare against the recently proposed generative depth estimation paradigm and assess the model's ablation points by comparing against the pretrained T2I model with and without the sequential Transformer module.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (.quick prototype development with only minor hyperparameter tuning)
PREDICTION: This modified T2I model is expected to achieve high-quality depth predictions, rivaling those from models specifically designed for depth estimation, although performance could degrade with images having intricate structures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Augmenting Pre-trained T2I Models with Spatial Information for Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: Incorporate a self-attention-based channel and spatial positional encoding mechanism into the pre-existing architecture of a pre-trained T2I model to exploit spatial patterns and structure in images that are relevant for depth estimation.
CONTROLS: Compare the robustness and accuracy of the modified T2I model against the sequential Transformer-based model from Proposal 1, especially on images with varying spatial complexity and lighting conditions.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (Hyperparameter search, additional experiments on spatially complex images)
PREDICTION: The spatially aware model is expected to achieve better generalization and depth accuracy, particularly for complex scenes and under various lighting conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Zero-Shot Depth Estimation through Multi-Modal Feature Fusion
PROPOSAL: Develop a spatial Transformer to selectively fuse features from intermediate layers of a pre-trained T2I model, leveraging both low-level image representations and high-level semantic features to enhance depth estimation performance.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of this multi-modal fusion model against existing methods, including the sequential Transformer and spatial-aware models, using ablations and parameter pruning to isolate the contributions of each feature fusion strategy.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (Extensive hyperparameter tuning and ablation experiments)
PREDICTION: The multi-modal fusion model is expected to achieve state-of-the-art depth estimation performance, as it combines the strengths of diverse feature representations.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISION of Zero-Shot Depth Estimation through Multi-Modal Feature Fusion
PROPOSAL: Develop and incorporate a supervision mechanism for guiding the spatial Transformer to selectively fuse features that are most relevant for depth estimation, alleviating the need for extensive hyperparameter tuning and validation.
CONTROLS: Validate the effectiveness of the supervision mechanism by comparing performance before and after incorporating it, as well as assessing its robustness against different masking ratios and imaging scenarios.
COST: 75 GPU-hours (Development of supervision mechanism and additional experiments)
PREDICTION: With the supervision mechanism, the multi-modal fusion model is expected to achieve faster convergence and more consistent performance, reaching depth accuracy that is even closer to state-of-the-art.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: REVISION of Zero-Shot Depth Estimation through Multi-Modal Feature Fusion
PROPOSAL: Integrate a coarse-to-fine upsampling strategy into the multi-modal fusion model's feature fusion process, enabling the model to produce high-resolution depth maps from its intermediate feature representations.
CONTROLS: Compare the upsampling strategy against existing upsampling methods, including nearest-neighbor interpolation and traditional deep upsampling networks, to assess its contribution to overall depth estimation performance and visual fidelity.
COST: 125 GPU-hours (Implementation and evaluation of the upsampling strategy)
PREDICTION: The coarse-to-fine upsampling strategy is expected to boost the model's depth estimation performance and visual quality, particularly in terms of preserving fine details and structural features in the output depth maps.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Incorporating Geometric Constraints for Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: Modify the pre-trained T2I model to incorporate geometric constraints, such as symmetries and space constraints, that are inherent in the real-world geometry of scenes, using 3D scene structure to guide the depth estimation process and enhance accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare the model's performance against the baseline and existing T2I-based depth estimation methods, with a focus on evaluating the model's ability to preserve geometric constraints and maintain accurate depth estimation under various viewing angles and lighting conditions.
COST: 175 GPU-hours (Implementation and evaluation of geometric constraints)
PREDICTION: The model incorporating geometric constraints is expected to improve depth estimation accuracy and robustness, particularly for complex scenes with hidden objects or strong visual occlusions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Effect of Pre-trained T2I Model Architecture on Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of different pre-trained T2I model architectures (e.g., ResNet-based vs. Transformer-based vs. hybrid models) on depth estimation performance, including the proposed models from previous experiments, and analyze their respective strengths and weaknesses.
CONTROLS: Compare the depth estimation performance across different pre-trained T2I model architectures, with a focus on understanding how architectural choices affect the model's ability to preserve geometric constraints and capture visual features relevant for depth estimation.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (Implementation and evaluation of different model architectures)
PREDICTION: The study is expected to reveal that certain pre-trained T2I model architectures are more suited for depth estimation tasks than others, providing insights into the design choices that are critical for achieving accurate and robust depth estimation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Active Learning Framework for Data-Efficient Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: Develop an active learning framework that selectively queries a human oracle to label the most uncertain and informative samples in the dataset, with the goal of efficiently obtaining high-quality depth annotations and improving the model's depth estimation performance.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effectiveness of the active learning framework by comparing its performance against traditional random sampling and human annotation of the entire dataset.
COST: 180 GPU-hours (Implementation and evaluation of the active learning framework)
PREDICTION: The active learning framework is expected to significantly reduce the annotation efforts required for achieving high-quality depth estimation, particularly for large and complex datasets, while also improving overall model performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Surface Normal Estimation via Self-Supervised Learning
PROPOSAL: Leverage the strength of the pre-trained T2I model to learn surface normal estimation through a self-supervised framework that uses depth estimation as a proxy task, reversing the flow of information to enable surface normal estimation from depth maps.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the self-supervised surface normal estimation framework against existing methods and evaluate its robustness against variations in illumination and viewing angles.
COST: 220 GPU-hours (Implementation and evaluation of the self-supervised framework)
PREDICTION: The self-supervised learning framework is expected to enable accurate and robust surface normal estimation, capitalizing on the depth estimation capabilities of the pre-trained T2I model and extending its utility to adjacent sensing tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Framework for Depth and Surface Normal Estimation with Uncertainty Quantification
PROPOSAL: Develop a unified framework that integrates the proposed methods for depth estimation and surface normal estimation, equipping it with uncertainty quantification to provide robust and interpretable predictions in real-world scenarios.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the unified framework on various benchmark datasets, enforcing a direct comparison against state-of-the-art methods for depth estimation and surface normal estimation.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (Implementation and evaluation of the unified framework)
PREDICTION: The unified framework with uncertainty quantification is expected to set a new benchmark for depth estimation and surface normal estimation, demonstrating robustness and interpretability in real-world scenarios and paving the way for future research in visual perception and interactive applications.

propositions.prediction: The coarse-to-fine upsampling strategy is expected to boost the model's depth estimation performance and visual quality, particularly in terms of preserving fine details and structural features in the output depth maps.
propositions.texte: Integrate a coarse-to-fine upsampling strategy into the multi-modal fusion model's feature fusion process, enabling the model to produce high-resolution depth maps from its intermediate feature representations.
propositions.titre: REVISION of Zero-Shot Depth Estimation through Multi-Modal Feature Fusion

propositions.controles: Compare the model's performance against the baseline and existing T2I-based depth estimation methods, with a focus on evaluating the model's ability to preserve geometric constraints and maintain accurate depth estimation under various viewing angles and lighting conditions.
propositions.cout_texte: 175 GPU-hours (Implementation and evaluation of geometric constraints)
propositions.prediction: The model incorporating geometric constraints is expected to improve depth estimation accuracy and robustness, particularly for complex scenes with hidden objects or strong visual occlusions.
propositions.texte: Modify the pre-trained T2I model to incorporate geometric constraints, such as symmetries and space constraints, that are inherent in the real-world geometry of scenes, using 3D scene structure to guide the depth estimation process and enhance accuracy.
propositions.titre: Incorporating Geometric Constraints for Depth Estimation

propositions.controles: Compare the depth estimation performance across different pre-trained T2I model architectures, with a focus on understanding how architectural choices affect the model's ability to preserve geometric constraints and capture visual features relevant for depth estimation.
propositions.cout_texte: 120 GPU-hours (Implementation and evaluation of different model architectures)
propositions.prediction: The study is expected to reveal that certain pre-trained T2I model architectures are more suited for depth estimation tasks than others, providing insights into the design choices that are critical for achieving accurate and robust depth estimation.
propositions.texte: Investigate the impact of different pre-trained T2I model architectures (e.g., ResNet-based vs. Transformer-based vs. hybrid models) on depth estimation performance, including the proposed models from previous experiments, and analyze their respective strengths and weaknesses.
propositions.titre: Evaluating the Effect of Pre-trained T2I Model Architecture on Depth Estimation

propositions.controles: Evaluate the effectiveness of the active learning framework by comparing its performance against traditional random sampling and human annotation of the entire dataset.
propositions.cout_texte: 180 GPU-hours (Implementation and evaluation of the active learning framework)
propositions.prediction: The active learning framework is expected to significantly reduce the annotation efforts required for achieving high-quality depth estimation, particularly for large and complex datasets, while also improving overall model performance.
propositions.texte: Develop an active learning framework that selectively queries a human oracle to label the most uncertain and informative samples in the dataset, with the goal of efficiently obtaining high-quality depth annotations and improving the model's depth estimation performance.
propositions.titre: Active Learning Framework for Data-Efficient Depth Estimation

propositions.controles: Compare the performance of the self-supervised surface normal estimation framework against existing methods and evaluate its robustness against variations in illumination and viewing angles.
propositions.cout_texte: 220 GPU-hours (Implementation and evaluation of the self-supervised framework)
propositions.prediction: The self-supervised learning framework is expected to enable accurate and robust surface normal estimation, capitalizing on the depth estimation capabilities of the pre-trained T2I model and extending its utility to adjacent sensing tasks.
propositions.texte: Leverage the strength of the pre-trained T2I model to learn surface normal estimation through a self-supervised framework that uses depth estimation as a proxy task, reversing the flow of information to enable surface normal estimation from depth maps.
propositions.titre: Surface Normal Estimation via Self-Supervised Learning

propositions.controles: Evaluate the unified framework on various benchmark datasets, enforcing a direct comparison against state-of-the-art methods for depth estimation and surface normal estimation.
propositions.cout_texte: 300 GPU-hours (Implementation and evaluation of the unified framework)
propositions.prediction: The unified framework with uncertainty quantification is expected to set a new benchmark for depth estimation and surface normal estimation, demonstrating robustness and interpretability in real-world scenarios and paving the way for future research in visual perception and interactive applications.
propositions.texte: Develop a unified framework that integrates the proposed methods for depth estimation and surface normal estimation, equipping it with uncertainty quantification to provide robust and interpretable predictions in real-world scenarios.
propositions.titre: Unified Framework for Depth and Surface Normal Estimation with Uncertainty Quantification

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Epistemic Uncertainty in Masked Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Compare the estimated semantic entropies (aleatoric uncertainty) and mutual information lower bounds (epistemic uncertainty) of a state-of-the-art masked diffusion model (MDM) with those of a strong autoregressive model (ARM) baseline on three real-world question answering datasets from the benchmark suite SuperGLUE.
CONTROLS: Include perplexity and F1-score as additional metrics, study the effect of different generation budgets on uncertainty estimates, and compare to uncertainty estimates obtained with diversity-oriented heuristics such as temperature scaling and nucleus sampling.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: MDMs will show comparable, yet slightly reduced, semantic entropies than ARMs, but demonstrate improved robustness to reduction in generation budget, reducing selectively across both uncertainties. Uncertainty estimates using heuristics will be biased and less reliable compared to direct computation.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revising Metrics for Semantic Aleatoric Uncertainty
PROPOSAL (1): Modified semantic entropy with inversely weighted word overlap: Replace the standard word overlap metric in computing semantic clusters with a weighted one that assigns lower importance to words appearing frequently across multiple clusters. This modification aims to balance the impact of common words and reduce sensitivity to rare, superficially similar responses.
CONTROLS: Same as before; now experiment with this modified metric alone on a subset of the datasets from proposal 1.
COST: Additional 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This modified entropy metric should yield more conservative and relevant estimates of semantic aleatoric uncertainty by distinguishing between generic and specific words, especially when rare answers are involved.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Evaluating Epistemic Uncertainty in Masked Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Refine proposal 1 by incorporating a control group to test the robustness of uncertainty estimates across languages, using the already-collected data for this sake.
CONTROLS: For ARM, include uncertainty estimates based on baseline language-specific models (e.g., English model for all-English queries), add native speaker-in-the-loop validation to collect scarce labels on uncertainty judgments for key-world pairs, aggregate robustness across three empirical datasets and specifying specific commonplace AQAs that do lead to utterable, often-and inaccurately, obvious query embarrassing variations.
COST: Additional 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ARM baselines will accurately compute significantly higher mutual information when controlled for a query by its nativeBODY.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving Epistemic Uncertainty Estimates with Denoising Techniques
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate a novel uncertainty-aware denoising technique that iteratively refines the model's estimates of epistemic uncertainty, leveraging the denoising process of MDMs to minimize the gap between the estimated epistemic uncertainty and the true model uncertainty.
CONTROLS: Compare the refined estimates to original estimates, measure the improvement in uncertainty-awareness of subsequent generations, and analyze the impact of different denoising schedules on uncertainty estimates.
COST: Additional 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This technique will lead to more accurate epistemic uncertainty estimates by iteratively refining the model's estimates, reducing the uncertainty gap, and improving uncertainty-awareness.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Evaluating Epistemic Uncertainty in Masked Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Expand the analysis of proposal 1 to explore the relationship between epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty. Specifically, investigate whether a causal relationship exists such that high epistemic uncertainty is accompanied by increased semantic entropy, and explore whether this relationship is transferable across different masked diffusion models and autoregressive models.
CONTROLS: Retain the existing controls, and introduce additional metrics to capture the correlation between epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty, such as Spearman's rank correlation coefficient.
COST: Additional 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: A moderate to strong positive correlation between epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty will be observed, indicating that higher epistemic uncertainty can indeed lead to increased semantic entropy, and this relationship will be transferable across models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying Uncertainty with Iterative Prompting
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate an iterative prompting approach to quantify epistemic uncertainty in language models. This involves iteratively refining the model's predictions through a sequence of carefully designed prompts, with uncertainty assessments after each iteration.
CONTROLS: Compare the iterative prompting approach to mutual information lower bounds, evaluate its robustness to different prompt designs, and assess its scalability to larger, more complex datasets.
COST: Additional 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The iterative prompting approach will provide more accurate and reliable estimates of epistemic uncertainty compared to mutual information lower bounds, especially for complex and nuanced questions.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Improving Epistemic Uncertainty Estimates with Denoising Techniques
PROPOSAL: Enhance the uncertainty-aware denoising technique developed in proposal 2 by incorporating a mechanism to handle abstraction and analogies, which are common sources of uncertainty in language models. This can be achieved through the use of intuitive prompts that elicit the model's ability to reason about abstract concepts and relationships.
CONTROLS: Introduce additional metrics to evaluate the denoising technique's ability to handle abstraction and analogies, such as a reasoning-assessment module that evaluates the model's understanding of abstract concepts.
COST: Additional 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By handling abstraction and analogies more effectively, the enhanced denoising technique will lead to more accurate and reliable estimates of epistemic uncertainty, especially in scenarios involving abstract and nuanced questions.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Quantifying Uncertainty with Iterative Prompting
PROPOSAL: Expand the iterative prompting approach in proposal 3 to incorporate a hybrid model that combines the strengths of autoregressive and masked diffusion language models. This hybrid model will be trained using an ensemble of both model types, allowing it to leverage the benefits of each architecture to improve uncertainty estimation.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the hybrid model to its constituent model types, evaluate its robustness to different prompt designs, and assess its scalability to larger, more complex datasets.
COST: Additional 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The hybrid model will provide more accurate and reliable estimates of epistemic uncertainty compared to individual autoregressive and masked diffusion models, especially in scenarios involving abstract and nuanced questions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Leveraging Passage Retrieval for Robust Uncertainty Estimation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of passage retrieval methods to improve robustness and accuracy of uncertainty estimation in language models. This involves retrieving relevant passages from a large corpus using the input query or question, and then using the retrieved passages to inform the uncertainty estimation process.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of passage retrieval to existing uncertainty estimation methods, evaluate its robustness to different input queries and datasets, and assess its scalability to large-scale settings.
COST: Additional 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The passage retrieval approach will provide more robust and accurate uncertainty estimates by leveraging the context and relationships present in the retrieved passages, especially in scenarios involving open-ended and abstract questions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Integrating Uncertainty Estimates into Question Answering Systems
PROPOSAL: Develop a framework that integrates the uncertainty estimates obtained from the previous proposals into question answering (QA) systems, enabling them to produce probability-weighted answers and uncertainty labels. This framework will also assess the impact of integrating uncertainty estimates on QA system performance.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of QA systems with and without uncertainty estimates, assess the impact of uncertainty estimates on answer quality and reliability, and study their influence on decision-making processes.
COST: Additional 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Integrating uncertainty estimates into QA systems will result in improved answer quality and reliability, as well as more informed decision-making processes, by providing explicit uncertainty labels and probability-weighted answers.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Uncertainty Estimation for Free-Form Question Answering
PROPOSAL: Experiment with adaptive importance sampling for marginalizing over output sequences to stabilize estimates of semantic aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty, using a small budget of generations from a pre-trained autoregressive language model.
CONTROLS: (1) Random sampling as a baseline, (2) fixed temperature sampling as a heuristic comparison, and (3) variation of importance sampling thresholds to study sensitivity.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expect improved estimates of uncertainty with a smaller budget of generations compared to random sampling and heuristic temperature scaling, but examine the sensitivity of importance sampling to threshold selection for robustness.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Extending to Masked Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Adapt the adaptive importance sampling approach from Proposal 1 to masked diffusion models (MDMs) by injecting noise into the input of the MDM and using the denoising process to stabilize the marginalization over output sequences.
CONTROLS: (1) Use the same adaptive importance sampling thresholds as in Proposal 1, (2) Compare with random sampling and fixed temperature sampling as done in Proposal 1, and (3) Evaluate the impact of the denoising schedule on uncertainty estimation.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expect the MDM-based approach to provide more stable estimates of uncertainty compared to random sampling, but may require careful tuning of the denoising schedule and adaptive sampling threshold to achieve optimal results.

Note: This proposal addresses the question of whether a single approach can serve both autoregressive and masked diffusion language models.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Adapting to Masked Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Modify Proposal 2 to use an iterative prompting regime to leverage the denoising process in masked diffusion models for uncertainty estimation, where each prompt is used to refine the output and stabilize the marginalization over output sequences.
CONTROLS: (1) Compare with the original adaptive importance sampling approach as in Revised Proposal 2, (2) Evaluate the impact of varying prompt iteration counts on uncertainty estimation, and (3) Assess the scalability of the iterative prompting regime to large-scale MDMs.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expect the iterative prompting approach to yield more accurate and stable estimates of uncertainty compared to the original adaptive importance sampling approach, with a marginal increase in computational cost.

Note: This revised proposal refines the initial approach for masked diffusion models using iterative prompting, which may provide more efficient and accurate uncertainty estimation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Semantic-Aware Sampling for aleatoric uncertainty
PROPOSAL: Develop a semantic-aware sampling strategy that selects samples based on their semantic distance or similarity to previously generated outputs, to cover distinct meanings instead of repeating the same ones and reduce the bias introduced by diversity heuristics.
CONTROLS: (1) Use a baseline approach where samples are selected randomly, (2) Compare with temperature scaling and nucleus sampling as commonly used diversity heuristics, and (3) Evaluate the impact of varying semantic distance thresholds on uncertainty estimation.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expect the semantic-aware sampling approach to effectively capture aleatoric uncertainty by amplifying the probability of distinct meanings, but may require careful tuning of the semantic distance threshold to avoid over-regularization.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Combining Aleatoric and Epistemic Uncertainty Estimation
PROPOSAL: Modify Proposal 1 to incorporate the semantic-aware sampling strategy developed in Proposal 3, allowing for joint estimation of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in a single framework by combining the output sequences obtained with and without semantic sampling.
CONTROLS: (1) Evaluate the bounds on uncertainty estimation using this hybrid approach, (2) Compare with using the semantic-aware sampling strategy alone, and (3) Assess the robustness of the hybrid approach to varying sampling budgets.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expect the combined approach to provide more comprehensive and accurate uncertainty estimates, capturing both the irreducible ambiguity among valid answers (aleatoric uncertainty) and the model's lack of knowledge or data coverage (epistemic uncertainty).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Mutual Information Lower Bounds for Epistemic Uncertainty
PROPOSAL: Develop an approach to compute lower bounds on epistemic uncertainty using mutual information between the model's output and a relevance mask, designed to capture the distribution shifts between the training and inference data. Evaluate this method on both autoregressive and masked diffusion language models.
CONTROLS: (1) Compare with the lower bound obtained from iterative prompting in Proposal 2, (2) Assess the scalability of the mutual information lower bound to large-scale language models, and (3) Evaluate the performance of the lower bound under varying relevance mask settings.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expect the mutual information lower bound to provide a useful estimate of epistemic uncertainty, but may require careful tuning of the relevance mask settings to achieve accurate results, especially for larger language models.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Enhancing Iterative Prompting with Semantic Distances
PROPOSAL: Modify the iterative prompting approach in Proposal 2 to incorporate semantic distances, as learned from Proposal 3, to more effectively sample from the model's output distribution and reduce the bias introduced by the denoising process in masked diffusion models.
CONTROLS: (1) Evaluate the improvement in uncertainty estimation using this enhanced iterative prompting approach, (2) Compare with the baseline iterative prompting approach, and (3) Assess the impact of varying prompt iteration counts and semantic distance thresholds on uncertainty estimates.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expect the enhanced iterative prompting approach to provide improved uncertainty estimates, by leveraging semantic aware prompting to better sample from the model's output distribution, and reducing biases introduced by the denoising process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Uncertainty Estimation on Real-World Question Answering Tasks
PROPOSAL: Apply the uncertainty estimation methods developed in this work to real-world question answering benchmarks, such as TriviaQA or QuAC, and evaluate their performance on tasks like predicting confidence scores and identifying plausible but incorrect answers.
CONTROLS: (1) Compare with state-of-the-art confidence scoring and uncertainty estimation methods on these benchmarks, (2) Assess the impact of varying sampling budgets on uncertainty estimates, and (3) Evaluate the robustness of the uncertainty estimation methods to noisy or adversarial input data.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expect the uncertainty estimation methods developed in this work to demonstrate strong performance on real-world question answering tasks, and provide a reliable approach to confidence scoring and identifying plausible but incorrect answers.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Ablation Study on the Influence of Diversity Heuristics
PROPOSAL: Conduct an ablation study to investigate the impact of incorporating diversity heuristics, such as temperature scaling or nucleus sampling, into the uncertainty estimation methods developed in this work, and assess their effectiveness in reducing redundancy and improving uncertainty estimates.
CONTROLS: (1) Ablate each diversity heuristic individually and evaluate the effect on uncertainty estimates, (2) Assess the impact of combining multiple diversity heuristics, and (3) Compare with the results obtained using the semantic-aware sampling strategy developed in Proposal 3.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expect the ablation study to provide insights into the relationships between diversity heuristics, uncertainty estimates, and sampling efficiency, and demonstrate that incorporating diversity heuristics can improve uncertainty estimates, but may also introduce biases and affecting reliability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Open-Ended Question Answering with Uncertainty Estimation
PROPOSAL: Integrate the uncertainty estimation methods developed in this work into an open-ended question answering system, and evaluate the effectiveness of using these methods to select the most confident and diverse responses.
CONTROLS: (1) Compare with state-of-the-art open-ended question answering systems that do not use uncertainty estimation, (2) Assess the impact of using uncertainty estimation on response quality and diversity, and (3) Evaluate the robustness of the integrated system to noisy or adversarial input data.
COST: 3500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expect the integrated system to improve response quality and diversity by effectively leveraging uncertainty estimation, and provide a reliable and transparent approach to open-ended question answering. This proposal caps off the experimental plan and provides a practical application of the uncertainty estimation methods developed throughout this work.

propositions.texte: Modify the iterative prompting approach in Proposal 2 to incorporate semantic distances, as learned from Proposal 3, to more effectively sample from the model's output distribution and reduce the bias introduced by the denoising process in masked diffusion models.

propositions.controles: (1) Use a baseline approach where samples are selected randomly, (2) Compare with temperature scaling and nucleus sampling as commonly used diversity heuristics, and (3) Evaluate the impact of varying semantic distance thresholds on uncertainty estimation.
